On my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, says the Lord God, there all the house of Israel shall serve me: all, I say, in the land in which they shall please me; and there I will require your firstfruits and the beginning of your tithes in all your sanctifications. In an odor of sweetness I will receive you, when I have led you out from the peoples and gathered you from the lands into which you were scattered, and I shall be sanctified in you in the eyes of the nations. And you shall know that I am the Lord. Of this mountain, on which all the house of Israel is to serve God, Isaiah and Micah sang with one voice: In the last days the mountain of the house shall be manifest on the summit of the mountains and shall be raised above the hills; and all the nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways and we will walk in his paths; […]

It must also be known that the Jews and the heirs of their error refer both this section which we have now expounded and the one like it in Isaiah to the thousand-year reign of Christ and of the saints; and that what is said: All peoples shall walk, each in the name of the Lord his God, they interpret in this way: that each nation is to be tormented with its idol and sent into the fire of eternal punishment. But they are refuted by what follows: this is said not of the end of the ages but of the first coming of Christ, in which the remnant of her that halts is gathered, and the nations are saved first. Isaiah, then, set down a testimony of this kind: The word that came to Isaiah son of Amoz concerning Judah and Jerusalem: for in the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, and the house of God upon the summit of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills, and all nations shall come to it. […]

Haply “to this mountain,” He said of Himself; for He is called a Mountain: “It shall come to pass in the last days, that the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest.” But this Mountain is placed above other mountains; because the Apostles also are mountains, supporting this Mountain. Therefore followeth, “In the last days the Mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, established in the top of the mountains.” Therefore passeth It the tops of all mountains, and on the top of all mountains is It placed; because the mountains are preaching The Mountain.
Who is meant by "mountain of strength" but our Redeemer?

This mountain is Christ. The Prophet speaks of this mountain, saying: “In the last days, the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established above the tops of the mountains” (Isa. 2:2). The mountains above whose tops the mountain of the house of the Lord is said to be established signify the Fathers of the Old Testament. Therefore the mountain of the house of the Lord is said to be established above their tops because they themselves foretold him, and when he came in the flesh, he surpassed them by a wondrous height. Therefore the house of the Lord, that is, the Church, was built upon this mountain, because it was founded upon Christ, as the Apostle Paul says: “For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3:11).

2:3.t: And when the Spirit of prophecy speaks as predicting things that are to come to pass, He speaks in this way: "For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And He shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people; and they shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into pruning-hooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more." And that it did so come to pass, we can convince you. For from Jerusalem there went out into the world, men, twelve in number, and these illiterate, of no ability in speaking: but by the power of God they proclaimed to every race of men that they were sent by Christ to teach to all the word of God; and we who formerly used to murder one another do not only now refrain from making war upon our enemies, but also, that we may not lie nor deceive our examiners, willingly die confessing Christ.

This "new covenant" Isaiah, another of the Hebrew prophets, calls the "new law,"when he says:

"3. For out of Sion shall go forth a law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And all the nations shall go, and all the peoples shall be gathered together, and shall say, Let us go up to the Mount of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob."

This law going forth from Sion, different from the law enacted in the desert by Moses on Mount Sinai, what can it be but the word of the Gospel, "going forth from Sion" through our Saviour Jesus Christ, and going through all the nations? For it is plain that it was in Jerusalem and Mount Sion adjacent thereto, where our Lord and Saviour for the most part lived and taught, that the law of the new covenant began and from thence went forth and shone upon all, according to the commands which He gave his disciples when He said:

"Go ye, and make disciples of all the nations, teaching them to observe all things, whatsoever I have commanded you." […]
2:3.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 4

2:3.t: And they shall say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths. The nations and peoples, by no means content with their own salvation, will exhort one another and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob. We have said above what the prepared mountain of the Lord is, and what the house of the Lord on the top of the mountains. And the house of the Lord is called the house of the God of Jacob, so that we may receive the old Instrument, and not, after the manner of Manichaeus, seek another house outside the house of the God of Jacob. And when we are in the house of the God of Jacob, then he will teach us his ways, by which we may go to him, and we shall walk in his paths, which the others too have given. So too Jesus, going up into the mountain, taught his disciples the eight beatitudes and the other things which the word of the Gospel contains (Luke 6). […]

The first law, the Old Testament, had come out of Mount Sinai by the lips of Moses; but it was foretold of the law Christ came to give: "The law shall come forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem." This explains why Christ ordered repentance to be preached in his name among all peoples but beginning in Jerusalem.

Came He to thee that thou shouldest have whereat to stumble, and not have whereto to go up? “Come ye, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord.” Isaiah saith this: “Come ye, and let us go up.” What is, “Come ye, and let us go up”? “Come ye,” is, Believe ye. “Let us go up,” is, Let us profit. But they will neither come, nor go up, nor believe, nor profit. They bark against the mountain. Even now by so often stumbling on Him they are broken, and will not go up, choosing always to stumble.

THE blessed prophet Isaiah has somewhere introduced those who by faith in Christ have been won unto life, as calling out eagerly, so to speak, unto one another, and saying; "Come, let us go up unto the mountain of the Lord, and unto the house of the God of Jacob, and they shall teach us His way, and we will walk in it." Now by the mountain here we affirm to be meant not any earthly mountain; for to imagine this would be foolish: but rather the church which Christ has rescued for Himself. For it is high and conspicuous to people everywhere, and, so to say, exalted, because there is nothing in it which brings men down to earth. For those who dwell within it care nothing for the things of earth, but rather desire those things that are above: and, as the Psalmist says, "They are exalted far above the earth;" as being altogether brave and courageous, and practising uninterrupted endeavours after all things whatsoever which please God.
2:3.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

2:3.t: It was opportune that the preaching of repentance and the forgiveness of sins through confession of Christ's name should have started from Jerusalem. Where the splendor of his teaching and virtues, where the triumph of his passion, where the joy of his resurrection and ascension were accomplished, there the first root of faith in him would be brought forth; [there] the first shoot of the burgeoning church, like that of some kind of great vine, would be planted. Just so, by an increase in the spreading of the word, [the church] would extend the branches of her teaching into the whole wide world.… It was opportune that the preaching of repentance and the forgiveness of sins, good news to be proclaimed to idolatrous nations and those defiled by various evil deeds, should take its start from Jerusalem, lest any of those defiled, thoroughly terrified by the magnitude of their offenses, should doubt the possibility of obtaining pardon if they performed fruits worthy of repentance, when it was a fact that pardon had been […]

2:4.t: The gospel will be this "way" of the new law and the new word in Christ, no longer in Moses. "And he shall judge among the nations," even concerning their error. "And these shall rebuke a large nation," that of the Jews themselves and their proselytes. "And they shall beat their swords into plowshares"; in other words, they shall change into pursuits of moderation and peace the dispositions of injurious minds, hostile tongues and all kinds of evil and blasphemy.… You learn here that Christ is promised not as powerful in war but pursuing peace.

Who is the one who has done this, or who is the one who has joined together in peace people who once hated one another, except for the beloved Son of the Father, the Savior of all, even Jesus Christ, who because of his own love suffered all things for our salvation? For from ages past the peace he would initiate was promised.
2:4.s: On the Incarnation of the Word 52:1

2:4.t: And he shall judge the nations, and rebuke many peoples. Therefore there is to be judgment among the nations too; nor are all unbelievers to be condemned by the same sentence, but according to the diversity of their merits they will suffer diverse things. And after he has judged the nations, then he will rebuke many peoples, or, as the Seventy translated, a great people. And note the order: the nations will be judged, because they are going to believe: For he who does not believe is already judged (John 3:18). But the great people, which is understood as Israel, will by no means be judged, but rebuked, because it did not receive the Son of God sent to it.

And they shall forge their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into sickles. Every zeal for war will be turned to peace, and instead of discord there will be concord in the whole world. Swords will be changed into ploughshares and spears into sickles, so that, putting aside the fury of war, they may serve agriculture and cut the richest harvests with sickles. This indeed can also be understood spiritually, when all the hardness of our heart is broken by the ploughshare of Christ, and the thorns of vices are rooted out, so that the seed of the word of God may grow into crops; and afterwards we shall eat the labors of our hands, when coming they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves (Ps 125 [126]:6).

Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they be trained any more for battle. […]

Another distinction is in relation to duality. The Old Testament comprises two times: before the Law, and under the Law. In the New Testament, likewise, there are two corresponding times: the time of the calling of the Gentiles that corresponds to the first, and the time of the calling of the Jews that corresponds to the second. This time is not yet, for then will be fulfilled these words of Isaiah: "One nation shall not raise the sword against another, nor shall they train for war again." For this is not yet fulfilled since both swords are still active: there are still disputes and heresies. Hence the Jews, who are waiting for this believe that Christ has not yet come.

The fact that the Jews will be converted is certain because of Isaiah and the Apostle who teaches authoritatively: "Though the number of the children of Israel are as the sands of the sea, the remnant shall be saved." And again: "A partial blindness only has befallen Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles should enter." […]

2:5.t: But as there the prophet says, 'And now, O house of Jacob, come and let us walk in the light of the Lord; for He has sent away His people, the house of Jacob, because their land was full, as at the first, of soothsayers and divinations;' even so it is necessary for us here to observe that there are two seeds of Judah, and two races, as there are two houses of Jacob: the one begotten by blood and flesh, the other by faith and the Spirit.

House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord: for you have cast off your people, the house of Jacob. After the calling of the nations and the showing of the mountain of the Lord on the top of the mountains, the Prophet turns to his own people, that is, the people of the Jews, which is called the house of Jacob, and exhorts them that, being in the darkness of error, they should receive the light of truth and walk in the light of the Lord. And in a manner he sings that word of David: Come to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be confounded (Ps 33 [34]:6). For everyone who does evil hates the light, and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved. But you, house of Jacob, house of my people, come with me, and let us walk together in the light of the Lord: let us receive the Gospel of Christ, let us be enlightened by him who says: I am the light of the world (John 8:12). […]

It cannot be questioned that what was predicted at sundry times by His prophets is now being realized,—namely, the announcement that He would disclaim His impious people (not, indeed, the people as a whole, because even of the Israelites many have believed in Christ; for His apostles themselves belonged to that nation), and would humble every proud and injurious person, so that He should Himself alone be exalted, that is to say, alone be manifested to men as lofty and mighty; until idols should be cast away by those who believe, and be concealed by those who believe not; when the earth is broken by His fear, that is to say, when the men of earth are subdued by fear, to wit, by fearing His law, or the law of those who, being at once believers in His name and rulers among the nations, shall interdict such sacrilegious practices. […]
2:5.s: The Harmony of the Gospels, Book 1, Chapter 28

2:6.t:
Such are his prophecies about all the Gentiles. Hear what he proceeds to add about the Jews:

" 6. For he has rejected his people, the house of the God of Jacob, for the land is filled as at the beginning with auguries, as the land of strangers, and many children of strangers are born to them. 7. For the land was filled with silver and gold, and there was no end of their treasures."

And that which follows after this, to which he adds:

"9. And they worshipped that which their own fingers had made, and a man bowed down, and was humbled, and I will not reject them. 10. And now enter ye into the rocks, and hide yourselves in the earth from the face of the fear of the Lord, and from the face of his glory, when he arises to shake the earth."

And in this he teaches that there will be a Resurrection of the Lord, at which all the land of the Jewish people will be shattered. […]
2:6.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

2:6.t: Because they have been filled of old, and have had soothsayers, like the Philistines. For Philistines the Seventy always translated foreigners, a common noun for a proper one: this is today the nation of the Palestinians, as it were of the Philisthinians, because the Hebrew tongue does not have the letter P, but uses the Greek PHI in its place. Hence what is said in the Psalms, with the enumeration of the other nations, The foreigners have been made subject to me (Ps 59 [60]:10), signifies not all foreign nations but properly the Palestinians. And he gives the reasons why God has cast off his people, the house of Jacob: because they have been filled, he says, as they were at the beginning, with soothsayers and omens and all the filth of idolatry. We know from the writing of Moses that the omens and auguries which the nations had whom the Lord drove out before Israel, the Canaanites, Amorites and Hittites, were not to be heeded. The commentators of the Church expound this passage in one way and another. […]

2:7.t: And the land is filled with silver and gold, and there is no end of its treasures. Among the other vices of the land of the house of Jacob is numbered also the abundance of gold and silver. Among omens and soothsayers, horses and chariots, which God forbade the kings of Israel to multiply, among idols, which are the works of men's hands, avarice is condemned. Hence the Lord commanded in the Gospel that we should not lay up for ourselves treasures on earth, and that we should not make treasures from which a thief can snatch, adding at the last: You cannot serve God and mammon (Matt 6:24). And finely has the Prophet expressed in other words that phrase of the little verse, The greedy man is ever in want, saying: And there is no end of its treasures; not that treasures have no end, but that the mind of those who possess them is not filled. And by these words both nations, the Jews and the Romans, are branded for avarice. […]

2:8.t: And its land is filled with idols; they have worshiped the work of their own hands, what their fingers have made; and man has bowed himself down, and the man has been humbled. Where once was the Temple and the worship of God, there the statue of Hadrian and the idol of Jupiter were set up. Which many interpret of that testimony which we read in the Gospel: But when you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place (Mark 13:14). And they bowed down to the work of their hands, and man, a rational animal, worshiped bronze and stone. But there are those who interpret these things of the Jews, that before they were taken by the Babylonians they did all these things, and were therefore abandoned by God. Hence at the end of the chapter too is set: Do not, therefore, forgive them. […]

2:9.t: Do not, therefore, forgive them. For which the Seventy translated: And I will not forgive them. If God is speaking, it is to be understood thus: Because they have done such things, I will not spare them, nor will I forgive such innumerable sins. If the Prophet, it is to be taken thus: Do not, therefore, forgive those who have committed such crimes. And if we understand it of the Romans, the interpretation is truer: who, overthrowing the temple of God, did not worship him who gave them the victory, but the idols of their own hands. But if of the Jews, it is a fierce sentence of the Prophet, so that he seems to pray against his own people, to whom he had said above: House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord.

2:10.t: Enter into the rock, hide yourself in the dug-out ground from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty. I indeed exhorted the people, saying, House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord. But because the Lord has cast off the people of Jacob, and has cast them off because they either did or suffered the things which we have expounded above, therefore I foretell to you the evils that are to come, and I exhort you to enter the rocks and hide in the caves from the face of the Babylonian or the Roman army, when all things will be laid waste, according to what we read in the Gospel: Then they will say to the mountains, Fall upon us; and to the rocks, Hide us (Luke 23:30). But according to the anagogy we are commanded, before the face of the Lord's majesty, to take on the strength of the rock, of which it is said: The rock is a refuge for the hares (Ps 103 [104]:18); and, On a rock you have exalted me (Ps 26 [27]:6). […]

2:11.t: The lofty eyes of man are humbled, and the height of men shall be bowed down; but the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day. When the enemies have come, and the Babylonian or Roman sword has laid waste the whole province, and the columns of warriors have besieged Jerusalem, then neither riches nor nobility of birth nor the power of offices will be able to defend anyone; but there will be one captivity for all, and God alone will be exalted, whose wrath no one will be able to avoid. Many understand these things of the day of judgment: that every creature, in comparison with the divine glory, will be humbled and bowed down, and will feel itself to be nothing.

2:12.t: For the day of the Lord of hosts is upon everyone proud and lofty, and upon everyone arrogant. These things too are joined to the former. In that day, he says, in which the Lord alone will be exalted, that is, in the day of the Lord's vengeance, all the lofty and the arrogant and the high will be subjected to captivity and the sword. Μεταφορικῶς the word is about the great and the princes: that the more they have been proud, the more they are brought low. For the Lord resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (1 Pet 5). Those who understand it of the day of judgment think that the devil is called proud and lofty and high and arrogant; who in his pride says: I will set my seat above the stars of heaven; I will sit on the lofty mountain, above all the lofty mountains, toward the North; I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High (Isa 14:13, 14): when out of the mouth of infants and sucklings praise will be perfected, that the enemy and the avenger may be destroyed (Ps 8:3).

2:13.t: And upon all the cedars of Lebanon, high and lifted up, and upon all the oaks of Bashan. In Psalm 28 (29) too it is sung: The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars; the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and will crush them like the calf of Lebanon (Ps 28 [29]:5, 6). And in Psalm 36 (37): I saw the wicked man exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found (Ps 36 [37]:35, 36). The oaks of Bashan too, which Aquila translated δρύας, Symmachus and Theodotion βαλάνους, we know to be acorn-bearing trees, which, even if they bear fruit, are food for swine, not for men. Bashan is a region of Arabia, over which Og ruled, who was called king of Bashan; and it means αἰσχύνη, that is, ignominy; and if we chose to translate it confusion, that would rather signify σύγχυσιν, that is, Babylon, than Bashan. Upon all, then, who are lifted up in pride, and do works of ignominy, and wallow in the mire of lusts, the vengeance of the Lord will rise. […]

2:14.t: And upon all the lofty mountains, and upon all the hills that are lifted up. Just as in a good sense, according to the variety of virtues, men are called mountains and hills, so among the impious, according to the diversity of vices, and above all of pride, some are mountains, others hills, upon which the day of the Lord will be; of whom it is written in Ezekiel: Thus says Adonai the Lord to the mountains and the hills: Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and your high places shall be scattered, and your altars shall be broken, and the rest (Ezek 6:3).

2:15.t: And upon every lofty tower, and upon every fortified wall. Those who refer these things to the times of Vespasian and Hadrian say that what is written was fulfilled bodily: that no lofty tower, no strongest wall, no multitude of ships and industry of trade could prevail against the might of the Roman army; but that the inhabitants of Judea came into such terror that they, with their wives and children, buried themselves in pits of the earth with the gold and silver which they thought would be a help to them, and sought out the deepest caves. For if the belly is the god of the gluttonous and the luxurious, why should not gold and silver be called the god of the avaricious? Others refer these things to Babylonian times. So I will run through each point according to the laws of tropology. A tower is built either for the defense of a city or for a lookout, so that the enemy may be seen coming from afar. […]

2:16.t: And upon all the ships of Tarshish, and upon all that is beautiful to see. For Tarshish, which all translated alike, the Seventy alone translated sea. The Hebrews think that in their own tongue the sea is properly called THARSIS (תרסים), and that when it is called IAM (ים), it is called so not in the Hebrew tongue but in the Syriac. Jehoshaphat too had ships which he sent to Tarshish (1 Kgs 22:49), but they were broken at Ezion-geber. Solomon too had ships which went to Tarshish (1 Kgs 10:22) and returned after three years and brought the king silver and gold, ivory and apes. But because both kings had sinned, the one given to pleasure and a lover of women of foreign nations, the other joining himself with the king of Samaria, both of which things are referred to the pagans and the heretics, in whom there is nothing but the glitter of eloquence, and a sense built up by diabolical art, and dead speech, which is interpreted in the ivory teeth, and a likeness of human reason, which is perceived in the apes; […]

2:17.t: And the loftiness of men shall be bowed down, and the height of men shall be humbled, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day, and the idols shall be utterly broken. Human speech seems to have reason so long as it has not been compared with divine knowledge. But when falsehood draws near to the truth, like stubble to fire, it is quickly devoured and perishes, and all the doctrines of falsehood, which are now called idols because they are feigned and fabricated, will be utterly broken.

2:20.t: In that day man shall cast away the idols of his silver and the images of his gold, which he had made for himself, to worship moles and bats; and he shall go into the clefts of the rocks and the caverns of the stones from the face of the terror of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth. We have often said that silver and gold are taken for speech and sense; and though these were given by God to men so that they might either speak of God or perceive God and praise their creator, they abuse this gift for the fashioning of idols; according to what is written: I gave them silver and gold, but they made Baal of my silver and gold (Hos 2:8). When, then, someone, terrified by the fear of the Lord, has first hidden his idols in the cave of his breast and concealed them in the abysses of the earth, not daring to bring out what he had wickedly fashioned, the second advance is that he cast away what he had first concealed and not suffer it to be in him. […]

2:21.t: And when these have been abandoned in the day of the Lord, those who have cast them away will enter the clefts of the rocks and the caverns of the stones, so as to dwell not in the dust of the earth and in vile mud but in firm reason, and find for themselves the various openings of the virtues, through which they may be able to come to the truth. These things, according to the anagogy, I have touched on as I could in brief words; the Hebrews refer them to Babylonian times and the overthrow of Jerusalem, when the Lord rose to strike the land of the Jews.

2:22.t: Cease, therefore, from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, for he himself is reckoned lofty. The Seventy omitted this, and in the Greek copies it was added by Origen under asterisks from the edition of Aquila; in the Hebrew it reads thus: HEDALU LACHEM MEN AADAM ASER NASAMA BAAPHPHO CHI BAMA NESAB HU. Where we have said, he himself is reckoned lofty, Aquila translated, in what is this one reckoned. The Hebrew word BAMA (במה) means either ὕψωμα, that is, a high place, which we read both in the books of Kingdoms and in Ezekiel, or else in what, and it is written with the same letters, BETH, MEM, HE; and according to the character of the passages, if we wish to read in what, we say BAMMA; but if high place or lofty, we read BAMA. The Jews, then, understanding that the prophecy is about Christ, interpreted the ambiguous word in the worse sense, so that they might seem not to praise Christ but to count him as nothing. […]

3:1.t: For behold, the ruler, the Lord of hosts, will take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the mighty and the strong: all the strength of bread, and all the strength of water. Up to this point they think it is spoken of the judgment. What follows concerns the captivity to come, which some refer to the Babylonians, others to the Romans. But it is better, as we said above, for everything to be referred to the Lord's passion. For after he was slain, all graces and gifts were taken away from the Jews, according to what is written in the Gospel: The Law and the Prophets until John the Baptist (Matt 11:13). And the order is this: Because you would not cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, who has been reckoned exalted, but on the contrary you shed the blood of the righteous one and devised the worst counsel, saying: Let us bind the righteous one, for he is useless to us (Wis 2:12), therefore you shall eat the fruit of your own devices. […]

3:2.t: The strong man and the man of war, the judge and the Prophet, and the soothsayer, and the old man. For strong man, which alone is in the Hebrew, the Seventy translated two words together, giant and strong man, meaning the same man to be the giant who is the strong man. Of the strong man we have spoken above. Now a giant in the good sense, that is, of the Lord and Savior, we read in the eighteenth psalm: He has exulted as a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the height of heaven, and his circuit even to its height (Ps 18 [19]:8). But if we read of Nimrod the giant (Gen 10), who was a hunter before the Lord, and of the giants (Gen 6) on whose account the flood came upon the earth, they are to be taken in the contrary sense. The man of war, too, we understand according to the history in this way: that they have been taken captive, and to this day are in servitude, and have not laid aside the yoke of slavery; […]

3:3.t: The captain of fifty. Συνεκδοχικῶς, the whole from a part. For just as those who command a hundred soldiers are called Centurions, and those who command a thousand Chiliarchs, whom we call Tribunes, from the fact that they command a tribe: so in the army of Israel those who were at the head of fifty soldiers were called captains of fifty. Hence too we call Decurions those who command ten men. Nor is it a wonder if among the Jews every rank of warriors has perished, since they have no power to serve under the sword and to bear arms. But since the number fifty is always referred to penitence, and Christ is the prince of penitence and the head of those who are saved through penitence, let us briefly lay open the mysteries of this number. In Genesis we read, when Abraham speaks to the Lord, that he said first that the city should be saved for fifty righteous, if they were found in it. And in Numbers there is the most celebrated festival of the seven weeks, that is, of Pentecost. […]

3:4.t: And I will give children to be their princes. If it is said in the person of the Prophet: For behold, the ruler, the Lord of hosts, will take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the mighty man and the mighty woman: all the strength of bread, and all the strength of water, and the rest, how does the same prophet now say: I will give children to be their princes, and the effeminate shall rule over them? Therefore, according to prophetic custom, while the Prophet is speaking, God suddenly speaks through the Prophet in his own person, and says: I will give children to be their princes: for having removed the things I had given before, and having taken away good things as though in anger, now on the contrary I will give evil things. I took away the old man and the captain of fifty, and the wonderful counselor, and the wise architect, and the prudent hearer, and so on. In their place I will give children as princes. […]

But to me something more sacred seems to lie hidden in the letter: that those are called young men in Scripture who fall away from the old authority and despise the gray-haired precepts of their parents; who, neglecting the commandment of God, desire to establish the traditions of men. Concerning them, in Isaiah too, the Lord threatens Israel, because it would not have the water of Siloam, which goes in silence, and turned away from the old pool, choosing for itself the streams of Samaria and the floods of Damascus. And I will give, he says, young men as their princes, and mockers shall rule over them.

3:5.t: And the people shall rush, man upon man, each one upon his neighbor: the boy shall riot against the old man, and the base against the noble. When the princes are young men, and mockers of the Lord, such as the prophetic discourse describes, then no order will be kept, whether of dignity or of age or of knowledge; but boys will rebel against old men, and the base against the noble, and they will fall upon one another. And that saying of the Apostle will be fulfilled: Biting one another, you have been consumed by one another (Gal 5:15). That these things befell the people of the Jews under Titus the son of Vespasian, Josephus writes (Jewish War, Book 5): and that, when they were being besieged by the Romans, Jerusalem was divided by sedition into three parts, and some held the citadel and the Temple, others the lower, others the upper part of the city.

3:6.t: For a man shall take hold of his brother, of the household of his father: You have a garment, be our prince; and let this ruin be under your hand. For ruin, Symmachus and Theodotion translated weakness; the Seventy, food. It signifies the scarcity of men, and above all the want of all things, so that whoever has food and clothing is believed to be powerful and rich and illustrious. And what it says according to the Hebrew, And let this ruin be under your hand, has this sense: Let our misery and calamity be sustained and protected by your help. And this must be considered, that each man chooses for himself his own prince, and that there is sedition in the choosing of princes, while some think some men worthy of rule and others others. Nor do they say to them, Your possessions and riches and revenues will be able to sustain us; but, This weakness, or my food, will be healed by your judgment and will hang upon it.

3:7.t: And he will answer in that day, saying, I am not a physician, and in my house there is neither bread nor garment; do not appoint me prince of the people. For physician, Symmachus and the Seventy translated prince; Theodotion, ἐπιδεσμεύοντα, one who binds up wounds and provides for health. He will answer is not found in the Hebrew, but has been added from the Seventy. For in the Hebrew it is joined to what is written above: In that day he will say, I am not a physician, and the rest. And he will say it who has been chosen prince. And just as the people desires to have as prince the one whom it perceives to be richer in comparison with itself, so the one who is chosen, considering his poverty and his weakness, testifies that he is unworthy of the honor conferred and cannot heal vices, that is, cure the sick, give food to the hungry, clothe the naked, since he himself is scarcely able to sustain himself. Let us not, then, at once acquiesce in the judgment of the multitude; […]

3:8.t: For Jerusalem has fallen, and Judah has collapsed: because their tongue and their devices are against the Lord, to provoke the eyes of his majesty. The recognition of their countenance has answered them: and they have proclaimed their sin like Sodom, and have not hidden it. It is the Prophet who says this, not, as many think, the one who had been chosen prince. And he says that no one is willing to be set over a sinful people for this reason, that both Judah and Jerusalem, both the city and the province of Judea, or the tribe of Judah, have fallen alike. And he gives the causes of their impiety: that they blasphemed against the Lord and said, Away, away, crucify such a one; we have no king but Caesar (John 19:15, 16), and by the fury of their tongue provoked the most merciful Lord to bitterness.

3:9.t: The climax of your sin is that you hate the righteous one whom you killed, as well as those who by his grace are godly, righteous and loving. It is for this reason that the Lord said, "Woe to their soul, because they have taken evil counsel against themselves, saying, 'Let us take away the just one, for he is distasteful to us.' " Although you did not offer a sacrifice to Baal, like your ancestors, and did not offer cakes in groves and on hills to the heavenly army, you did not accept the Lord's Christ. Whoever does not know Christ does not know the will of God. Whoever rejects and hates him obviously rejects and hates the one who sent him. Whoever does not have faith in him does not believe the words of the prophets who preached his good news and proclaimed him to all people.

And the prophet himself at once supplies the reason, why he called them rulers of Sodom, and people of Gomorrah: "For your hands are full of blood." And again a little further on :

"They have proclaimed their sin as Sodom and made it manifest. Woe to their soul, because they have taken evil counsel with themselves, saying, We will bind the just, for he is burdensome to us."

Since he so very clearly mentions some one's blood, and a plot against some one just man, what could this be but the plot against our Saviour Jesus Christ, through which and after which all the things aforesaid overtook them?
3:9.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

3:9.t: The Jews in their imaginings, and in their agreeing to act unjustly against the Lord, forgot that they were bringing wrath upon themselves. Therefore does the Word lament for them, saying, ‘Why do the people exalt themselves, and the nations imagine vain things?’ For vain indeed was the imagination of the Jews, meditating death against the Life, and devising unreasonable things against the ‘Word of the Father.’ For who that looks upon their dispersion, and the desolation of their city, may not aptly say, ‘Woe unto them, for they have imagined an evil imagination, saying against their own soul, let us bind the righteous man, because he is not pleasing to us.’ And full well is it so, my brethren; for when they erred concerning the Scriptures, they knew not that ‘he who diggeth a pit for his neighbour falleth therein; and he who destroyeth a hedge, a serpent shall bite him.’ […]

They bound Jesus and led him to the meeting place of the high priest. Can you recognize that this was already written? Isaiah says, "Woe to their souls because they have taken evil counsel against themselves, saying, 'Let us bind the just one, for he is troublesome to us.' " Woe to their souls indeed! Let us see why. Isaiah was sawn in two, but afterwards the people were restored. Jeremiah was thrown into the dungeon, but the Jews had their wound healed. In these instances the sin was against a man, and therefore less. However, when they sinned not against a man but against God become human, then woe to their souls!

It is the tribes, then, that are meant by the names of the patriarchs. From the tribe of Simeon come the scribes, from that of Levi the chief priests, who brought their wickedness to completion and filled up the entire measure of their fathers' ungodliness in the passion of the Lord. They took counsel against the Lord Jesus, to kill him, even as Isaiah says, "Alas for their souls! Because they have devised an evil counsel against themselves, saying. 'Let us bind the just one, for he is profitless to us.' " They killed the prophets and apostles who announced the coming of the Lord of salvation and preached his glorious passion and resurrection. Thereafter, in their greed and out of their desire for earthly wickedness, they fled from sharing in the divine, from chastity of body and moderation of spirit, contempt for money and profit in grace.
3:9.s: On the Blessings of the Patriarchs 3.13

3:9.t: The recognition of their countenance will answer them: that is, they have received back their own sins; or, as the Seventy translated, the confusion of their countenance has stood against them: that is, they have always had their own offenses before their eyes. And just as the Sodomites, sinning with all license and having not even any shame in their crime, said to Lot, Bring the men out, that we may lie with them (Gen 19:5): so these too, crying out publicly, proclaimed their sin and had no modesty in blaspheming. For to hide one's impiety is the second plank after shipwreck and a consolation of miseries. Hence they are also called princes of Sodom, because they had the sins of Sodom.

Woe to their soul, because evils have been repaid to them. Say to the righteous that it is well, because they have eaten the fruit of their own devices. Woe to the wicked unto evil: for the reward of his hands shall be done to him. According to the Hebrew and the other Translators it has this sense: Woe to them, because they have received back their crimes. Therefore you who hear, or who read the book of the Prophet, praise the righteousness of God, because he has done well: because the wicked have eaten the labors of their own hands. And woe to the wicked people unto evil: for it has received what it deserved. And he who handed over his prince to the Roman power himself lies subject to Roman servitude. But according to the Seventy Translators, who said: Woe to their soul, because they have devised the worst counsel against themselves, saying: Let us bind the righteous one, because he is useless to us; […]

3:10.t:
The aforesaid Scribes and Pharisees therefore placed James upon the pinnacle of the temple, and cried out to him and said: 'You just one, in whom we ought all to have confidence, forasmuch as the people are led astray after Jesus, the crucified one, declare to us, what is the gate of Jesus.'

And he answered with a loud voice, 'Why do you ask me concerning Jesus, the Son of Man? He himself sits in heaven at the right hand of the great Power, and is about to come upon the clouds of heaven.'

And when many were fully convinced and gloried in the testimony of James, and said, 'Hosanna to the Son of David,' these same Scribes and Pharisees said again to one another, 'We have done badly in supplying such testimony to Jesus. But let us go up and throw him down, in order that they may be afraid to believe him.'

And they cried out, saying, 'Oh! Oh! The just man is also in error.' […]
3:10.s: Memoirs (Book V), as quoted in Church History (Book II), Chapter 23, Sections 13-15 (as quoted by Eusebius of Caesarea, AD 339)

3:12.t: As individuals we have our own officers, but the whole multitude is handed over to several, according to that which is written in Isaiah: "my people, your officers plunder you, and those who are powerful lord it over you" — the officers lord it over us, if we owe anything.
3:12.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 35

3:12.t: But now, what wounds can the conquered show, what injuries to gaping vitals, what tortures of the limbs, when faith did not fail in combat but perfidy arrived before the combat? Nor does the necessity of the crime excuse the one who was caught, where the crime is of the will. I do not say this to burden the cases of the brothers but rather to stimulate the brothers to prayers of satisfaction. For since it is written, "They that call you blessed send you into error and destroy the way of your steps," one who consoles the sinner with flattering blandishments furnishes the means for sinning and does not check transgressions but nourishes them. But one who rebukes at the same time that he instructs with firmer counsels urges a brother on to salvation.

Isaiah also, filled with the Holy Spirit, cries out and chides the daughters of Zion who have been defiled by gold and raiment, and he reproves those who have an abundance of harmful riches and withdraw from God for the sake of the pleasures of time.… This, God blames; this, he brands with reproach. By this he declares that they have been defiled; by this they have departed from the true adornment and have merited disgrace and shame. Having put on silk and purple, they cannot put on Christ; adorned with gold and pearls and necklaces, they have lost the adornments of the heart and soul. Who would not detest and shun what has caused another's ruin? Who would seek and take what has served as a sword and weapon for the death of another? If, on draining the cup, he who had taken the potion should die, you would know that what he drank was poison; if, after taking food, he who had taken it should perish, you would know that what could kill, when taken, was deadly. […]
3:12.s: Treatise II. On the Dress of Virgins 13

3:12.t: Let us hearken to God, as he proclaims through Isaiah: "O my people, they that call you blessed lead you astray, throw you down headlong." Who is more guilty of throwing the people of God down headlong? He who relies on the power of the free will and scorns the help of the Creator and is secure in his own will, or he who fears the judgment of God at every thought of his precepts?

My people, their exactors have despoiled them, and women have ruled over them. For women, whom Symmachus alone translated so, and who in Hebrew are called NASIM (נשים), Aquila and the Seventy translated ἀπαιτοῦντας, which means exactors; Theodotion δανειστὰς, that is, usurers. Now the prophetic discourse speaks against the Scribes and Pharisees, who for the sake of base gain, to receive tithes and first-fruits, denied the Son of God. And he does not call them masters, scribes and teachers, but exactors (Luke 20), who think that piety is a means of gain, and devour, not, as in the Apostle, only the houses of widows, but the whole people; and, accusing their luxury and their shameful way of life, he calls them not only exactors, as men seen to exact money from the unwilling, but women, because they do everything for lust's sake and are given over to pleasures. Let us too, then, beware that we be not exactors among the people; […]

My people, those who call you blessed, they deceive you, and scatter the way of your steps, or throw it into confusion. He had called the Scribes and Pharisees exactors, not masters; and above, mockers, who because of gifts, which blind the eyes even of the wise, not only did not rebuke the sinners among the people, but for the sake of riches and profits extolled them with praises, calling them blessed, and pillars of the house of God, and the other things flatterers are wont to say. He, then, is the churchman teacher who moves tears, not laughter, who rebukes sinners, who calls no one blessed, no one happy, and does not anticipate the sentence of his judge, since holy Scripture says (Sir 11:30): Call no man blessed before death. But in another place too we read (Prov 27:14): He who blesses his friend in the morning with a loud voice differs in nothing from one who curses. Therefore, despising the judgments of men, let us neither be lifted up by their praises nor saddened by their disparagements; […]

3:13.t: The Lord stands to judge, and he stands to judge the peoples. The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people, and with its princes. The people, which was deceived through simplicity and inexperience, is still called the people of God, and is therefore judged that it may be saved. Nor does the Lord sit in the attire of one judging, as we read in Daniel: Thrones were set, and books were opened (Dan 7:9); but he stands to judge, and he stands to judge the peoples, wishing those to stand whose way had been scattered. But against the princes and elders of his people he comes to judgment, not to judge but to be judged alike with them, giving them room for defense, if they can have anything to answer, according to what is said in the fiftieth psalm: That you may be justified in your words, and may overcome when you are judged (Verse 6). In the prophet Micah too we read something of the kind (Mic 6), which we have interpreted in its place. […]

3:14.t: For you have grazed down my vineyard: the plunder of the poor is in your house. Why do you wear down my people, and grind the faces of the poor?, or crush them, and as the Seventy interpreted, put them to confusion. He keeps the prophetic custom of suddenly changing the persons: for above the Lord himself had said, My people, those who call you blessed, they deceive you; and afterwards the Prophet had added, The Lord stands to judge: the Lord will come to judgment. Therefore after the prophet, the Lord himself, who had come to judgment with the elders of his people and its princes, speaks to them and rebukes the offenders: Why do you graze down my vineyard?, of which it is written: You have brought a vine out of Egypt (Ps 79 [80]:9). And in this same prophet: The vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel (Isa 5:7). This vineyard the Lord in the Gospel too let out to most wicked husbandmen, who killed the son of the householder sent to them (Matt 21). The plunder of the poor, he says, is in your houses. […]

Therefore, coming with all Angels, together with Him He shall have the Saints also. For plainly saith Isaias also, “He shall come to judgment with the elders of the people.” Those “elders of the people,” then, those but now named Angels, those thousands of many men made perfect coming from the whole world, are called Heaven.

3:16.t: But shouldest thou enter into a church, thou geest forth, without getting anything but countless leers, and revilings, and curses, not from the beholders only, but also from the prophet. For straightway Isaiah, that hath the fullest voice of all, as soon as he hath seen thee, will cry out, "These things saith the Lord against the princely daughters of Sion; because they walked with a lofty neck, and with winkings of the eyes, and in their walking, trailing their garments, and mincing at the same time with their feet; the Lord shall take off their bravery, and instead of a sweet smell there shall be dust, and instead of a stomacher, thou shalt gird thyself with a cord." These things for thy gorgeous array. For not to them only are these words addressed, but to every woman that doeth like them.
3:16.s: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 89

3:16.t: And the Lord said: Because the daughters of Zion are lifted up, and have walked with outstretched neck, and went with nods of the eyes, and clapped, and walked, and stepped with their feet in measured gait. Above, both the prophet and the Lord had rebuked both the people and the princes; now the prophetic discourse turns to the women of whom he had said before, And women have ruled over them, lest they should think themselves strangers to the crime, they on account of whose luxuries and wantonness the exactors grazed down the Lord's vineyard, and the plunder of the poor is in their houses, and they wore down his people and put to confusion the faces of the poor. Some think these are truly the women of the Jews; others judge that it is said metaphorically of the cities of Judea, which are called daughters of Zion: the lesser towns, that is, villages and townships. […]

3:17.t: The Lord will make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion, and will lay bare their hair, and instead of adornment there will be disgrace. This will befall us too whose sins are concealed, when that which is written has been fulfilled: Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed (Luke 8:17). For so long as we are covered by the hair and garment of ignorance, and men think us, who are within full of dead men's bones, to be whitened sepulchers (Matt 23), we seem to have some cleanness. But when what is hidden has been laid open, all the hair will be taken away, and a foul baldness will appear to all.

3:18.t: In that day the Lord will take away the adornment of the shoes. In what day? The Jews think, that of the Babylonian captivity. We prove that it is more truly when they were taken by the Romans and lost all the ornaments of clothing and gems, of gold and jewels, and their various furnishings. Or else, through the metaphor of the women, all the adornment of the cities is related to have been destroyed. Understand the ornaments of the cities to be in the streets and porticoes, the forum and the gymnasia and the public walls. If we refer these to the state of souls, let us recall that we have read of the shod feet of him who is to eat the flesh of the lamb and celebrate the Pasch, and that neither the garments nor the shoes of those passing through the wilderness were worn out. What are these shoes? Those of which the Apostle writes to the Ephesians: Your feet shod in preparation of the Gospel of peace (Eph 6:15). […]

And the crescents, and the necklaces, and the jewels, and the bracelets, and the headbands, and the hair-ornaments, and the anklets, and the little chains, and the scent-boxes, and the earrings, and the rings, and the gems hanging on the forehead. He describes the jewels of the women, and through them the insignia of the cities; or, according to the anagogy, the ornaments of the various virtues. Women have little bosses hanging down in the likeness of the moon, which we transfer to the ornaments of the Church, which is illumined by the sun of righteousness. Necklaces too, hanging down as far as the breast, show the understanding and the ruling part (ἡγεμονικόν) of the mind in the heart. And jewels, which in a single word signify all ornaments; and the good works of bracelets, such as Rebecca received at her betrothal (Gen 24); and headbands, the ornaments of the head; hair-ornaments, that it may have judgment of each thing; […]

3:22.t: And the changes of raiment, and the mantles, and the linen cloths. For linen cloths the Seventy interpreted transparent Laconian garments, wishing to signify the very fine garments with which the bodies of the Lacedaemonians were covered, who were most ready for war and of a rather austere life; although neither the Hebrew nor any other of the translators has Laconian. Changes of raiment and mantles, which Symmachus translated more expressively ἀναβολαια, are ornaments of women's clothing, by which the shoulders and breasts are covered. Changes of raiment, according to the anagogy, are those of which it is said: They will go from strength to strength (Ps 83 [84]:8); and linen cloths, that, washed in the Lord, we may enjoy delights, according to what is written in the Psalms: You will give them to drink of the torrent of your pleasure (Ps 35 [36]:9). […]

And the pins, and the mirrors, and the fine linens, and the fillets, and the summer veils. Women have pins, by which the arrangement of the dressed hair is held together, so that it may not flow too loosely and be scattered into straggling locks. They have mirrors too, in which they look at their face, and if they see anything lacking, they add to their adornment. They have fine linens, which are called wraps; and fillets, with which the hair is bound, which they call ταινίας. They have summer veils too, which we can call mantles, with which Rebecca also was covered; and today too the women of Arabia and Mesopotamia are veiled with them. In Hebrew they are called ARDIDIM, in Greek θέριστρα, from the fact that in θέρει, that is, in summer and the heat, they protect the bodies of women. The daughters of Zion, therefore, because of their pride lost the pins by which the rule of all the precepts was held fast. […]

3:24.t:
And instead of a sweet odor there will be a stench, and instead of a girdle, a cord. The penitent says that sins stink: My wounds have putrefied and are corrupted because of my folly (Ps 37 [38]:6). The Apostle commanded the loins to be girded with a girdle, saying: Stand, having your loins girded in truth (Eph 6:14). And of the sinner we read: Each one is bound fast with the cords of his own sins (Prov 5:22). Therefore, instead of the good odor of the virtues, the daughters of Zion will have the rottenness of sins; and instead of the girdle of truth they will be bound with the cords of falsehood, such as those had upon their heads who with rags and filth begged their life from the king of Syria.

And instead of a breast-band, haircloth. For breast-band, as Symmachus interpreted it, the Seventy translated a tunic μεσοπορφύραν, that is, striped with purple, which Aquila expressed as girdle of exultation. Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, PHTHIGIL (פתיגיל), which is a kind of women's ornament. […]

3:25.t: Your most beautiful men too shall fall by the sword, and your strong ones in battle. For most beautiful men the Seventy interpreted, and your most beautiful son, whom you love, shall fall by the sword. If we understand this of the state of a soul which has sinned after the virtues, let us take her most beautiful son to be good works, which have fallen by the enemy's sword; and the strong too to have perished in battle, because the righteousness of the righteous man will not deliver him in whatever day he has gone astray (Ezek 33:12). But if we follow the history, we shall be taught by these words that the prophet's discourse is not about women whose husbands fell in battle, but about the cities of Judea, which he called daughters of Zion, and whose warriors fell in the conflict. Lastly, the following verse speaks of the same Zion.

3:26.t: And her gates shall lament and mourn, and the city itself, desolate, shall sit upon the ground. This we see with our eyes to this day. According to tropology the interpretation is easy: that whoever has given place to the devil and has not kept his heart with all watchfulness, his gates mourn; and, the bridegroom being absent, he is ever in mourning, and, falling from the heights, sits in the dust of the earth.

4:1.t: The "seven women" suffer "reproach" and go about seeking to receive the one who is able to "take away their reproach". These same "seven women" make a promise, that they will "eat their own bread and be clothed with their own garments". They have no need of the "bread" of him who "takes away their reproach"; they do not lack the "garments of a man" whom they "take". They have better "garments" than a "man" can supply to them; they have more sumptuous foods than the human condition can bestow. It is therefore worth considering whose these "seven women" are and what their "reproach" is. The "seven women" are one; for they are the "Spirit of God". And this one is seven; for the "Spirit of God" is "the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord". This "wisdom" suffers "reproach" from the many wisdoms that rise up against it; this true "understanding" bears "reproach" from false understandings; […]

"And He had in His right hand seven stars." He said that in His right hand He had seven stars, because the Holy Spirit of sevenfold agency was given into His power by the Father. As Peter exclaimed to the Jews: "Being at the right hand of God exalted, He hath shed forth this Spirit received from the Father, which ye both see and hear." Moreover, John the Baptist had also anticipated this, by saying to his disciples: "For God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto Him. The Father," says he, "loveth the Son, and hath given all things into His hands." Those seven stars are the seven churches, which he names in his addresses by name, old calls them to whom he wrote epistles. Not that they are themselves the only, or even the principal churches; but what he says to one, he says to all. For they are in no respect different, that on that ground any one should prefer them to the larger number of similar small ones. […]
4:1.s: Commentary on the Apocalypse of the Blessed John

4:1.t: HOW DO THE SEVEN WOMEN MENTIONED IN ISAIAH, “AND SEVEN WOMEN SHALL TAKE HOLD,” ETC. (Isa. 4:1), SIGNIFY THE SEVEN CATHOLIC CHURCHES? — “And seven women,” he says, “shall take hold of one man, saying, We will eat our own bread, and wear our own apparel: only let your name be called upon us; take away our reproach.” It is absolutely clear that by the seven women the seven Churches are signified: for although the Church is one, it is called sevenfold, so that the one body may consist of a sevenfold number of members. For not only we, but also the citizens above are members of the Church, whose head is Christ (Eph. 5:23). Whether therefore the Churches are called one or seven does not conflict. It is called one because it has one head, which is Christ; it is called seven because, just as the members are diverse, so also the spiritual powers, among which we too are reckoned, have diverse functions, on account of which they are called “of the air.” […]
4:1.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 47: HOW THE SEVEN WOMEN OF ISAIAH SIGNIFY THE SEVEN CHURCHES

4:1.t: And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying: We will eat our own bread, and be covered with our own garments; only let your name be called upon us: take away our reproach. When the most beautiful men of the city of Jerusalem have fallen by the sword, and the strong have perished in battle, and her gates have lamented and mourned, and she herself has been made desolate through the very great scarcity of men, the warriors having been slain, seven women will take hold of one man, desiring to have seed in Zion and a household in Jerusalem, saying that they have food and clothing, only so that they may not be seen to be without a husband and lie under that curse which is written: Cursed is the barren woman, and she who does not make seed in Israel (Deut 7). Zechariah too agrees with this sense: In those days ten men out of all the tongues of the nations shall take hold of the fringe of a Jewish man, saying: We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you (Zech 8:23). […]

And in Isaiah we read: Seven women shall take hold of one man, saying: We will eat our own bread and be clothed with our own garments; only let your name be called upon us, take away our reproach. Those, then, who there are called seven women, that is, Churches, whose number is contained also in the apostle Paul — for he writes to seven churches, to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians, to the Thessalonians. And in the Apocalypse of John the Lord, girded with variety and with purest gold, walks in the midst of the seven lampstands, that is, of the churches of the Ephesians, the Smyrnaeans, the Pergamenes, the Thyatirans, the Sardians, the Philadelphians, the Laodiceans —, are now named ten in the prophet Zechariah, whom the Lord also sought, so that, if he had found them in Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, he might deliver them from destruction.

Second, their fecundity is represented by the seven women in Isaiah: Seven women will take hold of one man on that day. A man, because these virtues produce virility; and one, because they do not divide him, but make him stable and fruitful.

4:2.t: In that day the bud of the Lord shall be in magnificence and in glory, and the fruit of the earth exalted, and exultation for those who shall have been saved of Israel. And it shall be that everyone who is left in Zion, and remains in Jerusalem, shall be called holy, everyone who is written in life in Jerusalem. When the daughters of Zion have lost all adornment because of their pride, and her gates have lamented and mourned, and she herself has fallen desolate, and all her warriors have perished in battle, so much so that many women can scarcely have one husband, then the bud of the Christian name will spring up, and the earth will give its fruit; and there will be exultation for those who have been saved of Israel, of whom it was said above as well: Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us a seed, we should have been as Sodom, and should have been like Gomorrah (Isa 1:9).

The Lord indeed gave of his generosity in that he arranged to liberate the human race from the crime of its transgression through his only-begotten Son. He gave of his generosity because with the grace of the Holy Spirit he consecrated for his entry the temple of a virginal womb. And our earth gave its fruit because the same virgin who had her body from the earth bore a son who was coequal to God the Father in his divinity but by the reality of [his] flesh consubstantial with her. Concerning this, Isaiah also, looking toward the time of human redemption, said, "On that day the branch of the Lord will be in magnificence and in glory, and the fruit of the earth will be sublime." The branch of the Lord was in magnificence and glory when the undying Son of God, appearing temporally in the flesh as a bright light, poured out upon the world the greatness of his heavenly virtues. […]

The third mode of generation is by means of propagation, and this in a fourfold way: as of a growth coming from a seed, a tree from a root, a conceived offspring from the belly or womb of the mother, or children from a begetting father. In the first mode of generation, formal beauty is lacking, for in the seed the form is vague and hidden. It is not so in the case of the Son. In the second, conformity is lacking, for although there is a single root, it is different in shape from the branches even though they produce a single tree. In the third, actuality is lacking, for although the mother is in a certain sense the active principle of the offspring, yet she is much more of a passive principle. In the fourth, eternal coexistence is lacking.

Now, take away these defects and suppose first formal beauty. In this sense, there is Isaiah: "The branch of the Lord will be luster and glory, and the fruit of the earth will be honor and splendor." […]

Fourth is the fullness of restoring fruits. Isaiah says: "The branch of the Lord will be luster and glory, and the fruit of the earth will be honor and splendor." And when was this? When the woman said: "Blessed art thou among women and blessed is the Fruit of thy womb!"

4:3.t: And note that not all Israel is saved, but the remnant of the people of Zion, and he who remains in Jerusalem: everyone who is written in life in Jerusalem, to whom the Lord too spoke: Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). It signifies the Apostles and those who believed through the Apostles.

4:4.t: The greatest cleansing is the spiritual washing that washes away the filth of the soul. The inspired word speaks of such a washing: "The Lord shall wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Israel and shall wash away the blood from their midst." This refers to the blood of immortality as well as the killing of the prophets. He means by this purification, seen from the added phrase, "by the spirit of judgment and by the spirit of burning." The washing of the body, however, is physical and is accomplished only by water. In fact, it can even be done in fields far away from the baths.

Then there follows: "when the days of their purification were fulfilled, according to the law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem". On account of the purification, he says, "of them". Of whom, "of them"? If it had been written: on account of her purification, that is, of Mary, who had given birth, no question would arise, and we would boldly say that Mary, who was human, had need of purification after childbirth. But now, in that it says: "the days of their purification", it seems to signify not one, but another or several. Did Jesus, then, have need of purification and was he unclean, or defiled with some filth? Perhaps I seem to speak rashly, but I am moved by the authority of the Scriptures. See what is written in Job: "no one is clean from filth, not even if his life should be of a single day". He did not say: "no one is clean from sin," but: "no one is clean from filth". For filth and sins do not signify the same thing; […]
4:4.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 14

4:4.t: When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall have washed the blood of Jerusalem from her midst by the spirit of judgment and by the spirit of burning. Then the remnant of Israel will be saved, when in the baptism of the Savior their sins have been forgiven them, and that blood has been washed away which the erring people invoked upon itself: His blood be upon us, and upon our children (Matt 27:25). Hence we read above: When you stretch out your hands, I will not hear you: for your hands are full of blood (Isa 1:15, 16). And afterwards, calling them to penitence, he adds: Wash yourselves, be clean. And note that he washed the filth of the daughters of Zion by the spirit of judgment, but the blood of Jerusalem by the spirit of burning. For what is light is washed; what is heavier is burned out. […]

To those who sin gravely he is a refining and consuming fire; but to those who commit light sins, fullers' herb, so as to restore cleanness to those who have been washed, according to what is written in Isaiah: The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst, by the spirit of judgement and by the spirit of burning. Those who have filth need the spirit of judgement, that they may be washed; those who are full of blood need the spirit of burning, that the blood which has been smeared on them from without may be taken away.

4:5.t: And the Lord will create over every place of mount Zion, and where he has been called upon, a cloud by day, and smoke and the brightness of flaming fire by night. For in Christ there is a new creation, of which we read elsewhere: The old things have passed away: behold, all things have been made new (2 Cor 5:17). For which the Seventy translated: And he will come, and it will be; every place of mount Zion, and all things that are round about it, a cloud will overshadow by day, and the light of flaming fire by night. And who will come, if not he of whom it is written: There will come out of Zion one who will deliver (Isa 59:20 LXX)? And of whom another prophet makes mention: Yet a very little while, and he who is to come will come, and will not delay (Hab 2:3). […]

4:6.t: And over all the glory a protection. And there shall be a tabernacle for a shade by day from the heat, and for security, and for a hiding place from the whirlwind and from the rain. This place the Jews refer to Antichrist, who they judge is signified by the whirlwind and the storm, when the Lord is to defend them from a most powerful adversary. But let us refer everything to the first coming of Christ, of which we read in the psalms as well: He has protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle: upon a rock he has exalted me (Ps 26 [27]:5); upon which the Church, being founded, is shaken by no storm, overthrown by no whirlwind and winds. Very many of the Jews understand both these things and all those with which they are joined of the Babylonian captivity and the return to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel and Ezra and Nehemiah.

5:1.t: And truly he was "a horn of salvation in the house of David", because this prophecy is sung in harmony: "For a vineyard was made on a horn". On what horn? On Christ Jesus, on him of whom it is now written: "he raised up a horn of salvation for us, in the house of David his servant, as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets".
5:1.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 10

5:1.t:
And the Son of Man came to free them and gather them together, but they did not receive Him. For He came to obtain fruit from them, and they did not give it to Him. For their vines were of the vine of Sodom and of the stock of Gomorrha, a vineyard in which thorns grew, and which bore wild grapes. Their vine was bitter, and their fruit sour. The thorns could not be softened, nor could the bitterness change to the nature of wine, nor could the sour fruit change to a sweet nature.

For Isaiah first set men of Judah as judges over them, and there was planted amongst them a new and beloved planting. But these are those judges who shall sit on twelve thrones and judge their twelve tribes. And thus He said to the judges:—Judge between Me and My vineyard, what further, O ye judges, should I have done to My vineyard, that I did not do? For lo! I planted it with vine scions, and they became strange vines. I surrounded it with a fence of heavenly Watchers and I built its tower, the holy Temple. […]
And in Isaiah it says, "I will sing to my beloved a song of my beloved touching my vineyard. My beloved has a vineyard." Who is the "Beloved" other than the only-begotten Son?

The sight of a vine, when observed by an intelligent eye, serves to remind you of your nature. Without doubt you remember the parable where the Lord calls Himself a vine and His Father the husbandman, and every one of us who are grafted by faith into the Church the branches. He invites us to produce fruits in abundance, for fear lest our sterility should condemn us to the fire. He constantly compares our souls to vines. “My well beloved,” says He, “hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill,” and elsewhere, I have “planted a vineyard and hedged it round about.” Evidently He calls human souls His vine, those souls whom He has surrounded with the authority of His precepts and a guard of angels. “The angel of the Lord encampeth round about them that fear him.” And further: He has planted for us, so to say, props, in establishing in His Church apostles, prophets, teachers; and raising our thoughts by the example of the blessed in olden times, He has not allowed them to drag on the earth and be crushed under foot. […]
5:1.s: The Hexaemeron, Homily 5: The Germination of the Earth

5:1.t: Similar to this vine are the members of the Church, who are planted with the root of faith and are held in check by the vine-shoots of humility. On this subject the Prophet beautifully says: ‘Thou hast brought a vineyard out of Egypt: thou plantest the roots thereof and it filled the land. The shadow of it covered the hills and the branches thereof the cedars of God. It stretched forth its branches unto the sea and its boughs unto the river.’ And the Lord Himself spoke through Isaias, saying: ‘My beloved had a vineyard on a hill in a fruitful place. And I fenced it in and dug around the vine of Sorech and I built a tower in the midst thereof.’ He fenced it in with a rampart, as it were of heavenly precepts and with the angels standing guard, for ‘the angel of the lord shall encamp round about them that fear him.’ He placed in the Church a tower, so to speak, of Apostles, Prophets, and Doctors, ready to defend the peace of the Church. He dug around it, when He had freed it from the burden of earthly anxieties. […]

I will sing now to my beloved the song of my cousin concerning his vineyard. The prophet sings a lamentable song to the people of Israel, which he composed of whom it is written in the Gospel: But when he had seen it (doubtless Jerusalem) he wept over it, and said: If you too had known the things that are for your peace, for the days will come upon you, and your enemies will throw up ramparts around you, and will hem you in, and will lay you low, and your children (Luke 19:41ff.). And again: How often would I have gathered your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not? Behold, your house will be left to you desolate (Matt 23:37, 38): to which this is like, which is now said in this song: I will abandon my vineyard. And that Christ is called the beloved and dearest one, whom Aquila interpreted πατράδελφον, uncle, or cousin, the title of the forty-fourth psalm teaches us: A song for the beloved. […]

5:2.t: And he fenced it, and chose out the stones from it, and planted the vine Sorec, and built a tower in its midst, and set up a winepress in it. Through the metaphor of the vineyard, as we said before, he describes the people of the Jews, which he fenced with the help of the Angels. And he chose out the stones from it, either idols or all things that could hinder the worship of God. And he planted it with the vine Sorec, which Symmachus alone interpreted as choice, expressing, as it seems to me, not word for word but the sense contained in the word. For the Hebrews say that Sorec is a kind of excellent vine, because it produces abundant and lasting fruit. Lastly, Sorec is interpreted by some as καλλίκαρπος, which we can render as of most beautiful fruit. He also built a tower in its midst, that is, the temple in the midst of the city; and set up a winepress in it, by which some think the altar is signified. […]

For thus He threatens her through Isaiah, “I will throw down her enclosure.” Wherefore? “For I looked that she should bring forth grapes, but she brought forth thorns.” I looked for fruit from thence, and I found sin. Why then dost thou ask, O Asaph, “Why hast Thou thrown down her enclosure?” For knowest thou not why? I looked that she should do judgment, and she did iniquity. Must not her enclosure needs be thrown down?

5:3.t: Now therefore, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard: what is there that I ought to have done further for my vineyard and have not done for it? Or is it that I waited for it to make grapes, and it made wild grapes? I have done, he says, all that I ought: I planted the vineyard in a most fertile place, I set a wall around it, I chose out the stones, and I propped up its shoots with stakes and reeds; the vine itself too was not one of many, but choice and καλλίκαρπος. I built a very strong tower, in which to store the crops and from which to watch the beasts that lie in wait for the crops. I set up a winepress, so that the grapes might be pressed above all in that same place and pour out wine. Since, then, I have done the things I ought to have done, let the inhabitants of Jerusalem and of Judah answer me; nay rather, let them judge between me and my vineyard, what is there that I ought to have done and have not done? […]

5:5.t: And now I will show you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away its hedge, and it shall be for plunder; I will break down its wall, and it shall be for trampling. And I will make it desolate; it shall not be pruned, and it shall not be dug: and briers and thorns shall come up over it. I challenged you above, he says, O inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of the tribe of Judah, to judge between me and my vineyard, and I asked you to say what I ought to have done that I have not done. And since, according to the Gospel parable, you will not answer what I ask, I myself will answer for you, showing what I am going to do: Since I have done for my vineyard all that I ought, and instead of grapes it has brought forth wild grapes, I will take away all that I had given. I will take away the help of the angels, of whom it is written in the psalms: The Angel of the Lord encamps round about those who fear him, and will deliver them (Ps 33 [34]:8); and it will be plundered by its adversaries. […]

And what his end will be, we learn from the words of Isaiah. For he says: "For the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the man of Judah: a plant new and well-beloved: and I looked that it would bring forth grapes, but it brought forth iniquity, and not righteousness, but a cry."
