And that Israel was thus punished for its neglect of that fruitfulness which was both fitting for itself and well pleasing to God; having neither obeyed His commands, nor consented to perform them; we learn again from' His words, where He says: "But now I will shew you what I will do to My vineyard. I will take away its fence, and it shall be wasted: and I will rend its wall, and it shall be trampled under foot. And I will abandon My vineyard: and it shall not be pruned, nor tilled: and thorns shall grow up in it as on waste ground; and I will command the clouds to rain no rain upon it." It is plain, therefore, to every man, that God hath no respect for the wicked soul that beareth thorns. […]
5:5.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

5:6.t: And I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it. These are the clouds which the Lord brought out from the end of the earth, of which we read in the psalm as well: Your truth reaches to the clouds (Ps 35 [36]:6). These clouds, since under Elijah all were idolaters, did not rain upon the land of Israel for three years and six months (1 Kgs 18). This indeed we can understand not only of the prophets but of the apostles: that after the passion of the Lord the Jews had neither prophets nor apostles, lest instead of grapes they should bring forth thorns, but that they might pray, for their barrenness and dryness, to him who can supply the rains of the virtues. Hence in Leviticus too he says to them: I will make the heaven of iron for you, and the earth of bronze (Lev 26:19). And in Deuteronomy: The heaven over your head shall be of bronze, and the earth beneath you of iron (Deut 28:23, 24). And again: The Lord will give rain to your land. […]

I will command, he says, the clouds not to rain rain upon them—that is, upon the people of the Jews. The clouds are the prophets: the Lord commanded them not to rain rain upon Israel. The prophetic word has been turned toward us. These clouds, if they are dashed against one another, make thunder and lightnings.

And what are His clouds? His Apostles, His preachers, by whom He thundered in precepts, lightened in miracles. The same are clouds who are also mountains: mountains for their height and firmness, clouds for their rain and fruitfulness. For these clouds watered the earth, of which it was said, “The Most High gave His Voice, and the earth was moved.” For it is of those clouds that He threateneth a certain barren vineyard, whence the mountains were carried into the heart of the sea; “I will command,” saith He, “the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.” This was fulfilled in that which I have mentioned, when the mountains were carried into the heart of the sea; when it was said, “It was necessary that the word of God should have been spoken first to you; but seeing ye put it from you, we turn to the Gentiles;” then was fulfilled, “I will command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.” The nation of the Jews hath just so remained as a fleece dry upon the ground.

What clouds? The preachers of the word of truth. What clouds? Those concerning which God doth menace a certain vineyard, which instead of grape had brought forth thorns and He saith, “I will command My clouds, that they rain no rain upon it.” In a word, the Apostles forsaking the Jews, went to the Gentiles: in preaching Christ among all nations, “the clouds have uttered a voice.”

5:7.t: But the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his delightful shoot. That is, of God; or, as the Seventy translated, a most beloved young planting. Israel and Judah differ from each other in this: that the whole people was at first called Israel, and afterwards, when David reigned over the tribe of Judah, and Rehoboam the son of Solomon over two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, those who were in Samaria, that is, the ten tribes, were called Israel; and those over whom men of David's line reigned were called Judah. And since calves were worshiped by Israel in Dan and in Bethel, Samaria was therefore taken first by the Assyrians; and a long time afterwards Judah was led away by the Chaldeans into Babylon, because they had sinned less. […]

5:8.t: Let him use those tenths and first-fruits, which are given according to the command of God, as a man of God; as also let him dispense in a right manner the free-will offerings which are brought in on account of the poor, to the orphans, the widows, the afflicted, and strangers in distress, as having that God for the examiner of his accounts who has committed the disposition to him. Distribute to all those in want with righteousness, and yourselves use the things which belong to the Lord, but do not abuse them; eating of them, but not eating them all up by yourselves: communicate with those that are in want, and thereby show yourselves unblameable before God. For if you shall consume them by yourselves, you will be reproached by God, who says to such unsatiable people, who alone devour all, "You eat up the milk, and clothe yourselves with the wool;" [Ezekiel 34:3] and in another passage, "Must you alone live upon the earth"? […]

But for us, men, there are far different sentiments. We desire change for various reasons: a wish for travel, for release from daily associations. We long for the approval of strangers and to remove the age-long boundaries which our ancestors have set up, adding estate to estate, household to household.

The earth alone does not suffice. We use the sea itself for our foundations. On the other hand, in compliance with individual whims, the land is excavated and sea water is brought in so as to form islands or straits for men’s use. Men claim the sea for themselves by right of ownership and boast that they have subjected fishes like slaves to a condition of servitude. This, they say, is my bay; that one belongs to another. Like sovereigns, they divide the elements among themselves. For some people, oysters are bred in water. For others, fish are enclosed in a fish pond.

The sea does not suffice for their luxuriant living. They must have reserve stores of oysters. They keep a reckoning of the age of each oyster bed. […]

Woe to you who join house to house, and link field to field, as far as the limit of the place: will you alone dwell upon the earth? For what we have said, as far as the limit of the place, the Seventy translated, that you may take something from your neighbor; Symmachus and Theodotion, until place fails, or there is none, so that, though the land fails, greed is by no means sated. This I think is said both generally against all for whom nothing is enough, and specially against the vineyard of the Lord, which instead of grapes made wild grapes, that is, instead of judgment iniquity, and instead of righteousness a cry. For what madness it is, when houses and fields ought to be had to keep off the rains and to sow crops, to desire to have those in all of which you cannot dwell and which you are not able to till, and to make another's need your pleasure! […]

And this you may learn from what He Himself says thereupon by the mouth of the holy prophets; "Therefore because you have bruised the heads of the poor, and taken from them chosen gifts, you shall build houses of carved stone, but you shall not dwell therein: and you shall plant desirable vineyards, but you shall not drink of their wine. For I know your many wickednesses, and mighty are your sins." And again, "Woe unto those who add house to house, and join field to field, that they may take away something from their neighbour. Will you dwell alone in the earth? For these things have been heard in the ears of the Lord of hosts. For though your houses be many, they shall be a desolation: though they be great and fair, there shall be none to inhabit them. […]
5:8.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

5:8.t: You evict your neighbors from their little farms, those nearest you from their houses and property. Would you "be placed alone in the midst of the earth," as it is written? This is the one end you cannot gain. Seize all that you can, occupy by force all that you can, still you shall always find a neighbor.
5:8.s: On the Government of God, Book 5, Chapter 11

5:9.t: These things of the Lord of hosts are in my ears: Unless many houses are made desolate, great and beautiful, without an inhabitant. For what we have rendered according to the Hebrew, These things of the Lord of hosts are in my ears, that is, the words which the Lord spoke still resound in my ears, the Seventy translated, These things have been heard in the ears of the Lord Sabaoth: not that the Prophet heard the words of the Lord, but that the things the Prophet was going to say were heard in the ears of the Lord; whereas it is more consistent to understand that the Prophet heard what the Lord spoke. And the Lord spoke this: that after the captivity great and most beautiful houses would be desolate, having no inhabitant.

We ask, according to the anagogy, how the houses of the heretics are great and beautiful, which, when the time of judgment has come, have no inhabitant. For all the pomp and structure of words and the arguments of dialectic will be reduced to nothing. And since, according to the apostle Paul (1 Cor 3), we are not only God's building but also his husbandry, which the heretics imitate and are dug under and rooted up by Jeremiah: therefore where ten acres of vineyards, or where ten yoke of oxen are at work, they will make one bath, and thirty measures of seed will make an ephi (Jer 18), so that from the number ten, which in the holy Scriptures is mystical and perfect, and from thirty, at which Ezekiel prophesied (Ezek 1) and the Lord was baptized (Luke 3), they are reduced to an ephi, which, in comparison with a manifold number, is confined to unity. […]

5:10.t: For ten acres of vineyards shall make one little flask, and thirty measures of seed shall make three measures. For little flask, which the Seventy alone translated, all the others interpreted bath, which in Hebrew is called BETH (בת). And for thirty measures, which we have set down for a cor, which in Hebrew is called OMER (תמר), the Seventy rendered six artabas, which is an Egyptian measure and makes twenty measures. In the excessive barrenness, then, which follows the captivity, ten acres of vineyards will make a bath, that is, three amphorae; and thirty measures of seed, that is, a cor, will make an ephi, which the Seventy interpreted as three measures, that is, three modii. Now bath is said of liquid kinds, and ephi or epha, of the same measure, of dry ones. As we read in Ezekiel according to the Hebrew: You shall have a just ephi, and a just bath. […]

5:11.t: Woe to you who rise early in the morning to pursue drunkenness, and to drink until evening, so as to be inflamed with wine. Harp and lyre, timbrel and pipe, and wine are in your feasts; and you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands. For drunkenness, as Aquila and Symmachus interpreted it, the Seventy set down the Hebrew word itself, SICERAM (שכר), which signifies every drink that can intoxicate and overturn the settled state of the mind. And, following the sequence of the explanation begun, he rebukes the husbandmen of the vineyard, who, with barrenness impending and the burning near at hand by which the briers and thorns are to be consumed, gave themselves over to luxury and pleasures, not only in eating and drinking but also in the delight of the ears and in the various kinds of the art of music. While they do these things, they do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider what is to come. […]

Hear also the words of the prophecy, and the "Woe" which was proclaimed for gluttons, "Woe unto those who rise up early in the morning and pursue strong drink, and who tarry long over it in the evening while wine inflameth them. With harps, and stringed instruments, and drums, and tabrets, they drink wine, and the works of God they understand not." And behold, the Spirit also hath taught thee that the man who ministereth unto his lusts is unable to understand the works of God. For as in our sleep we are not able to speak and to act as living beings who are awake, even so the man who is sunk in the sleep of lusts cannot understand the living works of God, neither doth he know how to contemplate His government, nor to wonder at the various forms of His dispensation; and he knoweth not admiration of the majesty of God, nor is he awake unto the knowledge of Him, nor is he ready to respond unto His wisdom. […]

Now this is the first lust which conquered the world, and because of it the first transgression of the law took place. Through it also the Prophet reproached the people, when he proclaimed, "Woe unto those who rise up early in the morning, and follow quickly thereafter."

5:13.t: Therefore my people has been led away captive, because it had no knowledge; and its nobles have perished with hunger, and its multitude is dried up with thirst. That these things befell the people of the Jews according to the letter under Vespasian and Titus, the Roman emperors, both Greek and Latin history relates. And this indeed they suffer spiritually today too, enduring not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God; because they neither regarded the work of the Lord nor considered the works of his hands, nor had knowledge of him who has always spoken through the Prophets (Amos 8). Hence in the Psalms too it is said of them: They shall return at evening, and shall suffer hunger like dogs, and shall go round about the city (Ps 58 [59]:16). And that every word of teaching is called bread and water, that saying of the Gospel teaches: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that goes forth from the mouth of God (Luke 4:4); […]
"Therefore my people are led into captivity, because they did not have knowledge," namely neither in the head nor in the members.

5:14.t: Therefore the underworld has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit, and its strong ones and its people, and its exalted and glorious ones, shall go down into it. And man shall be bowed down, and the man of rank shall be humbled, and the eyes of the lofty shall be brought low. Those who rose in the morning to pursue strong drink, and continued in drunkenness until evening, and, occupied with pleasure and delights, would not regard the work of the Lord nor contemplate the works of his hands, were therefore led into captivity, because they had no knowledge of the Son of God, who himself says to them, You know neither me nor him who sent me (John 8:19); and in the captivity itself they perished with hunger and were dried up with thirst. […]

5:16.t: And the Lord of hosts shall be exalted in judgment, and the holy God shall be sanctified in righteousness. When the people has been led away captive because it had no knowledge, and has perished with hunger and been dried up with thirst, and the underworld has enlarged its soul, and the strong and the exalted and glorious have gone down into the depth, and man has been bowed down and the man of rank humbled, and all have received according to their deserts: then the Lord will be exalted in judgment, whose judgment before seemed to be unjust, and the holy God will be sanctified by all in righteousness, so that what is said in the Gospel may be fulfilled: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name (Matt 6:9); and: Righteous Father, the world has not known you (John 17:25). […]

5:17.t: And the lambs shall feed according to their order, and strangers shall eat the deserts turned into fruitfulness. For the lambs feeding according to their order, which is taken in the good sense, the Seventy, intending I know not what, translated, those that are plundered shall feed like bulls, understanding bulls in place of lambs, and again interpreting lambs in place of strangers. But when the Lord has been exalted in judgment, and the holy one sanctified in his righteousness, so that the wicked husbandmen perish wickedly and the lofty cedar is cut down by the axe of the Lord, then those who are of the number of the lambs, not of the goats, will feed in the meadows of the Church and will say: The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing (Ps 22 [23]:1); and what the Jews have deserted, turned into fruitfulness, the people of the nations will eat. This is according to tropology. […]

5:18.t: Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as with the rope of a cart. Who say: Let his work make haste and come quickly, that we may see it; and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near and come, and we know it. For the rope of a cart the Seventy translated the strap of the yoke of a heifer, or of a cow. That sins are called bonds we read quite often; among them is this: Each one is bound fast with the cords of his own sins (Prov 5:22). And the Lord, rebuking the offending people, which had joined sins to sins, made a scourge of cords, showing them how they had made the house of God a den of robbers (John 2), and had turned the seat of prayer into a house of trade (Matt 21). The guest too at the Lord's supper, not having a wedding garment, is bound hand and foot and cast into the outer darkness (Matt 22). And the Lord came to say to those who were in bonds, Come out (Isa 49:9); and to those who were in darkness, Be revealed (Ps 145 [146]:8). […]

For indeed every man twists for himself a rope by his sins: "Woe to them who draw sins as a long rope?" Who makes a long rope? He who adds sin to sin. How are sins added to sins? When the sins which have been committed are covered over by other sins. One has committed a theft: that he may not be found out to have committed it, he seeks the astrologer. It were enough to have committed theft: why wilt thou add sin to sin? Behold two sins committed. When thou art forbidden to go to the astrologer, thou revilest the bishop: behold three sins. When thou hearest it said of thee, Cast him forth from the Church; thou sayest, I will betake me to the party of Donatus: behold thou addest a fourth sin. The rope is growing; be thou afraid of the rope. It is good for thee to be corrected here, when thou art scourged with it; that it may not be said of thee at the last, "Bind ye his hands and feet, and cast him forth into outer darkness." For, "With the cords of his own sins is every one bound." […]

But those “proud ones have hidden a trap for me;” they have sought to trip up my steps. And what have they done? “And have stretched out cords as traps.” What cords? The word is well known in holy Scripture, and elsewhere we find what “cords” signify. For “each one is holden with the cords of his sins,” saith Scripture. And Esaias saith openly, “Woe to them that draw sin like a long rope.” And why is it called a “cord”? Because every sinner who persevereth in his sins, addeth sin to sin; and when he ought by accusing his sins to amend, by defending he doubleth what by confession he might have removed, and often seeketh to fortify himself by other sins, on account of the sins he hath already committed.…

Our Lord shows what reward awaits hypocritical workers when he made a scourge of cords and drove them all out of the temple. They are cast out as sharers of the inheritance of the saints if, after they are chosen to be among the saints, they either perform good acts deceitfully or evil acts openly. He also drives out the sheep and oxen when he shows the life and teaching of such persons deserve condemnation. The cords with which he expelled the wicked persons from the temple by scourging them are the progressive development of [their] evil actions, which provide material to the strict Judge for condemning those who are to be rejected.… The person who heaps sins upon sins, for which he will be condemned more severely, is like one lengthening the cords with which he can be bound and scourged, adding to them little by little.

5:19.t: And the sense is: Woe to you who think that the day of judgment will not be, or that the captivity which the prophetic discourse foretells will not come; who say to the Prophet: How long will you threaten us with the wrath of God? We wish to know it; let it come now. And they say this in irony, because they think it will not come, but is feigned by the Prophet.

5:20.t: For, in like manner, they also who oppose martyrdoms, representing salvation to be destruction, transmute sweet into bitter, as well as light into darkness. Thus, by preferring this very wretched life to that most blessed one, they put bitter for sweet, as well as darkness for light.

Woe to you who call evil good, and good evil, putting darkness for light, and light for darkness, putting bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter. It is a crime of the same kind to call good, light and sweet by contrary names as to call evil, darkness and bitter by the names of virtues. This is against those who do not think it a sin if they disparage the good, and do not judge it an offense if they praise the evil. And the Jews put good as evil, and light as darkness, and sweet as bitter, when they took up Barabbas, the author of robbery and sedition, and crucified Jesus, who had come only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, to save what had perished. In Barabbas let us understand the devil, who, though he is night and darkness, transforms himself into an Angel of light (Matt 27). Hence the Apostle too says: What participation has righteousness with iniquity? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? (2 Cor 6:14, 15). […]

Hence it is said in Isaiah: Woe to those who call sweet bitter, and bitter sweet. This is said by those who in judging consider not the cases but the persons, and turn the fruit of Christ's righteousness, which is most sweet, into bitterness. Whoever, therefore, in judging is led either by kinship or by friendship, or, on the other hand, by hostile hatred or by enmities, perverts the judgment of Christ, who is righteousness, and turns his fruit into bitterness.

"Woe unto them that call evil good." For this text is to be understood to refer not to humans but to those things that make humans evil, and the prophet's accusation is rightly applied to one who calls adultery good. But if someone should call another good whom he believes chaste, not knowing that he is an adulterer, he is deceived not in his understanding of good and evil but through the secrets of human conduct. He is calling a person good whom he believes to possess that which indubitably is good. The adulterer he would call evil, the chaste person good, and he calls the person in question good simply through not knowing that he is an adulterer and not chaste.

Since this is true, what are we to do? Must we accede to the will of wicked men? Or if they wish even empty praise conferred on them, is it fitting to proffer silly and meaningless eulogies? Surely we must consider that, as men of honor should not mock even those who wish to make themselves ridiculous, so they should not laud in lying phrases those who yearn to be adorned by praise, however false. We must not take into account the preferences of individuals, but rather what is fitting for us to say, especially since the prophet said: "Woe unto them that put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter."

We must by every means hold fast to the truth, so that what a thing is in fact, it may also be in words, and those that contain sweetness be called sweet, and those that contain bitterness, bitter.
5:20.s: On the Government of God, Book 8, Chapter 1

5:20.t: Opposing adherence to peace, we have the spirit of malice and cruelty, of hatred and anger, and these two lead to complete perversion: the malicious man turns every good into evil, while the angry man turns every evil into good and considers good the actual rendering of evil. Hence they "change darkness into light, and light into darkness." Such as these are unqualified to listen to God's Law.

5:21.t: That the Black One may find no means of entrance, let us flee from every vanity, let us utterly hate the works of the way of wickedness. Do not, by retiring apart, live a solitary life, as if you were already [fully] justified; but coming together in one place, make common inquiry concerning what tends to your general welfare. For the Scripture saith, "Woe to them who are wise to themselves, and prudent in their own sight!"
5:21.s: The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter IV

5:21.t: Who is the greatest subverter of the people of God—he who, relying on the power of free choice, despises the help of the Creator and is satisfied with following his own will, or he who dreads to be judged by the details of the Lord's commandments?

Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes, and prudent in your own sight. You who seem to yourselves, he says, to be wise, who follow the prudence not of God but of men: and though you do not receive the power of God and the wisdom of God, you think yourselves wise (1 Cor 1). Between wisdom and prudence the Stoics say there is this difference: that wisdom is the knowledge of things divine and human, but prudence only of mortal things. And these things are said consistently against the Scribes and Pharisees, who, having the key of knowledge, neither enter in to Christ themselves nor allow others to enter (Luke 11).

Consider as your superiors one another, especially those who are not committed to your charge, your neighbors, because even those whom you see doing certain wicked things—you do not know what good things may lie hidden in them. Therefore let each one strive to be great, but yet in some way not know that he is, lest while he arrogantly attributes greatness to himself, he lose it. For hence it is said through the prophet: "Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes, and prudent before yourselves." Hence Paul says: "Be not wise in your own eyes." Hence against the proud Saul it is said: "When you were little in your own eyes, you were made head among the tribes of Israel." As if it were openly said: When you saw yourself as little, I made you great above others. But because you now see yourself as great, you are esteemed little by me.

5:22.t: Woe to you who are mighty to drink wine, and strong men to mix strong drink, that is, drunkenness. Of those to whom he had said above, Woe to you who rise early in the morning to pursue drunkenness, and to drink until evening, so as to be inflamed with wine, he speaks now too: who are mighty to drink wine, and strong men to mix strong drink (Deut 32). Drunk with the wine of the dragon and the incurable venom of asps, they slandered the power of the Lord. And being drunk themselves, they made the peoples drunk, so that, raving with a like fury, they cried out together against the Lord. According to tropology we have already said before that the priests who are to enter the Tabernacle of God ought not to drink wine and strong drink (Lev 10). To which we now add that it was commanded the Nazirites too, who sanctify themselves to the Lord, that they should neither drink nor eat wine and strong drink and anything that comes from grapes, not even a raisin, nor vinegar made from wine (Num 6). […]

5:23.t: You who justify the wicked for gifts, and take away from the righteous man his righteousness. This too is part of the vices of the vineyard which instead of grapes made wild grapes, and, when the Lord waited for it to do judgment, did iniquity, justifying the wicked for gifts, and considering not the cases but the presents, which blind even the eyes of the wise. Hence we must beware lest we be drunk with wine, in which is luxury (Deut 16:19; Eph 5), and the thighs of our shame be laid bare (Gen 9), and lest we flatter the wicked for gifts and despise the righteousness of the righteous man for his poverty. This is commanded in the Epistle of James as well: that we not become judges of iniquity by honoring the wicked rich and despising the holy poor.

5:24.t: Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours the stubble, and the heat of the flame burns it up, so their root shall be as ashes, and their bud shall go up as dust. For they have cast away the law of the Lord of hosts, and have blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel. For the causes given above, of pride and drunkenness and avarice, because instead of grapes they brought forth thorns, and hay, wood, stubble, and briers that are to burn, therefore the root of their malice will be reduced to ashes, and every flower and beauty of riches and of the body will be compared to dust (1 Cor 3). For they did not only do these things, but by these steps they came to blasphemy, so that they did not receive the law of the Lord and blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel; of which we read above: Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem (Isa 2:3). The root can be taken as evil thoughts, and the fruit and bud as evil works and words, so that what lies hidden in the root is shown in the bud; […]

5:25.t: Therefore the fury of the Lord is angered against his people, and he has stretched out his hand over it and struck it, and the mountains are troubled, and their carcasses have become like dung in the midst of the streets. For all this his fury is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out. Because they cast away the law of the Lord of hosts, which the Lord promises through Jeremiah that he will give, saying: Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will strike a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not according to the pact which I made with your fathers in the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt (Jer 31:31, 32). And they blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel, saying: He has a demon, and is a Samaritan (John 8:48); and: Is not this the son of the carpenter? (Matt 13:55). […]

5:26.t: I Glorify God, even Jesus Christ, who has given you such wisdom. For I have observed that ye are perfected in an immoveable faith, as if ye were nailed to the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, both in the flesh and in the spirit, and are established in love through the blood of Christ, being fully persuaded with respect to our Lord, that He was truly of the seed of David according to the flesh, and the Son of God according to the will and power of God; that He was truly born of a virgin, was baptized by John, in order that all righteousness might be fulfilled by Him; and was truly, under Pontius Pilate and Herod the tetrarch, nailed [to the cross] for us in His flesh. Of this fruit we are by His divinely-blessed passion, that He might set up a standard for all ages, through His resurrection, to all His holy and faithful [followers], whether among Jews or Gentiles, in the one body of His Church.
5:26.s: Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans

5:26.t: And he will lift up a signal among the nations far off, and will whistle to him from the ends of the earth; and behold, he will come swiftly in haste. There shall be none faint nor laboring among them; he shall not slumber nor sleep, nor shall the girdle of his loins be loosed, nor the latchet of his shoe be broken. His arrows are sharp, and all his bows bent; the hoofs of his horses are like flint, and his wheels like the rush of a tempest. His roaring is like a lion's; he shall roar like the lion's whelps, and gnash his teeth, and seize the prey, and embrace it, and there shall be none to rescue it. And he shall resound over it in that day like the sound of the sea: we shall look upon the land, and behold, the darkness of tribulation, and the light is darkened by its gloom. The Hebrews understand this place to be prophesied of the Babylonians and Nebuchadnezzar, that by the will of God he was brought into Judea and Jerusalem and overthrew the temple. […]

6:1.t: So long as "King Uzziah" lived, the prophet Isaiah could not "see the vision". For "Uzziah" was a sinner, "doing what was wicked before the sight of the Lord", and acting against the will of the divine law. "He entered the temple" and the holy of holies, and for this reason he was covered with "leprosy on his forehead", so that, going outside the city, he was reckoned among the unclean. Such a ruler of the soul, therefore, must die, that we may be able "to see the vision" of God; for not in vain is it written: "and it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord". For each one of us "Uzziah" is alive, or Pharaoh, and we do not "groan" while doing the "works" of Egypt. But if he "dies", then we "groan", as it is written in Exodus. If "Uzziah" lives, we do not "see the glory of God"; but if he "dies", then we "see"—as soon as "Uzziah dies"—"the glory of God", provided only that the Word "reign" in us, the Word who said: "but I have been appointed king by him", and that wrath does not "reign". […]

"It came to pass", he says, "in the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and lifted up". The "vision" is recorded; why is the time of the king signified? Give heed to when the "vision" arose: when "King Uzziah died", Isaiah "saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and lifted up". If any of us knows who "Uzziah" was and what he did, he can know what the prophet taught through the Spirit, what the divine word sets forth for us. I will go to the life of "King Uzziah" and inquire from the books of Kingdoms and from the history of Chronicles concerning "Uzziah", and there I see that it is necessary, if it is to come to pass that "I should see the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and lifted up", that "King Uzziah" must "die" for me. […]

[Passages quoted, Isa. vi. i; 8-10.]

THIS, too, is fulfilled in our Saviour, according to John, when he says:

"37. But though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him: 38. That the saying of Esaias the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spake, Lord, who hath believed our report? and to whom hath the arm of the Lord been revealed?" 39. Therefore they could not believe, because that Esaias said again, 40. He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them. 41. These things said Esaias, when he saw his glory, and spake of him."

Or according to Matthew:

"10. And the disciples came and said to him, Why speaketh thou unto them in parables? 11. He answered and said unto them, Because it is given unto you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given ... 13. […]

He was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him," and adding after this, "and the Word became flesh, and tabernacled among us"; so in the same strain the inspired prophet, about to proclaim God born of a Virgin, tells first the vision of His Divine glory, when he thus describes the Being of God:

6:1.t: If grace is greater and understanding clearer in the New Testament than in the Old, why did the prophet Isaiah see the Lord of hosts, who is Christ, seated on the throne of majesty, according to the interpretation of John the Evangelist? For he said among other things: “Isaiah said these things when he saw his majesty and spoke of him” (Isaiah 6:1; John 12:41). But in the New Testament Stephen the first martyr says that he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55). What does it mean that here he appears as subject after his victories, and there as Lord before he had conquered? — As the occasion required, so the Lord showed himself. To the prophet he appeared as a king rebuking the people: and he showed himself as what he was, that is, seated. For the reason lay in the peace of his divinity. But the slander of the Jews caused him to appear to Stephen as standing. In Stephen the cause of the Savior was suffering violence. […]
6:1.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 88: WHY CHRIST APPEARED SEATED TO ISAIAH BUT STANDING TO STEPHEN

6:1.t: What would you say of Isaiah or Ezekiel, who was an eyewitness of very great mysteries, and of the other Prophets; for one of these saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting on the Throne of glory, and encircled and praised and hidden by the sixwinged Seraphim, and was himself purged by the live coal, and equipped for his prophetic office. And the other describes the Cherubic Chariot of God, and the Throne upon them, and the Firmament over it, and Him that shewed Himself in the Firmament, and Voices, and Forces, and Deeds. And whether this was an appearance by day, only visible to Saints, or an unerring vision of the night, or an impression on the mind holding converse with the future as if it were the present; or some other ineffable form of prophecy, I cannot say; the God of the Prophets knoweth, and they know who are thus inspired. But neither these of whom I am speaking, nor any of their fellows ever stood before the Council and Essence of God, as it is written, or saw, or proclaimed the Nature of God.

In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up. That Isaiah prophesied under four kings, over Judah and Jerusalem, was shown by the title of the first vision; that is, under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. So when Uzziah was dead, under whom all the things we have expounded above were spoken, his son Jotham succeeded him, who reigned sixteen years, and did what was right in the sight of the Lord, and built the high gate of the temple. While he was ruling, Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, so as to show the bearing of one who reigns.

And the things that were under him filled the Temple, or, as Theodotion and Symmachus translated: And the things that were under his feet filled the Temple. For which the Seventy translated: And the house was full of his glory. […]

The sheer size of the volumes being woven in the explanation of the prophet Isaiah is enough for me, where to pass anything over is a loss to the understanding. Therefore in the individual books, which signify only their number and order, I have set brief little prefaces. And you, Eustochium, virgin of Christ, I beg to help me with your prayers in the exposition of a most difficult vision: in which God almighty is seen in his majesty; and two Seraphim standing round about him and crying: Holy, Holy, Holy, the Lord Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory; and the threshold of the temple moved and shaken, and the Jewish house filled with the darkness of error. And the Prophet, in comparison with the divine glory, saying that he has unclean lips and dwells in the midst of a blaspheming people, who cried out with the concordant voice of impiety: Crucify, crucify such a one; and, We have no king but Caesar (John 19:6 and 15). […]

There is a twofold dimension to the firmament: one concerned with the highest, the other with the lowest; one which makes known the eternal God, the other which reveals God made man. Of these two aspects, Isaiah says, in chapter six, in a vision which was the root of all his other visions: "I saw the Lord seated on a high and lofty throne, with the train of his garment filling the temple." And immediately there follows upon this the blinding of the Jews and the enlightenment of the Gentiles. Wherefore Isaiah says "I saw," that is, through the vision of understanding lifted up by faith and stabilized in the height of eternal wisdom, in which there is a twofold light, inflaming and seraphic.

In the mystery of prophetical revelation, Christ is symbolized through prophetical visions, and this in different ways: for one saw Christ as "a branch of the watching-tree," another saw Him "seated on a high and lofty throne," while yet another saw Him "dressed."

6:2.t: It is impossible to find the beginning of God. The beginning of God's movement you can nowhere grasp—not you, I say, and not anyone else, nor any other of the things that have subsistence. The Savior alone and the Holy Spirit, who have always been with God, see His "face"; and perhaps also the "angels", who "continually see the face of the Father who is in heaven", see also the beginnings of His works. And so too before men "the Seraphim hide their feet"; for the "last things", such as they are, cannot be recounted. "Who has announced concerning the last things?" says the Scripture. The things that we see—granting even that we do see something—are the middle things. What existed before the world we do not know; yet certain things did exist before the world. What is to follow after the world we do not apprehend for certain; yet other things will be after the world. Those things, therefore, that are written—"in the beginning God made heaven and earth. […]

"And the Seraphim stood round about him, six wings to the one, and six wings to the other". I see two "Seraphim", each of them having in itself "six wings". Then the arrangement of the "wings". "And with two wings indeed they covered the face"—not their own, but God's—"and with two wings they covered the feet"—not their own, but God's—"and with two wings they were flying". According to what is written, it seems contradictory: if they "stood", they could not "fly". But it is written: "they stood round about him, six wings to the one and six wings to the other; and with two they covered the face and with two they covered the feet, and with two they were flying; and they cried one to another". Truly these "Seraphim", who are around God, who by knowledge alone say: "Holy, Holy, Holy!", on this account keep the mystery of the Trinity, because they too are holy; for among all the things that are, nothing is holier than these. […]
To sum up my discourse:—Glorify Him with the Cherubim, who unite the Three Holies into One Lord, and so far indicate the Primal Substance as their wings open to the diligent.

Seraphim stood above it; six wings to the one, and six wings to the other: with two they covered his face, and with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew. And they cried one to another, and said: Holy, Holy, Holy, the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory. What we, following the other Translators and the Hebrew truth, in which is written MEMMALLO ממעללו, that is, ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ, which in Latin is said above it, have rendered, the Seventy translated round about him, so that the Seraphim are described as standing not above the Temple but round about the Lord. Again, where we said that one of the Seraphim covered his face and feet, by which is understood God's: in the Hebrew is written PHANAU פניו and REGLAU (רגליו), which can be interpreted both as his and as its own: so that, according to the ambiguity of the Hebrew speech, the Seraphim may be said to cover both the face and feet of God and their own face and feet. […]

Impiously, therefore, a certain one understands the two Seraphim as the Son and the Holy Spirit: since, according to the evangelist John and the apostle Paul, we teach that the Son of God was seen in the majesty of one who reigns, and that the Holy Spirit spoke. Some of the Latins understand the two Seraphim as the old and the new Instrument, which speak only of the present age. Hence they are said to have six wings, and to cover the face and feet of God, and to bring forth in rivalry the testimony of the truth, and in all that they cry to show forth the mysteries of the Trinity. And to marvel together that the Lord Sabaoth, being set in the form of God the Father, took the form of a servant and humbled himself even unto death, and the death of the cross (Phil 2), and that no longer, as before, do heavenly things alone know him, but earthly things also.

And thus also is it in respect of the spiritual natures and orders of celestial beings, and it is faith which maketh it possible to receive every word which is spoken concerning them; for otherwise there must necessarily be unbelief, since the Book calleth them "absolute spiritual beings" [in one place], and in another it speaketh of them as "compacted bodies," to which it attributeth forms which are different from each other. Concerning the Seraphim we are told by the word of the Book [that they have] wings and faces, and concerning the Cherubim [we are told that they have] other forms which are different from each other; which of these statements are we to accept as true? for according to the outward hearing of the word each contradicts the other. The statement that they are spirits we believe, the statement that they are compacted bodies we hold to be true, the statement that their construction consisteth of forms of different kinds we accept; and we receive them all by faith.

"Seraphim were stationed above; each of them had six wings: with two they veiled their faces, with two they veiled their feet, with two they hovered aloft." There are two Seraphim established in us through faith. Our intellect enlightened by faith is made to resemble a Seraph, that is, it is enlightened and inflamed through faith. Faith is both toward the eternal God and toward God made man. Faith toward the eternal God contains one explanation of the six wings: in reference to the distinction of the Persons, there are three articles—concerning the unbegotten Father, the only-begotten Son proceeding from the Father only, and the Holy Spirit breathed by both. These are the three wings on the right side, that is, in eternity. Likewise, on the left there are three wings inasmuch as there is diffusion into the creature out of a single essence, power and operation: the one God is the Creator, the Sanctifier and the Retributor. […]

Just as God completed the whole world in six days and rested on the seventh, so the lesser world may be led in most orderly fashion through six stages of successive illuminations to the repose of contemplation. As a figure of this, one ascended by six steps to the throne of Solomon; the Seraphim that Isaiah saw had six wings; after six days the Lord called Moses from the midst of the cloud, and Christ after six days, as is said in Matthew, led the disciples up the mountain and was transfigured before them.

These six considerations having therefore been traversed, as if they were the six steps of the throne of the true Solomon, by which one arrives at peace, where the true peaceful one rests in a peaceful mind as in an interior Jerusalem; and as if also the six wings of the Cherub, by which the mind of the true contemplative, filled with the illumination of supernal wisdom, may be borne upward; and as if also the first six days, in which the mind must be exercised, so that it may at last arrive at the sabbath of rest; after our mind has contemplated God outside itself through vestiges and in the vestiges, within itself through the image and in the image, above itself through the similitude of the divine light shining upon us and in that light itself, insofar as is possible according to the state of wayfaring and the exercise of our mind; […]

6:3.t: "And they cried out one to another", not "one" to many, but "one to another". For to hear the holiness of God, which is announced by the Savior, according to the dignity of the matter no one can except the Holy Spirit; just as, in turn, to indwell the sanctity of God, which is announced by the Holy Spirit, no one can except the Savior alone. On this account "they cried out one to another and said: Holy, Holy, Holy!" It does not suffice for them to cry 'Holy!' once, nor twice, but they take up the perfect number of the Trinity, that they may manifest the multitude of the holiness of God, which is the repeated commonalty of a threefold holiness; to the holiness of the Father is joined the holiness of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. "For both He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one". He who "sanctifies" is the Savior, according to this—that as a man He receives holiness from God the Father. And so they say: "Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Sabaoth!". […]

We make mention also of the seraphim, whom Isaiah in the Holy Spirit saw standing around the throne of God, and with two of their wings veiling their face, and with two their feet, while with two they flew, crying, "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts." For the reason of our reciting this confession of God, delivered down to us from the seraphim, is this, that so we may be partakers with the hosts of the world above in their hymn of praise.

But when I say God, I mean Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. For Godhead is neither diffused beyond these, so as to bring in a mob of gods; nor yet is it bounded by a smaller compass than these, so as to condemn us for a poverty-stricken conception of Deity; either Judaizing to save the Monarchia, or falling into heathenism by the multitude of our gods. For the evil on either side is the same, though found in contrary directions. This then is the Holy of Holies, which is hidden even from the Seraphim, and is glorified with a thrice repeated Holy, meeting in one ascription of the Title Lord and God, as one of our predecessors has most beautifully and loftily pointed out.

Cherubim and seraphim with unwearied voices praise him and say, "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of hosts." They say it not once, lest you should believe that there is but one; not twice, lest you should exclude the Spirit; they say not holies [in the plural], lest you should imagine that there is plurality, but they repeat three times and say the same word, that even in a hymn you may understand the distinction of persons in the Trinity and the oneness of the Godhead, and while they say this they proclaim God.

And in that they cry one to another, or, according to the Hebrews, this one to that one, that is, one to one, they exhort one another to the praises of the Lord, and say: Holy, Holy, Holy, the Lord of hosts, so as to show the mystery of the Trinity in one Godhead; and to testify that no longer the Temple of the Jews, as before, but the whole earth is full of the glory of him who for our salvation deigned to take a human body and to come down to the earth. Indeed, when Moses too was praying the Lord, after the calf had been worshipped, to spare the sinful people, the Lord answered: I will be propitious to them. But as I live, and as my name lives: for the whole earth shall be filled with my glory (Num 14:20-21). And the seventy-first psalm sings: The whole earth shall be filled with his glory (Ps 71 [72]:19). Hence also the Angels cried to the shepherds: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will (Luke 2:14).
Sabaoth: of armies, or of powers, or of warfares.
6:3.s: On Hebrew Names, On Isaiah the Prophet

6:3.t: "A thousand thousand stand before Him, and ten thousand times ten thousand minister unto Him"; now this concerneth the Seraphim who stand above Him, having their wings spread out to fly, and this one crieth to this, saying, "Holy, Holy, Holy." And concerning the Cherubim it is written that they were yoked unto a chariot, and while their faces looked downwards, the motions of their spiritual natures were directed whither was the Most High. And spiritual beings stand in this service, and the hosts and ranks of heaven are obedient unto the word of Jesus. And concerning the Apostles it is written, "They shall sit upon thrones," and this indicateth to us the greatness of their honour, and their equality with Him in inheritance.
6:3.s: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 9 -- Second Discourse on Poverty

6:3.t: he saw the Lord sitting on a throne high and lifted up, while the Seraphim stood in a circle around him, the one having six wings, and the other six wings, with which they did cover themselves, and the one cried out to the other and said: Holy, holy, holy Lord of Sabaoth! the whole earth is full of his glory.

God again used an expression ambiguously respecting the Trinity, repeating thrice through Isaiah the word Holy which he made applicable to one God, saying: The Lord of hosts, the whole earth is full of His glory; showing both the number of the three Persons and the unity of the Godhead.

For that the “Trisagium” refers not to the Son alone, but to the Holy Trinity, the divine and saintly Athanasius and Basil and Gregory, and all the band of the divinely-inspired Fathers bear witness: because, as a matter of fact, by the threefold holiness the Holy Seraphim suggest to us the three subsistences of the superessential Godhead. But by the one Lordship they denote the one essence and dominion of the supremely-divine Trinity. Gregory the Theologian of a truth says, “Thus, then, the Holy of Holies, which is completely veiled by the Seraphim, and is glorified with three consecrations, meet together in one lordship and one divinity.” This was the most beautiful and sublime philosophy of still another of our predecessors.
6:3.s: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 3, Chapter 10

6:3.t: To be sanctified is to be drawn away from any love that sullies and corrupts and may lead the soul to ruin. In this must the creature resemble the Creator: "You shall be holy," He said, "because I am holy." This holiness makes one God-conformed. That is why the Seraphic spirits cried out: "Holy, holy, holy."

Our intellect enlightened by faith cries out three times: "Holy, holy, holy." There are two Seraphim established in us through faith, and each one makes the triple exclamation, but refers only once to the Lord God. For the understanding of God is the understanding of three Persons with unity of essence. And so the intellect is made to resemble a Seraph, that is, it is enlightened and inflamed through faith, and cries out "Holy" three times. The other Seraph answers "Holy, holy, holy," for as in the eternal God there are trinity of Persons and oneness of essence, so also in God made man there are trinity of natures and unity of Person. And these are the two roots of faith, and a man who ignores them believes nothing: they refer to the body, the soul and the divinity. The holy Christ has a holy body, the holy Christ has a holy soul, the holy Christ has a holy divinity. He is holy without, holy within, and holy above.

This, indeed, is the Monarch who exerts power to the supreme degree, who is supremely wise in discerning the truth, supremely holy in loving the good, and supremely constant in distributing what is just. The Seraphim correspond to supreme holiness, for in them there is holy love, wherefore they cry out, Holy, Holy, Holy; the Cherubim, to wisdom, for in them there is the fullness of understanding; the Thrones, to constancy, for in them there is a high seat, open to receiving.

6:4.t: "And with two they were flying, and they said one to another: Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory. And the lintel was lifted up by the voice with which they cried", by the "voice" of Jesus Christ and the "voice" of the Holy Spirit. If any one of us hears the "voice" of Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit "crying out", the "lintel is lifted up" and becomes higher than at that time when "it was lifted up" and when it was said: "lift up the gates, your princes, and be lifted up, everlasting gates, and the king of glory shall enter in". "And the house was filled with smoke". From the remission of the fire the whole "house was filled". And "smoke" is the vapor of fire.

When therefore I have done all these things, "the lintel was lifted up by the voice with which they cried out". It is a blessed thing, then, for each one of us so to labor that he may become a partaker of the door and of the "lintel" of the door, which is according to the understanding of Christ God. For it is not, I think, unseemly to say that the flesh is called the door and the Word the "lintel". "The lintel was lifted up by the voice with which they cried out, and the house was filled with smoke", with that good "smoke" from the "glory" of God.

And the lintels of the hinges were moved at the voice of him who cried, and the house was filled with smoke. When the Seraphim cried and proclaimed the mystery of the Trinity in all the earth, when the whole earth came to know the passion of the Lord and Savior, at once the threshold of the Temple was moved, or taken away, and all its hinges fell down, the Savior's threat being fulfilled, when he said: Your house shall be left to you desolate (Matt 23:38). And how beautiful is the order of the words! After the earth was filled with the glory of the Lord Sabaoth, the Temple of the Jews was filled with the darkness of ignorance, and with gloom, and with smoke, which is harmful to the eyes. Or certainly by the smoke of the Temple a burning is signified. For first the Gospel of the Savior was preached in the whole world, and forty-two years after the Lord's passion Jerusalem was taken and the Temple burned. […]

6:5.t: "And I said: O wretched me, for I am pricked with compunction!". Before you "see the vision", do you not confess yourself to be "wretched", O Isaiah? He does not say: so long as "Uzziah" lived did it never come into my mind that I was "wretched"; for I begin to know that I am "wretched" when I "see the vision", when "Uzziah the leprous king" is "dying" for me, and I say: "O wretched me!"? Now I too begin to confess to the Lord and to say of my very self: "O wretched me!", as Isaiah says: "O wretched me!". And close to this the Apostle too says: "wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?". It is a blessed thing, then, that I should confess myself "wretched". If I humble myself and, repenting, weep over my sins, God will hear me and give me a deliverer, and I say: "thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!". In truth let us say from the heart: "wretched me". […]

"And I said: O wretched me, for I am pierced with remorse, since, although I am a man and have unclean lips". I cannot suppose that Isaiah humbled himself; rather, the Scripture says and gives testimony that his "lips are cleansed" by "one of the Seraphim", who "was sent" to "take away his sins". And "one" of the "Seraphim" is my Lord Jesus Christ, who was sent by the Father to "take away" our "sins", and he says: "behold, I have taken away your iniquities and have cleansed away your sins". And do not think it an affront to his nature, if the Son is sent by the Father. Indeed, that you may recognize the unity of the deity in the Trinity, Christ alone in the present reading now forgives "sins", and yet it is certain that "sins" are forgiven by the Trinity. For he who has believed in one, believes in all. Let there be brought to me, then, from the heavenly altar the "tongs", that it may touch my lips. If the "tongs" of the Lord touch "my lips", it "cleanses" them. […]

"And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth". Why should we not set forth in the present a certain tradition of the Jews, plausible indeed yet not true, and why should we not find its solution? They say that Isaiah was for this reason sawn asunder by the people, as one transgressing the law and proclaiming things beyond the Scriptures. For the Scripture says: "no one shall see my face and live", but this man says: "I saw the Lord of Sabaoth". Moses, they say, did not "see", and you have "seen"? And for this reason they sawed him and condemned him as impious; for they did not know that "with two wings the Seraphim covered the face of God". "I saw the Lord". If Isaiah "saw the face", Moses also "saw". Moses "saw the back parts", as it is written; nevertheless he "saw the Lord", even though he did not "see" his "face". And so this man too "saw", although he did not "see" the "face". Wrongly, therefore, did they condemn the prophet. "And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth; […]

"And it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died, that I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up; and the house was full of his glory. And the Seraphim stood round about him, six wings to the one and six wings to the other; and with two they veiled his face, and with two they veiled his feet, and with two they flew. And they cried one to another and said: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory", and the rest. But in order that we too may see the "vision" which Isaiah "saw", let us call upon Jesus, who has bestowed eyes upon those who do not see. For even now he can come and bring it about that we may behold with opened eyes the things that have been spoken in the reading of the sacrament; let us promise him that from now on we will no longer make "the body of Christ the body of a harlot", nor do works worthy of mourning. Let each one of us speak these things in his heart to God, and let us pray that his coming may take place even now; […]

JACOB IS CALLED “THE MAN WHO SEES GOD,” AND MOSES SAW GOD FACE TO FACE; LIKEWISE ISAIAH SAYS, “I HAVE SEEN THE LORD OF HOSTS WITH MY EYES.” BUT ON THE OTHER HAND JOHN THE EVANGELIST SAYS, “NO ONE HAS EVER SEEN GOD” (Gen. 32:28; Exod. 33:11; Isa. 6:5; 1 John 4:12); THIS, AS FAR AS IT APPEARS, IS CONTRADICTORY. — As far as true faith is concerned, absolutely no one has ever seen God, neither the Father nor the Son. For what is called “seeing” refers to understanding; for sight is as in an image. Just as when we do not know emperors personally, we see them in likeness, not in reality; so too God was seen so that it might be understood that the one who appeared was God, by reason, not by substance; because in His own nature God cannot be seen. And to reveal more truly the hidden things of the question set before us, let us strive to explain the Evangelist’s meaning. […]
6:5.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 71: ON WHETHER GOD CAN BE SEEN

6:5.t: According to the Hebrew, Isaiah cries out in anguish and says, "Woe is me because I have held my peace, because I am a man of unclean lips and I dwell in the midst of a people that has unclean lips, and I have seen with my eyes the Lord of hosts!" Because of his virtues, he deserved to enjoy the sight of God, and, because of his awareness of his sins, he confessed that his lips were unclean. Not because he had said anything that was contrary to the will of God, but because he had held his peace, deterred either by fear or modesty, and because he had not exercised the prerogative of a prophet, of condemning a sinful nation. When we, who flatter the rich and accept sinful persons, rebuke sinners, is it for the sake of base gain? Unless, perhaps, we speak with complete frankness to those whose wealth we stand in need of. We may act otherwise; we may refrain from every type of sin, but, if we keep silent about the truth, we are certainly committing a sin.

And I said: Woe is me, because I was silent, because I am a man polluted in lips, and I shall dwell in the midst of a people having polluted lips, and I have seen with my eyes the king, the Lord of hosts. Abraham too, after he saw the Lord and heard his voice, says that he is earth and ashes (Gen 18); and Isaiah, according to the Seventy Translators, testifies that he is pierced with compunction, not for other crimes, but because he had unclean lips. Happy the conscience that has sinned only in speech, and that not by its own fault, but by fellowship with a people having polluted lips, with whom he was very often compelled to speak. From this it is shown that it is harmful to live with sinners: For he who touches pitch shall be defiled by it (Sir 13:1). But since in the Hebrew we read: Woe is me, because I was silent, the Prophet bewails himself because he was not worthy to praise the Lord Sabaoth with the Seraphim, whom we understand as the Angelic powers. […]

Let us give another example too. Isaiah, when he had seen the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, what does he say? 'Woe is me, wretched that I am, for I am pricked with compunction, because I have unclean lips, and I sit in the midst of a people that has unclean lips.' See what he says, Woe is me, wretched, because I have unclean lips. And afterward what does he say? Because he had unclean lips, therefore one of the seraphim is sent, and takes a coal of fire from the altar, and touches his lips and his tongue, and purges it. And what does he say? 'Behold, this has touched your lips, and has cleansed your tongue.' And at once what does he say? 'Whom shall I send to this people, and who shall go?' O the mysteries of the Scriptures! As long as he had a deceitful tongue and unclean lips, it is not said to him, Whom shall I send, and who shall go? His lips are cleansed, and at once he is sent to speak. So then he who has unclean lips cannot prophesy, cannot be sent into the service of God.

And therefore with daily sighs all the saints grieve over this weakness of their nature and while they search into their shifting thoughts and the secrets and inmost recesses of their conscience, cry out in entreaty: "Enter not into judgment with Thy servant, for in Thy sight shall no man living be justified;" and this: "Who will boast that he hath a chaste heart? or who will have confidence that he is pure from sin?" and again: "There is not a righteous man upon earth that doeth good and sinneth not;" and this also: "Who knoweth his faults?" And so they have recognized that man's righteousness is weak and imperfect and always needs God's mercy, so that one of those whose iniquities and sinsGod purged away with the live coal of His word sent from the altar, after that marvellous vision of God, after his view of the Seraphim on high and the revelation of heavenly mysteries, said: "Woe is me! for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips." […]
6:5.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Theonas, Chapter 17

6:5.t: Purity of heart and simplicity, Peter, is of great force with almighty God, who is in purity most singular, and of nature most simple. For those servants of his, which do retire themselves from worldly affairs, avoid idle words, labour not to lose their devotion, nor to defile their soul with talking, do especially obtain to be heard of him, to whom, after a certain manner, and as they may, they be like in purity and simplicity of heart. But we that live in the world, and speak oftentimes idle words, and that which is worse, sometime those that be hurtful: our words and prayers are so much the farther off from God, as they be near unto the world: for we are drawn too much down towards the earth, by continual talking of secular business: which thing the prophet Esaye did very well reprehend in himself, after he had beheld the King and Lord of armies, and was penitent, crying out: Woe be to me for being silent, because I am a man that have defiled lips: and he sheweth straight after the reason why his lips were […]

6:6.t: "And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth". If ever we have thought about God while we are still sinners, we too say what the prophet now says: "and one of the Seraphim was sent to me". How good is God! Because, He says, I hear Isaiah confessing—for he said: "O wretched me!"—because I hear him repenting—for he says: "I am pricked with compunction"—because he has declared his own offenses, saying: "since I am a man and have unclean lips, I dwell also in the midst of a people having unclean lips", I too, "while he is yet speaking, say: behold, I am present". "And one of the Seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he had a coal". A "coal" is brought to the prophet, that through the burning of fire his "lips" might be purged, which had at some time sinned. Who is this "one of the Seraphim"? My Lord Jesus Christ: He, according to the dispensation of the flesh, was sent, having in His hand a "coal" and saying: "I came to send fire upon the earth, and would that it were already kindled!" […]

And one of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand a pebble, which he had taken from the altar with tongs, and he touched my mouth, and said: Behold, I have touched your lips with this, and your iniquity shall be taken away, and your sin shall be cleansed. One of the Seraphim, which is interpreted kindling, flew, or was sent, to cleanse the Prophet's unclean lips, and to purge them with the live coal, or pebble, which he had taken from the altar. Many, however, think that there are two Seraphim, because one cried to another, although among many too individuals can cry to individuals; and the edition of the Seventy rather signifies very many, who translated, Seraphim stood round about him. For if it were said of two, they would have said not round about, but on either side. And this fits the multitude of Angels, which is made ready for the ministry of God. And they are called Seraphim in the plural number, and Seraph in the singular: just as Cherubim and Cherub. […]

And the Lord put forth his hand and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me: Behold, I have given my words in your mouth. It is to be noted that here the hand of God is put forth to touch the mouth of the prophet, and it is said to him: behold, I have given my words in your mouth, whereas in Isaiah it is written: and one of the seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he had a coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar, and he touched my mouth and said: behold, this has touched your lips, and it will take away your iniquities and cleanse your sins. For there, because he was of firm and mature age, and he himself simply confesses that he has unclean lips and dwells in the midst of a people having unclean lips, one of the seraphim is sent, to touch his mouth not with a hand but with tongs and a coal, and to take away his iniquities and cleanse his sins. […]

And further the prophet Isaiah also said, that "He saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high, and lifted up: and around Him stood the Seraphim, praising Him. Then said He to himself, Alas for me a sinner, for I repent me: in that being a man, and of unclean lips, I dwell among a people of unclean lips, and have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth." But to this he adds, that " one of the Seraphim was sent unto me, and in his hand he had a live coal, which he had taken with the tongs from the altar, and he touched with it my mouth, and said, Lo! this has touched your lips, and it shall take away your sins, and cleanse you of your iniquities." What interpretation then are we to put upon the coal which touched the prophet's lips, and cleansed him from all sin? Plainly it is the message of salvation, and the confession of faith in Christ, which whosoever receives with his mouth is forthwith and altogether purified. And of this Paul thus assures us; […]
6:6.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

6:6.t: But Dionysius the Areopagite, that ancient and venerable Father, is said to declare that from the lesser hosts of angels some are sent forth to fulfill their ministry either visibly or invisibly, namely because angels or archangels come for human consolation. For those higher hosts never withdraw from the inner places, since those who are preeminent have no function of external ministry. This seems to be contradicted by what Isaiah says: "And one of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar, and he touched my mouth." But in this statement of the prophet, he wants it understood that the spirits who are sent receive the name of those whose office they perform. For the angel who carries a coal from the altar to burn up the sins of speech is called a Seraphim, which means burning. […]

Wherefore with all fear and a pure conscience and certain faith let us draw near and it will assuredly be to us as we believe, doubting nothing. Let us pay homage to it in all purity both of soul and body: for it is twofold. Let us draw near to it with an ardent desire, and with our hands held in the form of the cross let us receive the body of the Crucified One: and let us apply our eyes and lips and brows and partake of the divine coal, in order that the fire of the longing, that is in us, with the additional heat derived from the coal may utterly consume our sins and illumine our hearts, and that we may be inflamed and deified by the participation in the divine fire. Isaiah saw the coal. But coal is not plain wood but wood united with fire: in like manner also the bread of the communion is not plain bread but bread united with divinity. […]
6:6.s: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 4, Chapter 13

6:7.t: We read also in Isaiah that the prophet is purged by fire through "one of the seraphim, which was sent to him, when it took with tongs one coal from those which were upon the altar, and touched the lips of the prophet and said": "behold, I have taken away your iniquities". To me these things seem to be mystical and to indicate this, that to each one, according to that in which he sins, if he is worthy to be purified, coals are applied to his members. For since the prophet here says: "I have unclean lips, and I dwell also in the midst of a people having unclean lips", therefore the "coal taken up with the tongs" by the seraph purges his lips, in which alone he professes himself not to be clean. From which it is shown that only as far as the word was his sin found, but that in deed or work he had sinned in nothing; […]

Let the reproving word, therefore, touch the "lips" of our mind and soul, that we too may say: "and it touched my mouth". If I shall have cleansed "my mouth", so that I speak nothing idle, nothing foolish, nothing base, nothing scurrilous—to name them all at once—nothing of those things that are forbidden, then I can say: "it touched my mouth". But so long as I "have unclean lips" and carry on unclean affairs, because of the words of sin "the fire from the altar does not touch me", nor "is one of the Seraphim sent to me".

"And He said: behold, this has touched your lips, and it has taken away your iniquities, and has purged your sins round about". Let the divine word bite us, let it burn up our souls, and let us say as we hear: "was not our heart burning within us?", that "our iniquities and sins may be taken away", and that, made clean, with clean mouth and clean heart and a whole clean conscience, we may give thanks to almighty God in Christ Jesus, "to whom is glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen!"

Tell me, then, whoever you are who deny the divinity of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit could not be liable to sin, who rather forgives sin. Does an angel forgive? Does an archangel? Certainly not, but the Father alone, the Son alone and the Holy Spirit alone [can forgive sins]. Now one is obviously able to avoid that which he has power to forgive.But perhaps someone will say that the seraph said to Isaiah, "Behold, this has touched your lips and shall take away your iniquities and purge away your sins." Shall take away, he says, and shall purge, not I will take away, but that fire from the altar of God, that is, the grace of the Spirit. For what else can we piously understand to be on the altar of God but the grace of the Spirit? Certainly not the wood of the forests or the soot and coals. […]

But Dionysius the Areopagite, that ancient and venerable Father, is said to declare that from the lesser hosts of angels some are sent forth to fulfill their ministry either visibly or invisibly, namely because angels or archangels come for human consolation. For those higher hosts never withdraw from the inner places, since those who are preeminent have no function of external ministry. This seems to be contradicted by what Isaiah says: "And one of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar, and he touched my mouth." But in this statement of the prophet, he wants it understood that the spirits who are sent receive the name of those whose office they perform. For the angel who carries a coal from the altar to burn up the sins of speech is called a Seraphim, which means burning.

6:8.t: Isaiah, "seeing the Lord of Sabaoth seated upon a lofty and lifted-up throne", and "seeing" also "the Seraphim standing about him", and receiving the remission of sins through that fire which, brought "from the altar", "cleansed" his "lips" by its touch, says that "he heard the voice of the Lord" — not commanding, but rousing and "saying": "whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?" Then he says that "he answered" the Lord: "behold, it is I, send me". But when I take my place here and search into what is written, I find that Moses did one thing and Isaiah another. For Moses, chosen for the leading-out of the people from the land of Egypt, says: "provide another whom you may send", and he seems to contradict God; but Isaiah, not chosen, but "hearing": "whom shall I send, and who will go?", says: "behold, it is I, send me". […]

"And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? And I said: behold, here I am; send me. And he said: go and say to this people: with hearing you shall hear and you shall not understand" and the rest. Concerning this discourse of the prophet Isaiah which has now been read, let us pray to God that he may grant us grace and that we may be able to expound things worthy of the prophetic spirit. "And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: whom shall I send?" After the prophet's "lips" had been cleansed, being prepared he took up the ministry of God and says: "behold, here I am, send me". But that he might be the more prepared for this, he remembered the voice of Moses. For Moses too, using the same words: "send me", was made "ruler of the people" and judge and was called "the servant of God".

And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? And I said: Here am I, send me. In place of what both we and all the other translators rendered for us, which in Hebrew is said LANU (לנו), the Seventy, wishing I know not what, set down to this people, which is not found in the Hebrew at all. Now when for us is said in the person of God, it is to be taken in the sense in which we also read in Genesis: Let us make man to our image and likeness (Gen 1:26), so as to indicate the mystery of the Trinity. For just as we read in the Gospel, where the Lord says: I and the Father are one (John 10:30); and one we refer to the nature, are to the distinction of persons: so, when the Lord commands, the Trinity gives the order. And the Lord does not say whom he orders to go, but sets the choice before those who hear, so that the will may obtain the reward. […]

6:9.t: But let us look also at those things which the Lord commanded to be "said to the people": "go, and say to the people: with the ear you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will perceive and not see. For the heart of this people has been thickened, and with their ears they have heard heavily and have closed their eyes, lest at any time they see with their eyes and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart and turn back, and I heal them". Knowing that the hearing of words is twofold and recognizing a double constitution — that is, one of them bodily, the other spiritual — he says to "the people", prophesying about those things which were to be at the coming of Christ, that there would be a time when "they would hear and not understand" them, seeing that, when "they heard" my Lord Jesus Christ, they "heard" only the voice of the sayings, not the sense. And this is manifest from the fact that "he spoke in parables" "outside" to "the people", but "to the disciples in secret he unfolded" them. […]
