Properly, however, Neser means sucker, which grows at the roots of trees and, torn off by farmers, is thrown away as useless; hence we too translated useless stock. […]

Like a putrid corpse, you will not have fellowship with them even in burial. For you have destroyed your land, you have slain your people. LXX: As a garment mixed with blood will not be clean, so neither will you be clean, because you have destroyed my land and have slain my people. Since the Hebrew and the edition of the Seventy differ greatly from each other, let us discuss each separately. Like a putrid corpse, or, as Aquila translated, trampled, you will not have fellowship of burial, not even with those whom you slew. For you are the teacher, they were the disciples: and from him to whom more has been entrusted, more is required. For you have destroyed your land, you have killed your people, namely those who were entrusted to you to govern. Hence he dares to say to the Savior: All these have been delivered to me, and I will give them to you, if you will fall down and worship me (Matt 4:9). […]

14:20.t: For you have destroyed your own land, you have slain your own people. According to the Seventy interpreters, who said: Because you have destroyed my land, and slain my people, there is no doubt what they mean. For Nebuchadnezzar slew and destroyed the land of Judea and its people Israel. According to the Hebrew the understanding is difficult: how he destroyed his own land and slew his own people; unless perhaps it is to be taken in this sense: those whom God had given you for chastening, you have utterly destroyed. Or otherwise: the ancient kingdom of the Assyrians, through your great pride and your lifting up your neck against God, has been utterly destroyed. For had you behaved humbly and known your own measure, the Assyrian and the Babylonian would be reigning to this day. Or in this way: you were so cruel toward foreigners that in your fury you oppressed even the peoples subject to you.

The seed of the most wicked will not be named forever. Prepare his sons for slaughter in the iniquity of their fathers: they will not rise up, nor inherit the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities. All the histories agree that, after Belshazzar the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar was slain and Darius succeeded to the kingdom of the Chaldeans, no one of Nebuchadnezzar's stock reigned thereafter. This, then, is what Scripture foretells: that Babylon will come to such devastation that not even of the royal seed will anyone remain, but on account of the father's impiety all his offspring will be wiped out. And for what we translated in the last part of the sentence, nor fill the face of the world with cities, there is written in the Hebrew, for cities, ARIM (ערים), which we can also translate as adversaries; so that the sense is: no one of your seed will be raised up as an adversary who desires to restore the kingdom. […]

Seed of the most wicked, prepare your sons for slaughter for the iniquities of their fathers: they will not rise up nor inherit the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities. And I will rise up against them, says the Lord of hosts: and I will destroy the name of Babylon and its remnant, and its offshoot and offspring, says the Lord of hosts. LXX: Most wicked seed, prepare your sons for slaughter for the sin of your father: that they may not rise up and possess the land, and fill the land with cities. And I will rise up against them, says the Lord Sabaoth: and I will destroy their name and remnant and seed. For most wicked seed, which the Seventy translated, in the Hebrew is written ZERA MRIM (זרע מרעים), which the others translated seed of the most wicked. Not that the seed itself is evil of itself: for God made all things good (Gen 1); but that from those who are most wicked by their own will an evil seed has sprung, which comes about by will, not by nature. […]

14:21.t: And since the victory of men is not perfect: For unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it will keep watch in vain (Ps 126 [127]:1): therefore the Lord himself will rise up against the sons of the most wicked, and will destroy out of confusion their name and remnant, and every offshoot and offspring, so that they may no longer sprout in the cities of the Lord. We read in the Gospel (John 8) that the devil is a liar from the beginning, and his father, that is, of the lie; which many not understanding wish the father of the devil to be the dragon who reigns in the sea, whom the Hebrews call Leviathan. And they think this suits the present passage according to the Seventy translators, who said: for the sins of your father: whereas in the Hebrew ABOTHAM (אבתם) plainly signifies not of your father but of their fathers.

14:22.t: And I will rise up against them, says the Lord of hosts: and I will destroy the name of Babylon, and the remnant, and the offshoot, and the progeny, says the Lord. And I will make it a possession of the hedgehog, and pools of water: and I will sweep it with a broom, grinding it away, says the Lord of hosts. That Babylon was most mighty, and that, set foursquare on the plains, it extended sixteen thousand paces from corner to corner of the wall, that is, sixty-four thousand in all around its circuit, is reported by Herodotus and many others who have written Greek histories. And its citadel, that is, the Capitol of that city, is the tower which was built after the flood, and is said to reach four thousand paces in height, narrowing little by little from broad to narrow, so that the overhanging weight may be borne more easily by the broader parts. They describe marble temples there, golden statues, streets gleaming with stones and gold, and many other things that seem almost incredible. […]

14:23.t: And I will make it a possession of the hedgehog, and pools of waters: and I will sweep it with a broom, grinding it, says the Lord of hosts. LXX: And I will make Babylonia desert, says the Lord, so that hedgehogs dwell in it, and it will come to nothing. And I will make it a gulf of mud, for destruction. When the Lord of hosts has destroyed the name of Babylon, and its remnant, and its offshoot, and all its offspring, he will not be content with its destruction unless he gives it as a possession to the hedgehog, and as pools of waters, and sweeps it, not lightly and casually, but grinding, so that nothing of its old filth remains in it. In the Acts of the Apostles it is written (Acts 10 and 11) that in that linen vessel which, let down by four corners, hung from heaven, all kinds of four-footed beasts and creeping things and birds were contained; which the Apostle afterward explaining says: God has shown me that I should call no man unclean. […]

14:24.t: The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: If it is not so, that as I have thought, so it will be, and as I have pondered in my mind, so it will come to pass, that I will crush the Assyrian in my land, and tread him down upon my mountains: and his yoke will be taken from them, and his burden will be removed from their shoulder. He returns to the present, that is, to Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, who laid waste Samaria and Judea and, Jerusalem excepted, destroyed everything round about; and he joins things near at hand to things that are to come long afterward, so that the fear hanging over them may be removed: because those who heard could say: We are enduring a siege now, and this man promises things that will come many ages later. […]

The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: Surely as I have thought, so shall it be, and as I have purposed in my mind, so shall it come to pass: that I will crush the Assyrian in my land, and on my mountains I will trample him. And his yoke will be taken from them, and his burden will be removed from their shoulder. After the hedgehog has dwelt in deserted Babylon, and in place of well-watered and fertile fields pools have covered everything, so that nothing of the former seed and abundance remains in Babylon, the oath of the Lord will be fulfilled, and what he purposed in his mind will come to pass: that the Assyrian is crushed in his land and trampled on his mountains. For the reckless enemy hastens to seize not only the land of God and all its lower places, but also those who in the service of God have so advanced in virtues that they are compared to mountains, and it is said of them: Its foundations are on the holy mountains (Ps 86 [87]:1). And note the propriety. In the land he is crushed; […]

14:26.t: This is the counsel which he has purposed upon the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out upon all the nations. For the Lord of hosts has decreed, and who will be able to weaken it? And his hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back? For the whole earth the Seventy translated the whole world, at the end of the burden, or vision, against Babylon. What lay hidden is opened: that God purposed his counsel upon the whole earth, that is, the whole world, and not only against the land of the Chaldeans and the Assyrian and Chaldean king; and that his hand is stretched out, or raised, upon all the nations, and not upon the one Babylonian nation. From this it is shown that all the things which have been said pertain not specifically to one province, but generally to the whole world.

This is the counsel that I have devised upon the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out upon all the nations. For the Lord of hosts has decreed, and who will be able to weaken it? And his hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back? In this place some think that the prophecy is general, against the whole world, and that the devastation of Babylon and of the Assyrian city is a type of the consummation of the world. We by no means contradict them, so long as we know that here the whole land of the Assyrians is properly signified, and that all the nations allied with the Assyrian king are pointed out. Whatever has been decreed by the Lord is prevented by no one's power. And his hand, stretched out and ready to strike, no one will be able to hold back.

14:27.t: They were ready to expose him [Joseph] to death, or to sorrow, or to slavery—to the uttermost ills. But the overruling God used the wickedness of the conspirators for the trial and approval of him who was sold and betrayed. In order that this result may not be thought to arise from any casual coincidence or accidental revolution of things, God, by means of the very men who opposed it, brought to pass the very result which they opposed, using His enemies for the approval of His servants, in order that you may learn, that what God has willed no one will hinder, and that none will turn aside His high hand; in order that whenever you are plotted against, you may not stumble or be downcast, but be enabled to know that the plot will result in good in the end, if only you bear your lot well.
14:27.s: Discourse 4 on Lazarus and the Rich Man

14:27.t: They did not realize that if human hands had put an end to those things, then human hands could get them back for them. But it was God who destroyed their city, and no human power could ever change what God had decreed. "For what God, the Holy One, has planned who shall dissipate? His hand is stretched out; who will turn it back?" What God has reared up and wishes to remain, no man can tear down. In the same way, what he has destroyed and wishes to stay destroyed, no man can rebuild.

And what is said: Who will be able to weaken it, and who will turn it back? we ought to take not as of something difficult, as that is read: Who is wise, and will understand these things (Ps 106 [107]:43)? And: Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward (Luke 12:42)? and other things like these; but as of something impossible. For no one will be able to weaken the counsel of the Lord, and to turn back his hand, stretched out or lifted on high, from striking.

14:28.t: In the year in which King Ahaz died, this burden came. We read that four kings of Judea are placed at the head of the Prophet's title: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, each succeeding the other in order and by descent; of whom we read above that Uzziah had died, as Isaiah relates: In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up. From this we understand that both the Vision of the Lord seated and the things enjoined upon the Prophet, up to the place where it is written (Isa 6): Like a terebinth and like an oak that spreads out its branches: the holy seed will be its shoot, were prophesied under King Jotham (ibid., 7). The third to succeed is Ahaz, son of Jotham, son of Uzziah king of Judah, under whom Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to make war against it, and the rest that Scripture records. […]

In the year in which King Ahaz died, this burden came. Do not rejoice, all you Philistia, because the rod of him who struck you has been broken. For out of the root of the serpent will come forth a basilisk, and its seed swallowing the bird. And the firstborn of the poor will be fed, and the poor will rest confidently, and I will make your root perish with famine, and I will slay your remnant. LXX: In the year in which King Ahaz died this word came: Do not rejoice, all you foreigners, for the yoke of him who struck you has been broken. For out of the seed of the serpent will come forth the offspring of asps, and out of their offspring will come forth winged serpents: and the poor will be fed through him, and poor men will rest in peace. But he will slay your seed with famine, and will kill your remnant. When Ahaz, who is interpreted κατάσχεσις, that is, holding, or possession, whom we read was a most ungodly king, had died, this weight, or word, comes upon the Philistines. […]

14:29.t: Do not rejoice, all you Philistia, because the rod of him who struck you has been broken: for out of the root of the serpent will come forth a regulus, and its seed swallowing the bird. What we say is natural: when the king of a hostile nation dies, his enemies always rejoice, expecting from the new state of things civil wars and seditions and inexperience in ruling. When Ahaz the sinner died, therefore, who had walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and had been joined to them by kinship, we understand that the Philistines, from close by, rejoiced and mocked Israel, because, having lost a king of mature years, they were subject to the young Hezekiah. Now by Philistines, as we said above, he means the Palestinians, whom the common edition writes as foreigners, although this is the term not for one nation but for all foreign nations. Do not, he says, rejoice, O Philistia, do not mock my people because the rod of Ahaz who struck you has been broken; because the staff which used to strike you seems crushed by death; […]

It is commanded, therefore, to the Philistines, whom they now call Palestinians, and whom the Seventy always translate ἀλλόφυλοι, that is, foreigners; and it is said to them that they should not rejoice nor be glad because they have broken the rod, or the yoke, of him who struck them (Heb 12:6). For whom the Lord loves he rebukes, and he chastises every son whom he receives. And God instructs us as sons when he visits our iniquities with a rod and our sins with scourges, so as not to take away his mercy from us (Ps 88 [89]). This is the rod of which it is written in another Psalm: Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me (Ps 22 [23]:4). This is the rod, and this the yoke, which the Savior wishes to lay upon the necks of all, so that, having put off the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, they may bear the yoke of Christ. […]

But because this Leviathan is called in another place not merely a serpent, but also a basilisk, because he rules over unclean spirits, or reprobate men, as Isaiah says, Out of the serpent's root shall come forth a basilisk, we must attentively observe how a basilisk destroys, that by the doings of the basilisk, his malice may be more plainly made known to us. For a basilisk does not destroy with its bite, but consumes with its breath. It often also infects the air with its breath, and withers with the mere blast of its nostrils whatever it has touched, even when placed at a distance.
14:29.s: MORALS ON THE BOOK OF JOB 6:33.62

14:30.t:
And the firstborn of the poor will feed, and the poor will rest in confidence. When the regulus has struck you, and the flying dragon has laid waste your borders, you will by no means lie in wait for Judah, nor terrify my poor little people with your treachery; but, hard pressed by your own straits, you will weep over your calamity. And the humble and the poor, who trusted not in riches and in power but in my name, will rest in secure peace, and will dread the onslaught of no enemy.

And I will make your root perish by famine, and I will slay your remnant. He speaks entirely in figures. And the sense is that, while the people of God rest in confidence, the root of the Philistines is dried up, and all its remnant will be consumed.

But those who have not broken the rod and yoke of him who struck them, but have submitted their neck to the Lord, and are poor in spirit, will be fed, and will say: The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing (Ps 22 [23]:1). And they will hear from the Lord: In most rich pastures I will feed them (Ezek 34; John 10); and they will go in and go out and find pasture. And the poor will be fed through him who strikes them in order to amend them: and they will rest in peace, or, with a careful shepherd, they will live confidently and will rest with Lazarus in the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16). But those who have broken the yoke and rod of him who struck them will suffer perpetual famine, so that they are not nourished by the word of God: but all their remnant will perish, lest anything sprout from the evil seed.

14:31.t: Howl, O gate, cry out, O city, all Philistia is laid low: for smoke will come from the north, and there is none who escapes its column. He says the gate for those who are in the gate, and the city for the inhabitants of the city. And he directs his speech to the cities of the Palestinians, that they should wail and mourn as Sennacherib comes and lays everything waste like a torrent. For under King Hezekiah the Assyrian came, and among the other nations laid waste the Philistines. To them Jeremiah speaks: Behold, waters will rise up from the north, and they will be like an overflowing torrent: and they will cover the land and all that fills it, the city and its inhabitants (Jer 47:2). For from the north came the Assyrian, and those who went forth from its heat, subjugating Nineveh and the other nations. […]

Howl, O gate; cry out, O city: all Philistia is laid low. For smoke comes from the North, and there is none who escapes its column. And what will be answered to the messengers of the nation? That the Lord has founded Zion, and in him the poor of his people will hope. For messengers, that is, Angels, which Symmachus alone translated, all have translated kings, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, because, except for the one letter ALEPH, which is added in the word for Angels, kings and Angels are called by the same name among the Hebrews, that is, MALACHE (Kings מלכי, Angels מלאכי). In the book of Hebrew Names I have found that Philisthiim means falling by the cup. Those, therefore, who have been made drunk with the cup of Babylon and have drunk the wine in which is debauchery, and, among the other vices, have not obtained the kingdom of God because of drunkenness, according to the Apostle (Eph 5), are commanded that their gate should howl and their city cry out. […]

14:32.t: What will be answered to the messengers of the nation? That the Lord has founded Zion, and in her the poor of his people will hope. Because he had said, There is none who escapes its column, Judah too seemed to be included in the general statement. If, he says, the messengers of the Assyrian nation ask why Judah alone has escaped, answer them that the Lord has founded Zion, and has himself protected the humble people by his power. For messengers (מלאכי) the Seventy translated kings (מלכי), misled by an error over a single letter, ALEPH.

And when Philistia has fallen, and its smoke has penetrated all things, so that no one can escape it, what will be said to the Angels who preside over the several nations, who wonder and desire to know why Zion alone, set on a watchtower and on the heights, has escaped the bitterness of this smoke? What, then, will be said to them? Surely what follows: That the Lord has founded it, and he himself is its foundation. And he has founded it upon the foundation of prudence, righteousness, fortitude and temperance, under which names Christ is understood, of whom the Apostle also says: For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, Jesus Christ (1 Cor 3:11). But he who is foolish, and speaks foolish things, and whose heart understands vain things, builds his house upon the sand, which has no foundation. […]

15:1.t: The burden of Moab: because in the night Ar was laid waste, Moab has fallen silent: because in the night the wall was laid waste, Moab has fallen silent. Let it suffice to have spoken once about burden and weight. I give only this brief reminder: that sad things always follow a burden, whereas a vision is followed either by glad things at once, or by glad things at the end after the sad. Moab is a province of the Arabs, in which was Balak son of Beor (Num 22), who hired the soothsayer Balaam from Mesopotamia to curse Israel; where also the people were initiated into Baal-peor (ibid., 25). Its metropolis is the city AR (ער), which today is called Areopolis, a name compounded from the Hebrew and the Greek tongue; not, as many suppose, because it is the city of ἄρεος, that is, of Mars. And Ar also means ἀντίδικος, that is, adversary. How great its power was, Jeremiah testifies (Jer 48:2, 7ff.), saying: There is no more exultation in Moab. And again: You have trusted in your fortifications and in your treasures. […]

The burden of Moab. LXX: The word against the land of Moab. Symmachus and Theodotion: The taking up of Moab. Just as circumcision is both carnal and spiritual, and of the spiritual it is said by the Apostle: For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit, and glory in the Lord, and put no confidence in the flesh (Phil 3:3); and again, to distinguish the spiritual Israel, it is said of the carnal: Behold Israel according to the flesh (1 Cor 10:18): and, You Gentiles in the flesh (Eph 2:11); so Moab is to be taken spiritually, which means from the father, or paternal water, conceived of incest and drunkenness, because he would seem to have been begotten in a manner in the absence, or rather without the knowledge, of the father. […]

Because by night Ar has been laid waste, Moab has fallen silent; because by night the wall has been laid waste, Moab has fallen silent. LXX: By night the land of Moab perished, for by night the wall of the land of Moab perished. For AR (ער), which Theodotion alone set down thus, as it is read in the Hebrew, Aquila and Symmachus translated city, not considering that between the Hebrew letters AIN and RES it does not have the letter JOD, which, if it were there, would rightly be read as city. Worldly wisdom, of which the Lord speaks through the Prophet: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject (Obad 8; 1 Cor 1:19), because it has as its author the mind, which is begotten by God's creating, seems indeed to be born of the father, which is what Moab means; but because it is adulterous and an adversary to the people of God, it is begotten of incest, of a cave and of night. Hence it perished by night, namely in everlasting error. […]

15:2.t:
The house has gone up, and Dibon, to the high places to lament over Nebo, and over Medeba Moab will howl. Do not let it be irksome to you that I walk along the road of the history; for you yourself wished me to do this. Now what is understood is the royal house; and the city of Dibon goes up to the idols set on the heights: over Nebo and over Medeba, noble cities, the whole province will howl. For in Nebo was consecrated the idol Chemosh, which by another name is called Baal-peor.

On all its heads baldness, every beard will be shaved. Among the ancients the shaving of the beard and the head was a sign of mourning. By these things, therefore, the greatness of the grief is shown, as Jeremiah cries out the same things against Moab: Every head baldness, and every beard will be shaved, and on all hands a binding, and on every back haircloth (Jer 48:37).

The house has gone up, and Dimon, to the high places, to lament. LXX: Be sorrowful within yourselves, for Dimon will perish, where the altar is: thither you will go up to weep. The whole house of hostile wisdom, and Dibon, which means their flowing, goes up to the high places in which it had grown proud: not to sacrifice victims, but to lament the things in which it had formerly sinned. And truly falsehood passes like a river, and flows by, and can never stand firm in a stable dwelling. But the word of God, which is compacted, is stable. Hence the manna too, which is seen like ice upon the face of the earth, does not flow away, but stands firm. Moreover, according to the Seventy, the Moabites are commanded to grieve and lament, not over others (for this belongs to the perfect) but over themselves, because their Dibon too, that is, their composed discourse, which flowed like a torrent, is to perish: in which they had, as it were, the altar of their consecration, and all worldly riches. […]

Over Nebo and over Medeba Moab will howl: on all its heads baldness, every beard will be shaved. In its crossroads they are girded with sackcloth: and upon its roofs and in its streets everyone howls: he will go down in weeping. And Heshbon and Elealeh will cry out: their voice has been heard as far as Jahaz: for this the armed men of Moab will howl, his soul will howl to itself. My heart will cry out to Moab: its bars as far as Zoar, a heifer of three years: for by the ascent of Luhith he will go up weeping, and on the way of Horonaim they will raise a cry of crushing: for the waters of Nimrim will be desolate: because the grass has withered, the shoot has failed, all greenness has perished. According to the greatness of the work is also their visitation: they will lead them to the brook of the willows: for the cry has gone round the border of Moab: its howling as far as Eglaim, and its cry as far as the well of Elim: because the waters of Dimon are filled with blood. […]

15:3.t: In its crossroads they are girded with sackcloth; on its roofs and in its streets all howling will go down into weeping. The tears will not be private; public laments will resound for a public grief; neither matrons nor virgins, nor the tender age of children, nor the broken steps of old men will be kept within doors: the extremity of captivity will know neither shame nor weakness.

In their crossroads too, that is, in the byways of errors, while each one according to his own will fashions what he wishes, he is girded with the sackcloth of penance; and upon the roofs and housetops, on which at first they believed themselves to be lofty, and in the streets (because they do not enter by the narrow way that leads to life, but by the broad way that leads to death), there will be howling. And they will by no means go up into pride, but will go down into weeping.

15:4.t:
Heshbon and Elealeh will cry out. These are names of cities of the province of Moab, of which Heshbon was once the city of the king of the Amorites, about which the same Jeremiah says: Fire has gone forth from Heshbon, and flame from the midst of Sihon. Now Heshbon means thought, and so Jeremiah, alluding to the name: Against Heshbon, he says, they have thought evil things (Jer 48:2).

Even to Jahaz their voice has been heard. The city of Jahaz overlooks the Dead Sea, where the border of the province of the Moabites lies. This, then, indicates that the howling of the province will resound to its farthest borders. Hence Jeremiah too says: From the cry of Heshbon, up to Elealeh and Jahaz they have uttered their voice (Jer 48:34).

Over this the lightly armed of Moab will howl, its soul will howl for itself. […]

Then they will understand all their thoughts to be vain, which is the meaning of Heshbon, and the ascent of pride to be empty, which is what Elealeh sounds, so that their voice is heard as far as the evil works which they have done, and the command which they thought was God's, condemning themselves by their own confession. Therefore the bars, that is, those who have been firm in Moab and have understood their error, will howl, and will begin to have hope of progress, when their soul has howled to itself.

15:5.t:
My heart will cry out to Moab. The Prophet speaks with the feeling of one who grieves, either because the enemies too, upon whom so many evils come, are God's creatures, or because they were to be crushed by such great calamities that they become pitiable even to their enemies. Jeremiah says the very same: Therefore my heart will sound for Moab like a flute.

Its bars, as far as Segor, a heifer of three years. And Jeremiah: From Segor, he says, as far as Horonaim, a heifer of three years. Of this city we have spoken in the books of Hebrew Questions as well, and now we note briefly that it is the fifth city after Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which, being small, was preserved at the prayers of Lot. And it is called Bala, that is, swallowed up, the Hebrews relating that it was overthrown by a third earthquake. It is the city which today in the Syrian tongue is called Zoora, in the Hebrew Segor: in both, the little one. We can take the heifer of three years as signifying full age. […]

Hence the Prophet, with the feeling of one who suffers with them, speaks to those whose soul was howling to itself, and says: My heart will cry out to Moab, that I may call them to penance. And their bars and all the supports which they seemed to have in their heresies will come as far as Zoar, that is, as far as the little one: and they will be shown to be not strong but fragile. And this Zoar, that is, small penance, if it perseveres, will lead them to perfect salvation: which is what the heifer of three years signifies, according to what we read in Genesis, where Abraham is commanded to offer a heifer, a ram and a goat of three years, namely a perfect sacrifice, so that he might deserve to be the heir of the Lord (Gen 15). And when they have done penance, they will climb to higher things by Luhith, that is, by the tears of the cheeks. […]

15:6.t:
For the waters of Nimrim will be deserted. This town lies above the Dead Sea, with salt waters, and barren for that very reason. And either he has alluded to the name, or what had not been so before came about after the devastation: that even the waters were turned to bitterness.

For the grass has withered, the shoot has failed, all greenness has perished. It is not, as some think, that all the grass truly dried up because of the barren waters of Nimrim; rather, Scripture is speaking by metaphor. And the sense is: in all Moab there will be the salt and bitter waters of Nimrim; as no grass springs up there, so drought will overtake the whole province, that is, from Segor to Horonaim, from border to border. Jeremiah says the very same: The waters of Nimrim will be very bad (Jer 48:34).

And this will come about because the waters of Nimrim, that is, the doctrine of the heretics, which is compared to leopards and transgressors, will be desolate and will be brought to nothing. They are leopards whose varieties and spots, in Jeremiah, are not changed (Jer 13), and apostates, of whom we read in the Psalms: I have counted all the sinners of the earth transgressors (Ps 118 [119]:119). Every grass too, and shoot, and whatever seemed green in their discourse, has withered.

15:7.t: According to the greatness of the work, so also their visitation: they will lead them to the torrent of the willows. For willows we read in the Hebrew ARABIM (ערבים), which can also be understood as Arabs, and can be read ORBIM (עורבים), that is, a village situated on their borders, whose inhabitants are said by many to have provided food for Elijah on Mount Horeb: a name which, because of its ambiguity, is also translated as ravens, and as the West, and as level places. And the sense is: the visitation will be according to the greatness of the disease. Take visitation here not as a remedy but as a blow. I will visit, he says, their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with stripes (Ps 88 [89]:33). The torrent of the willows understand as the rivers of Babylonia, of which David says: On the willows in the midst of it we hung up our instruments (Ps 136 [137]:2); or else as the valley of Arabia through which one passes to the Assyrians.

And they have been visited by God according to the greatness of their sins, so that him whom they had not perceived through benefits they might come to know through scourges. Accordingly they will be led to the valley or brook of the willows, so that no fruit may remain in them. For they say this is the nature of the seed of these trees: that whoever drinks it in a cup is without children. Hence the saints too, who because of their sins have come to be in the confusion of this world, hang their instruments on the willows of the rivers of the Babylonians (Ps 136 [137]).

15:8.t: For the cry will go round the border of Moab, its howling as far as Eglaim, and its cry as far as the well of Elim. Jeremiah too writes almost all the same things. And these are cities and places of the Moabites, in which the crying and wailing of the captive people is described.

A cry goes round all the borders of the Moabites, either of those who call them to repentance, or of those who lament for their error: so that through their howling they may be able to offer the calves of the lips, and come as far as the fountain of the Lord's rams, or of the strong: because Elim signifies both.

15:9.t:
For the waters of Dibon are filled with blood. Where formerly there was luxuriance because of the watered fields and the ever-flowing springs, there, because of the multitude of the slain, streams of blood will flow.

For I will set additions upon Dibon: for those who flee from Moab, a lion, and for the remnant of the land. Lest anyone think it a fault of the scribe and, in wishing to correct an error, make one, the one city is written both with the letter M and with the letter B: of these, Dimon is interpreted as silence, Dibon as flowing. Both names having been given it because of the waters that flow silently, to this day this little town is called indifferently both Dimon and Dibon. And as for his saying: I will set additions upon Dibon, since it seemed to raise the question what these might be, he showed it in the following line, saying: For those who flee from Moab, a lion, and for the remnant of the land: so that even those who have slipped away in flight are consumed by beasts. […]

And the waters of Dimon, which means sufficient sorrow, or grief, which had polluted many by their sprinkling, will be shown to have been to the deceived peoples not for salvation but for blood. Hence the prophetic word promises that upon the flowing tears, which is the meaning of Dibon, they will redouble not one grief but many additions of grief: so that, after they have done full penance and have fled from Moab, they may have as their prince the lion, God, whom the Seventy called ariel, which means lion of God: whose edition I have forborne to discuss in this place, because it disagrees in very many points with the Hebrew truth, and from what we have translated its sense too can be understood.

16:1.t: Send forth the Lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion. What we are interpreting is not history but prophecy. And every prophecy is wrapped in enigmas, and with abrupt sentences passes, while speaking of one thing, to another: lest, if Scripture kept to order, it should be not prophecy but narrative. And the sense is: O Moab, upon whom the lion is about to rage, and from whom not even a remnant will be able to be saved, have this consolation: from you will go forth the spotless Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, who will rule over the whole world. From the rock of the desert, that is, from Ruth, who, widowed by the death of her husband, bore Obed by Boaz, and from Obed came Jesse, and from Jesse David, and from David Christ. And the mountain of the daughter of Zion we shall interpret either as the city of Jerusalem itself, or, according to the sacred understanding, as the Church, which is set upon the summit of the virtues.

Send forth the lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert, to the mountain of the daughter of Zion. And as a bird fleeing, and as young ones flying from the nest, so will the daughters of Moab be at the crossing of the Arnon. Enter into counsel, call a council: make your shadow like night at midday: hide those who flee, and do not betray the wanderers. My fugitives will dwell with you; Moab, be their hiding place from the face of the destroyer. For the dust is at an end, the wretch is consumed; he has failed who trampled the earth. And a throne will be prepared in mercy, and one will sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging and seeking judgment, and swiftly rendering what is just. […]

16:2.t: Then, as for Job, that pattern of patience, what mysteries are there not contained in his discourses? Commencing in prose the book soon glides into verse and at the end once more reverts to prose. By the way in which it lays down propositions, assumes postulates, adduces proofs and draws inferences, it illustrates all the laws of logic. Single words occurring in the book are full of meaning. To say nothing of other topics, it prophesies the resurrection of humankind's bodies at once with more clearness and with more caution than anyone has yet shown. "I know," Job says, "that my redeemer lives, and that at the last day I shall rise again from the earth; and I shall be clothed again with my skin, and in my flesh shall I see God. Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another. This my hope is stored up in my own bosom." […]

And it will be: as a bird fleeing, and young ones flying away from the nest, so will the daughters of Moab be at the crossing of the Arnon. He returns to the order he had begun: When I have set, he says, a most savage lion upon those who flee from Moab, and upon the remnant of the land, to break their limbs and bones, then they will fly away in terror, and all the daughters, that is, the villages and cities of the province of Moab, will migrate at the crossing of the Arnon, which is the border of the Amorites and the Moabites. And by putting crossing here too, he signifies captivity.

But he who has fled from the desert of Moab (to return from the prophecy to the anagogy), and, despising falsehood, has stood on the mountain of truth, will be like a bird fleeing; and like young ones flying from the nest, lest they be devoured by the Moabite serpents. Thus, he says, will all the daughters, that is, the Moabite souls, be at the crossing of the Arnon, which means their illumination: when, having abandoned their errors, they have crossed over to the knowledge of the truth.

16:3.t: And as I know of two kinds of fire, so also do I of light. The one is the light of our ruling power directing our steps according to the will of God; the other is a deceitful and meddling one, quite contrary to the true light, though pretending to be that light, that it may cheat us by its appearance. This really is darkness, yet has the appearance of noonday, the high perfection of light. And so I read that passage of those who continually flee in darkness at noonday; for this is really night, and yet is thought to be bright light by those who have been ruined by luxury. For what saith David? "Night was around me and I knew it not, for I thought that my luxury was enlightenment."

It is said therefore to Moab himself, or to him who has escaped from Moab: Do nothing without counsel (Prov 13): and do not be carried about by every wind of doctrine, but follow him who is the Angel of great counsel (Eph 4): and call a council, so that out of the wandering and straying you may make a Church of God. And your shade and tabernacle, in which you formerly thought you were resting, which belonged to night and darkness, set it at midday, that is, in the brightest light, in which you ought to hide those fleeing from error, and no longer betray those who were formerly wanderers.

Take counsel, call a council: make your shade like night at midday, hide the fugitives, and do not betray the wanderers. My refugees will dwell with you: Moab, be their hiding place from the face of the devastator; for the dust is at an end, the wretched one is finished, he who trampled the land has failed. For wretched one in the Hebrew one reads SOD (סד), which can also be understood as devastator. And he speaks to Moab, that it should find counsel for its safety, and, gathering its elders, convene a council for its salvation. Do you wish, he says, to be saved and to merit the mercy of God? In the clear light and the open flight of my people, be like night and shade; take in the fugitives, and do not betray the wanderers. And why he said this he adds at once: My refugees will dwell with you. For when Jerusalem has been laid waste, and all Judea, which borders on the Moabites, my people will migrate to you. […]

16:4.t: For, O Moab, my fugitives who had forsaken me, who had gone out of the Church and, abandoning the teaching of the Holy Spirit, were following their own sense; or those who had dwelt with you, when the destroyer, the devil, begins to persecute them, do you, turned with your whole mind to the fear of the Lord, offer them hiding places: and know that after the coming of the Lamb, who arose from the rock of the desert as ruler of the whole earth and came to the mountain of the daughter of Zion, all the power of the devil, which is compared to dust, is at an end. And the wretch is consumed who made many wretched: and he has failed who trampled the whole earth, namely those who were earthly.

16:5.t: And a throne will be prepared in mercy, and he will sit upon it in truth, in the tabernacle of David, judging and seeking judgment, and swiftly rendering what is just. The Hebrews interpret this place thus: When the Assyrian has been put to flight, Hezekiah, a righteous man, will reign over Judah and will hold the throne of David, judging in truth the people of God subject to him. Others understand it of Christ: when the dust of the Antichrist is at an end, and the devastator who trampled the whole earth has been taken away, Christ the king will come, who will sit in the tabernacle of David, and in the day of judgment will render to all according to their works. Nor is there any doubt that this passage prophesies of Christ. But we can understand the same thing of his first coming, and show it in the tabernacle of the Church: that throughout the whole land of Moab the trophies of the Churches as they rise bear witness to the dominion of Christ.

And when he has been consumed and brought to nothing and has utterly failed, a throne and an everlasting kingdom will be prepared. First in mercy (for we are all (Rom 3) under sin, and need the grace of God); and he will sit in the tabernacle of David, which had fallen and has been raised up, who after mercy will judge, and seek righteousness, and render to each according to his works. Let us consider from the beginning of the Burden, or of the word, of Moab, in which it is said: By night Ar of Moab has been laid waste, and the rest up to this place; and we shall see how by steps and in the order of penance Israelites are made from Moabites, and flee like birds and fly away like young ones from the nest, so as to cross over by the Arnon and dwell on the mountain of the daughter of Zion: and, all the power of the devil or of the Antichrist having been crushed, Christ reigns in them and sets his throne among those who have been saved by mercy and righteousness. […]

16:6.t: We have heard of the pride of Moab: he is exceedingly proud. His pride and his arrogance and his indignation are more than his strength. Therefore Moab will howl to Moab, all of him will howl: to those who rejoice over the wall of baked brick, speak of his wounds: for the suburbs of Heshbon are deserted, the vineyard of Sibmah. LXX: We have heard of the insolence of Moab: he is exceedingly insolent: his pride and his insolence and his fury are not like your divination: not so will Moab howl: for in Moab all will howl: but for the inhabitants of Deseth you will meditate, and you will not be confounded: the plains of Heshbon will mourn the vineyard of Sibmah. In how many obscurities this passage is wrapped according to the Seventy translators is evident from the fact that it can scarcely be read. Let us speak, therefore, according to the Hebrew. […]

We have heard of the pride of Moab, he is exceedingly proud: his pride, and his arrogance, and his indignation are greater than his strength. Therefore Moab will howl to Moab, all of it will howl: to those who rejoice over the walls of baked brick, tell of its wounds. Again he returns to the present, and accuses Moab of pride, because it was lifted up far more than its strength warranted; and because of this pride Moab will howl to Moab, that is, the people to the city, or the metropolis to the province, and the whole land will resound with howling over the walls of baked brick, of which Jeremiah too says: Therefore I will wail over Moab, and to all Moab I will cry out, to the men of the earthen wall, lamenting (Jer 48:31). And by these things he shows both the power of its former prosperity and the wounds of its sudden overthrow.

16:7.t: Therefore Moab will howl to Moab, that is, one to another: namely, all the varieties of the heretics and of worldly wisdom will bellow against one another when they are in torments (1 Kgs 6). For this reason, to those who have walls not built of squared stones, of which the Temple was built, and so polished that hammer and axe were not heard in the house of God, O you teachers of the Church, or you who have been saved from the error of Moab, announce their wounds, with which they have been wounded by the darts of the heretics. For all their thoughts, which is what Heshbon signifies, do not belong to the dwelling of the Lord's city, of which it is written: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God (Ps 45 [46]:5); […]

16:8.t:
For the suburbs of Heshbon are deserted: the vine of Sibmah. Between Heshbon and Sibmah there are scarcely five hundred paces; and by the metaphor of the vine he signifies the devastation of the whole province.

The lords of the nations have cut down its shoots. He keeps the metaphor he had begun, showing that the kings of the nations who had laid Moab waste ravaged all its hamlets and fortresses.

They have reached as far as Jazer: they have wandered in the desert: its offshoots have been left behind: they have crossed the sea. Understand the shoots and offshoots as its people and its fugitives; and the crossing of the sea as the captivity into Babylon, about which we shall read later: The burden of the desert of the sea.

The lords of the nations have cut down its branches: they have reached as far as Jazer. They have wandered in the desert: its shoots have been left: they have crossed the sea. For this I will weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vineyard of Sibmah: I will drench you with my tears, Heshbon and Elealeh: for upon your vintage and upon your harvest the voice of the treaders has burst in. And gladness and exultation will be taken away from Carmel: and in the vineyards he will not exult nor shout for joy: he who was accustomed to tread will not tread wine in the press: I have taken away the voice of the treaders. The suburbs of Heshbon, of which we spoke above, are deserted, and the vineyard of Sibmah, which can be interpreted not only as lifting up height but also as some conversion: because in the region of Moab it seems in some part to wish to be converted to the service of the Lord. […]

16:9.t:
Therefore I will lament with the weeping of Jazer, the vine of Sibmah: I will drench you with my tears, Heshbon and Elealeh. This is the voice of the Prophet lamenting, and attesting the greatness of the devastation by the greatness of his tears, and weeping for the vine of Jazer and of Sibmah, and for Heshbon and Elealeh, cities once most strong, cut down as the Assyrian pruned them.

For upon your vintage and upon your harvest the voice of the treaders has burst in. Understand the treaders of the grapes, gathering in the joy of the vintage, as the armies of the enemies; and that in the very season of joy the season of captivity has come.

And so the prophetic word laments the strength of the heretics, that is, Jazer, and the vineyard of Sibmah, which exalts itself against the knowledge of God. And I will drench you with my tears, Heshbon, namely their thoughts, and Elealeh, by which they climb to the heights. And why does he lament Jazer and the vineyard of Sibmah, and drench Heshbon and Elealeh with his tears? So that, while he himself weeps, he may teach them also to weep. For, he says, upon your vintage and upon your harvest the voice of the treaders has burst in. For the vineyard of the Moabites, because of the nearness of the place, is such as is the vineyard of the Sodomites too, of which it is said: For their vine is of the vineyard of the Sodomites, and their shoot of Gomorrah (Deut 32:31). And in Psalm 77 (78) we read of the Egyptian vine which God struck with hail. […]

16:10.t:
And joy and exultation will be taken away from Carmel. It is an idiom of the Scriptures always to liken Carmel, a rich and wooded mountain which overlooks Ptolemais and on which Elijah prayed, to fertility and abundance; and by this it signifies that all joy and fertility are to be taken away from cities once most fruitful.

And in the vineyards he will not exult, nor shout for joy. What is understood is the former vintager, that is, the husbandman of the province of Moabitis. Accordingly he immediately added:

He who used to tread will not tread wine in the press: I have taken away the voice of the treaders. By no means will the joyful vintager sing the vintage shout at the vintage; but everywhere hostile devastation and the clamor of the victors will arise.

The gladness and exultation of the heretics, in which they had formerly been accustomed to rejoice, will also be taken away: so that, after they have done penance, they may deserve to hear: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:5). And what he added, from Carmel, signifies this: not that the heretics truly have Carmel, that is, the knowledge of the spiritual circumcision, but that they falsely boast of having it. And when the vineyards have been cut down, and gladness and exultation taken away from the knowledge falsely so called, then there will be none of the former treaders to tread the grapes which he had trodden before: and their voice will be struck dumb in eternal silence.

16:11.t: Therefore my belly will sound for Moab like a harp, and my inmost parts for the wall of baked brick. Lest anyone should think the Prophet's lament a sign of exultation, by which he rejoiced that the enemies of the people of Israel were captives, he says that it is out of affection, and out of the inmost grief of his heart, that he mourns the overthrow of a city once most mighty.

For this my belly will sound for Moab like a harp, and my inward parts for the wall of baked brick. And it will be, when it has appeared that Moab has labored on his high places, he will enter into his holy places to entreat, and he will not prevail. This is the word which the Lord spoke to Moab from that time. When the error of Moab has been destroyed, or rather its false gladness changed into mourning and tears, my belly, the prophet's, which is composed with musical art like a harp, and which, conceiving from the fear of God, has begotten many children, so that there is no string that does not give back its sound, will resound with the mourning of Moab doing penance: and all my inward parts for the wall of baked brick: for which Theodotion translated for the scattered wall. For all the defenses of the adversaries, in which they formerly trusted, will be destroyed and will fall. […]

Moreover, according to the Seventy, who translated: The inner parts of the prophet, like a wall renewed by God, and that he is put to shame, that is, Moab, and enters to the altars and to the things that are made by hand, we can discuss it thus, saying that the inward parts of the prophet are always renewed and made stronger by God, so that the adversaries are confounded, and understand the things which have been fabricated by human hand to be empty and of no profit for salvation.

16:12.t: And it will come to pass, when it has become apparent that Moab has labored over its high places, it will enter its sanctuaries to pray, and it will not prevail. It is the last misery not to have help even in those whom it has always worshiped. Deserted, he says, by your own strength, and with all your defenders slain, you will go to the idols, you will venerate the shrines, and you will find no help in those upon whom the devastation will come together with you.

And when Moab has understood that he has labored in vain at the doctrines which he formerly thought lofty, he will enter into his holy places, not those which are holy of themselves, but those which in his error he thought holy, and he will not be able to find help. Or surely, having abandoned the error of falsehood, he will try to enter into the holy places of the Church, to make them his own, and to pray and entreat, but he will not prevail. For we cannot take hold of perfect virtue as soon as we wish.

16:13.t: This is the word which the Lord spoke to Moab from that time. From what time, do you suppose? Clearly from the time when Moab was created. And the Lord says: The Moabites and the Ammonites shall not enter into the Church of God (Deut 23:3). Or we may understand from that time as of ancient time: that these things were decreed long ago by the divine sentence; not that the foreknowledge of God brought about the cause of the devastation, but that the future devastation was known beforehand to the majesty of God.

And what he adds: This is the word which the Lord spoke to Moab from that time, let us know that an epilogue has been given back to the proem in which he had said, the word against Moab, or the burden, so that what he had begun there he has completed here. And from that time is to be understood as from when he began to speak to him, so that all that he said is one word of God, that is, one sentence.
In the mystery of prophetical revelation, Christ is symbolized by word, which people heard while they could see no one, as they said: "This is the word that the Lord spoke to Moab."

16:14.t: And now the Lord has spoken, saying: In three years, like the years of a hireling, the glory of Moab will be taken away, above all its great people, and it will be left small and slight, by no means many. This prophecy, as we said above, is directed against the Moabites after the death of Ahaz, in the reign of Hezekiah, under whom the ten tribes were led into captivity by Sennacherib king of the Assyrians. So, just as a hireling waits for the setting of the sun, and day and night looks for the end of his work so as to receive his fixed wage, so too after three years Moab will be destroyed when the Assyrian comes, and scarcely a few will be left in the land to inhabit the overthrown cities and to till the deserted fields. It can also be a prediction about the Babylonian captivity: that after Jerusalem had been taken and three years had passed, Moab was to be laid waste by the Chaldeans; or else that within the space of three years no rest was to be given them.

And now the Lord has spoken, saying: In three years, like the years of a hireling, the glory of Moab will be taken away over all his great people, and he will be left small and slight, by no means many. The three years in which the glory of Moab will be taken away over all his great people, or great riches, as the Seventy translated, are to be understood mystically. For just as the mercy of the Lord is in weights and measure, so torments and punishments too have their measure, so that after three years have passed, in which he will be left small and slight and by no means many, he may then cease to be without glory. And this is to be noted, that according to the prophecy of Ezekiel, when days are counted for years to Israel (Ezek 4), that is, to the ten tribes, which had sinned more grievously, three hundred and ninety years are reckoned in punishments, as it is contained in the Hebrew, not a hundred and ninety, as the common edition has: and to Judah, in which was the Temple of God, forty years. […]

17:1.t: The burden of Damascus: Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city, and it will be like a heap of stones in ruin. The cities of Aroer, abandoned, will be for flocks, and they will rest there, and there will be none to frighten them. And help will cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus, and the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the sons of Israel, says the Lord of hosts. After Babylon and the Philistines and Moab, the discourse turns to Damascus, that is, Aram, which itself was once a royal city too, and held the primacy in all Syria: Antioch and Laodicea and Apamea were not yet flourishing, cities which we know to have grown after Alexander and the empire of the Macedonians. Because, then, it always gave help to the ten tribes against Judah, as the history of Kings and Chronicles relates, he signifies that devastation by the Assyrians is drawing near to them too, as the king of the Assyrians says: I have taken Arabia, and Damascus, and Samaria. […]

The burden of Damascus. Symmachus and Theodotion: The taking up of Damascus; the LXX: The word against Damascus, adding something of their own, as they did at the beginning of Moab. We first read the name Damascus in Genesis: he was Abraham's home-born servant before Isaac, and was thought to be his heir, had not the son of Sarah been begotten by promise (Gen 15). Now it means either kiss of blood, or drinking blood, or blood of sackcloth, all of which suit the people of the heathen, who before the faith of Christ were friends of blood and cruelty, and did works worthy of lamentation and of sackcloth. In the book of Days (2 Chr 24) the history relates that when the year was completed the army of Syria went up against Joash king of Judah, and came into Jerusalem, and slew all the princes of the people, and sent all the spoil to the king of Damascus; it had come with few men, and God had delivered into their hand a very great multitude, because they had forsaken the Lord God of their fathers. […]

Behold, Damascus shall cease to be a city, and shall be as a heap of stones in ruin. The cities of Aroer shall be left for flocks, and they shall rest there, and there shall be none to make them afraid; and help shall cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria shall be as the glory of the children of Israel, says the Lord of hosts. As was shown in the title, by Damascus is signified the calling of the nations, which loved or drank blood; and once they have believed in Christ, they will cease to be cities of their former way of life, and will be as a heap of stones in ruin. For as heaps of stones that are scattered over the fields are carried together into one mound, so out of all the nations a heap of believers has been gathered at the ruin of the people of the Jews, they falling and we rising.

Some think that this prophecy is the same as the one we read in Jeremiah: Damascus is dissolved, it has turned to flight, trembling has seized it, anguish and pains have held it like a woman in labor (Jer 49:24, 27). And again: I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it will devour the ramparts of Ben-hadad. But it must be known that Jeremiah describes the Babylonian captivity of the city of Damascus, that is, of the few whom the king of the Assyrians had left in it; whereas Isaiah announces the captivity by the Assyrians that is close at hand. Others suppose that the Roman captivity is foretold, since the people of the Jews too was taken captive, and Damascus, over which Aretas ruled, endured a like servitude: so that all that is written about it is to be transferred to the time of Christ and to the mysteries of the Apostles.

17:2.t: The cities of Aroer, abandoned, will be for flocks. Aroer means tamarisk, which is properly a tree that grows in the wilderness and in salty soil; and by this the devastation is shown. They will rest there: the flocks is understood; and there will be none to frighten them. For the solitude will be so great that not even a robber lying in wait is to be feared.

The forsaken cities of AROER (ערוער), that is, of the tamarisk, shall also be for the flocks of the Church, so that we may inhabit those which the Jews forsook; or else, idolatry being destroyed, the Gospel shall be built up. This too we see fulfilled in our own times: the Serapeum at Alexandria and the temple of Marnas at Gaza have risen up as churches of the Lord, and the cities of Aroer have been made ready for the flocks of the Gospel. Aroer, that is, tamarisks, grow in desert places, according to what is written in the curse of the man who trusts in man, and whose heart departs from the Lord: He shall be, it says, like the tamarisk in the desert, and shall not see good when it comes; but he shall dwell in dryness, in the desert, in a land of salt and uninhabitable (Jer 17:6). Others again say that from this tree, by the arts of sorcerers, μίστρα, that is, hatreds, are stirred up. […]

17:3.t: And help will cease from Ephraim: by no means will the ten tribes have help in it against Judah. And the kingdom from Damascus: ἀπὸ κοινοῦ [from the common or popular edition] will cease is understood. But when he says that the kingdom ceases and rests, he does not signify a perpetual devastation, but takes away for the present the power by which it formerly reigned in all Syria. And the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the sons of Israel, says the Lord of hosts. As, he says, the ten tribes were destroyed when the Assyrian ravaged them, and all their glory was led into captivity, so the few who remain in Damascus will imitate them, and will have the glory of their allied nation. Take glory as said by irony, for ignominy. And all this will happen because the Lord has spoken, whose words cannot be made void.

Then the help of God shall cease from Ephraim, by whom in this place are understood the Scribes and Pharisees, according to the prophecy of Hosea, who names Ephraim those who are opposed to the people of God (Hos 5 and 8). And the kingdom shall cease from Damascus, so that sin, and the prince of sin, the devil, may no longer reign in Damascus, which formerly loved blood; but the remnant of Syria, that is, those from the nations who have believed, are to be as the children of Israel formerly were, the kingdom of God having been taken from them and given to the nations which bring forth its fruit, as the Lord God of hosts has spoken through all his prophets.

17:4.t:
"4. And there shall be in that day a failing of the glory of Jacob, and the riches of his glory shall be shaken. 5. And it shall be as when one gathers standing corn, and reaps the grain of the ears; 6. And it shall be as when one gathers ears in a rich valley, and stubble is left. Or as the berries of an olive tree are left, two or three on the topmost bough, or four or five on its branches, thus saith the Lord God of Israel. 7. In that day a man shall trust in him that made him, and his eyes shall look on the Holy One of Israel, 8. and they shall not trust in the altars, nor in the work of their hands, which their own fingers have made."

And in this it is clearly prophesied how Israel's glory and all her riches will be taken away, and how but a few, easily numbered, like the few berries on the branch of an olive tree, are said to be left; and these would be those of them who are believers in our Lord. […]
17:4.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

17:4.t: And it will come to pass in that day, the glory of Jacob will be made thin, and the fat of his flesh will waste away. When, he says, Damascus has been taken and has ceased to be a city, and such glory has crowned it as crowned Israel, that is, the ten tribes, then all the defense, and the fattest flesh, and the refuge of Jacob will waste away: for by no means will he have allies to join with him in laying Jerusalem waste. We have read above that Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to make war against it, and that it was announced to the house of David: Syria has rested upon Ephraim; of whom the Prophet speaks to Ahaz: Do not fear, and let not your heart be afraid of these two tails of smoking firebrands, in the wrath of the fury of Rezin king of Syria and of the son of Remaliah, because Syria, Ephraim and the son of Remaliah have taken most evil counsel against you.

And it shall come to pass in that day that the glory of Jacob shall be made thin, and the fatness of his flesh shall waste away. And it shall be as one gathering in the harvest what remains, and his arm shall glean the ears, and it shall be as one seeking ears in the valley of Rephaim. And there shall be left in it as a cluster of grapes, and as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three olives at the top of a branch, or four or five at its summits, its fruit, says the Lord God of Israel. After the remnant of Syria has become as the glory of the children of Israel once was, and through their trespass salvation has been given to the nations, then all the glory of the Jews, by which they were glorious in the whole world, shall be made thin, and the fatness of their flesh shall waste away, since they have no prophets, no signs and mighty works, no present help of God, no dignity of the priesthood; but the whole body of their nation shall wither and be brought to nothing.

17:5.t: And since it is said of the calling of the nations: The harvest is great, but the labourers are few (Matt 9), those poor ones shall glean the remnants of the harvest, which were saved through the Apostles, and the scantiest ears, not from the mountains and lofty places, but in the valley of Rephaim, that is, in the lowliness of the letter. And consider that Rephaim, which means giants, signifies the Pharisees and Scribes, as Ephraim did above. Indeed, for the valley of Rephaim the Seventy translated the hard valley, to express the hardness of the Jewish heart.

And it will be like one gathering in the harvest what has remained, and his arm will gather the ears: and it will be like one seeking ears in the valley of Rephaim. And there will be left in it as it were a cluster, and as at the shaking of an olive tree two or three olives at the top of a branch, or four or five on its topmost boughs, its fruit, says the Lord God of Israel. Those who understand the present devastation of Damascus as under the Roman empire maintain that these words signify the Apostles: that just as a few ears and olives are wont to remain in the field or on the trees, so the remnant of Israel is saved; especially since there follows: In that day man will bow down to his maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel, that is, to Christ. The two olives, and three, and four, and five they interpret as fourteen Apostles: that is, the twelve who were chosen, and a thirteenth, James, who is called the brother of the Lord, and also Paul the Apostle, the vessel of election (Acts 9:15). […]

17:6.t: Out of their lowliness those who shall be saved are chosen like ears among the stubble and like clusters at the vintage; and as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three olives, or four or five. For when the smiting of the people of the Jews came, that olive tree of the people of Israel, which under Moses had six hundred thousand armed men (Num 26), and under David, when Joab numbered them, a countless people (2 Sam 24), could scarcely offer a few fruits to the Lord the Savior: two olives, Paul and Barnabas; and three olives, Peter and James and John (Acts 13), who both beheld the Lord transfigured on the mountain and were found worthy to go with the Lord to the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue (Matt 17). The four and five olives make up the remaining nine Apostles, among whom Matthias took the place of Judas the betrayer; […]

17:7.t: In that day man will bow down to his maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel. And he will not bow down to the altars which his hands have made, and which his fingers have wrought: and they will not look to the groves and the shrines. They think that this was fulfilled in the times of Christ, when, the kingdom of Damascus having been destroyed, the everlasting empire of the Savior succeeded, and the error of idolatry was diminished. The intention of these interpreters is indeed pious, but it does not keep the order of the history. We, however, say that, when Damascus had been overthrown and the ten tribes had been led away to the Assyrians, those who were left of the tribes that belonged to Israel turned, at Hezekiah's letters, to the worship of God, and came to the temple at Jerusalem, as the history of Chronicles relates (2 Chr 30). […]

In that day man shall bow down to his maker, and his eyes shall look to the Holy One of Israel. And he shall not bow down to the altars which his hands have made, and which his fingers have wrought; they shall not look to the groves and the shrines. At that time, when from the people of Israel, to whom it was formerly said, The Lord your God has called you a fruitful olive tree (Jer 11:16), and of whom we read in the Psalms, Your children like young olive plants round about your table (Ps 127 [128]:3), the Lord in his hunger shall scarcely have found, for the drought of spiritual grace, two olives, and three, or four, or five, the fullness of the nations shall come in, and shall bow down not to idols made with hands but to its God, and looking to the Holy One of Israel they shall despise altars and groves and shrines, knowing what is written: Every plant which the heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up (Matt 15:13).

17:9.t: In that day the cities of its strength will be abandoned like ploughs, and the crops that were abandoned before the face of the sons of Israel, and it will be deserted. He does not say this against Damascus, but against the ten tribes, which were called Israel: that just as, at the coming of the people of God out of Egypt, all the nations that inhabited the land of promise, struck with sudden terror, abandoned their ploughs and the heaps of grain and their work half done, seeking safety in their feet, so the land of Israel too should remain desolate for a long time. Hence I wonder that for ploughs and heaps of grain Aquila chose to translate potsherd and Emir; Symmachus, forest and Amir; the Seventy, the Amorites and the Hivites. Theodotion alone set down the Hebrew word, ARS ET EMIR: which among them is read more correctly HORES (חרש) ET AMIR (והאמיר), that is, ploughshares and heaps of crops.

In that day the cities of his strength shall be forsaken like ploughs and standing corn, which were forsaken before the face of the children of Israel. And it shall be desolate, because you have forgotten God your Savior, and have not remembered your strong helper. LXX: In that day your cities shall be forsaken, as the Amorites and the Hivites forsook them before the face of the children of Israel. And they shall be desolate, because you have forsaken God your Savior, and have not remembered the Lord your helper. As under Moses and Joshua the son of Nun the Amorites and the Hivites, and the other nations that dwelt in the land of promise, forsook their ploughshares and standing corn and the heaps in the fields and fled, lest they be seized by their enemies, so the land of Judea and all its strongest cities were forsaken by their inhabitants when the Romans laid Judea waste and besieged Jerusalem.

17:10.t:
Because you have forgotten God your Savior, and have not remembered your strong helper. These things, he says, you will suffer, O Israel, because you have abandoned God your Savior, who freed you from Egypt, who subjected hostile nations to you: and you have not remembered your helper.

Therefore you will plant a faithful planting, and you will sow a foreign shoot. This is to be read more pointedly and as irony. Because, he says, you have forgotten God your Savior, and have not remembered your strong helper: will you on that account have to plant a faithful planting, and not rather sow a foreign shoot, for the enemy to snatch away? Or certainly thus: my sons, who were begotten from the stock of my people, you have established in the land for this purpose, that you might make them foreign and most wicked.

And an apostrophe is made to the land of Judea itself, that is, to those who dwelt in it: You have suffered all these things because you have forgotten God your Savior, which means Jesus, whose coming to you the Law and the Prophets continually announced; and you have not remembered your strong helper, who was always your succour. The cause, then, of the desolate cities of Judea is forgetfulness of the Savior, who had said at the beginning of this Prophet: Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood.

Therefore you shall plant a faithful plantation, and shall sow a strange seed. In the day of your planting wild grapes, and in the morning your seed shall flower: the harvest is taken away in the day of inheritance, and he shall grieve grievously. LXX: Therefore you shall plant an unfaithful plantation and an unfaithful seed, and in the day on which you plant you shall go astray. But if you sow in the morning, it shall flower for harvest in the day of inheritance, when, as the father of a man, he gives an inheritance to his sons. Where we, following Aquila and Symmachus and the Seventy, have translated in the day of inheritance, which in Hebrew is BIOM NEHELA (ביום נחלה), one can read in the Hebrew in the worst day. And where Aquila and Theodotion translated and man shall grieve, we, taught by the Hebrews, instead of man, which in their tongue is ENOS, have rendered ANUS (אנוש), that is, grievously. […]

17:11.t: In the day of your planting, wild grapes, and in the morning your seed will flower. The harvest has been taken away in the day of inheritance, and it will grieve grievously. These, he says, are the fruits of your works that you will reap: your vine of Sorek will degenerate into wild grapes, your seed will hold out hope in the blade; but when ripeness has come, it will be reaped by another. And then you will grieve grievously, when you lose what you hoped for and almost already held.

17:12.t: Woe to the multitude of many peoples; like the multitude of the roaring sea, and the tumult of the crowds, like the sound of many waters, they shall roar. The peoples shall roar like the multitude of overflowing waters; and he shall rebuke him, and he shall flee far off, and he shall be carried away like the dust of the mountains before the wind, and like a whirlwind before the tempest. At eventide, behold, trouble; in the morning, and he shall not stand. This is the portion of those who have wasted us, and the lot of those who plunder us. Above, under the name of Damascus, we read of the calling of the nations, and the casting off of the Jews, and, through the Apostles and in the Apostles, the election of the few of the Jews who believed. And since, in comparison with the whole world and all the nations, only a small part believed of the Christian people, of whom it was said above: And the remnant of Syria shall be as the glory of the children of Israel (for many (Matt 22:14) are called, but few are chosen); […]

Woe to the multitude of many peoples, like the multitude of the roaring sea: and the tumult of crowds, like the sound of many waters: the peoples will roar like the sound of flooding waters: and he will rebuke him, and he will flee far off: and he will be snatched away like the dust of the mountains before the wind, and like a whirlwind before the storm. At eventide: and behold, confusion in the morning, and he will not endure. This is the portion of those who have laid us waste, and the lot of those who plunder us. Those who suppose that the earlier captivity of Damascus was brought on by the Romans refer this also that is written: Man will bow down to his maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel, to the times of Christ and of the Apostles. And what follows as well: You will plant a faithful planting, and you will sow a foreign shoot: in the day of your planting, wild grapes, and the rest, they take to concern the unbelief of the Jews. […]

17:13.t: For the peoples shall roar in the spectacles of theatrical licence, and in the cruelty of the amphitheatre, and in the frenzies of the circus, like the sound of overflowing waters, when with a voice concordant in impiety they blaspheme and cry that the Christians be thrown to the lions and the beasts, and other things of the kind. But while they rage like the sea, the Lord shall rebuke the author of their sedition and drive him away from his people. And as dust stirred up on the mountains is carried off the more violently the higher it is, and as a whirlwind that rises from the earth is borne aloft by a sudden tempest, so he too shall be carried off and separated from the people of God and shall flee, lest he be banished to the abyss.

17:14.t: And when the day of consummation comes, which is what evening means, then there shall be trouble for him as he recognizes his own sins. And at morning time, that is, on the day of the resurrection, he shall not stand, which the Seventy translated shall not be. But if he shall not be, what will they answer who grant the devil repentance and, as far as in them lies, promise him the summit of an archangel? This is the portion of those who have wasted us, and the lot of those who plunder us. These words are spoken either by the Christian people, or by the prophet in the person of the believing people: that their persecutors, who oppressed the saints of God with exiles, prisons and confiscations of goods, shall have eternal destruction and shall possess everlasting punishments.

18:1.t: Woe to the land, the cymbal of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia. The Hebrew word SELSEL (צלצל), which Symmachus interpreted as sound and Theodotion as birds, we have rendered as cymbal. Aquila translated double shadow. But it must be known that a shadow is called SEL (צל), and here the syllable itself is doubled. From this we can understand the saying thus: Woe to the land that promises help in the shadow of its wings.
