21:5.t: And in testimony of the fact that Babylon was captured during a banquet, Isaiah clearly exhorts her to battle when he writes: "Babylon, my beloved, has become a strange spectacle unto me: set thou the table and behold in the mirrors those who eat and drink; rise up, ye princes, and snatch up your shields!"

Set the table, watch in the watchtower those eating and drinking: arise, princes, seize the shield. This place is taken in two ways. O Medes and Elamites, to whom I said above: Go up, Elam, besiege, O Mede, take food, prepare yourselves for the coming battle, lest, when the time of fighting has come, weariness hold you back. And when you have eaten and drunk, arise, seize your arms, vanquish the Babylonian. And his saying, watch in the watchtower, is read in this sense: look out diligently for what is to come. It can also be understood thus: O Babylon, prepare a table and a banquet for Belshazzar your king, son of Evil-merodach, grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, and see what happens after the meal, at which he will drink toasts to harlots and concubines from the vessels of the Lord. O princes, who recline at table with the king (and he means the Medes and Persians), arise and seize your arms to kill the king. We learn this more fully in the volume of Daniel (Dan 5).

21:6.t: For thus the Lord said to me: Go and set a watchman, and let him declare whatever he sees. And he saw a chariot of two horsemen, a rider on an ass, and a rider on a camel; and he gazed diligently with much attention, and a lion cried out. LXX: For thus the Lord said to me: Go and set for yourself a watchman, and whatever you see, declare it. And I saw two horsemen riding, a rider on an ass, and a rider on a camel; I heard much hearing, and I called Uriah to the watchtower. The Prophet is bidden to set a watchman in his heart, and to gaze more carefully at what is to come upon the world; and he saw two horsemen, a rider on an ass and a rider on a camel. These someone has interpreted so as to call the rider on the ass, according to the Gospel reading (Matt 21) and the prophecy of Zechariah (Zech 9), Christ; and on the contrary the rider on the camel the opposing power, on account of the foulness of that crooked animal. Others again refer the two riders, of the letter and of the spirit, to the two Testaments.

For thus the Lord said to me: Go and set a watchman, and let him announce whatever he sees. And he saw a chariot of two horsemen, a rider on an ass, and a rider on a camel. And he gazed diligently with much attention, and the lion cried out: Upon the watchtower of the Lord I stand continually by day, and upon my watch I stand whole nights. Behold, there comes this rider, a man of the two-horsed chariot; and he answered and said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the graven images of her gods are broken on the ground. My threshing, and son of my threshing floor, what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have announced to you. He gives the reasons for the fear above: why anguish possessed him like a woman in labor, and he fell down on hearing, and was terrified and surrounded with dark horror. Thus, he says, the Lord said to me: Go and appoint a watchman, to foretell the future to you in the prophetic spirit; […]

21:7.t: [Daniel 5:1] "Belshazzar the king made a great feast for his one thousand nobles; and each one drank in the order of his age." It should be known that this man was not the son of Nebuchadnezzar, as readers commonly imagine; but according to Berosus, who wrote the history of the Chaldeans, and also Josephus, who follows Berosus, after Nebuchadnezzar's reign of forty-three years, a son named Evilmerodach succeeded to his throne. It was concerning this king that Jeremiah wrote that in the first year of his reign he raised the head of Jehoiachin, king of Judah, and took him out of his prison (Jeremiah 52:31). Josephus likewise reports that after the death of Evilmerodach, his son Neriglissar succeeded to his father's throne; after whom in turn came his son Labosordach. Upon the latter's death, his son, Belshazzar, obtained the kingdom, and it is of him that the Scripture now makes mention. […]

21:8.t: And because there was doubt about the person of the watchman who had seen Cyrus coming up, he himself explains it more plainly, and says: Upon the watchtower of the Lord I stand continually by day, declaring himself to be the watchman of the Lord, who, always set in the prophetic office, and obeying the command of the Lord by day and by night, speaks whatever he commands.

But what the Seventy interpreters meant in this place, in translating uriam for lion, which in Hebrew is called ARIA (אריה), I do not well understand, especially since the aforementioned priest Urias, who is called to bear witness, is written with other letters.

And for what is said in the Hebrew, ARIE (אריה), for which Aquila and Symmachus translated lion and lioness, the Seventy, meaning I know not what, set down οὐρίαν, which a certain man thinks is to be interpreted light of the Lord, though light of the Lord, which is not found here, is written with other letters, and lion, which is read here, with others. And he would have this watchman, whom the Prophet is bidden to set in his heart, be called Uriah, and by the interpretation of the name he refers it to the understanding of Christ, so that, with him dwelling in us, we may be able to see what is to come. This indeed could also be fitted to the lion, since Jacob (Gen 49) and Balaam (Num 23 and 2) name the lion under the mystery of Christ.

I am upon the watchtower of the Lord, standing continually by day, and I am upon my guard, standing whole nights. Behold, this man comes, the rider of a chariot of horsemen, and he answered and said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the graven images of her gods are broken to the ground. My threshing, and the sons of my floor, what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have declared to you. LXX: The Lord said: I stood all day, and upon the camp I stood all night; and behold, he comes, the rider of a chariot, and answering he said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all her idols and the things made with hands are broken to the ground. Hear, you who are left and are grieving; hear what I have heard from the Lord Sabaoth; the God of Israel has declared it to us. The Prophet stands on the watchtower of the Lord, and, set in his light, looks forward to what is to come. And this is the guard he keeps, this the office entrusted to him: to see, in the darkness of this world, what is to come.

21:9.t: What, then, did the lion cry out? Behold, there comes this rider, a man of the two-horsed chariot: there is no doubt that Cyrus is indicated. And the lion himself, who had cried out above, answered and said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the graven images of her gods are broken on the ground. For when the rider of the two-horse chariot laid it waste, Babylon was destroyed forever, and the temple of Bel and all the idols were leveled to the ground.

Behold, he says, this man comes, signifying by what follows that he saw the Lord the Savior coming, seated on a chariot of two, and yoking to one car two horses, or rather two animals, the ass and the camel. And this rider of the chariot answered the Prophet, who longed and desired to hear his words, and said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, the confusion of the whole world; it fell at my coming, when I took a human body, and it will utterly collapse at the consummation of the world. And all her graven images are broken to the ground. For which the Seventy translated idols and things made with hands, signifying the scripture of the heretics and the various errors of heresies, who are makers of idols and worship what they have fashioned out of their own heart.

21:10.t:
"Hear ye isles, which are forsaken and tortured, hear, what I heard from the Lord of Sabaoth: the God of Israel has announced (it) to us.

Note the way in this passage also in which he does not call those of the Circumcision to hear the unspeakable words, but those only, whom he calls "forsaken and tortured," as were those in the apostolic age who bewailed and lamented the evil of the life of men.
21:10.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

21:10.t: And in what follows: My threshing, and son of my threshing floor, he makes an apostrophe to Jerusalem, and to the Temple which stands on the threshing floor of Ornan, and says to her: O Jerusalem, and you people, son of my Temple, let not what I have said seem incredible to you: for they are not my words but the Lord's, and it is his words that have resounded through my mouth. Some think, but wrongly, that this is said not to Jerusalem but to Babylon, of which he said above as well: Babylon, my beloved, has been made a wonder to me; and that the sense is: You who have crushed me will yourself be crushed too, not by my word, but by the power of the Lord, which foretells to you that these things will come.

And what follows, in the person of the Prophet saying, My threshing, and the sons of my floor, what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have declared to you, has this sense according to the Hebrew: O people, who are to be stored in my granaries, whom I have therefore threshed in various straits, that I might shake the chaff from you, and the purest wheat might be stored in my granaries: what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, is to come upon the whole world, this I have declared to all of you who are in the world. Others again say that the person is still the earlier one, namely the Lord the Savior, and that he himself speaks to the Apostles: What I have heard from the Father I have declared to you (John 15:15). […]

21:11.t: The Jews dream in vain that this prophecy is made against the city of Rome and the Roman empire; and that in what is written in Isaiah, The burden of Dumah, with the stroke of a letter slightly changed, res can be read in place of deleth, and it sounds Rome, since the letter vau in their language is taken both for u and for o.

The burden of Dumah: he calls to me out of Seir: Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? The watchman said: The morning comes, and the night. If you seek, seek; turn, and come. LXX: The vision of Idumea: he calls to me out of Seir: Guard the ramparts; I keep guard morning and night; if you seek, seek, and dwell with me. The Hebrew word ELAI (אלי), which all have translated to me, if you choose to read it ELI, means my God or my strong one. And what we have rendered he calls or he summons, that is, καλεῖ, may, by the ambiguity of the Hebrew and the Greek speech, be read call! or summon!; and the sense is: God, who is my watchman, calls me day and night to repentance, so that, leaving Seir, which means shaggy and hairy, I may return and dwell with him. Dumah sounds either likeness or silence; but Idumea is rendered earthly.

The burden of Duma. He calls to me out of Seir: Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? And the watchman said: The morning comes, and the night: if you seek, seek; turn, come. For Duma the Seventy put Idumaea. But Duma is not the whole province of Edom, but a certain region of it which lies toward the south, and is twenty miles distant from the city of Palestine which today is called Eleutheropolis: near it are the mountains of Seir, which took their name from their founder; for Seir means shaggy and hairy, which Esau was. In the prophet Obadiah we have discussed this nation more fully: there it was necessary to go over the ancient history, and to draw in as testimony the same Visions of Ezekiel and Jeremiah, and especially the prophecy against Mount Seir (Ezek 25 and 35; Jer 49); and that saying from the Psalms: Into Edom I will stretch out my shoe; and elsewhere: The tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek (Ps 59 [60]:10; Ps 82 [83]:7-8). […]

The Lord therefore speaks to the choir of the Apostles and commands it: Call to me those who are of Seir, so that the multitude of the nations may serve me, which, after the likeness of Esau, has nothing in itself soft and smooth and sleek, but is shaggy, wild, intractable. And you, O Apostles, after you have called the nations to me out of Seir, guard the ramparts of the Church, lest the enemy break in easily; lest the lion, roaring and going about, seeking an entrance by which he may get in, tear and scatter the flock shut up in the Church. And the multitude of the Church answered: Not only in prosperity but in adversity, that is, both by day and by night, I will keep your commandments, O God. To her God says: If you truly seek me, show by your works that you seek me; and let it not suffice you to have sought once, but seek always him whom you have found; and to hold him more perfectly, forget your people and your father's house, and, having forsaken the error of the Gentiles, abide with me in the Church. […]

Again he says, "Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? The watchman said, 'The morning comes, and also the night.' " For "the watchman came by night," in that the guardian of the human race even showed himself manifest in the flesh, and yet Judea, being close pressed by the darkness of its faithlessness, never knew him. Where it is well added in the voice of the watchman, "The morning comes, and also the night." For by his presence has a new light shone out upon the world, and yet the former darkness remained in the hearts of unbelievers. And it is well said, "They shall grope in the noonday as in the night," for we search out by groping that which we do not see with our eyes. Now the Jews had seen his undisguised miracles, and yet they still went on seeking him, as it were groping for him, when they said, "How long do you make us to doubt? If you be the Christ, tell us plainly." […]
21:11.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 6.34

21:13.t: Since we have understood what Kedar is, and what Arabia, and what Hazor, let us see what the prophet Isaiah says: In the forest at evening you will sleep, in the paths of Dodanim. The word ARAB (ערב), as we have often said already, is used for evening, and Arabia, and raven, and plain, and the West. And for what we, following the Seventy, have translated you will sleep, one can render you will stay or you will dwell, that is, αὐλιθήσεσθε, which in Hebrew is THALINU (תלנו). DODANIM (דדנים) too is rendered as kinsmen and relatives. So it is now foretold to the Jews who have been able to escape the Babylonian siege, and to cross from the devastation of the whole province to the neighboring desert, that they will dwell in the wilderness of Arabia, on the road that leads to their brothers.

The burden in Arabia. This is not found in the edition of the Seventy Translators; but what follows, In the forest at evening you shall sleep, in the paths of Dodanim, is joined to the preceding vision, so that it reads, if you seek, seek, and dwell with me in the forest. Arabia in our tongue sounds evening, which is the beginning of night and of darkness; and everyone who has the beginning of sins dwells in the evening. But he who comes to the height of them stands in the middle of the night. Hence in Egypt too the firstborn are slain at midnight (Exod 12). And the apostle Peter denied the Lord three times before the cock crew, which is understood as midnight (Matt 26); but after the night was far spent and the day began to draw near, when the darkness of midnight had been overcome and the cock, herald of the light, sounded, he wept bitterly and understood his sin, and at that time he could say: In the evening weeping shall linger, and in the morning gladness (Ps 29 [30]:6). So much meanwhile on the present place. […]

The burden in Arabia. In the forest at evening you will sleep, in the paths of Dodanim. Meeting the thirsty, bring water: you who dwell in the land of the south, meet the fugitive with bread. For they have fled from the face of the swords, from the face of the threatening sword, from the face of the bent bow, from the face of grievous battle. For thus says the Lord to me: Yet in one year, as in the year of a hireling: and all the glory of Kedar will be taken away, and the remnant of the number of the mighty archers of the sons of Kedar will be diminished: for the Lord God of Israel has spoken. As I sought, and long turned over with deliberation, what Arabia this was to which the prophetic word is directed, whether the Moabites, or the Ammonites and Edomites, and all the other regions which are now called Arabia, what follows in this same Vision gave me occasion to see that the Ishmaelites must be understood: All the glory of Kedar will be taken away, and the remnant of the number of the mighty archers of the sons of […]

21:14.t: And again the discourse turns to the Ishmaelites, and urges them to mercy: Run, and go to meet your brothers, weary and in peril from burning thirst, and bring them water: for so great is the heat of the sun that, unless you come to their aid, they will perish in the wilderness; and bring not only water but bread too to the fugitives, so that your clemency may relieve those whom the siege has worn out.

Moreover, that place in which we have translated: You who dwell in the land of the south, meet the fugitive with bread, and have read it in the imperative mood, as if in the person of the Lord, they affirm can be read in the Hebrew thus: Those who dwell in the land of the south met the fugitive with bread; so that, when God had said to them, Meeting the thirsty, bring water, they with hostile mind brought bread without water, to increase their thirst with food.

Coming to meet the thirsty, bring water, you who inhabit the land of the South; meet the fugitive with bread. For they have fled from the face of the swords, from the face of the threatening sword, from the face of the bent bow, from the face of the grievous battle. LXX: To meet the thirsty bring water, you who dwell in the region of Teman; meet those who flee with bread, because of the multitude of the slain, because of the throng of those who go astray, because of the multitude of the sword, and because of the multitude of the bent bows, and because of the multitude of those who fall in war. You who are in Teman, which means South and perfection, and who dwell in that place of which it is written, God shall come from the South (Hab 3:3), and who are consummated and perfect, and have within you the light of the knowledge of the Scriptures: meet those who flee from Arabia and from the forest with water and bread, and do not wait until they come to you, but imitate that father of the Gospel parable who ran to meet […]

Again, by bread is set forth the instruction of heavenly doctrine, as is said by the prophet, "You who dwell in the land of the south, meet with bread him that is flying away." For they dwell in the land of the south who, placed within [the] holy church, are breathed upon by the love of the Spirit from on high. But he is flying who is wishing to escape from the evils of this world. He then who dwells in the land of the south should meet with bread him that is flying; that is, he who is already full of the Holy Spirit within the church should console with words of instruction the one who is endeavoring to escape from his evil ways.
21:14.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 23.49

21:15.t: And at the same time he gives the reason why he commands this to be done, saying: They have fled the Babylonian sword, they have fled the bows of the Elamites, they have fled the threatening battle.

21:16.t: Some, from the words yet in one year, and all the glory of Kedar will be taken away, would have it that what is foretold is not the Babylonian captivity, of which Jeremiah too speaks, but that of the Assyrians, who, one year after the devastation of Judea, pursued the Saracens far and wide.

And do not despise the wretched: your captivity too will come quickly. For as the hireling's year is swift, and he thinks all labor short until he reaches the wage he longs for, so all the glory of the sons of Kedar will be taken from you, and your arrows will be broken, and a small number of fighters will remain.

For thus says the Lord to me: Yet within one year, as in the year of a hireling, all the glory of Kedar shall be taken away, and the remnant of the number of the mighty archers of the children of Kedar shall be diminished. For the Lord God of Israel has spoken. I tell you to meet with water and bread those who flee from the forest and from Arabia because the Lord has promised that these things shall be. As the year of a hireling passes quickly, who every day looks for nothing but the wage of his labour, or certainly is always at work and toil in order to receive the wage of his labour, so all the glory of Kedar, which means darkness, of which we read in the Psalm too, I have dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar (Ps 119 [120]:5), shall swiftly be taken away; […]

22:1.t: For not in every house are there vessels of gold and silver, but in most there are wooden ones; nor is every house full; for there are empty ones too, which the prophet knew, who said: What has happened to you now, that you have gone up into empty houses? The city is filled with those crying out. And he added: All your princes have fled, all who were wounded in you and have fallen from faith into unbelief. Sabellius was wounded, Valentinus was wounded, Arius was wounded; for they were found in an empty house.

The burden of the valley of Vision. The Seventy, although it is not found in the Hebrew, translated more plainly, the word of the valley of Zion. For this city is the seedbed of the prophets, in which the Temple was built and the Visions of the Lord were multiplied. Because, then, it is placed among the other nations and reckoned as one of many, it is by no means called a mountain, according to that prophetic saying: Its foundations are on the holy mountains: the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob (Ps 86 [87]:1); but a valley, because it has been humbled. Jeremiah says this very thing in other words, when he receives the cup full of wine and gives it to all the nations, and last of all holds it out to Jerusalem, that it may drink and vomit and fall and go mad: signifying that it too was to be laid waste by the Babylonians (Jer 25). The history of Kings and of Jeremiah tells this more fully. […]

The burden of the valley of vision. LXX: The word of the valley of Zion. In the book of Hebrew Names we have set down that Zion means watchtower, which, set on high places, beholds from afar the things that are coming. Since, then, Zion, according to the laws of tropology, is referred to the Church, as in that saying of the second Psalm in the person of the Lord the Savior, But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain (Ps 2:6); and, Those who trust in the Lord are as Mount Zion (Ps 124 [125]:1); and, The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob (Ps 86 [87]:2); and more plainly the Apostle: You have come, he says, to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22): we ask why in the present vision it is called the valley of Zion. […]

We do not wish to be valleys of Zion, but mountains of Zion. For Zion has its valleys, it has also its plains. Whoever is a sinner is a valley of Zion, he is not a mountain of Zion. Someone may say: You are speaking from your own opinion. Let us call Isaiah as a witness, at the time when Zion had sinned, after many visions, where it is said, A vision against Idumaea, a vision against Moab, a vision against Edom and the sons of Ammon, at the last is placed: 'A vision of the valley of Zion'. For because it had descended from the height of faith, therefore it collapsed from a mountain into a valley.

What is it with you too, that you also have gone up, all of you, onto the housetops, full of clamor, a crowded city, an exultant town? A Hebrew used to tell me that the present Vision does not belong to the time when Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem and led Zedekiah, bound and deprived of his eyes, to Babylon, but to the times of Sennacherib, when Shebna the high priest betrayed a great part of the city, and only Zion, that is, the citadel and the Temple, and the nobles remained, after the example of the city of Rome, which, when the Gauls burst in, preserved its patricians and the flower of its youth in the citadel. But we can also speak of it as of the Babylonian captivity; although Eusebius refers everything to the coming of Christ, and thinks it was fulfilled in the times of Vespasian and Titus. Let us then pick out each point, touching briefly on the threefold exposition. What is it with you too? What do you have, he says, O Zion, that you too have gone up, all of you, onto the housetops? […]

22:2.t: Now is the time to quote the words of the prophet and to say, “Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people.” Though they are wrapped in profound silence and lie stunned by their misfortune, robbed of all sense of feeling by the fatal blow, I at all events must not let such a fall go unlamented. If, to Jeremiah, it seemed that those whose bodies had been wounded in war, were worthy of innumerable lamentations, what shall be said of such a disaster of souls? “My slain men,” it is said, “are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle.” But I am bewailing the sting of the real death, the grievousness of sin and the fiery darts of the wicked one, which have savagely set on fire souls as well as bodies.

Full of clamour, a crowded city, an exulting town. LXX: The city is filled with those who cry out, an exulting city. The teaching of the heretics consists not in sense but in much speaking and clamour. Hence, on account of the multitude of those deceived, it is called a crowded city, and exulting on account of its pride. For being puffed up they swell, and boast that they have found holier things.

Your slain are not slain by the sword, nor dead in battle. LXX: Your wounded are not wounded by the sword, nor are your dead dead in battle. The greatest part is overthrown by the deceptions of the heretics without any struggle or debate, and this is a very great crowd. The slain, then, or as the Seventy translated, the wounded of the valley of Zion are not slain and wounded by the sword, but have gone over to the heretics of their own will; and in comparison with those who are overcome after battle, he is the more unhappily wounded and slain who has surrendered of his own accord. […]

Your slain are not slain by the sword, nor dead in war. All your princes have fled together, and have been harshly bound. All who were found have been bound together: they have fled far away. If you refer it to the times of Sennacherib, when the city was partly taken, they are rightly said not to have been conquered by the sword nor slain in war, but by treachery, some fleeing from the city, and others, whom the enemy overpowered, bound in chains. But if to the Babylonian captivity, which is also the truer view, we shall say that they were overcome not by battle but by siege. And if you wish to understand it tropologically, with Eusebius, of the coming of Christ, you will say that they were slain not by the sword but by unbelief, and that all their princes withdrew from God and were bound with the cords of sins, and that there was none of the Pharisees who was not bound in the nets of the devil.

22:3.t: All your princes have fled together, and have been harshly bound. In this place we have followed the translation of the Seventy, because in sense it is not far from the Hebrew. But to translate word for word from the Hebrew, it reads thus among them: All your chief men have departed together, they have been bound by the bow; and the other translators also followed this edition. For all the princes of the heretics have departed from the Church of Christ to the synagogue of Satan, and have gone over together, discordant in faithlessness, concordant in desertion; and they have been bound by the bow, of which it is written in the Psalm: Behold, the sinners have bent the bow, they have made ready their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in the dark at the upright of heart (Ps 10 [11]:2), and to send the fiery darts of the devil, which both wound and bind. […]

22:4.t: Grief is often capable of refreshing distressed souls, and of rendering a burdened conscience light: consider how often women, when they have lost their most beloved children, break their hearts, and perish, if they are forbidden to mourn, and to shed tears. But if they do all which those who are sad, are wont to do, they are relieved, and receive consolation. And what wonder that this should be the case with women, when you may even see a prophet affected in a similar manner? Therefore he was continually saying, "Suffer me—I will weep bitterly—labour not to comfort me, because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people." So that, oftentimes, sadness is the bearer of consolation; and if it is so with regard to this world, much more with regard to spiritual things.

Therefore I said: Depart from me, I will weep bitterly: do not press to console me over the devastation of the daughter of my people. If at the devastation of Babylon the Prophet weeps with the feeling of a mourner, and says: Anguish has possessed me, like the anguish of a woman giving birth: I fell down when I heard, I was troubled when I saw, my heart has withered, darkness has stupefied me: Babylon my beloved has been made a wonder to me, how much more now, at the ruin of his own city, can he accept no consolation, giving himself wholly to lamentation!

Therefore I said: Depart from me, I will weep bitterly; do not press to comfort me over the devastation of the daughter of my people. For it is a day of slaughter and of trampling and of weeping from the Lord God of hosts in the valley of vision, searching the wall, and magnificent upon the mountain. LXX: Therefore I said: Let me alone, I will weep bitterly; do not strive to comfort me over the breaking of the daughter of my race; for it is a day of tumult and of perdition and of trampling, and error from the Lord God Sabaoth in the valley of Zion; they err from the least to the greatest, they err upon the mountains. Samuel too mourned for Saul (1 Sam 15), and the Lord and Savior wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19; 2 Cor 12:21); and the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: Lest, when I come to you again, God humble me, and I mourn for many who sinned before and have not done penance. Hence, with the feeling of one who suffers with them, he says to others also: Who is weak, and I am not weak? […]

22:5.t: For it is a day of slaughter, and of trampling, and of weeping, for the Lord God of hosts in the Valley of vision. He gives the reasons, according to the threefold understanding, why he said: Depart from me, I will weep bitterly: because Zion has been trampled down, once the mountain of visions and now the valley of weeping.

For the day of judgment and slaughter and trampling will by no means be Jerusalem, which means vision of peace, but of its ancient name Jebus, which means trampling; a day of weeping too, or of error, as the Seventy translated, from the Lord Sabaoth: not that weeping and error come from the Lord, but through the occasion of the holy Scriptures, which the Lord gave to be read, an occasion of error arises for those who can say: Why have you made us err from your way? (Isa 63:17). And in another place: The Lord has mingled for them a spirit of error (ibid. 29:10): so that they should stand not on the mountain of Vision but in the valley of Zion. And this very day, which arises from the Lord of hosts in the valley of Vision to show the works of each, searches the wall of the heretics, which they have built against the Church like a most solid rampart; […]

Searching the wall, and magnificent upon the mountain: and Elam took up the quiver, the chariot of a horseman, and the shield laid bare the wall. The army of Babylon is described entering the city, occupying the temple, and proudly driving through the streets in four-horse chariots. And that the shield, which is wont to cover other things, laid bare the gilded doorposts and the walls clad with marble facing, sounds elegantly in the Hebrew, and the sense is most beautiful: that the shield protected no one, but laid bare, since all the riches were torn out by the strength of the soldiers. If, however, the Elamites are set in the battle, Elam being a city of the Assyrians, it cannot be referred to the times of the Roman overthrow, unless perhaps we interpret everything allegorically.

22:6.t: And Elam took up the quiver, the chariot of a man, a horseman, and the shield laid bare the wall. And your choice valleys shall be full of chariots, and the horsemen shall set their seats in the gate. And the covering of Judah shall be uncovered, and you shall see in that day the armoury of the house of the forest; and you shall see the breaches of the city of David, that they are multiplied. LXX: But the Elamites took quivers, riders, men upon horses, and a gathering of fighters; and your choice valleys shall be filled with chariots, and horsemen shall throng your gates; and they shall uncover the gates of Judah, and they shall look on that day into the choice houses of the city; and they shall uncover the hidden things of the houses of the citadel of David, and they shall see that they are many. Elam, which means their ascent, or the Elamites, as the Seventy translated, whom we render despisers, took up the quiver to shoot in the dark at the upright of heart; […]

These Elamites, according to the edition of the Seventy, have not one quiver but several; and they are riders of men, on whose souls they ride; and there is a very great multitude preparing itself for battle against the Church, so that all its valleys are filled; and the horsemen stop up their senses, and by their combat challenge to the contest the churchman, who is interpreted Judah; and when he brings forward the testimonies of the Scriptures and refutes all lies, the heretics will see the houses of the city of David, and will come to know all the things formerly secret: how in the citadel of David, which means strong of hand, that is, of Christ, are all the doctrines of truth. The places are obscure, not only according to the history but according to the ἀναγωγὴν. Those, then, whom our views displease ought to bring forward their own, so that we may acquiesce in their explanation, if it is true.

22:7.t: And your choice valleys, he says, and your lowly doctrines, O valley of Zion, shall be full of chariots, those which the Lord sank with Pharaoh, whose horsemen and riders shall set their seats in your gates, so as not to let those besieged and shut up in you go out.

And your choice valleys will be full of chariots, and the horsemen will set their seats at the gate. And the covering of Judah will be uncovered, and you will see in that day the armory of the house of the forest, and you will see the breaches of the city of David, that they have been multiplied. He plainly describes the captivity which took place in the eleventh year of King Zedekiah, of which Jeremiah too speaks: Behold, I will call together all the families of the kingdoms of the North, says the Lord, and they will come, and each will set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, and upon all its walls round about (Jer 1:15). And lest we should think this foretold in word and not fulfilled in deed, the same Jeremiah says: In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the fifth of the month, the city was opened, and all the princes of the king of Babylon entered, and sat in the middle gate (Jer 39:2). […]

22:8.t: Then almighty God, through churchmen, shall uncover the coverings of Judah and all the secrets of those who stand in the confession of the faith; and then, O valley of Zion, in that day and in the clear light of truth, you shall see the whole armour of the Apostle, and of the house of the forest, in which the throng of the nations stands; as it is sung also in Psalm 131 (132): Behold, we have heard of it in Ephrathah; we have found it in the fields of the forest (Ps 131 [132]:6). And when the covering and secret of Judah, which formerly was hidden on account of the mystery, has been uncovered, and you have seen the armour of the Church, then you will understand the schisms of the city of David, which you have multiplied in order to gather to yourself deceived peoples.

22:9.t: And you gathered the waters of the lower pool, and you numbered the houses of Jerusalem, and you destroyed houses to fortify the wall. And you made a reservoir between the two walls, and the water of the old pool: and you did not look up to him who had made it, and you did not see its maker from afar. He relates how they prepared the city for the siege: they transferred the waters of the lower pool, which could be captured, to the upper fortification; they destroyed houses and built walls; family by family they reckoned up how much water each house should receive; they made a cistern between the two walls, and restored the old pool to store the waters; and they did not rather call upon the help of God, who is the founder of the city and the Lord of the pool; as if he had said in other words: You have placed your trust in man, and not in God, who is the maker of man. […]

And you gathered the waters of the lower pool, and you numbered the houses of Jerusalem, and you pulled down houses to fortify the wall. And you made a reservoir between the two walls, and the water of the old pool; and you did not look to him who had made it, and you did not see its maker from afar. LXX: And they turned the water of the ancient pool into the city, and they pulled down the houses of Jerusalem to strengthen the walls of the city; and you made yourselves water between the two walls within the ancient pool; and you did not look to him who made it from the beginning, and you did not see its creator. You who will see, or do see, the breaches of the city of David, that is, of the Church, which have been multiplied throughout the whole world; […]

22:12.t: And in that day the Lord God of hosts shall call to weeping and to mourning, to baldness and to the girding of sackcloth; and behold joy and gladness, killing calves and slaughtering rams, eating flesh and drinking wine: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. And it was revealed in my ears by the Lord of hosts: Surely this iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die, says the Lord God of hosts. Daily the Lord God of hosts calls to repentance the heretics, who, despising the water of the old pool between the two walls, have dug themselves a reservoir and gathered the water of the lower pool, which has its waters not from heaven but from the earth; and he calls them to weeping, for blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh (Matt 5:5); and to mourning, lest afterwards they hear: We have lamented to you, and you have not mourned (ibid. 11:17); and to baldness, that they may shave off all the works of death, and remove from their body whatever does not live in the body; […]

And the Lord God of hosts will call in that day to weeping, and to lamentation, and to baldness, and to the girding of sackcloth. And behold, joy and gladness, slaying calves and slaughtering rams, eating flesh and drinking wine: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. And it has been revealed in my ears by the Lord of hosts: If this iniquity will be forgiven you until you die, says the Lord God of hosts. When the captivity was at hand and Jerusalem besieged, while sword, famine and thirst pressed hard upon the city, Jeremiah called the people to repentance (Jer 34); and on the contrary the kings and princes, and the wretched multitude, with the despair of men perishing, gave themselves over to feasting. But nothing so offends God as a stiff neck after sins, and contempt born of despair. This he says through Amos too: For three and for four impieties I will not turn him back: because he both devised it and did it, and did not repent, and moreover taught evil. […]

22:13.t: That too great lust of food is not to be desired. In Isaiah: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. This sin shall not be atoned for to you, even until you die." Also in Exodus: "And the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play." Paul, in the first [letter] to the Corinthians: "Food does not commend us to God; neither if we eat shall we abound, nor if we do not eat shall we lack." And again: "When you come together to eat, wait one for another. If any is hungry, let him eat at home, that you may not come together for judgment." Also to the Romans: "The kingdom of God is not food and drink but righteousness and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit." In the Gospel according to John: "I have food of which you don't know. My food is that I should do his will who sent me and should finish his work."
22:13.s: Treatise XII. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews 3:60

22:13.t: Now we say that the wicked are dead, but not in an ascetic life opposed to sin; nor do they, like the saints, bear about dying in their bodies. But it is the soul which they bury in sins and follies, drawing near to the dead, and satisfying it with dead nourishment; like young eagles which, from high places, fly upon the carcases of the dead, and which the law prohibited, commanding figuratively, ‘Thou shalt not eat the eagle, nor any other bird that feedeth on a dead carcase;’ and it pronounced unclean whatsoever eateth the dead. But these kill the soul with lusts, and say nothing but, ‘let us eat and drink, for to morrow we die.’ And the kind of fruit those have who thus love pleasures, he immediately describes, adding, ‘And these things are revealed in the ears of the Lord of Hosts, that this sin shall not be forgiven you until ye die.’ Yea, even while they live they shall be ashamed, because they consider their belly their lord; […]

Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. This was said by Isaiah the prophet on account of those who, as if there were to be nothing after death, cared only for the belly, like cattle (Isa. 22:13), as did those also who were corrupting the Corinthians.

But they, on the contrary, instead of weeping and mourning, baldness and haircloth, had joy and gladness, and, as if all things ended with death, killing calves and slaughtering rams, to eat flesh and drink wine, they spoke the words of blasphemers: While we are in the present world, let us abound in delights; for tomorrow, that is, the time to come, will be without sensation. While they were saying these things, the Lord heard the words of blasphemy, and threatened that he would not forgive this iniquity until they either die to sin and vices, or are dragged down to the underworld with their offences. This indeed can be understood not only of the heretics but of every sinner who, neglecting his sins, becomes worse through despair, and, ensnared by pleasures, joins blasphemy to sin, so as to think that all the sensation of the living ends with death, saying that saying of Epicurus: "After death there is nothing, and death itself is nothing."

22:15.t: Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Go, enter in to him who dwells in the tabernacle, to Shebna who is over the temple, and you shall say to him: What are you doing here, or as whom are you here? For you have hewn yourself a tomb here; you have hewn a memorial on high carefully, a tabernacle for yourself in the rock. Behold, the Lord will cause you to be carried away as a cock is carried away, and he will lift you up like a garment. Crowning, he will crown you with tribulation; like a ball he will cast you into a land wide and spacious: there you shall die, and there shall be the chariot of your glory, the shame of the house of your Lord. And I will drive you from your station, and depose you from your ministry. And it shall come to pass in that day that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and I will clothe him with your tunic, and strengthen him with your girdle, and I will give your power into his hand; and he shall be as a father to those who dwell in Jerusalem, and to the house of Judah. […]

And what almost escaped us in the haste of dictation: Shebna means turn now, or conversion. It is said, therefore, to the prince of the Jews, that he should turn from the Law to the Gospel, and, forsaking the images of the victims, pass over to the truth of the spiritual sacrifice.

The Prophet, then, is commanded to go in to the high priest, who dwelt, according to the Seventy, in the pastophorium; according to Aquila, in the tabernacle; for which Theodotion, following the Hebrew truth, says: Go in to this Socen, which can be interpreted fair and upright (so that, namely, κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν, unjust and crooked is to be understood), to the high priest of the temple, and you will say to him: You who dwell in the house of God, whose crimes run riot through the whole city, why are you secure in your works, as though you did not fear captivity? Have you hewn yourself a tomb in the rock, and built so proudly that your ambition should follow you even in death?

Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Go, enter in to him who dwells in the tabernacle, to Shebna, who is over the Temple, and you will say to him: What are you doing here? or as whom are you here, that you have hewn out a tomb for yourself here? You have hewn out a monument on high, a tabernacle for yourself carefully in the rock. Behold, the Lord will cause you to be carried away, as a cock is carried away, and he will lift you up like a cloak. Crowning, he will crown you with tribulation; like a ball he will throw you into a broad and spacious land: there you will die, and there will be the chariots of your glory, the shame of the house of your Lord. And I will drive you out from your station, and depose you from your ministry. And it will come to pass in that day, I will call my servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah. And I will clothe him with your tunic, and strengthen him with your girdle, and I will give your power into his hand: and he will be like a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. […]

Those who take everything according to ἀναγωγὴν would have the priesthood of the Jews fall in the high priesthood of Shebna, and the mysteries of the Gospel worship shown in the succession of Eliakim, which means God rising again: so that what follows: In that day, says the Lord of hosts, the peg that had been fixed in the sure place will be removed, and it will be broken and fall, pertains to the ruin of the former people. And no one doubts, both according to the history and according to the allegory, that, because he had said peg, the metaphor is kept in the hanging up of vessels of different kinds; and that when the former have been broken, others are hung up.

22:16.t: To this tradition and teaching, then, it is said: What are you doing here? Why do you wish to build yourself a house in the letter that kills, and to fix your tabernacle, which has no foundation, in the firmness of the rock, which ought to be called not so much a tabernacle and a house as a tomb and a memorial?

22:17.t: And I tell you this because you ought not to toil at hewing a tomb, since the Lord will carry away your priesthood, as GEBER (גבר) is wont to be carried, which all have translated man. But the Hebrew who instructed us in the reading of the Old Testament rendered it cock. As a cock, he says, is carried from one place to another on the shoulder of a porter, so the Lord will lightly carry you away from your place.

Hear what the Lord's sentence upon you is: as a cock is carried off on the shoulder of the one carrying it, and men each lift their cloak onto the shoulder, so your removal into captivity will be easy. You will have a crown, not of the golden plate and of the sanctification of the Lord, but of tribulation and anguish. For as a ball, if it is thrown down a slope, cannot stand still but rolls on in swift course, so you too will be led away to a most broad land, which we may understand as either Egypt or the plains of Babylonia, and there you will die; and there will be the chariots of your glory, all the powers and riches on which you now lean as you go about. There you will feel the shame of the house of your Lord: because you will suffer these things on account of your evil works and the violation of the Temple of your God.

22:18.t: And you who once had the crown of the high priest, and the sanctification on the plate of gold on which the name of God was written (Exod 28), shall be crowned with tribulation and distress. And as a ball, if it is thrown down a sloping and spacious place, cannot stand still but rolls on without end, so all your people shall be scattered to the ends of the world. And there you shall die with your letter, and all your glory, and the chariots in which you were formerly borne in renown; and the splendour of the house of God shall be turned into shame.

22:19.t: For the Lord shall take you away from your station and from your ministry, that is, from the ceremonies of the victims, so that what is written to the Hebrews may be fulfilled: For when the priesthood is changed, there must of necessity be a change of the law also (Heb 7:12).

I will drag you down from your rank and cast you out of the office of high priest, and in your place I will clothe Eliakim my servant, son of Hilkiah, with your garments, and adorn him with your girdle, just as Eleazar was clothed with the garments of his father Aaron. To him I will give the authority of the Temple, so that he may have the people, not subject to him as a slave, but loving him as a son.

22:20.t: And when you have been cast out of your ministry, I will call my servant Eliakim, to whom I have said in another place also: It is a great thing for you to be called my servant (Isa 49:6, LXX). Eliakim means God rising again, or the resurrection of God. This God rising again, then, who is the son of Hilkiah, that is, of the portion of the Lord, shall receive your place, and shall be clothed with your robe and strengthened with your girdle, so that what you had in the letter he may possess in the spirit; and he shall be the father of those who dwell in Jerusalem, that is, in the vision of peace, which is interpreted as the Church, and to the house of Judah, where the true confession of faith is. Hence he himself says to the Apostles: Little children, yet a little while I am with you (John 13:33). And to another: Son, your sins are forgiven you (Matt 9:2). And to another woman: Daughter, your faith has made you whole (Luke 7:50).

22:22.t: He will receive the key of my house, and carry it on his shoulder; he will have authority over all the ceremonies.

I will give him, he says, the key of the house of David, he who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens (Rev 3). And this very key shall be upon his shoulder, that is, in his passion, according to what is written in another place: Whose government is upon his shoulder (Isa 9:6). For what he has unlocked by his passion cannot be shut; and what he has shut in the ceremonies of the Jews shall be opened by no one else.

22:23.t: And as, when a peg is fixed in the wall of the Temple and set in a very firm place, all the vessels of the priests and Levites are hung upon it, both those needed in the sacrifices and those of the musicians of every kind, so the whole people will hang upon the authority of Eliakim my servant.

For I will fasten him as a peg in a sure place, where the assembly of the Faithful is; hence too those who believe in Christ are called the faithful. And he shall be for a throne of glory of his father's house, that is, of the Church; and they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father's house. Hence it is written in the Gospel also: All the people hung upon him (Luke 19). And this indeed was done not only at that time, but is fulfilled to this day, so that there hang upon him, as it were, divers vessels of God: wisdom and righteousness and all the things by which Christ is called. Divers kinds of vessels: for these Aquila translated SASAIM (צאצאים) and SEPHOTH (הצפעית), which Symmachus rendered grandsons and mixed ones, so that the Apostles and all believers, that is, the sons of sons, and those mixed from all the nations, may hang upon him. From the vessels of bowls, for which Theodotion set down AGANOTH (אגנות): for both small and great shall believe in the Lord. […]

22:25.t: And as for his saying: In that day the peg that had been fixed in the sure place will be removed, and it will be broken and fall, and what had hung upon it will perish, because the Lord has spoken, many refer it to Shebna: that when Eliakim had been fixed as a peg, the former peg, which had been fixed, collapsed. But since there follows: And what had hung upon it will perish, which by no means happened when Shebna was cast down, we understand this to be said: that when Shebna was deposed, Eliakim received the high priesthood, the dignity of whose priesthood the final captivity overthrew.

What follows seems contrary to our sense: how this peg, which had been fastened in a sure place, is taken away and broken, and what had hung upon it falls and perishes, and this happens because the Lord has spoken. This can be resolved thus, if we read that saying of the Gospel, that in the last days the love of many shall grow cold (Matt 24), and the Lord himself says: Do you think the Son of man, when he comes, will find faith upon the earth? (Luke 18:8). It is not, then, the peg that will be broken and fall and perish, which it is impious to say; but the peg will be taken away from the sure place, that is, from the Church, through the impiety that daily grows up, and those who before hung upon him by faith will afterwards through unbelief be broken and fall and perish. And this shall happen in the last days, because the Lord has spoken. For peg, which in Hebrew is called JATHED (יתד), and is rendered alike by all, the Seventy alone translated above prince, and here man.

23:1.t: The burden of Tyre. Howl, you ships of the sea, for the house is laid waste from which they were wont to come: from the land of Cethim it has been revealed to them. Be silent, you who dwell in the island, the merchandise of Sidon. The prophet Ezekiel sets forth more plainly and more fully both the overthrow of Tyre and the causes of the overthrow, saying: Son of man, because Tyre has said of Jerusalem: Aha, the gates of the peoples are broken, she has turned to me, I shall be filled, she is deserted. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, O Tyre, and I will cause many nations to come up against you, as the sea comes up in waves, and I will scatter the walls of Tyre, and destroy its towers, and I will scrape its dust from it (Ezek 26:2ff.). […]

The word of Tyre. What we thought about the burden, or word and taking up, of Tyre according to the Hebrews, we have said above in the book of the historical explanation of the ten Visions. Now we shall run briefly through the whole prophecy against Tyre according to the ἀναγωγὴν and the edition of the Seventy. Tyre is called SOR (צר) in the Hebrew tongue, and is rendered into our speech as distress. Every soul, then, that is taken up with vices and evil thoughts can be called sor.

Howl, you ships of Carthage, for they have perished, and shall come no more. From the land of the Kittim she has been led captive. To whom are the inhabitants of the isle become like? The merchants of Phoenicia, crossing the sea in many waters, the seed of merchants like harvests brought in, the merchants of the nations. For Carthage, in the Hebrew is written THARSIS (תרשיש), which all have translated alike. And Tharsis means contemplation or searching out of joy. Kittim too, which in Hebrew is called CHETIM (כתים), means sea congealing; […]

23:2.t: And in naming it an island he does not lie: for afterwards it was made part of the mainland by Nebuchadnezzar or by Alexander, when many mounds were heaped up in the narrow strait for its capture. He also calls it the merchandise of Sidon, in keeping with the following line, in which he says: Be ashamed, O Sidon. For the histories relate that Tyre is a colony of Sidon.

Those crossing the sea have filled you; in many waters the seed of the Nile, the harvest of the river is its produce. That Tyre delights in trade and is the emporium of the whole world, both present times prove and Ezekiel describes at length. And that merchants cross the seas in carrying their goods, there is no one who doubts; nor does the city itself have such great wealth from the land of its own region, which is very narrow and hemmed in by the borders of Galilee and of Damascus, as it has from the shipping of goods.

For those who dwell in this isle are like no others than merchants, or carriers, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine and pass from one vice to another. And we dwell in an isle as long as we are beaten by the temptations of this world, and on every side our isle and little boat is struck by the waves of the sea. Now the merchants of this isle are from Sidon, which means huntress, and in which dwell very many hunters, of whom it is written: He will deliver you from the snare of the hunters (Ps 90 [91]:3). And in another place the saint rejoices that he has been delivered from their snares, saying: Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters (Ps 123 [124]:7).

23:3.t: The whole Nile and the fertility of Egypt pour into Tyre from close at hand. For Nile, which we read among the Hebrews as SIOR (שיחר), the Seventy and Theodotion interpreted merchants; this word means turbid, and by this signifies the waters of the Nile, as Jeremiah testifies: What have you to do with Egypt, that you should drink the waters of Geon? (Jer 2:18): for which in the Hebrew there is Sior, that is, turbid.

And all the merchants of the nations are compared to crops which quickly wither, or to the harvests of the river, which have their rain not from heaven but from the earth; and therefore they will perish with the nations. Where we read the seed of merchants, in the Hebrew is written the seed of sior, by which the Nile is understood, because it has turbid waters with which the crops of Egypt are watered.

23:4.t: Therefore, after being so often ploughed by returning merchants, "Be ashamed, O Sidon, has said the sea." This is the voice of the fatigued element, as it were, saying, "Be ashamed, Sidon"; that is: Merchant, you accuse my waves although you yourself are more restless than they. Blush indeed for shame since you are not disturbed by peril. More modest are the winds than your desires. They have their rests; never do your cravings for gain take holiday. Even when the weather is quiet, never are your ships quiet. The water is churned under the oar when it is at rest from the blast. "I have not been in labor," it says, "nor have I reared, nor have I nourished up young men." Why do they disquiet me whom I do not know, whom I do not acknowledge?

But this is far from the accepted opinion. As a matter of fact, the farmer cleaves the earth ‘with deep-driven plough’; ‘stripped he ploughs, stripped he sows’; stripped in the glowing ‘heat he thrashes on the floor the parched ears.’ The merchant, impatient when the east winds are blowing, ploughs the sea often when the course is unsafe. Insolent and rash men such as these are condemned by the Prophet, who says: ‘Be thou ashamed, O Sidon, the sea speaketh,’ that is to say, if dangers do not move you, then shame can check and modesty confound you. ‘Be thou ashamed, O Sidon,’ in which there is no place for virtue, no care for safety, no young men exercised in arms and ready to fight in defense of their country. They are anxiously and entirely preoccupied with gain and the benefits derived from commerce. ‘What the merchant sows, so does he reap.’

Be ashamed, O Sidon: for the sea has spoken, the strength of the sea, saying: I have not travailed, and I have not brought forth, and I have not nourished young men, nor brought up virgins. I said above that Tyre is a colony of the Sidonians. Hear, then, O mother, all the seas crying out together against your daughter, and in a manner uttering a voice, though by nature they cannot speak: In vain have I brought riches together; to no purpose have I gathered wealth from the whole world into Tyre: she that was rich, she that was luxurious, and once rejoiced in a multitude of peoples, in which a throng of mortals was born, a troop of children, swarms of youth, whose streets rang with the games of virgins and infants, of young men and girls, has now been reduced to solitude. It is customary to make προσωποποιΐας out of mute things.

Be ashamed, O Sidon, said the sea; and the strength of the sea said: I have not travailed, nor brought forth, nor nourished young men, nor brought up virgins. And when it is heard in Egypt, pain shall seize them over Tyre. The sea of this world, in which dwell small animals with great, and the dragon which God formed to be mocked, seeing that those who had formerly been taken by the demons have been taken by the hunters of Christ, who hunt from every mountain and hill, speaks to the opposing power of the hunters, which Sidon means, and says to it: Be ashamed, O Sidon; for I have not travailed nor brought forth, nor nourished the young men taken by you, nor brought up the virgins whose folly is condemned in the Gospel (Matt 25). For my travail and childbearing, and my nourishing and bringing up of virgins, have been blotted out by the travail of the Apostles of Christ, one of whom said: My little children, of whom I travail again until Christ be formed in you (Gal 4:19). […]

Sidon is brought to shame, as it were, by the voice of the sea, when the life of one who is fortified and supposedly steadfast is reprobated in comparison with the lives of those who are worldly and are being tossed about in this world. For often there are those who, returning to the Lord after their sins of the flesh, evince themselves the more zealous in doing good works, as they realize they were worthy of condemnation for their deeds. And often certain people who persevere in preserving the integrity of the flesh, on perceiving that they have less to deplore, think to themselves that the innocence of their lives is sufficient and do not arouse themselves by zealously striving to be fervent in spirit.

Divine Providence has compassed us about and cut off all excuse. All openings to people's equivocating arts are in every way closed. A Gentile, one without the law, is brought forward to confound the iniquity of those that are under the law; which is well and summarily shown by the prophet, when he says, "Be ashamed, O Sidon, says the sea." For in Sidon we have a figure of the steadfastness of those settled upon the foundation of the law, and in the sea of the life of the Gentiles. Accordingly, "Be ashamed, O Sidon, says the sea," because the life of those under the law is convicted by the life of Gentiles, and the conduct of people in a state of religion is put to confusion by the conduct of those living in the world, so long as the first do not, even under vows, observe what they hear enjoined in precepts. The latter by their manner of life keep those ways so that they are not in any wise bound by legal enactments.
23:4.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Preface to Book 1, Section 5

23:5.t: When it has been heard in Egypt, they will grieve when they hear of Tyre. This is plain: that the Egyptians, after they have heard that a most mighty and neighboring nation has been destroyed by a long siege, know that destruction is drawing near to them too.

When Egypt hears this, which in Hebrew is called MESRAIM (מצרים), which means ἐκθλίβουσα, that is, afflicting and constraining, it too will be terrified, understanding that it too will suffer the same things that Tyre has suffered. And while this is referred to all vices, it can also be perceived in the diversity of the heresies, when, one heresy being taken, another trembles, and in the confusion of one the other perceives that it is to be taken. And as it is said of Sodom: For if the signs had been done in them which were done in Capernaum, they would have remained until this day; and it is added: But it shall be more tolerable for Sodom in the day of judgment than for you: so we learn of Tyre and Sidon, the Savior saying: But it shall be lighter for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for that city (Matt 11:21ff.). Hence too the Canaanite woman, who understood that her daughter, that is, her soul, was grievously vexed by a demon, is said to have come out of the borders of Tyre and Sidon to pray to Christ. […]

23:6.t: Cross the seas, howl, you who dwell in the island. Again, for sea and Tharsis the Seventy translated Carthage. We read in the histories of the Assyrians that the besieged Tyrians, when they saw no hope of escape, embarked on ships and fled to Carthage, or to other islands of the Ionian and Aegean sea. Hence too it is said in Ezekiel: No wage has been paid to him, nor to his army, for Tyre (Ezek 29): because all the wealth of the city had been carried away, and all the nobles had left it empty.

Go to Carthage; howl, you who dwell in this isle. Is not this your disgrace from the beginning, before she was delivered up? Her feet shall lead her far off to sojourn. What follows, Her feet shall lead her far off to sojourn, has been added from the Hebrew, and is marked beforehand with an asterisk, that is, with shining stars. O Tyrians, you who dwell in distress and abide in an isle, exposed on every side to the waves of temptations, depart from it, and go to Carthage, that is, Tharsis, and hasten to true joy, mourning your old sins and the ancient disgrace which you either inflicted on others or suffered from them. And I command this because you see Tyre, your city, about to move from its seats and purpose to other borders, when, having laid aside their old error, they have bowed their necks to the Gospel of the Savior; so that those who formerly dwelt in distress may depart far off and become sojourners and dwellers in the teaching of the Lord the Savior.

23:7.t:
Is not this yours, which gloried from the days of old in its antiquity? He convicts Tyre of pride, because it gloried in the antiquity of its founding and did not look to God, but, recalling the names of its fathers, thought itself eternal.

Its own feet will lead it far away to sojourn abroad. He means those who had remained in the city and were led captive to Babylon.

23:8.t:
Who has devised this against Tyre, once crowned? Read Ezekiel again (Ezek 27), and you will learn from the lament over its prince how great the glory of Tyre was. He calls it crowned because, as a king among a great multitude of men raises his head adorned with a diadem, so Tyre, gleaming and lofty in riches, and shining with gold and gems and silk and purple, was esteemed a queen among all nations.

Whose merchants are princes, its traders the renowned of the earth. We marvel that the envoy of Pyrrhus once said of the city of Rome: I have seen a city of kings. Behold, long before those times the merchants and traders of Tyre are described as princes and renowned men: so that by this the greatness of its opulence is shown, since a merchant of Tyre could be a king in the other's words.

Who has purposed these things against Tyre? Is she less, or does she not prevail? Her merchants are princes of Canaan, the renowned of the earth. The Lord Sabaoth has purposed to dissolve all the insolence of those who glory, and to dishonour all that is renowned upon the earth. The word Canaan has been added from the edition of Theodotion; for it Aquila translated merchants. The Holy Spirit therefore asks, or rather by the question affirms, that the Lord has purposed these things against the princes of Tyre, whose whole industry is to seek wealth by trading. And as in the Gospel we read of dealers in pearls (Matt 13), who, having sold all, long to buy one pearl, and who surely are to be called renowned merchants, not of earth but of heaven, so, on the contrary, the merchants of Tyre, that is, of tribulation and distress, are to be called the renowned of the earth, because whatever they do looks to the earth; and princes of Canaan, which means tossed about and shaken. […]

23:9.t: The Lord of hosts has devised this, to pull down the pride of all glory, and to bring into ignominy all the renowned of the earth. Because above, in the manner of one asking, he had said: Who has devised this against Tyre, once crowned?, now he himself answers: It is not that the threads of the fates have been spun thus, as fools think; it is not that the wheel of fortune has run; but it has been accomplished by the judgment of God and by his will, who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Jas 4); and he reminds the arrogant of their condition, so that through misery they may learn the power of him whose clemency they had refused to feel through his benefits.

The Lord of hosts, then, purposed this counsel: to dissolve the most wicked bonds of the merchants, or rather to scatter the compacted injury through which all who are subject to Tyre grow proud. And as for what he added, and to dishonour all that is glorious upon the earth, the Lord is not the author of dishonour, but shows to be shameful what lies open to shame of itself. This indeed we read in Leviticus also concerning the Priests: With defilement he has defiled him (Lev 21), the priest, no doubt: not that he is the author of the defilement, but that he shows him to be defiled who formerly seemed clean to very many.

23:10.t: Pass through your land like a river, daughter of the sea: there is no girdle for you any more. As, he says, a river, or, as the Hebrew has it more expressively, a stream, for it is called IOR (יאר), is easily crossed on foot, so you too, led into captivity, will pass through your land, O daughter of the sea, either because you are an island, or because it was written of you above: The sea has spoken, the strength of the sea: I have not travailed, and I have not brought forth. And what sense his next words have, there is no girdle for you any more, Symmachus teaches more openly: you will no longer be able to resist, that is, you will not have the strength, nor your loins girded for fighting, so as to be able to go out against your adversaries.

Work your land; for ships no longer come from Carthage, and your hand no longer prevails, which provokes kings on the sea. The edition of the Seventy differs greatly in this place from the other translators and from the Hebrew itself; but let us pursue our purpose. Above he had said: Go to Carthage; howl, you who dwell in the isle. Now he says the opposite: since ships no longer come from Carthage, work your land. For it profited Tyre that the foreign ships perished, so that she is compelled to work her own land, of which it is said in the Proverbs: He who works his land shall be filled with bread (Prov 12:11): so that she may live not from the uncertain hazard of the waves and of shipwrecks, but from the fruits of her own work, of which it is sung in the psalms to the righteous man: You shall eat the labours of your hands (Ps 127 [128]:2). […]

23:11.t: He has stretched out his hand over the sea, he has troubled kingdoms. Who stretched out his hand? From the very tenor of the discourse there is no doubt that it is God, of whom he said above: The Lord of hosts has devised this, to pull down the pride of all glory. He stretched out his hand, then, over all the seas, signifying the world and the earth, and troubled all the nations, among which you too, O Tyre, were troubled; or else over the sea, in which you are properly situated.

The Lord has given command against Canaan, to crush its strong ones. He shows what the sea is over which the Lord stretched out his hand, saying: He has given command against Canaan. For Tyre was founded in the land of Canaan. Read the Scriptures, and especially the Gospel (Mark 7), where the Syrophoenician woman, pleading for her daughter, comes out of the land of Canaan, and is called a Canaanite woman. And at the same time, because he had said: He has stretched out his hand, lest you should believe that the Lord works with limbs and by bodily function, he added, he has given command, so that for God to have done is to have commanded.

The Lord Sabaoth has commanded concerning Canaan to destroy its strength, and they shall say: You shall no more do injury and iniquity to the virgin daughter of Sidon. That Tyre and Sidon are in the land of Canaan we have shown above also, setting forth the testimony of the Gospel, in which we read that the Canaanite woman, or Syrophoenician, came out of the borders of Tyre and Sidon and met the Lord the Savior. Now every soul that is set amid the waves of the world and is carried about by every wind of doctrine is to be called Canaan, which means as it were a tossing or a shaking. Hence it is said also to the adulterous old man: Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you (Dan 13). It profits Tyre and its distresses, then, that the Canaanite strength should perish, so that it may be said to its inhabitants that they can no longer do injuries and oppress by iniquity the virgin daughter of Sidon. […]

23:12.t: And he said: You will no more glory, suffering calumny, O virgin daughter of Sidon; rise, cross over to Cethim: there too there will be no rest for you. God, who devised to pull down the pride of all glory, who gave command against Canaan to crush its strong ones, himself says: You will by no means glory any longer, nor trust in your own power. O virgin daughter of Sidon, that is, colony of the Sidonians, you will indeed flee in ships to the islands of the West, or to Cyprus, and the other lands of Macedonia and Greece; but there too, with God against you, you will not be able to find rest. Besides, everyone who is a wanderer and a stranger in the world, and of uncertain abode, is always in straits, continually in grief.

If you go to the Kittim, not even there shall there be rest for you; and if to the land of the Chaldeans, it too has been laid waste by the Assyrians. Siim founded it; they set up its ramparts, they raised its tower: its wall has fallen. What follows has been added from the edition of Theodotion under asterisks: Siim founded it; they set up its ramparts; they raised its tower; and joined without asterisks: its wall has fallen. The Kittim are interpreted a stroke consummated or perfect; the Chaldeans in this place, as it were breasts; the Assyrians, reproving. The etymology of Siim we too have not been able to find, and the other translators rendered it by the very name with which it is written among the Hebrews. It is said, therefore, to Tyre, that although she strive to go to the Kittim and avoid the stroke of her distresses, she cannot find perfect rest even there. […]

23:13.t: Behold the land of the Chaldeans, such a people there was not: Assyria founded it for captivity; they carried away its mighty men, they undermined its houses, they made it a ruin. Howl, you ships of the sea, for your strength has been laid waste. Because he had said above: Its own feet will lead it far away to sojourn abroad; and again, Pass through your land like a river; and because the people of Tyre was twofold, those who had fled and crossed over to Cethim, and those who had remained in the city, he speaks to both. Of those who had fled he said above: Rise, cross over to Cethim, there too there will be no rest for you. Of those who had remained and were led into captivity: Behold, he says, the inhabitants of the land of the Chaldeans, whose power no peoples had before, and which was founded by the Assyrian, have carried away the mighty men of Tyre. They undermined not only the walls but all the dwellings of the city, and made it a ruin. […]

23:14.t: "Howl," he says—he repeats it—"O you ships of Carthage, for your strength is laid waste. And it shall come to pass in that day, Tyre shall be abandoned;" and below, "but after seventy years, Tyre shall be as the song of a harlot." Behold what words the prophet employs, and how he does not avoid the baseness of words of this kind. We ourselves sometimes avoid them, not because our tongue is more chaste than theirs, but our authority inferior. For very great is the force of words in the vivid exposition of such things, so that they who do not blush at their sins blush at least at the names of their sins. "Tyre shall be," he says, "as the song of a harlot." Beware, lest, when someone sees those dances being performed, and unseemly words being sung, he says, "Behold, Tyre has become the song of a harlot."

Furthermore, the Hebrews claim that Tarshish generally represents the sea, as in the psalms: "With a violent wind, you will destroy the ships of Tarshish," that is, the sea, and in Isaiah: "Wail, ships of Tarshish." I recall speaking about this several years ago in a letter to Marcella. The prophet, therefore, was not seeking to flee to a specific place, but he was hastening to continue toward wherever it was the sea would take him. Indeed, a terrified fugitive is rightly more interested in seizing the first opportunity to sail than he is in selecting a place of refuge. This also we are able to say: he who thought that "God is known in Judea" only and that "his name is great in Israel" only, once he felt him in the waves of the sea, confessed and said, "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord of heaven who made the sea and the dry land." But if he made the sea and the dry land, how can you who abandoned the dry land think it possible to avoid the Creator of the sea in the midst of the sea? […]

Howl, you ships of Carthage, for your strength has perished. The ships of Carthage, that is, of Tharsis, are bidden to howl; for they have not, as above, perished or shall not come, but their strength has perished. For Tharsis, according to another interpretation, is rendered into our tongue consummation of six, or of gladness. Now we read that this world was made in six days, and according to the traditions of the Church it will afterwards be consummated. All the goods of this world, then, and the whole labour of mortals, are compared to the uncertain course of ships, because they will quickly perish, and all the strength of those who sail will be dissolved. Hence it is written in Solomon also: The wise man has gone up to strong cities, and has destroyed their fortifications (Prov 21:22). For whatever is composed by the art of the heretics, of worldly wisdom, and of opposing doctrines, the churchman destroys, and teaches that it is subject to his feet.

23:15.t: On this account he was the overshadowing Cherub; who destroyed the Prince of Tyre, because he rejoiced over the children of Israel, for that they were carried away captive from their land, and because his heart was exalted. This Tyre also lay waste seventy years like Jerusalem which sat in desolation seventy years. For Isaiah said concerning it:—Tyre shall wander seventy years, as the days of one king, and shall commit fornication with all the kingdoms that are upon the face of the earth.

And it will come to pass in that day, you will be in oblivion, O Tyre, for seventy years, like the days of one king.
