From this place to the end of this prophecy prosperous things are announced to Tyre: that it ought to repent; that it is to be built again; that the overthrow of Tyre is to last only seventy years, the years during which the temple of God too was desolate: so that the city that mocked at the ruins of another should also match the time of that one's ruins. The seventy years of one king many think to be said of Nebuchadnezzar, the years during which the kingdom of the Assyrian nation continued in Jerusalem. Others think it is said in general: that he who has had a long time of reigning cannot go beyond seventy years.

And it shall come to pass in that day that Tyre shall be forsaken seventy years, as the time of one king, as the time of a man. And after seventy years Tyre shall be as the song of a harlot. Take a harp, go about, harlot city given over to forgetfulness. Play well on the harp, sing much, that you may be remembered. And after seventy years God will visit Tyre, and she shall be restored again to her former state; and her trade shall be with all the kingdoms of the world upon the face of the earth. And her trade and her hire shall be holy to the Lord; but it shall not be gathered for themselves, but for those who dwell before the Lord. All her trade, to eat and drink and be filled in common store, a memorial before the Lord. What is said, a memorial before the Lord, and upon the face of the earth, and as the time of a man, is not found in the Hebrew, but has been added in the Greek. […]

23:16.t: But after seventy years it will be for Tyre like the song of a harlot. Take a harp, go about the city, harlot given over to oblivion; sing well, repeat the song, that you may be remembered. Because you have committed fornication with very many nations, and your former lovers have despised you, desolate and naked and filthy with the squalor of captivity, take up the harp now, redouble your songs, go about the city, lament your former brothel, and wash away with tears the traces of your old error, so that you may call forth the mercy of God upon you.

23:17.t: And it will come to pass after seventy years, the Lord will visit Tyre, and will bring it back to its wages, and again it will commit fornication with all the kingdoms of the earth upon the face of the earth. That all these things were fulfilled according to the history is shown by the concordant writings of the Greeks and Phoenicians: that after seventy years it was restored and returned to its former power, and became the mart of all the nations; and these, I think, are called fornications: so that, as he who commits fornication enters the brothel and pays the wage of debauchery, so the trader, flocking in from the whole world, has filled up the beauty of the city as of a harlot.

23:18.t: And its merchandise and its wages will be sanctified to the Lord: they will not be hidden away nor laid up. For its merchandise will be for those who dwell before the Lord, that they may eat to the full and be clothed even to old age. We find that these things have not yet been done according to the history; unless perhaps it is to be thought that after the building of Jerusalem and the restoration of Tyre the cities were friendly to each other, and Tyre often sent gifts to the temple of God: as we read in Ezra too (Neh 13:16), that he drove off the Tyrians who were selling fish on the sabbath, and did not allow them to enter the city: and from this one item of trade one must judge of the rest as well. The Jews put off their vain hopes into the future, declaring that these things are to be fulfilled after the Antichrist, in the thousand years. […]

24:1.t: Behold, the Lord will scatter the earth, and will lay it bare, and will afflict its face, and will disperse its inhabitants; and as the people is, so will the priest be; and as the servant, so his master; as the handmaid, so her mistress; as the buyer, so he who sells; as the lender, so he who receives the loan; as he who demands repayment, so he who owes. With scattering the earth will be scattered, and with plundering it will be despoiled: for the Lord has spoken this word. After the particular rebuke of the individual nations, Judea, Babylon, the Philistines, Moab, Damascus, Israel, Egypt, the desert of the sea, Edom and Arabia, the valley of vision, and at the last Tyre, in the explanation of which we have said what we could, the prophetic discourse now describes what the whole world is going to suffer at the consummation, and the prophecy is by no means about the individual nations, but about all of them alike. And first, what torments the impious are going to suffer; […]

24:2.t: Then there will be no difference between noble and base, priest and layman, servant and master, handmaid and mistress, rich and poor, the lender and him who is pressed by debt, buyer and seller. For all will stand on equal terms before the judgment seat of Christ, and there will be no respect of persons with God (Rom 14; Col 3). Of this Job too speaks in almost the same words: The small and the great are there, and the servant who does not fear his master (Job 3:19). And the Savior in the Gospel, to whom all judgment has been committed, bears witness in full discourse.

We are put as guards in the vineyards, but we do not cultivate our own. When we are involved with external affairs, we neglect to watch over our own activities. I think that God suffers greater outrage from no one, dearly beloved, than from priests. Those he has placed to reprove others he sees giving an example of wickedness in their own lives. We who ought to have restrained sin, ourselves commit it. More seriously, priests who ought to give of their own possessions frequently plunder the goods of others. If they see others living humbly and chastely, they often make fun of them. Consider what will become of the flocks when wolves become shepherds! They undertake to guard the flock and are not afraid to waylay the Lord's flock.We do not seek to gain souls; we devote ourselves daily to our own pursuits, we attend to earthly matters, we strive for human praise with all our will. […]

And this indeed is what the Lord, in the wrath of just retribution, menaced through the prophet, saying, "And there shall be like people, like priest." For the priest is as the people, when one who bears a spiritual office acts as do others who are still under judgment with regard to their carnal pursuits.

What is written has surely been fulfilled in us: And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest. For the priest does not differ from the people when by no merit of his own does he transcend the common conduct.

24:3.t: The earth, therefore, will be scattered, and all earthly works will be reduced to nothing, so that, the image of the χοϊκοῦ having been abolished, the image of the heavenly may remain. For the first man was from the earth, earthly, and the second from heaven, heavenly: as is the earthly, such also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, such also are the heavenly; so that, as we have borne the image of the earthly, we may bear also the image of the heavenly (1 Cor 15:47-49). Hence the same Apostle says: Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God (ibid., 50). Not that, as the heretics say, the nature of bodies perishes, but that this corruptible puts on incorruption, and this mortal puts on immortality. And all these things will come to pass, because what is to come the Lord has spoken through the prophets.

24:4.t:
"4 b. The lofty men of the earth mourned, 5. and the earth waxed lawless through her inhabitants. 6b. Therefore, the inhabitants of the earth shall be poor, and few men shall be left."

Here again having rebuked the transgressors of the law of the covenant of God who belong to the people of the circumcision, and threatened them with what was written, he prophesies that some few men of them will be left. And these would be those named of the apostle "the remnant according to the election of grace."
24:4.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

24:4.t: The earth has mourned and has wasted away, and has been weakened; the world has wasted away, the height of the people of the earth has been weakened, and the earth has been slain by its inhabitants. LXX: The earth has mourned, the world has been corrupted, the lofty of the earth have mourned, but the earth has acted impiously because of its inhabitants. God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6). Hence the first sentence is against those who are lofty on the earth, that all things which are now strong may be weakened because of those who have mingled blood with blood, and, in the manner of the blood of Abel, have made the gore of the slain cry out to God (Gen 4).

24:5.t: Because they have transgressed the law, they have changed the ordinance, they have broken the everlasting covenant. Because of this a curse will devour the earth, and its inhabitants will sin; therefore its tillers will go mad, and few men will be left. LXX: Because they have transgressed the law, they have changed the precepts, the eternal testament. Because of this a curse will devour the earth, because its inhabitants have sinned; therefore the inhabitants of the earth will be poor, and few men will be left. Let the Jews hear, who boast that they alone have received the law of the Lord, that first all the nations and the whole world received the natural law, and that the law was given afterwards through Moses for this reason, because the first law had been broken. Of it the Apostle speaks: For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things that are of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves: who show the work of the law written in their hearts (Rom 2:14). […]

24:6.t: And as in the beginning God blessed every creature that he had made (Gen 1), so at the consummation of the world he will curse those who are earthly, and who were not sojourners but inhabitants of the earth, and sinned in it; who, forgetting their condition, have raged against one another in mutual fury. And few will remain who have the heavenly image; or, according to the Seventy, the inhabitants of the earth will be poor, because they have lost their spiritual riches.

24:7.t: The vintage has mourned, the vine has been weakened, all who were glad of heart have groaned. The joy of the timbrels has ceased, the sound of those who rejoice has been stilled, the sweetness of the harp has fallen silent; they shall not drink wine with song, the drink will be bitter to those who drink it. The city of vanity has been crushed, every house has been shut, with no one entering. There will be an outcry over wine in the streets; all gladness has been forsaken, the joy of the earth has been carried away. And desolation has been left in the city, and calamity will overwhelm the gates: for these things will be in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the peoples. At the consummation of the world, the remembrance of past delights will be the matter of torments. Hence also that rich man clothed in purple at his banquet, who had received his good things in his life, lifting up his eyes from hell, sees Lazarus at rest (Luke 16). […]

24:10.t: The city of vanity will be crushed, or every city, or the spiritual Babylon, which sits clothed in purple upon seven hills, whose punishments we read in the Apocalypse of John (Rev 18). And he did well to say the city of vanity. For if it is said of heaven and earth and of all things that are earthly: Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity (Eccl 1:2), how much more must this be said of one city, which is a small part of the whole world! Then the houses whose ceilings are now gilded, and whose walls, while the poor die of cold without roof or hut, are clothed with veneers of marble and shine with the gleam of sawn ivory, will remain empty.

24:11.t: There will be an outcry in the streets over wine, not in the strait and narrow way that leads to life, but in the broad and spacious one that leads to death (Matt 7): over the wine and drunkenness of the error of those who have slept their sleep, and all the men of riches have found nothing in their hands (Ps 75 [76]). For the joy of the earth has been carried away into heaven, and desolation has been left in the once most crowded city, and the calamity of its inhabitants will overwhelm the gates of the busy streets, through which the throngs of the peoples used to stream in.

24:13.t: And that we might know plainly that the destruction of the whole world is being announced, he added: These things will be in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the nations, or of the peoples.

As if a few olives that are left were shaken from the olive tree, and the grape clusters when the vintage is finished. These will lift up their voice and give praise; when the Lord has been glorified, they will neigh from the sea: therefore glorify the Lord in teachings, in the islands of the sea the name of the Lord God of Israel. How far the translation of the Seventy differs in this place from the Hebrew truth, the following words will show. LXX: As if someone were to shake an olive tree, so they will shake them; and if the vintage ceases, these will cry out with clamor. But those who have been left upon the earth will rejoice together with the glory of the Lord; the water of the sea will be troubled; therefore the glory of the Lord will be in the islands of the sea, the name of the Lord will be glorious, of the Lord God of Israel. […]

According to the Seventy, all that we have understood of the saints can be referred to the impious: that when the vintage is finished, then they cry out, set in punishments. But those who have escaped the number of the impious rejoice in the glory of the Lord, and the waters of the peoples of this world are troubled.

24:14.t: These, then, who remain, and after the vintage and the pressing of the world have been able to escape the hands of the persecuting Antichrist, or the burning of the impending punishment, will lift up their voices on high and will praise God. When the Lord comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels, and they see him reigning in majesty, then they will neigh in the likeness of horses, exulting in the greatness of their joy, and they will neigh from the sea of this world.

24:15.t: Therefore you who are now instructed in the Holy Scriptures, and know that such great joy and such great rewards are reserved for you, glorify the Lord in teachings, hearing that which is written: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord (2 Cor 10:17). Not at all in the land of Judea, but in the islands, that is, in the Churches of this sea and world, in which is blessed and praised the name of the Lord God of him who was once Israel, or, of the man who sees God.

24:16.t: From the ends of the earth we have heard praises, the glory of the Righteous One; and I said: My secret is mine, my secret is mine: woe is me. LXX: From the wings of the earth we have heard portents: hope for the righteous; and they will say ※ my mystery is mine ⁚. This, which is said, my mystery is mine, is not found in the Seventy, but has been added in the Greek from the translation of Theodotion. Again, for what they put as woe, so as to join it to the following verse, in the Hebrew is said OI LI (אוי לי), which properly means woe is me. Also for ends, which we have set down for the sake of explaining the sense more openly, the Hebrew has MECCHENAPH (מכנף), which means wing, not end. […]

The transgressors have transgressed, and with the transgression of transgressors they have transgressed. Terror and the pit and the snare are upon you, who are an inhabitant of the earth; and it shall be that he who flees from the voice of terror shall fall into the pit, and he who extricates himself from the pit shall be held by the snare. LXX: Woe to the transgressors who transgress the law. Fear and the pit and the snare are upon you who inhabit the earth. And it shall be that he who flees fear shall fall into the pit, and he who comes out of the pit shall be caught by the snare. This is the cause of my mourning and groaning, on account of which I said a second time, my secret is mine, my secret is mine: because all have transgressed the law of God, and the Lord's punishment is by no means put off, nor is it foretold as future, but it is imminent, and holds the inhabitants of the earth captive. […]

24:18.t: For the floodgates from on high have been opened, and the foundations of the earth will be shaken. With breaking the earth will be broken, with crushing the earth will be crushed, with shaking the earth will be shaken. With tossing the earth will be tossed like a drunken man, and it will be removed like a tent of one night, and its iniquity will weigh it down, and it will fall, and will not add to rise again. Therefore no one will escape the terror and the snare and the pit of the Lord, because the floodgates from on high, or, as the Seventy translated more plainly, the windows of heaven have been opened, so that the Lord might look down upon all the sins of men, which before, because he did not punish them, he seemed to sinners not to know. But after he has seen all the works of mortals through the opened windows, the foundations of the earth have been shaken, according to what is written in another place of the gaze of God: Who looks upon the earth, and will make it tremble (Ps 103 [104]:32).

24:19.t: Then the earth will be broken and crushed, and shaken and tossed in the likeness of a drunken man: not that the earth itself is reduced to dust and to nothing, but that all earthly things pass away, and another manner of life succeeds. And as a drunken man does not know what he is doing, but, his sinews growing dull with drunkenness, neither foot nor mind stands to its duty: so the whole earth, that is, all men who dwell on the earth, will be drunk with the greatness of the evils and the punishments, and will be stupefied at all that they see. And as a tent or pavilion of one night is moved from place to place, and the place of the former tent is abandoned by the traveler, so that no trace remains of the past lodging: so the fashion of this world will pass away, and the earth will be deserted which has been weighed down by its iniquity, whose weight and most grievous burden is described in Zechariah: Who sat upon a talent of lead (Zech 5:7). And it will fall, he says, and will not add to rise again. […]

24:21.t: And this is the sense of the whole passage: The windows of heaven have been opened, so that, as the Lord looked out upon earthly sins, every fashion of earthly works might pass away and fall, and by no means rise again to its former state. In that day, that is, in the day of judgment, the Lord will visit upon the host, or upon the adornment, of heaven on high, so that he may judge not only earthly but also heavenly things. And what the adornment or host of heaven is, let us learn from the writing of Moses: Beware lest, looking up to heaven and seeing the sun and the moon, the stars and all the adornment of heaven, you be deceived and worship them (Deut 4:19). And the Lord will visit, according to the idiom of the Scriptures, the host and army of heaven as one sick and in need of the knife and cautery, according to this: I will visit their sins with a rod, and their iniquities with scourges (Ps 88 [89]:33). For in what follows too we read: My sword has been made drunk in heaven (below, Isa 34:5); […]

24:22.t: These princes, then, who did not keep their rank, the Lord will gather in the day of judgment, bound together as in one bundle, and will cast them into the pit of hell, so that in them too may be fulfilled what is written of the impious: He opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the ditch which he made (Ps 7:16). And they will be shut up in prison, according to what the Lord says: Depart into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt 25:41). But what follows, And after many days they will be visited, seems to applaud my friends who grant repentance to the devil and the demons, in that after long times they are visited by the Lord. But let them consider that the divine Scripture did not say openly, They will be visited by the Lord, or, they will be visited by the angels, but absolutely, they will be visited. […]

24:23.t: He [Isaiah] was pricked by the thorn of sin; you are decked with the flowers of virtue. "The moon shall be ashamed, and the sun confounded, when the Lord shall punish the host of heaven on high." This is explained by another passage. "Even the stars are unclean in his sight";21 and again, "He charges his angels with folly." The moon is ashamed, the sun is confounded, and the sky covered with sackcloth. Shall we fearlessly and joyously, as though we were free from all sin, face the majesty of the Judge? After all, the mountains shall melt away, that is, all who are lifted up by pride, and all the host of the heavens, whether they are stars or angelic powers, shall fade away like heavens when the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll.

And it will be in that day: the Lord will visit upon the host of heaven on high, and upon the kings of the earth who are upon the earth. And they will be gathered together in the gathering of one bundle into the pit, and they will be shut up there in prison, and after many days they will be visited. And the moon will blush, and the sun will be confounded, when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and has been glorified in the sight of his elders. For what we have translated, and the moon will blush, and the sun will be confounded, the Seventy translated, the brick will melt, and the wall will fall; what the cause of the error is, the following words will show. The sun in the Hebrew language is called by three names: SEMES (שמש), and HAMMA (המה), which means heat, and HERES (חרס), which signifies ὄστρακον, that is, potsherd or dryness. MAOR (מאר), however, which in Greek is called φωστήρ and in Latin luminary, is common to the sun and the moon. […]

Then the moon will blush, and the sun will be confounded, according to what the Apostle says: For the creation itself groans and travails (Rom 8:22), seeing that men who enjoyed its light have done nothing worthy of the goodness of God, who makes his sun rise upon the righteous and the unrighteous (Matt 5): as if a steward and bailiff, when the master comes, were to see the household subjected to various torments and not having fulfilled his precepts at all. Of this same passage the Savior teaches more fully in the Gospel: The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be moved, when the sign of the Son of man has appeared in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth have beaten their breasts, and have seen the Son of man coming with the clouds of heaven in power and much glory (Matt 24:29, 30). […]

The stars on the day of judgment will be seen obscurely, not because of a gradual waning of their own light but due to the overwhelming brilliance of the true light, who is the supreme Judge coming in majesty, and the light of the Father and the holy angels. Nevertheless, nothing should prevent us from understanding that the sun, the moon and other stars will be deprived temporarily of their own light, as happened to the sun at the Lord's passion. But because the moon, which should have been full at that time, lay hidden behind the earth, Joel's prophesy remains unfulfilled still today, for after he had said "the sun will be turned to darkness," he added, "and the moon to blood before the great and magnificent day of the Lord comes." Isaiah also spoke about the day of judgment, saying, "The moon will be ashamed and the sun confounded when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem and is glorified in the presence of Jerusalem's elders."

25:1.t:
And this very thing the great prophet Isaiah wonderfully foreknew by the Holy Spirit, and foretold. And he therefore says thus:

"O Lord, my God, I will glorify thee, I will hymn thy name, for thou hast done marvellous things."

And he goes on to explain what these things so truly "wonderful" are:

"And the Lord of Sabaoth shall make a feast for all the nations. They shall drink joy, they shall drink wine, they shall be anointed with myrrh (on this mountain). Impart thou all these things to the nations. For this is God's counsel upon all the nations."

These were Isaiah's "wonders."the promise of the anointing with ointment of a good smell, and with myrrh made not to Israel but to all nations. Whence not unnaturally through the chrism of myrrh they gained the name of Christians. But he also prophesies the "wine of joy "to the nations, darkly alluding to the sacrament of the new covenant of Christ, which is now openly celebrated among the nations.
25:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 10

25:1.t: But others, both better and more correctly, understand it as said in the person of the prophet, giving thanks to the Father for the passion of the Lord Savior, because he has done wonders and has fulfilled his ancient designs in truth, when those standing at the right hand will hear: Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world (Matt 25:34). Understanding this, Paul too said: As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and spotless (Eph 1:4); and, desiring that what he prophesies should come to pass, he adds the Hebrew word AMEN (אמן), for which the Seventy translated so be it. And the Lord in the Gospel often uses this word: Amen, amen, that is, truly, truly I say to you (John 6:54).

O Lord, you are my God: I will exalt you, I will confess to your name, for you have done wonders, ancient faithful designs: amen. For you have made the city a heap, the strong city a ruin, the house of strangers, so that it is no city, and will never be built for ever. Because of this a strong people will praise you, the city of mighty nations will fear you. For you have become strength to the poor, strength to the needy in his tribulation, a hope from the whirlwind, a shade from the heat: for the spirit of the mighty is like a whirlwind driving against a wall. Like heat in thirst, you will bring low the tumult of strangers; and as with scorching heat under a cloud, you will make the offshoot of the strong wither. LXX: O Lord my God, I will glorify you; I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things, an ancient true counsel, so be it. For you have made cities a heap, strong cities, that their foundations might fall. The cities of the impious will not be built for ever. […]

O COME, all ye who love the glory of the Saviour, and thereby weave crowns for your heads, come once again, that we may rejoice in Him, and as we extol Him with endless praises, let us say in the words of the prophet Isaiah: "O Lord, my God, I will praise Thee; and I will laud Thy name; for Thou hast wrought wonderful works, even a counsel true from the beginning." What then is the counsel and purpose of God the Father, which was from the beginning, and was true? Plainly that respecting us. For Christ foreknew, even before the foundations of the world, His mystery: but it was in the last ages of the world that He arose for the inhabitants of earth, that having borne the sin of the world, He might abolish both it and death, which is its consequence, and was brought upon us by its means. For so He Himself plainly said, "I am the resurrection and the life:" and "he that believeth on Me hath everlasting life, and shall not come into judgment, but hath passed from death unto life."
25:1.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

25:2.t: And why he praises and confesses to the name of the Lord, and what these wonders are, and the ancient designs which he showed true in deed, follows: For you have made the city a heap, the strong city a ruin, the house of strangers, so that it is no city, and will never be built for ever. The once strong city is understood as Jerusalem, which has become the house of strangers; of whom the Savior says in the psalm: Strange children have lied to me, strange children have grown old and have limped in their paths (Ps 17 [18]:46). This city, when it has been destroyed, will never be built for ever, so that the dreams of a thousand-year kingdom and of a golden and jeweled Jerusalem may be laid to rest.

25:3.t: And when Jerusalem has been destroyed for its impiety, a strong people will praise the Lord. And who the strong people is, the following verse shows: The city of mighty nations will fear you. While those blaspheme, the people of the nations will fear you. For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Prov 9:10). And a strong people will praise you, and the city of mighty nations will fear you, that is, the Church gathered from the nations.

25:4.t: For you have become strength to the poor, to your Christ, of whom we read also in the Psalms: Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor (Ps 40 [41]:1). And in Zechariah, according to the Hebrew truth, the poor man, that is, EBION (אביון), is described as sitting upon the colt of an ass (Zech 9). Strength to the needy, in the tribulation of his passion, a hope from the whirlwind of the cross, and a shade from the heat, when he said: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit (Luke 23:46). For as when the wind is dashed against a wall and passes by, so the whirlwind of the blaspheming Jews could not harm him.

25:5.t: And to use another comparison: as an offshoot is scorched by most grievous heat and droops, so you will make the tumult and clamor of the strangers, that is, of those who have become strangers to you, wither and perish. According to the Seventy translators, I could not find in this place, I do not say the sense, but the order and sequence of the words. And for that place where we have translated, like heat in thirst, for which in the Hebrew is written BASAION (בציון), which among them means pathless place or thirst: why they turned pathless place and in thirst into in Zion, the error is plain, from the likeness of the words SAION and SION (Both ציון), since it is marked with the same letters.

25:6.t: Having been counted worthy of this holy chrism, you are called Christians, verifying the name also by your new birth. For before you were deemed worthy of this grace, you had properly no right to this title but were advancing on your way toward being Christians.Moreover, you shall know that in the old Scripture there lies the symbol of this chrism. For at the time Moses imparted to his brother the command of God and made him high priest, he anointed him after bathing him in water. And Aaron was called Christ or anointed, evidently from the typical anointing. So also the high priest, in advancing Solomon to the kingdom, anointed him after he had bathed in Gihon. To them, however, these things happened in a figure, but to you not in a figure but in truth; because you were truly anointed by the Holy Spirit. Christ is the beginning of your salvation. He is truly the first fruit, and you are what follow. If the first fruit is holy, obviously its holiness will pass to the remainder also. […]

After the passion of the Lord, then, when he has freed him from thirst and heat and whirlwind, the Lord will make, not at all for the people of the Jews, but for all nations, on Mount Zion a fat feast, burnt offerings full of marrow, and the wine of a vintage refined from the lees, so that he may cast down and cause to be swallowed up the face of death and of the bond by which all peoples were bound; and he will break the net of death, and the web that had caught all nations. And according to the Apostle, death will be swallowed up for ever (1 Cor 15). And the Lord will take away the tear from every face, when, death being overcome, the kingdom of Christ has come, and the reproach of the human race, which had been made to the image of the Creator, has escaped the slavery of the devil and of death. […]

25:7.t: And the Lord of hosts will make for all peoples on this mountain a feast of fat things, a feast of the vintage: of fat things full of marrow, of a vintage refined from the lees. And he will cast down on this mountain the face of the bond that was bound upon all peoples, and the web that he wove over all nations. And he will cast down death for ever, and the Lord God will take away the tear from every face, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth: for the Lord has spoken. LXX: And the Lord Sabaoth will make for all nations upon this mountain: they will drink gladness, they will drink wine. They will be anointed with ointment on this mountain. Deliver all these things to the nations, for this counsel is upon all nations: death, prevailing, has devoured. And again: The Lord God has taken away every tear from every face, and the reproach of his people he has taken away from all the earth. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken. […]

25:8.t: Now the laws of love summoned Him even as far as Death and the dead themselves, so that He might summon the souls of those who were long time dead. And so because He cared for the salvation of all for ages past, and that "He might bring to naught him that hath the power of death," as Scripture teaches, here again he underwent the dispensation in His mingled Natures: as Man, he left His Body to the usual burial, while as God He departed from it. For He cried with a loud cry, and said to the Father: "I commend my spirit," and departed from the body free, in no wise waiting for death, who was lagging as it were in fear to come to Him; nay, rather, He pursued him from behind and drove him on, trodden under His feet and fleeing, and He burst the eternal gates of his dark realms, and made a road of return back again to life for the dead there bound with the bonds of death. […]
25:8.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 4, Chapter 12

25:8.t: In the Old Testament the jaw of death is bitter, since it is said, "Strong death is all devouring." In the New Testament the jaw of death is sweet, for it has swallowed death, as the apostle says: "Death is swallowed up in victory! O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?"

Stricken by the indecency of this act [the golden calf], Moses broke the tablets and shattered the head of the calf and beat it to powder in order to destroy all traces of impiety. The first tablets were broken so that the second ones might be repaired whereon, through the teaching of the gospel, faithlessness, now utterly destroyed, vanished. Thus Moses shattered that Egyptian pride and by the authority of the eternal law checked that loftiness overreaching itself. Therefore David says, "And the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and shatter them like the calf of Lebanon. Thus the people swallowed all faithlessness and pride, so that impiety and haughtiness might not swallow them. For it is better that each person be master of his flesh and its vices, that it may not be said of him that all-powerful death has devoured him, but rather, "death is swallowed up in victory!"

It is death that has brought men to old age and corruption: death therefore has made old, that is to say, has corrupted: for "that which is made old, and is growing aged, is near corruption," as Scripture saith: but Christ renews, in that He is "the Life." For He Who in the beginning created, is able again to renew unto incorruption and life. For one may well affirm that it is the office of one and the same energy and power, to effect both the one and the other. As therefore the prophet Isaiah says, "'He hath swallowed up death, having become mighty." And again, "The Lord hath taken away all weeping from every countenance. He hath taken away the reproach of the people from all the earth." By the reproach of the people he means sin, which disgraces and depraves men: and which, together with destruction, shall be slain, and sorrow and death shall perish, and the tears cease which are shed on its account.
25:8.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

25:8.t: For the prophet Isaiah again assures us that death which entered in because of sin does not retain its power over the dwellers upon earth for ever, but is abolished by the resurrection from the dead of Christ, Who renews the universe, and refashions it to that which it was at the beginning—" for God created all things for incorruption," as it is written; for he says, "He has swallowed up death, having waxed mighty: and God shall again take away all weeping from every countenance; He shall remove the reproach of the people from the whole earth." Now sin is what he calls the reproach of the people, and when this has been taken away, death also is extinguished with it, and corruption departs from the midst: and by having brought it to an end, He removes every one's weeping; and lamentation also is put to silence; for henceforth there is no more cause for men to weep and lament.
25:8.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

25:9.t: And they will say in that day: Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us: this is the Lord, we have waited patiently for him; we will exult and be glad in his salvation. For the hand of the Lord will rest on this mountain; and Moab will be threshed under him as straw is crushed in the wagon. And he will stretch out his hands under him, as a swimmer stretches them out to swim, and his glory will be brought low with the dashing of his hands. And the fortifications of your lofty walls will fall, and will be brought low and pulled down to the ground, even to the dust. When death has been swallowed up for ever, the people of God which has been freed from the hand of death will say to the Lord: Behold, this is our God, whom the unbelieving thought only a man; and we have waited for him, that is, we have believed his words, that he will fulfill his promises, and he will save us. Therefore, snatched by his help from the jaws of death, we will exult and be glad in him; […]

25:10.t: So the prophetic discourse, although it weaves its prophecy generally about the consummation of the world, yet, so as not to seem to neglect present things entirely, names Moab, which was an enemy of Israel, so much so that it made them commit fornication with the Midianites and be consecrated to the idol Baal-peor, which means Priapus; against which Jeremiah speaks: Chemosh will go forth into captivity, his priests and his princes together (Jer 48:7); and again: Moab will be confounded in Chemosh, as the house of Israel was confounded in Bethel (ibid., 13), and other things like these. And from one idol and the demon who presided over this idol, he indicates that all the adverse powers are to be brought low and led down into Tartarus, and crushed like dust. But if this is how it will be, where is the repentance of the devil?

25:11.t: And as one who swims is wont to stretch out his whole body, so he will be dashed from his power to the ground, and in falling will make a noise.

25:12.t: And all the fortifications of his lofty men, or of his walls, as is contained in the Hebrew, will fall and be brought low, and will be pulled down to the ground, broken to the dust.

26:1.t: In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: The city of our strength, the Savior, a wall and an outer wall will be set in it. LXX: In that day they will sing this song in the land of Judea: Behold a strong city, and our salvation will set a wall and a surrounding wall. When Moab has been brought low and pulled down to the ground, even to the dust, and all enemies laid beneath the feet of Christ, then this song will be sung in the land of Judah, or Judea, each of which means confession: so that, as we have understood Zion and Jerusalem as the heavenly city, so we may also understand the region of this city as the heavenly confession. Indeed, the saints, unwilling to sing the song of Judea in a foreign land, say: How shall we sing a song to the Lord in a foreign land? (Ps 136 [137]:4). I think that this is the song which in another place too the saints are commanded: Sing to the Lord a new song (Ps 95 [96]:1). And this song will be what follows: The city of our strength, the Savior (Matt 5). […]

This is the wall of which the prophet says: “Our strong city is Zion; the Savior shall be set within it as a wall and fortification” (Isa. 26:1). By this wall, therefore, Christ is signified together with all his members, so that its foundation represents him, while the rest of its structure represents his members.

26:2.t: Open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter, keeping the truth. The old error has gone; you will keep peace: peace, because we have hoped in you. You have hoped in the Lord for everlasting ages. LXX: Open the gates, let the people enter which keeps righteousness, and keeps the truth, laying hold of the truth, and keeping peace: peace, because they have hoped in you, O Lord, for ever. This whole song, which the saints are to sing in the land of confession and praise, suddenly changes persons, and is woven as if by question and answer. The people of God had said: The city of our strength, the Savior, a wall and an outer wall will be set in it. The Lord answered, or rather commanded, not those who had said this, but the angels who presided over the gates of the Lord's city, that they should open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter through them, keeping the truth, or, as is said in the Hebrew, EMMUNIM (אמונים), which in our language is rendered faiths, in the plural number, not the singular. […]

After the words of the people and the answer of the Lord, and again the voice of the people, the Prophet speaks to the believers: You have hoped, or hope in the Lord, for everlasting ages, and the rest that follows. According to the Seventy, he enters the gates of the Lord who keeps righteousness in good works, and keeps or embraces the truth in the truth of faith, so that through good works and faith he may come to the peace which surpasses all understanding, and may merit to receive that peace; because he has believed in God, who is the eternal rewarder of good works (Phil 4). Hence also in another place it is written: You have desired wisdom: keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to you (Sir 1:33).

26:3.t: After the word of God, the people answered in Hebrew JESER SAMUCH (יצרסמך), which Aquila and Symmachus translated alike, πλᾶσμα ἐπηρεισμένον, that is, our error has been taken away, or our thought has been made firm, which before wavered between you and the idols, so that we are by no means carried about by every wind of doctrine, but believe with our whole mind in you, the Lord Savior. For this, so that the sense might be made plainer, we translated, the old error has gone. And because our thought has been made firm, therefore you will keep for us the peace which you promised to the Apostles, saying: My peace I give you, my peace I leave you (John 14:27); and not once only but a second time, so that the recompense which is promised with a double word may be secure, according to what the Apostle too said: Rejoice, again I say rejoice (Phil 4:4). And this he obtains of whom it is said in Leviticus: Man, man, of the children of Israel (Lev 17); […]

26:4.t: In the Lord God, the strong one, for ever: for he will bow down those who dwell on high; he will bring low the lofty city, he will bring it low even to the ground; he will pull it down even to the dust. The foot will trample it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy. LXX: O great eternal God, who have brought low and pulled down those who dwell on high, you will destroy strong cities, and will bring them down even to the pavement, and the feet of the meek and the lowly will trample them. These things too the Prophet speaks, who answered from that place where he had said above, Hope in the Lord for everlasting ages; and he joins to it what we have now set forth: In the Lord God, the strong one, for ever, and the rest. For the Lord God, the strong one, the Hebrew has three names, IA (יה) and ADONAI (יהוה) and SUR (צור), of which one signifies invisible, another ineffable, another mighty; the first of them is placed as the last syllable in ALLELUIA (הללו יה). […]

26:5.t: For he will bow down those who dwell on high, because everyone who exalts himself will be humbled; those who boasted that they had Abraham as their father, and said in insult of the Lord: We were not born of fornication (John 8:41). He will bring low the lofty city: as the Jews think, Rome; as we prove to be more correct, Jerusalem, which killed the Prophets and stoned those who were sent to it, and at the last killed the son of the householder, so that, the heir being slain, the inheritance might perish (Luke 13). Nor is it called a city, which in Hebrew is said IR (עיר), but CARIA (כריה), which Aquila translated πολίχνην, which we can call either little city or hamlet or small town; and Jerusalem is frequently called by this name in the Scriptures. And he did well to set down a double humbling, He will bring low, he will bring it low: first under the Babylonians, when the temple was destroyed; the second time under Titus and Vespasian, whose ruin remains until the end.

And because it is said in the words of the Savior, Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11), we can refer this not only to men but also to the adverse powers. According to the Seventy, the Prophet sings praises to God because he brings low all the proud, and razes the fortifications of all cities to the ground, and the feet of the saints, the meek and the lowly trample them.

26:6.t: The foot will trample it, and he repeats and joins the feet of the poor, without doubt of Christ, of whom we have said above too: He has become strength to the poor, strength to the needy in his tribulation. The steps of the needy, namely of the Apostles, who, imitating the poverty of the Lord, obtained also the privilege of his power; who, not being received, shook off upon it the dust of their feet.

26:7.t: The path of the righteous is straight, straight is the track of the righteous for walking; and in the path of your judgments, O Lord, we have waited for you; your name and your memorial are in the desire of the soul: my soul has desired you in the night. LXX: The way of the righteous is straight, the way of the righteous has been made straight, and prepared. For the way of the Lord is judgment; we have hoped in your name, and in the remembrance which our soul desires. The Prophet is still speaking of Christ, of whom he had said above: The foot will trample it, the feet of the poor. The path of this righteous one, then, is straight, or, to coin a new word, straightnesses, which the Greeks call εὐθύτητας, and which we can call more in the Latin manner equities; and in Hebrew they are called MESSARIM (משרים). In the one path of Christ, then, all righteousnesses are found; and for that reason he trod and wore it with his own foot, so that whoever wishes to walk along it may walk with an unstumbling course.

26:8.t: In this path of the Lord's judgments the saints have waited for him, and have hoped in him, because hope does not confound. And they have had his name and memorial in the desire of their soul, saying: My soul has longed to desire your judgments at all times (Ps 118 [119]:20); and again: My soul desires, and has fainted for your salvation (ibid. 81). And he who has the name of the Lord in his desire desires nothing else. And this must be noted, that the desire for the Lord is not in the flesh but in the soul, according to what we read in another psalm: My soul has thirsted for God, the strong, the living (Ps 41 [42]:2). For the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal 5). For these are opposed to one another, so that we do not do the things we wish.

26:9.t: But, as I said, at the crowing of the cock their President comes, and gently touching the sleeper with his foot, rouses them all. For there are none sleeping naked. Then as soon as they have arisen they stand up, and sing the prophetic hymns with much harmony, and well composed tunes. And neither harp nor pipe nor other musical instrument utters such sweet melodies, as you hear from the singing of these saints in their deep and quiet solitudes. And the songs themselves too are suitable, and full of the love of God. "In the night," they say, "lift up your hands unto God. With my soul have I desired Thee in the night, yea with my spirit within me will I seek Thee early."

And what follows, In the night, according to the Seventy is joined to the following passage, according to the Hebrew to the former one. And he can say, My soul has desired you in the night, who says confidently with the Psalmist: Every night I will wash my bed, I will water my couch with tears (Ps 6:7). Night and darkness can also be taken for tribulation and distress. Hence in another psalm too the Prophet sings of the security of the righteous: The sun will not burn you by day, nor the moon by night (Ps 120 [121]:6), that is, neither in prosperity nor in adversity will you ever be moved from your place.

But also with my spirit within my breast, from the morning I will watch for you. LXX: From the night my spirit rises early to you, O God: for your judgments are a light upon the earth. We wish both to follow the Hebrew and not to pass over the common edition entirely, and by this necessity of things we are compelled to seek different understandings in a different order and wording. So what is said, from the night, is, according to the Seventy, as we said, the beginning of this passage; according to the Hebrew, the end of the preceding one; although even according to the Seventy it can be taken at the end of the preceding testimony, so that the sense is: My soul desires you in the night; and afterwards it begins: in the morning my spirit rises to you, O God. And it rises in the morning for this reason, because your precepts are a light upon the earth. […]

When you have done your judgments on the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn righteousness. Let us have mercy on the impious, and he will not learn righteousness; in the land of the saints he has done wickedly, and he will not see the glory of the Lord. LXX: Learn righteousness, you who dwell upon the earth. For the impious has ceased, and he will not learn righteousness upon the earth; he will not do truth; let the impious be taken away, that he may not see the glory of the Lord. Let us speak first according to the Hebrew, and when we have chosen to express the sense of the Prophet, then let us pass to the Seventy translators. As long as you do not exercise your judgments upon the earth, and neither repay good to the good nor evil to the evil, your righteousness, O Lord God, is unknown on the earth. […]

According to the Seventy, the inhabitants of the earth are commanded to learn righteousness. For every man seems righteous to himself; but God knows the hearts of all, who will render to each according to his works (Prov 21). And in another place of the same book it is said: There are ways of a man which seem straight; but their ends look into the depth of hell (Prov 14:12). Hence we ought to learn righteousness, and not trust in our own judgment. For there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness (Eccl 7); not because he is righteous, but because he seems to himself to be righteous. But if Christ has been made for us by God wisdom and righteousness, sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1), those who are commanded to know righteousness are commanded this: to learn and know Christ. And I command you, he says, to learn righteousness for this reason, because the impious has been taken away, and his kingdom destroyed, who, as long as he reigned on the earth, could neither know righteousness nor do truth; […]

For "night" is this present life, and as long as we are in it, we are covered with a mist of uncertain imaginations as far as the sight of inward objects is concerned. For the prophet was sensible that he was held by a certain mist in his sight of the Lord, when he says, "My soul longed for you in the night." As if he were to say, I long to behold you in the obscurity of this present life, but I am still surrounded by the mist of infirmity.
26:9.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 23, Section 39

26:9.t: Anyone who has been able to reach out for the truth has been on fire with this love. For this reason David said, "My soul has thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?" And he counseled us, saying, "Seek his face continually." And for this reason the prophet said, "My soul has desired you in the night, and with my spirit within my breast I will watch for you in the morning." And again the church says to the Lord in the Song of Songs, "I have been wounded with love."It is right that the soul, after bearing in its heart a wound of love brought on by its burning desire, should reach out for healing at the sight of the doctor. And so, again, it says, "My soul melted when he spoke." The heart of a person who does not seek the face of his Creator is hardened by his wickedness, because in itself it remains cold. But if it now begins to burn with the desire of following him whom it loves, it runs since the fire of love has melted it. Its desire makes it anxious. […]

26:10.t: For our Lord Jesus Christ came, not only that we might behold His glory here, but also that which shall be. For therefore He saith, "I will that these also be with Me where I am, that they may behold My glory." Now if the glory here was so bright and splendid, what can one say of that which shall be? for it shall appear not on this corruptible earth, nor while we are in perishable bodies, but in a creation which is imperishable, and waxes not old, and with such brightness as it is not possible even to represent in words. O blessed, thrice blessed, yea many times so, they who are deemed worthy to be beholders of that glory! It is concerning this that the prophet says, "Let the unrighteous be taken away, that he behold not the glory of the Lord." God grant that not one of us be taken away nor excluded ever from beholding it.

To which the Lord answered: Let us have mercy on the impious; which all, except the Seventy, translated alike. And the sense is: rather let the impious obtain mercy, and learn my clemency, while he too is saved. And again, to the Lord as he speaks, the Prophet answered in the person of human impatience: And he will not learn righteousness. And the sense is: and how will he be able to know your righteousness, if he has experienced only clemency? And he gives the reasons why he wishes him to learn the righteousness of God: because he has acted wickedly in the land of the saints, and has fought continually against your saints, he ought to feel torments. And again the Lord, tempering the sentence, says: And let him not see, or he will not see the glory of the Lord. And the sense is: it is enough for him, in place of all punishment, that he will not see me reigning with my saints in my majesty. […]

O Lord, let your hand be exalted, and let them not see: let them see, and let the zeal of the people be confounded, and let fire devour your enemies. LXX: O Lord, your arm is lofty, and they did not know; but knowing they will be confounded: zeal will seize the untaught people, and now fire will eat the adversaries. What he had said above, and he will not see the glory of the Lord, can be understood thus: You ask, O Prophet, that I should not have mercy on the impious, lest, if I have had mercy on him, he who has acted wickedly in the land of the saints should begin not to know righteousness; I answer you: will he then not see the glory of the Lord? Will he then not behold my triumphs, he who rather ought to see me reigning, so that he may know how great a good he lacks? And this is to be read more pointedly, with the voice of one asking a question.

In this human form the good will see him in whom they have believed; the wicked, him whom they have despised. But the wicked will not see him in the form of God in which he is equal to the Father, for as the prophet says, "The wicked shall be taken off that he may not see the glory of the Lord," and, on the other hand, "Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God."

Then, therefore, we shall come and we shall enjoy the one thing; but the one thing will be all things to us. For what was it I said, my brothers, when I began to speak? What is that sufficiency which we shall possess when we shall have no need? What is the sufficiency which we shall possess? I had intended to say, "What will God give to us which he will not give to them?" "Let the wicked be taken away that he may not see the glory of God." Hence God will give his glory to us so that we may enjoy it; and the wicked will be taken away that he may not see the glory of God. God himself will be the entire sufficiency which we shall possess as our own. Greedy one, what did you seek to gain? What does anyone, for whom God is not enough, seek from God?

His coming means his return from the judgment to his kingdom. The Lord comes to us after the judgment, because he lifts us up from his human appearance in the contemplation of his divinity; his coming means that he leads us to the vision of his glory. We see in his divinity after the judgment the one we beheld in his humanity at the judgment. At the judgment he comes in the form of a servant and appears to everyone, since it is written, "They will look on him whom they pierced." When the condemned fall down to their punishment, the righteous are led to the brightness of his glory, as is written: "The wicked is taken away, so that he will [not] see the glory of the Lord."

26:11.t: To which the Prophet answered: O Lord, let your hand be exalted, and be stretched out to strike, so that the impious may not see you, and may not enjoy the light of your glory, not even for repentance. To whom the Lord answered: Let them rather see and be confounded, either the zeal of the people or those zealous for the people, and let fire devour and consume your adversaries, that is, those of the people of the saints. And it is the fire of repentance, which tortures their hearts because they have lost such a Lord. This can also be understood of the Jews, who did not know Christ, the arm of the Lord, and when they have seen and recognized him whom they had fastened to the gibbet, will be confounded. […]

Note that there are two kinds of zeal, one full of love, the other full of hatred. The former is indicated in the words, "The zeal of your house has devoured me"; the latter, in the words, "Zeal has taken hold of the senseless people, and now fire shall devour your opponents."

26:12.t: Whenever you see a man living in wickedness, and enjoying great prosperity, and suffering no calamity, on this account lament for him the more, because, being under the power of disease and grievous corruption, he increases his own weakness, becoming worse by luxury and indolence. For punishment is not in itself an evil, but the real evil is sin. The latter separates us from God; the former leads us to God, and mitigates His wrath. How is this shown? Hear the prophet saying, "O priests, comfort ye, comfort ye my people. Speak to the heart of Jerusalem, and say that she has received of the Lord's hand double for her sins." And again: "O Lord our God, give us peace, for thou hast repaid all to us."
26:12.s: HOMILIES ON LAZARUS AND THE RICH MAN 3

26:12.t: But I say all this now, and select all the histories that contain trials and tribulations, and the wrath of kings, and their evil designs, in order that we may fear nothing, save only offending God. For then also was there a furnace burning; yet they derided it, but feared sin. For they knew that if they were consumed in the fire, they should suffer nothing that was to be dreaded; but that if they were guilty of impiety: they should undergo the extremes of misery. It is the greatest punishment to commit sin, though we may remain unpunished; as on the other hand, it is the greatest honour and repose to live virtuously, though we may be punished. For sins separate us from God; as He Himself speaks; "Have not your sins separated between you and Me?" But punishments lead us back to God. As one saith, "Give peace; for Thou hast recompensed us for all things." Suppose any one hath a wound; which is the most deserving of fear, gangrene, or the surgeon's knife? the steel, or the devouring progress of the ulcer? […]

O Lord, you will give us peace: for you have wrought all our works for us. LXX: O Lord our God, give us peace: for you have rendered all things to us. It must be noted that after he has rendered to us our works, he is going to give peace, and how they set out the reasons why they ask for peace. For they say that for all the works which they have wrought upon the earth they have endured torments, and that it is just that after punishments and tortures they should obtain mercy. Or otherwise: Because the consummation of the world has come, and all that you spoke through the Prophets has been fulfilled in deed, and you have rendered all that you promised, grant us peace, which surpasses all understanding.

Through all that we do, therefore, let us return with a careful mind to the fountain of true light. Let us give thanks to our Creator for the good things we receive, and let us humbly say to him with the prophet Isaiah: "All our works you have worked for us." For our good works are the works of him whose heart it did not suffice to raise us up unless he also bowed down himself for us. For if God, coeternal with the Father before the ages, had not become man in time, when would temporal man have tasted eternal things? Therefore the descent of truth became the ascent of our humility.

"A man's steps are directed by the Lord." Whoever walks a straight path composed of human steps does so not by the freedom of human judgment but by the governance of him to whom Isaiah said, "All of our works were accomplished by you." "What man can understand his way?" In this it becomes clear that whatever goodness anyone possesses from himself he does not have except through the grace of God, because no one is able to understand through the freedom of his own judgment either what kind of future he will have or the quality and duration of conquests to come.

All our merits are rooted in the merit of Christ, whether satisfactory for punishment or meritorious of eternal life, because we are worthy neither to be absolved from offense against the highest good, nor to gain the immensity of the eternal reward, which is God, except through the merit of the God-man, to whom we can and ought to say: All our works you have wrought in us, O Lord.

26:13.t: For the Son of God indeed, being himself the Word, is Lord of all. But we once were subject from the first to the slavery of corruption and the curse of the law. Then by degrees fashioning for ourselves things that were not, we served, as says the blessed apostle, "them which by nature are no gods." Ignorant of the true God, we preferred things that were not to the truth. But afterwards, as the ancient people when oppressed in Egypt groaned, so when we too had the law "engrafted" in us, according to the unutterable sighings of the Spirit made our intercession, "O Lord our God, take possession of us"; then, as "he became a house of refuge" and a "God and defense," so also he became our Lord. Nor did he then begin to be, but we began to have him for our Lord.

O Lord our God, lords have possessed us without you: only in you may we remember your name. LXX: Lord our God, possess us: O Lord, besides you we know no other, we call upon your name. For this reason we seek mercy and peace, which is to be granted after all things, because lords have possessed us without you, namely the idols, or the demons who sit by the idols; and we ask nothing else but that, after very many errors, we may be worthy to remember your name. According to the Seventy, those who said, Lord God, possess us, pray for this, that after peace has been restored to them they may become the possession of God. This indeed we read also of Wisdom, which according to the Hebrew speaks in Proverbs: God possessed me, the beginning of his ways (Prov 8:22), although some copies wrongly have creature for possession. Then it follows: But before all the hills he begot me. For how can begetting be fitted to a creature, when it rather suits possession? […]

26:14.t: Let the dying not live; let the giants not rise again. Therefore you have visited and crushed them, and have destroyed all memory of them. LXX: For the dead will not see life, nor will physicians raise them up. Therefore you have brought on, and destroyed, and taken away every male of theirs. Symmachus, in his manner, more plainly: The dead will not give life; the giants will not raise up. Therefore you have visited and crushed them, and have utterly destroyed all memory of them. Let us speak first according to the Seventy. The question seems difficult, how the dead do not see life. It is solved thus: they do not see life so long as they are dead. As if we were to say, a blind man does not see the light so long as he is blind; but if he has recovered his health, he will look upon the light: so too he who is dead in iniquity and sins cannot live before he is given life by righteousness and the virtues, through him who says, I am the life (John 14). […]

For hence it is said by the prophet, "The dead shall not live; the giants shall not rise up again." For whom does he call "the dead" except sinners, and whom does he designate "giants" except those who over and above take pride in sin. Now the former do "not live," because by sinning they have forfeited the life of righteousness; these latter too "cannot rise up again" after death because after their transgression they are swollen with pride and do not have recourse to the remedies of penitence.
26:14.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 17, Section 30

26:15.t: You have been indulgent to the nation, O Lord, you have been indulgent to the nation. Have you been glorified? You have removed far all the ends of the earth. LXX: Add evils to them, O Lord, add evils to the glorious of the earth: you have made far off all the ends of the earth. The evils which the Seventy put twice are not found in the Hebrew; but because he had said above, Therefore you have brought on and destroyed, and taken away every male of theirs, following the same sense they added of their own, evils: so that those who are glorious on the earth may be crushed by double evils. Further, according to the Hebrews the sense is far otherwise, and in agreement with the earlier discussion. The Lord had said: Let us have mercy on the impious. The Prophet had answered: And where is your righteousness? especially since he has wrought such great evils against your saints. To which the Lord: And he will not see, he says, the glory of the Lord. […]

Theodore: Sometimes holy Scripture is wont by an improper use of terms to use "evils "for "affliction;" not that these are properly and in their nature evils, but because they are imagined to be evils by those on whom they are brought for their good. For when divine judgment is reasoning with men it must speak with the language and feelings of men. For when a doctor for the sake of health with good reason either cuts or cauterizes those who are suffering from the inflammation of ulcers, it is considered an evil by those who have to bear it. Nor are the spur and the whip pleasant to a restive horse. Moreover all chastisement seems at the moment to be a bitter thing to those who are chastised, as the Apostle says: "Now all chastisement for the present indeed seemeth not to bring with it joy but sorrow; […]

26:16.t: O Lord, in distress they have sought you; in the tribulation of murmuring your teaching was to them. LXX: O Lord, in tribulation I remembered you; in small tribulation your teaching was to us. Because, being indulgent, you have often been despised and not glorified, but on the contrary all have withdrawn from the knowledge of you, therefore, O Lord, strike them, so that in distress they may seek you, and in the tribulation of murmuring your teaching may be to them: when so great a weight of evils presses upon them that they do not even dare to cry out confidently, but swallow their pain in silence. According to the Seventy, the Prophet remembers the Lord in tribulation, according to what is said in the psalm: Out of tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard me in a broad place (Ps 117 [118]:5). And in another place: To the Lord I cried when I was troubled, and he heard me (Ps 119 [120]:1). Hence the Apostle says: We are troubled, but not distressed; we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken (2 Cor 4:8). […]

26:17.t: As a woman who has conceived, when she draws near to the birth, cries out in pain in her pangs: so have we become before your face, O Lord. We have conceived, and as it were travailed, and have brought forth spirit. LXX: And as a woman in travail, when she draws near to the birth, cries out in her pain: so have we become ÷ to your beloved ⁚ because of fear of you, O Lord; we have received in the womb, and have travailed, and have brought forth the spirit of your salvation, which we have made upon the earth. As a woman drawing near to the birth is compelled by pain to cry out, so we seek you in distress, and before the face of the dread of you we have conceived, and travailed, and brought forth, not children of the flesh, but of the spirit: so that we may believe in you with our whole mind, and learn through torments him whom we did not perceive through benefits. […]

A time to give birth and a time to die. A time to plant and a time to pluck up what has been planted. No one doubts that both the rising and the passing away of men is known to God and fixed by him, and that to give birth is the same as to plant, and to die the same as to pluck up what has been planted. But since we read in Isaiah: From fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived and been in labor and given birth, this must be said: that in the perfect man that offspring which was born of fear dies, once he has begun to love God. For perfect indeed love casts out fear.

26:18.t: That there are also some souls that conceive offspring, the prophet made clear when he said: "from fear of you, Lord, we conceived in the womb and travailed and gave birth to a spirit of salvation which you made upon the earth". For just as in those who are pregnant the seed is formed and shaped, so also in the soul that receives the word, the conception of the word is gradually formed and shaped within it. And this I think is what Paul says to the Galatians: "my children, whom I again bring forth in travail until Christ be formed in you", which is as though he were to say: until the word be formed and made manifest in you. In the epistle to Timothy he says likewise that a woman shall be saved "through the bearing of children, if she abide in faith and love and holiness with chastity". But who is this woman, if not the soul that conceives the word of God and of truth, and gives birth to good works like to Christ? […]

The soul therefore conceives from this seed of the word and forms the conceived word within itself, until it brings forth the spirit of the fear of God. For thus through the prophet the souls of the saints say: "from your fear, O Lord, we have conceived in the womb and have been in labor and have brought forth; we have made the spirit of your salvation upon the earth". This is the childbearing of holy souls, this the conception, these are the holy nuptials which are fitting and suited to the great high priest Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!".

Their cows did not miscarry, therefore, but gave birth, so that their labor would be increased and that they would beget everything they conceived without reverence for God. The righteous, however, take delight in an altogether different way. They glory not in the abundance of their wealth or the fruitfulness of their livestock but in the Lord, saying, "We were impregnated with reverence for you, and we brought forth the spirit of salvation."

Isaiah also, proclaiming the resurrection to the people, says that he is the announcer of the Lord's message, for we read thus: "For the mouth of the Lord has spoken, and they shall speak in that day." And what the mouth of the Lord declared that the people should say is set forth later on, where it is written: "Because of your fear, O Lord, we have been with child and have brought forth the Spirit of your salvation, which you have poured forth upon the earth. They that inhabit the earth shall fall; they shall rise that are in the graves. For the dew which is from you is health for them, but the land of the wicked shall perish. Go, O my people, and enter into your chambers; hide yourselves for a little until the Lord's wrath pass by."

If such, therefore, be our experience in the flesh, let us turn to an examination of what is proper to the soul. There is no question that we have to deal here with something that is without sex, yet it fulfills all the offices of both sexes in that the soul conceives and, as in marriage, gives birth. Nature provides woman with a womb in which a living person is brought to birth in the course of time. Such, too, is that characteristic of the soul which is ready to receive in its womb-like recesses the seeds of our thoughts, to cherish them and to bring them forth as a woman gives birth to a child. This and no other is the meaning of the words of Isaias: We have conceived and brought forth the spirit of salvation. Some of these conceptions are associated with the female sex, such as malice of thought, petulance, sensuality, self-indulgence, immodesty, and other vices of that nature which tend to enervate the traits associated with what is distinctively masculine. […]
26:18.s: On Cain and Abel, Book 1, Chapter 10

26:18.t: Salvations we have not wrought on the earth; therefore the inhabitants of the world have not fallen. LXX: We shall not fall, but the inhabitants of the earth will fall. A different translation must needs have a different sense too. According to the Hebrew this is said: Because we have done nothing worthy of your mercy, therefore the impious have not fallen, but to this day prevail and possess the earth. But the Seventy assert this: that while the saints make the spirit of salvation upon the earth, those who are inhabitants of the earth fall; although between world, which in Hebrew is called THEBEL (תבל) and in Greek οἰκουμένη, and earth there is much difference. Whoever, then, have given themselves to dwelling on the earth, and have been grounded with a fixed root in earthly works, will fall; and they will not fall who sit in the world and rest in the Church, which is the dwelling place of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

For they have crushed, or cut asunder, with iron carts the women with child of Gilead. These are the women with child of whom the Lord speaks in the Gospel: Woe to those who are with child, and to those who give suck in those days. The women with child are the souls of believers, who at the beginning of faith can say: From fear of you, Lord, we have conceived and been in labour; and if they have not been cut up and pierced with iron by the carts and the iron and toothed wheels, of which the psalmist says: The sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, they can also say what follows: And we have brought forth; we have made the spirit of your salvation upon the earth. And consider at the same time that they cannot cut up men of mature age, but only those who are still in the womb, or who cannot take solid food and are still nourished with the milk of infancy.

I speak to you a wondrous thing, but a true one. Our Zion, in which at times there are foreigners, and Tyre, and the Ethiopian: that watchtower, that harlot, that Rahab, that Babylon, she who spread apart her feet to everyone passing by, according to Ezekiel: that harlot, if she wills, suddenly becomes a virgin. She becomes a virgin, and conceives the Son of God, and gives birth. 'From the fear of you, O Lord, we conceived and were in labor; we brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth.' See, then, that the harlot conceives from God and gives birth, and brings forth the Savior. We brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth. Therefore our soul, that Rahab, that harlot, can conceive and bring forth the Savior.

And what did they? “There pains as of a woman in travail.” What are the pains “as of a woman in travail,” but the pangs of a penitent? See the same conception of pain and travail: “Of Thy fear” (saith Isaiah) “we have conceived, we have travailed of the Spirit of salvation.” So then the kings conceived from the fear of Christ, that by travailing they brought forth salvation by believing on Him whom they had feared. “There pains as of a woman in travail:” when of travail thou hearest, expect a birth. The old man travaileth, but the new man is born.

"When a woman gives birth, she is sorrowful because her hour has come." He refers to holy church as a woman on account of her fruitfulness in good works and because she never ceases to beget spiritual children for God. He says also in another place about this, "The kingdom of heaven is like yeast which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until the whole [mass] was leavened." A woman took some yeast when the church, by the Lord's generosity, secured the energy of love and faith from on high. She hid this "in three measures of flour until the whole [mass] was leavened" when she performed her ministry of imparting the word of life to parts of Asia [Minor], Europe and Africa, until all the bounds of the world were on fire with love for the heavenly kingdom. The one who said sadly to those who were departing from the purity of the faith, "My little children, for whom I am again in travail, until Christ be formed in you," was indicating that he was among this woman's members. […]

26:19.t: Then, too, Isaiah himself has plainly declared that there shall be joy of this nature at the resurrection of the just, when he says: "The dead shall rise again; those, too, who are in the tombs shall arise, and those who are in the earth shall rejoice. For the dew from Thee is health to them."

Unquestionably, if the people were indulging in figurative murmurs that their bones were become dry and that their hope had perished—plaintive at the consequences of their dispersion—then God might fairly enough seem to have consoled their figurative despair with a figurative promise. Since, however, no injury had as yet alighted on the people from their dispersion, although the hope of the resurrection had very frequently failed among them, it is manifest that it was owing to the perishing condition of their bodies that their faith in the resurrection was shaken. God, therefore, was rebuilding the faith that the people were pulling down. But even if it were true that Israel was depressed at some shock in their existing circumstances, we must not on that account suppose that the purpose of revelation could have rested in a parable. […]
26:19.s: ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH 31
