26:19.t: Isaiah the prophet says, "The dead men shall rise again, and those who are in the tombs shall awake." And the prophet Ezekiel, now before us, says most plainly, "Behold, I will open your graves and bring you up out of your graves." And Daniel says, "Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall arise, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting shame."67And there are many Scriptures that testify of the resurrection of the dead. For there are many other sayings on this matter. But now, by way of remembrance only, we will make a passing mention of the raising of Lazarus on the fourth day and just allude, because of the shortness of the time, to the widow's son also who was raised. And merely for the sake of reminding you, let me mention the ruler of the synagogue's daughter, and the rending of the rocks, and how "there arose many bodies of the saints which slept," their graves having been opened. But especially be it remembered that "Christ has been raised from the dead."

Do not listen to those who say that this body is not raised up; for raised it is, as Isaiah witnesses, saying, "The dead shall arise, and they in the tombs shall be raised." Or, as Daniel says, "Many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall arise, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting shame." But while rising again is the common lot of all people, the manner of rising again is not alike for all. For while we all receive everlasting bodies, those bodies are not alike for all. That is to say, the righteous receive such bodies as may enable them to join with the band of angels throughout eternity, while sinners received bodies in which to undergo through the ages the torture of their sins.

Let your dead live, let my slain rise again: awake and give praise, you who dwell in the dust, for your dew is a dew of lights, and the land of the giants you will pull down to ruin. LXX: The dead will rise again, and they will rise again from the tombs, and those who are in the earth will rejoice. For your dew is their healing, but the land of the impious will fall. While the saints travail and bring forth the spirit, and the inhabitants of the earth fall, because they have not wrought salvations on the earth, those whom the Apostle calls the dead in Christ, and who have been slain for the name of the Lord, will rise again in glory (1 Thess 4). And because their death is sleep, they are said, not, as according to the Seventy, to rise again, but to awaken and to wake up. Hence Lazarus too, who was to be awakened, is called sleeping by the Lord (John 11). […]

But the heavens too shall give their dew, the heavens of which it is written in Psalm 18 (19): The heavens tell the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands. Of these heavens it is said in the song of Deuteronomy: Rejoice, O heavens, with him, that is, with the Lord and Savior, whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son; it is he who speaks with Moses: Let my speech be awaited like the rain, and let my words come down like the dew. For those who were dead in sins shall rise again, and those who lay in whitewashed sepulchres, which are full of dead men's bones, shall be raised up, and those who dwell in the earth shall rejoice. And what the cause of the joy is, the following words show: For the dew which is from you is their healing.

The first part [of the verse] concerns the resurrection of the just, but the last few words may be taken to mean "the bodies of the wicked will fall into the ruin of damnation." In regard to the resurrection of the just, the attentive reader will notice some distinction. "The dead shall rise" refers to the first resurrection; "those in the graves" refers to the second; and in the following words we may not improperly find a reference to the saints whom the Lord will find alive on earth. As for the word "your dew is their health," we are not wrong in taking "health" to mean "immortality," that most perfect health which needs no daily medicine of ordinary food.

Those persons therefore who were restored to life by the power of Christ, we take as a pledge of the hope prepared for us of a resurrection of the dead: and these were, this young man, and Lazarus of Bethany, and the daughter of the chief of the synagogue. And this truth the company of the holy prophets proclaimed before: for the blessed Isaiah said, "The dead shall arise, and those in the graves shall be restored to life: for the dew from Thee is healing to them." And by dew he means the life-giving operation of Christ, which is by the instrumentality of the Holy Ghost.
26:19.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

26:19.t: The prophet Isaiah therefore has said to us, "Your dead men shall arise: and those in the graves shall be raised; and they who are in the earth shall rejoice: for the dew from You is healing to them." And by the dew I imagine he means the life-giving power of the Holy Spirit, and that influence which abolishes death, as being that of God and of life.
26:19.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

26:19.t: Further Isaiah says: The dead shall rise again, and they that are in the graves shall awake. And it is clear that the souls do not lie in the graves, but the bodies.
26:19.s: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 4, Chapter 27

26:20.t: When we read, "Go, my people, enter into your closets for a little while, until my anger passes away," we have in the closets graves, in which they will have to rest for a little while, who shall have at the end of the world departed this life in the last furious onset of the power of Antichrist. Why else did he use the expression closets in preference to some other receptacle, if it were not that the flesh is kept in these closets or cellars salted and reserved for use, to be drawn out thence on a suitable occasion? It is on a similar principle that embalmed corpses are set aside for burial in mausoleums and sepulchers, in order that they may be removed from there when the Master shall order it. […]
26:20.s: ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH 27

26:20.t: He builds, therefore, the ark and makes in it nests, that is, certain storerooms, in which animals of diverse kinds may be received. Of which the prophet also says: "Go, my people, enter into your storerooms, hide yourself for a little while, until the fury of my wrath passes by." This people, then, which is saved in the Church, is compared to all those, whether men or animals, which were saved in the ark.

But according to the anagogy, the people of God is commanded to enter into its chambers, or storerooms, for ταμεῖα means both: to shut, according to the precept of the Gospel, the door of its chamber (Matt 6), and to say with the Prophet: Set a guard, O Lord, on my mouth, and a fortified door to my lips (Ps 140 [141]:3); and to hide itself a little, however little, until the wrath of the Lord passes, so that it does nothing for the sake of glory, but enjoys the good of conscience and awaits God alone as judge. And the storerooms which are to be shut and hidden by those who have become rich in works and words are prudence, temperance, fortitude, justice, so that the left hand may not know what the right hand does, so that we may enjoy the riches of the Law and the Prophets and the Gospel. And that all the days of our life are short and very small, Jacob, exceeding a hundred years, says: Small and very evil are my days (Gen 47:9). […]

Go, my people, enter into your chambers, shut your doors upon you: hide yourself a little for a moment, until the indignation passes. For behold, the Lord will come forth from his place, to visit the iniquity of the inhabitant of the earth against him; and the earth will disclose its blood, and will no longer cover its slain. LXX: Go, my people, enter into your chambers, shut your door: hide yourself a little, however little, until the wrath of the Lord passes. For behold, the Lord from the holy place will bring wrath upon the inhabitants of the earth, and the earth will disclose its blood, and will no longer hide the slain. Above he had said of the saints, The dead will rise again, and those who are in the tombs will rise again; for the dew from you is their healing; and on the contrary of the impious, but the land of the impious will fall. […]

26:21.t: And what follows, For behold, the Lord from the holy place will bring his wrath, signifies this: that the wrath of God begins from the saints, or that all his vengeance is just and holy, not coming down from disturbance of mind, as is usual among men, but from zeal to correct. And I consider the earth of the inhabitants to be that of which it is written: Let the earth hear the words of my mouth (Deut 32:1). And: Give ear, O earth (Isa 1:2). And again: Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord (Jer 22:29). For as those who dwell on the earth, so those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Rom 8). And earth in this place signifies the soul that lives carnally. And it will disclose its blood, if it has caused anyone to stumble, and deserves to hear with Cain: The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood (Gen 4:10, 11). All blood, then, will be required on the day of judgment, nor will the earth hide its blood; […]

27:1.t: In the same way the serpent, which is the author of sin, is called crooked, and the sword of God is drawn against the dragon, the crooked serpent, which makes many twists and turns in its progress. As the coiling movement of the serpent trails along, it is traced unevenly on the ground, since, if it were otherwise, the first parts would hasten along, the next follow transversely and the tail bend aside in the opposite direction. Therefore, he who follows the serpent shows that his life is crooked, uneven, and filled with contrarieties; but, he who follows after the Lord makes his paths straight and his footprints right.

In that day the Lord will visit with his hard and great and strong sword upon Leviathan the bar serpent, and upon Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the whale that is in the sea. LXX: In that day God will bring the holy and great and strong sword upon the dragon, the fleeing serpent, upon the dragon, the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea. The Hebrews hand down that the devil, that is, the slanderer, which is a Greek name, is called in Hebrew SATAN (שטן), that is, adversary. Hence in Zechariah too it is said: Satan, that is, the adversary, stood at his right hand to oppose him (Zech 3:1). And he is also called BELIAL (בליעל), that is, apostate, transgressor, and without yoke. Hence the Apostle too: What fellowship, he says, has Christ with Belial? (2 Cor 6:15). And wherever the Seventy put sons of pestilence, in the Hebrew is written sons of Belial. […]

For "Leviathan" is interpreted to be "their addition." Whose "addition," then, but the "addition" of people? And it is properly styled "their addition," for since by his evil suggestion he brought into the world the first sin, he never ceases to add to it day by day by prompting to worse things.Or indeed it is in reproach that he is called Leviathan, that is, styled "the addition of men." For he found them immortal in Paradise, but by promising the divine nature to immortal beings, he as it were pledged himself to add somewhat to them beyond what they were. But while with flattering lips he declared that he would give what they did not have, he robbed them cunningly even of what they had. And hence the prophet describes this same Leviathan in these words, "Leviathan, the serpent: even Leviathan that crooked serpent." For this Leviathan crept near to people with tortuous windings through the false promise of what he would give them; […]
27:1.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 4, Sections 15-16

27:1.t: For who is described by the designation of the "serpent" but our old enemy, at once slippery and crooked, who for the deceiving of humankind spoke with the mouth of a serpent? Of whom it is said by the prophet, "Leviathan the serpent, the crooked one"; who was for this reason allowed to speak with the mouth of a serpent, that by Leviathan's vessel humanity might learn what he was that dwelt within. For a serpent is not only crooked but slippery as well; and so because he stood not in the uprightness of truth, he entered into a crooked animal.… He spoke to man by means of a slippery animal because if one does not resist him, he secretly slips into the interior of the heart. Now "the dens" of this serpent were the hearts of wicked people.
27:1.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 17, Section 51

27:2.t: In that day the vineyard of pure wine will sing to him. I the Lord, who keep it, will suddenly give it to drink: lest perhaps it be visited, I keep it night and day. LXX: In that day the good vineyard is his desire, that he may be its prince. I am a strong city, a city which is besieged: in vain will I give it drink. For they will be taken by night, and by day the wall will fall. The Hebrew in this place differs much from the edition of the Seventy; therefore let us discuss the particulars as we have set them out. The vineyard of which Isaiah speaks above, A vineyard was made for the beloved on a horn, in a fertile place: how it ought to be understood, let us learn from his own teaching: For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel (Isa 5:1); of which it is sung in the psalm: You brought a vine out of Egypt, and so on (Ps 79 [80]:9). To this vineyard too he gives the cup of purest wine to drink through Jeremiah (Jer 25). […]

27:3.t: It is the soul, too, that says, "I am a strong city, a city besieged." The city is besieged through Christ, the city is that heavenly Jerusalem, in which there are interpreters of God's law and men skilled in doctrine in great abundance; through them one seeks the Word of God.

Therefore let us flee these evils and elevate our soul to the image and likeness of God. The flight from evils is the likeness of God, and the image of God is gained through the virtues. And so, like a painter, he has painted us with the colors of the virtues. "See, I have painted your walls, Jerusalem." Let us not wipe away with the brush of neglect the props of the painted walls of our soul. And so "I have painted the walls," with which we can turn away the enemy. The soul has its walls; from them it stands forth and concerning them it says, "I am a strong city, a city besieged." By these walls it is guarded, and by them it is protected under siege. And truly the soul is a wall, which stretches forth over the camp. And therefore the bride says in the Song of Solomon, "I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers." The wall that the Lord painted is good, even as he says: "On my hands I have painted your walls, and you are always in my sight."

27:4.t: Indignation is not in me: who will make me a thorn and a brier in battle? I will march upon it; I will burn it up together. Or rather shall I hold fast my strength? It will make peace for me, peace it will make for me. LXX: There is none that has not laid hold of it. Who will set me as keeper of stubble in a field? Because of this adversary I have driven it back. Therefore the Lord has done all that he arranged: I have been burned; its inhabitants will say, we will make peace with him, we will make peace with him. According to the Hebrew, this is the sense: I, who by days and nights have always preserved my vineyard, lest the boar out of the wood should lay it waste, lest the beasts should devour it, have I no indignation, and do I not know how to strike the sinner, and to render to each what he deserves? Where Aquila put thorn and brier, in the Hebrew is written SAMIR (שמיר) and SAITH (ושית), which signify adamant and places full of brambles. […]

27:6.t: Those who come forth from the root of Jacob, Israel will blossom and bud, and they will fill the face of the world with seed. LXX: Those who come are the sons of Jacob: Israel will bud and blossom, and its fruit will fill the world. After the Apostles, preaching the Gospel in the whole world, have said, We will make peace with Christ, we will make peace with him, those who were of the seed of Jacob on high, and have attained to the apostolic dignity, will be called sons of Jacob. Then Israel will bud and blossom, seeing that the whole world has been filled with the teaching of its sons and has borne most abundant fruits, which while it remained in Judea it had not borne.

27:7.t: Has he struck him according to the stroke of him who struck him? Or as he killed his slain, so was he killed? This place is understood in two ways: either against Jerusalem, so as to say that it was not struck by God as it itself struck Christ and his Apostles; or against the multitude of the nations, in that, while they persecuted and shed Christian blood, the Apostles and apostolic men nonetheless took care of their salvation and reconciled them to God.

27:8.t:
In measure against measure, when it has been cast off, you will judge it. LXX: Quarreling and reproaching, he will send them away. According to the Hebrew, this is the sense: As Jerusalem did, so will it receive, and according to the measure with which it measured, it will be measured back to it. And it will receive the measure heaped up when the time of judgment has come and God has cast it off. According to the Seventy, what is said depends on what precedes. For Israel will not be struck as it struck, nor killed as it killed: Israel, which quarreled against the Apostles, and reproached its teachers, and commanded them not to speak in the name of Christ. Therefore the Lord will cast them off and drive them out of his flock.

He has meditated in his hard spirit through the day of heat. LXX: Was it not you who meditated with a hard spirit to kill them, with a spirit of fury? According to the Hebrew this is said: with the measure with which it measured, Jerusalem will receive; […]

27:9.t: Therefore by these things iniquity will be forgiven to the house of Jacob, and this is all the fruit, that his sin may be taken away: because he has made all the stones of the altar like stones of ash dashed to pieces; the groves and the shrines will not stand. LXX: Therefore the iniquity of Jacob will be taken away, and this will be his blessing, when I have taken away his sin, when he has made all the stones of the altars crushed like ash ground small, and their trees will not endure, nor the idols. He gives the reasons why, after the Jews have laid hands on the Lord, they may obtain pardon if they are willing to do penance, so that the prayer of the Savior may be fulfilled: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do (Luke 23:34). Therefore, he says, iniquity will be forgiven to the house of Jacob, and its sin will be taken away, so that it may merit the blessing of God, which had called down a curse upon itself, saying: His blood be upon us and upon our children (Matt 27:25); […]

27:10.t: For the fortified city will be desolate; the beautiful one will be left, and abandoned as a desert. There the calf will feed, and there he will lie down and consume its topmost shoots. LXX: Their idols will be cut down like a grove, and the flock dwelling far off will be abandoned like a forsaken flock, and it will be for a long time for pasture, and there the flocks will rest, and after a long time there will not be in it anything green, because it has been dried up. Jerusalem, the city once firm and fortified, because it did not receive the son of the householder, but said, Come, let us kill him, for this is the heir, and the inheritance will be ours (Matt 21:38), will be desolate. […]

27:11.t: The women, returning from the sepulcher and from this vision of the angels, were foreseen by Isaiah, when he says, "Come, you women, who return from the vision," that is, "come" to report the resurrection of the Lord. It was well, however, that the unbelief of the disciples was so persistent, in order that to the last we might consistently maintain that Jesus revealed himself to the disciples as none other than the Christ of the prophets.

And there were many women there, watching from afar, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him; among whom was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee (27, 55. 56). They report that Isaiah prophesied concerning these women when he said: Women coming to the spectacle, come; for it is not a people having wisdom. For he calls women those who had been from afar and from afar were watching Jesus; he calls them to the word, that they may indeed forsake the senseless and forsaken people and come to the new covenant. And I judge those women to be blessed who are built up unto blessedness by the spectacle of the word and by the death of the body of Jesus; for everything that is in Christ, if it be truly seen, makes the beholder blessed.

Therefore they look upon the mortification of the body of Jesus and the manner in which he commended "his spirit" to the Father by his prayers. […]

In the drought of its harvest the women coming and teaching it will be crushed. For it is not a wise people: therefore he who made it will not have mercy on it, and he who formed it will not spare it. LXX: Women coming from the spectacle, come: for it is not a people having understanding; therefore he who made them will not have mercy on them, and he who formed them will not spare. What is said, In the drought of its harvest they will be crushed, for which the Seventy translated, there will not be in it anything green, because it has dried up, according to the Hebrew is coupled with what follows, according to the Seventy with the preceding sense. Let us speak first, then, according to the Hebrew. When the time of the drought and the harvest of Jerusalem, and, to speak more openly, of its devastation, has come, the throng of the synagogues will run together from the whole world to lament Jerusalem and console her evils. Or he is speaking openly of the women who, with bared breasts, strike their arms till they bleed; […]

27:12.t: And it will be in that day: the Lord will strike from the channel of the river to the torrent of Egypt. LXX: And it will be in that day: the Lord will shut in from the trench of the river to Rhinocorura. Had he not added, in that day, by which we are taught that what he is about to say is to be coupled with what precedes, we could have expounded a sense proper to this passage; but now everything is to be referred to what precedes. Since the fortified city will be desolate, and the once beautiful one will be left as a desert, and there the calf will lie down and consume the shoots of the vineyard, and all things will be dried up, since it is not a people having understanding, and because of its folly it has obtained no mercy from its Creator: therefore the Lord will strike, or shut in, from the channel or stream of the river to the torrent of Egypt, so that in all Judea, which was once the land of promise, no word of teaching may be found, nothing of the knowledge of the Scriptures; […]

27:13.t: And it will be in that day: a blast will be sounded on a great trumpet; and those who had been lost from the land of the Assyrians, and those who had been cast out into the land of Egypt, will come, and they will worship the Lord on the holy mountain in Jerusalem. LXX: And it will be in that day: they will sound with a great trumpet; and those who had perished in the region of the Assyrians, and those who had perished in Egypt, will come, and they will worship the Lord upon the holy mountain in Jerusalem. In this place the Jews promise themselves empty hopes: that at the consummation of the world, when the Antichrist, their ἠλειμμένος, as it is said, has come, the dispersed people will be gathered from the Assyrians and from the land of Egypt, and will come to Jerusalem, and, the temple having been built, will worship the Lord their God. This cannot stand at all according to the letter. For not from the Assyrians and from Egypt only, but from the whole world, those who are to believe in Christ will be called. […]

28:1.t: Woe to the crown of pride, to the drunkards of Ephraim, and to the falling flower of the glory of its exultation, who were on the summit of the most fertile valley, going astray from wine. Behold, the strong and mighty one of the Lord, like the onrush of hail, a whirlwind that shatters; like the onrush of many waters overflowing and sent forth upon a spacious land. With feet shall the crown of pride of the drunkards of Ephraim be trodden down. And the falling flower of the glory of its exultation, which is upon the summit of the valley of the fat, shall be like an early fruit before the ripeness of autumn, which, when the beholder has looked upon it, as soon as he has taken it in his hand, he will devour it. LXX: Woe to the crown of insolence, the hirelings of Ephraim: a flower falling from glory upon the summit of the fat mountain, you who are drunk without wine. […]

28:3.t:
" 3. The crown of pride, the hirelings of Ephraim shall be beaten down. 4. And the fading flower of glorious hope on the top of the high mountain shall be as the early fig: he that sees it will desire to swallow it, before he takes it into his hand. 5. In that day the Lord shall be the crown of hope, the garland of glory to the remnant of his people; for they shall be left in the spirit of judgment."

And here he prophesies that the Lord will be "a crown of hope and glory" to the remnant of his people, not to all their nation, but to those only signified by the remnant, and names the others in contrast to the remnant of his people "a crown of shame and hirelings of Ephraim."
28:3.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

28:5.t: In that day the Lord of hosts shall be a crown of glory and a garland of exultation to the remnant of his people, and a spirit of judgment to him who sits upon judgment, and strength to those returning from war to the gate. But these also have not known because of wine, and have gone astray because of drunkenness; the priest and the prophet have not known: they are swallowed up by wine because of drunkenness, they have gone astray in drunkenness: they have not known the seer, they have been ignorant of judgment, or wonderfully. For all the tables are filled with vomit and filth, so that there was no more room. LXX: In that day the Lord Sabaoth shall be a crown of hope, which is woven of glory, for the remnant of the people. They shall be left in a spirit of judgment upon judgment, and strength forbidding to kill. For these have been deceived by wine: they go astray because of strong drink; the priest and the prophet have lost their minds because of strong drink; […]

28:8.t: According to the anagogy, that Hebrew text in which we said: For all their tables are filled with vomit and filth, so that there is no more room, can be referred to the heretics, and to the scribes and Pharisees, in this way: that we say all their teaching and all their mysteries are full of vomit and filth, since they do not digest the food of the holy Scriptures nor make it life-giving to the whole body, but void it unripe and stinking, so that God finds no place in them. But I wonder what Theodotion meant, that for the Hebrew word called CISOA (קיאצאה), for which Aquila translated vomit of filth and Symmachus simply vomit, he should say ἐμετὸν δυσαλίας, that is, vomit of dysalia, a word I have not been able to find read anywhere among the Greeks, unless perhaps he coined a new name for a new thing. Indeed among the Hebrews too it is a compound, since vomit is called CI, and SOA filthy. Whatever, then, causes nausea and vomiting can be called δυσαλία.

28:9.t: Whom shall he teach knowledge, and whom shall he make to understand what is heard? Those weaned from the milk, those drawn from the breasts: for command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little there, a little there. For with speech of lip and with another tongue he will speak to this people, to whom he said: This is my rest; refresh the weary, and this is my refreshment, and they would not hear. And the word of the Lord shall be to them: command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little there, a little there; that they may go and fall backward, and be broken, and be snared, and be taken. LXX: To whom shall we announce evils, and to whom shall we announce tidings? those who are weaned from the milk, who are drawn from the breast. Expect tribulation upon tribulation; wait for hope upon hope; […]

"Whom shall he teach knowledge, and whom shall he make to understand the message? Those weaned from milk and drawn away from the breasts." We dispose ourselves to receive the gift of understanding through holiness of life. Milk signifies the sweetness of carnal delights, by which sweetness the carnal and the infantile are nourished, that is, those who follow infantile impulses. And as long as a man is joined to these carnal consolations, he is called a nursing infant and is not fit to receive the solid food of life and understanding. If we wish to bless God and receive this gift, it is necessary that we be drawn away from these consolations and separate ourselves from the milk of concupiscences.

28:10.t: Only let our spirit be kept unbroken, the firmness of our faith in Christ be maintained unshaken, and ere long our Champion will appear; He will come and will not tarry. Expect tribulation after tribulation, hope upon hope; yet a little while; yet a little while. Thus the Holy Ghost knows how to comfort His nurslings by a promise of the future. After tribulations comes hope, and what we are hoping for is not far off, for let a man name the whole of human life, it is but a tiny interval compared with the endless age which is laid up in our hopes.

"My conscience is at rest, and I know that it is not from any fault of mine that I am suffering; moreover affliction in this world is a ground for expecting a reward hereafter." When the enemy was more than usually forward and ventured to reproach her to her face, she used to chant the words of the Psalter.… When she felt herself tempted, she dwelt upon the words of Deuteronomy.… In tribulations and afflictions she turned to the splendid language of Isaiah: "You that are weaned from the milk and drawn from the breasts, look for tribulation upon tribulation, for hope also upon hope. Yet a little while must these things be by reason of the malice of the lips and by reason of a spiteful tongue." This passage of Scripture she explained for her own consolation as meaning that the weaned, that is, those who have come to full age, must endure tribulation upon tribulation that they may be accounted worthy to receive hope upon hope.

We read in the book of Job how, while the first messenger of evil was yet speaking, there came also another; and in the same book it is written, "Is there not a temptation"—or as the Hebrew better gives it—"a warfare to man upon earth?" It is for this end that we labor, it is for this end that we risk our lives in the warfare of this world, that we may be crowned in the world to come. That we should believe this to be true of people is nothing wonderful, for even the Lord was tempted, and of Abraham the Scripture bears witness that God tested him. It is for this reason also that the apostle says, "We glory in tribulations … knowing that tribulation works perseverance; and perseverance, character; and character, hope. Now hope does not disappoint." And in another passage [we read], "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation or distress or persecution or family or nakedness or peril or sword? As it is written, 'for your sake we are killed all the day long; […]

28:11.t: These gifts were first bestowed on us the apostles when we were about to preach the Gospel to every creature, and afterwards were of necessity afforded to those who had by our means believed; not for the advantage of those who perform them, but for the conviction of the unbelievers, that those whom the word did not persuade, the power of signs might put to shame: for signs are not for us who believe, but for the unbelievers, both for the Jews and Gentiles. For neither is it any profit to us to cast out demons, but to those who are so cleansed by the power of the Lord; as the Lord Himself somewhere instructs us, and shows, saying: "Rejoice not because the spirits are subject unto you; but rejoice, because your names are written in heaven." [Luke 10:20] Since the former is done by His power, but this by our good disposition and diligence, yet (it is manifest) by His assistance. It is not therefore necessary that every one of the faithful should cast out demons, or raise the dead, or speak with tongues; […]

For in the Law it is written: That in other tongues and in other lips I will speak to this people, and not even so will they hear me, says the Lord (Isa. 28:11). The Lord said this of those whom he foreknew would not believe even the Savior. For to speak in other tongues and in other lips is to preach the new testament, as the prophet Jeremiah says: Behold, the days will come, says the Lord, and I will accomplish for the house of Israel and for the house of Judah a new testament, not according to that which I appointed for their fathers (Jer. 31:31): that is, with the order changed, to speak otherwise than the words of the old law run; when they hear that the sabbath is loosed, the new moons made void, circumcision ceasing, the sacrifices changed, foods long forbidden permitted to be eaten, Christ preached as God from God: this is to speak in other tongues and in other lips; and not even so were the faithless willing to obey God. […]

Just as sometimes all the utterances of the Old Testament together in the Holy Scriptures are signified by the name of the Law. For the apostle, in citing a text from the prophet Isaiah, where he says, "With divers tongues and with divers lips will I speak to this people," yet prefaced it by, "It is written in the Law." And the Lord Himself says, "It is written in their Law, They hated me without a cause," whereas this is read in the Psalm.

28:14.t: What, then, are the burdens that he censures? None but those which they were accumulating of their own accord, when they taught for commandments the doctrines of men; for the sake of private advantage joining house to house, so as to deprive their neighbor of his own; cajoling the people, loving gifts, pursuing rewards, robbing the poor of the right of judgment, that they might have the widow for a prey and the fatherless for a spoil. Of these Isaiah also says, "woe to them that are strong in Jerusalem!"

When you renounce Satan, trampling underfoot every covenant with him, then you annul that ancient "league with hell," and God's paradise opens before you, that Eden, planted in the east, from which for his transgression our first father was banished.

Therefore hear the word of the Lord, you scornful men, who rule over my people that is in Jerusalem. For you have said: We have struck a covenant with death, and with hell we have made a pact: when the overflowing scourge passes through, it shall not come upon us, because we have made a lie our hope, and by a lie we are protected. LXX: Therefore hear the word of the Lord, you afflicted men and princes of this people that is in Jerusalem: Because you have said: We have made a testament with hell, and a pact with death: if the passing tempest rushes on, it shall not come upon us, since we have made a lie our hope, and by a lie we shall be protected. What we said above, that the princes of the Jews used to say to the prophets with mockery: Command, command again; wait, wait again, and other things like these, by which it is shown that they in no way believed the words of the prophets but held their prophecy in contempt, the present chapter shows, in which they are called scornful men. […]

28:16.t: And again the prophet says, "Since as a mighty stone He is laid for crushing, behold I cast down for the foundations of Zion a stone, precious, elect, a corner-stone, honourable." Next, what says He? "And he who shall trust in it shall live for ever." Is our hope, then, upon a stone? Far from it. But [the language is used] inasmuch as He laid his flesh [as a foundation] with power; for He says, "And He placed me as a firm rock."
28:16.s: The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter VI

28:16.t: If at any time in reading the Scripture you stumble at something which is a fair stone of stumbling, and rock of offence, blame yourself; for you must not despair of finding in this stone of stumbling and rock of offence thoughts to justify the saying, "He that believeth shall not be ashamed." First believe, and thou shalt find beneath what is deemed a stumbling-stone much gain in godliness. For if we really received a commandment to speak no idle word, because we shall give account of it in the day of judgment; and if we must with all our might endeavour to make every word proceeding out of our mouths a working word both in ourselves who speak and in those who hear, must we not conclude that every word spoken through the Prophets was fit for work? and it is no wonder if every word spoken by the Prophets had a work adapted to it. Nay, I suppose that every letter, no matter how strange, which is written in the oracles of God, does its work. […]

He ordained that the former Law should stand till He came, and He was revealed as the originator of the second Law of the new covenant preached to all nations, as being responsible for the Law and influence of the two religions, I mean Judaism and Christianity. And it is wonderful that divine prophecy should accord:

"Behold, I lay in Zion a stone, choice, a cornerstone; precious, and he that believes on him shall not be ashamed."

Who could be the corner-stone but He, the living and precious stone Who supports by His teaching two buildings and makes them one? For He set up the Mosaic building, which was to last till His day, and then fitted on to one side of it our building of the Gospel. Hence He is called the corner-stone.
28:16.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 7

28:16.t:
And furthermore Isaiah also prophesied beforehand with regard to this stone. For he said:—Thus saith the Lord, Behold I lay in Zion a chosen stone in the precious corner, the heart of the wall of the foundation. And he said again there:—Every one that believeth on it shall not fear. And whosoever falleth on that stone shall be broken, and every one on whom it shall fall, it will crush. For the people of the house of Israel fell upon Him, and He became their destruction for ever. And again it shall fall on the image and crush it. And the Gentiles believed on it and do not fear.

And He shows thus with regard to that stone that it was laid as head of the wall and as foundation. But if that stone was laid as the foundation, how did it also become the head of the wall? How but that when our Lord came, He laid His faith in the earth like a foundation, and it rose above all the heavens like the head of the wall and all the building was finished with the stones, from the bottom to the top. […]

Was his tomb made with hands? Does it rise above the ground, like the tombs of kings? Was the sepulcher made of stones joined together? And what is laid upon it? Tell us exactly, O prophets, about his tomb also, where it lies, and where we shall look for it. But they answer, "Look upon the solid rock which you have hewn," look and see.… I, who am "the chief corner stone, chosen, precious," lie for a while within a stone, I, who am "a stone of stumbling" to the Jews but of salvation to them that believe.

Jacob also, hastening to seek a bride, met Rachel unexpectedly at the well. And a great stone lay upon the well, which a multitude of shepherds were wont to roll away when they came together, and then gave water to themselves and to their flocks. But Jacob alone rolls away the stone, and waters the flocks of his spouse. The thing is, I think, a dark saying, a shadow of what should come. For what is the stone that is laid but Christ Himself? for of Him Isaiah says, "And I will lay in the foundations of Sion a costly stone, precious, elect:" and Daniel likewise, "A stone was cut out without hands," that is, Christ was born without a man. For as it is a new and marvellous thing that a stone should be cut out of the rock without a hewer or stone-cutting tools, so it is a thing beyond all wonder that an offspring should appear from an unwedded Virgin.

The foundation of justice therefore is faith, for the hearts of the just dwell on faith. And the just man that accuses himself builds justice on faith, for his justice becomes plain when he confesses the truth. So the Lord says through Isaiah: "Behold, I lay a stone for a foundation in Zion." This means Christ as the foundation of the church. For Christ is the object of faith to all; but the church is as it were the outward form of justice; it is the common right of all.
28:16.s: On the Duties of the Clergy 1.29

28:16.t: Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will lay in the foundations of Zion a tried stone, a corner stone, precious, founded with a foundation: he who believes, let him not hasten. And I will set judgment in the weight, and righteousness in the measure: and hail shall overthrow the hope of falsehood, and waters shall overflow the protection. And your covenant with death shall be blotted out, and your pact with hell shall not stand; when the overflowing scourge passes through, you shall be trodden down by it. When it passes through, it shall take you away: for in the morning, at daybreak, it shall pass through, in the day and in the night, and vexation alone shall give understanding to the hearing: For the bed is straitened, so that one must fall out, and a short cloak cannot cover both. LXX: Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will put into the foundations of Zion a precious stone, chosen, a corner stone, honorable, in its foundations; and he who believes shall not be confounded. […]

To the one group, the infant at birth is shown as the chief cornerstone announced by the prophet; to the other group he is manifested at the very outset of his career. He has already begun to weld together in himself the two walls originally set in different directions, bringing shepherds from Judea and magi from the East.

And it is seemly for us first of all to uproot wickedness, and then to lay in ourselves the foundation of the edifice of virtues, in order that the rock may receive our foundation, as it is written, and that on a sure stone may be our building, even as it is said. And in this respect we should be like unto the physicians of our nature who, until they have removed and cleansed the matter from the sore, do not lay upon it the plaster which buildeth up and maketh to grow the living flesh; and so must it be with us also when we have uprooted the matter of the lust of the belly, and have made accusations against its filthy and loathsome forms.

Christ is the foundation of this faith. For other foundation no one can lay, but that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. For He is the cornerstone of which Isaiah and Peter speak: See, I am laying a stone in Sion, a stone that has been tested, a precious cornerstone as a sure foundation. And the Apostle: You are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ Jesus Himself as the chief cornerstone.

28:17.t: God promises also to set in it the judgment of the weight: For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). And righteousness, or mercy, in the measure, so that he may render to each according to his works, and temper righteousness and mercy each by the other, according to what we read in the psalms too: Mercy and truth have met each other: righteousness and peace have kissed (Ps 84 [85]:11). Your hope also, he says, and your lie, that is, the devil, the father of every lie, the hail of my punishments shall overthrow.

And the protection under which you thought you would be safe, a mighty tempest and a multitude of waters shall destroy, so that the friendship and covenant you had with death and with hell, that is, with the devil, shall perish forever. And the scourge, or tempest, of which you had said: When the overflowing scourge passes through, it shall not come upon us, shall come, and you shall be trodden down by it, that is, you shall suffer all the torments which, in your despairing mind, you thought you would never suffer.

28:19.t: For it will always rush upon you, and in prosperity as in adversity you will feel the wrath of the Lord, and cruel death will lay you waste. What shall I say of the punishments? The mere dread of punishments and the fear of torments will correct you unto salvation, and will make you understand your evils. And when you have been vexed, then you will know that my prophets spoke the truth.

Further, as for what is read in the Seventy: Learn to hear, you who are afflicted: we cannot fight, and we ourselves are too weak to be gathered together, what sense it has, and how it is connected with what goes before, I am entirely ignorant. Unless perhaps the divine word is speaking to the princes of the people and exhorting them to have hope in God and not in death and hell, and to learn to hear the oracles of the prophets; and they answer that, for the weakness of their strength, they cannot fight against the opposing powers, nor be gathered together among the people of God.

Now righteous people conceive a dread of God before his indignation is stirred up against them; they fear him at rest, lest they should feel him as moved. But, on the other hand, the wicked then for the first time fear to be smitten when they are under the rod, and terror then rouses them from the sleep of their insensibility when vengeance is troubling them. And hence it is said by the prophet, "And only the vexing alone shall supply understanding to the hearing." For when they have begun to be stricken in vengeance for the contempt and neglect of God's precepts, then they understand the thing that they heard.
28:19.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 11, Section 41

28:20.t: And what follows: For the bed is straitened, so that one must fall out, and a short cloak cannot cover both, has the sense we read in the Apostle: You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and of the table of idols (1 Cor 10:20-21); and elsewhere: What participation has righteousness with iniquity? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? What part has the believer with the unbeliever? What consent has the temple of God with idols (2 Cor 6:14-15)? He speaks under the metaphor of a most chaste husband, who says to an adulterous wife: One little bed cannot hold me and the adulterer with you, and a short cloak cannot cover both the husband and the paramour. […]

And the glory of the God of Israel was there, not because it took delight in such a neighbor, but so that by its presence it might destroy the idol of jealousy and the temple; hence the overthrow of the city and of the temple also follows after a short time; and it is written in Isaiah that a narrow bed can by no means hold two, and a short cloak cannot cover both, Scripture signifying that saying of the Apostle: What agreement has Christ with Belial? The temple of God with an idol?

28:21.t: For as on the mountain of divisions the Lord shall stand, as in the valley of Gibeon he shall be angry, that he may do his work, his strange work, that he may perform his work, his work is foreign to him. And now do not mock, lest perhaps your bonds be tightened. For I have heard from the Lord God of hosts a consummation and a cutting short upon the whole earth. LXX: As a mountain of the ungodly the Lord shall rise up, and he shall be in the valley of Gibeon; with fury he shall do his works, a work of bitterness, and his fury shall deal as with strangers: and his bitterness is strange. And do not you rejoice, lest your bonds be strengthened, since I have heard from the Lord God Sabaoth things completed and cut short, which he will do upon all the earth. The Lord promised that he would lay a precious stone in the foundations of Zion, so that hail might overthrow the lie and the hope of the ungodly, and a mighty tempest might blot out the covenant with death and the pact with hell. […]

According to the Seventy, the Lord himself is said to be about to rise like a mountain of the ungodly and to be in the valley of Gibeon, that he may do his works, which are all one work of bitterness: and this should by no means seem blasphemous. For it does not say that the Lord will be a mountain of the ungodly, but like a mountain, which seems most heavy to the ungodly and those who bear it. Just as a negligent son and a sick man may think a father and a physician cruel if they restore them to health with blows and with the cautery of discipline. For the Lord will rise up and will be in the valley of Gibeon on account of those who, though for their sins they stand in a low place, are lifted up into pride by the swelling of their mind. For Gibeon means hill: that he may do his works, which are works of bitterness, when he is compelled to change his clemency and, instead of sweet, becomes bitter.

Hence Isaiah, contemplating our salvation and [Christ's] passion, well said: "That he may do his work, his strange work; that he may perform his work, his work is strange to him." For the work of God is to gather the souls that he created and call them back to the joys of the eternal light. But it is not the work [of] God in his essence to be flogged, to be smeared with spittle, to be crucified, to die and to be buried, but this is the work of a sinful person who deserved all these things for his sins. But [Jesus] himself bore our sins in his own body on the tree. And he who in his own nature always remains incomprehensible deigned to be comprehended in our nature and to be flogged, because if he had not assumed the attributes of our weakness he could never have raised us to the power of his fortitude.… And he does his strange work that he might do his proper work, because insofar as he bore our sins in infirmity he led us who are his creatures to the glory of his fortitude in which he lives and reigns with God the […]

28:22.t: Since, then, the Lord is going to rise up from his patience and will by no means spare, just as he did not spare on Mount Pharasim and in the valley of Gibeon, I warn you, O scornful men, by no means to laugh at my prophets, nor to think that what they announce will not come, lest, if you persist in mocking, the bonds of your sins be tightened (For each one is bound fast by the cords of his own sins (Prov 5:22), or the time of captivity come upon you. For what the Lord was postponing in time, the bonds, the captivity and the punishments, or the last day of judgment, he is now about to fulfill in fact, and to consummate and cut short. Therefore I, the prophet, announce to you the things I have learned from the Lord God almighty are to come upon the whole earth, so that you may forestall the impending wrath by repentance.

Therefore you who are one day to suffer these things, do not now rejoice with that joy with which the rich man too rejoiced, clothed in purple at his banquet and neglecting the poor man Lazarus (Luke 16), lest perhaps your bonds become stronger. For what the Lord is going to do, and to fulfill his sentence in fact, this I have both heard and announced to you in full. And as for what he added: Upon all the earth, according to the history understand the borders of Judea; according to the anagogy, of the whole world.

28:23.t: Give ear and hear my voice: attend and hear my speech. Will the plowman plow all day that he may sow, will he break up and hoe his ground? When he has leveled its surface, will he not sow gith, and scatter cumin, and put wheat in rows, and barley, and millet, and vetch in their borders? And he will instruct him in judgment; his God will teach him. For gith shall not be threshed with saws, nor shall the wheel of the cart go round over the cumin; but gith shall be beaten out with a rod, and cumin with a staff: but bread shall be crushed. Yet the thresher shall not thresh it forever, nor shall the wheel of the cart vex it, nor shall he crush it with its hoofs. And this has gone forth from the God of hosts, that he might make his counsel wonderful and magnify righteousness. LXX: Give ear and hear my voice: attend and hear my words. Will he who plows plow all day, or will he prepare the seed before he prepares the ground? […]

28:24.t: I praise wedlock, I praise marriage, but it is because they give me virgins. I gather the rose from the thorns, the gold from the earth, the pearl from the shell. "Does the plowman plow all day to sow?" Shall he not also enjoy the fruit of his labor? Wedlock is the more honored, the more what is born of it is loved. Why, mother, do you grudge your daughter her virginity? She has been reared on your milk, she has come from your womb, she has grown up in your bosom. Your watchful affection has kept her a virgin. Are you angry with her because she chooses to be a king's wife and not a soldier's? She has conferred on you a high privilege; you are now the mother-in-law of God.

Will the farmer, he says, always plow so that he may cast the seed? Will he not first break up the ground and turn over the furrows with the plowshare, and break the lumps lying there with rake and hoe, so that when he has leveled the surface of the earth and first softened the hard fields, he may then scatter gith or cumin, and sow wheat, and barley, and millet, and spelt in their borders, according to the variety of the land and of the seasons: for all things are not sown at once. For spelt, which the Greeks call ζέαν, some understand vetch.

God dispenses the human race in various ways: now he punishes, now he has mercy; now he rebukes, now he defends; that is, now he plows, now he sows, now he reaps the ripe fruits, and when they are reaped he threshes them on the floors, and governs his world as he will. Gith and cumin, that is, all the nations that did not receive the knowledge of him nor have the precepts of the Law, he corrects with a rod and a staff; but the wheat, that is, the people of the Jews, he will torment with great punishments. For to whom more is entrusted, from him more will be required. And the servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12:47); and in another place it is written: The mighty shall suffer torments mightily (Wis 6:7). Yet he will not torment them forever. For it is one thing to be ungodly, another to be a sinner. […]

28:26.t: And God by his judgment instructs the farmer himself, that is, the sower, by nature, and teaches him to know what cultivation to apply to which seed.

28:27.t: Then, when the time of reaping has come, gith and cumin, which are the weaker seeds, are not ground by the wheels of the carts, which, made of iron like saws, are driven round and dragged over the reaped crops; but they are beaten out with a rod and a staff, which are commonly called flails.

Where we have translated: gith shall be beaten out with a rod, and cumin with a staff, the Seventy, meaning I know not what, translated: but cumin is eaten with bread. Indeed the old Greek translators too, in rendering the Hebrew, were silent about this expression, perhaps because they had nothing to say.

28:28.t: But bread, that is, the wheat from which bread is made, is ground by iron wheels, and all its stalk is crushed into chaff. Yet it is not always vexed and ground, nor at all times crushed by the hoofs of the wheels; for which in the Hebrew it says by their horses: so that, since he had spoken of the hoofs of the wheels, he might keep the metaphor in the rest. Some would have it that, because he named hoofs and horses, herds of mares are meant, which are usually let into the threshing floors to tread out the grain; but Scripture could not say what the province of Judea did not have.

And that passage in which we, according to the Hebrew, have put: Yet the thresher shall not thresh it forever, nor shall the wheel of the cart vex it, nor shall he crush it with its hoofs, the Seventy translated not word for word but according to the sense: For I will not be angry with you forever, nor shall the voice of my bitterness trample you down: showing that refreshment is to come to sinners after torments, and that these things have gone forth from the Lord as portents and wonders. Hence sinners who are afterward to be punished are commanded to take counsel and exalt their consolation, by no means a vain one, as was added by the Seventy, but consolation absolutely. For God would never command them to exalt their vain consolation, which would be of no profit to them.

28:29.t: But this, that is, that gith and cumin are beaten out with a rod and a staff, while wheat and barley and spelt, and perhaps millet too, are ground by iron wheels, not forever, is the judgment of God, who in all things shows his wonderful counsel and displays the greatness of his righteousness in all. These things we have said παραφραστικῶς, so that we may more easily understand the sense for which they are said.

29:1.t: Woe to Ariel, Ariel, the city which David besieged. Year has been added to year, the solemnities have rolled round. I will surround Ariel with a rampart, and it shall be sad and mourning; and it shall be to me like Ariel. And I will set as it were a ring round about you, and I will cast up a mound against you, and set up fortifications for your siege. You shall be brought low, you shall speak from the earth, and your speech shall be heard from the ground, and your voice shall be like that of a python from the earth, and from the ground your speech shall mutter. And the multitude of those who winnow you shall be like fine dust, and the multitude of those who have prevailed against you like passing ash. And it shall be suddenly, at once: it shall be visited by the Lord of hosts with thunder and the shaking of the earth, and with the great noise of whirlwind and tempest, and of the flame of devouring fire. […]

At the beginning of this chapter too, where we have said: Year has been added to year, or taken away, they translated: gather the fruits, or produce, year upon year: eat, for you shall eat with Moab. And the sense is: before the acceptable year of the Lord, of his preaching, comes, or rather the two years, of which we read in the Canticle of Habakkuk according to the Hebrew: In the midst of two times you shall be known (Hab 3), sow for yourselves in tears, that you may reap in joy (Ps 125 [126]). It is written in the Gospel according to John that the Lord came to Jerusalem at three Passovers, which make two years (John 2:13). And what follows: For you shall eat with Moab, is not in the Hebrew. Of this we can say that, unless they gather for themselves the fruits of repentance, they will begin to eat with those who do not enter the Church of the Lord forever. The other points in which they seem to differ are plain, and from what we have expounded their interpretation is easy.

I know that I have read that Ariel means my light of God, which is far otherwise. For here the first syllable is written with ALEPH and RES (אר): but light, which in Hebrew is called OR, has between ALEPH and RES the middle letter VAU, which is not found in the present name. And they refer all that is now said against Ariel to the heretics, who reckon their own doctrine to be the light of God, and who are to be overcome by the true David: and all their solemnities are to be taken away, and their present joy changed into future sorrow; and God commands them to do penance, lest they begin to eat with the Moabites and be like the Gentiles. For he himself will overcome Ariel, and will encompass all their strength and riches with his army. And with towers, that is, with the teachers of the Church, he will bring their words low to the earth, so that they will by no means set their mouth against heaven, but will be written in the earth and speak from the earth, and become like dust shaken off by a wheel; […]

29:2.t: And the Lord says that he will surround Ariel with a rampart, with the Babylonian army, and that it will be sad and mourning when it has been destroyed by them. And again, under Jeshua son of Jozadak the high priest, and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and Ezra and Nehemiah, when Haggai and Zechariah prophesied, it will be like Ariel, in that it will have the likeness of the ancient temple, but not have its magnificence and adornment.

29:3.t: A second time also the Lord threatens that he will surround Ariel with a ring, and cast up a mound against it, and set up fortifications for its siege, and that what he himself says, lamenting Jerusalem in the Gospel, will be fulfilled: If you knew the things that are for your peace, for days shall come upon you, and your enemies shall surround you with a rampart, and besiege you, and you shall be brought low to the ground (Luke 19:42ff.). And Jerusalem shall be trodden down by the nations until the time of the nations is consummated.

29:4.t: For in other words the prophet now says the same thing: that, brought low, it speaks from the earth, and its speech is heard from the ground; and its voice is like that of a python from the earth, and from the ground it mutters like sparrows; so that by these words he signifies the νεκυομαντείαν of the magicians, by which they are said to call up souls and to hear the thin voices of shades, or rather of demons. Indeed for python Aquila translated magician, which in Hebrew is called CHEB (כאב), for which the Seventy translated those speaking from the earth. By these words it is indicated that the ruin of the temple will remain until the consummation of the world, so that, having collapsed into ashes, it will never be raised again.

29:5.t: And so great an army of Roman power will encompass you, O Ariel, that it will be compared to countless dust, like ash flying through the air. Hence he compares to dust and ash not the weakness of those who made war against them, but their multitude, which is equal to the countless sands.

29:6.t: And this will be suddenly, at once, so that in the midst of peace sudden wars arise under Nero, and the Lord of hosts visits Jerusalem with thunder, and with the shaking of the earth, and with the whirlwind of tempest, and with the flame of devouring fire, by which he signifies that the temple was to be burned.

29:7.t: And the Romans, who, when the Jews had been overcome and Jerusalem overthrown under Titus and Vespasian, offered to the Capitol spoils from the vessels that once were God's, and thought that what they had done was the work of their own valor and of the power of their gods, not of the wrath of God, will possess all their riches as in a dream and in a vision of the night. And as one who is hungry thinks, while sleeping, that he is eating in his dreams, and one who is thirsty, his throat parched with thirst, drinks rivers, and when he has awakened his thirst becomes fiercer, having been mocked by an empty drink: so the multitude of all the nations which, subject to Roman power, fought against Mount Zion, will have their riches as in a shadow and a cloud and a dream of the night, riches which they will leave behind by an early death. In the place where we have put: all who have made war and besieged and prevailed against it, the Seventy translated: and all who have fought against Jerusalem, which is not in the Hebrew.

29:8.t: Let us speak of him who thought he was happy since he was chief butler and believed that this was the summit and crown of all power, that he would give the cup to the king. This was his glory, this was his grandeur in this world; when he was deprived of this he felt sorrow, and when he was restored to it he rejoiced. But this is a dream, and all worldly power is a dream, not a reality. To be sure, he saw by way of a dream that his preeminent position was restored to him. Isaiah also says that people of this kind are such as take delight in prosperity in this world. One who eats and drinks in his sleep thinks he is filled with food and drink, but when he awakens, he begins to be more hungry; then he understands how insubstantial were that dreamer's food and drink. Just so, one who is asleep in this world and does not open his eyes to the mysteries of God, as long as he is in a deep corporeal sleep, supposes that such worldly power is of some importance, seeing it, as it were, in his dreams. […]

But that we may know that waters and cups signify teaching, the Lord speaks to the Samaritan woman: Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will not thirst for ever. Therefore whoever drinks of the waters of the Samaritan woman, that is, of the heretics, will always thirst and will not be able to cool the burning of a parched throat, as Isaiah cries aloud about this very thing: As one who is thirsty dreams that he drinks, and when he has risen he still thirsts, and his soul has hoped in vain; so shall all the nations be that fight against Jerusalem. For truly whoever drinks of the waters of the heretics, and fights against Jerusalem, the Church of God, drinks in his sleep, and his soul is mocked by empty images. And when he thinks himself satisfied, then he will have the beginning of thirst.

29:9.t: Be stupefied and wonder: waver and stagger, be drunk, and not with wine; reel, and not with drunkenness. For the Lord has mingled for you a spirit of deep sleep: he will close your eyes; your prophets and your princes, who see visions, he will cover. And the vision of all shall be to you like the words of a sealed book, which, when they give it to one who knows letters, they will say: Read this, and he will answer: I cannot, for it is sealed. And the book shall be given to one who does not know letters, and it shall be said to him: Read; and he will answer: I do not know letters. For spirit of deep sleep the Seventy translated compunction; Theodotion ecstasy of mind; Aquila καταφορὰν, that is, heavy sleep; which in Hebrew is called THARDEMA (תרדמה), and which Scripture records was sent by God upon Adam (Gen 2), when the woman was made from the rib of his side. And Jonah snored in this same sleep in the ship (Jonah 1). […]

But we should notice the ways in which the Lord points out that the soul is weighed down: for He did not mention adultery, or fornication, or murder, or blasphemy, or rapine, which everybody knows to be deadly and damnable, but surfeiting and drunkenness, and the cares or anxieties of this world: which men of this world are so far from avoiding or considering damnable that actually some who (I am ashamed to say) call themselves monks entangle themselves in these very occupations as if they were harmless or useful. And though these three things, when literally given way to weigh down the soul, and separate it from God, and bear it down to things earthly, yet it is very easy to avoid them, especially for us who are separated by so great a distance from all converse with this world, and who do not on any occasion have anything to do with those visible cares and drunkenness and surfeiting. […]
29:9.s: The First Conference of Abbot Isaac, Chapter 5

29:10.t: Not to recognize sins lest penance follow is the wrath of God, as it is written: "And the Lord gave to them the spirit of a deep sleep," lest they actually return and be cured and be healed by their lamentations and just satisfactions after their sins.…The first degree of felicity is not to sin; the second, to recognize the sins committed. In the former, innocence runs upright and unimpaired to save; in the latter, there follows the remedy to cure. They have lost both of these by offending God.… Or do you think, brother, that crimes against God are light matters, small and of little moment, because through them the majesty of an offended God is not sought, because the wrath and fire and day of the Lord are not feared, because, with Antichrist at hand, the faith of a militant people is disarmed while vigor and the fear of Christ are taken away?

29:11.t: And plainly, if we hear negligently, if we bring no zeal to erudition and understanding, not only the Scripture of the law and the prophets, but even that of the Apostles and the Gospels is covered from us with a great veil. But I fear lest, through excessive negligence and dullness of heart, the divine volumes be for us not only veiled but even sealed, so that, "if a book to be read is given into the hands of a man who does not know letters, he says: I do not know letters; if it is given into the hands of a man who knows letters, he says: it is sealed." Whence it is shown that we must not only apply zeal to learning the sacred letters, but must also entreat the Lord and "day and night" beseech him, that the Lamb "from the tribe of Judah" may come and himself, taking the "sealed book," may deign to open it. For he it is who, "opening the Scriptures," kindled the hearts of the disciples, so that they said: "was not our heart burning within us, when he opened to us the Scriptures?"

Isaiah [prophesied] that the Jews would not understand the holy Scriptures, but that they would become intelligible in the last times, after Christ had come: "And all these words shall be to you as the words of a book that is sealed, which, if you shall give to a man that knows letters to read, he shall say, I cannot read, for it is sealed.… But in that day the deaf shall hear the words of the book, and they who are in darkness and in a cloud; the eyes of the blind shall see."
29:11.s: Treatise XII. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews 1:4

29:11.t: Instead of "Seal the vision and the prophet,'' Aquila gives, I think, a more suitable rendering, viz. "And for fulfilling vision and prophet." For our Lord Jesus Christ did not come as it were to seal up the visions of the prophets, for He rather opened and explained those that were of old obscure and sealed, tearing away so to say the seals impressed on them, and taught His disciples the meaning of the Holy Scriptures. Hence He says, "Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah hath prevailed, and he has opened the seals that were set on the book," in John's Apocalypse. What are these seals but the obscurities of the prophets? Isaiah knew them well and definitely says too: "And these words shall be as the words of the sealed book." The Christ of God did not come then to shut up the vision and the prophet, but rather to open them and bring them to the light.
29:11.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 2

29:11.t: But Thou, O Daniel, shut up the words and seal the book, even to the time appointed. Many shall pass over, and knowledge shall be manifold. He who had revealed manifold truth to Daniel now signifies that the things he has said are matters of secrecy, and he orders him to roll up the scroll containing his words and set a seal upon the book, with the result that many shall read it and inquire as to its fulfilment in history, differing in their opinions because of its great obscurity. And as for the statement, "Many shall pass over" or "go through," this indicates that it will be read by many people. For it is a familiar expression to say: "I have gone through a book," or, "I have passed through an historical account." Indeed this is the idea which Isaiah also expressed in regard to the obscurity of his own book: "And the sayings of that book shall be like the words of a book that is sealed. And if they shall give it to an illiterate man, saying, 'Read it,' he will reply, 'I do not know how to read.' […]

Hence he significantly did not say that the vision of all the prophets is sealed to all who read; but to you, he says, it shall be sealed, to whom I now speak, to whom I foretell that these things will come; or he will close forever the eyes of your princes, who, according to the Septuagint, boasted that they saw things hidden and secret. And all holy Scripture, he says, shall be to you closed and sealed, so that you, who suppose you know the letters of the Law and the oracles of the prophets, and meditate day and night with unwearied mouth on the volumes of the Scriptures, may not understand what you read; as it is written in the Apocalypse of John: Who is worthy to open the book and to loose its seals (Rev 5:2)? And when no one had been found to open the seals, he says that he wept, and that at last he was granted a word of God to him: Do not weep: behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has prevailed to open the book and to loose its seals. […]

[Daniel 12:4] "But Thou, O Daniel, shut up the words and seal the book, even to the time appointed. Many shall pass over, and knowledge shall be manifold." He who had revealed manifold truth to Daniel now signifies that the things he has said are matters of secrecy, and he orders him to roll up the scroll containing his words and set a seal upon the book, with the result that many shall read it and inquire as to its fulfilment in history, differing in their opinions because of its great obscurity. And as for the statement, "Many shall pass over" or "go through," this indicates that it will be read by many people. For it is a familiar expression to say: "I have gone through a book," or, "I have passed through an historical account." Indeed this is the idea which Isaiah also expressed in regard to the obscurity of his own book: "And the sayings of that book shall be like the words of a book that is sealed. And if they shall give it to an illiterate man, saying, 'Read it,' he will reply, 'I do not know how to read.' […]
29:11.s: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER TWELVE

29:11.t: Since, therefore, the teachers of the Jews to this present day cannot read and open the seals and lay open the mysteries of the Scriptures, if you give that book to the unlearned people, who are devoured by their own teachers, they will confess that they do not know letters and therefore cannot read. And of two evils it is much lighter to confess ignorance of the Law than to boast of wisdom and not be able to know what is said.

Moreover, since the enemy of our salvation was keeping a watchful eye on virgins, according to the prophecy of Isaiah, who said, Behold a virgin shall conceive and bare a Son and shall call His name Emmanuel, which is, being interpreted, ‘God with us,’ in order that he who taketh the wise in their own craftiness may deceive him who always glorieth in his wisdom, the maiden is given in marriage to Joseph by the priests, a new book to him who is versed in letters: but the marriage was both the protection of the virgin and the delusion of him who was keeping a watchful eye on virgins.
29:11.s: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 4, Chapter 14

29:11.t: Sacred Scripture is compared to the water of the sea on account of the profundity of its mysteries. The sea is deep, nor can a man wade across it: so great is the profundity of the mysteries of sacred Scripture that, however illuminated a man may be and however great his industry, he cannot attain to their depth. Hence Isaiah says: "The vision of all things shall be to you as the words of a sealed book, which when they give to one who knows letters, they will say: Read this; and he will answer: I cannot, for it is sealed. And the book shall be given to one who does not know letters, and it shall be said to him: Read; and he will answer: I do not know letters." Neither the learned nor the unlearned will be able to read it. Who then will read it? I say that he who wishes to enter the sanctuary of God with pride will not be able to, even if he is learned; similarly, if a learned man wishes to enter, he would be foolish. It is necessary, therefore, that one have both learning and the spirit.

29:13.t: Let us cleave, therefore, to those who cultivate peace with godliness, and not to those who hypocritically profess to desire it. For [the Scripture] saith in a certain place, "This people honoureth Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me." [Isaiah 29:13] And again: "They bless with their mouth, but curse with their heart." [Psalm 62:4] And again it saith, "They loved Him with their mouth, and lied to Him with their tongue; but their heart was not right with Him, neither were they faithful in His covenant." [Psalm 78:36-37] "Let the deceitful lips become silent," [and "let the Lord destroy all the lying lips, ] and the boastful tongue of those who have said, Let us magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is lord over us? For the oppression of the poor, and for the sighing of the needy, will I now arise, saith the Lord: I will place him in safety; I will deal confidently with him." [Psalm 12:3-5]
29:13.s: Clement's First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 15

29:13.t: What is this obstinacy or what is this presumption to place human tradition before the divine plan and not to notice that God is offended and angered as often as human tradition subverts and disregards the divine precepts? He cries and says through Isaiah, the prophet, "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far separated from me. In vain, moreover, they honor me, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men."

For the speaking in this way or in that is not the cause of the thought within us; but the hidden conception of the heart supplies the motive for such and such words; "for from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh." We make the words interpret the thought; we do not by a reverse process gather the thought from the words. Should both be at hand, a man may certainly be ready in both, in clever thinking and clever expression; but if the one should be wanting, the loss to the illiterate is slight, if the knowledge in his soul is perfect in the direction of moral goodness. "This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." What is the meaning of that? That the right attitude of the soul towards the truth is more precious than the propriety of phrases in the sight of God, who hears the "groanings that cannot be uttered." Phrases can be used in opposite senses; the tongue readily serving, at his will, the intention of the speaker; […]

Again the form of righteousness is described and magnified when Scripture says, "The law of his God is in his heart, and his stride will not be broken." The law of God is in the heart of the righteous. Which law? It is not the written law but the natural law, because "the law was not laid down for the righteous but for the unrighteous." The law is in his heart, not superficially, as it is on the lips of the Jews, for "he who believes with his heart is justified." The one who believes also speaks, but the one who speaks does not necessarily believe. For instance, the people did not believe about whom it is written: "This people honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me."
29:13.s: Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms 36.69

29:13.t: For if we, when sending children to teachers, should we see them reaping no benefit thereby, begin to be severe in blaming the teachers, and remove them often to others; what excuse shall we have for not bestowing upon virtue even so much diligence as upon these earthly things, but forever bringing our tablets home empty?
