And the service of righteousness silence, so that they may worship the Lord not with the much speaking of the Jews but with the brevity of faith; and may rest secure in eternal peace, and in their tabernacles may be the riches of which the Apostle spoke (1 Cor 1:5): I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ, because in everything you have been made rich in him, in all speech and in all knowledge.

He that suffers from a flux of seed is pronounced unclean, because, being addicted to much speaking, he defiles himself by that which, had it been orderly issued, might have produced the offspring of right thought in the hearts of hearers; and, while he incautiously spends himself in loquacity, he sheds his seed not so as to serve for generation, but unto uncleanness.
32:17.s: The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 2, Chapter 4

32:17.t: It is the practice of the impertinent ever to answer by the opposite what is said aright, lest, if they assent to the things asserted, they should seem inferior. And to these the words of the righteous, however small in number they have been heard, are 'much,' in that as they cut their evil habits to the quick, they fall heavy upon the hearing, whence that is even wrested to a crime, which by a right declaration is pronounced against crimes. For the very person, who had delivered strong sentences on grounds of truth, Zophar rebukes and calls full of words, in that, whereas wisdom reprimands sins by the mouth of the righteous, it sounds like superfluity of talkativeness to the ears of the foolish. For froward men account nothing right, but what they themselves think, and they reckon the words of the righteous idle in the degree that they find them differing from their own notions. […]
32:17.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 10, Section 2

32:18.t: And when the Christian people sits, or dwells, in beauty, or, as the Seventy translated, in the city of peace, which is without doubt in the Church, then hail and tempest and the raging wrath of the Lord will come down upon the forest, of which it was said above: And Carmel will be counted as a forest; and the city of Jerusalem will be brought low, and, according to another Scripture, will speak from the earth.

32:20.t: The prophet says, "Blessed is he that sows into all waters, whose ox and donkey tread," [that is] the people, from the law and from the Gentiles, gathered into one faith.

Blessed is he from whom Jesus asks drink, as He did from that Samaritan woman, and gives a well of water springing up unto eternal life. Blessed is he that soweth beside all waters, and upon every soul, tomorrow to be ploughed and watered, which today the ox and the ass tread, while it is dry and without water, and oppressed with unreason. And blessed is he who, though he be a "valley of rushes," is watered out of the House of the Lord; for he is made fruitbearing instead of rushbearing, and produces that which is for the food of man, not that which is rough and unprofitable. And for the sake of this we must be very careful not to miss the Grace.

Accordingly, like a perfect man learned in the law and made firm in the gospel, accept the faith of both Testaments, for, as we read today, "Blessed is he who sows upon every water, where the ox and the donkey tread," that is, who sows upon the people who follow the teaching of both Testaments. This is the ploughman's ox, wearing the yoke of the law, of which the law says, "You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out your corn," for this ox has the horns of holy Scripture. But in the Gospel the Lord, representing the people of the Gentiles, mounts the colt of a donkey.

Do we ask where we have read of the ox and the ass together? In Deuteronomy it is written: You shall not plough with a calf and an ass together (Deut 22:10). And in this same Isaiah: Blessed is he who sows upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread (Isa 32:20). Ebion ploughs with the ox and the ass together, worthy, for the lowliness of his understanding, of the poverty of his name; for he so receives the Gospel as not to abandon the ceremonies of the Jewish superstitions, which went before in shadow and image. But blessed is he who sows in the words of the Scriptures, of the old as well as of the new Instrument, and treads the waters of the letter that kills, so as to reap the fruit of the life-giving spirit.
At the end of the section too they translated thus: Blessed are those who sow upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread.

Since these things are so, and we have learned from the prophetic oracle how great the goods are that the Church will possess, and how great the evils that Jerusalem will suffer: blessed are you, Apostles, and you other teachers, who sow upon all the waters of Holy Scripture, in which the ox and the ass tread. The ox is a clean animal, on account of the election of the fathers; the ass unclean, on account of the former idolatry of the Gentiles; so that the Church of the Lord may be gathered both from the Circumcision and from the Uncircumcision.

Something of the same kind, I think, is said in Isaiah too: Blessed is he who sows upon the water, where the ox and the ass tread. That is, that teacher is held worthy of blessedness who sows upon the well-watered breast of his hearers, a people gathered from the Jews as well as from the Gentiles.

By water peoples are denoted, as it is said by John, "Now the waters are peoples." By water likewise not only the tide of peoples drifting away, but also the minds of good men that follow the preachings of faith, are denoted, as the Prophet saith, "Blessed are ye that sow upon all waters." And it is said by the Psalmist; "The voice of the Lord is upon the waters."
32:20.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 19

32:20.t: What else is meant by 'seed,' but the word of preaching? As the Truth says in the Gospel, "A sower went forth to sow"; and as the Prophet says; "Blessed are ye who sow upon all waters." What else but the Church, ought to be understood by the threshing floor? Of which it is said by the voice of the Forerunner; "And He will throughly purge His floor."
32:20.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 31

33:1.t: Woe to you who plunder: will you not yourself be plundered? And you who despise: will you not yourself be despised? When you have finished plundering, you will be plundered: when, wearied, you have ceased to scorn, you will be scorned. LXX: Woe to those who make you wretched: for no one makes you wretched. And those who reject you do not reject you: those who reject will be taken, and will be handed over, and like a moth in a garment so will they be overcome. He had spoken of the Apostles and of the teachers of the churches: Blessed are those who sow upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread: now he directs a curse at their persecutors, nay, at their prince, who possesses the hearts of the impious: that whatever they have done they may receive back, and their present power may be the material of future torments. Hence according to the LXX it is said: Woe to those who make you wretched: for no one makes you wretched. […]

33:2.t: O Lord, have mercy on us: for we have waited for you: be their arm in the morning, and our salvation in the time of tribulation. At the voice of the Angel the peoples fled, at your exaltation the nations were scattered. And your spoils will be gathered as the young locust is collected, as when the ditches are full of it. The Lord is magnified, for he has dwelt on high: he has filled Zion with judgment and righteousness. And there will be faith in your times: the riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge: the fear of the Lord is itself his treasure. LXX: O Lord, have mercy on us, for we trust in you: the seed of the unbelieving has come to perdition, but our salvation is in the time of tribulation: because of the voice of fear the peoples were astonished at the fear of you, and the nations were scattered. But now your spoils will be gathered, small and great: as if someone were gathering locusts, so will they mock you: holy is God who dwells on high. Zion is filled with judgment and righteousness; […]

33:6.t: Whoever then has been established in this perfect love is sure to mount by a higher stage to that still more sublime fear belonging to love, which is the outcome of no dread of punishment or greed of reward, but of the greatest love; whereby a son fears with earnest affection a most indulgent father, or a brother fears his brother, a friend his friend, or a wife her husband, while there is no dread of his blows or reproaches, but only of a slight injury to his love, and while in every word as well as act there is ever care taken by anxious affection lest the warmth of his love should cool in the very slightest degree towards the object of it. And one of the prophets has finely described the grandeur of this fear, saying: "Wisdom and knowledge are the riches of salvation: the fear of the Lord is his treasure." […]
33:6.s: The First Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, Chapter 13

33:6.t: But "true wealth" signifies either the joy of eternal life itself, concerning which it is written, "the riches of his inheritance in the saints," or those spiritual virtues with which the fullness of life is attained, about which Isaiah said, "the riches of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge; the fear of the Lord himself is its treasure.""And if you are unfaithful with goods that are not yours, who will give you something of your own?" The resources of this world are alien to us, that is, external to the nature of our habitat, "for we brought nothing into this world and we are without doubt unable to take anything from it." Our possession is the kingdom of heaven, our life is Christ, and our wealth consists in the fruitfulness of spiritual works, about which Solomon said, "The redemption of a man's soul is his wealth."

33:7.t: Behold, those who see will cry outside: the Angels of peace will weep bitterly. The ways are laid waste, the one who passed along the path has ceased, the covenant has been made void, he has cast off the cities, he has not regarded men. The earth has mourned and languished, Lebanon is confounded and has become deaf, and Sharon has become like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel are shaken. Now I will rise up, says the Lord: now I will be exalted, now I will be lifted up. You will conceive burning heat, you will bring forth stubble; your spirit, like fire, will devour you. And the peoples will be like ashes from a burning: thorns gathered together will be burned with fire. […]

But if you want to see that the ancient prophets were terribly sad and aggrieved about the future blinding of their nation, which was the cause of our illumination, listen to Isaiah, for when he was sent to announce beforehand the grace of the Lord's coming, saying that "a light has arisen upon those who dwell in the region of the shadow of death," he responded immediately to the advent of the same light, saying "you have enlarged the nation; you have not increased its joy." And elsewhere, while commemorating the despondency of this people, Isaiah said, among other things, "the messengers of peace will weep bitterly, referring to the prophetic heralds of the divine word."

33:9.t: The earth has mourned and languished for those who dwelt in the land (Gen 15 and 22). Lebanon is confounded and has become deaf: without doubt it signifies the Temple, of which we read in Zechariah: Open your gates, O Lebanon, that fire may devour your cedars (Zech 11:1). Or Jerusalem, which in Ezekiel is called Lebanon, when the Prophet says: A great eagle with great wings, which has the design of entering into Lebanon (Ezek 17:3); which the divine word afterward interprets: when, it says, Nebuchadnezzar came to Jerusalem; plainly explaining the Eagle as the king of Babylon, and Lebanon as Jerusalem. Sharon has become like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel are shaken. For Bashan, the LXX translated Galilee, the province in place of one place of the province. Sharon, moreover, is the name of the whole region around Joppa and Lydda, in which very broad and fertile plains stretch out. Bashan too is a region beyond the Jordan, which the two and a half tribes possessed, and which means most fruitful and fat (Deut 3); […]

33:10.t: Therefore the Lord says that he will rise up, either from his very great patience, or from the underworld, and will be exalted among the nations, and lifted up on the cross.

33:11.t: And he turns in apostrophe to the Jews themselves: You will conceive burning heat, and you will bring forth stubble, and your spirit will kindle a fire for you, so that the devouring flame may consume what was conceived and brought forth.

33:12.t: And the peoples of the Jews, he says, will be like ashes from a burning, showing the greatness of their misfortune by the remnants of the embers. For their thorns, which have been gathered together by the multitude of their sins, will be devoured by the burning; which most refer to the last captivity and overthrow of Jerusalem. Others affirm that it will come about more fully and perfectly at the time of judgment.

33:13.t: He speaks moreover concerning our ears, how He hath circumcised both them and our heart. The Lord saith in the prophet, "In the hearing of the ear they obeyed me." And again He saith, "By hearing, those shall hear who are afar off; they shall know what I have done." And, "Be ye circumcised in your hearts, saith the Lord." ... Therefore He hath circumcised our ears, that we might hear His word and believe.
33:13.s: The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter IX

33:13.t: Hear, you who are far off, what I have done, and you who are near, know my strength. The sinners in Zion are terrified, trembling has seized the hypocrites. Who of you can dwell with devouring fire? Who of you will dwell with everlasting burnings? He who walks in acts of righteousness, and speaks truths, who casts away avarice from calumny, and shakes his hands free of every bribe, who stops his ears lest he hear blood, and shuts his eyes lest he see evil. He will dwell on high; fortresses of rocks are his height: bread has been given him, his waters are faithful. His eyes will see the king in his beauty: they will behold the land from afar. Your heart will meditate fear. Where is the scribe? Where is he who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of little ones? You will not see the imprudent people, the people of deep speech, so that you cannot understand the eloquence of its tongue, in which there is no wisdom. […]

33:14.t: The Scripture itself … expressly distinguishes between Abraham's bosom, where the poor man dwells, and the infernal place of torment. "Hell" (I take it) means one thing, and "Abraham's bosom" another. "A great gulf" is said to separate those regions and to hinder a passage from one to the other. Besides, the rich man could not have "lifted up his eyes," and from a distance too, except to a superior height, and from the said distance all up through the vast immensity of height and depth.… There is some determinate place called Abraham's bosom, and it is designed for the reception of souls of Abraham's children, even from among the Gentiles (since he is "the father of many nations," which must be classed amongst his family), and of the same faith as that with which he himself believed God, without the yoke of the law and the sign of circumcision. This region, therefore, I call Abraham's bosom. […]

The sinners, or the impious, who were in Zion are terrified, or have departed, and trembling has seized the hypocrites, to whom the Lord said in the Gospel: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites (Matt 23:14)! Who of you can dwell with him who is a devouring fire? Who will dwell with everlasting burnings? Or according to the LXX: Who will announce to you that the eternal fire is burning, which God has prepared for the devil and his angels?

33:15.t: Who, then, will be able to dwell with God, or to announce the punishments to come? Everyone who is such as the prophetic word describes: who walks in many acts of righteousness, and loves acts of righteousness not once but always, and speaks truths not on one occasion but continually; who casts away avarice, which is the mother of calumny. For money is not heaped up for one man except with another's loss and harm. And he shakes his hands free of every bribe; for bribes blind the eyes even of the wise. He stops his ears lest he hear the judgment of blood. All iniquity and oppression and injustice is a judgment of blood: and though one does not kill with the sword, yet he slays by his will. And he shuts his eyes lest he see evil. Happy the conscience that neither hears nor beholds evil.

There are some who indeed do not receive rewards of money from ordination, yet bestow sacred orders for human favor, and from that very generosity seek only the recompense of praise. These certainly do not bestow freely what was freely received, because from the service of holiness they have rendered, they seek the coin of favor. Hence the prophet spoke well when describing the just man, saying: Who shakes his hands free from every gift. For he does not say: Who shakes his hands from a gift, but added from every, because one thing is a gift from service, another a gift from the hand, another a gift from the tongue. A gift from service is deference unduly rendered, a gift from the hand is money, a gift from the tongue is favor. Therefore he who bestows sacred orders shakes his hands free from every gift when in divine matters he seeks not only no money, but also no human favor.
33:15.s: 40 Homilies on the Gospels, Homily IV

33:15.t: We must bear in mind too that there are three ways in which deceit itself is practised, in that, surely, the object aimed at in it is either the secret interest of our fellow creatures' feelings, or the breath of applause, or some outward advantage; contrary to which it is rightly said of the righteous man by the prophet, "Blessed is he that shaketh his hands clear of every favour." For as deceit does not consist only in the receiving of money; so, no doubt, a favour is not confined to one thing, but there are three ways of receiving favours after which deceit goeth in haste. For a favour from the heart, is interest solicited in the opinion, a favour from the mouth is glory from applause, a favour from the head a reward by gift. Now every righteous man 'shaketh his hands clear of every favour,' in that in whatever he does aright, he neither aims to win vainglory from the affections of his fellow creatures, nor applause from their lips, nor a gift from their hands. […]
33:15.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 9

33:16.t: He, then, who is such will dwell on high, that is, in the kingdom of heaven, or in a lofty cave of a very strong rock, in Christ Jesus: the rock that followed the people of Israel, that they might drink from it and be protected by its strength. Bread will be given him, and his waters are faithful: which the fables of the Gentiles understand as ambrosia and nectar. But we shall interpret the bread and the most faithful waters as the law of God.

By the name of bread the teaching of perfection is shown, as Paul attests, who, rousing the weak to conversion, says: "I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. For you were not yet able, nor are you yet able." For if milk belongs to little ones, bread belongs to none but the perfect. Whence also it is said of the strength of the perfect man: "He shall dwell on high, the fortifications of rocks shall be his loftiness, bread has been given to him." Therefore in the house of bread a king is sought for anointing, because those are profitably advanced who are nourished in the order of perfect conduct. For he is able to make others strong who has not been nourished in lax and negligent conduct.

33:17.t: He, then, who is such will behold Christ the king in his brightness, of whom it is said above (cf. Isa 32:1): Behold, a righteous king will reign, and princes will rule in judgment. And his eyes will see from afar the land which they had long desired, the land of the meek and gentle, of which it is written in the Gospel: Blessed are the meek, for they will possess the land (Matt 5:4); or, set in heaven, they will look down on earthly things.

Through the sacraments of his humanity with which we have been imbued, we may be able to attain the contemplation of the glory of his divinity, that contemplation which he himself in his faithful benevolence pledged to his faithful servants when he said, "One who has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. One who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him." He says, "I will manifest myself"—that is, "Not in such a way that everyone can look at me, or in such a way that even the unfaithful can see me and crucify me, but in such a way that only the pure eyes of the saints can see 'the King of ages in his beauty.' " In this way I will show myself to those who love me, so as to reward them for their love. […]

The disciples indeed saw him coming in his kingdom, for on the mountain they saw him shining in that brightness with which he will be seen in his kingdom by all the saints when the judgment has been brought to completion. But since the eyes of the disciples were still mortal and corruptible, they were then unable to sustain what the whole church of the saints will have the power to look upon when she has become incorruptible through resurrection. Concerning this it is written, "Their eye will see the king in his beauty."

33:18.t: Your heart will meditate fear: so that when you have attained all things, you may say with the Apostle: I who am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God (1 Cor 15:9). For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. Where is the scribe? Where is he who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of little ones? (Prov 9:1). Where, he says, are the scribes and Pharisees, who, weighing the words of the Law in the balance, deceived the unhappy people? whom the Scripture now calls little ones: little in sense, little in understanding.

33:19.t: And when the eyes of the believer have beheld the king in his majesty, and his heart has meditated fear, then he will not see the imprudent people, the people of the Jews, or of the philosophers and orators of the world, who applaud themselves for secular learning and eloquence, of whom he now says: A people of deep speech, so that you cannot understand the eloquence of its tongue; whose whole adornment is in words, who have only the leaves and the shade of speech, and do not possess the fruit of truth. Then there follows: In which there is no wisdom; of whom it is also said in another place: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will reject (1 Cor 1:19). Why? Because God has made foolish the wisdom of this world.

33:20.t: Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnity: your eyes will see Jerusalem, a wealthy habitation: a tabernacle that can by no means be moved, nor will its pegs be taken away for ever, and none of its cords will be broken. For only there is our Lord magnificent: a place of rivers, streams very broad and open; no ship with oars will pass through it, nor will a great trireme cross it. For the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king; he himself will save us. Your cords are loosened, and will not hold: so will your mast be, that you cannot spread out the ensign. Then the spoils of many preys will be divided: the lame will seize the plunder. Nor will the neighbor say, I am faint: the people that dwells in it, iniquity will be taken away from it. […]

33:21.t: For the plainly spoken words of these interpreting have made the sentences of the ancient Fathers henceforth clear to us. Hence the Prophet Isaiah viewing the words plain by the interpretation of Holy Church, not obscured by the darkness of allegories, exclaimed, saying, "The place of rivers, the broadest and open streams." For the sayings of the Old Testament were as narrow and close streams, which bound up the sentences of their lore in the darkest gathering together. But on the other hand the teaching of Holy Church are 'streams both broad and open,' because her declarations are at once many in number to those that find them, and plain to those that seek.
33:21.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 18

33:23.t: But now he speaks to the earthly Jerusalem: that the cords of its tabernacle are loosened, and could not hold up the tent, and its mast, on which the most beautiful sails once hung, has fallen with its ropes broken, so that it is useless not only for sailing but also for an ensign. And after their ship has been broken up and the tabernacle scattered, so that the cords are torn apart on both sides, the plunder will be divided among the victors: who will be so weak in their own strength that they are called lame; and nonetheless, since the wrath of God gives them strength, they will feel no weakness, nor will they say: I have labored. For whoever is among them, iniquity and sin will be taken away from him, because he has carried out the will of God.

34:1.t: Come near, you nations, and hear, and you peoples, attend: let the earth hear, and its fullness, the world and all its offspring. For the indignation of the Lord is upon all the nations, and his fury upon all their host: he has slain them and given them over to slaughter. Their slain will be cast out, and from their corpses a stench will rise: the mountains will melt with their blood. And all the host of the heavens will waste away: the heavens will be rolled back (or folded together) like a book: and all their host will fall away, as a leaf falls from the vine and from the fig tree, for my sword has been made drunk in heaven. Behold, it will come down upon Idumea, and upon the people of my slaughter, to judgment. The sword of the Lord is filled with blood, it is fattened with fat: with the blood of lambs and goats, with the blood of rams full of marrow; for the Lord has a victim in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Edom. And the unicorns will come down with them, and the bulls with the mighty. […]

34:2.t: For the indignation of the Lord is described as coming not upon the one nation of Judea alone, and upon the Assyrians and Chaldeans, the Egyptians, the Moabites and the Ammonites and the Philistines, but against all the nations, and upon all their host, or, as the LXX translated, their number, to slay them and to make the stench of rotting bodies rise on high, signifying the sins of all the nations; so that the mountains are filled with their gore and filth and blood: all the lofty powers and the Angels who presided over the several nations; and all the host or strength of the heavens wastes away: the heavens are rolled back, or folded together, like a book, and all their host and army, and, as the LXX translated, the stars will fall away, in the likeness of leaves which, as the cold draws near, fall withered and shrivelled from the vine and the fig tree. […]

34:4.t: But they forsook Him, and worshipped idols, as Jeremiah said concerning them:—Go to the distant isles, and send to Kedar, and consider well and see, whether there has been (anything) like this, whether the nations change their gods, those that are no gods. But My people has changed My honour for that which is not profitable. Be astonished, ye heavens, at this; and quake and fear greatly, saith the Lord; because My people have done two wickednesses; they have abandoned Me, the fountain of the water of life, and they have gone and dug for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns which cannot hold water. For the broken cisterns are the fear of images and idols. And He calls the heavens to astonishment, because they worshipped the hosts of the heavens. And the heavens shall receive as a penalty, that they shall be rolled up as a scroll, and all the host of them shall fall down.

So, our Lord Jesus Christ comes from heaven, and he comes with glory at the last day to bring this world to its close. For this world will accomplish its course, and the world that once came into being is hereafter to be renewed. For seeing that corruption, theft, adultery and every form of sin has been poured out on the earth, and in the world fresh blood has been ever mingled with previous blood, this astonishing habitation filled with iniquity is not to last. This world passes away that the fairer world may be revealed. Now would you have this proved by the express words of Scripture? Listen to these from Isaiah: "And the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll; and all the stars shall fall down, as the leaf falls off from the vine, and as a falling fig from the fig tree."

34:5.t: All these things will come about because his sword has been made drunk in heaven: the punishment and sentence and vengeance upon sinners which is pronounced by the Lord. This sword and blade is sharpened against the impious in Ezekiel (Ezek 21), and, when very many have been slain, is commanded to go back into its sheath. And when it has been made drunk and filled in heaven, that is, in the air, which by the usage of the Scriptures is called heaven, then it will come down to Idumea too, that is, to earthly things: so that after the punishment of the demons the souls of men too may be judged. For Idumea in our language means earthly.
And because God did not spare the angels who sinned, who by their own fault lost their heavenly dwelling, therefore he himself says through Isaiah: My sword has been made drunk in heaven.

34:6.t: And it is filled with blood and fattened with the fat of lambs and goats, and of rams full of marrow, and of bulls: so as to signify that princes and people alike are to be punished. For the Lord has a victim in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Edom. Of this Bozrah and Idumea the same Prophet also testifies in what follows (cf. Isa 63:1), saying: Who is this who comes from Edom, with his garments red from Bozrah? And some think that, because Bosor means flesh, the torments of all in the flesh are shown by the Lord's victim in Bozrah: they fall into a pious error. For in the present place it is written not with the letter SIN, which is set in BOSOR (בשר), that is, flesh, but with SADE, and it is called BOSRA (בצרה), which according to Joshua and Jeremiah is found not in Edom, that is, Idumea, but in the land of Moab (Jer 48). […]

34:8.t: For it is the day of the Lord's vengeance, the year of the recompenses of the judgment of Zion. And its torrents will be turned into pitch, and its ground into sulphur: and its land will become burning pitch. Night and day it will not be quenched, for ever: its smoke will go up: from generation to generation it will be desolate; for ages of ages there will be none passing through it. And the pelican and the hedgehog will possess it, and the ibis and the raven will dwell in it, and the measuring line will be stretched over it, to bring it to nothing, and the plummet unto desolation. Its nobles will not be there: they will rather call upon the king, and all its princes will be as nothing. And thorns will spring up in its house and nettles, and the thornbush in its fortresses: and it will be the lair of dragons and the pasture of ostriches. And demons will meet with onocentaurs, and the hairy one will cry out one to another: there will lie down the lamia, and will find rest for herself. […]
What we have said is prophesied of Jerusalem, and what the Jews suspect is said of the Roman empire, some refer to the whole world, so as not to seem to disagree with what precedes.

Sacred Scripture has stature, because it directs conduct toward standing, so that the minds of hearers may not be bent toward earthly desire. It has height, because it promises the joys of eternal life in the heavenly homeland. It also has a horrible appearance, because it threatens all the reprobate with the punishments of hell. Therefore it shows its stature in the building of conduct, it shows its height in the promise of rewards, it shows its horrible appearance in the terrors of punishments. For it is upright in precepts, lofty in promises, horrible in threats. ... It has a horrible appearance when, describing hell, it says: "The day of vengeance of the Lord, the year of retribution for the judgment of Zion; and its torrents shall be turned into pitch, and its soil into sulphur; and the land shall be burning pitch, day and night it shall not be extinguished forever."

34:9.t: and therefore we judge that after the general consummation of the whole world the Scripture returns to Jerusalem, to which it was speaking at that time, and describes its devastation at full length: namely, that after the time of the Roman siege has come, all things will be filled with pitch and sulphur and burning flames, and its smoke will remain for ever, and the pelican and the hedgehog and the ibis and the raven will dwell there, animals which are accustomed to dwell in desert places; and that this will come about because the line and the plummet of the Lord, that is, his sentence, cannot be changed.

34:11.t: But those who follow tropology affirm that, once the people of the Jews has been driven out, idolaters and those who serve various superstitions will dwell in Jerusalem under the names of beasts and monsters; and that these are the pelicans and hedgehogs, the ibis and the raven, the dragons and ostriches, and the onocentaurs, and the demons, and the hairy ones, and the lamia, which in Hebrew is called LILITH (לילית), and was translated lamia by Symmachus alone, and which some of the Hebrews suspect to be ἐριννὴν, that is, a fury. And indeed, if we consider that colonies brought from various nations were settled in Jerusalem, and that according to the rite of their own provinces the several households worshipped the monstrous forms of their own demons, we shall affirm that all these dwelt in Jerusalem.

34:12.t: Its nobles, that is, the Apostles and the believers, will not be there, nor will they be joined to the number of the lost, but will rather call upon Christ the king. But all its princes, namely the scribes and Pharisees, will be brought to nothing, and in the once most adorned houses thorns and nettles and the thornbush will spring up. And it will be the lair of dragons and the pasture of ostriches, which are themselves also signs of utter desolation.

34:13.t: But it would take too long to search through the whole of Scripture and run through the different kinds of them, as they are termed by the prophets onocentaurs, satyrs, sirens, witches, howlers, ostriches, urchins; and asps and basilisks in the Psalms; and are called lions, dragons, scorpions in the gospel, and are named by the Apostle the prince of this world, rulers of this darkness, and spirits of wickedness. And all these names we ought not to take as given at random or hap-hazard, but as alluding to their fierceness and madness under the sign of those wild beasts which are more or less harmful and dangerous among us, and by comparing them to the poisonous wickedness or power which among other beasts or serpents, some pre-eminence in evil confers on them, they are called by their names, in such a way that to one is assigned the name of lion because of the fury of his rage and the madness of his anger, to another that of basilisk because of his deadly poison, which kills a person before it is perceived, and to […]
34:13.s: First Conference of Abbot Serenus, Chapter 32

34:13.t: Which conduct the Lord by the Prophet well reproves, under the character of Babylon, saying; "Thorns and nettles shall spring up in her houses, and the bramble in the fortresses thereof." For what do we understand by 'nettles,' but the irritations of thoughts, and what by 'thorns,' but the piercings of sins? Nettles therefore and thorns spring up in the houses of Babylon, because in the disorder of a reprobate mind there arise longings of thoughts which exasperate, and sinful deeds which wound. But they who act thus have others also more wicked than themselves as their defenders. Whence he there fitly subjoined immediately, "And the bramble in the fortresses thereof." For the bramble is crowded with such a circle of thorns, that it can hardly be touched from its roughness. The nettle and the thorn therefore spring up within, but both of them are fortified without by the bramble: because, namely, smaller offenders commit any kinds of evil, but greater and most abandoned ones defend them.
34:13.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 33

34:14.t: And there will meet one another in it, according to the LXX, various phantoms of demons, or, as all the others translated according to the Hebrew, SIIM (ציים) and IIM (איים), onocentaurs and hairy ones and the lamia, which the fables of the Gentiles and the fictions of the poets describe.

34:15.t: The hedgehog too rears its young there, and has a most secure lodging: thither the kites are gathered, a most rapacious bird, which in Hebrew is called DAJOTH (דיות), or, as the LXX translated, stags, of which we shall speak below.

And what the LXX translated: There the stags met one another, and saw one another's faces: they passed by in number, not one of them perished, nor did one seek the other. For the Lord commanded them, and his spirit gathered them: and he himself gave them lots, and his hand will divide for them, that they may feed for ever, and possess it from generation to generation, and rest in it: this we shall interpret allegorically, to teach that the stags, that is, the Apostles and all holy teachers, of whom it is written: As the stag longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God (Ps 41 [42]:1); and elsewhere: The voice of the Lord perfecting the stags (Ps 28 [29]:9); and again: Let the stag of friendship and the foal of your graces speak with you (Prov 5); and in Job: But you have watched the months of the stags, and you will bring forth their young (Job 39:2); and in the Song of Songs it is said: My kinsman is like a roe, or a young stag upon the mountains of spices (Song 2:9); […]

Hence it is rightly said through the prophet, under the similitude of Judah, to the soul that sins and excuses itself, "There the urchin had her nest." For by the name of urchin is denoted the duplicity of a mind that is insincere, and cunningly defends itself; because, to wit, when an urchin is caught, its head is perceived, and its feet appear, and its whole body is exposed to view; but no sooner has it been caught than it gathers itself into a ball, draws in its feet, hides its head, and all is lost together within the hands of him that holds it which before was all visible together. So assuredly, so insincere minds are, when they are seized hold of in their transgressions. For the head of the urchin is perceived, because it appears from what beginning the sinner has advanced to his crime; the feet of the urchin are seen, because it is discovered by what steps the iniquity has been perpetrated; […]
34:15.s: The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 3

34:16.t: Among these things the Prophet speaks to his hearers: O men who hear me speaking, what I announce as to come will all be fulfilled in deed. For they are written in the book of the Lord, and his sentence is fixed, and not even one will be void. For what proceeds from my mouth, he has commanded; that is, I indeed speak, but the words are the Lord's, and by his spirit whatever has been said will be accomplished. By his decree and measure each thing will be fulfilled, and they will not abandon their order unto everlasting generations. Let these things be said according to the Hebrew and the historical explanation.

35:1.t:
[Passage quoted, Isa. xxxv. 1-7.]

HERE also the Coming of God for salvation, bringing many blessings, is precisely foretold. The prophet says that there will be a cure for the deaf, sight for the blind, yea, even healing for the lame and tongue-tied, and this was only fulfilled at the Coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ, by Whom the eyes of the blind were opened, and the deaf regained their hearing; why need I say, how many palsied and deaf and lame also received physical cure by the hands of His disciples? And how many others, afflicted with various diseases and maladies, received of Him healing and salvation, according to the inspired prediction of prophecy, and according to the unimpeachable testimony of the Holy Gospels? And the prophecy here disguises under the name of "desert" the Church of the Gentiles, which for long years deserted of God is being evangelized by those of whom we are speaking, and it says that besides other blessings the glory of Libanus will be given to the desert. […]
35:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 21

35:1.t:
[Passage quoted, Isa. xxxv. 3-6.]

THIS, too, was fulfilled, was clearly fulfilled, by our Saviour's miraculous works after John's preaching. Notice therefore how He bears good tidings to the desert, not generally, or to any desert, but to one particular desert by the bank of Jordan. This was because John lived there and baptized there, as Scripture says:

"John was in the desert baptizing, and there went out unto him all the land of Judaea, and all they of Jerusalem, and were baptized of him in Jordan."

I think the desert here is a symbol of that which of old was void of all God's good things, I mean the Church of the Gentiles, and the river by the desert that cleanses all that are bathed therein is a figure of some cleansing spiritual power, of which the Scriptures speak, saying, "The movements of the river make glad the city of God." And this means the ever-flowing stream of the Holy Spirit welling from above and watering the city of God, which is the name for life according to God. […]
35:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 9, Chapter 6

35:1.t:
But she that was desolate and rejected by men received the consummation which we behold in consequence of her patience toward God, so that the prophecy of Isaiah was spoken of her:

'Rejoice, thirsty desert, let the desert rejoice and blossom as the lily, and the desert places shall blossom and be glad.' 'Be strengthened, ye weak hands and feeble knees. Be of good courage, ye feeble-hearted, in your minds; be strong, fear not. Behold our God recompenseth judgment and will recompense, he will come and save us.' 'For,' he says, 'in the wilderness water has broken out, and a pool in thirsty ground, and the dry land shall be watered meadows, and in the thirsty ground there shall be springs of water.'

These things which were prophesied long ago have been recorded in sacred books; but no longer are they transmitted to us by hearsay merely, but in facts. […]

For this cause I will not refrain from sacred expressions when I am telling of Divine Power. "Let the desert rejoice, and let her blossom like the lily" (that is, the Church, which but yesterday seemed a widow, and husbandless, as well as everyone that was withered up by the envious and joyless winter of ungodliness), "because the Lord hath had compassion upon His people, neither hath He abandoned His own inheritance:" because He hath done marvellous things, and His ancient, true counsel, the which was to be favourable towards them that fear Him and that hope in His mercy, forasmuch as He hath broken down the gates of brass, and smitten asunder the bars of iron; because we have been humbled for our transgressions, and the snare has been broken, and we are set free, in the joy of the God that hath called us, and who comforts the lowly in heart."

And where shall we place that oracle of Isaiah, which cries to the wilderness, "Be glad, O thirsty wilderness: let the desert rejoice and blossom as a lily: and the desolate places of Jordan shall blossom and shall rejoice"? For it is clear that it is not to places without soul or sense that he proclaims the good tidings of joy: but he speaks, by the figure of the desert, of the soul that is parched and unadorned, even as David also, when he says, "My soul is unto Thee as a thirsty land," and, "My soul is athirst for the mighty, for the living God."

And "the excellency of Carmel" is given to the soul that bears the likeness to the desert, that is, the grace bestowed through the Spirit. For since Elijah dwelt in Carmel, and the mountain became famous and renowned by the virtue of him who dwelt there, and since moreover John the Baptist, illustrious in the spirit of Elijah, sanctified the Jordan, therefore the prophet foretold that "the excellency of Carmel" should be given to the river.

And "the glory of Lebanon," from the similitude of its lofty trees, he transfers to the river. For as great Lebanon presents a sufficient cause of wonder in the very trees which it brings forth and nourishes, so is the Jordan glorified by regenerating men and planting them in the Paradise of God: and of them, as the words of the Psalmist say, ever blooming and bearing the foliage of virtues, "the leaf shall not wither," and God shall be glad, receiving their fruit in due season, rejoicing, like a good planter, in his own works.

The desert and the pathless land will be glad, and the wilderness will exult, and will flower like the lily. Budding, it will bud forth, and will exult, joyful and praising. The glory of Lebanon has been given to it, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon. They will see the glory of the Lord, and the beauty of our God. LXX: Rejoice, thirsty desert, and let the wilderness exult, and let it flower like the lily. The deserts of the Jordan will flower and exult: the glory of Lebanon has been given to it, and the honor of Carmel: and my people will see the glory of the Lord, and the height of our God. Since Jerusalem has been turned into pitch, and its everlasting smoke has gone up, and the pelican and the hedgehog, the ibis and the raven, dragons and ostriches, demons and onocentaurs, the lamia and the hairy ones dwell in it, and the sentence of the Lord has been fulfilled upon it: Your house will be left to you desolate (Luke 13:35): therefore she who before had been deserted, of whom it is said in the psalm: The voice of the […]

After John was killed, the Lord saw the time drawing near and withdrew to a deserted place called Bethsaida. This teaches mystically that a deserted Judah, which had beheaded its prophets by not believing them, would later become fruitful in the desert of a church that possessed no man of the Word. Hence, the beautiful Bethsaida means "house of fruitfulness." For it was about it that Isaiah said, "The desert and the dry land will rejoice, and the wilderness will exult and bloom like the lily," and again, "they will see the glory of the Lord and the beauty of our God."

35:2.t: And what is set down in the LXX, and the deserts of the Jordan will exult, is indeed not found in the Hebrew; but we can say that by the river Jordan John's baptism of repentance is shown, which the Lord sealed and confirmed by his own washing. And since this is said figuratively of the wilderness, which refers to the nations, and in which John was, the Jordan can fittingly be joined to it, so that through the desert of the nations we may come to the baptism of the Savior. And what follows, the glory of Lebanon has been given to it, and the beauty of Carmel and Sharon, we must take according to the earlier explanation, in which we said that by Lebanon the Temple or Jerusalem is understood, as Zechariah says: Open your gates, O Lebanon (Zech 11:1); and Ezekiel: A great eagle with great wings, full of talons, which has the design of entering into Lebanon and Carmel (Ezek 17:3); […]

Because a multitude of Gentiles followed it after Judah came to faith in the Lord's incarnation and an astonished partaker of the same grace hastened its own unexpected conversion, Judah exclaimed in surprise, "Who is this that ascends from the desert, flowing with delights, leaning upon my beloved?" The church of the Gentiles ascends from the desert because the one who was deserted by its Creator for a very long time now arrives at his grace by the incremental steps of faith and good works, thus fulfilling what the prophet Isaiah said: "The desert and the dry land will rejoice, and the wilderness will exult and bloom like the lily." Indeed, she is truly flowing with those delights about which the spouse spoke above: "How beautiful you are, and how lovely, my dear, with delights," that is, with the delights of heavenly life. […]
35:2.s: Commentary on the Song of Songs 5:8.4-5

35:3.t: The sick of the palsy is healed, and that in public, in the sight of the people. For, says Isaiah, "they shall see the glory of the Lord and the excellence of our God." What glory, and what excellence? "Be strong, you weak hands and feeble knees" refers to the palsy. "Be strong; fear not." "Be strong" is not vainly repeated, nor is "fear not" vainly added; because with the renewal of the limbs there was to be, according to the promise, a restoration also of bodily energies: "Arise, and take up your couch"; and likewise moral courage not to be afraid of those who should say, "Who can forgive sins, but God alone?"

The same prophet says: "Be ye strengthened, ye relaxed hands, and ye feeble knees; be consoled, ye that are cowardly in heart; be strong; fear not. Lo, our God shall return judgment; He Himself shall come, and shall save you: then shall the eyes of the blind be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear; then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb shall be eloquent." Since the prophet says that at God's advent these should be the signs which come to pass; let men acknowledge either that Christ is the Son of God, at whose advent and by whom these wonders of healings were performed; or, overcome by the truth of Christ's divinity, let them rush into the other heresy, and refusing to confess Christ to be the Son of God, and God, let them declare Him to be the Father. For, being bound by the words of the prophets, they can no longer deny Christ to be God. […]

[Passage quoted, Isa. xxxv. 3.]

Now we have this prophecy fulfilled in the Gospels, partly, when they brought to our Lord and Saviour a paralytic lying on a bed, whom He made whole with a word; and partly, when many that were blind and possessed with daemons, yea, labouring under various diseases and weaknesses, were released from their sufferings by His saving power. Nor should we forget how even now throughout the whole world multitudes bound by all forms of evil, full of ignorance of Almighty God in their souls, are healed and cured miraculously and beyond all argument by the medicine of His teaching. Except that now we call Him God as we should, as One Who can work thus, as I have already shewn in the evidence of His Divinity. Yea, surely it is right now to acknowledge Him to be God, since He has given proof of power divine and truly inspired. […]
35:3.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 9, Chapter 13

35:3.t: Therefore the traders came from Gilead, that is, from their possessions of or dwelling in the law, and brought their wares to the church, so that that balm might heal the sins of the nations. Of them it is said, "Be strong, you hands that are feeble and you knees that are without strength." The balm is unspoiled faith. Such a faith Peter exhibited when he said to the lame man, "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, arise and walk." And he arose and walked, as was right. Such a faith Peter had when he said to the paralytic, "Aeneas, the Lord Jesus heals you; get up and make your bed." And he got up and made his bed. Such a faith he had when he said to the dead woman, "Arise in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ." And the departed woman arose. With the mortar made from this cement those stones are fastened together from which God is able to raise up children to Abraham.

Then let us flee the wickedness of this world, in which "the very days are evil," and flee it relentlessly. On that account Isaiah cries out, "Be strong, you hands which are feeble and you knees which are without strength." This means: Be strong, you knees, not of the body but of the soul, so that the footstep of the spirit can rise up straightway to the heights of heaven. Thus conduct will be more stable, life more mature, grace more abundant and discretion more guarded.

Strengthen the slackened hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Say to the faint-hearted (or to the fearful), Be strengthened, and do not fear; behold, your God will bring the vengeance of recompense: God himself will come and will save you (or, as the LXX translated, us). Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped (or will hear). Then the lame man will leap like a stag, and the tongue of the dumb will be opened, for waters have broken out in the desert, and torrents in the wilderness, and what was dry ground will become a pool (or marshes), and the thirsty land springs of water. In the lairs in which dragons dwelt before, the green of reed and rush will spring up (for which the LXX translated: There will be the gladness of birds, and folds of flocks). And there will be a path there, and a way (or a clean way), and it will be called the holy way; the polluted will not pass through it. […]

35:5.t: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a stag, and the tongue of the dumb will be opened. And although this was fulfilled by the greatness of signs, when the Lord said to the disciples of John who had been sent to him: Go and report to John what you have heard and seen: the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise again, the poor have the gospel preached to them (Luke 7:22); yet it is fulfilled daily among the nations, when those who before were blind, and stumbled against wood and stones, behold the light of truth. And those who with deaf ears could not hear the words of the Scriptures now rejoice at the precepts of God; when those who before were lame, and did not keep the right way, leap like stags, imitating their teachers; and the tongue of the dumb is opened, whose mouths Satan had shut, so that they could not confess the one Lord.

35:6.t: And that it was predicted that our Christ should heal all diseases and raise the dead, hear what was said. There are these words: "At His coming the lame shall leap as an hart, and the tongue of the stammerer shall be clear speaking: the blind shall see, and the lepers shall be cleansed; and the dead shall rise, and walk about." And that He did those things, you can learn from the Acts of Pontius Pilate.

That [Jesus] healed the lame and the blind, and that therefore we hold him to be the Christ and the Son of God, is manifest to us from what is contained in the prophecies: "Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened."

Now what can they [i.e., those who deny the incarnation] say to this, or how can they dare to face this at all? For the prophecy not only indicated that God is to sojourn here but also announces the signs and the time of his coming. For they connect the blind recovering their sight, and the lame walking, and the deaf hearing, and the tongue of the one who stammers being made plain, with the divine coming which is to take place. Let them say, then, when such signs have come to pass in Israel, or where in Judah anything of the sort has occurred. Naaman, a leper, was cleansed, but no deaf man heard nor lame walked. Elijah raised a dead man; so did Elisha;64 but none blind from birth regained his sight. For in good truth, to raise a dead man is a great thing, but it is not like the wonder wrought by the Savior. […]
35:6.s: On the Incarnation of the Word 38

35:6.t: And for this reason the eyes will be opened, the ears will hear, the lame will leap, and the tongue of the dumb will be opened: because in the once deserted Church the waters of saving baptism have broken out, or burst forth, and torrents and streams in the wilderness, namely the various spiritual graces; and what was dry ground has been turned into a pool and marshes, so that it is not only free from the burning of thirst, but is navigable and well watered, and has very many springs, which the stag longs for, and of which whoever has drunk can bless the Lord, according to what is written: Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel (Ps 67 [68]:27).

35:7.t: But since I have not quoted to you such Scripture as tells that Christ will do these things, I must necessarily remind you of one such: from which you can understand, how that to those destitute of a knowledge of God, I mean the Gentiles, who, 'having eyes, saw not, and having a heart, understood not,' worshipping the images of wood, [how even to them] Scripture prophesied that they would renounce these [vanities], and hope in this Christ. It is thus written: 'Rejoice, thirsty wilderness: let the wilderness be glad, and blossom as the lily: the deserts of the Jordan shall both blossom and be glad: and the glory of Lebanon was given to it, and the honour of Carmel. And my people shall see the exaltation of the Lord, and the glory of God. Be strong, ye careless hands and enfeebled knees. Be comforted, ye faint in soul: be strong, fear not. Behold, our God gives, and will give, retributive judgment. He shall come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear. […]

In the lairs of the Gentile souls, in which dragons dwelt before, there will be the reed and the rush, with which the faith of the Lord may be written, and on which limbs once weary may rest; or there will be the gladness of birds, and folds of flocks: so that they may take the wings of a dove, and, leaving lowly things, hasten to the heights, and be able to say with the Psalmist: The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing: in a place of pasture, there he has set me: beside the waters of refreshment he has brought me up.

The Lord promises concerning holy Church through another prophet, saying: "There shall spring up in her the greenness of the reed and the rush." I remember having explained this in another place, that by the reed we should understand writers, and by the rush, hearers. But since both rush and reed are accustomed to grow near the moisture of water, and both spring forth from one and the same water, and the reed indeed is taken up for writing, while with the rush one cannot write, what should we understand by the rush and the reed, except that there is one doctrine of truth which irrigates many hearers? But some who are irrigated advance in the word of God even to the point that they also become writers, that is, like reeds; but others hear the word of life, maintain the greenness of good hope and right works, yet cannot advance to writing at all. What are these in the water of God except certain rushes, so to speak? They indeed advance by growing green, but they cannot express letters at all.

35:8.t: There will be a path there, and a most clean way, which will be called holy, and which says of itself: I am the way (John 14:6), through which he who is polluted will not be able to pass. Hence it is also said in the psalm: Blessed are the undefiled in the way (Ps 118 [119]:1). And this way, that is, our God, will be for us so straight and level and plain that it has no error: and fools and the senseless may be able to walk in it, to whom Wisdom speaks in Proverbs: If anyone is a little one, let him come to me. And to the unwise she said: Come, eat my bread, and drink the wine which I have mixed for you. Leave childishness, and live, and walk in the ways of prudence (Prov 9:4-6). For God has chosen the foolish things of the world (1 Cor 1): the prince of which fools speaks in the psalm: O God, you know my foolishness. And the foolishness of God is wiser than men (Ps 68 [69]:6). […]

35:9.t: There follows: There will be no lion there: our adversary the devil, who goes about roaring, seeking how he may enter the sheepfold of the Lord (1 Pet 5). And the evil beasts, his attendants, will not go up by it. For the track of a serpent cannot be found upon a rock. But those will walk in it who have been set free from the chains of sins, and redeemed by the blood of the Savior, and have repented, and have come to Zion, of which we have often spoken: You have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22); lest after the Jewish fashion we seek a golden Zion and a jewelled Jerusalem, which, according to the prophecy of Daniel, has been dissolved into everlasting ashes (Dan 9).

35:10.t: "Everlasting joy," says Isaiah, "shall be upon their heads." Well, there is nothing eternal until after the resurrection. "And sorrow and sighing," he continues, "shall flee away." The angel echoes the same to John: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes," from the same eyes indeed which had formerly wept and which might weep again if the loving kindness of God did not dry up every fountain of tears. And again: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death," and therefore no more corruption, it being chased away by incorruption, even as death is by immortality.
35:10.s: ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH 58

35:10.t: [God] is the same one who said to Jeremiah, "Behold, I place my words in your mouth as a fire." David, therefore, also received this tongue of fire, so that he could speak of divine knowledge while enkindled with zeal: "Make known to me my end, O Lord." He was not here asking about his own death or about the final resurrection. He was inquiring into that end of which the apostle spoke: "For the end will come when the Lord Jesus hands over the kingdom to God the Father and when he destroys every principality and power and when death is the last of all things to be destroyed," such that evil is defeated and eternal goodness is ignited. Therefore it was said, "Pain and wailing will flee."
35:10.s: Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms 38.16

35:10.t: And the everlasting gladness of those who praise the Lord will be upon their head, so that after they have conquered the world they may be able to say with the Apostle and with the Prophet: I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; for the rest, there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness (2 Tim 4:7, 8); and, O Lord, as with the shield of your good will you have crowned us (Ps 5:13). Then, as joy and gladness take their place, sorrow and groaning will flee away, when he comes out of Zion who will deliver. All these things we, following the apostle Paul, interpret of the first coming of the Savior: but the Jews, and our Judaizers, refer them to the second, on the strength of a single little verse, They will return and come to Zion with praise, longing for the blood of victims, and the servitude of all the nations, and the beauty of wives.

36:1.t: I have read in someone's Commentary that this Sennacherib is the same who also took Samaria, which is altogether false. For the sacred history relates that first Pul king of the Assyrians, under Menahem king of Israel, laid waste the ten tribes; second, that Tiglath-pileser came to Samaria under Pekah son of Remaliah of Israel; third, that Shalmaneser under Hoshea king of Israel took all Samaria (2 Kgs 15, 17); fourth, that it was Sargon who stormed Ashdod (Isa 20); fifth, Esarhaddon, who, when Israel had been carried away, sent the Samaritans into the land of Judea as guards (2 Kgs 17); sixth, Sennacherib, who under Hezekiah king of Judah, having taken Lachish and the other cities of Judea, besieged Jerusalem (2 Kgs 18). Others, however, think that one and the same king is called by many names.

And it came to pass in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them. And the king of the Assyrians sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem to king Hezekiah with a heavy hand, and he stood at the aqueduct of the upper pool, in the way of the fuller's field. And there went out to him Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder; and Rabshakeh said to them: Say to Hezekiah: Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians: What is this confidence in which you trust? Or with what counsel and strength are you planning to rebel? In whom do you have confidence, that you have withdrawn from me? Behold, you are trusting in this broken staff of reed, in Egypt: on which if a man leans, it will enter into his hand and pierce it: so is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him. […]

36:3.t: Ioach [Joah]: whose brother he is, but better: confessing, or glorifying.
36:3.s: On Hebrew Names, On Isaiah the Prophet

36:6.t: Of a reed staff of this kind Rabshakeh too vainly reproaches Hezekiah king of Judah, saying: Behold, trusting in this reed rod, and a broken one, upon Egypt; whoever leans on it, it goes into his hand: so is Pharaoh king of Egypt and all who trust in him; and he indeed was lying about a righteous king in recalling these things — he who is interpreted as 'much with a kiss': for he was drunk from the golden cup of Babylon, and therefore he was thrusting his own things upon the people, while it was confessing the Lord —; here, however, Pharaoh is reproached for having been to the house of Israel a rod or reed staff, promising them help that was vain and fragile and soon to be shattered.

Let us then consider the words of Rabshakeh; and first, what he says: You are trusting in this broken staff of reed, in Egypt, is false: for no history relates that Hezekiah sent to the Egyptians and asked for Pharaoh's help. And what he adds: If you answer me, We trust in the Lord our God, is true. But again he joins a lie to the truth: that Hezekiah had taken away His high places and altars. For he had done this not against God but for God, so that, idolatry and the old error being destroyed, he might command God to be worshiped in Jerusalem, where his Temple was; although we read that by a very bad custom the people sacrificed victims to God on the mountains and hills, even when the altar had already been built. […]

36:10.t: They could have stayed there, then, and were not afraid, but surely the heavenly hand that had dragged them thither to punish the vices of the Spanish compelled them also to cross the straits to devastate Africa. In fact, they themselves confessed that they did not act of their own volition, for they were driven and urged on by a divine command. From this we may learn how great are our misdoings, since to destroy and punish us the barbarians are compelled to move against their will, following the words of the devastator of the land of Israel, the king of the Assyrians, when he said: '' And now without the will of the Lord am I come up against this land? The Lord said unto me, 'Go up against this land, to destroy it.' " And elsewhere the Sacred Word says: "Therefore thus saith the Lord of Hosts, the God of Israel: 'Behold, I will send and take Nabuchodonosor the king of Babylon, my servant, and when he cometh, he shall smite the land of Egypt.' […]
36:10.s: On the Government of God, Book 7, Chapter 13

36:11.t: And Eliakim and Shebna and Joah said to Rabshakeh: Speak to your servants in the Syrian tongue, for we understand it: do not speak to us in the Jewish tongue in the ears of the people who are on the wall. And Rabshakeh said to them: Has my lord sent me to your lord and to you to speak all these words, and not rather to the men who sit on the wall, that they may eat their own dung and drink the urine of their feet with you? And Rabshakeh stood and cried out with a loud voice in the Jewish tongue, and said: Hear the words of the great king, the king of the Assyrians. Thus says the king: Let not Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to rescue you; and let not Hezekiah give you confidence in the Lord, saying: The Lord will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of the Assyrians. Do not listen to Hezekiah. For thus says the king of the Assyrians. […]

36:12.t: In order then that both our houses may be continually open to the one, and our ears to the others, let us purge away the filth from the ears of our soul. For as filth and mud close up the ears of our flesh, so do the harlot's songs, and worldly news, and debts, and the business of usury and loans, close up the ear of the mind, worse than any filth; nay rather, they do not close it up only, but also make it unclean. And they are putting dung in your ears, who tell you of these things. And that which the barbarian threatened, saying, "Ye shall eat your own dung," and what follows; this do these men also make you undergo, not in word, but in deeds; or rather, somewhat even much worse. For truly those songs are more loathsome even than all this; and what is yet worse, so far from feeling annoyance when ye hear them, ye rather laugh, when ye ought to abominate them and fly.
36:12.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 37:7

36:16.t: Make a blessing with me, and come out to me, and eat each one of his vine, and each one of his fig tree, and drink each one the water of his cistern: until I come and take you away to a land that is like your land: a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards. Let not Hezekiah trouble you, saying: The Lord will deliver us. Have the gods of the nations delivered each one his land from the hand of the king of the Assyrians? For which in the volume of Kings one reads: Do with me what is profitable, and come out to me (2 Kgs 18:31). So the sense is the same. Do, he says, what may benefit you and turn to your blessing. Or he says this: Bless the Assyrian king and praise him, and confess him your lord, so that you may obtain rewards; and until I return from Egypt, or, having taken Libnah, come back, dwell in your city and enjoy your goods. But afterward I will come and transfer you to a land which is like your land, of grain, wine and olives. […]

36:19.t: Where is the God of Hamath and Arpad? Where is the God of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand? Who is there among all the gods of these lands that has rescued his land out of my hand, that the Lord should rescue Jerusalem out of my hand? And they were silent and answered him not a word. For the king had commanded them, saying: Do not answer him. This shows that Samaria served all these gods, and was taken for that reason. But if, he says, with so many gods presiding, we easily overcame the ten tribes, how much more easily shall we conquer you, nay, Jerusalem alone, with one God as its guardian?

36:21.t: And all the people kept silent and answered him nothing; for they had received the king's command not to answer him. Truly righteous was Hezekiah, doing all things faithfully and everything with counsel. And he had commanded that the blaspheming Assyrian not be answered for this reason: lest he provoke him to greater blasphemies. Hence it is written: Do not kindle the coals of the sinner (Sir 8:13); and in the psalm we read: When the sinner stood against me, I was dumb, and was humbled, and kept silent from good things (Ps 38 [39]:2-3); and again: Set, O Lord, a guard to my mouth, and a fortified door to my lips: incline not my heart to words of malice (Ps 140 [141]:3).

36:22.t: And Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, came in to Hezekiah with their garments torn, and reported to him the words of Rabshakeh. And it came to pass, when king Hezekiah had heard, he tore his garments, and was covered with sackcloth, and went into the house of God. And he sent Eliakim, who was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah, the son of the prophet Amos, and they said to him: Thus says Hezekiah: This day is a day of tribulation and of rebuke and of blasphemy, for the children have come to the birth, and there is no strength to bring forth. If by any means the Lord your God may hear the words of Rabshakeh, whom the king of the Assyrians his master sent to blaspheme the living God and to reproach him with words which the Lord your God has heard. Lift up therefore a prayer for the remnant that is found. And the servants of king Hezekiah came to Isaiah; […]

37:3.t: And they said, it says, to him: Thus says Hezekiah, not 'the king', not swelling with the title of empire: This day is a day of tribulation and of rebuke and of blasphemy: of our tribulation, of God's rebuke, of the enemies' blasphemy. And he sets down the likeness of a woman in labor and in pain, who has come up to the birth and cannot bring forth, nor say: From fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived, and have been in pain, and have brought forth the spirit of salvation.

37:4.t: There follows: If by any means the Lord your God may hear the words of Rabshakeh (Isa 26:18 LXX). For we do not dare to call the Lord of all our Lord, since through his anger we suffer so much; but we call him your Lord. And we have this confidence of vengeance: that the living God is blasphemed by a worshiper of dead idols. And they have reproached with words which the Lord your God has heard. Lift up therefore a prayer, our prayer, which lies prostrate: not for the whole people, which has already perished, but for the remnant, which is besieged.

37:5.t: And when the servants of king Hezekiah had come to Isaiah: again he was silent about the name of Prophet, in order to keep the humility he had begun. And Isaiah anticipated them: for by the same spirit by which he knew things to come, he had heard the king too, though absent; and he tells them what they should answer to their master, humbled in this confidence of conscience. Say, he says, to your master, who is your lord; for my Lord says this: Do not fear the words with which not you but I have been blasphemed. Nor do I tell all that I am going to do to the king of the Assyrians, lest I seem to boast of my power; but only that a spirit is to be given him, not of God but an adverse one. And having heard a report, let him return to his own land and fall in it by the sword: so that Hezekiah might hear both things he desired together, that he was to be freed from siege and danger, and that the hostile and angry king would die in his own land. […]

37:8.t: And Rabshakeh returned and found the king of the Assyrians fighting against Libnah: for he had heard that he had departed from Lachish. And he heard concerning Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, people saying: He has come out to fight against you. And when he heard it, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying: Thus shall you say to Hezekiah king of Judah, speaking: Let not your God, in whom you trust, deceive you, saying: Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of the Assyrians. Behold, you have heard all that the kings of the Assyrians have done to all the lands which they overthrew, and will you be able to be delivered? Have the gods of the nations rescued them, whom my fathers overthrew, Gozan and Haran, and Rezeph, and the sons of Eden who were in Telassar? Where is the king of Hamath, and the king of Arpad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, Ana and Ava? […]

37:9.t: We pass quickly over the plain things in order to dwell on the doubtful ones. That Sennacherib king of the Assyrians fought against the Egyptians and besieged Pelusium, and that, when the mounds had already been built to take the city, Tirhakah king of the Ethiopians came to its help, and that in one night near Jerusalem one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrian army fell by pestilence, is related by Herodotus, and most fully by Berosus, the writer of Chaldean history, whose credibility must be sought from their own books.

37:13.t: In the enumeration of the other nations he sets down ANA (הנע) and AVA (ועוה), which the Seventy ran together, saying anavegava; and the conjunction and, that is, vau, between the two nations Ana and Ava, they set down in the Hebrew tongue, so that to the ignorant it seems one nation or city.

37:14.t: And Hezekiah took the books from the hand of the messengers and read them; and he went up into the house of the Lord and spread them out before the Lord, and prayed to the Lord, saying: O Lord of hosts, God of Israel, who sit upon the Cherubim, you alone are God of all the kingdoms of the earth: for you made heaven and earth. Incline, O Lord, your ear and hear; open, O Lord, your eyes and see, and hear all the words of Sennacherib which he sent to blaspheme the living God. For truly, O Lord, the kings of the Assyrians have made desolate the lands and their regions, and have given their gods to the fire: for they were not gods, but works of men's hands, wood and stones; and they broke them in pieces. And now, O Lord our God, save us from his hand, and let all the kingdoms of the earth know that you alone are God. Against the blasphemies of king Sennacherib Hezekiah seized his accustomed weapons. And again he goes to the Temple and spreads out his letters before the Lord. […]

37:18.t: And what he adds: For truly, O Lord, the kings of the Assyrians have made desolate the lands and their regions, and have given their gods to the fire: for they were not gods, but works of men's hands, wood and stones; and they broke them in pieces, is proved by many histories, which write that the kings of the Persians came into Greece and overthrew and plundered the temples of the Greeks.

37:20.t: And he asks for vengeance, so that through his occasion all kingdoms may know that he alone is God, who can deliver his own from danger.

37:21.t: And Isaiah son of Amos sent to Hezekiah, saying: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: As to what you have asked me concerning Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, this is the word which the Lord has spoken concerning him: The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and mocked you; behind you the daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head. Whom have you reproached, and whom have you blasphemed, and against whom have you raised your voice and lifted up the height of your eyes? Against the Holy One of Israel? By the hand of your servants you have reproached the Lord and have said: With the multitude of my chariots I have gone up to the height of the mountains, the ridges of Lebanon, and I will cut down its lofty cedars and its choice fir trees, and I will enter the height of its summit, the forest of its Carmel. I dug, and drank water, and dried up with the sole of my foot all the streams of the embankments. […]

37:23.t: And she has said this: Not against me, but against the Lord you have been proud; and not you yourself, but through your servants, so that the arrogance of the blasphemer might be the greater. For you said that with the multitude of your chariots you would climb the height of the mountains and the ridges of Lebanon, and cut down its lofty cedars and fir trees. This we ought to take either μεταφορικῶς of all the nations and their princes, or of Jerusalem, which is what Lebanon means, so that we refer its cedars and firs to all its powerful and noble men, and the height of its summit and the forest of Carmel to the Temple. For he himself had said above: Have you not heard what the kings of the Assyrians have done to all the lands which they overthrew? Therefore neither will you be able to be delivered.
