And in another place He repeated the great things which He had done, and the works which He had established by the nod of His Will, and how all created things hang upon the power of His word, and the natural things keep their bounds, and the creation is yoked beneath the dispensation of His Will; before Whom the mountains are placed in scales, and the hills in a balance, Who hath meted out heaven with His span, and hath comprehended the dust of the earth in His palm, and before Whom the nations and peoples of the world are accounted as nothing. These things He spake by the hand of the Prophet, that through them He might make His majesty known, and that by the report of His majesty he might work fear in those who listened unto him. […]
40:12.s: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 7 -- Second Discourse on the Fear of God

40:12.t: Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand and weighed the heavens with his palm? Who hath poised with three fingers the bulk of the earth? This the Word did, through whom all things were made. His hand, by which all things are created, that is, formed or made distinct and adorned, with three fingers lifts and suspends the earth, that is, the ecclesiastic hierarchy which He creates, distinguishes and adorns. This hand measures the waters, this hand holds all things as an object is held in the fist. This is the hand of the eternal Word. This witnessing transcends any judgment by a creature.

40:13.t: For who has known the mind of the Lord? who has instructed him (Isa. 40:13)? The mind of God is this, that he commanded these things to be done spiritually, by which the wisdom of the world, denying that what has been done can be done, would be proved foolish. There is no one who has known this mind and is displeased with it, so as to correct the counsel of God; for he who has known it praises the power of God, whereas he who denies that God can do all things does not believe that he made the world either. For what great thing is it that he should be believed to have begotten from himself, who is not doubted to have made all things out of nothing? seeing that the Savior says: But with God all things are possible (Matt. 19:26).

"Yet to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we to him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him." … The apostle says according to the prophecy of Isaiah, "Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?" And he added, "For him and through him and in him are all things," which Isaiah said of the artificer of all, as you have it. "Who has measured the water with his hand, and the heaven with his palm?" And the apostle has added, "For of him and through him and in him are all things." What is "of him"? That the nature of all things is of his will, and he is the author of all things that come into existence. "Through him" means what? That establishment and continuance are seen to have been bestowed on all things through him. "In him" means what? […]

Who, he says, has helped the spirit of the Lord, or who was his counselor and showed him? etc. For which Symmachus translated: Who has prepared the spirit of the Lord, and who has shown him the man of his counsel? With whom did he take counsel, and who gave him understanding, and taught him the way of judgment, and instructed him in knowledge, and showed him the road of prudence? By this he shows more plainly that the spirit was prepared, or established, the one of whom one reads in the Apostle: Now the Lord is the Spirit. And: Upon whom the Spirit of God rested, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, and the rest. Who says in what follows: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me: because he has anointed me (Isa 61:1). For he himself is the spirit of the Lord and the man of his counsel, in whom dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily (Col 2). With him he took counsel, of whom we spoke above (cf. Isa 9:6): Wonderful, Counselor. […]

40:15.t: For it was fitting that (since all the nations are reckoned as a droplet of the bucket) he who for the salvation of all became all things should become also a droplet, to set them free. For what did he not become for our salvation? We are empty; and he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. We are a foolish people and not wise; and he became the foolishness of preaching, that the foolishness of God might be made wiser than men. We are weak; the weakness of God was made stronger than men.
40:15.s: HOMILIES ON THE SONG OF SONGS, HOMILY 2

40:15.t: And the wicked shall not arise in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous. And even as the righteous who are perfected in good works shall not come into the judgment to be judged, so of the wicked also whose sins are many, and the measure of whose offences is overflowing, it shall not be required that they should draw nigh unto the judgment, but when they have risen again they shall turn back to Sheol, as David said, The wicked shall turn back to Sheol, and all the nations that forget God. And Isaiah said, All the nations are as a drop from the bucket, and as the turning of the balance. And the isles as a grain of sand shall be cast away, and all the nations are esteemed as nothingness by Him. For destruction and the sword are they esteemed by Him. Therefore learn and be persuaded, that all the nations that know not God their Maker, are esteemed by God as nothingness, and shall not come nigh to judgment, but as soon as they have risen shall turn back to Sheol.
40:15.s: Demonstration 22 (Of Death and the Latter Times), Section 17

40:15.t: All the nations that did not know their Creator, or the whole race of mortals, are in comparison with God like a drop of a bucket, and like the tipping of a balance, which with a light weight inclines to one side. And just as, if a small drop flows from a bucket, it is disregarded by the one who carries it, so the whole multitude of the nations, compared with the heavenly ministries and the multitude of the Angels, is counted as nothing. The islands too are counted as spittle, or, as Symmachus and Theodotion have it, setting down the Hebrew word itself, as DOC (דק), which falls off: for which Aquila translated λεπτὸν βαλλόμενον. And the Hebrews say that this word signifies the finest dust, which, snatched up by the wind, is often thrown into the eyes and is felt rather than seen. The tiniest and almost invisible particles of dust, then, are called by this word: what perhaps Democritus with his Epicurus calls atoms. […]

They know not how great is that nature which the mind cannot understand nor speech describe, and which rules over all. For to it all things are small: and so the blessed prophet Isaiah teaches us where he says; "If it is true that all the nations are as a drop from a cask, and are reckoned as the turn of a balance, and shall be counted as spittle, to what have you likened the Lord?" For what is one drop from a cask? and what is the turn of a balance? and what too is spittle?—that is, a single expectoration? If therefore this be the position of all things towards God, how can it be a great matter to Him, or one that occasions Him trouble, to have the care of all things? The noxious sentiments therefore of the heathen are bereft of reason.
40:15.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

40:15.t: And just as all things compared to the divine power can do virtually nothing, so all things compared to the divine essence are virtually the least. Whence in respect to the divine being this entire world is as something minimal. And this is what is said in Wisdom eleven: For as a grain in the balance, so is the whole world before you, and as a drop of morning dew that falls upon the earth: and in Isaiah forty: Behold, the nations are as a drop from a bucket and are accounted as a grain in the balance: and afterward: All nations are as though they were not, so are they before him, and they are accounted as nothing and emptiness.
40:15.s: Quaestiones Disputatae, De Mysterio Trinitatis, Question 4

40:16.t: And at the same time, to draw men away little by little from idolatry, he takes away the ceremonies of victims, and teaches that all the wood of Lebanon and the herds that graze on it could not suffice for his burnt offerings.

40:17.t: But if all the nations are in his sight as if they were not, and are counted as nothing and void (and among all the nations is Israel too), then Israel too is as if it were not, and is counted as nothing and void. This we say so that its pride may be broken, and they may know that they are like the other nations.

And the Prophet said, "He rebuketh the sea, and maketh it dry, and drieth up all the rivers;" and again, "He looketh on the earth and it trembleth; He rebuketh the mountains, and they smoke." And again the prophet Isaiah saith, "All the nations are accounted as nothing by Him." Now these things the Spirit of God spake concerning the power of God, that those things which were not He called to come into existence, and that what did exist He called and changed into nothing. To this power also He compareth faith.

40:18.t: To whom then have you likened God, or what image will you set up for him? Has the smith cast a graven image, or has the goldsmith shaped it with gold, and the silversmith with plates of silver? The wise craftsman has chosen strong and incorruptible wood: and he will seek how to set up an idol that will not be moved. Having described the greatness of God and shown his power in part, the nations and islands being counted as a drop of a bucket and the tipping of a balance, and as dust, and the ceremonies of victims being rejected, he teaches in what follows why all the nations are as nothing in his sight and are counted as void: To whom have you likened God, or what image will you set up for him, who is spirit, and is in all things, and runs everywhere, and holds the earth as in his fist?

40:19.t: And at the same time he mocks the folly of the nations, that a craftsman or bronze-smith, or goldsmith or silversmith, should make a god for themselves, and fasten it together with plates and nails and set it firmly, lest it be pushed over by the blasts of the winds. And what he added: the wise craftsman has chosen strong and incorruptible wood, in the Hebrew is said AMSUCHAN (המסכן); which is a kind of incorruptible wood from which idols are especially made. He says these things so that, idols being rejected, he may prepare the way for the teaching of the Gospel, and all crooked things may be directed into straight; the valleys exalted and the hills brought low; and the glory of the Lord revealed, so that all flesh may see the salvation of God. According to tropology we can say that the chiefs of the heretics are rebuked, who fashion various idols from their own heart: whether by the charm of eloquence, which silver signifies; or by the splendor of gold, which is referred to the understanding; […]

40:21.t: Will you not know? Will you not hear? Has it not been announced to you from the beginning? Have you not understood the foundations of the earth? He who sits upon the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like locusts; who stretches out the heavens like nothing, and spreads them out like a tent to dwell in; who makes the searchers of secrets as though they were not; he has made the judges of the earth as void. Indeed, their stock was neither planted, nor sown, nor rooted in the earth: suddenly he blew upon them and they withered, and the whirlwind will carry them off like stubble. And to whom have you likened me and made me equal? says the Holy One. Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these things: who brings out their host by number, and calls them all by name. Because of the greatness of his might and strength and power, not one was left behind. LXX: Will you not know? Will you not hear? Has it not been announced to you from the beginning? Have you not known the foundations of the earth? […]

40:22.t: As to its form, what Isaias has said about the firmament of the heavens makes it more than clear that God created ‘heaven like a vault,’ because within the range of heaven all things which move in the sea and land are enclosed. This is the implication, too, of what we read that ‘God stretched out the heavens.’ He stretched it out as you would stretch skins over tents, the dwelling places of the saints, or as a scroll, that the names of many be inscribed therein who merited the grace of Christ by their faith and devotion. To all such it is said: ‘Rejoice in this that your names are written in heaven.’

This is the first heaven, shaped like a vaulted chamber, which was created on the first day along with the earth, and of it Isaiah speaks thus: He that hath established the heaven as a vaulted chamber. But the heaven, which is bound to the first at the middle, is that which was created on the second day, to which Isaiah refers when he says: And having stretched it out as a tent to dwell in. David also says concerning it: Stretching out the heaven as a curtain, and indicating it still more clearly he says: Who layeth the beams of his chambers in the waters.

He made therefore the heaven, not a sphere, as those vain babblers conceive—for He did not make a rolling sphere, but, as the prophet says: Who hath made the heaven as a vaulted chamber and stretched it out as a tent to dwell in; for none of us is so impious as to be persuaded by these triflers, and not by the words of the Prophet, which declare that the heaven has a beginning and an end.
40:22.s: The Christian Topography, Book 10 (quoting Severianus of Gabala, Hexaemeron)

40:22.t: For, contending against the divine words, which say: He that established the heaven as a vault, these most superior persons cry out in opposition and say: "It is not so, for it is spherical, and this is manifest from the eclipses which we have already adduced."

Others have pictured the heaven as a hemisphere. This idea is suggested by these words of David, the singer of God, Who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain, by which word he clearly means a tent: and by these from the blessed Isaiah, Who hath established the heavens like a vault: and also because when the sun, moon, and stars set they make a circuit round the earth from west to north, and so reach once more the east. Still, whether it is this way or that, all things have been made and established by the divine command, and have the divine will and counsel for a foundation that cannot be moved. For He Himself spoke and they were made: He Himself commanded and they were created. He hath also established them for ever and ever: He hath made a decree which will not pass.
40:22.s: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 2, Chapter 6

40:23.t: And he who stretched out the heavens and spread them out, so that either the multitudes of Angels might dwell above or men might abide beneath, and made, as it were, a great house for rational creatures, he himself according to the character of the times appoints princes, or searchers of secrets, so that they are as though they were not; and he has made the judges of the earth as void. For which the Seventy translated: and has made the earth as nothing; since also at the beginning of Genesis, where it is written: But the earth was invisible and unformed (Gen 1:2), the others translated: But the earth was void and nothing. How many kings Greek and Barbarian and Roman history recounts! Where is that countless army of Xerxes? Where the multitude of Israel in the desert? Where the incredible power of kings? Why should I speak of ancient things? Present examples teach us that princes are as nothing, and that the judges of the earth are counted as void.

40:24.t: These princes and judges of the earth (or, as others suspect, of heaven) were neither sown nor planted nor made firm with a solid root, and suddenly, at God's command, they are carried off and perish, as stubble is snatched away by whirlwind and tempest; according to what is written: And I passed by, and he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found (Ps 36 [37]:36).

40:25.t: God is one thing, and what belongs to God is another thing.… How will you employ in a comparison with God an object as your example, [such as a king] which fails in all the purposes that belong to a comparison? Why, when supreme power among kings cannot evidently be varied but only unique and singular, is an exception made in the case of him (of all others) who is King of kings, and (from the exceeding greatness of his power and the subjection of all other ranks to him) the very summit, as it were, of dominion?
Since, then, so great is the power and majesty of the Creator, to what likeness do you compare God? And do you not rather understand the maker from the greatness of his creatures?

40:26.t: In many places in scripture is the phrase "Lift up your eyes" set forth by the divine word, urging us to elevate and raise our thoughts and our vision, which is cast down and stooped, unable to fully look up and to rise on high; just as in Isaiah: "Lift up your eyes on high and see: who has created these things?" And the Savior, when about to proclaim the Beatitudes to those gathered on the plain, lifted up his eyes to his disciples and said, "Blessed are they" and so forth; for no true disciple of Jesus is below, just as neither is the one resting in Abraham's bosom. Thus the rich man, being in torments, lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham and Lazarus in his bosom. Moreover, the woman "bowed together and could in no wise lift up herself" was straightened by Jesus so that she might lift up her eyes. […]
40:26.s: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 13:274

40:26.t: If you do not believe words, at least believe your eyes; and from the service of the heavens and of all the elements consider the power of the Lord. Who brings out their host by number, that is, of the heavens; and calls them all by name: understand, the stars. Of which it is also sung in the Psalms: Who numbers the multitude of the stars, and calls them all by name (Ps 146 [147]:4). Or let us interpret the host of heaven as the Angels and all the armies of the heavens, of whom Daniel also speaks: Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten times a hundred thousand stood before him (Dan 7:10). Hence he is also called the Lord Sabaoth, which in our language is said the Lord of the army and of hosts, or of powers. […]

As for their other assertion, that God's knowledge cannot comprehend things infinite, it only remains for them to affirm, in order that they may sound the depths of their impiety, that God does not know all numbers. For it is very certain that they are infinite; since, no matter of what number you suppose an end to be made, this number can be, I will not say, increased by the addition of one more, but however great it be, and however vast be the multitude of which it is the rational and scientific expression, it can still be not only doubled, but even multiplied. Moreover, each number is so defined by its own properties, that no two numbers are equal. They are therefore both unequal and different from one another; and while they are simply finite, collectively they are infinite. Does God, therefore, not know numbers on account of this infinity; and does His knowledge extend only to a certain height in numbers, while of the rest He is ignorant? Who is so left to himself as to say so? […]

40:27.t: Why do you say, Jacob, and speak, Israel: My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment will pass away from my God ? Do you not know, or have you not heard? The everlasting God, the Lord who created the ends of the earth, will not fail, nor will he labor, nor is there any searching out of his wisdom. He gives strength to the weary, and to those who have no might he multiplies strength. Boys will fail and will labor, and young men will fall in weakness. But those who hope in the Lord will change their strength, they will take on wings like the eagle, they will run and not labor, they will walk and not fail. LXX: For do not say, Jacob, and why have you spoken, Israel: My way is hidden from God, and my God has taken away my judgment and has departed? And now do you not know, and have you not heard? The eternal God, the God who created the ends of the earth, will not hunger, nor will he labor, nor is there any finding out of his understanding. He gives strength to the hungry, and sorrow to those who do not grieve. […]

40:28.t: If they shall assign the toil of making all things as the reason why God only made the Son, the whole creation will cry out against them as saying unworthy things of God; and Isaiah, too, who has said in Scripture, "The everlasting God, the Lord, the Creator of the ends of the earth, does not faint, neither is he weary: there is no searching of his understanding." And if God made the Son alone, as not lowering himself to make the rest but committed them to the Son as an assistant, this on the other hand is unworthy of God, for in him there is no pride. No, the Lord reproves the thought when he says, "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing?" … If then it is not unworthy of God to exercise his providence, even down to things so small, a hair of the head and a sparrow and the grass of the field, also it was not unworthy of him to make them. For what things are the subjects of his providence, of those he is Maker through his proper Word. No, a worse absurdity lies before the people who speak this way; […]

To them God answered: Do you not know, and have the words of the preceding Scriptures not taught you? or, according to the Seventy, are you ignorant, because you have not heard, that the eternal God and Creator of all, the Lord, knows all things, holds all things together, and orders all things by his majesty? Nor does he ever fail or labor, so that he should not understand your judgment, and your ways should be hidden from him. Nor is there, he says, any searching out of his wisdom; from which place I think that saying of the Apostle was taken: Incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways (Rom 11:33); or, as the Seventy translated, he will not hunger, and he will not labor. For where there is food, there is often hunger, if you take the food away; and where there is hunger, there is also labor. But since these things are not in God, why do you attach human passions to him?

40:29.t: Rather, he himself gives strength to the hungry and the weary, and to those who seem to be as nothing in the world he multiplies power and might; or, according to the Seventy, he gives sorrow to those who do not grieve; for there is a sadness that leads to death, and there is a sadness that leads to life. Hence to those who have an impenitent heart he gives sadness, so that they may understand their sins.

40:30.t: And because many rejoice in the health of the body, and think youth and boyhood to be perpetual, he adds and says that the flowering age quickly falls, and robust bodies wither.

40:31.t: But those who have their trust not in their own strength but in God, and always await his mercy, change their strength and go from strength to strength, and take on wings like the eagle, and hear: Your youth will be renewed like the eagle's (Ps 102 [103]:5); they run to the Lord and do not labor in their desire for him; they walk and never fail. We have often said that the old age of eagles grows green again by the changing of their feathers, and that they alone can look at the radiance of the sun and gaze with flashing eyes upon the splendor of its rays, and that by this test they prove their young, whether they are true-born. So too the saints grow young again, and, having put on an immortal body, do not feel the labor of mortals, but are caught up in the clouds to meet Christ, and, according to the Seventy, never hunger, because they have the Lord present as their food.

The second disposition for the inflowing of the gift of fortitude is through the imperturbable consolation of hope. "Those who hope in the Lord shall renew their strength: they shall take wings as eagles, they shall run and not labor: they shall walk and not grow faint." A man would gladly bear a great burden for a mark of gold. If a fly refreshes so much, then you ought greatly to be moved to endure for the hope of a future and eternal reward. In God we ought to trust, because he "gives strength to the weary."

41:1.t: Scripture correctly says: Be renewed, O islands. For we are surrounded by the waves of sin, like islands in the sea of this world. Therefore, these islands were renewed by the coming of the Lord through the forgiveness of sins, that is, men were immersed in the water as if placed in the midst of the sea like islands, they were struck by the waves like islands, resounding with the waves of sins as if they were islands, in which, before, there were frequent shipwrecks for the simple reason that there was deceit in their hearts and flattery on their lips.
41:1.s: The Interrogation of Job and David, Book 2, Chapter 9

41:1.t: Let the islands be silent before me, and let the nations change their strength; let them approach, and then let them speak; let us draw near together to judgment. Who raised up the Righteous One from the East, called him to follow him? He will give the nations before him, and he will hold kings. He will give them as dust to his sword, as stubble swept off by the wind to his bow. He will pursue them; he will pass on in peace; the path will not appear in his feet. Who has wrought and done these things, calling the generations from the beginning? I the Lord, I am the first and the last. The islands saw and were afraid; the ends of the earth were astounded; they drew near and came. Each will help his neighbor, and will say to his brother Be strong. The coppersmith strengthened the one who was forging at that time, striking with the hammer, saying, It is good for gluing; and he strengthened it with nails, so that it should not be moved. LXX: Be renewed toward me, you islands, for the princes will change their strength; […]

41:2.t: The prophet declares that "righteousness" is a living thing and alive, and we used to think that it had been said by the Apostle alone that Christ is "righteousness and sanctification and redemption and wisdom". But perhaps the Apostle too, instructed by the prophets, knew "righteousness" to be a living being and alive. What is this "righteousness"? "The only-begotten God". But that it did not originate with the Apostle that Christ is "righteousness", and a living and subsisting "righteousness", but rather that, finding it in the prophetic words, he set forth this mystery for us, is certain from the chapter at which our reading has now come to rest. For it says: "Who made righteousness rise up from the east, and called it to his feet?". He "called" "righteousness"; it is plain that it is a living being, if it walks when "called". […]

And he so questions them and challenges them to answer, as to teach by questioning what they do not know: Who raised up the righteous one from the East, or righteousness? For he is not the God of the Jews only, but also of the nations, who called Christ the Lord, the Savior, who was made for us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1); in whom, according to the same Apostle, the righteousness of God is revealed (ibid.). And he called him to follow him in all things and to do the works of the Father, and to fulfill that which he says: O God, I have willed to do your will (Ps 39 [40]:9). In his sight kings and nations will bow their necks, and to his sword and arrows the adverse powers will be made subject like stubble and dust.

Some of the Hebrews think it is said of Abraham, who was called righteous from the East, that is, from the Chaldeans, because he alone was found righteous; and he followed him, going out of his native land into a land he did not know; and God delivered into his hand the kings who had come against Sodom and Gomorrah, and before his sword and bow made them like stubble and dust; and he pursued them and returned in peace, and did not feel the course of the long journey; and this he did not by his own strength but by the mercy of the Lord, who from the beginning knew that these things would come.

What we have interpreted of the person of Christ, and the calling of the nations, and the preaching of the Gospel, and the condemnation of idols, some refer to Cyrus king of the Persians: that God raised him up from the East against the Babylonians and made him obey his command, laying many nations low before him and subjecting all things to his sword and bow; and they refer what follows to his person, namely that their idols, made by human effort and called into being by the coppersmith's art, did not profit the Babylonians.

41:3.t: He will pursue them, namely the kings and princes of the several nations; and he will pass through in peace, calling all to peace, so that they may be reconciled to God. The path will not appear in his feet, that is, he will not feel the labor of the way, nor any weariness of human weakness, but will drink of the brook in the way, and therefore will lift up his head (Ps 109 [110]).

41:4.t: The great Isaiah thus speaks of the Divine nature with reference to these doctrines, in his exalted utterance,—who speaks in the person of the Deity, "I am the first, and hereafter am I, and no God was before Me, and no God shall be after Me." … Since, then, neither is that God which was before God, nor is that God which is after God, (for that which is after God is the creation, and that which is anterior to God is nothing, and Nothing is not God;—or one should rather say, that which is anterior to God is God in His eternal blessedness, defined in contradistinction to Nothing;)—since, I say, this inspired utterance was spoken by the mouth of the prophet, we learn by his means the doctrine that the Divine Nature is one, continuous with Itself and indiscerptible, not admitting in Itself priority and posteriority, though it be declared in Trinity. Since, then, the saying is the saying of God, whether you grant that the words are the words of the Father or of the Son, the orthodox doctrine is equally upheld by either. […]

Who, he says, has wrought and done these things? Who raised up the righteous one, or righteousness? Who delivered nations and kings to him? Who subjected all things to his sword and bow? Surely he who from the beginning of the world foretold that these things would come, who is the Founder of all. And because he had said, with the feeling of one inquiring, Who raised up the righteous one from the East, and so on, while all were silent he answered himself: I am the Lord, I am the first and the last. It is he who speaks also in the Apocalypse of John: I am the alpha and the ω, the beginning and the end (Rev 1:8; and 22:13).

41:5.t: The islands saw, that is, the nations, or the Churches gathered from the nations, which endure the storms of this world; and they feared the Lord: For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Prov 9:10). All the ends of the lands trembled at the words of the Apostles, drawing near and coming together to the Gospel of Christ.

Saw, he says, the islands, that is, the nations round about, and were terrified by his power: and the ends of the earth: namely Shem the son of Noah, who at the furthest time of the lands had escaped from the Flood with his father and his brothers, and had been preserved until that time (Gen 14). Him they want to be understood as Melchizedek, and that he came to meet Abraham as he returned from the battle, and received him, and blessed him, and strengthened him with the blessings of God; and that he is the coppersmith who forged Abraham and with the hammer of his art brought him out into better things, and said to him: It is good that you be glued to the fear of the Lord and joined to him. And he strengthened him, or made him solid, with the nails of the Lord's precepts, so that he should not be moved but should abide in his fear,

41:6.t: And when they saw that they themselves were saved, they fulfilled in deed what they had heard above: let them approach, and then let them speak, so that they helped their neighbors and wished to strengthen their brothers in the Lord, and said to them: Depart from idols, despise the ancient images of demons, which a human hand fashioned, which were produced by the beating hammer, which were joined with glue, which were made fast with nails so that they should not be moved, and which, when they stand, cannot walk.

41:8.t: Abraham, styled "the friend," [Isaiah 41:8] was found faithful, inasmuch as he rendered obedience to the words of God. He, in the exercise of obedience, went out from his own country, and from his kindred, and from his father's house, in order that, by forsaking a small territory, and a weak family, and an insignificant house, he might inherit the promises of God. For God said to him, "Get you out from your country, and from your kindred, and from your father's house, into the land which I shall show you. And I will make you a great nation, and will bless you, and make your name great, and you shall be blessed. And I will bless them that bless you, and curse them that curse you; and in you shall all the families of the earth be blessed." [Genesis 12:1-3] And again, on his departing from Lot, God said to him, "Lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you now are, northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward; for all the land which you see, to you will I give it, and to your seed forever. […]
41:8.s: Clement's First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 10

41:8.t: And you, Israel my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, seed of Abraham my friend. In whom I took hold of you from the ends of the earth, and called you from its far places, and said to you: You are my servant; I have chosen you and have not cast you off. Do not fear, for I am with you; do not turn aside, for I am your God; I have strengthened you and have helped you and the right hand of my righteous one has upheld you. Behold, all who fight against you will be confounded and will blush; they will be as though they were not; and the men who contradict you will perish. You will seek them and will not find them; the men who rebel against you will be as though they were not; and the men who war against you, as a thing consumed. For I the Lord your God have taken hold of your hand, saying to you: Do not fear, I have helped you. Do not fear, worm Jacob, you who are dead out of Israel. I have helped you, says the Lord, and your redeemer is the Holy One of Israel. […]

41:9.t: For in him he took hold of them from the end of the earth, and from its far-off borders he called Israel out of all the nations, gathering first the people of the Jews, of whom the Apostle Paul also says: It was necessary that the word be preached first to you; but since you turn us away, we go to the nations (Acts 13:46).

41:10.t: For to none other than to God does it belong to implant courage in the fearful, saying to the faint-hearted, "Fear not, for I am with thee, be not dismayed," as says the Psalmist, "Yea though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death I will fear no evil, for Thou art with me." Nay, the Lord Himself says to the fearful,—"Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid," and, "Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith?" and, "Be of good cheer, it is I, be not afraid," and again, "Be of good cheer: I have overcome the world."

To you, therefore, who are both my servant and my chosen one, who are to preach among the nations and to suffer very many persecutions, I say: Do not fear, for I am with you, to whom I speak in the Gospel: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age (Matt 28:20). Do not go astray, nor turn aside from the truth, nor deceive yourself with a false persuasion that by your own strength, unskilled and naked, you will penetrate the forest of the nations and call the fiercest peoples to gentleness. It is I who have strengthened you and have helped you; and the right hand of my righteous one has upheld you, or protected you, that is, of the Lord the Savior; or my right hand, as the Seventy translated.

41:11.t: For behold, your adversaries, the people of the Jews, and all who fight against you, and your persecutors, will be turned into nothing, and you will seek your adversaries and will not find them. And the reason is given why he does not find his adversaries: Because they will be as though they were not. These adversaries are said to rage against the Apostles, or, according to the Hebrew, to be consumed.

41:13.t: And for this reason you ought not to fear, because I have taken hold of your hand, I who say to you: Do not fear, I have helped you; do not fear, worm Jacob, you who are dead out of Israel, or, as the Seventy have it, very few out of Israel. What we have set down, I have helped you: do not fear, worm Jacob, is not found in the Seventy. Now the worm, which in Hebrew is called THOLATH (תולעת), is the name given, for its lowliness and contempt, to the choir of the Apostles, imitating the Savior, who speaks in the psalm: I am a worm, and no man, a reproach of men, and the outcast of the people (Ps 21 [22]:7). For as a worm penetrates the earth, so the apostolic word penetrated the cities of the nations, and entered first into the hardest hearts. And rightly they are called few out of Israel, because in comparison with the whole world very few of the Jewish nation believed, to whom the Lord says in the Gospel: Do not fear, little flock (Luke 12:32). […]

41:15.t: And what follows, I have made you like a new threshing wagon, having sawing teeth, signifies this: that the preaching of the Gospel crushes the adverse powers and the spiritual wickedness that lifts itself up against the knowledge of God, which, according to the variety of their pride, are called mountains and hills; and when these are carried off and scattered after the manner of a whirlwind, let Israel exult and rejoice in the Lord, the Holy One of Israel. We can also say that the churchman, having the sawing teeth of the Gospel preaching on a new wagon, which works not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the spirit, crushes the hardest hearts of unbelievers, separating the wheat from the chaff and crushing the mountains and hills, that is, all the chiefs of the heretics, so that, crushed and ground down, they are reduced to dust and are taught that they are nothing, so that those who had been wrongly gathered together may be divided for their own good.

41:17.t: The needy and the poor seek water, and there is none; their tongue is parched with thirst. I the Lord will hear them; I the God of Israel will not forsake them. I will open rivers on the sloping hills, and fountains in the midst of the plains. I will make the desert into a pool of waters, and the trackless land into streams of waters. I will put in the wilderness the cedar and the thorn, and the myrtle, and the olive tree. I will set in the desert the fir, the elm and the box together, that they may see and know and consider and understand together that the hand of the Lord has done this, and the Holy One of Israel has created it. LXX: And the poor and the needy will exult; for they will seek water, and there will be none; their tongue has dried up for thirst. I the Lord God will hear them, the God of Israel, and I will not forsake them; but I will open rivers on the mountains, and fountains in the midst of the plains; I will make the desert into marshes, and the thirsty land into watercourses. […]

41:18.t: Therefore the Lord, the God of Israel, did not wholly forsake them, nor let them perish for ever, but opened rivers on the sloping hills, or on the mountains, and fountains in the midst of the plains. These rivers took their beginning from that river which is read of in the Psalms: The rush of the river gladdens the city of God (Ps 45 [46]:4); and in another place: The river of God is filled with waters. These waters and fountains flowed from that fountain who speaks through Jeremiah: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water (Jer 2:13). And above in this same Prophet it is said: They will drink waters from the fountains of the Savior. Of these also it is sung in the Psalms: Bless the Lord God from the fountains of Israel (Ps 67 [68]:27). And he made, he says, the desert into a pool of waters, and the trackless land into streams of waters. Of these waters the Savior too spoke in the Gospel in mystical language (John 4:13-14): Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will not thirst for ever; […]

41:19.t: Since, then, the multitude of the Church, once a desert, had been watered with life-giving waters, therefore, according to the Seventy, there spring up in it the cedar, and the box, and the myrtle, and the cypress, and the poplar; according to the Hebrew and the other translators, the cedar, the setta, and the myrtle, and the olive tree, and the fir, and the elm, and the box together. These varieties of trees signify the diversity of spiritual grace. And because the nature of the others is known to all, let us discuss only the Hebrew SETTA (שטה), which Theodotion translated thorn. It is a kind of tree growing in the desert, resembling the white thorn, of which all the wood of the ark and the furnishings of the tabernacle were made, which are called Settim (Exod 37): a wood that does not rot and is very light, and that surpasses all woods in solidity and beauty, as much in strength as in sheen. The cedar, too, and the cypress and the myrtle are of the finest fragrance and do not rot. […]

41:21.t: Bring your judgment near, says the Lord; bring forward whatever you may have, said the king of Jacob. Let them approach and tell us whatever things are to come; tell the former things that have been, and we will set our heart on them and we will know their last end; and show us the things that are to come. Declare the things that are to come hereafter, and we will know that you are gods. Do good also, or evil, if you can, and let us speak and see together. Behold, you are of nothing: and your work is of that which is not; an abomination is he who has chosen you. LXX: Your judgment is near, says the Lord God; your counsels have come and drawn near, says the king of Jacob. Let them draw near and declare to us the things that are to come; or tell the former things that were, and we will apply our mind, and we will know what the last things are. Tell us also the things to come, and declare the things that are to come at the last, and we will know that you are gods. […]

41:22.t: And at the same time an apostrophe is made to the idols themselves, which are without sense and possess the faculty neither of hearing nor of answering. Tell us, he says, either things past or things to come, and show your power by the outcome of events. Now this signifies that after the coming of Christ all the idols fell silent. Where is Delphic Apollo, and Loxias, and the Delian, and the Clarian, and the other idols that promised knowledge of the future, which deceived the most powerful kings? Why could they foretell nothing of Christ, nothing of his Apostles, nothing of the ruin and abolition of their temples? If, then, they could not foretell their own destruction, how could they announce what concerned others, whether evil or good? But if anyone says that many things were foretold by idols, it must be known that they always joined falsehood to truth, and so tempered their sentences that whether something good or something evil happened, either could be understood. […]

41:23.t: Or else it must be said that mute images of men, without sense, can do neither good nor evil, nor know things past nor things to come, because they are of nothing and of that which is not, and it is not so much they as he who worships them that is worthy of abomination. For the idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of men's hands. They have a mouth, and will not speak (Ps 113 [115]:13). How then can they know and announce things to come, or relate things past, and do good or evil, when they have neither the sense of men nor that of brute animals? Nor does it matter of what material they seem to be made, since all are earthly.

41:25.t: I have raised up from the North, and he will come from the rising of the sun; he will call upon my name, and he will bring on rulers as mud, and as a potter treading the ground. Who has announced it from the beginning, that we may know; and from the first, that we may say: You are righteous? There is none announcing, nor foretelling, nor hearing your words. The first will say to Zion: Behold, they are here; and to Jerusalem I will give a bearer of good tidings. And I looked, and there was not even any of these who would enter into counsel, and, when asked, would answer a word. Behold, all are unrighteous, and their works are vain; their images are wind and emptiness. LXX: But I have raised up him who is from the North, and him who is from the rising of the sun; they will be called by my name. Let princes come, and as the clay of the potter, and as a potter treading clay, so you will be trodden down. […]

The Hebrews interpret the one raised up from the North and coming from the rising of the sun as the Assyrian and the Persian, who came to Jerusalem and trod down all its princes; and none of the idols which they worshiped knew that this would come, but the Lord alone, who punished them for their sins.

41:26.t: These things, which, according to prophetic custom, I say that I have done as though they were already past, or, according to Symmachus, which I promise as future, none of the demons and idols can foretell. Hence all the oracles fell silent, because there is no one who announces, no one who hears, while the once brutish hearts of the Gentiles have understood their error and forsaken false prophecies.

41:27.t: And the Lord will speak first to Zion, that is, to his Church, and will say to her: Behold, here are your sons, whom I have given to you through faith in me. And he means the Apostles, who preached the Gospel in the whole world. Zion and Jerusalem differ in name; but as there is one city, so also there is one Church.

41:28.t: Let all the nations, therefore, which follow the error of idols, be questioned by us, so that they may answer whence they are. And this will be the answer of them all: that all follow vanity and the winds, and worship the works of their own hands. Whatever we have said of the idols and the nations, let us refer to the doctrines of perversity, and to their chiefs, the heresiarchs: that while Christ announces the peace of the Church and shows them the way of truth, they follow error and are likened to wind and whirlwind.

42:1.t:
[Passage quoted, Isa. xlii. 1-7.]

THE Evangelist alludes to this passage, when the Pharisees went out and took counsel against our Saviour to put Him to death, when He healed the sick on the Sabbath day. But Jesus, knowing, as He says, this conspiracy against Him, departed thence, and great multitudes followed Him, and He healed them all, and He straitly charged them that they should not make Him known. And He adds to this the words, "All this was done" (that is to say His departure, and His yielding to those that plotted, and His effort to escape notice in the miracles that He did, and His pledging those that were healed not to make Him known), in order that what was said by the prophet might be fulfilled, when He said:

"Behold, my son, in whom I am well pleased, my beloved in whom my soul delighteth; I will put my spirit upon him, and he shall bear forth judgment to the Gentiles; he shall not strive nor cry, neither shall his voice be heard in the streets. […]
42:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 9, Chapter 15

42:1.t:
And the same Isaiah, continuing, prophesies these things about Christ:

"Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased, he shall bring judgment to the nations."

And he adds: "Till he place judgment upon the earth, and in his name shall the Gentiles trust."

Here, then, the second time the prophet states that the Gentiles will hope in Christ, having said above "In Him shall the Gentiles trust." Though here it is "In His name shall the Gentiles trust."
42:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 3, Chapter 2

42:1.t: It is possible, with the help of God, easily to distinguish the presence of the good and the bad; a vision of the holy ones is not agitated. "He shall not protest and cry out; none will hear his voice." It occurs so quietly and gently that joy and gladness and confidence are at once born in the soul.… The soul's thoughts remain untroubled and calm, so that, enlightened of itself, it contemplates those who appear. LIFE OF ST.

Behold my servant, I will uphold him; my chosen one, in him my soul is well pleased. I have put my spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations. He will not cry out, nor will he accept a person, nor will his voice be heard outside. A bruised reed he will not break, and smoking flax he will not quench; in truth he will bring forth judgment. He will not be sad nor troubled, until he sets judgment in the earth; and the islands will wait for his law. LXX: Jacob my child, I will take him up; Israel my chosen one, my soul has received him. I have put my spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations; he will not cry out, nor will he let go, nor will his voice be heard outside. A broken reed he will not break, and smoking flax he will not quench; but in truth he will bring forth judgment. He will shine and will not be broken, until he sets judgment upon the earth; and in his name the nations will hope. […]

Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved, and the rest. This is said through the prophet Isaiah in the person of the Father: I will put my Spirit upon him. The Spirit is put not upon the Word of God and upon the Only-begotten who came forth from the bosom of the Father, but upon him of whom it was said: Behold my servant.

What does it mean that it is written in Matthew: 'A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench' (Matthew 12:20). For the explanation of this passage, the whole testimony that Matthew takes from the Prophet Isaiah must be set forth, even the words of Isaiah (Isaiah 42): according to the Septuagint interpreters and the Hebrew itself, to which Theodotus, Aquila, and Symmachus agree. Thus of the four Evangelists, only Matthew relates: "And Jesus knowing it, retired from thence: and many followed him, and he healed them all. And he charged them that they should not make him known. That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaias the prophet, saying: Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul hath been well pleased. I will put my spirit upon him, and he shall shew judgment to the Gentiles." (Chapter 12, verses 15-18) He will not strive, nor cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. […]

The passage reads, "Jacob, my son, I will uphold him; Israel, my elect, my soul has assumed him." … It is true, indeed, that the Vulgate text has "my servant" in place of "Jacob" and "Israel," but the Septuagint translators preferred to make the meaning more explicit, namely, that the prophecy concerns the "Highest" insofar as he became the "lowliest," in the form of a servant. Hence they placed the name of that man from whose stock the "form of a servant" was assumed. It was to him that the Holy Spirit was given.

42:2.t: He will not cry out: for he will be gentle and meek; and he will not accept a person in judgment, or he will not lift up (it is understood) his voice on high. Or, according to Symmachus, he will not be deceived, understanding all the snares of the devil; or, according to the Seventy, he will not let go, namely the people of the Jews, calling them to repentance. Nor will his voice be heard outside: for he did not preach the Gospel outside Galilee and Judea among the other nations. And if we read that he was in the borders of Tyre and Sidon (Matt 15), or in the region of Caesarea Philippi, which is now called Paneas, still it must be known that it is not written that he entered those cities themselves.

Nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. Wide indeed and spacious is the way that leads to perdition, and many enter by it. Who are the many? Those who do not hear the voice of the Savior, because they are not on the narrow way but on the spacious one.

42:3.t: The prophets, therefore, did not openly behold the actual face of God, but [they saw] the dispensations and the mysteries through which man should afterwards see God. As was also said to Elias: "Thou shalt go forth tomorrow, and stand in the presence of the Lord; and, behold, a wind great and strong, which shall rend the mountains, and break the rocks in pieces before the Lord. And the Lord [was] not in the wind; and after the wind an earthquake, but the Lord [was] not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake a fire, but the Lord [was] not in the fire; and after the fire a scarcely audible voice" (vox aurae tenuis). For by such means was the prophet-very indignant, because of the transgression of the people and the slaughter of the prophets-both taught to act in a more gentle manner; and the Lord's advent as a man was pointed out, that it should be subsequent to that law which was given by Moses, mild and tranquil, in which He would neither break the bruised reed, nor quench the smoking flax. […]

And therefore it was prophesied of Christ, because he was not to be bent down to earthly things: A bruised reed he will not break, since the flesh which sins had bruised he made solid by the power of the resurrection. A good reed is the flesh of Christ, which fixed the head of the serpent devil and the allurements of worldly desire to the gibbet of the cross.

A bruised reed, or a broken one, he will not break. For he will be easy to appease toward all, and will give pardon to sinners, saying to the woman: Take heart, daughter, your sins are forgiven you (Luke 7:48). And smoking flax, or, as the others translated, dim and dark, he will not quench: those who were near to being quenched were preserved by the clemency of the Lord (which we have discussed in the works mentioned above concerning the Jews and the nations); but he will judge all things with truth, in no way fearing the scribes and Pharisees, whom he boldly called hypocrites (Matt 7, 15, 22, 23 throughout, and Luke 6, 12).

A battered reed he will not break, and smoldering flax he will not put out. He who does not hold out a hand to a sinner and does not carry the burden of his brother, he breaks the battered reed. And he who despises the small spark of faith in little ones, he puts out the smoldering flax. Christ did neither of these things; for he had come for this, to save what had perished.

42:4.t: The words, "And in his name shall the Gentiles trust," have also been exactly fulfilled. For the nations of Christians trust only in the Name of our Saviour Jesus Christ, and are marked with His Name as that of the Father of the religion with which they are associated. For it was foretold that He should be given for a Light to none but the Gentiles. And by Him in accordance with the prediction, the eyes of the blind—those that had long been impaired in understanding, and not only of these but of those who had lost their very bodies, and those who before were involved, bound and chained in sin, in darkness and ignorance of true religion, by Him freed from their sins— were accounted worthy of the light of knowledge and of the freedom of God. And if you at your leisure test the rest of the passage, as I have so far done, you will find each one of its predictions fulfilled in our Lord and Saviour, and in Him alone.
42:4.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 9, Chapter 15

42:4.t: But what follows, He will shine and will not be broken, until he sets judgment upon the earth, the Evangelist Matthew did not set down (Matt 12); or else the words in the middle, between judgment and judgment, were removed by a scribe's error. And it signifies that, rising from the dead, he enlightened all, and was not broken by death, until he set judgment upon the earth, he who said in the Gospel: For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind (John 9:39). For this we translated: He will not be sad, nor troubled, but he will keep an evenness of countenance at all times: what the philosophers falsely boast of Socrates, that he was never sadder or happier than usual. For this Aquila and Theodotion translated: He will not darken, and he will not run, until he sets judgment in the earth. And the sense is: he will deter no one by sadness of countenance, nor will he hasten to punishment, he who has reserved the truth of judgment for the last time. […]

42:5.t: For the breath of life, which also rendered man an animated being, is one thing, and the vivifying Spirit another, which also caused him to become spiritual. And for this reason Isaiah said, "Thus saith the Lord, who made heaven and established it, who founded the earth and the things therein, and gave breath to the people upon it, and Spirit to those walking upon it;" thus telling us that breath is indeed given in common to all people upon earth, but that the Spirit is theirs alone who tread down earthly desires. And therefore Isaiah himself, distinguishing the things already mentioned, again exclaims, "For the Spirit shall go forth from Me, and I have made every breath." Thus does he attribute the Spirit as peculiar to God which in the last times He pours forth upon the human race by the adoption of sons; but [he shows] that breath was common throughout the creation, and points it out as something created. Now what has been made is a different thing from him who makes it. […]

And so says Isaiah;—"He that spread forth the earth and that which cometh out of it; he that giveth breath unto the people upon it, and Spirit to them that trample on it"; for they that trample down earthly things and rise above them are borne witness to as worthy of the gift of the Holy Ghost. What then ought to be thought of Him whom the world cannot receive, and Whom saints alone can contemplate through pureness of heart? What kind of honours can be deemed adequate to Him?
The Son is both sent and given, and the Spirit also is both sent and given; they have assuredly a oneness of Godhead who have a oneness of action.

Thus says the Lord God, who creates the heavens and stretches them out, who makes firm the earth and the things that spring from it, who gives breath to the people that is upon it, and spirit to those who tread on it: I the Lord have called you in righteousness, and have taken hold of your hand, and have kept you, and have given you as a covenant of the people, as a light of the nations, that you might open the eyes of the blind, and bring the bound out of confinement, out of the prison house those who sit in darkness. I am the Lord, that is my name; my glory I will not give to another, nor my praise to graven images. The former things, behold, they have come; new things too I declare; before they spring up, I will make you hear of them: It was uncertain who had said before: Behold my servant, I will uphold him; my chosen one, in him my soul is well pleased. I have put my spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations. […]

Isaiah again says: Thus saith the Lord, he that made the heaven and pitched it; and the Apostle in like manner says: Of the true Tabernacle which the Lord pitched and not man. They both speak of the heaven as standing on and fixed on the earth, and not as revolving round it.

42:6.t: Moses then received it, but they proved themselves unworthy. Learn now how we have received it. Moses, as a servant, received it; but the Lord himself, having suffered in our behalf, hath given it to us, that we should be the people of inheritance. But He was manifested, in order that they might be perfected in their iniquities, and that we, being constituted heirs through Him, might receive the testament of the Lord Jesus, who was prepared for this end, that by His personal manifestation, redeeming our hearts (which were already wasted by death, and given over to the iniquity of error) from darkness, He might by His word enter into a covenant with us. For it is written how the Father, about to redeem us from darkness, commanded Him to prepare a holy people for Himself. The prophet therefore declares, "I, the Lord Thy God, have called Thee in righteousness, and will hold Thy hand, and will strengthen Thee; […]
42:6.s: The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter XIV

42:6.t: He, then, whose praises are so great, spoke these things to him whose law the islands and the nations await: I the Lord have called you in righteousness: of whom he himself speaks in the Gospel: Righteous Father, the world does not know you (John 17:25); so that he might be the God not only of the Jews but also of the nations. And I have taken hold of your hand, because whatever the Son works, the Father works. And I have kept you, you who yourself preserve all things. And I have given you as a covenant of the people of Israel, to whom I had promised beforehand that you would come. And as a light of the nations, which sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, that you might open the eyes of the blind, who before did not see God. And bring the bound out of confinement (Prov 5); for each one is bound fast by the cords of his own sins. And in the Gospel the Lord loosed him whom Satan had bound (Matt 8). Out of the prison house those who sit in darkness, those who were living in the night and gloom of error.

Those also whose heart was of old obscured by the darkness of the devil, He has illuminated by rising as some Sun of Righteousness, and making them the children no longer of night and darkness, but of light and day, according to Paul's word, And those who were blind,—for the Apostate had blinded their hearts,—have recovered their sight, and acknowledged the truth; and, as Isaiah says, "Their darkness has become light:" that is, the ignorant have become wise: those that once were in error, have known the paths of righteousness. And the Father also says somewhere unto the Son Himself, "I have given Thee for a covenant of kindred, for a light of the Gentiles, to open the eyes of the blind, to bring out the prisoners from their bonds, and from the guard-house those that sit in darkness." For the Only-begotten came into this world and gave a new covenant to His kindred, the Israelites, of whom He was sprung according to the flesh, even the covenant long before announced by the voice of the prophets. […]
42:6.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

42:7.t: "The opened eyes of the blind" means [Christ] provided clear knowledge of the Father through the Son.

42:8.t: Who says by the prophet, "I am God, and there is none beside me." Who says by the same prophet, "Because I will not give my majesty to another," that He may exclude all heathens and heretics with their figments; proving that that is not God who is made by the hand of the workman, nor that which is feigned by the intellect of a heretic. For he is not God for whose existence the workman must be asked.

[Eunomius says:] "…receiving glory from the Father, not sharing His glory with the Father, for the glory of the Almighty is incommunicable, as He hath said, 'My glory will I not give to another.'" Who is that "other" to whom God has said that He will not give His glory? The prophet speaks of the adversary of God, and Eunomius refers the prophecy to the only begotten God Himself! For when the prophet, speaking in the person of God, had said, "My glory will I not give to another," he added, "neither My praise to graven images." For when men were beguiled to offer to the adversary of God the worship and adoration due to God alone, paying homage in the representations of graven images to the enemy of God, who appeared in many shapes amongst men in the forms furnished by idols, He Who healeth them that are sick, in pity for men's ruin, foretold by the prophet the loving-kindness which in the latter days He would show in the abolishing of idols, saying, "When My truth shall have been manifested, My glory shall no more be […]

And what he adds, I am the Lord, that is my name; my glory I will not give to another, does not exclude the Son; for when he says in the Gospel, Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world was (John 17:5), the Father himself answered: I have both glorified it, and will glorify it. For he did not say: My glory I will give to no one, for if he had said that, he would have excluded the Son too; but my glory I will not give to another, besides you, to whom I have given it, to whom I will give it. Hence I greatly admire the propriety of holy Scripture, in that all the translators, who are accustomed to disagree in many other places, translated the word AHER (אחר) with one voice another. And that we may know that by this sentence not the Son but the idols are excluded, the following words bear witness: Nor my praise to graven images. For which the Seventy have: nor my powers to images. […]

42:9.t: There follows: The former things, behold, they have come. And the sense is: What I have spoken, what I have promised through Moses and the Prophets, all has been fulfilled. But now I announce to you the Gospel, the calling of the nations, the passion of Christ, the newness of faith: so that as you see the former things fulfilled in fact, so you may also believe that the things I now promise will come,

42:10.t: Well, in as much as the Word was from the first, He was and is the divine source of all things; but in as much as He has now assumed the name Christ, consecrated of old, and worthy of power, he has been called by me the New Song. This Word, then, the Christ, the cause of both our being at first (for He was in God) and of our well-being, this very Word has now appeared as man, He alone being both, both God and man-the Author of all blessings to us; by whom we, being taught to live well, are sent on our way to life eternal. This is the New Song, the manifestation of the Word that was in the beginning, and before the beginning. The Saviour, who existed before, has in recent days appeared.

These indeed try to pursue, but you go down into the water and come out unharmed, and, the filth of your sins being washed away, you ascend "a new man" ready "to sing a new song." But the Egyptians, pursuing after you, are drowned in the abyss, even though they seem to beg Jesus not to send them meanwhile into the abyss.

Sing to God a new song, his praise from the ends of the earth, you who go down to the sea, and its fullness, the islands and their inhabitants. Let the desert and its cities lift up; Kedar will dwell in houses; give praise, you inhabitants of Petra; from the top of the mountains they will cry out. They will give glory to the Lord, and will declare his praise in the islands. The Lord will go forth as a mighty one, as a man of war he will stir up zeal; he will shout and cry aloud; he will prevail over his enemies. I have always held my peace, I have kept silent, I have been patient; like a woman giving birth I will speak; I will scatter and swallow up at once. I will make the mountains and hills desolate, and I will dry up all their grass; and I will turn the rivers into islands, and I will dry up the pools. And I will lead out the blind into a way that they do not know, and in paths of which they are ignorant I will make them walk. I will turn darkness before them into light, and crooked things into straight. […]

42:11.t: Let, he says, the desert and its cities lift up their voice, of which we have also spoken above. Or let the desert rejoice, and its villages, and Kedar, which was once an uninhabitable region beyond Arabia, of the Saracens; and the inhabitants of Petra, which itself is also a city of Palestine. And this signifies that the people of the nations, formerly a desert as regards the knowledge of God and bound by the errors of idolatry, is turned to the praises of the Lord. Or, because Kedar means darkness, and, according to the Apostle (1 Cor 10), the rock is Christ, all believers are commanded that those who were before in darkness, and now believe in the Lord the Savior, should cry aloud from the top of the mountains and openly preach Christ, those to whom it was said also above (cf. Isa 40:9): Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem. And I will set his glory in the islands, of which we spoke before.

42:13.t: And the prophetic word describes the glorious coming of the Savior, of which the Apostle Paul also speaks: According to the illumination of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4; 2 Tim 1:10); and compares him to a most mighty man, who is about to fight against his adversaries and to stir up zeal. Of this it was prophesied also in the Song of Deuteronomy: They have moved me to jealousy with that which was not God, and have provoked me with their idols; and I will move them to jealousy with a nation that is not, and with a most foolish nation I will provoke them (Deut 32:21).

42:14.t: It is sufficiently discovered that He suffered shame for man's sake, to set him free from death; and that He exclaimed, as in the words of the prophet, "I have endured as a travailing woman." In very deed did He endure for our sakes sorrow, ignominy, torment, even death itself, and burial. For thus He says Himself by the prophet: "I went down into the deep." Who made Him thus to go down? The impious people. Behold, ye sons of men, behold what recompense Israel made unto Him! She slew her Benefactor, returning evil for good, affliction for joy, death for life. They slew by nailing to the tree Him who had brought to life their dead, had healed their maimed, had made their lepers clean, had given light to their blind. Behold, ye sons of men! behold, all ye people, these new wonders! They suspended Him on the tree, who stretches out the earth; they transfixed Him with nails who laid firm the foundation of the world; they circumscribed Him who circumscribed the heavens; they bound Him who absolves sinners; […]

“I have long time holden my peace. Am I to hold my peace for ever? Shall I still further endure to enforce against myself the hardest punishment of silence, by neither writing myself, nor receiving any statement from another? By holding fast to this stern determination up to the present time I am able to apply to myself the prophet’s words, “I endure patiently like travailing woman.” Yet I am ever longing for communication either in person or by letter, and ever, for my own sins’ sake, missing it.

Nevertheless I thought that I ought to bear my troubles in silence, waiting for some indication to come out of them. I did not even think that what was said against me proceeded from ill will; I thought it was the result of ignorance of the truth. But now I see that hostility increases with time, and that my slanderers are not sorry for what they said at the beginning, and do not take any trouble to make amends for the past, but go on and on and rally themselves together to attain their original object. This was to make my life miserable and to devise means for sullying my reputation among the brethren. I, therefore, no longer see safety in silence. I have bethought me of the words of Isaiah: “I have long time holden my peace, shall I always be still and refrain myself? I have been patient like a travailing woman.” […]

WHAT IS GOD? — [God is] good, just, merciful. Good, because He brought into existence things that were not; just, because whatever He made to advance He left to the free judgment of their own liberty; yet because they are not so perfect that they cannot fall, He decreed that seeds of law should naturally exist in them, adding the help of revealed law, so that His authority might be complete for humankind; merciful, because He does not quickly repay those who sin, but bears with them so that He may forgive the repentant. He is also severe, so that, through fear, the things well created by Him may be preserved, lest negligence give rise to the downfall of life. And, lest we omit what is more wondrous, His mercy is so great that He endures insults from those He has made and Himself first calls them to peace. Is this not an act of greater power than having created the creature? Yet if His excessive goodness remained without limit in this, it would harm the creature. […]
42:14.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 1: WHAT IS GOD?

42:14.t: He will also shout and cry aloud against his enemies, openly rebuking their unbelief and declaring with a loud cry: I have held my peace, I have always kept silent, I have been patient, or, as the Seventy translated: I have held my peace; shall I always hold my peace (Eccl 3:7)? So that what is said through Solomon may be fulfilled: A time to keep silence, and a time to speak. And the sense is: For a long time I have often borne you when you sinned; but because I had kept silent before, I will no longer keep silent. And as a woman giving birth pours forth the infant into the light, and makes open what was before held shut in her womb, so I will now bring forth my pain and the forbearance which I always had over your crimes, and I will scatter your counsels; and at one time I will swallow up the whole nation, and all the pride of your mountains and the swelling of your hills. And the grass, of which it was said above, Truly the people is grass, that is, princes as much as the common herd, I will reduce to a desert. […]

Which same truth he conveys by the Prophet in few words, saying, "I have long time holden my peace, I have been still and refrained myself; now will I cry like a travailing woman." For as we have already before said, a woman in travail with pain gives forth that which she bore for long in her inner parts, He then that for long time held his peace, 'crieth like a travailing woman,' in that the Judge that shall come, who for long bore with the deeds of men without taking vengeance, sooner or later brings to light with hotness of examination, as if with pain of mind, the sentence of direful visiting which He kept within. Therefore let none despise this Lamp, when it is out of sight, lest He burn up His despisers when He shineth from heaven. For to whomsoever He does not now burn to give pardon, He shall then assuredly burn to award punishment. […]
42:14.s: MORALS ON THE BOOK OF JOB 10:31

42:16.t: And I will lead the blind by the way which before they did not know, of whom we also read above: I have given you as a covenant of the people, as a light of the nations, that you might open the eyes of the blind. These will be led by the way of which Christ speaks: I am the way, or by the way of the knowledge of God; and I will make them walk by the paths of the Prophets. Then their darkness will be changed into light, and crooked things will be turned into straight, so that they may understand what they read, and with the eyes of the heart behold the clear light of Christ in the Old Testament. And at the same time he adds: These words which I have done, or I will do for them: no longer promising things to come, but rendering what I had promised before.

If, dearly beloved, we comprehend faithfully and wisely the beginning of our creation, we shall find that man was made in God’s image, to the end that he might imitate his Creator, and that our race attains its highest natural dignity, by the form of the Divine goodness being reflected in us, as in a mirror. And assuredly to this form the Saviour’s grace is daily restoring us, so long as that which, in the first Adam fell, is raised up again in the second. And the cause of our restoration is naught else but the mercy of God, Whom we should not have loved, unless He had first loved us, and dispelled the darkness of our ignorance by the light of His truth. And the Lord foretelling this by the holy Isaiah says, “I will bring the blind into a way that they knew not, and will make them walk in paths which they were ignorant of. I will turn darkness into light for them, and the crooked into the straight. These words will I do for them, and not forsake them.” […]

42:17.t: But while I say these things, the people of the Jews has turned back, so as not to believe him who promises, and to be confounded in its errors, and to neglect the pledge of God, having before believed in idols. Or, when the fullness of the nations has come in, then the people of Israel too will be converted (Rom 11), and will repent of its error, through which it had before served idols. Or certainly, after the calling of the nations, he returns to the beginning, so as to say that all the nations which refused to believe the Gospel are to be confounded in their idols.

42:18.t: And since the keenness of the inner hearing is in our power, the prophet says: "Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see. Who is so deaf as My servants, and who is so blind as those who rule over them?" Even the servants of God are blinded.

You deaf, hear, and you blind, look, that you may see. Who is blind but my servant? and deaf but he to whom I have sent my messengers? Who is blind but he who has been sold? and who is blind but the servant of the Lord? You who see many things, will you not keep them? you who have open ears, will you not hear? And the Lord willed to sanctify him, and to magnify the law and exalt it. But this is a people plundered and laid waste; all are the snare of young men, and they are hidden in prison houses; they have become a prey, and there is none to rescue; a plunder, and there is none to say: Give back. Who is there among you who will hear this, who will attend and listen for the time to come? Who gave Jacob up to plunder, and Israel to those who lay waste? Was it not the Lord himself, against whom we have sinned? And they would not walk in his ways, and they did not hear his law. And he poured out upon him the indignation of his fury, and strong war; and he burned him round about, and he did not know it; […]

42:20.t: To him it is said: O Israel, you who see many things, and have very many Prophets through whom to know the commandments of God, will you not keep what has been commanded you? You who have open ears, will you not hear what is said? Of whom we also read above: Hearing you will hear, and will not understand; and seeing you will look, and will not see; for the heart of this people has been made fat (Isa 6:9).

42:21.t: The Lord, he says, willed to sanctify him, and to magnify his Law, and to exalt and raise up the people lying prostrate.

42:22.t: But he refused to do the will of God, and therefore he was plundered and laid waste by his adversaries, whom we ought to understand either as demons or as enemies. All are the snare of young men, and they are hidden in prison houses. Or, as the Seventy translated, There is a snare in the chambers everywhere, and in the houses together, in which they hid them: signifying the scribes and Pharisees, who deceived the wretched common people and everywhere laid snares against the Lord the Savior and his Apostles (Luke 11), having the key of knowledge, neither entering themselves, and forbidding others who wished to enter.
