And beautifully he called their breasts, in which the worst thoughts dwelt, prisons. Therefore they became a prey and a plunder, and there was none to free them and to speak a word on their behalf.

42:23.t: And at the same time the Prophet exhorts them that, if all cannot hear, at least a few may know the things to come and understand from whom they have suffered these things, and may recognize the causes of their devastation, they who would neither hear nor do what had been commanded in the Law.

42:24.t: In this part of the Lord's Prayer, [Christ] shows that the enemy is powerless against us without God's prior permission. During temptation, consequently, all our fear and devotion and attention should be focused on God, since evil has only such force as he himself permits. … Moreover, evil is given power over us according to our [willful] sins. As Isaiah writes, "Who gave Jacob up to the looters and Israel to the ponderers." It was the Lord, against whom we sinned, in whose ways we would not walk and whose law we refused to obey. So he unleashed the fury of his anger against us. And again, when Solomon strayed from the precepts and paths of the Lord, it was recorded, "The Lord stirred up Satan against Solomon himself."
42:24.s: Treatise IV. On the Lord's Prayer 25

42:25.t: Therefore the Lord poured out upon them all his anger and an indignation full of fury, so that he who before had kept silent would no longer hold his peace, and would chastise them not with words but with punishments and torments; and a most mighty war would seize them, which they could in no way escape, showing the ferocity of the Romans. And though he has been burned on every side and has no soundness in him, yet he does not understand the cause of his punishment: that he has been punished because he did not receive the Son of God.

43:1.t: And now thus says the Lord who creates you, Jacob, and forms you, Israel: Do not fear, for I have redeemed you, and I have called you by your name: you are mine. When you pass through the water , I will be with you, and the rivers will not cover you. When you walk into the fire, you will not be burned, and the flame will not burn in you; for I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior; I have given Egypt as your propitiation, Ethiopia and Saba for you. Since you have become honorable in my eyes and glorious, I have loved you, and I will give men for you, and peoples for your life. Do not fear, for I am with you; from the East I will bring your seed, and from the West I will gather you. I will say to the North: Give; and to the South: Do not hold back; bring my sons from afar, and my daughters from the end of the earth. And everyone who calls upon my name, I have created him for my glory, and I have formed him, and I have made him. […]

43:2.t: "Even if we cross over, they shall not slip, says the Lord." We shall not slip into corruption, we who are crossing over into incorruption, because he himself will support us. For so he himself has said and so he has willed.

There is a way to the tree of life, so that it may come to pass: "If you pass through fire, the flame shall not burn you." What fire? "He stationed the Cherubim and the flaming sword that turns, to guard the way of the tree of life." So for this reason the blessed ones waited there, carrying out a dispensation and not being able to come where the tree of life is, where the paradise of God is, where God is husbandman, where the blessed and chosen and holy ones of God are.

It happened one day, that a man, who is called wise amongst the Jews, questioned me, saying:—Jesus, Who is called your Teacher, wrote for you, that If there shall be in you faith like one grain of mustard, ye shall say to this mountain, Remove, and it shall remove from before you; and (ye shall say) even, Be lifted up and fall into the sea, and it shall obey you. So apparently there is in all your people not one wise man, whose prayer is heard, and who asks of God that your persecutors should cease from you. For clearly it is written for you in that passage, There is nothing which ye shall not be able to do.

And when I saw that he was blaspheming and speaking much against the Way (the Christian religion), my mind was disturbed, and I understood that he would not admit the interpretation of the words that he quoted to me. Then I also questioned him on sayings from the Law and from the Prophets, and said to him:—Do ye trust that even when ye are dispersed God is with you? […]

We are wayfarers in this life; many walk, but it is needful that we walk aright, for then is the Lord Jesus with us, as we read, When thou passest through the waters I will be with thee, and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee; when thou walkest through the fire thou shalt not be burned. But if a man take fire in his bosom, the fire of lust, the fire of immoderate desire he walketh not through, but burns this clothing of his soul. A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour than silver and gold! Faith is sufficient for itself, and in its own possession is rich enough. And to the wise man nothing is foreign, but what is contrary to virtue; wherever he goes, he finds all things to be his own. All the world is his possession, for he uses it all as if it were his own.

And what he adds, waters and rivers, and fire and flames, describes the onslaught and fury of the persecutors, who begrudge the salvation of the nations and do not want the word of the Gospel to be preached. The Jews, however, would have the Egyptians understood by the waters, the Babylonians by the rivers, the Macedonians by the fire, the Romans by the flame.

And through the prophet the Lord promises saying, "When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee, and the rivers shall not overflow thee." For the rivers overflow those whom the active business of this world confounds with perturbation of mind. But he who is sustained in mind by the grace of the Holy Spirit passes through the waters, and yet is not overflowed by the rivers, because in the midst of crowds of peoples he so proceeds along his way as not to sink the head of his mind beneath the active business of the world.

Knowledge is not able to make anything without materials. Knowledge does not venture to step over unto the domain which lies outside nature. How then? That the dissolved nature of water does not suffer the footsteps of flesh on its back, that he who excites fire is burnt by it, and that it is dangerous to act contrary to these [rules]. Such lore is cautiously guarded by knowledge. And it is absolutely impossible to persuade it to order an advance into this domain.

Faith on the other hand commands this with authority, saying: If thou tread on fire it will not burn thee; and floods ‘will not drag thee along. And faith has done these things many times before the eyes of all creatures. If knowledge had been given an opportunity in this domain, it would not have given the permission to try such things at all. Through faith many have entered the mouth of the flames, and have checked the power of the burning fire, and have persevered in it without injury, and have walked on the back of the sea as if it were dry land. […]

43:3.t: And he commands them not to fear for this reason, that the Lord God, their Savior and the Holy One of Israel, is with them, who has made them preach to Egypt, Ethiopia and Syene, and to the furthest bounds of the world. For Syene the other translators put SABA (סבא), whence came the queen of the South, who came to hear the wisdom of Solomon (1 Kgs 10).

43:4.t: Therefore the choir of the Apostles has become honorable in the sight of God and beloved by him; and the salvation of all the men and peoples who have been called through them to the Gospel will also be reckoned to the salvation of their own souls.

43:5.t: Hence he adds and says: Do not fear, I am with you, I who say to you in the Gospel: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age (Matt 28:20). For from the East and from the West I will bring your sons, to rest in the bosom of Abraham; and from all parts of the world a people of my sons and daughters will be gathered, who either call upon my name or are called by my name, so that they are called Christians, to the glory of their founder.

43:6.t: The same thing is signified also by that which is written: I will say to the north wind: Bring; and to the south-west wind: Do not hold back. For the south wind and the east wind are never commanded to bring, because those who are afterwards to be led to the east and the south must be in other regions. The north wind, therefore, brings its inhabitants to the south, and the south-west wind brings its own to the east. For they cannot make progress if they remain in their former seats.

43:7.t: Thou, Master almighty, didst create all things for Thy name's sake; Thou gavest food and drink to men for enjoyment, that they might give thanks to Thee; but to us Thou didst freely give spiritual food and drink and life eternal through Thy Servant. Before all things we thank Thee that Thou art mighty; to Thee be the glory for ever.

43:8.t: And what follows, Bring forth the people that is blind and has eyes, that is deaf and has ears, many think is said of the people of the nations, who through the teaching of the Apostles began to hear and to see. But let us understand this too of scattered Israel, which was called through the Apostles and believed first; to whom Paul also says: It was necessary that the word of God be preached first to you (Acts 13:46). And the Lord himself in the Gospel: Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 10:6). Then follows: All the nations are gathered together, and the tribes are assembled, that is, together with the people that believed from among the Jews, so that the calling may be twofold, of the circumcision and of the uncircumcision. And what is said, Bring forth, is a word addressed to the Son. Or, according to the Seventy, the Father speaks of the Son, that he has brought forth his blind and deaf people, and joined them to the nations, and made of them many princes of the Church. […]

And with the same meaning the Lord rebukes by the prophet the unnatural but freely chosen blindness of the Jews, which they by their obstinacy brought upon themselves, saying: "Hear ye deaf, and ye blind, behold that you may see. Who is deaf but My servant? and blind, but he to whom I have sent My messengers?" And that no one might ascribe this blindness of theirs to nature instead of to their own will, elsewhere He says: "Bring forth the people that are blind and have eyes: that are deaf and have ears;" and again: "having eyes, but ye see not; and ears, but ye hear not." The Lord also says in the gospel: "Because seeing they see not, and hearing they hear not neither do they understand." And in them is fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah which says: "Hearing ye shall hear and shall not understand: and seeing ye shall see and shall not see. […]
43:8.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, Chapter 12

43:10.t: What then do the divine Scriptures intend to say, for example, here: "Before Me there was no God, and after Me there shall be none," and "I am, and there is no God besides Me"? Do not suppose that in these utterances the unity is applied to the God of the universe … apart from Christ, and, of course, not to Christ alone apart from God. But let us speak of this as Jesus Himself taught: "I and the Father are one."

Still I should like to ask our objectors, what means that which is said by the Prophet, "Before Me there was no God formed, nor is there any after Me"? For if the Son is younger than the Father, how, says He, "Nor is there any after me"? Will you take away the being of the Only-Begotten Himself? You either must dare this, or admit one Godhead with distinct Persons of the Father and Son.
43:10.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 4

43:10.t: Or else God himself is the witness and performer of his own words, and so is his child and servant whom he has chosen. There is no doubt that he means Christ, to whom he says also above: It is a great thing for you to be called my child. And all these things will take place so that the truth may be preached to the world, and that those whose mind was before brutish and senseless may know and believe and understand that besides the one God there is no other God, neither before nor after. For the founder of the times never has a beginning, since this very word, ever, belongs to time. And as he has now said, I am a witness, says the Lord God, and the child whom I have chosen, the Lord saying this same thing in the Gospel: The testimony of two men is true. I am he who bears witness of myself, and the Father who sent me (John 8:17-18), so too we must think of his divinity: that there is no God but he who speaks and his child whom he has chosen. […]

And according to what he commands in another place: Be my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord God, and the servant whom I have chosen, the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit is a witness for us, so that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand. And it seems to me that the sentence stands rather in this way, and that the truth is confirmed under these three witnesses, rather than through the letter. For there were two witnesses against Susanna, and against the Lord Savior himself, and yet the word did not stand in their mouth. Against Naboth, too, almost the whole city bore witness, and the agreement of most wicked witnesses had not the firmness of truth but the conspiracy of a crime.

43:11.t: And what follows, And besides me there is no Savior, shows that the Son saves all things in the Father. Of him the same prophet testifies: And the Lord will send them a Savior, who will save them (Isa 19). For God, who is wise and strong, cannot be without his own wisdom and power.

43:12.t: Since, then, I foretold from the beginning that these things would come, there will be no one who can refuse my will, nor indeed make void what I shall have done. These things are said indeed to Jacob and Israel, but they refer to the apostolic choir and to all of the people of the Jews who have been willing to believe in Christ.

43:14.t: Thus says the Lord, your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: For your sake I have sent to Babylon, and I have pulled down all the bars, and the Chaldeans glorying in their ships. I am the Lord, your Holy One, the Creator, Israel, your King. LXX: Thus says the Lord God, who redeemed you, the Holy One of Israel: For your sake I will send to Babylon, and I will rouse up all the fugitives, and the Chaldeans will be bound in ships. I am the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel, who have shown Israel your king. According to the Hebrew, the prophetic word is still directed to Israel: that their redeemer, the Lord and the Holy One of Israel, has spoken these things to them: For your sake, you who preach the Gospel with me, to whom I said above, Do not fear, for I am with you, who are witnesses of my will, and who announce my child to an unbelieving world as a second witness, I have sent my Son into Babylon and the confusion of this world. […]

43:16.t: Thus says the Lord, who made a way in the sea, and a path in the rushing waters; who brought forth the chariot and the horse, the army and the strong man: together they have fallen asleep, and they will not rise again; they are crushed like flax, they are quenched. Do not remember the former things, and do not look upon the things of old. Behold, I am doing new things; now they will spring forth; surely you will know them. I will make a way in the desert, and rivers in the trackless land. The beast of the field will glorify me, the dragons and the ostriches; for I have given waters in the desert, rivers in the trackless land, to give drink to my people, my chosen one. This people I have formed for myself; they will tell my praise. LXX: For thus says the Lord, who gives a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty water; who brings forth chariots and horses and a most mighty multitude. But they have fallen asleep, and they will not rise again; they are quenched like quenched flax. […]

43:18.t: Therefore I command you this: that among my signs and wonders, by which Babylon, the mightiest city, was overthrown, and by which a way was opened for my people in the Red Sea and in the Jordan, you should in no way remember the old things, since in the Gospel I am going to do far greater things, in comparison with which past things ought to be passed over in silence. For no longer will I find a way in the Red Sea, but in the desert of the whole world. Nor will one river or fountain burst forth from the rock, but many rivers, to refresh not bodies, as before, but thirsting souls; and that will be fulfilled which we read above: You will drink waters from the fountains of the Savior (cf. Isa 12:3).

43:19.t: The Word says, "Look, I am doing something new, which no eye has seen, no ear heard, no human heart felt." These are to be seen, heard and grasped by a new eye, a new hearing and a new heart when the Lord's disciples speak, listen and act in the Spirit.

For of this number I find figurative hints up and down the Creator's dispensation in the twelve streams of Elim. … Now the same number of apostles was thus portended, as if they were to be fountains and rivers that should water the Gentile world, which was formerly dry and destitute of knowledge, as he says by Isaiah, "I will put streams in the unwatered ground."

But as often as water is named alone in the holy Scriptures, baptism is referred to, as we see intimated in Isaiah: "Remember not," says he, "the former things, and consider not the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing.…" There God foretold by the prophet that among the nations, in places that previously had been dry, rivers should afterwards flow plenteously and should provide water for the elected people of God, that is, for those who were made children of God by the generation of baptism. Moreover, it is again predicted and foretold before, that the Jews, if they should thirst and seek after Christ, should drink with us, that is, should attain the grace of baptism. "If they shall thirst," he says, "he shall lead them through the deserts, shall bring forth water for them out of the rock. The rock shall be cloven, and the water shall flow, and my people shall drink," which is fulfilled in the Gospel, when Christ, who is the Rock, is cloven by a stroke of the spear in his passion; […]

But He, although He took on Him our flesh, although He was made man that He might redeem man, and recal him from death, still, as being God, came upon earth in an extraordinary way, that as He had said, 'Behold I make all things new,' so also He might be born of an immaculate virgin, and be believed to be, as it is written, 'God with us.' But from their perverse ways they are induced to say 'She was a virgin when she conceived, but not a virgin when she brought forth.' Could she then conceive as a virgin, and yet not be able to bring forth as a virgin, when conception always precedes, and birth follows?

43:20.t: Then what never was done will be done: all the beasts and dragons and ostriches that dwelt in the wilderness of the nations, and were like beasts in the blood of idolatry and the savagery of their manners, will glorify me and praise me together. For dragons, which Theodotion alone, as it is written in the Hebrew, called THANNIM (תנים), the others translated Sirens: monstrous creatures which by their sweet and deadly song cast sailors headlong to be torn apart by Scylla's dogs. And this signifies that those who were formerly given over to pleasure and luxury are turned to the service of the Lord; although it is better to understand dragons, since ostriches are joined to them, so that, since he was speaking once of the beasts of the wilderness, he set down these animals, which are at home in the desert. […]

43:21.t: And those of them who declare that God would make a new covenant with men, not such as that which He made with the fathers at Mount Horeb, and would give to men a new heart and a new spirit; and again, "And remember ye not the things of old: behold, I make new things which shall now arise, and ye shall know it; and I will make a way in the desert, and riven in a dry land, to give drink to my chosen people, my people whom I have acquired, that they may show forth my praise," -plainly announced that liberty which distinguishes the new covenant, and the new wine which is put into new bottles, [that is], the faith which is in Christ, by which He has proclaimed the way of righteousness sprung up in the desert, and the streams of the Holy Spirit in a dry land, to give water to the elect people of God, whom He has acquired, that they might show forth His praise, but not that they might blaspheme Him who made these things, that is, God.

43:22.t: You have not called upon me, Jacob, nor have you labored in me, Israel. You have not offered me the ram of your burnt offering, and with your victims you have not glorified me. I have not made you serve with offering, nor have I given you labor with incense. You have not bought me sweet cane with silver, and with the fat of your victims you have not made me drunk. But you have made me serve in your sins; you have given me labor in your iniquities. LXX: Not now have I called you, Jacob, nor have I made you labor, Israel. You have not brought me the sheep of your burnt offering, nor have you magnified me with your victims; nor have I made you serve with sacrifices, nor have I given you labor with incense; nor have you bought me incense with silver, nor have I desired the fat of your sacrifices; but in your sins I have defended you, and in your iniquities. […]

43:23.t: And as for your thinking that you have offered me victims and sacrificed rams, know that they were not accepted by me, because they were shared by me and the idols. And he repeats that sense of which he had spoken above: To what purpose is the multitude of your victims to me, says the Lord? I am full of the burnt offering of rams, and of the fat of lambs, and the blood of bulls and goats I do not want. For I have not, he says, required anything precious from you, so as to make you labor in preparing it. I have not exacted offerings from you, nor sought frankincense, nor sweet cane, nor incense and spices of various kinds, with whose smoke you might make me drunk and sate me. But obedience, which is above sacrifice, and the sacrifice of which David says in the Psalms, A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise (Ps 50 [51]:19): these I wanted, these I sought. But you have made me serve and labor in your sins, so that I was compelled to say: I have labored in bearing; […]

43:24.t: But because sweat is usually wiped away from workers by a cloth, the labor of God can also be expressed by the name of cloth—He who indeed always remains quiet and unchangeable in Himself, yet nevertheless declares that He labors when He bears the harsh depravities of men. Whence He also says through the prophet: "I have labored in enduring." Now God appeared in the flesh, He labored from our infirmity. When unbelievers saw this labor of His passion, they refused to venerate Him. For they disdained to believe that He whom they saw mortal in the flesh was immortal in His divinity.

43:25.t: For he himself now instigates us to sin, he himself also, when we have sinned, accuses. If, therefore, in this life we forestall him and are our own accusers, we escape the malice of the devil, our enemy and accuser. For so also elsewhere the prophet says: "do you", he says, "tell your iniquities first, that you may be justified". Does he not evidently show the mystery of which we treat, when he says: "do you tell them first?" — that he may show you that you ought to forestall him who is ready to accuse.

You have blotted it out, indeed, in your hearts and minds, but the Word of God is not blotted out, the Holy Spirit is not blotted out but turns away from impious minds. It is not grace but iniquity that is blotted out; for it is written, "I am he, I am he who blots out your iniquities."

Groan bitterly, sacrifice confession, (for, saith he, "Declare thou first thy transgressions that thou mayest be justified,") sacrifice contrition of heart. These victims turn not to ashes nor dissolve into smoke nor melt into air; neither need they wood and fire, but only a deep-pricked heart. This is wood, this is fire to burn, yet not consume them. For he that prayeth with warmth is burnt, yet not consumed; but like gold that is tried by fire becometh brighter.

I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins. Put me in remembrance, that we may be judged together; tell, if you have anything, that you may be justified. Your first father sinned, and your interpreters have transgressed against me. And I have defiled the holy princes; I have given Jacob to slaughter, and Israel to blasphemy. LXX: I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them. But you, remember, and let us be judged. Tell your iniquities first, that you may be justified. Your fathers sinned, and your princes have acted unjustly against me, and the princes have defiled my holy things. And I have given Jacob up to destruction, and Israel to reproach. You, he says, Jacob and Israel, have made me labor in your sins, and I could scarcely carry the burdens of your iniquities; you whom I in no way call my servants or my children, but address by the bare names of Jacob and Israel, so as to expose and reprove you as sinners. […]

Germanus: And whence can there be aroused in us this holy and salutary contrition from humiliation, which is described as follows in the person of the penitent: "I have acknowledged my sin, and mine unrighteousness have I not hid. I said: I will acknowledge against myself mine unrighteousness to the Lord," so that we may be able effectually to say also what follows: "And Thou forgavest the iniquity of my heart;" or how, when we kneel in prayer shall we be able to stir ourselves up to tears of confession, by which we may be able to obtain pardon for our offences, according to these words: "Every night will I wash my bed: I will water my couch with tears;" if we expel from our hearts all recollection of our faults, though on the contrary we are bidden carefully to preserve the remembrance of them, as the Lord says: "And thine iniquities I will not remember: but do thou recollect them?" […]

43:26.t: And it is ours to flee to God. And let us endeavor after this ceaselessly and energetically. For he says, "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." And prayer and confession with humility are voluntary acts. Therefore it is enjoined, "First tell your sins, that you may be justified." What afterwards we shall obtain, and what we shall be, it is not for us to judge.
43:26.s: Fragments Found in Greek Only in the Oxford Edition

43:26.t: For so also elsewhere the prophet says: "do you", he says, "tell your iniquities first, that you may be justified". Does he not evidently show the mystery of which we treat, when he says: "do you tell them first?" — that he may show you that you ought to forestall him who is ready to accuse. "Do you", therefore, he says, "tell them first", lest he forestall you; for if you tell them "first" and offer the sacrifice of repentance according to the things which we said above are to be offered, and hand over your flesh to destruction, "that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord", it will be said to you also that "you have received your evils in your life, but now rest here".

We are just when we acknowledge that we are sinners, and our justice depends not on our personal merit but rather on the mercy of God, as holy Scripture says: "The just is an accuser of himself in the beginning of his plea." And in another place, "State your sins, that you may be justified."

Put me, then, in remembrance: if you have anything righteous to answer me, I will gladly receive it, that we may be judged together, and you may convict me of not having done for you what I ought to have done. This sense we read more fully in Micah: My people, what have I done to you, and in what have I troubled you? Answer me: for I brought you up out of the land of Egypt, and freed you from the house of bondage, and sent before your face Moses and Aaron and Miriam. And in the fiftieth Psalm David says to God: That you may be justified in your words, and may prevail when you are judged (Ps 50 [51]:5). Tell, then, if you have anything, that you may be justified. And the sense is: I will not speak first against you, lest you say you have been overwhelmed by a multitude of words; but if you have anything righteous, speak for yourself, so that you may be seen to endure undeservedly the things you suffer.

According to the Seventy, who added on their own, Tell your iniquities first, that you may be justified, God calls them to repentance, so that they may understand their crimes and sins and obtain pardon. For it is written also in another place: The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech (Prov 18:17).

43:27.t: And that you may know that I have mercy on you not for your merit but for my own clemency, I will go back to your fathers and forebears, so that you may understand that you were begotten of sinners: Your first father sinned in the wilderness, namely the whole people of Israel. Or else the author of your race, Abraham, is convicted of having sinned when, as the Lord promised the land of promise to his seed, he answered: Whereby shall I know that I shall possess it? And your interpreters, he says, have transgressed against me (Gen 15:8): Aaron and Moses at the water of contradiction, who spoke as mediators between me and you (Exod 17). And that we may understand that this is not a forced exposition, there follows: And I have defiled the holy princes, of whom it is also sung in the psalm: Their judges have been swallowed up beside the rock (Ps 140 [141]:6). These he says he has defiled for this reason, that they did not enter the land of promise. […]

And their princes and fathers are said to have violated the holy things of the Lord, not serving the Law of God, but seeking the traditions and commandments of men; on account of whom Jacob perished, and Israel was given to reproach, cast out of his own province, an exile and a stranger throughout the whole world.

44:1.t: And now hear, Jacob my servant, and Israel, whom I have chosen. Thus says the Lord, who makes you and forms you from the womb, your helper: Do not fear, my servant Jacob, and you, Most Upright, whom I have chosen. For I will pour out waters upon the thirsty, and streams upon the dry ground; I will pour out my spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your offspring. And they will spring up among the grass, like willows beside flowing waters. This one will say, I am the Lord's; and that one will call in the name of Jacob; and this one will write with his hand, To the Lord; and he will be likened in the name of Israel. LXX: But now hear, Jacob my child, and Israel whom I have chosen. I am the Lord God, who made you and fashioned you from the womb; you will yet have help. Do not fear, my child Jacob, and beloved Israel whom I have chosen; yet I will give water in thirst to those who walk in the waterless land; I will put my spirit upon your seed, and my blessings upon your sons. […]

44:2.t: Thus says the Lord, your maker and former, who helped you from the womb (Gen 25), so that while still in your mother's womb you seized your brother's heel; or who at the beginning of the newborn Church preserved you from the persecutors. Do not fear their cruelty, Jacob my servant, and Most Upright, whom I have chosen. He calls Israel by another name; for the Hebrew word ISURUN (ישרון) the others translated εὐθύτατον, or εὐθῆ, that is, most upright and upright; the Seventy alone most beloved, adding Israel of their own. For properly, according to the Hebrews and the faithfulness of the letters, ISRAEL (ישראל) means upright of God; whereas a man seeing God lies not in the letters but in the sound of the word. Hence also the book of Genesis is called εὐθεῖς, that is, of the righteous: Abraham, Isaac and Israel.

44:3.t: God himself testifies that the Holy Spirit presides over his blessings, saying, "I will put my Spirit on your seed and my blessings on your children." For no blessing can be full except through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

Do not fear, then, Jacob and Israel, because I will pour out waters upon the thirsty and the dry ground, of which it has often been said: And I will pour out, or I will put my spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your offspring, which will be born again of water and the Holy Spirit in baptism. This the Savior also promised in the Gospel, saying: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. And at once it is added: But this he said of the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed were to receive (John 7).

44:4.t: He also compares those who are born again in baptism to green grass, and to the willow which springs up beside flowing waters and, against the nature of things, bears fruit, though before it was barren, or rather its seed, taken as food, makes people barren. This indeed is read in the first psalm: And he will be like a tree which is planted by the streams of waters, which will give its fruit in its season, and its leaf will not fall. Others understand by the grass and the willows springing up anew a twofold calling: so that the people of the nations is in the grass, and in the willows those of Israel who believed.

44:5.t: And at the same time he describes the variety of believers: One will say, I am the Lord's, he who trusts that the works of righteousness are in him; another will call (understand: sinners to repentance) in the name of Jacob, so that they too may supplant vices and sins. Another will write with his hand, I am God's; or, as the Seventy translated, he will write on his hand, I am God's, so that he glories in being a soldier in the new service of Christ's warfare. And he will be likened in the name of Israel. For not all from Israel, but a great part from the multitude of the nations will be likened in the name of Israel, so as to receive the Law and the Prophets and all the graces of the Holy Spirit which were promised to the people of Israel.

44:6.t: For God is one and only and first. But this is not said to the denial of the Son; perish the thought. For he is in that One and First and Only, as being of that One and Only and First the only Word and Wisdom and Radiance. And he too is the First, as the fullness of the godhead of the First and Only, being whole and full God.

For we do not count by way of addition, gradually making increase from unity to multitude, and saying one, two, and three,—nor yet first, second, and third. For "I," God, "am the first, and I am the last." And hitherto we have never, even at the present time, heard of a second God. Worshipping as we do God of God, we both confess the distinction of the Persons, and at the same time abide by the Monarchy.

Again, where do you get your Unbegotten and Unoriginate, those two citadels of your position, or we our Immortal? Show me these in so many words, or we shall either set them aside, or erase them as not contained in Scripture; and you are slain by your own principle, the names you rely on being overthrown, and therewith the wall of refuge in which you trusted. Is it not evident that they are due to passages which imply them, though the words do not actually occur? What are these passages?—I am the first, and I am the last, and before Me there was no God, neither shall there be after Me. For all that depends on that Am makes for my side, for it has neither beginning nor ending. When you accept this, that nothing is before Him, and that He has not an older Cause, you have implicitly given Him the titles Unbegotten and Unoriginate. And to say that He has no end of Being is to call Him Immortal and Indestructible. The first pairs, then, that I referred to are accounted for thus.

"I am the first, and hereafter am I, and no God was before Me, and no God shall be after Me." For knowing more perfectly than all others the mystery of the religion of the Gospel, this great prophet, who foretold even that marvellous sign concerning the Virgin, and gave us the good tidings of the birth of the Child, and clearly pointed out to us that Name of the Son,—he, in a word, who by the Spirit includes in himself all the truth,—in order that the characteristic of the Divine Nature, whereby we discern that which really is from that which came into being, might be made as plain as possible to all, utters this saying in the person of God: "I am the first, and hereafter am I, and before Me no God hath been, and after Me is none."
I have not read of, or heard of or found any varying degree in God. Never have I read of a second, never of a third God. I have read of a first God; I have heard of a first and only God.

Thus says the Lord, the King of Israel, and his redeemer, the Lord of hosts: I am the first and I am the last, and besides me there is no God. Who is like me? Let him call and declare, and set out the order for me, since I established the ancient people; let them declare to them the things to come and the things that shall be. Do not fear, nor be troubled: from that time I have made you hear, and I have declared; you are my witnesses. Is there a God besides me, and a former whom I have not known? The makers of an idol are all nothing, and their most beloved things will not profit them. They themselves are their witnesses, that they do not see nor understand, so that they may be confounded. Who has formed a god, and cast a graven image that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all its partners will be confounded; for the craftsmen are of men; they will all assemble, they will stand, and they will be afraid, and they will be confounded together. The ironsmith has worked with the file; […]

44:7.t: Let him call the things that are not as though they were, and set out the order of my creation, I who have balanced all things by reason, since I made man upon the earth. Nor do I want this only, but I also ask for knowledge of things to come.

44:8.t: Hence you, Israel, whose king and redeemer I am, do not fear the images, which you learned on Mount Sinai are nothing. Or is there perhaps another Creator, whom I have not known? Or besides this is there another world, to show the power of an unknown God?

44:9.t: And not only the things that are made, but those also who make them, will be held as nothing. And when the time of vengeance has come, the works of their hands will in no way be able to free them; blind and senseless, they confound their own craftsmen.

And the prophetic discourse on the mockery of idols is woven more fully, but these things are easy to understand and do not call for a long-winded, nay, a superfluous exposition. On this Flaccus too writes in a Satire, deriding the images of the nations (Satires, book 1, 8): Once I was a fig-tree trunk, a useless log, when the craftsman, uncertain whether to make a stool or a Priapus, preferred that I be a god: thence I am a god, of thieves and birds the greatest terror. . . . . . . . . . . . . And whatever has been said of idols can be referred also to the chiefs of the heresies, who with a crafty heart put together the images of their doctrines and lies, and venerate what they know to have been feigned by themselves. Nor is their own error enough for them, unless they have deceived all the simple into worshiping them. […]

44:11.t: When, however, the Scripture terms them [gods] which are no gods, it does not, as I have already remarked, declare them as gods in every sense, but with a certain addition and signification, by which they are shown to be no gods at all. As with David: "The gods of the heathen are idols of demons;" and, "Ye shall not follow other gods." For in that he says "the gods of the heathen"—but the heathen are ignorant of the true God—and calls them "other gods," he bars their claim [to be looked upon] as gods at all. But as to what they are in their own person, he speaks concerning them; "for they are," he says, "the idols of demons." And Esaias: "Let them be confounded, all who blaspheme God, and carve useless things; even I am witness, saith God." He removes them from [the category of] gods, but he makes use of the word alone, for this [purpose], that we may know of whom he speaks.

How could he fail to pity them in this also, seeing that they worship them that cannot see. In hearing, they pray to them that cannot hear. Born with life and reason, people, as they are, call gods things that do not move at all but do not even have life. Strangest of all, do they serve as their masters beings whom they themselves keep under their own power?

44:12.t: For who could believe that a god is formed by adze, file and auger and hammer? And that images are either cast in the coals, or by rule, plane and corner tools and compass suddenly rise up into gods? Especially since the cheapness of the art is shown by the hunger and thirst of the craftsman. For a wooden statue is made, expressing the human form, and the more beautiful it is, the more august a god it is thought. It is set in a shrine and shut up in an eternal prison, the thing that grew for a long time in the forests and, according to the variety of trees, was a cedar or a holm oak or an oak or a pine. And in a wondrous manner its chips and shavings are thrown into the fire to warm the god's craftsman and to cook various stews; but the other part is formed into a god, so that, when the work is finished, its maker may worship it and invoke the help of his own work.

44:15.t: And neither do we honour with many sacrifices and garlands of flowers such deities as men have formed and set in shrines and called gods; since we see that these are soulless and dead, and have not the form of God (for we do not consider that God has such a form as some say that they imitate to His honour), but have the names and forms of those wicked demons which have appeared. For why need we tell you who already know, into what forms the craftsmen, carving and cutting, casting and hammering, fashion the materials? And often out of vessels of dishonour, by merely changing the form, and making an image of the requisite shape, they make what they call a god; which we consider not only senseless, but to be even insulting to God, who, having ineffable glory and form, thus gets His name attached to things that are corruptible, and require constant service.

44:18.t: Nor does he understand or consider, nay, he does not see with the eyes either of the flesh or of the mind, that that cannot be God of which a part has been burned in the fire, nor can the divine majesty be made by the hand of a man.

44:21.t: Remember these things, Jacob and Israel, for you are my servant; I have formed you, you are my servant, Israel; do not forget me. I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Return to me, for I have redeemed you. Praise, O heavens, for the Lord has done it; shout for joy, you ends of the earth; resound with praise, you mountains, you forest and every tree in it; for the Lord has redeemed Jacob, and Israel will glory. LXX: Remember these things, Jacob and Israel, for you are my child; I have formed you as my child; and you, Israel, do not forget me. For behold, I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like darkness. Return to me, and I will redeem you. Rejoice, O heavens, for God has had mercy on Israel. Sound the trumpet, you foundations of the earth; cry out with gladness, you mountains, you hills and all the trees that are in them; for God has redeemed Jacob, and Israel will be glorious. […]

44:22.t: And thus, through each and every kind of malice, as though by diverse colors gathered together, you paint upon yourself this "image of the earthly," which God did not make in you. Therefore he is to be entreated by us who says through the prophet: "Behold, I blot out your iniquities as a cloud, and your sins as a mist." And when he has blotted out in you all those colors which were taken from the dyes of malice, then there shines forth again in you that image which was created by God. You see, then, how the divine scriptures introduce forms and figures by which the soul may be taught unto the acknowledgment or the cleansing of itself.

And since these are to be utterly destroyed at the coming of my child whom I have chosen, therefore know with all the eagerness of your mind that, as a cloud and darkness and mist is either dissolved by the heat of the sun or thinned out by a sweeping wind, so I will cause your iniquities to be dissolved, and all the sins with which you had before offended me. Only return to me and do penance, for you are to be redeemed with precious blood.

44:23.t: If you do this, know that heaven and earth rejoice in your salvation, and all the elements sing together; or the angels who dwell in heaven, and the other powers by which the foundations of the earth are borne; or certainly the Apostles and Prophets, of whom the Apostle also spoke: Built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets (Eph 2:20). The mountains also and the forests, or the hills, which, according to the variety of their virtues, have held the first, the middle and the last places, are bidden to shout for joy and to sound the trumpet, knowing that the Lord has redeemed Jacob, and that he rejoices in the conversion of Israel; or that Israel himself, turned from error, becomes glorious.

44:24.t: And when the prophet says concerning the creation, "That stretches forth the heavens alone," and when God says, "I only stretch out the heavens," it is made plain to everyone that in the "Only" is signified also the Word of the Only, in whom "all things were made" and without whom "was made not one thing." Therefore, if they were made through the Word, and yet he says, "Only," and together with that Only is understood the Son, through whom the heavens were made, so also then, if it is said, "One God," and "I Only," and "I the First," in that "One" and "Only" and "First" is understood the Word co-existing, as in the Light the Radiance. And this can be understood of no other than the Word alone. For all other things subsisted out of nothing through the Son and are greatly different in nature, but the Son himself is natural and true offspring from the Father. And thus the very passage that these insensate have thought fit to adduce, "I the First," in defense of their heresy, does rather expose their perverse spirit. […]

Thus says the Lord, your redeemer, and your former from the womb: I am the Lord who makes all things, who alone stretches out the heavens, who establishes the earth, and there is none with me; who makes void the signs of the diviners, and turns the soothsayers to madness; who turns the wise backward, and makes their knowledge foolish; who raises up the word of his servant, and fulfills the counsel of his messengers; who say to Jerusalem: You will be inhabited , and to the cities of Judah: You will be built, and I will raise up its deserts; who say to the deep: Be desolate, and I will dry up your rivers; who say to Cyrus: You are my shepherd, and you will fulfill all my will; who say to Jerusalem: You will be built; and to the temple: You will be founded. LXX: Thus says the Lord who redeemed you, and who forms you from the womb: I am the Lord who accomplish all things; I alone stretched out the heaven, and made firm the earth. Who else has scattered the signs of the pythons, and divinations from the heart? […]

44:25.t: He, then, being so great and such, when the time of the foreordained mystery has come, that all idols may be destroyed and the knowledge of God alone may be preached in the world, will destroy and overturn all the prophecies of the diviners, and the signs and portents of the pythons and soothsayers, by which they have deceived the human race; and he will show to be foolish the wisdom of the philosophers, which itself also is the greatest part of error, since by human thoughts they are in no way shown to have comprehended the wisdom of God.

44:26.t: He will also fulfill in deed the word of his child, or servant, of whom we spoke above, and the counsel of his messengers, namely of the Apostles and all the teachers, who will announce the will of their master to the nations. He, then, who is to do such great things, whose power I have described in a brief discourse, now says also to Jerusalem, which was to be destroyed by the Babylonians, before it is destroyed, that it will again be inhabited by peoples; and to the cities of Judea, that they will be restored; he who will also raise up its solitudes, so that all may be filled with inhabitants.

44:27.t: However, a time will come, when all shall be consumed by fire; as Isaiah says of the God of the universe in these words, “That saith to the deep, Be dry, and I will dry up thy rivers.” Reject then the foolish wisdom of this world, and receive with me the more simple but infallible doctrine of truth.
44:27.s: The Hexaemeron, Homily 3: On the Firmament

44:27.t: He, then, who says to Jerusalem and to Judea and its deserts that it will be inhabited and built and raised up, says to the deep or abyss, that is, to Babylon, Be desolate, and I will dry up your rivers, all the power of its kings. Or, because he had spoken of the deep and the abyss, rightly by metaphor he set down rivers too, of which the Psalmist also sings: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept (Ps 136 [137]:1).

44:28.t: And he who restores Jerusalem and destroys Babylon also says to Cyrus, king of the Persians, who first destroyed Babylon and the Chaldeans: You are my shepherd, or, as the Seventy translated, that he should be wise. The cause of this difference is plain. For if we read the Hebrew word ROI with the letter RES (רעי), it is understood as my shepherd; if with DALETH (דעי), as knowing or my understanding one; and the likeness of these letters is distinguished by a small stroke, and for this reason they are often confused. It is written at the beginning of Ezra that at the edict of Cyrus, king of the Persians and Medes, the captivity of the people of Israel was loosed, and those who wished to return were sent back to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest. For the Lord inspired him to do his will and to fulfill his commands. And significantly he added, who say to Jerusalem: You will be built; and to the Temple: You will be founded. […]

45:1.t: Thus says the Lord to my anointed, Cyrus, whose right hand I have taken hold of, to subdue nations before his face, and I will turn the backs of kings, and I will open doors before him, and the gates will not be shut. I will go before you, and I will humble the glorious ones of the earth; I will break the gates of bronze, and I will shatter the bars of iron. And I will give you hidden treasures and the secrets of hidden places, that you may know that I am the Lord, who call your name, the God of Israel. For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I have also called you by your name; I have likened you, and you have not known me. I am the Lord, and there is none besides; apart from me there is no God; I girded you, and you have not known me; that they may know, those who are from the rising of the sun and those who are from the west, that besides me there is none. I am the Lord, and there is no other. I form light and create darkness; I make peace and create evil. I am the Lord who does all these things. […]

His right hand he took hold of and held, so that no one could resist his strength. Let us read Xenophon's history of the elder Cyrus in eight books, and we shall see the prophecy of Isaiah fulfilled. For what city was not opened to him? What city did not bow beneath him the backs of its kings? What walls, before impregnable, were not overthrown by his siege? Hence God makes an apostrophe to Cyrus himself: I have given you the treasures and the hidden wealth of all the cities, so that you, who before worshiped idols, might perceive the one God through his benefits, especially since you know that your name was foretold long before you were born. Josephus too relates this in the eleventh book of the Jewish Antiquities: that Cyrus read that Isaiah had prophesied of him by his very name, and that for this reason he loved the Jews very much as God's intimates.

According to tropology we can say these things also of the churchman, to whom God has given speech and wisdom, so that by his disputation he may overturn all the sects contrary to the truth, as holy Scripture records of Stephen too (Acts 6), that no one could resist his wisdom; and so that he may subject kings, that is, the patriarchs of the several heresies, to his power, and may open and break what before seemed shut fast by the art of dialectic, and may bring into the open the secrets of the heretics, overcoming and refuting them, so that they may come to know the secrets of Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2). Such a man God calls by his own name, because he is the defender of his child Jacob and of his chosen Israel. Him he takes up and likens to his own word; and he must beware lest he think that what he speaks is his own, but must refer all to the glory of the giver, lest he too deserve to hear: I girded you, and you have not known me. […]

For taking into his hands the book of Isaiah he found as he read the section which contained the prophecy concerning himself; since Isaiah says in that section: Thus saith the Lord to his Anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden to subdue nations before him, and I will loose the loins of kings. I will open the doors before him, and the gates shall not be shut. I will go before thee and will level mountains. I will break in pieces the doors of brass, and cut in sunder the bars of iron; and I will give thee the treasures of darkness, and hidden riches of secret places will I present to thee, that thou mayest know I am the Lord, which call thee by thy name, even the God of Israel. For Jacob my servant's sake and Israel my chosen, I have called thee by thy name and I will accept thee; and shortly afterwards: I have raised him up a king in righteousness, and I will make straight all his ways. He shall build my city, and lead back the captivity of my people, not for price nor reward, saith the Lord of hosts. […]

45:2.t: Therefore, let us fear nothing so much as sin and transgression. Let us not fear punishment, and then we shall escape punishment. Even as the Three Children were not afraid of the furnace, and so escaped from the furnace. Such indeed it becomes the servants of God to be. For if those who were brought up under the Old dispensation, when death was not yet slain, nor his "brazen gates broken down," nor his "iron bars smitten in sunder;" so nobly encountered their end, how destitute of all defence or excuse shall we be, if, after having had the benefit of such great grace, we attain not even to the same measure of virtue as they did, now when death is only a name, devoid of reality. For death is nothing more than a sleep, a journey, a migration, a rest, a tranquil haven; an escape from trouble, and a freedom from the cares of this present life!

And of these passions as the occasions are recognized by everybody as soon as they are laid open by the teaching of the elders, so before they are revealed, although we are all overcome by them, and they exist in every one, yet nobody knows of them. But we trust that we shall be able in some measure to explain them, if by your prayers that word of the Lord, which was announced by Isaiah, may apply to us also-"I will go before thee, and bring low the mighty ones of the land, I will break the gates of brass, and cut asunder the iron bars, and I will open to thee concealed treasures and hidden secrets" -so that the word of the Lord may go before us also, and first may bring low the mighty ones of our land, i.e. these same evil passions which we are desirous to overcome, and which claim for themselves dominion and a most horrible tyranny in our mortal body; […]
45:2.s: The Twelve Books on the Institutes of the Coenobia, Book 5, Chapter 2

45:4.t: And these things, he says, I have granted you for the sake of Jacob my servant, and Israel my chosen, and I have called you by your name, as I called Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and foretold you long before, as I did Isaac and Josiah: lest you should be thought to be that Christ to whom you have been likened, and whose type and image you went before. But you have not known me, that is, you have worshiped images, not God. I girded you with strength; I made you victor over many nations, and you have not known your helper. In this place I cannot sufficiently marvel at the folly of readers, that they refer these things to Christ, through whom the world was reconciled to God. I, he says, am the Lord, and there is none besides apart from me. For besides my Word and Reason, and my power and wisdom, which is in me, there is no other God. And I have done these things so that the whole world, from the East and the West, may acknowledge that there is no other God besides me. I am the Lord, and there is no other. […]

45:6.t: And inasmuch as this Son is undivided and inseparable from the Father, so is he to be reckoned as being in the Father, even when he is not named. The fact is, if he had named him expressly, he would have separated him, saying in so many words, "Beside me there is none else, except my Son." In short, he would have made his Son actually another, after excepting him from others.

45:7.t: Now (like many other persons nowadays, especially those who have a heretical proclivity), while morbidly brooding over the question of the origin of evil, Marcion's perception became blunted by the very irregularity of his researches. When he found the Creator declaring, "I am he that creates evil," Marcion had already concluded from other arguments that satisfy only twisted minds that God is the author of evil. So Marcion now applied to the Creator the figure of the corrupt tree bringing forth evil fruit, that is, moral evil, and then presumed that there ought to be another god, after the analogy of the good tree producing its good fruit. Accordingly, finding in Christ a different disposition—one of a simple and pure benevolence, differing from the Creator—Marcion readily argued that in his Christ had been revealed a new and strange divinity; and then with a little leaven he leavened the whole lump of the faith, flavoring it with the acidity of his own heresy.

In the same way also we explain the expressions, "I, who make peace and create evil"; for he calls into existence "corporeal" or "external" evils, while purifying and training those who would not be disciplined by the word and sound doctrine. This, then, is our answer to the question, "How is it that God created evil?"

Who, similarly wishing still more to come into our knowledge, and, by way of stirring up our minds to His worship, said, "I am the Lord, who made the light and created the darkness;" that we might deem not that some Nature,—what I know not,—was the artificer of those vicissitudes whereby nights and days are controlled, but might rather, as is more true, recognise God as their Creator.

He calls this evil therefore which chastens them, which makes them purer, which renders them more zealous, which leads them on to love of wisdom; not that which comes under suspicion and is worthy of reproach; for that is not a work of God, but an invention of our own will. He calls then by the name of evil the affliction, which arises from our punishment; thus naming it not in regard to its own nature, but according to that view which men take of it. For since we are accustomed to call by the name of evil, not only thefts and adulteries, but also calamities; so he has called the matter, according to the estimate of mankind. This then is that which the prophet saith "There is no evil in the city which the Lord hath not done." This too by means of Isaiah God has made clear saying "I am God who maketh peace and createth evil," again naming calamities evils. This evil also Christ hints at, thus saying to the disciples, "sufficient for the day is the evil thereof," that is to say the affliction, the misery. […]

I, then, who gave you strength, and am the only God, myself make things contrary to one another, light and darkness, that is, day and night; peace and evil, that is, leisure and war; by which he signifies both that he was angry with his people, when it endured the darkness of captivity and the evils of bondage, and again that he had mercy on it, when, sent back to their homeland, they received peace and joy. For as darkness is contrary to light, so war is contrary to peace. Hence let the heresy be confounded which thinks God the founder of evils; since here evil is set not as the contrary of good, but for affliction and war, according to what is written in the Gospel: Sufficient for the day is its own evil (Matt 6:34).

But the evil which the Lord does in the city is not the contrary of virtue, but affliction and torment, of which we read: Sufficient to the day is its own evil, that is, tribulation and distress. And in the prophet we read: I am God, who made light and darkness, who make peace and create evils. For just as darkness is contrary to light and day, so war too is contrary to peace; it is not evil in itself, but seems to be evil to those who endure it. And that we may know that in the holy Scriptures evil is sometimes taken not as the contrary of virtue but as affliction, punishments and distress, let us take one more example, from Jonah: And God saw their works, that they had turned from their most wicked ways, and he repented over the evil which he had spoken of doing to them. The evil there is surely the overthrow of the Ninevites, which God had threatened through the prophet, and not the evil contrary to virtue, which belongs to sin, on account of which he was threatening torments to sinners.

Germanus: We often read in holy Scripture that God has created evil or brought it upon men, as is this passage: "There is none beside Me. I am the Lord, and there is none else: I form the light and create darkness, I make peace, and create evil." And again: "Shall there be evil in a city which the Lord hath not done?"

Theodore: Sometimes holy Scripture is wont by an improper use of terms to use "evils "for "affliction;" not that these are properly and in their nature evils, but because they are imagined to be evils by those on whom they are brought for their good. For when divine judgment is reasoning with men it must speak with the language and feelings of men. For when a doctor for the sake of health with good reason either cuts or cauterizes those who are suffering from the inflammation of ulcers, it is considered an evil by those who have to bear it. Nor are the spur and the whip pleasant to a restive horse. […]

His permission, therefore, is usually spoken of in the Holy Scripture as His energy and work. Nay, even when He says that God creates evil things, and that there is no evil in a city that the Lord hath not done, he does not mean by these words that the Lord is the cause of evil, but the word ‘evil’ is used in two ways, with two meanings. For sometimes it means what is evil by nature, and this is the opposite of virtue and the will of God: and sometimes it means that which is evil and oppressive to our sensation, that is to say, afflictions and calamities. Now these are seemingly evil because they are painful, but in reality are good. For to those who understand they become ambassadors of conversion and salvation. The Scripture says that of these God is the Author.

It is, moreover, to be observed that of these, too, we are the cause: for involuntary evils are the offspring of voluntary ones.
45:7.s: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 4, Chapter 19

45:8.t: Drop down dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one: let the earth be opened, and let it bud forth the Savior, and let righteousness spring up together: I the Lord have created him. LXX: Let the heaven rejoice from above, and let the clouds sprinkle righteousness: let the earth bud forth, and let mercy spring up, and let it bud forth righteousness together: I am the Lord who created you. The interpretation of this passage is twofold. For some think that it clings to what was said above, and that, when King Cyrus sets the captives free, heaven and earth rejoice: μετωνυμικῶς, that is to say, those who dwell in heaven and on earth. Others separate it from what precedes and want it to be the proper beginning of this chapter, and a prophecy of the Lord's coming: that command is given to the clouds, of which it is written above (cf. Isa 5:6): I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it, that is, upon the vineyard of Israel; […]

Or else, according to the LXX, who said: He has risen from his holy clouds, understand the patriarchs, prophets and apostles, whom the Lord commanded not to rain rain upon Israel. These are the clouds of which it is written: And let the clouds sprinkle justice; for these bodily clouds, into which the denser air is gathered, cannot rain justice.

In this nativity of Christ, according to the prophecy of David, “truth sprang out of the earth, and righteousness looked down from heaven.” In this nativity also, Isaiah’s saying is fulfilled, “let the earth produce and bring forth salvation, and let righteousness spring up together.” For the earth of human flesh, which in the first transgressor, was cursed, in this Offspring of the Blessed Virgin only produced a seed that was blessed and free from the fault of its stock. And each one is a partaker of this spiritual origin in regeneration; and to every one when he is re-born, the water of baptism is like the Virgin’s womb; for the same Holy Spirit fills the font, Who filled the Virgin, that the sin, which that sacred conception overthrew, may be taken away by this mystical washing.

45:9.t: But what the Seventy mean, who at the beginning of this chapter translated: What better have I made than the potter's clay? Will he who ploughs plough the earth? I am not able to know: unless perhaps I follow the edition of Theodotion, who put in place of this: Woe to him who contends against his maker, ploughing those who plough the earth: namely, that he wounds the hearts of mortals unto penitence, and, after the manner of furrows, breaks them up and overturns them. But this too is a frivolous interpretation. Further, that God, our Creator and maker, is called a potter, the apostle Paul too says in the Epistle to the Romans: Does the thing formed say to him who formed it: Why have you made me thus? Has not the potter power over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom 9:20)? […]

Woe to him who contradicts his maker: a potsherd of the Samian earth. Does the clay say to its potter, What are you making? and, Your work is without hands? Woe to him who says to a father, What are you begetting? and to a woman, What are you bringing to birth? Thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, his fashioner: Ask me about things to come concerning my sons, and concerning the work of my hands give charge to me. I made the earth, and I created man upon it: my hands stretched out the heavens, and I gave command to all their host. I have raised him up to righteousness, and I will direct all his ways. He will build my city, and he will let my captivity go, not for a price nor for gifts, says the Lord of hosts. LXX: What better have I made than the potter's clay? Will the ploughman plough the earth? Will the clay say to the potter, What are you making? because you do not work and have no hands? Woe to him who says to a father, What are you begetting? and to a mother, What are you bringing to birth? […]

But one who refers the understanding so begun to Christ frames the words of his explanation thus: Woe to those who contradict God and do not think that Christ will come; as if clay and a potsherd from among potsherds should contradict its potter. Woe to him who says to the Almighty Father, Why do you beget a Son? and to the woman, holy Mary, What are you bringing to birth? Of whom the Apostle too writes (Gal 4): That Christ was made of a woman, and made under the law. These things, then, says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, who fashioned the Savior in the virginal womb, saying through Gabriel: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you (Luke 1:35): and the holy thing that will be born in you will be called the Son of God: let the potsherd question me and search out the secrets of things to come. And let it instruct me how I ought to regenerate the adopted sons who are to believe in my Son. […]

45:11.t: How then are there mansions in the Father's house, and these not different ones but the same, which already exist in a sense in which they can admit of no preparation, and yet do not exist, inasmuch as they are still to be prepared? How are we to think of this, but in the same way as the prophet, who also declares of God, that He has [already] made that which is yet to be. For he says not, Who will make what is yet to be, but, "Who has made what is yet to be." Therefore He has both made such things and is yet to make them. For they have not been made at all if He has not made them; nor will they ever be if He make them not Himself. He has made them therefore in the way of fore-ordaining them; He has yet to make them in the way of actual elaboration.

45:12.t: And what is written: I gave command to all the stars, has given some an occasion to hold that the stars are rational and have soul and sense. For, they say, he would not command any but beings who understand: not remembering that it is written in Jonah: The Lord commanded the scorching wind (Jonah 4:8). And again: He commanded the morning worm (ibid., 7). And that in the Gospel the Savior rebuked the winds and the sea (Luke 8), in which it is plain that there is neither sense nor reason.

For I am God, who did not create the earth for emptiness, that it should be deserted and squalid, but that men should dwell in it. I stretched out, or made firm, the heavens, that they might be the dwelling place of the angels. And I distinguished them with the variety of the stars, and commanded each in what order to run, and to complete the different spans of days and months and years. I, then, who made heaven and earth, what great thing is it if I have created one king to keep my commands, and if I direct all his ways? For he will order that my city Jerusalem be built, and that the captives return to Judea. Not for a price, nor for gifts, but because of my will, says the Lord God of hosts.

But if I made the earth to be inhabited by men, and stretched out the heavens above, and adorned them with the variety of the stars, so that worshipers of God might dwell on the earth, what wonder is it if I have sent my Son, a righteous king, into the world, or raised him up from the underworld, all of whose ways are straight? For he committed no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth (1 Pet 2:22). He it is who is to build my city upon the rock, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail (Matt 16); and which, set on a mountain, cannot be hidden (ibid., 5); and to let go free all who were formerly bound with demonic chains, not for a price nor for gifts: for we have been saved freely, the Apostles hearing and doing: Freely you have received, freely give (Matt 10:8).

45:13.t:
[Passage quoted, Isa. xlv. 12-13.]

IN these words God the Creator of the Universe first foretells by the prophet a King and Saviour who will come to build up a holy constitution, and ransom all men who are enslaved by the errors of daemons.
45:13.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 4

45:13.t: Some refer these things to Zerubbabel, who led the captives out of Babylon, and built the city, and constructed the temple, while Haggai and Zechariah prophesied and said: The hands of Zerubbabel have founded this house, and his hands will complete it (Zech 4:9). But we say more rightly and more truly that neither did Cyrus build the city, which was constructed afterwards under Nehemiah, nor were all his ways made straight, he to whom it was said above: I took you and girded you, and you did not know me; and that all that is said exceeds the station of Zerubbabel, who was under the nod and power of the Medes and Persians. For Zerubbabel neither constructed the city, nor let the captivity go, nor can he be called king who, living under other kings, lacked this name.

45:14.t:
[Passage quoted, Isa. xlv. 12-13.]

IN these words God the Creator of the Universe first foretells by the prophet a King and Saviour who will come to build up a holy constitution, and ransom all men who are enslaved by the errors of daemons. And next in order the prophetic Spirit darkly tells of the subjection of the different nations, which shall be subject to the One of Whom he prophesies, and how they will worship Him as God, how they will pray in His name, because of the greater God dwelling in Him, that is to say the Most High Father and God of the Universe. And this is how it is expressed.

"14. Thus saith the Lord: Egypt hath laboured for thee, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians, and the Sabeans, great in stature, shall pass over to thee, and shall be thy servants; and they shall follow thee bound in fetters, and shall worship thee anew, and shall pray in thy name, because God is in thee, and there is no God but thee. 15. For thou art God, and we knew it not, God of Israel, Saviour. 16. […]
45:14.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 4

45:14.t: BY WHAT REASONING CAN THE WICKEDNESS OF ARIUS BE SIMPLY REFUTED FROM THE LAW? — If we grant authority to reason, the very meaning of the names “Father” and “Son” shows their unity. You ask, how? For the true Son of God would not be so called unless He had come forth from the substance of God the Father. Truth and justice in God would not permit Him to call someone “Son” truly if that Son were not from Himself. He is not truly the Son of God if He is not from Him. But Scripture says He is true; therefore He is from Him. Whoever denies that Christ was born of God does an injustice to Scripture, which calls Him the true Son of God precisely in order to signify that He was born of God. For if He is not from God, and yet is called the true Son of God, then Scripture is deceitful. But if Scripture does not deceive, then whoever does not confess that Christ came forth from God both nullifies Scripture and denies Christ to be the true Son of God. It is not will that makes a true Son, but birth. […]
45:14.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 97: REFUTING THE WICKEDNESS OF ARIUS FROM THE LAW

45:14.t: Would you receive yet a third testimony to Christ's godhead? Hear Isaiah saying, "Egypt has labored, and the merchandise of Ethiopia," and soon after, "In you shall they make supplication, because God is in you, and there is no God except you. For you are God, and we knew it not, the God of Israel, the Savior." You see that the Son is God, having in himself God the Father, saying almost the very same which he has said in the Gospels. … And again he has not said, "I and the Father am one" but "I and the Father are one," that we should neither separate them nor make a confusion of Son-Father.

That Egypt, and the Ethiopians, and the Sabaim, lofty and exalted men, served him, no one doubts, since one sees the world subjected to him, and perceives that, under the name of a few nations which dwell at the furthest ends of the earth, all the hinges of the heavens and all the shores of the earth are to believe in him. Hence it is beautifully said, as to men laboring in the error of idolatry, that the labor of Egypt ceases. For no nation was so given over to idolatry, and venerated such innumerable monstrosities, as Egypt, of which we read above (Isa 19:1): Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud, and will enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt will melt in its midst.

Thus says the Lord: The labor of Egypt, and the merchandise of Ethiopia, and the Sabaim, men of stature, will pass over to you, and will be yours: they will walk behind you, they will go bound in manacles: and they will worship you, and make supplication to you: only in you is God, and there is no God apart from you. Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Savior. They are confounded and have blushed, all of them: together the makers of errors have gone off into confusion. Israel is saved in the Lord with an eternal salvation: you will not be confounded, and you will not blush, for ever and ever. LXX: Thus says the Lord Sabaoth: Egypt has labored, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians and of the Sabaim: lofty men will pass over to you, and they will be your servants, and they will follow you bound in manacles, and they will pass over to you, and will worship you, and will pray in you: because God is in you, and there is no God apart from you. […]

The Hebrews strive with foolish contention to assert that, up to the place where we read: Only in you is God, and there is no God apart from you, it is said either to Jerusalem or to Cyrus; but that what follows: Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Savior, is suddenly an apostrophe made to the almighty God; though it is plain even to fools that the texture of the discourse is one, and that a sense which is joined together in the very order and reasoning of the narration cannot be divided.

45:16.t: Further, what is added in the Seventy: Be renewed unto me, islands, we can expound thus: we may say that the Churches gathered from the nations are renewed in Christ, and are called islands because they endure the rage and the storms of persecutors, and, founded upon the rock, are shaken by no mass of whirlwinds.

They are confounded and have blushed, all together, namely the Scribes and Pharisees. And the makers of error have gone off into confusion, who spread a lie through the whole world, saying that he had been stolen away by the Apostles (Matt 28). But Israel, saved in the Lord with an eternal salvation, is understood as the choir of the Apostles, and those who believed through the Apostles. Hence it is said to them: You will not be confounded nor will you blush, not only in the present age but also in the one to come.

45:18.t: For thus says the Lord, who creates the heavens, God himself who forms the earth and makes it, he himself its fashioner: he did not create it in vain; that it might be inhabited he formed it: I am the Lord, and there is no other. I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth. I did not say to the seed of Jacob: Seek me in vain. I am the Lord who speaks righteousness, who declares right things. Gather together, and come, and draw near together, you who have been saved from among the nations: they have not known, who lift up the wood of their graven image, and pray to a god that does not save.
