Declare, and come, and take counsel together: who has caused this to be heard from the beginning, has foretold it from that time? Is it not I the Lord, and there is no God besides me? A righteous God and one who saves, there is none besides me. Be converted to me, and you will be saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is no other. […]

For the very Prophet through whom the retrogression of the sun was effected, when, by means of the dread sign, he had in reality confuted the theory of the Babylonians, by showing that the heaven is not a revolving sphere, and that they held an opinion that is erroneous, this very Prophet not long afterwards speaks thus of the figure of the heaven: He that established the heaven as a vaulted chamber; and again: The Lord God who made the heaven and fixed it, thus declaring at once that it is a vault, and that it is established and fixed and not in revolution

45:19.t: For on Mount Sinai too, from its lofty summit, he spoke these things in the hearing of the peoples: You shall have no strange gods besides me, nor shall you make yourself an idol (Exod 20:3, 4). But it is better that we believe this was said of the preaching of the Gospel: for Moses spoke in a hidden wilderness to one people only. But the sound of the Apostles went out into the whole world, and their words reached to the ends of the earth (Ps 18 [19]). I did not say, he says, to the seed of Jacob, Seek me in vain. For I promised them the kingdoms of heaven, and I spoke to them first: I came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 15:24). And therefore I spoke righteousness and declared right things, or truth, so that, leaving behind the images and ceremonies of the Law, they might follow the truth of the Gospel.

45:20.t: But because they would not believe, and judged themselves unworthy of salvation, therefore I say to the nations: Gather together from the whole world; and come and draw near to me together, you who have been saved from among the nations. By this he shows that not all the nations will believe at once, but gradually and in parts. Finally he rebukes those who remained in their former error, saying: They have not known, who lift up the wood of their graven image, and pray to a god that does not save. And the sense is: They did not understand my words, weighed down by the burden of their idols, and hoping in those in whom there is no salvation.

45:21.t: AGAINST THE PAGANS. — By what reasoning the pagans dare to confront us or attack our faith, while thinking themselves innocent, I do not see. For they have no evidence for their assertions, of their superstition, I would rather say, than of religion. Whatever they have without safeguards they put forward, so that they may themselves be regarded as authors and defenders of novelties. First of all, they claim to worship gods, yet those gods give no marks, no testimonies. They call those beings gods who did not dare to be called by that name, so that men are made the authors of gods, though God ought to be the author of men; and therefore their assertion is vain and empty. Whatever is without God cannot be stable. […]
45:21.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 114: AGAINST THE PAGANS

45:21.t: Hence the Apostles are commanded to proclaim the truth in season and out of season (2 Tim 4), and to enter on counsel for the salvation of the nations. And this, that is, that very many from the nations should be gathered and come and be saved, God spoke from the beginning, and the mouths of all the Prophets sang it, who spoke by the word of the Lord, besides whom there is no other. For the Son is God not apart from him, but in him.

45:22.t: And beautifully he joins: A righteous God, not of one nation at all, but of the whole world, to which he says: Be converted to me, and you will be saved, all the ends of the earth; fulfilling what the Father promised the Son: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession (Ps 2:8).

45:23.t: And he swears by himself that the sentence of his mouth, and the word he has once uttered concerning the salvation of the nations, will by no means be made void; but that the promise of him who said above: Be converted to me, and you will be saved, all the ends of the earth, will be fulfilled in deed. And he swears, according to the Apostle (Heb 6), so that through two immovable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have firm consolation; but he also swears this: that, idols abandoned, every knee should bow to him, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue of mortals should swear by him (Phil 2). In this the Christian people is plainly signified. For it is the custom of the Church to bend the knee to Christ: which the Jews, displaying the pride of their mind, do not do at all. And every tongue too of all the barbarian nations confesses God, not in synagogues but in the Churches of Christ.

45:24.t: And every tongue that confesses Christ will speak in the Lord, and will say: Mine are righteousnesses, and mine is the dominion, not the Jewish people's. To him all the nations will come, and those who formerly resisted his Gospel will be confounded; and all the seed of Israel will be justified and praised, whose preaching and most fertile sowing has borne the richest fruits throughout the whole world. Or, according to the Seventy, every tongue that swears by and confesses God will say that the righteousness and glory of the whole world comes to him, and that the Jews, who separate themselves from him, are confounded. But those who have sprung from the stock of the sons of Israel, and who have sprouted from the seed of the Apostles, and have believed in Christ, may they have righteousness and everlasting glory.

46:1.t: Bel is broken, Nebo is crushed: their idols are made over to beasts and cattle, your burdens with heavy weight even to weariness. They have wasted away and are crushed together: they could not save the one who carried them, and their soul shall go into captivity. LXX: Bel has fallen, Dagon is crushed: their graven images are made into beasts and cattle; you carry them bound together like a burden for one who labors, and faints, and hungers, and has no strength besides, who will not be able to save from war: but they themselves have been led captive. After the calling of the nations, and the election of believers from Israel, he testifies that the idols have collapsed. Bel has fallen, has fallen, or is broken: whom the Greeks call Belus, the Latins Saturn. So great was his worship among the ancients that they sacrificed to him not only human victims, captives and mortals of low birth, but even their own children. […]

These idols, he says, which cannot save those who carry them, are nothing else but burdens for the priests, weighing them down even to weariness. And when captivity comes, they are the first to be led captive, for the value of the metals of which they are made, and they cannot set free their own soul, or that of those who carry them. Not that dumb idols, which are without sensation, have a soul and some sense of pain; but that soul and members are spoken of καταχρηστικῶς in things that are without sense and members. Otherwise, too, we read in Proverbs: In the hand of the tongue are death and life. Or else this must be said: that the heaviest burden among the nations was the error of idolatry, which weighed its worshipers down to the earth, and could not save them, and made their souls captives of the devil and of demons.

46:3.t: Hear me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, who are carried from my womb, who are borne from my matrix. Even to old age I myself, and even to gray hairs I will carry you: I have made, and I will bear: I will carry, and I will save. To whom have you likened me, and made me equal, and compared me, and made me like? You who lavish gold from the purse, and weigh silver on the scales, hiring a goldsmith to make a god: and they fall down and worship. They carry it on their shoulders, bearing it and setting it in its place, and it will stand, and will not move from its place. But when they cry to it, it will not hear: it will not save them from tribulation. LXX: Hear me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of Israel, who are carried from the womb, and are instructed from a little child even to old age. I am, and until you grow old I am: I sustain you: I have made, and I will carry: I will take you up, and I will save you. To whom have you likened me? […]

According to the Seventy, who said: Who are carried from the womb, and are instructed from infancy even to old age, this signifies that they meditate on the law of God day and night in vain, having no knowledge of God, but venerating images of men and beasts: so much so that they need prophetic rebuke, through which God speaks to them: To whom have you likened me, and made me equal? and the rest: that they lavished gold and silver, and, hiring a sculptor, made idols, and worshiped the works of their own hands, which are carried on shoulders, and, fixed and set firm, cannot move themselves, nor profit those by whom they are worshiped. We pass quickly over what is plain, so that by the mercy of Christ we may unlock what is closed.

46:4.t: O Lord our God, under the shadow of your wings let us hope; defend us and support us. You will bear us up when we are little, and even down to our gray hairs you will carry us. For our stability, when it is in you, is stability indeed; but when it is in ourselves, then it is all unstable. Our good lives forever with you, and when we turn from you with aversion, we fall into our own perversion. Let us now, O Lord, return that we be not overturned, because with you our good lives without blemish—for our good is you yourself.

Woe to the audacious soul that hoped that by forsaking you it would find some better thing! It tossed and turned, on back and side and belly, but the bed is hard, and you alone give rest. Yet you are near. You deliver us from our wretched wanderings and establish us in your way. You comfort us and say, "Run, I will carry you. I will lead you home, and I will set you free."

46:8.t: Remember this, and be grounded, and return, transgressors, to heart. Recall the former age, for I am God, and there is no God beyond, nor is there any like me. Declaring from the start the last things, and from the beginning things not yet done, saying: My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done. Calling a bird from the East, and from a far land the man of my will; and I have spoken, and I will bring it about; I have created, and I will do it. LXX: Remember these things, and groan: repent, you who err. Return in heart, and remember the former things from of old; for I am God, and there is no other besides me. I who declare beforehand the last things before they happen and are fulfilled, and I have said, all my will shall stand, and all that I have planned I will do. I who call a bird from the East, and from a far land, those concerning whom I have planned: I have spoken, and I have brought it about: I have created and I have done it. […]

Behold, there he is, wherever truth is known. He is within the inmost heart, yet the heart has wandered from him. Return to your heart, O you sinners, and hold fast to him who made you. Stand with him, and you shall stand firmly. Rest in him, and you shall be at rest.

And we, who see in one way, and hear in another way, how know we this? We return perhaps to ourselves, if we are not the trangressors to whom it is said, "Return, O trangressors, to your heart." Return to your heart: why go from yourselves, and perish from yourselves? Why go the ways of solitude? You go astray by wandering: return ye. Whither? To the Lord. 'Tis quickly done: first return to thine own heart; thou hast wandered abroad an exile from thyself; thou knowest not thyself, and yet thou art asking by whom thou wast made! Return, return to thy heart, lift thyself away from the body: thy body is thy place of abode; thy heart perceives even by thy body. But thy body is not what thy heart is; leave even thy body, return to thy heart. In thy body thou didst find eyes in one place, ears in another place: dost thou find this in thy heart? Or hast thou not ears in thy heart? Else of what did the Lord say, "Whoso hath ears to hear, let him hear?" Or hast thou not eyes in thy heart? Else of what saith the apostle. […]

46:9.t: Consider from the beginning of the world that there is no God besides me, and that no other could know things to come, except me, who announce through the Prophets what I am going to do: so that, when I have fulfilled what was foretold, I may prove my divinity by divination. For I now say that the mystery which in times past was unknown to all generations, or rather my counsel, will stand; so that, when you see it brought to pass, you may know no God but him who knew that these things would be, nay, commanded them to be done.

46:11.t: I am he who calls a bird from the East: as the Hebrews think, Cyrus king of the Persians, or Darius prince of the Medes; and from a far land the man of my will, to fulfill all my will against Babylon and the Chaldeans. Or, as we prove to be true, the Lord Savior, of whom Balaam too prophesies: A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man out of Israel (Num 24:17), whose name is the East (Zech 6), whom the Magi coming from the East worshiped. For he it is who speaks in the Psalms: O God, I have willed to do your will (Ps 39 [40]:9), of whom the Father spoke: and he proved his pledge by deed. In place of what we have rendered from the Hebrew, the man of my will, the Seventy put, those concerning whom I have planned. According to them, then, by the birds called from the East we can understand the ministries of the angels, which run to and fro through the whole world at the Lord's command; who are ministering spirits, and are sent for the salvation of believers. […]

46:12.t: The inner man possesses a heart. "Listen to Me, you who have lost heart!" Those to whom the prophet is speaking have a heart by the flesh: it cannot be lost. But when a man is careless about the cultivation of his intellectual being, then, on account of much idleness, the faculty of thought evaporates from him, he loses his heart, and it is precisely of such people that it is said: "Listen to Me, you who have lost heart!"

Hear me, you hard of heart, who are far from righteousness. I have brought my righteousness near: it shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not delay: I will give salvation in Zion, and in Israel my glory. LXX: Hear me, you who have lost heart, who are far from righteousness. I have brought near my righteousness, and the salvation that is from me I will not make to tarry. I have given salvation in Zion, and to Israel glory. Those to whom he had said above: Hear me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, and again: Return, transgressors, to heart, even now he calls, according to the Hebrew, hard of heart because of their unbelief, and, according to the Seventy, men who have lost heart and mind. Following this, the most learned man Stephen the martyr, worthy of his name, says in the assembly of the Jews: Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did (Acts 7:51). […]

47:1.t: Go down, sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon: sit on the ground, there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans, for no more shall you be called soft and tender. Take the millstone, and grind meal: lay bare your shame, uncover your shoulder, reveal your legs, pass over the rivers. Your disgrace shall be revealed, and your reproach shall be seen: I will take vengeance, and no man shall withstand me. LXX: Go down, sit upon the ground, virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground. There is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans, for no more at all shall you be called soft and tender. Take the millstone, grind meal. Reveal your covering, lay bare your gray hairs, uncover your shins, pass over the rivers: your disgrace shall be revealed, your reproaches shall appear. What is just I will take from you, no more at all will I hand you over to men. […]

47:2.t: As Fabiola was not ashamed of the Lord on earth, so he shall not be ashamed of her in heaven. She laid bare her wound to the gaze of all, and Rome beheld with tears the disfiguring scar that marred her beauty. She uncovered her limbs, bared her head and closed her mouth. She no longer entered the church of God but, like Miriam the sister of Moses, she sat apart, outside the camp, till the priest who cast her out should himself call her back. She came down like a daughter of Babylon from the throne of her daintiness, she took the millstones and ground meal, she passed barefoot through rivers of tears.

But because there follows: Lay bare your shame, the millstone too is understood figuratively by the Hebrews, namely that, after the manner of a harlot, she lies open to the lust of the victors. And what is written in the book of Judges about Samson (Judg 16), that he was condemned by the Philistines to the mill, they wish to signify this: that, being the strongest of men, he was compelled, for the sake of offspring, to do this with foreign women. In the place where we have translated, lay bare your shame, for which the Seventy translated, reveal your covering, Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, SAMTHECH (צמתך); Aquila SEMMATHECH; Symmachus τὸ σιωπηλόν σου: which we can express as your silent part, because it ought to be kept silent for modesty. This indeed we also read in the Song of Songs, where the beauty of the bride is described: at the end he adds: Apart from your silent part (Song 4): the translators being unwilling to render a word which in holy Scripture would sound shameful. […]

47:4.t: Our Redeemer, the Lord of hosts is his name, the Holy One of Israel. Sit silent, and go into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans; for no more shall you be called mistress of kingdoms. I was angry with my people, I defiled my inheritance, and I gave them into your hand: you showed them no mercies. Upon the old man you made your yoke exceedingly heavy, and you said, For ever I shall be mistress: you did not lay these things to heart, nor did you remember your latter end. LXX: He who delivered you has said, the Lord Sabaoth, his name is the Holy One of Israel. Sit pierced with grief, enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans: no more at all shall you be called the strength of the kingdom: I was angry against my people, I defiled my inheritance. I gave them into your hand, but you gave them no mercy: on the old man you made the yoke exceedingly heavy, and you said, For ever I shall be mistress: you did not understand these things in your heart, nor did you remember the last things. […]

47:5.t: And again the discourse is directed to Babylon itself. Sit silent, or pierced with grief, and remember your crimes. Enter into darkness: because for confusion and disgrace you cannot bear the light: no more at all shall you be called mistress, not of one kingdom, nor even of all kingdoms.

47:6.t: And at the same time, because a hidden question arose, why God should be angry against the Chaldeans whom he himself had sent to take Israel, he answered that, being angry against his people, he had wished to chastise them, not to destroy them; to scourge them, not to kill them. But they had given free rein to their own cruelty, and had laid on more stripes than God's vengeance demanded: and it is a great sign of Babylonian cruelty that they did not spare even old men, whose age is venerable even among enemies. And this too is a sign of pride, that, deceived by present prosperity, she did not consider the uncertainties of the future. We ought therefore always, in prosperity, to beware of what is to come, and not to oppress those handed over to us, who are being instructed for this purpose, that they may become better.

47:8.t: And now hear these things, you delicate one, who dwell confidently, who say in your heart: I am, and there is none besides me any more: I shall not sit as a widow, and I shall not know barrenness. And these two things shall come upon you suddenly in one day, barrenness and widowhood: all things have come upon you, because of the multitude of your sorceries, and because of the hardness of your enchanters, exceedingly. And you trusted in your wickedness, and you said: There is none who sees me: your wisdom and your knowledge, these have deceived you, and you said in your heart: I am, and besides me there is no other. Evil shall come upon you, and you shall not know its rising, and calamity shall rush upon you which you shall not be able to expiate, misery shall come upon you suddenly which you shall not know. […]

47:9.t: What you have suffered, he says, is not only because of your pride and the abundance of all wealth and your delights, but also because of the multitude of your sorceries, and of your enchanters, in whom you trusted. And evil shall come upon you which you did not know before, and whose rising you did not know. Or, as the Seventy translated: Destruction shall come upon you, and you shall not know it: a pit, and you shall fall into it: so that you who were preparing the evil of captivity for all the nations may yourself fall into the pit that you prepared. What is plain we pass over in brief speech.

47:12.t: Stand with your enchanters, and with the multitude of your sorceries, in which you have labored from your youth, if perhaps anything may profit you, or if you can become stronger. You have failed in the multitude of your counsels: let the augurs of the heaven stand and save you, who gazed at the stars and reckoned the months, that from them they might announce to you things to come. Behold, they have become as stubble, fire has burned them: they shall not deliver their souls from the hand of the flame: there are no coals to warm them, nor a hearth to sit by: so have they become to you, all those things in which you had labored: your traders from your youth have gone astray, each in his own way: there is none to save you. LXX: Stand now in your enchantments and in your many sorceries, which you learned from your youth, if they can profit you: and you have labored in your counsels: let the astrologers of the heaven, who gaze at the stars, stand and save you: let them announce to you what is to come upon you. […]

47:13.t: So also His Father makes great account of prophecy, when He sets Himself against the honor paid to idols: "Let them declare to you," saith He, "what shall come upon you"; and again, "I have declared, and have saved, and there was no foreign God amongst you"; and He brings this forward through all prophecy. Because prophecy is especially the work of God, which devils cannot even imitate, though they strive exceedingly. For in the case of miracles there may be delusion; but exactly to foretell the future belongs to that pure Nature alone. Or if devils ever have done so, it was by deceiving the simpler sort; whence their oracles are always easily detected.
47:13.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 19

47:13.t: Let these, then, who reckon the months and count up the years, and, weighing the moments of the hours, promise knowledge of the future, tell you what the Lord has planned against you; and, since they are silent about what is to come, the Prophet answered: Behold, they have become as stubble, fire has devoured them; so that those who promised salvation to others did not know their own punishments: and there is no doubt that, when the city was burning, the devouring flame consumed its inhabitants. And what follows: There are no coals to warm them, nor a hearth to sit by, the Hebrews explain thus: They have no knowledge of warmth, nor an enlightening sense that could dispel their darkness and drive out the cold of error. For which the Seventy, meaning I know not what, translated: You have coals of fire, you shall sit upon them: these shall be a help to you; unless perhaps we can say this, that fire and burning are much more useful to Babylon than the magi and Gazarenes, the astrologers and enchanters, were. […]

47:14.t: Let us ask those who assert that there are different natures whether Babylon is of an evil nature or a good one. If they say of an evil one, which there is no doubt they will answer, how is she called to repentance, and told: Sit pierced with grief, enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans? And then, after the enumeration of her sins and crimes: You have coals of fire, you shall sit upon them: these shall be a help to you? And what is meant by what is added according to the same Seventy: You have labored in exchange from your youth? What is this exchange? Surely from good to evil. From which it is plain that men are good by nature, and become evil by will. Finally it is added: Man has gone astray in himself, not by nature, but by the choice of the mind.

47:15.t: All her labor and her traders, whom we understand as the magi, achieved this: that each went astray in his own way; and, himself lost, could not offer salvation to another.

48:1.t: Hear these things, house of Jacob, you who are called by the name of Israel, and have come forth from the waters of Judah: who swore in the name of the Lord, and make mention of the God of Israel, not in truth nor in righteousness. For they are called after the holy city: and upon the Lord of Israel they are established: the Lord of hosts is his name. These things I foretold would come upon the Chaldeans and Babylonians, and what I have spoken through my Prophets must be fulfilled in deed. But you, house of Jacob, and you who are called by the name of Israel, and who have come forth from the water of Judah, and the rest that follows, hear more attentively what I am about to say. And it is to be noted that he by no means calls them Jacob, but the house of Jacob; nor Israel, since they are falsely called by this name, not having the work of the name. […]

48:3.t: The former things I declared from of old, and they went forth from my mouth, and I made them heard: suddenly I worked, and they came to pass. For I knew that you are hard, and your neck is a sinew of iron, and your brow is bronze. I foretold it to you from of old: before they came, I made it known to you, lest perhaps you should say: My idols have done these things, and my graven images and my molten images have commanded them. What you have heard, see it all: but you have not declared it. I have made you hear new things from that time: and things kept in store which you do not know: they are created now, and not from of old: and before the day, and you did not hear them, lest perhaps you should say: Behold, I knew them. You have neither heard, nor known, nor from of old was your ear opened: for I know that you will deal very treacherously, and I have called you a transgressor from the womb. For my name's sake I will put my fury far off: and with my praise I will bridle you, lest you perish. […]

Most of our writers, to touch briefly on a few things according to the Seventy Translators, hold that the coming of Christ is prophesied: that he comes suddenly, unhoped for, and shows his presence to a most hard people, whose ears God never opened, because its heart had grown fat, and it heard heavily with its ears. And that, as soon as the Lord was poured forth from the virginal womb, it was called transgressor and wicked, seeking to kill him. And as for what he joins: For my name's sake I will show you my fury, and my glorious things I will bring upon you, he draws on the sense of the Apostle, or rather the apostle Paul (Rom 1) takes his testimony from this passage, that the wrath of God is revealed to terrify those who sin, and afterwards glory is offered to those who have turned: Behold, he says, I have sold you, not for money, but I have sold you in your sins, and I have rescued you from the furnace of poverty. […]

48:6.t: Behold, you have heard all the things that are to come, and yet you hide the truth in silence. Nor do I recount the past things by which my power has often been proved: how I led the people out of Egypt, drowned the Egyptians in the Red Sea, handed over the land of promise, subjugated various nations to you. But I announce the new things that I am going to do against Babylon, so that the shameless lie of your mouth may be refuted, you who claim to know what you do not know.

48:8.t: For from the beginning you have been a transgressor of my commandments; and God called you a transgressor from the womb, when, set free from Egypt, you were, as it were, conceived in my womb, and brought up, and instructed. You longed for the ox's head of Egypt, saying: These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.

48:9.t: Not for your merit, then, but by my mercy I have put off my fury, lest you should perish utterly, and for the praise of my name I will bridle you, so that, like a beast of burden and a horse in bridles, you may follow me against your will.

But in one matter vainglory is found to be a useful thing for beginners. I mean by those who are still troubled by carnal sins, as for instance, if, when they are troubled by the spirit of fornication, they formed an idea of the dignity of the priesthood, or of reputation among all men, by which they maybe thought saints and immaculate: and so with these considerations they repell the unclean suggestions of lust, as deeming them base and at least unworthy of their rank and reputation; and so by means of a smaller evil they overcome a greater one. For it is better for a man to be troubled by the sin of vainglory than for him to fall into the desire for fornication, from which he either cannot recover at all or only with great difficulty after he has fallen. […]

48:10.t: Behold, I have refined you, that is, I have tested you, as silver is smelted. Or, I wished to test you not in riches but in the furnace of poverty. From this it is shown that most men are tempted both by riches and by poverty, if they either badly abuse the former or by no means bear want with virtue.

48:11.t: For my own sake, then, I will do it, lest my name be blasphemed among the nations, and they think that you were overcome not by my anger but by the help of their idols. And what he adds, my glory I will not give to another, signifies this: lest the idols be thought to have crushed the people of God. Or certainly, when he says, I will not give to another, he shows that he has already given it to another; for 'to another' is said to distinguish it from the former.

48:12.t:
[Passage quoted, Isa. xlviii. 12-15.]

SEE now how He that says, "I am the first, and I am the last. He that established the earth and the heaven," clearly confesses that He was sent by "the Lord, the Lord," calling the Father Lord twice, and you will have undeniable evidence of what we seek. And He says that He is first among beings begotten in all reverence, since He allots Being, original, unbegotten, and beyond the first, to the Father. For the customary meaning of first in the sense of "first of a greater number," superior in honour and order, would not be applicable to the Father. For the Almighty God of course is not the first of created things, since the idea of Him does not admit of a beginning. He must be beyond and above the first, as Himself generating and establishing the First, and the Divine Word alone is to be called the First of all begotten things. […]
48:12.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 6

48:12.t: Hear me, Jacob, and Israel, whom I call. I myself, I am the first, and I am the last. My hand also founded the earth, and my right hand measured the heavens: I called them, and they will stand together. Gather together, all of you, and hear: who among them has declared these things? The Lord has loved him: he will do his will in Babylon, and his arm upon the Chaldeans. I, I have spoken and called him: I have brought him, and his way is made straight. Draw near to me, and hear these things: not from the beginning have I spoken in secret: from the time before it came to be, there I was. And now the Lord God has sent me, and his spirit. LXX: Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call. I am the first, and I am for ever: and my hand founded the earth, and my right hand made firm the heaven. I will call them, and they will stand together: and all will be gathered, and will hear: Who has announced these things to them? Loving you, I have done your will upon Babylon: to take away the seed of the Chaldeans. […]

48:13.t: My hand founded the earth. Hence in Proverbs too he says: God by his wisdom founded the earth, and his right hand measured (Prov 3:19), or made firm the heavens, or the heaven, as the Seventy translated. And he calls the heavens, that they may obey his command and tell forth his glory. But if the heavens obey the will of the Lord and run in their order, why does earth and ashes glory (Sir 10), and not know its own frailty?

48:14.t: Gather together, all of you, and hear: either heavens, or the whole creation, or the whole multitude of Israel. What are the things they are bidden to hear? That the Lord has loved him: there is no doubt that he means Cyrus and Darius, who did the will of the Lord against Babylon, and exercised his arm upon the Chaldeans. And he himself spoke and called him by his name, and brought him, and his way was made straight, so that none dared to resist his might.

But according to Symmachus, who translated: Who has announced these things to him? whom the Lord has loved, who does his will in Babylon: and according to the Seventy, to take away the seed of the Chaldeans, it is referred to the person of the Lord: who is truly beloved by the Father, and who did all the will of the Father, and who overthrew in Babylon, that is, in the confusion of this world, all the seed of the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as demons. He himself spoke, and heard the Son, and brought him, who says to believers: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened (Matt 11:28).

48:16.t:
[Passage quoted, Isa. xlviii. 12 and 16.]

You have here the Lord sent and the Lord sending, that is to say the Father and God of the Universe, entitled Lord twice as was usual.
48:16.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 22

48:16.t: Hence he summons them to draw near and hear, and, as the Lord foretells it, to know that the king of the Persians and Medes will come, to overthrow Babylon and destroy the Chaldeans. And to announce these things, the Prophet says that he has been sent by the Lord and by his spirit. This is according to the Hebrews and their opinion.

And hear these things which from the beginning I have spoken in secret, that is, through the riddles and mysteries of the Prophets, which had been unknown to all past generations. When all things were being made by the Father, he himself was with him, who rejoiced with him, who even now says: I, who was always with the Father, and in the Father, and was never without the Father, even now speak (John 14): and according to the frailty of the flesh I assumed, I say that the Lord God has sent me, and his spirit: and in one short verse the mystery of the Trinity is shown to us.

Now it is Jesus Christ who is speaking here as the "Lord God"; yet this would not have been obvious if he had not added the final words, "And now the Lord God has sent me and his Spirit." These words were spoken by Christ in his "form" as a "servant." He used a verb in the past tense to indicate a future event.

Moreover, He could not be sent by the Father without the Holy Spirit, not only because the Father, when He sent Him, that is, when He made Him of a woman, is certainly understood not to have so made Him without His own Spirit; but also because it is most plainly and expressly said in the Gospel in answer to the Virgin Mary, when she asked of the angel, "How shall this be?" "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee." And Matthew says, "She was found with child of the Holy Ghost." Although, too, in the prophet Isaiah, Christ Himself is understood to say of His own future advent, "And now the Lord God and His Spirit hath sent me."

48:17.t: Thus says the Lord, your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: I am the Lord your God, who teach you profitable things, who guide you in the way in which you walk. Would that you had heeded my commandments; your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the whirlpools of the sea. And your seed would have been like the sand, and the offspring of your womb like its pebbles: they would not have perished, and his name would not have been worn away from before my face. Since he has promised Israel things to come, he gives the reasons why he afflicted them before: if they avoid these, they will by no means suffer the like. If, he says, you had heeded my commandments, as the Seventy translated: or certainly, with the feeling of one who wishes, would that you had heeded my commandments: if you had done them, your peace would have been like rivers, and your righteousness like the whirlpools of the sea: signifying abundance and plenty of all things.

The authority of the one commanding ought to move us to observe the commandments of God. He is of great authority, because by His wondrous wisdom He governs us. Whence Isaiah says: "I am the Lord, teaching you profitable things, governing you in the way in which you walk. Would that you had heeded my commandments! Your peace would have been as a river."

48:18.t: Set before yourself any river. It springs from its fountain but is of one nature, of one brightness and beauty. And you assert rightly that the Holy Spirit is of one substance, brightness and glory with the Son of God and with God the Father. I will sum up everything in the oneness of the qualities without any dispute over degrees of greatness. For in this point also Scripture has provided for us. For the Son of God says, "Whoever shall drink of the water that I will give him, it shall become in him a well of water springing up unto everlasting life." This well is clearly the grace of the Spirit, a stream proceeding from the living Fountain. The Holy Spirit, then, is also the fountain of eternal life.You observe, then, from his words that the unity of the divine greatness is pointed out and that Christ cannot be denied to be a fountain even by heretics, since the Spirit, too, is called a fountain. […]

This water is good, then. I mean here the grace of the Spirit. Who will give this Fountain to my heart? Let it spring up in me, let that which gives eternal life flow on me. Let that Fountain overflow on us and not flow away. For Wisdom says, "Drink water out of your own vessels and from the fountains of your own wells, and let your waters flow abroad in your streets." How shall I keep this water so that it does not seep out or glide away? How shall I preserve my vessel, lest any crack of sin penetrating it should let the water of eternal life exude? Teach us, Lord Jesus, teach us as you taught your apostles, saying, "Lay not up for yourselves treasures on the earth, where rust and moth destroy and where thieves break through and steal."8Our rust is wantonness, our rust is lust, our rust is luxury, which dim the keen vision of the mind with the filth of vices. […]

48:19.t: And as for what follows: and your seed would have been like the sand, and the offspring of your womb like its pebbles: it seems indeed to hold good in the people of the Jews, who to this present day sprout sons and grandsons like little worms; but how is this to be taken as a promise, when they have neither peace nor righteousness? For either he is angry with them, or appeased. If angry, how is his seed multiplied daily? If appeased, how are they in servitude, and do not possess peace and righteousness? From this it is plain that he now speaks of the Apostolic seed, of which we also read above (cf. Isa 1): Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us a seed, we should have been like Sodom. Since this is by no means seen fulfilled at that time, it is fulfilled in the coming of Christ: and the seed of Israel remains before his face.

48:20.t: Go forth from Babylon, flee from the Chaldeans: declare it with a voice of exultation, make this heard, carry it to the end of the earth, and say: The Lord has redeemed his servant Jacob. They did not thirst in the desert when he led them out; he brought forth water from the rock for them, and he split the rock, and the waters flowed. There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord. Those who understood the place above, where it is written: I, I have spoken, and called him: I have brought him, and his way is made straight, of Cyrus and Darius, refer these things too to his times, when the people went forth from Babylon, and fled from the Chaldeans, and was redeemed by the Lord its God.

But those who, more truly and more rightly, refer these things to the Savior's coming (cf. below, Isa 61:1), of which it is said: He has sent me to announce good news to the poor, to preach release to the captives (Luke 4:18, 19), understand it to be an exhortation of those who announce the Gospel of the Lord Savior himself, that we should go forth from Babylon, that is, from the confusion of this world, and flee the Chaldeans, of whom it has often been spoken. For the Lord redeemed his servant Jacob with his most precious blood, and led him through the desert of the world, and split water from the rock. Concerning which the Apostle too says: And the rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4). And the divine word is split, and divided into many parts, so that what we cannot receive whole we may take in parts. […]

"Come forth out of Babylon." If we take the command of the prophet in a spiritual sense, it means that we should fly from the city of this world, from the fellowship of wicked angels and wicked [people], with the feet of that faith that works through love, and we should press onward unceasingly toward the living God.

48:21.t: This also that is said: They did not thirst in the desert when he led them out, he brought forth water from the rock for them; and he split the rock, and the waters flowed, although they cannot show it fulfilled according to the history (for under Zerubbabel and Ezra they did not come through a desert, nor did a split rock furnish them waters, as is related to have happened to those going out of Egypt), they nevertheless maintain was fulfilled hyperbolically, in the likeness of the former happiness, when they came into Judea through the desert of the nations, and were set free from captivity.

48:22.t: And so that we may know, they say, that it was prophesied not of Christ but of Cyrus, there is joined: There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord: and the sense is: Perfect happiness will not be except under Christ, which is reserved for the last time.

49:1.t: Consider how he who was not yet born could have a people, unless he were in being before he was born. The prophet says this in his person, "From my mother's womb he gave me my name"; because the angel foretold that he would be called Jesus. Again, concerning the plots of Herod, he says, "He … concealed me in the shadow of his arm."

Hear, islands, and give heed, peoples from afar: the Lord called me from the womb, from the belly of my mother he remembered my name. And he made my mouth like a sharp sword: in the shadow of his hand he protected me. And he made me like a chosen arrow: in his quiver he hid me; and he said to me: You are my servant, Israel, for in you I will glory. And I said: I have labored in vain, without cause and vainly I have spent my strength: therefore my judgment is with the Lord, and my work with my God. LXX: Hear me, islands, and give heed, nations. After a long time it shall stand, says the Lord. From the belly he called me, and from the womb of my mother he called my name. And he made my mouth like a sharp sword, and under the protection of his hand he hid me. He made me like a chosen arrow, and in his quiver he hid me. And he said to me: You are my servant, Israel: and in you I will be glorified. And I said, I have labored without cause, in vain, and I have given my strength for nothing. […]

49:2.t: Therefore, if anyone can with a capacious mind conceive and consider the beauty and comeliness of all these things which were created in Him, being struck by the very loveliness of things and pierced by the magnificence of their splendor as by a chosen arrow, as the prophet says, he will receive from Him a saving wound, and will burn with the blessed fire of His love.
49:2.s: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, PROLOGUE

49:2.t: He also made his mouth like a sharp sword, so that with the spirit of his mouth he may slay the wicked one. Of which sword he himself also speaks in the Gospel: I came not to send peace upon the earth, but a sword, separating the evil from the good: For I came to divide a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law (Matt 10:34, 35). And in the shadow, he says, of his hand he protected me, so that the lowliness of the flesh might be covered by the power of the divinity, as the angel announced to the Virgin: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you (Luke 1:35). He made me, he says, like a chosen arrow, in his quiver he hid me. When he says, a chosen arrow, he shows that God has very many arrows, but not chosen ones: which arrows are the Prophets and the Apostles, who run through the whole world. Of whom it is sung in another place too: Your arrows are sharp, O most mighty; […]

According to tropology this place can be explained thus: Judah is stretched as a bow when the Lord and Savior is sent by the Father into this world, he who is himself both the bow and the archer and the arrow. The bow, as in the present place. The archer, as in Psalm 44 (45): Your arrows are sharp, most mighty; and when someone has been wounded by them, he says: I am wounded with love. And the arrow is he himself who speaks through Isaiah: He has set me as a chosen arrow, and in his quiver he has hidden me. The chosen arrow is the Word of God; the quiver in which the arrow is hidden is the dispensation of the flesh he assumed.

49:3.t: And he said to me: You are my servant, Israel: for in you I will be glorified (Song 4:9). A servant, because, though he was in the form of God, he deigned to take the form of a servant (Phil 2), and Israel, because he was born of the seed of the Jews. And, what can be understood of no other of the servants, there is joined: For in you I will glory. For he himself also says in the Gospel, Father, glorify your name (John 12:28). He it is who in the psalm says to the Son: Arise, my glory, and arise, psaltery and harp (Ps 56 [57]:9), that is, the choir of all the virtues.

49:4.t: And when the Father said to me these things that I have related, I answered him: How are you glorified in me, Father, since I have labored in vain, and could not call back to you a great part of the Jewish people? And all these things are said to show the free will of man. For it is God's to call, and ours to believe: nor, if we do not believe, is God at once powerless; but he leaves his power to our choice, so that the will of the righteous may obtain its reward. Since, then, they would not believe in you through me, my judgment is with you, that I have done all things that I ought to have done for them, saying in the Gospel: I have glorified you on the earth, having completed the work which you gave me to do (John 17:4); and again: I have manifested your name to men. And my work, or my labor and pain (for this is what πόνος signifies), is in your sight. […]

49:5.t: And now says the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant, that I might bring Jacob back to him, and Israel will not be gathered: and I am glorified in the eyes of the Lord, and my God has become my strength. And he said: It is a small thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to turn back the dregs of Israel. I have given you as a light of the nations; that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth. LXX: And now thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant, that I might gather Jacob to him, and Israel: I shall be gathered and glorified before the Lord, and my God shall be my strength. And he said to me: It is a great thing for you to be called my child, and to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to turn back the dispersion of Israel. Behold, I have set you for a covenant of the race, for a light of the nations, that you may be salvation to the end of the earth. […]

49:6.t: Next is the fact of His being called Servant and serving many well, and that it is a great thing for Him to be called the Child of God. For in truth He was in servitude to flesh and to birth and to the conditions of our life with a view to our liberation, and to that of all those whom He has saved, who were in bondage under sin. What greater destiny can befall man's humility than that he should be intermingled with God, and by this intermingling should be deified, and that we should be so visited by the Dayspring from on high, that even that Holy Thing that should be born should be called the Son of the Highest, and that there should be bestowed upon Him a Name which is above every name? And what else can this be than God?—and that every knee should bow to Him That was made of no reputation for us, and That mingled the Form of God with the form of a servant, and that all the House of Israel should know that God hath made Him both Lord and Christ? […]

It is one thing to be named Son according to the divine substance; it is another thing to be so called according to the adoption of human flesh. For, according to the divine generation, the Son is equal to God and Father, and, according to the adoption of a body, he is a servant to God the Father. "For," it says, "he took upon him the form of a servant." The Son is, however, one and the same.… According to his glory, he is Lord to the holy patriarch David but David's son in the line of actual descent, abandoning nothing of his own but acquiring for himself the rights that go with the adoption into our race. Not only does he undergo service in the character of man by reason of his descent from David, but also by reason of his name, as it is written: "I have found David my servant";4 and elsewhere: "Behold, I will send to you my Servant, the Orient is his name." […]

Nor is it any wonder that men, holy though they are, are nobly called servants of God, since through the prophet Isaiah the Father speaks to the Son: "It is a great thing for you to be called my child (puer)" (Isa. 49:6), which in Greek is said: μέγα σοί ἐστι τοῦ κληθῆναί σε παῖδά μου. Now because "child" (puer), that is, παῖς, can according to the Greeks signify both servant (famulus) and son, we inquired in the Hebrew, and found written not "my son" but "my servant", that is, ABDI (עבדי). Hence also the prophet Obadiah (Abdias), whose name means "servant of the Lord", received his name from his service to God. If it disturbs anyone that the Lord and Savior, who is the founder of the universe, is called a servant of God, he will not be disturbed if he hears him speaking to the apostles: "Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be the servant of all"; and: "The Son of man came, not to be served, but to serve" (Matt. 20:27, 28); and, lest he should seem to teach this by words alone, he showed it by example. […]

49:7.t: Thus says the Lord, the redeemer of Israel, his Holy One, to the contemptible soul, to the abhorred nation, to the servant of lords. Kings shall see, and princes shall rise up, and they shall worship for the Lord's sake, for he is faithful: and the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you. LXX: Thus says the Lord who delivered you, the God of Israel. Sanctify him who despises his own soul, who is an abomination to the nations, who is the servant of princes. Kings shall see him, and princes shall rise up, and they shall worship him for the Lord's sake: for the Holy One of Israel is faithful, and he has chosen you. In place of what we have said: to the contemptible soul, to the abhorred nation, to the servant of lords, Theodotion translated: to him who despises his soul, who is an abomination to the nation, who is the servant of princes: which plainly fits the person of Christ. […]

49:8.t: For thus the God of all, after the manner of wise Solomon, distributes everything in time and season, to the end that, in due time, the salvation of men should be everywhere spread abroad. Thus the ‘Wisdom of God,’ our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, not out of season, but in season, ‘passed upon holy souls, fashioning the friends of God and the prophets;’ so that although very many were praying for Him, and saying, ‘O that the salvation of God were come out of Sion!’—the Spouse also, as it is written in the Song of Songs, was praying and saying, ‘O that Thou wert my sister’s son, that sucked the breasts of my mother!’ […]

In an acceptable time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have helped you (Isa. 49:8): this is written in Isaiah the prophet. He teaches that the grace of God was predestined for the time of Christ; for God decreed that his mercy should abound in such a way that he would bestow help on those who ask in the name of Christ.

Thus says the Lord: In a pleasing time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have helped you. And I have kept you, and given you as a covenant of the people, that you might raise up the land, and possess the scattered inheritances: that you might say to those who are bound: Go forth; and to those who are in darkness: Be revealed. In the ways they shall feed, and in all the plains shall be their pastures. They shall not hunger nor thirst, and the heat and the sun shall not strike them: for he who has compassion on them shall rule them, and shall give them drink at the springs of waters. And I will make all my mountains a way, and my paths shall be raised up. Behold, these shall come from afar, and behold, those from the North and the sea, and these from the land of the South. Praise, O heavens, and exult, O earth: shout praise for joy, O mountains, for the Lord has comforted his people, and will have mercy on his poor. […]

And he kept him, or formed him, when death had been overcome, and gave him as a covenant of the people of the Jews, that is, of those among them who were willing to believe: that he might raise up the land, which lay in the errors of idolatry, and possess the scattered, or deserted, inheritances, which did not have God as their inhabitant, and might say to those who were in bonds, Go forth, those who were held fast by the bonds of sins, since each one is bound fast with the cords of his own sins (Prov 5); and to those who were in darkness, Be revealed: those who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, and could not see the light. And after they have been converted, and have beheld the clear light of Christ, they shall feed in the ways and in the paths of the holy Scriptures, and shall say: The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture there he has set me: he has brought me up beside the waters of refreshment (Ps 22 [23]:2).

49:10.t: And he who has been fed and nourished in such ways and paths shall neither hunger nor thirst, nor feel the heat of the sun: and in him what is written will be fulfilled: The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night (Ps 120 [121]:6). So that he feels neither the adversities nor the prosperities of this world. Since the Lord is merciful and compassionate, he himself will comfort them and rule them, and lead them to the springs of waters. Or, he will give them drink at the springs, of which it is written: Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel (Ps 67 [68]:27). And in another place: Draw waters from the springs of the Savior (Isa 12:3). These springs are in the Old Testament and the New.

But since they have been called to the light of truth, they have become pastures for them, and feeding-grounds that nourish them toward spiritual manliness, and to the desire for every good thing. And God promises them the abundance of His grace, and help, and spiritual consolation. For they shall not hunger, nor shall they thirst, he says. For long ago they were in want of spiritual consolation, for there was among them no divine law, no prophet, no guide, no instructor, no teacher, no spring of spiritual waters. But since they have received mercy from God, the supply of spiritual goods has now become most abundant for them, as they have received soul-profiting nourishment. For they ate bread from heaven, they drank living water, about which Christ Himself spoke, addressing the woman in Samaria: "Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again. But whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will have in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life." […]

49:11.t: And all the stumbling-blocks that could hinder the steps of believers the Lord will turn into level ground for them, and he will bring low the high places and raise up the low, that they may have a level and open road.

49:12.t: And who these are for whom the way is prepared, he sets out more plainly: Behold, these shall come from afar: and behold, those from the North and the sea, and these from the land of the South. Showing the four regions of the world, East and North, West and South, he put afar for the East: for the southern region, in the Hebrew is read SINIM (סינים), which the Seventy translated of the Persians. The rest expressed it as it is read in the Hebrew, sinim, which we have translated from the South: suspecting this, that Mount Sinai is situated in the southern part, according to the Prophet Habakkuk: God will come from the South, and the holy one from Mount Paran, shady and thick (Hab 3). But if by sinim, as the Seventy translated, we understand the Persians, who are situated toward the East, we shall be able to refer what is said above, Behold, these shall come from afar, to the South.

49:13.t: For He raised up the falling, healed the sick, satisfied those who were hungry, and filled the poor, and, what is more wonderful, raised us all from the dead; having abolished death, He has brought us from affliction and sighing to the rest and gladness of this feast, a joy which reacheth even to heaven. For not we alone are affected by this, but because of it, even the heavens rejoice with us, and the whole church of the firstborn, written in heaven, is made glad together, as the prophet proclaims, saying, ‘Rejoice, ye heavens, for the Lord hath had mercy upon Israel. Shout, ye foundations of the earth. Cry out with joy, ye mountains, ye high places, and all the trees which are in them, for the Lord hath redeemed Jacob, and Israel hath been glorified.’ And again; ‘Rejoice, and be glad, ye heavens; let the hills melt into gladness, for the Lord hath had mercy on His people, and comforted the oppressed of the people.’

And the heavens and the earth are commanded, either the powers that dwell in heaven and on earth, or angels and men, to sing together the praises of God. And those who are set on the height of the virtues are to testify to the gladness of their mind with jubilation and exultation. For the Lord has comforted his people, those of the Jews who were willing to believe. And he has had mercy on his poor and lowly ones: or on all his people, who were called to him from East and West, North and South, having neither Law nor Prophets nor spiritual riches, but, deserted, poor and lowly, lay subject to all the demons.

49:14.t: And Zion said: The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me. Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have pity on the son of her womb? And if she should forget, I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on my hands: your walls are always before my eyes. Your builders have come: and those who destroyed you and scattered you shall go forth from you. Lift up your eyes round about, and see, all these are gathered together, they have come to you. As I live, says the Lord, you shall be clothed with all these as with an ornament, and you shall put them about you like a bride, for your deserts and your solitudes, and the land of your ruin, shall now be too narrow for the inhabitants, and those who swallowed you up shall be chased far away. Still they shall say in your ears, the sons of your barrenness: The place is too narrow for me, make room for me to dwell. And you shall say in your heart: Who has begotten these for me? […]

And again speaking by the comparison of a wife, He says: "Even if she shall have forgotten, yet will I not forget thee." For who can be ignorant, that the memory of God is neither broken off by oblivion, nor yet repaired by recollection? But when He neglects and passes over some things, He is said, after the manner of minds, to forget, and when, after a long time, He visits the things He wills, He is said, after the fashion of our changeableness, to have remembered. For how does oblivion weaken the strength of that Godhead, with Which even praiseworthy memory itself has no essential agreement. For men remember no things, except those which are either past or absent. How then does God remember past things, when the very things which in themselves pass away, stand ever present at His beck? Or how does He call to mind things absent, when every thing that is, is present to Him, from the fact that it exists in Him? For if it were not present to Him, it would not exist at all; […]
49:14.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 32, Section 7

49:15.t: To it God answered, using a likeness from nature: If it can happen that a mother forgets her infant, and is not moved by pity toward the offspring of her own womb, then I too will forget you. I will say something more: even if she should forget, overcoming the laws of nature by hardness of mind, yet I will not forget my creature, and I will always hold the souls of the Saints in my heart.

This providence and love of God therefore, which the Lord in His unwearied goodness vouchsafes to show us, He compares to the tenderest heart of a kind mother, as He wishes to express it by a figure of human affection, and finds in His creatures no such feeling of love, to which he could better compare it. And He uses this example, because nothing dearer can be found in human nature, saying: "Can a mother forget her child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb?" But not content with this comparison He at once goes beyond it, and subjoins these words: "And though she may forget, yet will not I forget thee."
49:15.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, Chapter 17

49:15.t: The blessed Virgin paid that price as a woman strong and devout with the piety of mercy toward the world, and especially toward the Christian people. Isaiah: "Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have mercy on the son of her womb? And if she should forget, yet I will not forget you." This is said of Christ. And it can be understood here that the entire Christian people was brought forth from the womb of the glorious Virgin, which is signified to us by the woman formed from the side of the man, who signifies the Church.

49:16.t: ‘Attend to thyself alone,’ says Scripture. In fact, we must distinguish between ‘ourselves,’ ‘ours,’ and ‘what surrounds us.’ ‘Ourselves’ refers to body and soul. ‘Ours’ are the members of our bodies and our senses. ‘What surrounds us’ consists of our money, our slaves, and all that belongs to this life. ‘Attend to thyself,’ therefore, ‘know thyself,’ that is to say—not what muscular arms you have, not how strong you are physically, or how many possessions or power you have. Attend, rather, to your soul and mind, whence all our deliberations emanate and to which the profit of your works is referred. Here only is the fullness of wisdom, the plenitude of piety and justice of which God speaks—for all virtue comes from God: ‘Behold, Jerusalem, I have painted thy walls.’ That soul of yours is painted by God, who holds in Himself the flashing beauty of virtue and the splendor of piety. That soul is well painted in which shines the imprint of divine operation. […]

To the soul of such a man He says: ‘Behold, Jerusalem, I have painted thy walls.’ He did not say ‘I have painted thy belly’ or ‘thy lower parts,’ but ‘I have painted thy walls,’ thus proclaiming that the strong protection of walls was granted to man. In this way, by keeping careful watch on the walls, man can ward off the dangers involved in a siege. He says, therefore: ‘I have given you neither delights nor the allurements of desire, neither incentives to luxurious living nor eagerness to possess another’s dignities. You have been granted a substantial basis for erecting walls and lofty turrets by means of which you can banish fear of an enemy’s assault and the dread of terrifying raids from legions of soldiers.’

For know, you who think yourself utterly forsaken, that you are engraved and painted on my hands, and that your walls remain continually before my eyes. From this we learn that Jerusalem is by no means to be sought in the region of Palestine, which is the worst of the whole province, and rough with rocky mountains, and suffers a dearth of water, so that it uses the rains of heaven, and consoles the scarcity of springs by the construction of cisterns; but in the hands of God, to whom it is said: Your builders have hastened. Or, according to the Seventy: Quickly you shall be built by those by whom you had been destroyed. For destroyed by the Jews, it was built by the Jews. Deserted because of the guilt of the Scribes and Pharisees, it was gathered together at the preaching of the Apostles of Christ, both from the Jews and from the nations. There follows: And those who destroyed you and scattered you shall go forth from you: the most wicked teachers; […]

49:18.t: And he added: And in the blood of the grape, his garment: that is, in the suffering of his body, he washed the nations with his blood. For indeed, the nations are the garment of the Word, as it is written: As I live, says the Lord, unless I clothe them all as a garment. And elsewhere: You will change them as a garment, and they will be changed. Therefore, he has cleansed not with his own blood, their sins which they did not have, but with our sins which we have committed.
49:18.s: On the Blessings of the Patriarchs, 4.24

49:18.t: And she is told to lift up her eyes round about, and see the sons who had been gathered to her. Of whom the Lord too spoke: Lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are already white for harvest (John 4:35). And to make us secure: As I live, says the Lord (which, according to the Old Testament, is said by the custom of swearing), you shall be clothed with all these as with an ornament, and you shall put them about you, as a bride puts a necklace about herself. Happy is he who is of such merit and such virtue that he is called an ornament of the Church. I think, moreover, that these signify the various spiritual graces by which the bride's array is adorned. Of her too it is sung in Psalm 44 (45): The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded with variety (Ps 44 [45]:10).

We have often said already that blessed Job stands for a type of Holy Church. But all they, who are joined to it by the unity of the Faith, are the garments of the Church. Of which the Lord says to the same Church by the Prophet, "As I live, thou shall be clothed with all these, as with an ornament." But by the south wind, which is doubtless warm, is designated, not improperly, the Holy Spirit, for when any one is touched by It, he is freed from the torpor of his iniquity. The garments, therefore, of Holy Church are warm, while the earth is breathed upon by the south wind; because they, who cling to her by faith, glow with fervent zeal of charity, while their mind is streamed through by the breath of the Holy Spirit.
49:18.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 27, Section 38

49:18.t: If anyone asks what the Lord's garments, which became white as snow, represent typologically, we can properly understand them as pointing to the church of his saints. Of them Isaiah said, "You will be clothed with all of these as though with an ornament."

49:19.t: For what had before been deserted, and had fallen into solitudes and ruins, will, at the coming of the Gospel of Christ, be restored, and will have so great a multitude of inhabitants that it cannot hold them. Provided only that the persecutors be chased far away, or those of whom we spoke above: Those who destroyed you and scattered you shall go forth from you.

49:20.t: And the sons of your barrenness, whom you thought you had utterly lost, and by them to have been widowed, shall say in your ears: The place is too narrow for me in the synagogues, make room for me in the Churches, to dwell more widely, so that I may not be crushed by the blasphemies of the Jews, so that your breadth may hold the whole world together with me.

49:21.t: We are to be a model for everyone around us, not just in our actions but also in our speech, in our chastity and in our faith. Let us be what we should wish others to think us, and let us show our feelings as they really are. We should never mutter a word that is unjust, even in our own heart, thinking to ourselves that it is hidden under a veil of silence; for the One who made the secret places hears words that are spoken in secret, and the One who implanted the power of thought in our innermost parts knows the hidden things that those innermost parts contain. So as people who live under the eyes of their Judge, let us remember that everything we do is exposed to the light, and in this way it will be manifest to all.
49:21.s: On the Duties of the Clergy 2.19.96

49:21.t: But you, unable to utter with your mouth the greatness of your joy, will ponder silently in your heart, and will say: Who has begotten these for me? I was barren and a widow, deserted and captive among the people of the Jews; I had ceased to have sons; for a long time I had not given birth. After Haggai and Zechariah and Malachi I had seen no other Prophets until John the Baptist; and how is it that I, who had been alone and destitute of a husband's help, have now begun to have so many sons? And so that we may know that Zion is built from both peoples upon the rock and foundation of Christ, Paul says to believers: Built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief cornerstone. (Eph 2:20.) From this it is plain that the one foundation of the Apostles and Prophets is our Lord Jesus Christ.

49:22.t: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I lift up my hand to the nations, and to the peoples I will raise up my standard: and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and carry your daughters upon their shoulders. And kings shall be your foster fathers, and queens your nurses. With face bowed to the ground they shall worship you, and lick the dust of your feet: and you shall know that I am the Lord, in whom those who wait for him shall not be confounded. LXX: Thus said the Lord God: Behold, I raise my hand over the nations, and over the islands I will lift up my standard, and they shall bring your sons in their bosom, and carry your daughters on their shoulders. And kings shall be your foster fathers: and princesses your nurses: on the face of the earth they shall worship you, and lick the dust of your feet; and you shall know that I am the Lord, and those who wait for me shall not be confounded. To what the Church had said: I was barren and captive, who has begotten these for me? […]

49:23.t: But the kings who are foster fathers, and the queens and princesses who are nurses, plainly point to the Apostles and to Apostolic men: such as Abraham too was, to whom it is said: You are a king from God among us (Gen 23:6); and whose heart is in the hand of God (Prov 21): who say to believers: As newborn babes, rational and without guile, desire milk (1 Pet 2:2). The princess also, that is, ἄρχουσα, which is the sound of Sarah's name, and the queens, or the queen, of whom it is sung in Psalm 44 (45): The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, nourishes Christ's little ones daily, and leads them to perfect age: and every age, sex and rank will worship Zion for the sake of him who dwells in her. For if Christ is the head of the Church, the head is worshiped in the body. And if it is said to certain people: Exalt the Lord our God, and worship the footstool of his feet (not that the footstool is to be worshiped; […]

49:24.t: Shall the prey be taken from the strong? or can what has been captured by the mighty be safe? For thus says the Lord: Indeed even the captivity shall be taken from the strong: and what has been carried off by the mighty shall be saved. But those who have judged you, I will judge: and your sons I will save. And I will feed your enemies with their own flesh, and they shall be drunk with their own blood as with new wine: and all flesh shall know that I am the Lord who saves you, and your redeemer, the strong one of Jacob. LXX: Shall anyone take spoils from a giant? And if anyone leads a captive away unjustly, he shall be saved. Thus says the Lord: If anyone captures a giant, he shall take spoils, and he who takes from the strong shall be saved. But I will judge my judgment. And I will rescue my sons, and those who afflicted you shall eat their own flesh, and shall drink their own blood like new wine, and shall be drunk: and all flesh shall know that I am the Lord who rescued you, and the help of the strength of Jacob. […]

49:25.t: Therefore the Lord, judging those who had oppressed Zion, or judging her judgment, will set free her sons who had been captured by the giant, and will save them, and he will feed the adverse powers with their own flesh, and make them drunk as with new wine, so that they may be glutted not by the slaughter of others but by their own death. And those who are flesh, because they have lost the spirit of God, are to feed on their own flesh. This indeed the Saint also says in the Psalms: When those who afflicted me drew near to eat my flesh (Ps 26 [27]:2). For it is not the spirit, which is incorporeal, that is eaten, but the flesh, which lies open to the bites of fierce beasts. And then Zion will learn, nay, all flesh which will see the salvation of God, that her Redeemer and Savior is he who wrestled with Jacob, or who was the helper of the strength of Jacob: so that in his passion, lifted up on high, he blessed those who crucified him: Father, forgive them: for they do not know what they are doing (Luke 23:34).

50:1.t: But hear what the prophet says: "By your sins you were sold, and for your iniquities I dismissed your mother." You see, then, that we are indeed all the creature of God, but each one is sold by his own sins and for his own iniquities departs from his own creator. We are, therefore, God's, according as we were created by him; but we became slaves of the devil, according as we were sold by our sins. But Christ, coming, "redeemed us," while we were serving that lord to whom we had sold our very selves by sinning. And so he seems to have received back as his own those whom he had created, but to have acquired as aliens those who by sinning had sought for themselves an alien lord.

[Passages quoted, Isa. 1. 1, 2 a, b.]

HERE the Lord Himself recording plainly His Coming among men rebukes the Jewish people, because they will not receive Him when He comes, nor hear Him when He calls. And He teaches, as if by way of apology, that this is the cause of their own rejection. "For when I came," He says, "I was not among you as a man: I called, and there was none that heard: therefore," He says, "ye were sold for your sins, inasmuch as ye were of yourselves divorced from my call, not that I had given you a bill of divorcement." This is clearly addressed to the Jews, and at the same time reveals their outrages on Him at His Passion, when it says: "I gave my back to scourges, and my cheeks to blows," and that which follows. But these words shall be properly interpreted at leisure.
50:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 23

50:1.t: But Joseph was sold into Egypt, because Christ was going to come to those to whom it was said: For your sins you have been sold. And therefore, He redeemed them with His own blood, who had sold themselves by their own sins. But Christ, who was sold, is held by the assumption of the condition, not by the price of guilt, because He Himself did not commit sin. Therefore, He contracted our debt, not His own money; He took away the handwriting, removed the lender, stripped off the debtor: He alone paid what was owed by all.

Thus says the Lord: What is this bill of divorce of your mother, with which I put her away? Or who is my creditor, to whom I sold you? Behold, for your iniquities you were sold, and for your crimes I put away your mother. For I came, and there was no man: I called, and there was none to hear. LXX: Thus says the Lord: What kind of bill of divorce of your mother is it, with which I put her away? Or to which creditor and exactor of mine did I sell you? Behold, for your sins you were sold, and for your iniquities I put away your mother, for I came, and there was no human being: I called, and there was none to obey. After the calling of the nations, and the kings and princes, the foster fathers and nurses, and the captivity of the one formerly strong and mighty, whose prey has been distributed to the Apostles, and after the madness of the demons, who have been glutted with their own flesh and made drunk with their own blood, when all flesh has known that the Redeemer and the strong one is himself the God of Jacob, he […]

And this law the Apostle also calls spiritual saying: "But we know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin." For this law is spiritual which bids us eat in the sweat of our brow that "true bread which cometh down from heaven" but that sale under sin makes us carnal. What, I ask, or whose is that sin? Doubtless Adam's, by whose fall and, if I may so say, ruinous transaction and fraudulent bargain we were sold. For when he was led astray by the persuasion of the serpent he brought all his descendants under the yoke of perpetual bondage, as they were alienated by taking the forbidden food. For this custom is generally observed between the buyer and seller, that one who wants to make himself over to the power of another, receives from his buyer a price for the loss of his liberty, and his consignment to perpetual slavery. And we can very plainly see that this took place between Adam and the serpent. […]
50:1.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Theonas, Chapter 12

50:2.t: They were ignorant of the words of the prophet Isaiah, who prophesied these very same things concerning him, and said in the person of the Lord and Savior himself: "what, that I came, and there was no man? I called, and there was none who would obey? Is my hand not able to rescue? Or can I not deliver? Behold, at my rebuke I will make the sea a desert, and I will set the rivers a desert. And their fish shall be dried up because they have no water, and shall die of thirst. And I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and make its covering like sackcloth.
