The Lord gives me the tongue of instruction, that I may know how it behooves me to speak the word; he set me in the morning, he applied to me an ear to hear, and the instruction of the Lord shall open my ears; but I am not unbelieving, nor do I contradict. I offered my back to the scourges, and my cheeks to the palms of hands, but I did not turn away my face from the confusion of spittings, and the Lord God became my helper". […]

And so that you may know that your mother was not repudiated by me, but withdrew by her own will, after many benefits I took a human body, and spoke no more through the Prophets, but in person. I came, and there was no man, or human being. For all, abandoning the image of man and of a human being, took on the images of beasts and serpents. Hence it is said to Herod because of his malice: Go and tell that fox (Luke 13:32). And to the Pharisees: Brood of vipers (Matt 23:33). And to the lustful: They have become horses mad after females (Jer 5:8). And of the pleasure-lovers: Do not cast your pearls before swine. And to the shameless: Nor give what is holy to dogs (Matt 7:6). And in common of them all: The vision of the four-footed beasts that were in the desert (Isa 30). The Lord therefore came, and did not find a man. For man, when he was in honor, did not understand: he was compared to senseless cattle, and became like them (Ps 48 [49]:13). […]

According to the anagogy, at the rebuke of the Lord the sea becomes a desert when all the bitterness of this world is dried up, and the rivers are made desolate, of which the spiritual dragon in Egypt said: The rivers are mine, and I made them (Ezek 29:9). And of which we read in another place: What have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the waters of the rivers (Jer 2:18)? The fish too, when the net has been cast into the sea, shall rot, those which have been separated from the good fish.

Is my hand shortened, and made very small, so that it cannot redeem? Or is there no power in me to deliver? Behold, at my rebuke I will make the sea a desert, I will turn the rivers into dry land: the fish shall rot for lack of water, they shall die of thirst. I will clothe the heavens with darkness, and make sackcloth their covering. LXX: Is my hand not able to deliver, or is it not strong enough to rescue? Behold, by my threat I will make the sea a desert, and make the rivers deserts, and their fish shall dry up, because there is no water, and they shall die of thirst. And I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and make its covering as haircloth. […]

50:3.t: And as for what follows: I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and its covering shall be as haircloth, either let us understand by heaven all that is above us, as the birds which are in the air are called heavenly, and the adverse powers, which run to and fro between heaven and earth, are said to be heavenly. Or certainly the heaven is clothed with darkness when it is covered with clouds. According to what is written: Who covers the heaven with clouds, and gives rain to the earth (Ps 146 [147]:8). And in threatening drought God says: I will make the heaven bronze, and the earth iron (Deut 28:23). Not that the nature of the elements is changed, but that by bronze and iron the greatness of the punishments is shown. The philosophers say that the clouds are not raised up more than ten stadia from the earth, and hide the brightness of the sun. It is not, then, the heaven that is wrapped in sackcloth, but, the light of heaven being shut off, the air that is beneath is darkened by the darkness of the cloud. […]

Yes! creation itself bewailed its Lord: for the sun was darkened, and the rocks were rent, and the very temple assumed the garb of mourners, for its "veil was rent from the top to the bottom." And this is what God signified to us by the voice of Isaiah, saying, "And I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and wrap it around with sackcloth."
50:3.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

50:4.t: For the power of His strong word, by which He always confuted the Pharisees and Scribes, and, in short, all your nation's teachers that questioned Him, had a cessation like a plentiful and strong spring, the waters of which have been turned off, when He kept silence, and chose to return no answer to any one in the presence of Pilate; as has been declared in the memoirs of His apostles, in order that what is recorded by Isaiah might have efficacious fruit, where it is written, "The Lord gives me a tongue, that I may know when I ought to speak." Again, when He said, "Thou art my God; be not far from me," He taught that all men ought to hope in God who created all things, and seek salvation and help from Him alone; and not suppose, as the rest of men do, that salvation can be obtained by birth, or wealth, or strength, or wisdom.

Now what ought we to learn before everything else, but to be silent that we may be able to speak? Lest my voice should condemn me before that of another acquits me, for it is written: "By your words you shall be condemned." What need is there, then, that you should hasten to undergo the danger of condemnation by speaking when you can be more safe by keeping silent? How many have I seen to fall into sin by speaking, but scarcely one by keeping silent; and so it is more difficult to know how to keep silent than how to speak … a person is wise, then, who knows how to keep silent. Lastly, the Wisdom of God said, "The Lord has given to me the tongue of learning, that I should know when it is good to speak." Justly, then, is one wise who has received of the Lord to know when he ought to speak. Wherefore the Scripture says well: "A wise person will keep silence until there is opportunity."
50:4.s: On the Duties of the Clergy 1.2.5

50:4.t: The Lord has given me a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain by a word him who is weary. He rouses in the morning, in the morning he rouses my ear, that I may hear him as a master. The Lord God has opened my ear: and I do not gainsay; I have not gone backward. I gave my body to those who struck, and my cheeks to those who plucked them. I did not turn away my face from those who rebuked and spat. The Lord God is my helper, therefore I am not confounded: therefore I have set my face like a very hard rock, and I know that I shall not be confounded. LXX: The Lord gives me a tongue of discipline, that I may know when I ought to speak a word. He set me in the morning, he added to me an ear for hearing; and the discipline of the Lord opens my ears. But I do not refuse, nor do I gainsay. I gave my back to the scourges, and my cheeks to blows. But I did not turn away my face from the shame of spittings. […]

And so learn from your own experience to sympathize with those in trouble, and never to terrify with destructive despair those who are in danger, nor harden them with severe speeches, but rather restore them with gentle and kindly consolations, and as the wise Solomon says, "Spare not to deliver those who are led forth to death, and to redeem those who are to be slain," and after the example of our Saviour, break not the bruised reed, nor quench the smoking flax, and ask of the Lord that grace, by means of which you yourself may faithfully learn both in deed and power to sing: "the Lord hath given me a learned tongue that I should know how to uphold by word him that is weary:" for no one could bear the devices of the enemy, or extinguish or repress those carnal fires which burn with a sort of natural flame, unless God's grace assisted our weakness, or protected and supported it.
50:4.s: Second Conference of Abbot Moses, Chapter 13

50:6.t: For how shall patience be looked for, if there be not previously labours and sorrows? Or how can fortitude be tested with no assault from enemies? Or how shall magnanimity be exhibited, unless after contumely and injustice? Or how can long-suffering be proved, unless there has first been the calumny of Antichrist? And, finally, how can a man behold virtue with his eyes, unless the iniquity of the very wicked has previously appeared? Thus even our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ comes before us, when He would shew men how to suffer, Who when He was smitten bore it patiently, being reviled He reviled not again, when He suffered He threatened not, but He gave His back to the smiters, and His cheeks to buffetings, and turned not His face from spitting; and at last, was willingly led to death, that we might behold in Him the image of all that is virtuous and immortal, and that we, conducting ourselves after these examples, might truly tread on serpents and scorpions, and on all the power of the enemy.

And so it is shewn to all that the Body was not the Word, but Body of the Word. And it was this that Thomas handled when it had risen from the dead, and saw in it the print of the nails, which the Word Himself had undergone, seeing them fixed in His own Body, and though able to prevent it, did not do so. On the contrary, the incorporeal Word made His own the properties of the Body, as being His own Body. Why, when the Body was struck by the attendant, as suffering Himself He asked, ‘Why smitest thou Me?’ And being by nature intangible, the Word yet said, ‘I gave My back to the stripes, and My cheeks to blows, and hid not My face from shame and spitting.’ For what the human Body of the Word suffered, this the Word, dwelling in the body, ascribed to Himself, in order that we might be enabled to be partakers of the Godhead of the Word. And verily it is strange that He it was Who suffered and yet suffered not. Suffered, because His own Body suffered, and He was in it, which thus suffered; […]

[This is] as though he were to say, "Though I knew beforehand that they would strike me, I did not even turn aside my cheek; for how could I have nerved my disciples to undergo death for the truth if I had been afraid?"

What do I mean by this, hold fast to Christ? It was for this reason that He chose to suffer on earth Himself. Ye have heard, while the prophet was being read, how He “did not turn away His back from the smiters, and His face from the spittings of men,” how “He turned not His cheek from their hands;” wherefore chose He to suffer all these things, but that He might console the suffering? He could have raised His flesh at the last day: but then thou wouldest not have had thy ground of hope, since thou hadst not seen Him. He deferred not His resurrection, that thou mightest not still be in doubt. Suffer then tribulation in the world with the same end as that which thou hast observed in Christ: and let not those who do evil, and flourish in this life, move thee.

50:7.t: Nevertheless, you will say, adversity is a terrible thing and grievous to be borne. Yet look at it again compared with another image and then also learn to despise it. For the railings, and insults, and reproaches, and gibes inflicted by enemies, and their plots are compared to a worn-out garment, and moth-eaten wool when God says "Fear ye not the reproach of men, neither be ye afraid of their revilings, for they shall wax old as doth a garment, and like moth-eaten wool so shall they be consumed." Therefore let none of these things which are happening trouble thee, but ceasing to invoke the aid of this or that person, and to run after shadows (for such are human alliances), do thou persistently call upon Jesus, whom thou servest, merely to bow his head; and in a moment of time all these evils will be dissolved.

50:8.t: Near is he who justifies me: who gainsays me? Let us stand together. Who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. Behold, the Lord God is my helper: who is he that will condemn me? Behold, they shall all be worn away like a garment, the moth shall eat them. LXX: He who is near justifies me: who is he that is judged with me, let him resist me together? And who is he that enters into judgment against me? Let him draw near to me. Behold, the Lord is my helper, who will afflict me? Behold, all of you shall grow old like a garment, and like a moth it shall eat you. If anyone, he says, thinks that I was justly given over to the cross and had committed some sin, let him resist me. Who is he that is judged with me, so that he may be overcome not by the power of my majesty but by reason? Now a man is judged with the Lord not by the authority of one who reigns but by comparison of virtues: as the Apostles also judge the twelve tribes of Israel, and the Ninevites and the queen of Sheba judge the people of the Jews. […]

50:9.t: Since, then, no one can be justified in the presence of the Lord, all shall grow old like a garment (Ps 101 [102]). And what grows old is near to perishing. And like a moth, he says, it shall eat them: namely the conscience of sins, and jealousy over the nations that have been saved. Of this it is said at the end of this volume: Their worm shall not die. And in Micah, against the perverse princes: I will take away their goods like a moth that eats them up, and walks upon the rule in the day of watching (Mic 7:4 LXX). And in Proverbs: An understanding heart is a moth of the bones (Prov 14:30 LXX). For moth in the present place Symmachus translated rust, Aquila worm.

50:10.t: Who among you fears the Lord, hearing the voice of his servant? He who has walked in darkness and has no light, let him hope in the name of the Lord, and lean upon his God. LXX: Who is there among you that fears the Lord, let him hearken to the voice of his child: those who walk in darkness have no light. Trust in the name of the Lord, and lean upon God. You scourged me, you spat upon my face: yet I call my persecutors to repentance. For I do not will the death of the sinful people, but only that it turn back and live (Ezek 33). And I say: who is there among you that fears the Lord and hears the voice of the servant, or child, that is, of his Son? Of these the one belongs to the flesh he assumed, the other to his nature. Nor let us think it a small thing to fear the Lord, according to what is said in Proverbs: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Prov 9:10). For perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment; and he who fears is not perfect in love. […]

50:11.t: That "fire" is not "from the altar". The fire which is "from the altar" is the fire of the Lord; but that which is outside the altar is not the Lord's, but is the proper fire of each one of those who sin, of which it is said: "their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished". That "fire" therefore is of those very ones who kindled it, as also elsewhere it is written: "walk in your fire and in the flame which you have kindled for yourselves". But to Isaiah not his own fire is applied, but the fire of the altar, which will "purge around" his "lips".

Behold, all of you who kindle a fire, girded with flames, walk in the light of your fire, and in the flames that you have kindled: by my hand this has been done to you; you shall sleep in sorrows. LXX: Behold, all of you kindle a fire and strengthen the flame; walk in the light of your fire, and in the flame that you have kindled; because of me these things have been done to you. You shall sleep in grief. Exhortation profits nothing, nor is there hope of salvation after crimes. All have turned aside, together they have become useless (Ps 13 [14]); all kindle a fire for themselves and strengthen the flame. For they have in themselves hay, wood, stubble, thorns and thistles and darnel, which are to be handed over to the eternal burning. Hence it is also written in Proverbs: In much wood the fire thrives (Prov 25:21). But if a little fire lays hold of great material, how much will a great flame lay waste? […]

Moreover, what we have set down according to the Seventy: A man who is estranged from me and sets his thoughts in his heart, and the torment (or punishment) of his iniquity before his face, agrees with that testimony which is written in Isaiah: Walk in the light of your fire, and in the flame which you have kindled; for each one kindles for himself the blazing of flames and prepares punishments for himself, while he is unwilling to correct his errors by repentance, but remains in errors that deserve the burning of flames.

It is impious to blame God's severity for our misfortunes: we should instead accuse ourselves. For when we commit the sins that cause our torture, we are ourselves the authors of our torments. Why then do we complain of the bitterness of our punishments? Each one of us punishes himself.

This is why the prophet said to us: "Behold, all ye that kindle a fire, that have added fuel to the flame; walk in the light of your fire and in the sparks that ye have kindled." For the whole human race is rushing headlong into eternal punishment by the very course that the Scriptures describe. First we kindle the fire, then add fuel to the flames, and lastly enter the flames that we have prepared. When does man first kindle eternal fire for himself? Surely when he first begins to sin. But when does he add fuel to the flames? When he heaps up sins upon sins. When shall he enter the everlasting fire? […]
50:11.s: On the Government of God, Book 4, Chapter 8

50:11.t:
As all things, are subject to sacred authority and the will of God rules everything, whatever evils and whatever punishments we bear daily are the censure of his divine hand, which censure, indeed, we constantly arouse and kindle by our sins. We kindle the fire of the celestial wrath and arouse the flames by which we are burned, so that the words of the prophet may rightly be used against us as often as we endure such ills: "Make your way into the flames of the fire that you have kindled.'' From this we see that according to the sacred sentence each sinner is preparing for himself the suffering that he endures. None of our misfortunes can be imputed to God; we are the authors of our own misery. For God is gracious and merciful and, as the Scripture says, he wishes no one to perish or be injured. So whatever is done against us is done by our own actions; there is nothing more cruel to us than ourselves; we, I say, are torturing ourselves even against God's will.

But, forsooth, I seem to be contradicting myself; […]
50:11.s: On the Government of God, Book 8, Chapter 1

51:1.t: Hear me, you who pursue what is just, and seek the Lord. Look to the rock from which you were hewn, and to the cavern of the pit from which you were cut out. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you: for I called him alone, and blessed him, and multiplied him. The Lord therefore will comfort Zion, and will comfort all her ruins, and will make her desert like delights, and her wilderness like the garden of the Lord. Joy and gladness shall be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise. LXX: Hear, you who pursue what is just, and seek the Lord. Look to the strong rock which you hewed out, and to the hole of the pit which you dug. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you, for he was one, and I called him, and blessed him, and loved him, and multiplied him: and now I will comfort you, Zion. […]

51:4.t: For the law promulgated on Horeb is now old, and belongs to yourselves alone; but this is for all universally. Now, law placed against law has abrogated that which is before it, and a covenant which comes after in like manner has put an end to the previous one; and an eternal and final law-namely, Christ-has been given to us, and the covenant is trustworthy, after which there shall be no law, no commandment, no ordinance. Have you not read this which Isaiah says: "Hearken unto Me, hearken unto Me, my people; and, ye kings, give ear unto Me: for a law shall go forth from Me, and My judgment shall be for a light to the nations. My righteousness approaches swiftly, and My salvation shall go forth, and nations shall trust in Mine arm?" And by Jeremiah, concerning this same new covenant, He thus speaks: "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah; […]

Attend to me, my people, and my tribe, hear me: for a law shall go forth from me, and my judgment shall rest for a light of the peoples. Near is my righteous one, my savior has gone forth: and my arms shall judge the peoples. The islands shall wait for me, and shall wait upon my arm. LXX: Hear me, hear me, my people, and kings, attend to me: for a law shall go forth from me, and my judgment for a light of the nations. My righteousness draws near swiftly, and my salvation shall go forth like a light: and in my arm shall the nations hope. The islands shall wait for me, and in my arm they shall hope. Once in the Hebrew it is said, Attend; twice according to the Seventy, hear me, hear me: to teach us that we ought to hear both with the ears of the body and with the sense of the soul. And the multitude of the nations, which is the people of God, is called to listen carefully to what is said; of which Zechariah says: Many nations, he says, shall flee to the Lord, and shall be his people (Zech 2:11). […]

51:5.t: And lest perhaps we should think that what he promised would come after a long time, he adds: near is my righteous one, or righteousness. For Christ has been made for us by the Father wisdom and redemption (1 Cor 1), holiness and righteousness, and all the names by which virtue is called. And it is beautifully said that righteousness will go forth, so that not one nation only but the whole world may be saved. And that the Son of God, who was sent by the Father, is called Savior, or salvation, which in Hebrew is said Jesus, Simeon declares, holding the child in his arms: Now you dismiss your servant, O Lord, for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples, a light for the revelation of the nations (Luke 2:29ff.). […]

51:6.t: Again, as to their malignantly asserting that if heaven is indeed the throne of God, and earth His footstool, and if it is declared that the heaven and earth shall pass away, then when these pass away the God who sitteth above must also pass away, and therefore He cannot be the God who is over all; in the first place, they are ignorant what the expression means, that heaven is [His] throne and earth [His] footstool. For they do not know what God is, but they imagine that He sits after the fashion of a man, and is contained within bounds, but does not contain. And they are also unacquainted with [the meaning of] the passing away of the heaven and earth; but Paul was not ignorant of it when he declared, "For the figure of this world passeth away." […]

But, however, we say thus: That which our Redeemer said to us is true:—Heaven and earth shall pass away. And the Apostle said, Hope which is seen is not hope. And the Prophet said, The heavens shall pass away as smoke, and the earth as a garment shall wear away; and its inhabitants shall become like it. And Job said concerning those that sleep, Till the heavens wear out, they shall not be aroused, nor shall they wake out of their sleep. From these things be thou persuaded that this earth, in which the children of Adam are sown, and the firmament that is over men, (even) that firmament which is set to divide the upper heavens from the earth and this life, shall pass away, and wear out, and be destroyed. And God will make a new thing for the children of Adam, and they shall inherit inheritances in the Kingdom of Heaven. If He shall give them inheritance in the earth, it shall be called the kingdom of heaven. And if in Heaven, it is easy for Him to do.
51:6.s: Demonstration 22 (Of Death and the Latter Times), Section 24

51:6.t: Upon the essence of the heavens we are contented with what Isaiah says, for, in simple language, he gives us sufficient idea of their nature, “The heaven was made like smoke,” that is to say, He created a subtle substance, without solidity or density, from which to form the heavens. As to the form of them we also content ourselves with the language of the same prophet, when praising God “that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in.”
51:6.s: The Hexaemeron, Homily 1: In the Beginning God Made the Heaven and the Earth

51:6.t: It is sufficient, therefore, to set forth what we find in the writings of Isaias concerning the nature and the substance of the heavens. In modest and familiar language he described the nature of the heavens when he said that God ‘hath fixed the heavens like smoke,’ desiring to declare it to be not of solid but of subtle nature.

Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath: for the heavens shall melt away like smoke, and the earth shall be worn away like a garment, and its inhabitants shall perish like these. But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not fail. LXX: Lift up your eyes to heaven, and look upon the earth beneath, for heaven has been made firm like smoke. But the earth shall grow old like a garment, and its inhabitants shall die like these. But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not fail. This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away (Matt 24:35). And David sings in the psalm: In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; and they shall all grow old like a garment; and like a cloak you shall roll them up, and they shall be changed (Ps 101 [102]:26). […]

51:7.t: Hear me, you who know what is just, people: my law is in their heart. Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies. For as a garment, so shall the worm eat them; and as wool, so shall the moth devour them. But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness to generations of generations. LXX: Hear me, you who know judgment, my people, of whom my law is in their heart. Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be overcome by their contempt. For like a garment they shall be consumed by time, and like wool they shall be eaten by the moth. But my righteousness shall be for ever, and my salvation to generations of generations. […]

51:8.t: For as a garment is consumed by the worm, or by time, and as wool is devoured by the moth, so all the reproach of the persecutors will pass away with the persecutors. Hence the Apostles too gloried that they had been counted worthy to suffer insults for the Lord (Acts 5). And they gloried because the salvation and righteousness of the Lord, which had promised them victory and rewards, that is, the Lord and Savior, abides for ever, or in each generation, of the former people and of the later, who received his coming; of whom it is also said above: Near is my righteous one, my savior has gone forth.

51:9.t: Arise, arise; put on strength, O arm of the Lord. Arise as in the days of old, in the generations of ages. Was it not you who struck the proud one, who wounded the dragon? Was it not you who dried up the sea, the water of the mighty deep, who made the depth of the sea a way, that the freed might pass over? And now those who have been redeemed by the Lord shall return and come into Zion praising; and everlasting gladness shall be upon their heads: they shall hold joy and gladness; sorrow and groaning shall flee. LXX: Rise up, rise up ÷ Jerusalem ⁚ and put on the strength of your arm. Rise up as in the beginning of the day, as an everlasting generation. Are you not she who cut down the breadth, who undid the dragon? Are you not she who made the sea a desert, the many waters of the deep; who made the depth of the sea a way of passage for those who had been freed and redeemed? For by the Lord they shall be led back, and shall come into Zion with gladness and everlasting exultation. […]

51:12.t: I, I myself will comfort you. Who are you, that you should have feared a mortal man, and the son of man, who shall wither like grass? And you have forgotten God your maker, who stretched out the heavens and founded the earth; and you have been in dread continually all the day at the face of the fury of him who afflicted you and had made ready to destroy. Where now is the fury of the afflicter? He shall come quickly, walking, to open, and he will not kill unto utter destruction, nor shall his bread fail. But I am the Lord your God, who trouble the sea, and its waves swell: the Lord of hosts is my name. I have put my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I have protected you, that you may plant the heavens and found the earth, and say to Zion: You are my people. LXX: I am, I am he who comforts you. Know who you were, and that you feared a mortal man, and the son of man, who have withered like grass; and you have forgotten God your maker, who made heaven and founded the earth; […]

According to the Seventy it is said to every believing soul that, though created in the image and likeness of God, she did not know her own dignity, but feared man and the son of man, who can kill only the body, and did not know that she is immortal, nor say with the Prophet: The Lord is my light and my savior, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life, of whom shall I be afraid (Ps 26 [27]:1, 2)? And again: The Lord is my helper, I will not fear what man may do to me. The Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon my enemies (Ps 117 [118]:6, 7). And what man is, is shown by another verse: In the Lord I will hope: I will not fear what flesh may do to me (Ps 55 [56]:5). Hence it is now said too: You feared a mortal man, and the son of man, who have withered like grass. For all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass (Isa 40); and, terrified by the power of the judge, you forgot that he himself was your protector, who made heaven and earth and all the elements we see; […]

51:14.t: My son will come quickly, walking and trampling your adversaries, to open to you the way of victory; or to unbar the underworld; who will not kill unto utter destruction, but wills to save those who turn. Then too his bread, which, as the Gospel proves, means doctrine, shall never fail, but shall always lie open to those who wish to eat.
And what is said above, And he will not kill unto corruption, and his bread shall not fail, was added from Theodotion's edition out of the Hebrew.

Symmachus, in the place where we said, He shall come quickly, walking, to open, and he will not kill unto utter destruction, translated thus: Quickly the underworld shall be opened, and he shall not die unto corruption, Christ being understood, who speaks in the fifteenth psalm: You will not leave my soul in the underworld, nor will you give your holy one to see corruption. In that place too where we, according to the Hebrew and Aquila, rendered, I have put my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I have protected you, that you may plant the heavens, and found the earth, and say to Zion: you are my people, he translated thus: I will put my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I will protect you, by which I planted heaven and founded the earth, and that I may say to Zion: you are my people.

51:15.t: He troubles the sea and makes its waves resound, he to whom it is also sung in the Psalms: You rule the strength of the sea, and the tossing of its waves you calm (Ps 88 [89]:10). In Jeremiah too it is written: Will you not fear me, says the Lord, and will you not tremble before my face, who set the sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting decree which it shall not pass (Jer 5:22)? The seas were troubled when the Lord's dragnet drew out a multitude of fish (Matt 13).

And at the same time he makes an apostrophe to the Son, whom he promises will come quickly, and whose bread he says is everlasting: that he himself, according to the dispensation of the flesh he assumed, is his Lord God, who makes the sea troubled and its waves swell, so that the pride of the persecutors is puffed up against his servants, and then, with the Lord's help, grows calm again. And he says that he has put his words in his mouth. For whatever the Son speaks are the words of the Father; and that he protected him in the shadow of his hand; and that he was protected for this reason, that he might plant new heavens and found a new earth, and say to Zion, that is, to the Church: You are my people. Therefore Zion is nothing other than the people of God.

51:16.t: And the Lord put his words in the mouth of the believer, and protected him in the shadow of his hand. He also says in the Gospel: When they hand you over, do not think how or what you are to speak; for what you are to speak will be given you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the spirit of your Father who speaks in you (Matt 10:19, 20). And in another place he says to the righteous man: Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it (Ps 80 [81]:12). And again: Open your mouth to the word of God: For the Lord will give the word to those who preach the good news with great power. Hence God speaks to the inner man of Jeremiah, after he touched his mouth: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth (Jer 1:9). He could sing with the Psalmist: He put a new song in my mouth, a hymn to our God (Ps 39 [40]:4). And who has wrought all these things but the Lord and Savior, who made heaven and earth, and says to Zion, You are my people? Which properly suits the Church gathered from the nations. […]

51:17.t: Discourse awhile on our present heavy blow, about the just judgments of God, whether we grasp their meaning, or are ignorant of their great deep. How again "mercy is put in the balance," as holy Isaiah declares, for goodness is not without discernment, as the first labourers in the vineyard fancied, because they could not perceive any distinction between those who were paid alike: and how anger, which is called "the cup in the hand of the Lord," and "the cup of falling which is drained," is in proportion to transgressions, even though He abates to all somewhat of what is their due, and dilutes with compassion the unmixed draught of His wrath. For He inclines from severity to indulgence towards those who accept chastisement with fear, and who after a slight affliction conceive and are in pain with conversion, and bring forth the perfect spirit of salvation; […]

Lift yourself up, lift yourself up, arise, Jerusalem, who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath: you have drunk to the bottom of the cup of stupor, and have drained it to the dregs. There is none to sustain her, of all the sons whom she has borne; and there is none to take her by the hand, of all the sons whom she has brought up. Two things there are that have befallen you; who shall be grieved over you? devastation and destruction, and famine, and the sword: who shall comfort you? LXX: Rise up, rise up, lift yourself up, Jerusalem, who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury. For the cup of ruin, the κόνδυ of fury, you have drunk off and emptied: and there was none to comfort you of all your sons whom you bore; and there was none to take you by the hand, nor of all your sons whom you raised up. These two things are against you: who shall be grieved with you? ruin and destruction, famine and the sword: who shall comfort you? […]

We can understand these things according to the anagogy also of the sinful soul, which, not wishing to drink the cup of the Lord's fury, says in the psalm: O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chastise me in your wrath (Ps 6:1). But if she has drunk it, it is good for her to feel her punishments, and to hear the Lord saying: When the wrath of my fury has passed, I will heal again. And elsewhere: Shall he who falls not rise again, says the Lord (Jer 8:4)?

51:18.t: And at the same time we must consider that from then on there was no prophet, no Apostle in Judea to comfort her, and take her by the hand, and lift her up as she lay. From this it is plain that these things are said of the time after the last captivity: otherwise, history relates that in Babylon and after Babylon she had Ezekiel and the other Prophets.

51:19.t: And as for what he says, Two things there are that have befallen you, or these two things are against you: who shall be grieved over you?, and in place of two he names four, devastation and destruction, famine and the sword: like this is what is sung in the Psalter: Once God has spoken, these two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, O Lord, mercy: for you will render to each according to his works (Ps 61 [62]:12, 13). For there too God speaks once, that he is almighty, and the Prophet hears two things, that his omnipotence prevails on both sides, so that he both grants mercy to the penitent and renders to those who persist in sin the punishments they deserve. In the same way in this other place two things befell Jerusalem, each of which has two parts. For destruction follows ruin, or devastation; and death follows famine and the sword.

51:20.t: Your sons have been cast out, they have slept at the head of all the ways, like an ensnared oryx: full of the indignation of the Lord, of the rebuke of your God. LXX: Your sons, in want and sleeping at the head of all the ways, like a half-cooked beet, full of the fury of the Lord, and failing from the Lord God. For half-cooked beet the other translators rendered an oryx caught and ensnared, which in Hebrew is called THO (תוא), a kind of beast born in the desert, which is placed among the clean animals in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. For this the Seventy supposed the Syriac word thoreth, which means beet. From the name let us pass to the sense. Your sons, like an oryx caught in the snares of the hunters, have slept at the crossroads and in the streets, and, laying their naked limbs upon the naked ground, have shown by their own miseries the indignation of the Lord and the rebuke of their God. […]

51:21.t: Therefore hear this, poor little one, and drunk, but not with wine. Thus says your ruler, the Lord, and your God, who fought for his people: Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of stupor, the bottom of the cup of my indignation: you shall not drink it again any more. And I will put it in the hand of those who humbled you, and said to your soul: Bow down, that we may pass over; and you made your body like the ground, and like a road for those passing over. LXX: Therefore hear, you who are humbled and drunk, but not with wine. Thus says the Lord God who judges his people: Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of ruin, the κόνδυ of my fury: and you shall not drink it again any more: and I will give it into the hands of those who unjustly oppressed you and humbled you; who said to your soul, Bend down that we may pass over; and you made your middle parts level with the ground for those passing outside. […]

But to come, according to the Seventy, to the spiritual understanding: it is said to the soul humbled by vices and drunk with passions, that she may know that she has the Lord as her judge, and that she will render account for all things. And if she has been turned to better things, the cup of ruin is to be taken from her hands, and the bowl of the Lord's fury, which held punishments, of which Ezekiel also says to Jerusalem: You shall drink the cup of your sister Samaria, deep and wide, that you may be drunk (Ezek 23:32), is to be handed over into the hands of those who had humbled her. There is no doubt that he signifies the adverse powers, which said to her soul: Bow down, that we may pass over. Here it is likewise to be noted that they did not bend her down, nor use force so that she who was formerly upright should be bowed to the ground, but left it to her own choice. And she of her own will laid down her neck, or her back, or her whole body, not inside but outside, for those who trampled her. […]

51:22.t: Therefore, if you do penance, and, lifted up, arise, you will know that the cup of stupor and of ruin, or according to Symmachus and Theodotion, of tearing and of commotion, is to be taken from your hand; and that you will no more drink the condy, for which in this place too Symmachus translated bowl; but that it is to be handed over to your adversaries, who said to your soul, Bow down, that we may pass over: and when they said it, you bent down of your own will. And you made your body like the ground, or your back; or according to the Seventy, your middle parts and your necks for those passing outside. Let this be said according to the history: that Jerusalem, if she is willing to lift herself up and arise, shall by no means drink the cup of the Lord's fury, nor suffer any more what she endured before.

51:23.t: Of these enemies, indeed, it is said through the prophet: "They say to your soul: Bow down, that we may pass over." For the soul standing upright is sublime, bowed down it is lowly, because through the height of virtues and through heavenly desire it is raised to lofty things; but when it falls away to vices or to love of the world, it falls to that place where the enemy, rushing in, easily tramples it. They say therefore to your soul, "Bow down, that we may pass over," because if they do not humble it to doing or thinking earthly things, they neither penetrate it with malign persuasions nor disturb it with the warfare of vices. From this, therefore, we can gather how far we ought to distance ourselves from the world in deed, word, and thought.
51:23.s: Commentaries on the Book of 1 Kings, Book 5

51:23.t: Hence another prophet says concerning unclean spirits: Who said to your soul, Bow down that we may pass over. For the soul stands upright when it desires heavenly things, and is by no means bent toward the lowest things. But when malign spirits see it standing in its uprightness, they cannot pass through it. For their passing through is to scatter unclean desires upon it. Therefore they say, Bow down that we may pass over, because if the soul does not cast itself down to desiring the lowest things, their perversity by no means prevails against it; and they cannot pass through her whom they fear standing rigid against them in heavenly intention.

Why does he not know, unless because, bending himself down to these lowest and earthly things, he heaps up earth for himself? Assuredly he does not know, concerning those things which he commits to the earth, for whom he gathers them: whether for the moth that destroys, or for the thief that digs through; for the enemy that plunders, or for the fire that devours. And thence that lamentable voice from the psalm belongs to the wretched man bending himself down and brooding over the things that are upon the earth: "I am made wretched and bowed down utterly; all the day long I went about in sadness." In himself indeed he experiences the truth of that sentence of the Wise Man: "God made man upright, but he has entangled himself in many sorrows." And immediately the voice of mockery comes to him: "Bow down, that we may pass over."
51:23.s: Sermons on the Song of Songs, Sermon 80

52:1.t: Arise, arise, put on your strength, Zion: put on the garments of your glory, Jerusalem, city of the Holy One: for the uncircumcised and the unclean shall no more pass through you. LXX: Rise up, rise up, ÷ Zion: ⁚ put on your strength, Zion, and put on your glory, Jerusalem, holy city. No more shall the uncircumcised and the unclean pass through you. Here again the name Zion, as above, was added by the Seventy, and therefore it has been transfixed with the spit. To her, then, to whom he had said above (Isa 51:17), Lift yourself up, lift yourself up, arise, Jerusalem, he now says: Arise, arise, put on your strength, Zion. And who Zion is, the following verse shows: Put on the garments of your glory, Jerusalem. We have said this to prove that Jerusalem and Zion are one city. And she is commanded to put off her garments of mourning and to put on those which she had before she drank from the hand of the Lord the cup of fury. […]

Just as the body is adorned by its garment, so the soul is adorned by fortitude; therefore it is called the clothing of the soul; nor is fortitude only the clothing of the soul, or of the glorious Virgin, but indeed of Mother Church. Whence Isaiah says: "Arise, arise, O daughter of Sion; put on the garments of thy glory." The discourse concerns the habit of fortitude, how we may be clothed with it. If we wish to describe fortitude rightly, we must note that it is from heaven.

52:2.t: Shake yourself from the dust: arise, sit down, Jerusalem: loose the bonds of your neck, captive daughter of Zion. For thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without silver. LXX: Shake off the dust, and rise up, Jerusalem. Loose the bond of your neck, captive daughter of Zion. For thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money. That the Prophet's word is by no means addressed to Jerusalem, that is, to the ruins of her stones, and her ashes and embers, but to the people that dwells in her, and that it is called daughter on account of the effeminacy of its spirit, the following verse shows, in which he says: Loose the bonds of your neck, captive daughter of Zion. For truly captive is the people of the Jews, which to this day bears the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, and is bound fast by the cords of its sins and blasphemies; which was sold for nothing, and did nothing worthy for which it could be redeemed. […]

52:4.t: For thus says the Lord God: My people went down into Egypt at the beginning, to sojourn there; and Assyria oppressed him without any cause. And now what have I here, says the Lord? For my people has been taken away for nothing: its rulers act unjustly, says the Lord, and continually all the day my name is blasphemed. Therefore my people shall know my name in that day: for I myself who spoke, behold, I am here. LXX: For thus says the Lord: My people went down into Egypt formerly, to sojourn there; and they were violently led away to the Assyrians; and now what shall be here, says the Lord? Because my people has been taken away for nothing, wonder, and howl. Thus says the Lord: Because of you my name is always blasphemed among the nations. Therefore my people shall know my name in that day: for I myself who spoke am here. […]

According to the Seventy, God says to Israel that it went down into Egypt of its own will, as Moses says in Deuteronomy: With seventy souls your fathers went down into Egypt (Deut 10:22); and they were led away captive violently by the Assyrians. Hence it is said to them: And now what are you here? What are you doing in the land of Judea, you who after the murder of the Prophets laid hands on the Son of God? Or else God speaks to the angelic powers and the Angels who presided over the Temple: What are you doing here, why do you not leave the blaspheming people? As Josephus also relates (Antiquities of the Jews, Book 6, ch. 12): when the gates of the Temple were suddenly opened and unbarred of their own accord, gates which many men could scarcely shut, a voice came forth from the inner sanctuary of the Temple, of those saying: Let us pass over from these seats. Here we must consider the exactness of the words: that they did not say, Let us depart, but, Let us pass over, namely to the people of the nations. […]

52:5.t:
[Passage quoted, Isa. lii. 5-10.]

THE prophecy of Christ's Passion immediately succeeds this in one and the same passage, which I shall expound at leisure. One and the same Lord, who said in the previous quotation to the Jewish people, "You were sold for your sins, and for your iniquities I sent away your mother, because I came, and there was no man: I called and there was none to hear," says in the passage before us to the Jews again: "Because of you my name is blasphemed among the Gentiles."

Then, as though having another people besides them, he adds, "Therefore my people shall know my name," and teaches that not another, but the same Lord that spoke in the prophets, will sojourn some day in our life, saying, "I am he that speak; I will come."
52:5.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 24

52:5.t: Hence he adds: And now what have I here, says the Lord? And the sense is: I have nothing left for which I should remain in this region, from which my people has been taken away for nothing, and sold for its sins, and caught like an oryx in a net, either by the forces of the Romans or by the snares of the devil, in which it is held bound to this day. And that they should suffer these things, their rulers and teachers acted unjustly; who, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, shall howl, according to Aquila, shall weep, when they have been handed over to torments. For they are the ones who stirred up the people against the Savior, so that they cried with one voice: Crucify, crucify such a one (John 19:15). Of them he had already said before: The Lord himself will come with the elders of the people and with its princes. But why have you burned my vineyard, and the plunder of the poor is in your houses (Isa 3:14)? […]

52:6.t: For who is our joy and boast, but our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, Who suffered for us, and by Himself made known to us the Father? For He is no other than He Who of old time spake by the Prophets; but now He saith to every man, ‘I Who speak am near.’ Right well is this word spoken, for He does not at one time speak, at another keep silence; but continually and at all times, from the beginning without ceasing, He raises up every man, and speaks to every man in his heart.

That is, he extended his hands to a people who did not believe and contradicted: not seeking an ambassador or messenger, but desiring to save his own people, the Lord himself: 'I, who spoke, behold I am here,' he said. And so, openly, I appear to those who do not seek me, and I am visible to those who do not ask me.

While they, then, blaspheme and curse the Lord, his people, of whom much has already been said, that is, the Christian people, shall know the name of him who is to come in the name of the Father. And it shall know it because he himself who formerly spoke through the Prophets will instruct the peoples in person.

Therefore he who has the knowledge of the name of God, and is not ignorant that he was created in his image and likeness, will dwell in light. And he will be in the day which Abraham rejoiced to have seen (John 8), of which holy David also speaks: This is the day which the Lord has made, let us exult and rejoice in it (Ps 117 [118]:24). For those who have lit for themselves the light of knowledge, and have the everlasting light which has been promised to believers, The Lord shall be to you an everlasting light (Isa 60:20), walk honestly in the day, and are sons of light and of the day; and they know him who says to Moses, Go, say to the sons of Israel: He who is has sent me (Exod 3:14); and him whom they had known before in the saints they will know to be present to themselves too.

52:7.t:
The prophecy before us shews it to be essential that Christ Himself should be the originator and leader of the Gospel activity, and the same prophet foretells that after Him His own disciples should be ministers of the same system:

"How beautiful are the feet of them that bring good tidings of good things, and of those that bring good tidings of peace."

Here he says very particularly that it is the feet of those who publish the good news of Christ that are beautiful. For how could they not be beautiful, which in so small, so short a time have run over the whole earth, and filled every place with the holy teaching about the Saviour of the world?
52:7.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 3, Chapter 1

52:7.t:
And the words, "As a season upon the mountains, as the feet of one preaching a message of peace, as one preaching good things, I will make thy salvation known, saying, Sion, thy God reigneth," the other translators make it clearer. For Aquila says: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of Him that preacheth the gospel, who publisheth peace, who preacheth the gospel of good things, publishing salvation, saying to Sion, Thy God reigneth."

And Symmachus says, "How lovely on the mountains are the feet of him that preacheth the gospel, making peace known, publishing good things, making salvation known, saying to Sion, Thy God reigneth": and instead of "The voice of thy guards is lifted, and they shall rejoice with the voice together, because they shall see eye to eye." Symmachus translates thus: "The voice of thy guards; they have raised their voice. Together, will they praise: For they will see openly." […]
52:7.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 24

52:7.t: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who announces and proclaims peace, and announces good, who proclaims salvation, and says to Zion: There shall reign your God. The voice of your watchmen: they have lifted up their voice; together they shall praise, for they shall see eye to eye, when the Lord has turned Zion back. LXX: As an hour upon the mountains, so are the feet of him who brings good news of the hearing of peace, who brings good news of good things: for I will make my salvation heard, saying: Zion, your God shall reign. The voice of those who guard you has been lifted up, and with the voice together they shall rejoice, for eyes shall see to eyes, when the Lord has had mercy on Zion. Consequently, of him who had said above, I myself who spoke, behold, I am here, the Prophet now testifies that he himself preached the Gospel upon the mountains, that is, upon the Apostles, of whom it is written: Draw near to the everlasting mountains (Mic 2:9 LXX); and whose doctrine is the illumination of God. […]

What the Seventy translated, as ὥρα, that is, an hour upon the mountains: so the feet of him who brings good news of the hearing of peace, and the rest, Paul, following the sense of the Hebrew Truth, sets down in the Epistle to the Romans: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of good things, who bring good news of peace (Rom 10:15): wishing the Apostles to be understood, whose feet the Lord washed (John 13), that they might be clean and beautiful for preaching, and might run through the whole world, and in a short time fill the world with the doctrine of Christ. Now ὥρα, that is, hour, according to the Seventy and the ambiguity of the Greek word, signifies either time or beauty. If time, this will fit it: In an opportune time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have been your helper (Isa 49:8). Hence the Apostle adds: Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor 6:2). […]

But you, "O elect people," set in the firmament of the world, who have forsaken everything that you may follow the Lord, follow him now and confound the mighty! Follow him, O beautiful feet, and shine in the firmament, that the heavens may declare his glory, dividing the light of the perfect ones—though not yet so perfect as the angels—from the darkness of the little ones, who are nevertheless not utterly despised.

52:8.t: And what follows, The voice of your watchmen, or of your guards, signifies the Apostles, of whom God speaks to the Church in another place too (below, Isa 62:6): Upon your walls I have set guards, who shall never be silent, remembering the Lord, who will lift up their voice, discoursing of lofty things. Hence it is said to them (above, Isa 40:9): Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion. Lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good news to Jerusalem. These will praise God with one voice, and see with eyes to eyes; which the Apostle says in other words, Face to face (1 Cor 13); when the Saint sings, My eyes are ever toward the Lord (Ps 24 [25]:15), and, To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven (Ps 122 [123]:1). And the Lord will answer him: For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears toward their prayer (Ps 33 [34]:16).

52:9.t: Rejoice and praise together, deserts of Jerusalem, for the Lord has comforted his people: he has redeemed Jerusalem. The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations: and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. LXX: Let the deserts of Jerusalem break forth into gladness together, for the Lord has had mercy on her, and has rescued Jerusalem. The Lord will reveal his holy arm in the sight of all the nations. And all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. When the people of the Jews had been led into captivity and the city burned, there was in Jerusalem either a rare inhabitant or none. But after he who formerly spoke in the Prophets, and was in the beginning with God, God the Word, dwelt among us and was made flesh, the deserts of Jerusalem were restored; […]

52:9.s: On Hebrew Names, On Isaiah the Prophet

52:10.t:
After this the call of the Gentiles to the worship of God is very clearly shown in the words, "And the Lord God will reveal His holy arm before all nations; and the high places of the earth shall see the salvation of our God." And consider that the arm of the Lord is nothing else but the Word and Wisdom, and the Lord Himself, Who is the Christ of God.

It is easy to shew this from many instances. In the Exodus you have Israel saved by the arm of God from slavery to the Egyptians. While the prophecy before us says that that same arm of the Lord, which of old appeared to save His people will be revealed to all nations, as if it formerly were hidden from them. And "the salvation, which "he says "all the high places of the earth shall see," and which he mentioned before when he said, "I will make my salvation known," know that it is the Hebrew for the name of Jesus.
52:10.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 24

52:10.t: And so that we may know that these things are by no means said of the people of the Jews, but of all who were to believe in the Lord through the apostles, he sets it down and says: he who comforted her, or had mercy on her, and who rescued or redeemed her, he himself prepared or revealed his holy arm in the sight of all the nations: and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. From this it is plain that, once the spiritual Jerusalem, that is, the Church, which had been abandoned by the Jews, was built up through the Apostles, the arm of the Lord is revealed to all the nations, and all the ends of the earth see his salvation. This is understood in two ways. For either the Father reveals his arm to all the nations, or the Son reveals his strength, of which it is written: For power went out from him and healed all (Luke 6:19). And again: I perceived that power went out from me, which healed the woman with the issue of blood (Mark 5:30). […]

And therefore, although the narrative which is read to us from the Gospel properly records those days on which the three men, who had neither been taught by the prophets’ predictions nor instructed by the testimony of the law, came to acknowledge God from the furthest parts of the East, yet we behold this same thing more clearly and abundantly carried on now in the enlightenment of all those who are called, since the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled when he says, “the Lord has laid bare His holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the nations upon earth have seen the salvation which is from the Lord our God;” and again, “and those to whom it has not been announced about Him shall see, and they who have not heard, shall understand.” […]

52:11.t: "Be separated", indeed, "you who carry the vessels of the Lord, and go out from the midst of them, says the Lord". "Separate yourself" from earthly deeds, "separate yourself" from the concupiscence of the world: "for everything that is in the world", according to the Apostle, "is the concupiscence of the flesh and the concupiscence of the eyes, which is not from God". When therefore you have separated yourself from all these things, devote yourself to God as a firstborn calf; let sin not work through you, nor let malice impose a yoke upon you, but be set aside and set apart, given over only to priestly uses like a firstborn animal.… But we say that one is set apart not by places, but by deeds, and not by regions, but by manners of life. Finally, the very word which in the Greek language is spoken, ἅγιος, signifies as it were to be outside the earth. For whoever shall have consecrated himself to God will rightly be seen to be outside the earth and outside the world; […]

Who is there among those destined to be born and die who will not at some point have to leave his country and suffer the loss of his estate? But by no means let Christ be forsaken. The loss of salvation and an eternal home is a much greater threat. See how the Holy Spirit cries to the prophet, "Leave. Depart. Get out of here. Do not touch any unclean thing. Get out of the middle of such things and be separate, you who bear the vessels of the Lord." And yet, those who are the vessels of the Lord and the temple of God do not go out from the middle of all this and leave so that they wouldn't have to be compelled to touch the unclean things or be polluted and corrupted with deadly food. In another place, a voice is heard from heaven, warning them ahead of time what servants of God should be doing. It says, "Come out of her, my people, so that you do not become partakers of her sins and so that you do not receive her plagues." The one who goes out and leaves does not become a partaker of the guilt. […]

But we, having heard above, How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who announces and proclaims peace, and, The Lord will reveal his arm in the sight of all the nations, and, all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God, understand this by no means of the Jews, but of the choir of the Apostles and of all the Saints. They are commanded to depart from Jerusalem and to preach the Gospel in the whole world, as the Lord the Savior says: Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matt 28:19): so that they may by no means stay with the blaspheming Jews, for whose slaughter the Roman army was being made ready, but may leave the polluted, and that those who carry the vessels of the Lord may be separated from them and be cleansed. For they are the Temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 3), and the vessels of gold and silver of a great house. Such was the Apostle Paul, who is called a vessel of election (Acts 9); […]

Depart, depart, go out from there, do not touch what is polluted: go out from the midst of her, be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord. For you shall not go out in tumult, nor shall you hasten in flight. For the Lord will go before you, and the God of Israel will gather you. LXX: Depart, depart, go forth from there, and do not touch what is unclean: go out from the midst of her: be separated, you who carry the vessels of the Lord, for you shall not go out with tumult, nor go with flight: but the Lord will go before you, and the God of Israel who gathers you. This too the Jews try to expound thus: Go out from Babylon, and abandon their idols. Go out from the midst of her, and bring back into the temple the vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had carried off when Jerusalem was taken (2 Kgs 15), now that Cyrus releases the captives under Zerubbabel and Ezra (Ezra 1); […]

52:12.t: There follows: You shall not go out in tumult, nor shall you hasten in flight. For they departed from Jerusalem not as the vanquished but as victors: so that they who, preaching the Gospel of God daily in the Temple, had brought many thousands of the Jews under the faith of Christ, might subdue the world too to his Gospel. For they had the Lord going before them, to gather them, the God of Israel, that is, to make one flock out of the whole world, so that what the Lord says to the Father in the Gospel might be fulfilled (John 17:21): Grant that, as I and you are one, so these too may be one in us: so that, with the same mind and the same judgment, forsaking the vices that fight one another and are contrary, they might lay hold of the one and only virtue. For vices and passions do not follow one another, as is said of the virtues, in which there are neither ὑπερβολαὶ nor ἐλλείψεις, that is, neither more nor less, but all things are tempered. […]

52:13.t: Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted, and lifted up, and shall be very high. As many were astonished over you, so shall his appearance be without glory among men, and his form among the sons of men. He shall sprinkle many nations: over him kings shall shut their mouth: for those to whom it had not been told of him have seen; and those who had not heard have beheld. LXX: Behold, my child shall understand, and shall be exalted, and shall be greatly glorified. As many shall be astonished over you, so shall your appearance be in glory from men, and your glory from the sons of men: so shall many nations marvel over him, and kings shall shut their mouth, for those to whom it has not been announced of him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand. […]

Wherefore let those evil applauders of Christ, who refuse to become Christians, desist from making the allegation that Christ did not teach that their gods were to be abandoned, and their images broken in pieces. For the God of Israel, regarding whom it was declared aforetime that He should be called the God of the whole earth, is now indeed actually called the God of the whole earth. By the mouth of His prophets He predicted that this would come to pass, and by Christ He did bring it eventually to pass at the fit time. Assuredly, if the God of Israel is now named the God of the whole earth, what He has commanded must needs be made good; for He who has given the commandment is now well known. But, further, that He is made known by Christ and in Christ, in order that His Church may be extended throughout the world, and that by its instrumentality the God of Israel may be named the God of the whole earth, those who please may read a little earlier in the same prophet. That paragraph may also be cited by me. […]
52:13.s: The Harmony of the Gospels, Book 1, Chapter 31

52:14.t: All which things the prophet Isaiah foretold, thus proclaiming beforehand, and by one word intimating all this insolence. For "like as many were astonished at thee," he saith, "so shall thy form be held inglorious of men, and thy glory of the sons of men." For what could be equal to this insolence? On that face which the sea, when it saw it, had reverenced, from which the sun, when it beheld it on the cross, turned away his rays, they did spit, and struck it with the palms of their hands, and some upon the head; giving full swing in every way to their own madness. For indeed they inflicted the blows that are most insulting of all, buffeting, smiting with the palms of their hands, and to these blows adding the insult of spitting at Him.
52:14.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 85:1

52:15.t: And we have not in vain believed in Him, and have not been led astray by those who taught us such doctrines; but this has come to pass through the wonderful foreknowledge of God, in order that we, through the calling of the new and eternal covenant, that is, of Christ, might be found more intelligent and God-fearing than yourselves, who are considered to be lovers of God and men of understanding, but are not. Isaiah, filled with admiration of this, said: "And kings shall shut their mouths: for those to whom no announcement has been made in regard to Him shall see; and those who heard not shall understand. Lord, who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?"

He shall sprinkle many nations, cleansing them with his blood and consecrating them in baptism to the service of God. Over him kings shall shut their mouth, and the princes of the world, all of whose wisdom has been overthrown by the preaching of the cross; and those who had not had the Law and the Prophets, and to whom nothing had been announced of him, they themselves shall see and understand. Of them the Savior also speaks: Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed (John 20:29). In comparison with them the hardness of the Jews is reproved, who, seeing and hearing, fulfilled in themselves the prophecy of Isaiah, who says: Hearing you shall hear, and shall not understand: and seeing you shall look, and shall not see. For the heart of this people has been made fat, and with their ears they have heard heavily (Isa 6:9, 10).

Listening to God’s providential leading of the Ancients be estimated by thee as precious drugs for weak eyes. And let the recollection of it be kept with thee at all times of the day. Meditate and think of it and learn wisdom from it, that thou be able to receive in thy soul with honour the recollection of God’s greatness and find for thyself everlasting life in Jesus Christ, the mediator of God and mankind, who was one in his two natures. Though the legions of the angels are not able to look upon the glory surrounding His majestic throne, yet for thy sake He has appeared before the world the most contemptible and humble of man; without form or comeliness; and while His invisible nature was not within the reach of the apprehension of created beings, He accomplished His providential dealings by [covering Himself] with a veil [made of the stuff] of our limbs, in order to save the life of all.

This is he through whom He has purified many peoples and on whom the Lord has laid the sin of us all as Jesaja says. […]

53:1.t: For Christ is of those who are humble-minded, and not of those who exalt themselves over His flock. Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Sceptre of the majesty of God, did not come in the pomp of pride or arrogance, although He might have done so, but in a lowly condition, as the Holy Spirit had declared regarding Him. For He says, "Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed? We have declared [our message] in His presence: He is, as it were, a child, and like a root in thirsty ground; He has no form nor glory, yea, we saw Him, and He had no form nor comeliness; but His form was without eminence, yea, deficient in comparison with the [ordinary] form of men. He is a man exposed to stripes and suffering, and acquainted with the endurance of grief: for His countenance was turned away; He was despised, and not esteemed. He bears our iniquities, and is in sorrow for our sakes; yet we supposed that [on His own account] He was exposed to labour, and stripes, and affliction. […]
53:1.s: Clement's First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 16

53:1.t: Now he would most certainly have said "your arm" if he had not wished us to understand that the Father is Lord and the Son also is Lord.

And the miracle of His birth Isaiah teaches sometimes mysteriously, and sometimes more plainly: mysteriously, when he says:

"Lord, who hath believed our report? And the arm of the Lord to whom hath it been revealed? we proclaimed him before as a child, as a root in a thirsty soil."

Instead of which Aquila interpreted thus: "And he shall be proclaimed as a suckling before his face, and as a root from an untrodden ground." And Theodotion: "And he shall go up as a suckling before him, and as a root in a thirsty land."

For in this passage, the prophet having mentioned "the Arm of the Lord," which was the Word of God, says: "In his sight we have proclaimed (him) as a sucking child, and one nurtured at the breast, and as a root from untrodden ground." […]
53:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 3, Chapter 2

53:1.t: Who has believed our report? and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? And he shall go up like a sapling before him, and like a root out of a thirsty land: there is no form in him, nor comeliness: and we saw him, and there was no appearance, and we desired him. Despised and the lowest of men, a man of sorrows, and knowing infirmity; and his face was as it were hidden, and despised: whence we did not esteem him. Truly he bore our sicknesses, and our sorrows he carried: and we thought him as it were a leper, and struck by God, and humbled. LXX: Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We announced as a little child before him, as a root in a thirsty land. There is no form in him nor glory, and we saw him, and he had no form nor comeliness: but his form was without honor, and failing beyond the sons of men. A man in a stroke, and knowing how to bear infirmity, for his face is turned away, despised and not esteemed. […]

At the beginning of the chapter, in which according to the Seventy it is said, Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed (Rom 10), a testimony which the apostle Paul also uses to the Romans, expounding it of the Lord's passion, Lord is not found in the Hebrew, but was added to make clear the person to whom it is said.

The evangelist thereafter brings forward what has formed the brief subject of to-day's reading, and says, "But though He had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on Him: that the saying of Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spake, Lord, who hath believed our report and to whom hath the arm of the Lord been revealed?" Where he makes it sufficiently plain that the Son of God is Himself the arm of the Lord; not that the person of God the Father is determined by the shape of human flesh, and that the Son is attached to Him as a member of His body; but because all things were made by Him, and therefore He is designated the arm of the Lord. For as it is with thine arm that thou workest, so the Word of God is styled His arm; because by the Word He elaborated the world. For why does a man, in order to do some work, stretch forth his arm, but because the doing of it does not straightway follow his word? […]

Keep far from your hearts, dearly beloved, the poisonous lies of the devil’s inspirations, and knowing that the eternal Godhead of the Son underwent no growth while with the Father, be wise and consider that to the same nature to which it was said in Adam, “Thou art earth, and unto earth shalt thou go,” it is said in Christ, “sit Thou on My right hand.” According to that Nature, whereby Christ is equal to the Father, the Only-begotten was never inferior to the sublimity of the Father; nor was the glory which He had with the Father a temporal possession; for He is on the very right hand of the Father, of which it is said in Exodus, “Thy right hand, O Lord, is glorified in power;” and in Isaiah, “Lord, who hath believed our report? and the arm of the Lord, to whom is it revealed?”

The first thing, then, is that a man possess Scripture, not like a Jew who is content with the rind. For instance, a certain Jew was reading one day this passage from Isaias: "Who would believe what we have heard?" He was reading it literally and was quite unable to relate it to anything nor to make any sense of it, and therefore he cast the book on the ground, begging loudly that God confound Isaias, because it seemed to him that what he said could not stand.

53:2.t: For this reason [it is, said], "Who shall declare His generation?" since "He is a man, and who shall recognise Him?" But he to whom the Father which is in heaven has revealed Him, knows Him, so that he understands that He who "was not born either by the will of the flesh, or by the will of man," is the Son of man, this is Christ, the Son of the living God. For I have shown from the Scriptures, that no one of the sons of Adam is as to everything, and absolutely, called God, or named Lord. But that He is Himself in His own right, beyond all men who ever lived, God, and Lord, and King Eternal, and the Incarnate Word, proclaimed by all the prophets, the apostles, and by the Spirit Himself, may be seen by all who have attained to even a small portion of the truth. Now, the Scriptures would not have testified these things of Him, if, like others, He had been a mere man. […]

And that the Lord Himself was uncomely in aspect, the Spirit testifies by Esaias: "And we saw Him, and He had no form nor comeliness but His form was mean, inferior to men." Yet who was more admirable than the Lord? But it was not the beauty of the flesh visible to the eye, but the true beauty of both soul and body, which He exhibited, which in the former is beneficence; in the latter-that is, the flesh-immortality.

There are, indeed, admitted to be recorded some statements respecting the body of Jesus having been "ill-favored"; not, however, "ignoble," as has been stated, nor is there any certain evidence that he was "little."

It is possible also in another way to see a twofold coming of Christ, that is, the coming of the Word into the soul. First indeed the untrained and those then beginning to know Christ, because they cannot see the brightness of his beauty, say: "we saw him, and he had no form nor comeliness, but his appearance was without honor". Now the unhonored appearance of the Word is the foolish preaching about Christ, when we preach Christ born and crucified. But the second coming is the coming of Christ among perfect men, concerning whom the steward of his word says: "but we speak wisdom among the perfect". And these perfect ones have become lovers of his beauty and beseech the Word, that he gird upon himself his rational sword and set it about the mystery of the fleshly nativity, which is called mystically the thigh. […]

Such were the thoughts of Hebrews long ago about the birth of Christ among men. Do they, then, describe in their prophecy some famous prince or tyrant, or some one in any other class of those who have great power in earthly things? One cannot say so, for no such man appeared. But as He was in His life, so they prophesied that He would be, in no way failing in truth. For Isaiah said: "We proclaimed him before, as a child, as a root in thirsty soil.'' And then he proceeds saying:

"2. He hath no form or glory, and we saw him, and he had no form or beauty, 3. And his form was dishonourable and slight even compared with the sons of men, a man in suffering, and knowing to bear sickness he was dishonoured, and not esteemed." What remains for him to say?
53:2.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 3, Chapter 2

53:2.t: Therefore, Christ is both the great mountain and the small mountain: truly great because He is the great Lord and His power is great; small because it is written: You have made him a little lower than the angels. Wherefore also Isaiah says: We beheld Him, and He had no form nor comeliness. Nevertheless, He became less from great and greater from less. Less from great, because, when He was in the form of God, He emptied Himself and took the form of a servant; greater from less, because Daniel says: And the stone which was cut out of the mountain, became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.

For not by any means in working wonders only was He wonderful, but even when merely showing Himself, He was full of great grace; and to declare this the prophet said, "Fair in beauty beyond the children of men." And if Esaias saith, "He hath no form nor comeliness," he affirms it either in comparison of the glory of His Godhead, which surpasses all utterance and description; or as declaring what took place at His passion, and the dishonor which He underwent at the season of the cross, and the mean estate which throughout His life He exemplified in all respects.

Further: He did not first give "commandment to depart unto the other side," nor until He had healed them. For surely they could not have borne it.
