As therefore on the mountain they not only continued with Him while exhorting them, but also when it was silence followed Him; so here too, not in His miracles only did they wait on Him, but also when He had ceased again, from His very countenance receiving no small benefit. […]
53:2.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 27:2

53:2.t: And as for what follows, He shall go up like a sapling before him, for which the Seventy translated, We announced as a little child before him: for sapling Symmachus translated branch, to show the man assumed, who came forth from the virginal womb. Of him he adds: Like a root out of a thirsty land. For thirsty Aquila translated pathless, to show the privilege of virginity: that he was created without any human seed from an earth previously untrodden. This is he of whom we read above too: A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall go up from his root (Isa 11:1), so as to signify his birth and his going up in the world. But if he had no form nor glory, but his form was ignoble and failing beyond the sons of men, or, as it stands in the Hebrew, despised and the lowest of men, how is it said in the Psalms: Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty, in your beauty and comeliness (Ps 44 [45]:4)? This is easily resolved. […]

53:3.t:
Surely, if they predicted His tribe and race and manner of birth, and the miracle of the Virgin, and His manner of life, it was impossible for them to pass over in silence that which followed, namely His Death: and what does Isaiah prophesy about it?

"3. A man" he says "in suffering, and knowing to bear sickness, he was dishonoured and not esteemed. 4. This man bears our sins, and is pained for our sake. And we thought him to be in trouble, in suffering, and in evil; 5. He was wounded for our sins, and bruised for our iniquities. The chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his stripe we are healed. 6. All we as sheep have gone astray, and the Lord delivered him for our sins, and he because of his affliction opens not his mouth. He was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb dumb before her shearers, so he opens not his mouth. 8. Who shall declare his generation? for his life is taken from the earth."

In this he shews that Christ, being apart from all sin, will receive the sins of men on Himself. […]
53:3.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 3, Chapter 2

53:3.t: Nor is even his death passed over in silence: on the contrary, it is referred to in the divine Scriptures, even exceedingly clearly.… He suffers it not for his own sake but for the immortality and salvation of all, and the counsels of the Jews against him and the indignities offered him at their hands.… O marvel at the loving-kindness of the Word, that for our sakes he is dishonored, that we may be brought to honor.
53:3.s: On the Incarnation of the Word 34:1-2

53:3.t: And what he adds, A man in pain, and knowing how to bear infirmity, or a man of sorrows, and knowing infirmity, shows the true body of a man and a true soul, he who, knowing how to bear infirmities, overcame them all by his divinity. And his face was hidden and despised, so that the divine power was concealed by the human body; of whom it was said above: You are a hidden God, and we did not know.

A man sees the slaughter of bodies, he grieves greatly. He therefore who sees the slaughter of souls, how can he restrain himself from tears? I know the infirmities of others: I ought to suffer with them. Isaiah: "We have seen him, a man of sorrows and knowing infirmity." There is no spirit of the knowledge of God in that member when it sees a member of its head wounded and does not grieve with it. David grieved over the death of Absalom, who nevertheless had persecuted him. There is therefore the grief of compunction for oneself, and the grief of compassion for one's neighbors.

53:4.t: Now the Greeks are accustomed to use for "carry" a word that also signifies "to take away." … Whatever were the cures that Jesus effected, he is mine.

While then the better, the great and worthy and divine sacrifice was not yet available for men, it was necessary for them by the offering of animals to pay a ransom for their own life, and this was fitly a life that represented their own nature. Thus did the holy men of old, anticipating by the Holy Spirit that a holy victim, dear to God and great, would one day come for men, as the offering for the sins of the world, believing that as prophets they must perform in symbol his sacrifice, and shew forth in type what was yet to be. But when that which was perfect was come, in accordance with the predictions of the prophets, the former sacrifices ceased at once because of the better and true Sacrifice.

This Sacrifice was the Christ of God, from far distant times foretold as coming to men, to be sacrificed like a sheep for the whole human race. As Isaiah the prophet says of him:

"As a sheep he was led to slaughter, and as a lamb dumb before her shearers."

And he adds:

"4. He bears our sins and is pained for us; […]
53:4.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 10

53:4.t: You grieve, then, Lord, not for your own wounds but for mine, not for your own death but for our weakness: and we reckoned you to be in sorrows, when you grieved not for yourself but for me; for you were made weak, but because of our sins, not because that weakness was yours, taken from the Father, but because it was taken on for me, since it profited me that the instruction of our peace should be in you and that by your bruise you should heal our wounds.

He truly bore our sicknesses and sins, and suffers pain for us, not in seeming, that is, τὸ δοκεῖν, as an old and a new heresy suppose; but he was truly crucified. He truly suffered pain, saying in the Gospel: My soul is sorrowful even unto death (Matt 26:38). And: Now my soul is troubled (John 12:27). And we thought him unclean, or in pain, as the Seventy translated; for which Aquila and Symmachus put leprous, Theodotion scourged. This, in other words, by Hebrew idiom is understood as leprosy, according to what is written in the psalm: And the scourge shall not come near your tent (Ps 90 [91]:10). And the sense is: We thought him struck by God for his own sins, he who was humbled for our sake and crucified with robbers. Where Symmachus translated Ἐν ἁφῇ ὄντα, that is, in leprosy, Aquila put ἁφημένον, that is, leprous; which many, not understanding, take to mean abandoned, and others read καθήμενον, that is, sitting.

Therefore in assuming true and entire manhood He took the true sensations of the body and the true feelings of the mind. And it does not follow because everything in Him was full of sacraments, full of miracles, that therefore He either shed false tears or took food from pretended hunger or feigned slumber. It was in our humility that He was despised, with our grief that He was saddened, with our pain that He was racked on the cross. For His compassion underwent the sufferings of our mortality with the purpose of healing them, and His power encountered them with the purpose of conquering them. And this Isaiah has most plainly prophesied, saying, “He carries our sins and is pained for us, and we thought Him to be in pain and in stripes and in vexation. But He was wounded for our sins, and was stricken for our offences, and with His bruises we are healed.”

53:5.t: And concerning the suffering of Christ, David said:—They pierced my hands and my feet, and all my bones cried out. They gazed and looked upon me, and divided my garments amongst them, and upon my vesture did they cast the lot. And Isaiah said:—Lo! My servant shall be known and shall be revealed and shall be lifted up, so that many shall be astonished at Him. As for this man, His visage shall be marred more than that of man, and His aspect more than that of the sons of men. And he said:—He will purify many nations, and kings shall be amazed at Him. And he said in that passage:—He came up as a little child before Him, and as a root from the dry ground. And in the end of the passage he said:—He shall be slain for our sins; He shall be humiliated for our iniquity; the chastisement of our peace is upon Him, and by His bruises shall we be healed. By what wounds were men healed? David was not slain; for he died in a good old age, and was buried in Bethlehem. […]
53:5.s: Demonstration 17 (Of Christ the Son of God), Section 10

53:5.t: It did not say, "He remedied our infirmities," lest, as being external to the body and only healing it, as he has always done, he should leave people subject still to death. Rather, he carries our infirmities, and he himself bears our sins, that it might be shown that he has become human for us, and that the body that in him bore them was his own body.

But he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our crimes. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we have been healed. All we like sheep have gone astray, each one in his own way has turned aside: and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth. LXX: But he was wounded for our sins, and was weakened for our iniquities. The discipline of our peace was upon him: by his bruise we have been healed. All like sheep have gone astray, man has gone astray in his own way. And the Lord handed him over for our iniquities, and he, because of affliction, did not open his mouth. We, he says, thought him a man of sorrows, or, according to the Seventy, to be in pain, and struck by God, and bearing his own sins. But he was wounded for our iniquities, saying in the psalm: They dug my hands and feet (Ps 21 [22]:18), so that by his wound he might heal our wounds; […]

Kish, who is called harsh, signifies not only his elect, but also the Redeemer himself. For no one was harsher toward himself than he. For the prophet, indicating the severity of this harshness, says: "Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he himself carried our sorrows" (Isa. 53:4). For to die is not to suffer for mortals, who are subject to the suffering of a condemned nature. He therefore was exceedingly harsh toward himself, who had nothing in himself by which he might suffer; but in order to free us by suffering, he graciously assumed that by which he might be harsh toward himself and be able to suffer.

53:6.t: Isaiah says [about Christ], "The Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all," that is, to correct our iniquities and set them right. For that reason, he alone is able to forgive our sins, he who has been appointed by the Father of all as our educator, for he alone is able to separate obedience from disobedience.

All, he says, like sheep have gone astray, and we have needed the mercy of God, saying in the psalm: I have gone astray like a lost sheep (Ps 118 [119]:176); the sheep which in the parable of the Gospel was carried back on the shoulders of the good and careful Shepherd (Matt 18). And who these sheep are, the following verse shows: Man has gone astray in his own way; or each one has turned aside in his own way, to follow his own error, and, forsaking the right way, to hold differing opinions about the Crucified. The Lord, however, has laid on him the iniquity of us all, or handed him over for our sins, so that what we could not bear through the weakness of our strength, he might carry for us, he who was offered because he himself willed it.

53:7.t:
When this one came from heaven to earth for the sake of the one who suffers, and had clothed himself with that very one through the womb of a virgin, and having come forth as man, he accepted the sufferings of the sufferer through his body which was capable of suffering. And he destroyed those human sufferings by his spirit which was incapable of dying. He killed death which had put man to death.

For this one, who was led away as a lamb, and who was sacrificed as a sheep, by himself delivered us from servitude to the world as from the land of Egypt, and released us from bondage to the devil as from the hand of Pharaoh, and sealed our souls by his own spirit and the members of our bodies by his own blood.

This is the one who covered death with shame and who plunged the devil into mourning as Moses did Pharaoh. This is the one who smote lawlessness and deprived injustice of its offspring, as Moses deprived Egypt. […]

Now those who are saved are called sheep because of their meekness, which they learned from him who says: "learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart," and because "even unto slaughter" they were ready to come, imitating Christ, who "was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before the one shearing it, without voice" — and not simply "without voice," but "before the one shearing it, without voice," that is, before the one taking away what is his own and plundering it.

For thus the patriarch Abraham rejoiced not to see his own day, but that of the Lord; and thus looking forward ‘he saw it, and was glad.’ And when he was tried, by faith he offered up Isaac, and sacrificed his only-begotten son—he who had received the promises. And, in offering his son, he worshipped the Son of God. And, being restrained from sacrificing Isaac, he saw the Messiah in the ram, which was offered up instead as a sacrifice to God. The patriarch was tried, through Isaac, not however that he was sacrificed, but He who was pointed out in Isaiah; ‘He shall be led as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers he shall be speechless;’ but He took away the sin of the world. And on this account [Abraham] was restrained from laying his hand on the lad, lest the Jews, taking occasion from the sacrifice of Isaac, should reject the prophetic declarations concerning our Saviour, even all of them, but more especially those uttered by the Psalmist; ‘Sacrifice and offering Thou wouldest not; […]

For this is the price of our liberty, as Peter says, ye were redeemed with the precious Blood, not indeed of a lamb, but of Him Who came as a lamb, in meekness and humility, and redeemed the whole world with the one offering of His Body, as He himself says, I was brought as a lamb to the slaughter. Wherefore John also says, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.

For he endured the cross not by necessity but by will, saying in the Gospel: The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not drink it (John 18:11)? And to Peter, who was scandalized at the name of the cross, because he did not know the mystery and trembled with human fear: Get behind me, Satan, you are a scandal to me, for you do not savor the things that are of God, but those that are of men (Matt 16:23). Otherwise, if he had not been offered by his own will, he who could point out and foretell the traitor, and said to the Apostles, All of you will be scandalized in me this night, could have avoided those who had been sent against him; but he went to meet them fearlessly, and offered himself of his own accord, saying: Whom do you seek (John 18:4, 6)? And at once they fell backward; for they could not bear the voice of God present before them. And beautifully he added: And he did not open his mouth. When Pilate said, Do you not speak to me?, he would not answer. […]

As a sheep he shall be led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer he shall be dumb, and he shall not open his mouth. From distress and from judgment he was taken away. Who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off from the land of the living: for the crime of my people he struck them. And he shall give the ungodly for burial, and the rich man for his death: because he did no iniquity, nor was there deceit in his mouth. And the Lord willed to bruise him in infirmity. LXX: As a sheep he was led to the sacrifice, and as a lamb dumb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth. In humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who shall declare his generation, for his life is taken from the earth? By the iniquities of my people he was led to death; and I will give the worst men for his burial, and the rich for his death. For he did no iniquity, nor was there deceit in his mouth: and the Lord wills to cleanse him from the stroke. […]

"When Pilate, therefore, heard that saying, he was the more afraid; and entered again into the judgment hall, and saith unto Jesus, Whence art thou? But Jesus gave him no answer." It is found, in comparing the narratives of all the evangelists, that this silence on the part of our Lord Jesus Christ took place more than once, both before the chief priests and before. Herod, to whom, as Luke intimates, Pilate had sent Him for a hearing, and before Pilate himself; so that it was not in vain that the prophecy regarding Him had preceded, "As the lamb before its shearer was dumb, so He opened not His mouth," especially on those occasions when He answered not His questioners. For although He frequently replied to questions addressed to Him, yet because of those in regard to which He declined making any reply, the metaphor of the lamb is supplied, in order that in His silence He might be accounted not as guilty, but innocent. […]

Yet when He suffered, He said none of these things; not that He had not what to say, but He waited for them to fulfil all things, and that all the prophecies might be fulfilled of Him, of whom it had been said, “And as a sheep before her shearer is dumb, so openeth He not His mouth.” It behoved Him to be silent in His Passion, though not hereafter to be silent in Judgment. For He had come to be judged, then, who was hereafter coming to judge; and who was for this reason to come with great power to judge, that He had been judged in great humility.

And hearken unto the prophet who also proclaimed our Lord with his simple teaching, and who likened Him unto a lamb and a sheep, the most innocent of all animals: "Like a lamb was He led to the slaughter, and like a sheep before the shearer He was silent." The lion and the wolf and bear are crafty, together with the other wild beasts, because craftiness was mingled with their evil nature when they were made; but sheep and lambs and ewes are simple and innocent in their ways and movements, and to them was our Lord likened, and by their name are believers called. Our Lord did not liken Himself unto a lion, which bringeth suffering and death, and He did not call His flocks by the names of wild animals, which by the nature in which they were created are cunning in respect of evil things, but He was called "lamb" and "sheep", and being meek like unto them He was led to suffering and to death, for "like a sheep before his shearer He was silent", and thus He in His humility opened not His mouth. […]
53:7.s: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 5 -- Second Discourse on Simplicity

53:7.t: He was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before the shearer, so was he dumb. The Ethiopian eunuch on reading this passage asked Philip to interpret it to him, and he at once explained that it was spoken by the Prophet with reference to the Lord Christ.

53:8.t: And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God; not begotten of things which are not, but of Him who is the Father; not in a corporeal manner, by excision or division as Sabellius and Valentinus thought, but in a certain inexplicable and unspeakable manner, according to the words of the prophet cited above: "Who shall declare His generation?" Since that His subsistence no nature which is begotten can investigate, even as the Father can be investigated by none; because that the nature of rational beings cannot receive the knowledge of His divine generation by the Father. But men who are moved by the Spirit of truth, have no need to learn these things from me, for in our ears are sounding the words before uttered by Christ on this very thing, "No man knoweth the Father, save the Son; and no man knoweth who the Son is, save the Father."

But with regard to these questions, let men decide them as they will. It is enough for me to repeat again that true and blessed saying, and so conclude my quest, the saying which I have often repeated: "Who shall describe His generation? "For of a truth the generation of the Only-begotten of God is seen to be beyond the reach not only of men, but of the powers that are beyond every being, as also our Lord and Saviour Himself says in mystic language this very thing to His own disciples. "No one knows the Father save the Son." To which he adds "and no one knows the Son save the Father."
53:8.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 1

53:8.t:
No language is sufficient to express the origin and the worth, the being and the nature of Christ. Wherefore also the divine Spirit says in the prophecies, "Who shall declare his generation?" For none knoweth the Father except the Son, neither can any one know the Son adequately except the Father alone who hath begotten him.

For who beside the Father could clearly understand the Light which was before the world, the intellectual and essential Wisdom which existed before the ages, the living Word which was in the beginning with the Father and which was God, the first and only begotten of God which was before every creature and creation visible and invisible, the commander-in-chief of the rational and immortal host of heaven, the messenger of the great counsel, the executor of the Father's unspoken will, the creator, with the Father, of all things, the second cause of the universe after the Father, the true and only-begotten Son of God, the Lord and God and King of all created things, the one who has received […]

For he it is who proceeded from a virgin and appeared as man on the earth and whose generation after the flesh cannot be declared. For there is none who can tell his father after the flesh, his body not being of a man but of a virgin alone. Thus, no one can declare the corporeal generation of the Savior from a man in the same way as one can draw up a genealogy of David and Moses and of all the patriarchs.
53:8.s: On the Incarnation of the Word 37

53:8.t: This sheep is equally called shepherd and says "I am the good Shepherd." By his manhood he is sheep; by his divine loving-kindness he is shepherd.

The Sheep, as the Victim: The Lamb, as being perfect: the Highpriest, as the Offerer; Melchisedec, as without Mother in that Nature which is above us, and without Father in ours; and without genealogy above (for who, it says, shall declare His generation?) and moreover, as King of Salem, which means Peace, and King of Righteousness, and as receiving tithes from Patriarchs, when they prevail over powers of evil.

And as for what follows, From distress and from judgment he was taken away, or as the Seventy translated, in humiliation his judgment was taken away: it signifies either that from tribulation and judgment he ascended victorious to the Father; or that he, the judge of all, did not find the truth of judgment, but without any fault was condemned by the sedition of the Jews and the voice of Pilate. Hence the Prophet marvels that the God of all handed himself over to suffering. Of which Paul speaks: For if they had believed, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor 2:8). There follows: Who shall declare his generation? This is understood in two ways: for either it is to be taken of his divinity, that it is impossible to know the mysteries of the divine birth, of which he himself speaks in Proverbs, Before all the hills he begot me (Prov 8:25), according to what we read elsewhere, Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor (Rom 11:34)? that is, no one; […]

The book of the generation of Jesus Christ. In Isaiah we read: His generation, who shall declare it? Let us not think, then, that the Gospel is contrary to the prophet, so that what he said was impossible to utter, this one begins to narrate; for there it is said of the generation of the divinity, here of the incarnation. And he began from the things of the flesh, so that through the man we might begin to learn of God.

It is said in Isaiah concerning the Lord Savior, "Who shall declare his generation?" When it is said, "Who?" every creature is excluded. For he did not say, "Which of men shall declare his generation?" but generally, "Who?" — that is, not an angel, not an archangel, not a cherub, not a seraph. For if that which is spoken of was hidden in God from the heavenly creatures, what wonder if it seems unknown to us who were made from clay?

The evangelist Matthew has commenced his narrative in these terms: "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham." By this exordium he shows with sufficient clearness that his undertaking is to give an account of the generation of Christ according to the flesh. For, according to this, Christ is the Son of man,—a title which He also gives very frequently to Himself, thereby commending to our notice what in His compassion He has condescended to be on our behalf. For that heavenly and eternal generation, in virtue of which He is the only-begotten Son of God, before every creature, because all things were made by Him, is so ineffable, that it is of it that the word of the prophet must be understood when he says, "Who shall declare His generation?" Matthew therefore traces out the human generation of Christ, mentioning His ancestors from Abraham downwards, and carrying them on to Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born. […]
53:8.s: The Harmony of the Gospels, Book 2, Chapter 1

53:8.t: The things which are connected with the mystery of to-day’s solemn feast are well known to you, dearly-beloved, and have frequently been heard: but as yonder visible light affords pleasure to eyes that are unimpaired, so to sound hearts does the Saviour’s nativity give eternal joy; and we must not keep silent about it, though we cannot treat of it as we ought. For we believe that what Isaiah says, “who shall declare his generation?” applies not only to that mystery, whereby the Son of God is co-eternal with the Father, but also to this birth whereby “the Word became flesh.”

53:9.t: WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT THE PROPHET ISAIAH SAYS OF CHRIST, “HE COMMITTED NO SIN,” WHILE THE APOSTLE, ON THE CONTRARY, SAYS, “HIM WHO KNEW NO SIN, HE MADE SIN FOR US” (Isa. 53:9; 2 Cor. 5:21)? — As far as the sense is concerned, the questions are different, but the words are similar: in one respect they are alike, in another they differ. “He made” and “did not make” are opposed; “knew not” and “did not commit” are similar. The prophet spoke in the person of Christ, because “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in His mouth”; but the Apostle speaks of the person of God the Father, who made Him, that is, Christ, who knew no sin, “sin for us.” This must be understood in two ways. First, He made Him sin by willing that He be incarnate, so that He whom fate did not touch should take a body from sinful flesh; by this He is said to have been “made sin.” Then, by offering Him for sins, He made Him sin. For in the Law the victim offered for sins was called “sin.” […]
53:9.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 74: WHY ISAIAH SAYS CHRIST COMMITTED NO SIN YET PAUL SAYS HE WAS MADE SIN

53:9.t: WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT THE PROPHET ISAIAH SAYS OF CHRIST, “HE COMMITTED NO SIN,” WHILE THE APOSTLE, ON THE CONTRARY, SAYS, “HIM WHO KNEW NO SIN, HE MADE SIN FOR US” (Isa. 53:9; 2 Cor. 5:21)? — With regard to the point at issue, not only do the words differ, but the persons are different. “He made” and “did not make” are opposed. But since what is said to have been made is not understood as having been made by Him who is declared not to have made it, it cannot be called a contradiction. For the statement of the prophet refers to the person of Christ, but that of the Apostle to the person of the Father. For God the Father reconciled the world to Himself through Christ; and therefore it came about that He, that is, Christ, was made sin. For this is what “He made Him sin” means: He gave Him into the virginal womb, that He might be born as man, made sin in respect of the flesh, because flesh is the flesh of sin, namely that one whom fate and condition did not touch, to bring forth as man. […]
53:9.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 40: WHY ISAIAH SAYS CHRIST COMMITTED NO SIN YET PAUL SAYS HE WAS MADE SIN

53:9.t: He gave the ungodly for his burial, and the rich man for his death; or the worst men for his burial, and the rich for his death: signifying both peoples, so that in the evil and the worst, who before had no knowledge of God (Rom 9), the multitude of the nations is shown; in the rich, to whom belonged the Testament and the Lawgiving and the Prophets, the Jewish people is pointed out. Therefore the Lord suffered and was buried for this reason, that he might gather to himself a Church from both peoples. Or this must be said: that the Scribes and Pharisees, and Sadducees, the priests and high priests, who formerly reigned among the people and abounded in excessive wealth, God handed over to the Romans after the Lord's passion, and subjected to everlasting servitude. He for whose burial and death the ungodly and the rich were handed over did no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth. […]

53:10.t:
It would have sufficed for him to have concluded the prophecy at this point, if he had not seen that something else would happen after the death of Christ. But as He after His death and entombment is to return and rise again almost at once, he adds this also concerning Him, saying next:

"The Lord also is pleased to purify him from his stroke—if ye can give an offering for sin, your soul shall see a life-long seed. And the Lord wills to take away from the travail of his soul, to shew him light."

He said above: "A man stricken, and knowing to bear weakness"; and now after his death and burial, he says: "The Lord wishes to cleanse him from his strokes." And how will this be done? "If ye offer," he says, "for sin, your soul shall see a seed that prolongs its days." For it is not allowed to all to see the seed of Christ that prolongs its days, but to those only who confess and bring the offerings for sins to God. […]
53:10.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 3, Chapter 2

53:10.t: And the Lord willed to cleanse him from the stroke which he had received when pierced by the soldier's lance. Or to bruise him in infirmity and wound; of which he himself also said: For they persecuted him whom you struck (Ps 68 [69]:27). And through Zechariah God says: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered (Zech 13:7). Therefore his suffering was not of necessity, but of the will of the Father and of his own, he who said to him: O God, to do your will, I have willed it (Ps 39 [40]:9). Of which we also read above: He was offered because he himself willed it.

If he lays down his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall be directed in his hand. Because there has labored his soul, he shall see, and be satisfied: by his knowledge he himself, the righteous one, shall justify my servants who are many, and he himself shall bear their iniquities. LXX: If you give an offering for sin, your soul shall see a long-lived seed: and the Lord wills to take away his soul from pain, to show him light, and to form understanding; to justify the righteous one who serves many well: and he himself shall bear their sins. According to the Hebrew this is the sense: If he whom the Lord willed to bruise, or to cleanse, lays down his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, which he sowed in good ground. Of which it is written in the Gospel: The sower went out to sow; and again: The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field (Matt 13:3). […]

According to the Seventy this is said: O you for whose sins the Son of God was led to death, you who, the worst men and rich in evil, were given for his burial and death: if you are willing to do penance, and to offer for your sins a sacrifice pleasing to God, a contrite spirit, your soul shall see a seed of long time, the Lord the Savior himself. Of whom it is sung in Psalm 88 (89): His seed endures for ever, and his throne like the sun in my sight. And again: I will establish his seed for ever and ever, and his throne like the days of heaven. Which in other words Gabriel says to the Virgin: Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, who shall be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord shall give him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end (Luke 1:31, 32). […]

53:11.t: And he shall see an everlasting seed, and the will of the Father shall be directed in his hand, because his soul labored for a long time, finding no rest among the Jews, and saying in the Gospel: Foxes have holes, and the birds of heaven nests; but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head (Matt 8:20). And in this same Prophet: I have labored, bearing it (Isa 1:14). Because, then, he labored, he shall see the Churches rise up in the whole world, and shall be satisfied with their faith. Indeed, when, hungry and thirsty, he had sat down by the well of Jacob (John 4) at midday under the scorching sun, he would not use the food that had been bought, because he was already satisfied with the faith of the Samaritan woman and of the city of Shechem coming out to him. In this sense he said among the eight beatitudes: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt 5:6). […]

And to show him light, so that he may see all enlightened through him. And to form with understanding, him being understood, upon whom the spirit of wisdom and understanding shall have come down. And to justify the righteous one, who has served many well; for he came not to be served but to serve (Matt 20), washing away in Peter's feet (John 13) the sins of all the Apostles. He appeared in the flesh, was justified in the spirit. Of him Judas the traitor too confesses: I have sinned, betraying righteous blood (Matt 27:4). And Pilate's wife: Have nothing to do with that righteous man: for I have suffered many things today in dreams because of him. And it is to be noted that he was not justified so that from being unrighteous he might become righteous; but the righteous one is justified, not so that he might begin to be what he was not, but so that what he was might appear to all. This righteous one suffered for the unrighteous, that he might offer us all to God. […]

53:12.t:
And since He willed it, and being willing took away the travail of His soul, and shewed Him light, the prophet rightly proceeds with the words: "Therefore he shall inherit from many, and shall divide the spoil of the strong."

Here it remained for him to mention the heritage of Christ, in agreement with the Second Psalm, in which the prophetic word foretells the plot that was hatched against Him, giving His name:

"2. The kings of the earth stood up,

And the rulers were gathered together

Against the Lord and against his Christ."

And it adds next:

"3. The Lord said to me, Thou art my son,

To-day I have begotten thee;

Ask of me and I shall give thee the Gentiles for thine inheritance

And the bounds of the earth for thy possession." It was to these Gentiles that the Prophet darkly referred, saying: "He shall inherit from many, and shall divide the spoil of the strong." For he rescued the subject souls from the opposing powers, which of old ruled over the Gentiles, and divided them as spoils among his disciples. […]
53:12.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 3, Chapter 2

53:12.t:
And when He went to His Father, He sent to us His Spirit and said to us I am with you till the world shall end. For Christ sitteth at the right hand of His Father, and Christ dwelleth among men. He is sufficient above and beneath, by the wisdom of His Father. And He dwells in many, though He is one, and all the faithful each by each He overshadows from Himself, and fails not, as it is written:—I will divide Him among many. And though He is divided among many, yet He sits at the right hand of His Father. And He is in us and we are in Him, as He said:—Ye are in Me and I am in you. And in another place He said:—I and Father are one.

And if anyone, whose conscience lacks knowledge, should dispute about this and say:—“Since Christ is one and His Father is one, how does Christ dwell, and His Father dwell, in faithful men? And how do righteous men become temples for God that He should dwell in them? […]

Concerning the robbers who were crucified with him it is written, "And he was numbered with the transgressors." Both of them were before this transgressors, but one was so no longer. For the one was a transgressor to the end, stubborn against salvation; who, though his hands were fastened, struck with blasphemy by his tongue. When the Jews passing by wagged their head, mocking the crucified and fulfilling what was written, "When they looked on me, they shook their head," he also reviled with them. But the other rebuked the reviler; and it was to him the end of life and the beginning of restoration, the surrender of his soul a first share in salvation.

Therefore I will allot him very many, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong: because he handed over his soul to death, and was reckoned with the wicked: and he bore the sins of many, and prayed for the transgressors. LXX: Therefore he shall possess many, and shall divide the spoils of the strong: because his soul was defiled in death, and he was reckoned with the unrighteous, and he took up the sins of many, and for their iniquities he was handed over. He gives the reasons why after his passion Christ obtains many rewards. Because, he says, he suffered, and did all the things which the preceding discourse described, and himself bore the iniquities of many: therefore I will allot him very many, so that, in place of Jacob, the portion of the Lord, and Israel, the line of his inheritance, they may believe in him, coming from the East and the West, and recline in the kingdom of God with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matt 8): when that is fulfilled which is written: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your […]

For Christ was not discerned by the ungodly, but was condemned with the ungodly; for it was said concerning Him, "He was accounted among the wicked." The robber escaped, Christ was condemned. He who was loaded with criminal accusations received pardon; He who has released from their crimes all who confess Him, was condemned.

Christ suffered a most universal passion, a most bitter passion, a most ignominious passion, a death-dealing passion, yet one that was life-giving.

He suffered also a most ignominious passion, both on account of the gibbet of the cross, which was the punishment of the worst criminals, and on account of the company of the wicked, namely the thieves, with whom He was reckoned.

Because the swelling of pride sometimes rises inwardly from presumption, and sometimes outwardly from ostentation and the praise of others: therefore, to remedy all pride, Christ suffered both kinds of ignominy, both in himself as the one suffering and in the company he had in his passion.

54:1.t: For all the Gentiles were "desolate" of the true God, serving the works of their hands; but the Jews and Samaritans, having the word of God delivered to them by the prophets, and always expecting the Christ, did not recognise Him when He came, except some few, of whom the Spirit of prophecy by Isaiah had predicted that they should be saved.

And the conclusion of the prophecy of Isaiah, tells of the soul once sterile and empty of God, or perhaps of the Church of the Gentiles, agreeably to the view I have taken. For since Christ has borne all for its sake, he rightly goes on after the predictions about them, to say:

"Rejoice, thou barren that bearest not; break forth and cry, thou that travailest not; for more are the children of the desolate, than of her that hath a husband, for the Lord has said, Enlarge the place of thy tent, and the skins of thy hangings peg down, do not spare. Widen thy cords, and strengthen thy pins: spread out still more to the right and left, and thy seed shall inherit the heathen."

This is the good news the Word gives the Church gathered from the Gentiles scattered throughout the world and stretching from sunrise to sunset, shewn forth very clearly when it says: "And thy seed shall inherit the Gentiles."
54:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 3, Chapter 2

54:1.t: WHAT DOES THE PROPHET MEAN WHEN HE SAYS, “REJOICE, O BARREN ONE WHO DOES NOT BEAR; BREAK FORTH AND CRY ALOUD, YOU WHO DO NOT LABOR, BECAUSE THE CHILDREN OF THE DESOLATE ARE MORE THAN THOSE OF HER WHO HAS A HUSBAND." — Since the children of earthly Jerusalem have fallen away from God, joy cannot be ascribed to her, but rather sorrow. Therefore, as a criticism to this Jerusalem, the prophet says that that higher Jerusalem should rejoice, the one the Apostle calls “our mother” (Gal. 4:26): because without groaning and pains she has far more children than this Jerusalem, which in tears gives birth carnally, namely, the Jews, whereas the other gives birth to Christians spiritually through faith. He calls her “desolate” because she is the life that Adam, the first man, abandoned when he followed death. So when people are reborn, they return to the life they had deserted. This life is Christ, because he says, “I am the life” (Jn. 14:6). […]
54:1.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 40: ON “REJOICE, O BARREN ONE”

54:1.t: WHAT IS IT THAT THE PROPHET SAYS: REJOICE, BARREN WOMAN, YOU WHO DO NOT GIVE BIRTH; BREAK FORTH AND CRY OUT, YOU WHO DO NOT LABOR IN CHILDBIRTH, BECAUSE THE CHILDREN OF THE DESOLATE ARE MORE NUMEROUS THAN THOSE OF HER WHO HAS A HUSBAND? — In this passage we understand two mothers: the heavenly and the earthly, that is, the free Jerusalem, of which the Apostle says that she is our mother, and this Jerusalem which he says is in slavery with her children, that is, the Jews. For the prophet, proclaiming the coming of the Lord and seriously calling out in joyful voice for the time of grace, exhorts the heavenly Jerusalem, called “desolate” because she did not yet have dwelling in her the children generated through faith, to rejoice. For the time had come when she should have the children foretold long ago, and many more than those of this Jerusalem, because Christians have surpassed the number of Jews. […]
54:1.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 15: ON “REJOICE, O BARREN ONE”

54:1.t: For it is written: Rejoice, barren one, you who do not bear; break forth and cry out, you who are not in labor; for many are the children of the deserted one, more than of her who has a husband (Isa. 54:1). He says that this earthly Jerusalem has a husband, because she bears according to the flesh; but that heavenly Jerusalem, which he calls our mother, he calls barren, because she does not bear according to the flesh, nor suffer pains, that is, she is not in labor. But she bears spiritually, without suffering, crying out in joy; for, once deserted (and by whom, if not by Adam, who deserted life and followed death), she now has more children than this one who has a husband, that is, who bears carnally. For Christians are many more than the Jews, as is said in the Apocalypse: And I saw a great crowd, which no one could number, from every tribe and nation (Rev. 7:9).

For it is written: Rejoice, barren one, you who do not bear; break forth and cry out, you who do not travail: for many more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband (Isa. 54:1.)

The synagogue had the Law as her husband; and, according also to the prophecy of Hannah, she was once fruitful in children (1 Sam. 1). But the barren Church, without Christ as husband, without any address of the Bridegroom's word, lay long in the desert. But after the synagogue received the bill of divorce into her hands, and turned all her husband's ornaments into the ornament of an idol, then the husband, his former girdle rotting, wove another belt for his loins, another loincloth out of the Gentiles; and she, as soon as she was joined to her husband, conceived and gave birth. And in Isaac the Lord cries out through the prophet: "Is a nation born all at once?" (Isa. 66:8): when in a single day, in the Acts of the Apostles, three thousand and five thousand men believed (Acts 3 ff.). […]

I know that I have often said, Eustochium, that the Apostles and Evangelists, wherever they set down testimonies from the Old Instrument, were accustomed, if there is no difference between the Hebrew and the Septuagint, to use either their own words or those of the Seventy Translators; but if the sense is one thing in the Hebrew and another in the old edition, they follow the Hebrew rather than the Seventy Translators. In short, just as we have shown that they set down many things from the Hebrew which are not found in the Seventy, so let our rivals show some testimonies taken from the Seventy which are not in the books of the Hebrews, and the dispute is finished. We have said this because the present passage, though it is one in sense, differs in words. With its explanation the fifteenth book on Isaiah begins.

Praise, O barren one, who do not bear; sing out praise and neigh, you who were not in labor: for more are the sons of the deserted one than of her who had a husband, says the Lord. LXX: Rejoice, O barren one, who do not bear: break forth and cry out, you who are not in labor: for more are the sons of the deserted one than of her who has a husband. For the Lord has said. Symmachus translated this passage thus: Rejoice, O barren one, who have not borne. Be glad in exultation, and neigh, you who have not been in labor: For more are the sons of the scattered one than of her who was under a husband. From him Theodotion and Aquila do not differ, apart from a few words. […]

Fulfilled be that prophecy wherein Isaiah in Thy person speaketh to Thy Church, Thy holy City, that barren one of whom many more are the sons of Her forsaken than of her that hath a husband. To Her indeed hath been said, “Rejoice, thou barren, that bearest not,” etc., more than of the Jewish nation which hath a Husband, which hath received the Law, more than of that nation which had a visible king. For thy king is hidden, and more sons to thee there are by a hidden Bridegroom.…The Prophet addeth, “Enlarge the place of Thy tabernacle, and Thy courts fix thou: there is no cause for thee to spare, extend further thy cords, and strong stakes set thou again and again on the right and on the left.” Upon the right keep good men, on the left keep evil men, until there come the fan: occupy nevertheless all nations; bidden to the marriage be good men and evil men, filled be the marriage with guests; it is the office of servants to bid, of the Lord to sever. […]

What, then, do these men, who are at once the perverse applauders of Christ and the slanderers of Christians, say to these facts? Can it be that Christ, by the use of magical arts, caused those predictions to be uttered so long ago by the prophets? or have His disciples invented them? Is it thus that the Church, in her extension among the Gentile nations, though once barren, has been made to rejoice now in the possession of more children than that synagogue had which, in its Law or its King, had received, as it were, a husband? or is it thus that this Church has been led to enlarge the place of her tent, and to occupy all nations and tongues, so that now she lengthens her cords beyond the limits to which the rights of the empire of Rome extend, yea, even on to the territories of the Persians and the Indians and other barbarous nations? or that, on the right hand by means of true Christians, and on the left hand by means of pretended Christians, His name is being made known among such a multitude of peoples? […]
54:1.s: The Harmony of the Gospels, Book 1, Chapter 32

54:1.t:
Then he will think of how He again will destroy this, so that perishes the wondrous order, the ornament of kinds, the prescribed course of the creatures, the times and occasions, the harmony of night and day, the useful seasons of the year, the embellished earth, the different kinds sprouting from it; the fine buildings of the cities and the beautiful palaces in them; the continual course of mankind, nature submitted and tormented from man’s entering it until he leaves it.

And how suddenly this wonderful order will be destroyed and how a new world will begin in which no recollection whatever of the first creation will occur to any man’s mind, in which there will be a different mode of life, different deliberations and different thoughts. Then human nature will no longer recollect this world nor the former way of life in it. For the gaze of their mind will be captivated by the sight of that [new] order, and it will not be able to turn in its memory towards the races of flesh and blood; […]

54:2.t: They see this temple here, the holy place of the Trinity, the habitation of sanctity, the holy Church, in which gleam those celestial curtains of which it is said: ‘Enlarge the place of thy tents and of thy curtains; fasten, spare not, lengthen thy cords and strengthen thy stakes; stretch further on the right and on the left; and thy seed shall inherit the Gentiles and thou shalt inhabit the desolate cities.’ The Church, therefore, has its curtains, by which it raises aloft the good life, shields the sinner, and overshadows the fault.

Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles: do not spare: make your cords long, and make your stakes firm. For you shall penetrate to the right and to the left, and your seed shall inherit the nations, and shall inhabit the deserted cities. LXX: Enlarge the place of your tabernacle, and fix the skins of your curtains, do not spare. Lengthen your cords, and strengthen your stakes; yet more to the right, and to the left spread out, and your seed shall possess the nations, and you shall make the deserted cities to be inhabited. To her to whom he had said: Praise, O barren one, who do not bear; break the bonds, by which you were formerly held bound, and cry out in confession of the Lord, you who had no children, it is now commanded, in the likeness of the tabernacle of Moses which he once had (Exod 36) in the desert, that she enlarge her tent and stretch out the skins; […]

54:4.t: Do not fear, for you shall not be confounded, nor shall you blush: for you shall not be ashamed, because you shall forget the confusion of your youth, and shall no more remember the reproach of your widowhood. For He who made you shall rule over you, the Lord of hosts is His name: and your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, shall be called the God of all the earth. LXX: Do not fear, because you have been confounded: nor be confounded, because you have been reproached: for you shall forget the eternal confusion, and of the reproach of your widowhood you shall not be mindful: for the Lord who made you, the Lord Sabaoth is His name: and He who delivered you, the God of Israel, shall be called of all the earth. A question arises: if it is said to the Church gathered from the nations: Rejoice, O barren one, who do not bear; […]

54:5.t: Here indeed we have a wonderful fact, which is not remarked by those few pagans who have remained such,—namely, that this God of the Hebrews who was offended by the conquered, and who was also denied acceptance by the conquerors, is now preached and worshipped among all nations. This is that God of Israel of whom the prophet spake so long time since, when he thus addressed the people of God: "And He who brought thee out, the God of Israel, shall be called (the God) of the whole earth." What was thus prophesied has been brought to pass through the name of the Christ, who comes to men in the form of a descendant of that very Israel who was the grandson of Abraham, with whom the race of the Hebrews began. For it was to this Israel also that it was said, "In thy seed shall all the tribes of the earth be blessed." […]
54:5.s: The Harmony of the Gospels, Book 1, Chapter 14

54:6.t: For the Lord has called you as a woman forsaken and mourning in spirit: and as a wife cast off from her youth, says your God. For a moment, for a little while, I forsook you: and with great mercies I will gather you. In a moment of indignation I hid my face from you for a little while: and with everlasting mercy I have had pity on you, says your redeemer, the Lord. LXX: Not as a woman forsaken and faint-hearted has the Lord called you, nor as a woman who is hated from her youth, says your God. For a little time I left you: and with great mercy I will have pity on you. In a little wrath I turned away my face from you: and with everlasting mercy I will have pity on you: says the Lord who delivered you. Here the friends of the Jews debase the forsaken woman and the wife cast off from her youth, whom the Lord forsook for a moment and for a little while, saying that she is Jerusalem; and that He, hiding His face for a little while, took her up again in everlasting mercies and changed her past grief into joy. […]

54:7.t: I seem indeed to hear that voice, from Him Who gathers together those who are broken, and welcomes the oppressed: Enlarge thy cords, break forth on the right hand and on the left, drive in thy stakes, spare not thy curtains. I have given thee up, and I will help thee. In a little wrath I smote thee, but with everlasting mercy I will glorify thee. The measure of His kindness exceeds the measure of His discipline. The former things were owing to our wickedness, the present things to the adorable Trinity: the former for our cleansing, the present for My glory, Who will glorify them that glorify Me, and I will move to jealousy them that move Me to jealousy. Behold this is sealed up with Me, and this is the indissoluble law of recompense.

54:9.t: Consider and observe, my hearer, that if God had given a hope to Sodom and to her fellows, He would not have overthrown them with fire and brimstone, the sign of the last day of the world, but would have delivered them over to one of the kingdoms to be chastised. As it is written that when Jeremiah caused the nations and kingdoms to drink the cup of wrath, he said concerning each one of the cities, that after they shall drink the cup, I will turn back the captivity of Elam, of Tyre, of Zidon, of the children of Ammon, and of Moab, and of Edom. Concerning each one of these kingdoms he said:—In the last days I well turn back her captivity. Now we see that Tyre was inhabited, and was opulent after she had wandered seventy years, and after she had received the reward of her harlotries and after she had committed fornication with all kingdoms. And she took the harp, and played it sweetly, and multiplied her music. And also the region of Elam is inhabited and opulent. […]

As in the days of Noah, so is this to me, to whom I swore that I would no more bring the waters of Noah upon the earth: so I have sworn not to be angry with you and not to rebuke you. For the mountains shall be moved, and the hills shall tremble: but my mercy shall not depart from you, and the covenant of my peace shall not be moved, says the Lord who has compassion on you. LXX: From the water which was under Noah this is to me: as I swore to him at that time that I would by no means any more be angry with the earth over you, nor in threatening you remove the mountains: nor shall your hills be removed. So neither shall my mercy fail, nor shall the covenant of my peace be taken away, says the Lord who is merciful to you. […]

54:11.t:
And when he had made the ground of all your minds clean and clear, he finally committed it to this all-wise and God-beloved Ruler, who, being endowed with judgment and prudence, as well as with other gifts, and being able to examine and discriminate accurately the minds of those committed to his charge, from the first day, so to speak, down to the present, has not ceased to build. Now he has supplied the brilliant gold, again the refined and unalloyed silver, and the precious and costly stones in all of you, so that again is fulfilled for you in facts a sacred and mystic prophecy, which says,

'Behold I make thy stone a carbuncle, and thy foundations of sapphire, and thy battlements of jasper, and thy gates of crystals, and thy wall of chosen stones; and all thy sons shall be taught of God, and thy children shall enjoy complete peace; and in righteousness shalt thou be built.'

Building therefore in righteousness, he divided the whole people according to their strength. […]

Poor little one, torn by the tempest, without consolation. Behold, I will lay your stones in order: and I will found you on sapphires: and I will make your battlements of jasper, and your gates of carved stones, and all your borders of desirable stones: All your sons taught by the Lord, and a multitude of peace for your sons, and in righteousness you shall be founded. LXX: Lowly and unstable, without consolation. Behold, I prepare for you the carbuncle as your stone, and sapphire as your foundations: and I will make your battlements jasper, and your gates stones of crystal, and your walls choice stones: and all your sons disciples of God, and great peace shall be for your sons, and in righteousness you shall be built. Where we have said: I will lay your stones in order, in the Hebrew is written BAPHPHUCH (בפך), which all except the Seventy have translated alike: I will lay your stones in stibium, in the likeness of an adorned woman who paints her eyes with stibium, so as to signify the beauty of the city. […]

54:12.t: And the walls of the city, or the borders and περίβολος, are built of choice stones, by which we can understand the remaining stones, and that all her sons are taught, or are disciples of God: a testimony the Lord uses in the Gospel of John, saying: No one can come to me unless my Father who sent me draws him, and everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me (John 6:44, 45). And shortly after: It is written in the prophets: They shall all be taught by God. He also speaks through Jeremiah: Putting my laws in their minds, and I will write them on their heart; and they shall no more teach each his neighbor and his brother, saying: Know the Lord. For all shall know me, from the least to the greatest. For I will be merciful to their iniquities, and their sins I will not remember (Jer 31:33, 34). And the teaching of the disciples of God has a multitude of peace, which was left to them by the Lord; […]

54:14.t: Withdraw far from calumny, for you shall not fear; and from terror, for it shall not come near you. LXX: Withdraw from the unjust man, and you shall not fear, and trembling shall not come near you. A most beautiful order. He had consoled the poor and lowly one, promising her spiritual graces. Now he teaches what she ought to do if she does not wish to dread the assaults of her adversaries. And the sense is: You do not wish to fear your enemies? Do what I say: Withdraw far from calumny, or from iniquity, for all iniquity and plunder is born of calumny; and you shall not fear, and trembling and terror shall not come near you, so that you fear not men but God, saying with Moses: I am trembling and fearful (Deut 9:19); and with one of Job's friends: Horror and trembling came upon me, and shook my bones greatly (Job 4:14); and with the prophet: At the voice of my prayer trembling entered into my bones (Hab 3:16); […]

54:15.t: Behold, the sojourner shall come who was not with me; he who was once a stranger to you shall be joined to you. LXX: Behold, proselytes shall come to you through me, and they shall be your settlers, and shall flee to you for refuge. These things too the Jews think are said to Jerusalem: that many of the nations will be proselytes and will take up the law of Moses and its ceremonies. We, according to the interpretation we have begun, refer this to the Church, which has been gathered through the apostles from both peoples, which has neither spot nor wrinkle, which is free, and the mother of all believers (Eph 5; Gal 4). To gather these proselytes and strangers the Lord sent His disciples, saying: Teach all nations (Matt 28:19), so that they might flee to the Gospel and take up the new Law, and that those who were once dwellers in idolatry might become settlers of the Church. Of them it is said in the psalms: The Lord makes the blind wise. […]

54:16.t: Behold, I have created the smith who blows the coals in the fire, and brings forth a vessel for his work: and I have created the slayer to destroy. Every vessel that is fashioned against you shall not prosper: and every tongue that resists you in judgment you shall judge. This is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord: and their righteousness is with me, says the Lord. LXX: Behold, I have created you, not as a coppersmith blowing the coals in the fire and bringing forth a vessel for work. But I have created you not for perdition, to destroy: every vessel that is made against you shall not prosper: and every voice shall rise against you in judgment: you shall overcome them all ÷ and they shall be liable to you in it ⁚ There is an inheritance for those who serve the Lord, and you shall be righteous to me, says the Lord. Let us speak first according to the Hebrew: If you wish not to fear, and that dread be far from you, do what the preceding discourse has related; […]

Further, according to the Seventy this seems to me the sense: I, your Creator, have not made you as the devil, that worst of smiths, forges vessels of iniquity with an unclean spirit and brings them forth to perdition; and he ought to know that vessels of this kind do not have a prosperous course, but are broken in mid-career. What the vessels are he shows in the following words: And every voice that shall rise against you in judgment, you shall overcome them all. The vessels of iniquity have a voice, and this voice rises against the Church when the heretics set their mouth on high and their tongue passes through the earth. And what follows, And they shall be liable to you in it, we have marked beforehand with an obelus, because it seems to have been added not so much by the Seventy as by bad copyists. And when the Church has overcome every voice that rises against her, then those who serve and obey the Lord will have an inheritance, an eternal possession; […]

54:17.t: And all who have been fashioned against you by the blowing smith shall not prosper, but shall feel both present punishments and those to come. And what before seemed hidden is said more plainly in what follows: And every tongue that resists you in judgment you shall judge, destroying the wisdom of the wise and rejecting the prudence of the prudent. And all the leaders of the heretics, and the teachers of the Jews, and the philosophers of the world, whom that smith had forged, you will condemn by your judgment; as the Queen of Sheba also condemned the unbelievers, and the Ninevites; and on the contrary Sodom will be justified by comparison with a worse Jerusalem (Matt 12). After this he adds what the rewards to come are, lest they think the contest is in vain and ends with the present death. […]

55:1.t: But if without any labour and trouble at all you may obtain that which you desire, what folly it is to put off the gift: "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters," Esaias invites you, "and he that hath no money, come buy wine and milk, without money and without price." O swiftness of His mercy: O easiness of the Covenant: This blessing may be bought by you merely for willing it; He accepts the very desire as a great price; He thirsts to be thirsted for; He gives to drink to all who desire to drink; He takes it as a kindness to be asked for the kindness; He is ready and liberal; He gives with more pleasure than others receive. Only let us not be condemned for frivolity by asking for little, and for what is unworthy of the Giver.

He then who is wise is free, bought with the price of the heavenly oracles, with that gold, that silver of the Divine Word; bought with the price of blood (for it is no small thing to acknowledge one's Redeemer;) bought with the price of Grace: he who heard and understood the words, Ho every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money, come ye, buy and drink and eat.

All you who thirst, come to the waters, and you who have no money, hasten, buy and eat: come, buy without silver and without any exchange wine and milk. Why do you weigh out silver not for bread, and your labor not for fullness? LXX: You who thirst, go to the water, and as many as have no money, go, buy, and eat, and walk, and buy without money and without price wine and fat. Why do you buy with money, and your labor not for fullness? The Hebrew word OI (הוי), of which I had said above, in the prophecy against Ariel (cf. Isa 29), that it was ambiguous, and signified either the interjection of one calling or woe, set here at the beginning of the passage, is read not with the feeling of one lamenting but of one calling. […]

THE prophet Isaiah bids those who embrace a life of piety towards Christ to go to the proclamations of the Gospel, saying, "You who thirst, go to the waters." But these waters are not the material waters of earth, but rather are divine and spiritual, poured forth for us by Christ Himself. For He is the river of peace, and the torrent of pleasure, and the fountain of life. And so we have heard Himself plainly saying, "Whosoever thirsts, let him come to Me and drink."
55:1.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

55:2.t: And at the same time he rebukes those who follow worldly wisdom and the perverse and feigned doctrines of the heretics, and the traditions of the Pharisees, and all knowledge falsely so called which is lifted up against God, and who at great prices and with unceasing labor weigh out silver for a discipline in which there is no bread, and sweat for foods in which there is no fullness. From this it is shown that the wisdom to be pursued is the one which lies not in the leaves and flower of words but in the marrow and fruits of meanings; which does not fly past the ear but refreshes the mind. To learn it we do not cross the seas, nor do we need great expense, but the word is near, in our mouth and in our heart.

Hear, you who hear me, and eat what is good, and your soul shall delight in fatness. Incline your ear, and come to me: hear, and your soul shall live. And I will strike with you an everlasting covenant: the faithful mercies of David. LXX: Hear me, and eat good things, and your soul shall delight in good things. Attend with your ears, and follow my ways: and hear me, and your soul shall live in good things. And I will establish for you an eternal testament, the faithful holy things of David. Lest anyone think that the hearing to which the divine word exhorts those who are to hear is of the flesh and not of the mind, it promises them good things not of the flesh but of the soul. For if, he says, you hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land (Isa 1:19). Or the good: He who says, I am the good shepherd (John 10:11). And your soul shall delight in good things and in fatness. […]

55:3.t: Finally he adds: Hear me, and your soul shall live (Isa 55:3). The promise of all good things is life everlasting. If you are willing to hear, and your soul lives forever, I will strike with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David. Of these the same Psalmist sang: The mercies of the Lord I will sing forever. From generation to generation I will proclaim your truth (Ps 88 [89]:1, 2). And so that we may know what these mercies are, he shows in the following words: Once I have sworn by my holy one: if I lie to David, his seed shall remain forever, and his throne as the sun in my sight, and as the full moon forever, and a faithful witness in heaven. He is called faithful for this reason, that He has fulfilled His promises. For these the Seventy translated the faithful holy things of David (Acts 13:34), which can be taken as firm and strong; as is this: All His commandments are faithful, confirmed for ever and ever (Ps 110 [111]:8). […]

God moreover said by Isaiah, "And I will make with them an everlasting covenant, even the holy, the sure things of David: behold I have given Him as a testimony among the gentiles, a ruler and commander of the gentiles." For it was fitting that Moses, as a servant, should be the minister of the shadow that endureth not: but Christ, I affirm, was the eternal publisher of a lasting and abiding worship. And what is the eternal covenant? It means the sacred prophecies of Christ, Who is of David's seed according to the flesh, and which produce in us holiness, and sureness: just as also the fear of God is pure, because it makes us pure: and the word of the Gospel is life, because it produces life: "for the words, He says, "that I have spoken unto you are spirit and life," that is, spiritual and life-giving. But mark well the exactness of the prophecy. […]
55:3.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

55:4.t: Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and teacher to the nations. Behold, you shall call a nation which you did not know: and nations which have not known you shall run to you, because of the Lord your God and the Holy One of Israel, because He has glorified you. LXX: Behold, I have given him as a testimony among the nations, a prince and commander to the nations: nations which did not know you shall call upon you: and peoples who were ignorant of you shall flee to you for refuge: because of the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, who has glorified you. He had summoned the people of the Jews to believe, to incline their ear and receive the everlasting covenant which the Lord had promised to David, and to Abraham and his seed, saying: In your seed the nations shall be blessed (Gen 22:18). The apostle Paul, explaining this: He did not say, he says, in seeds, but, in seed, which is Christ (Gal 3:16). […]

55:6.t: And wherefore, my beloved? For it is right that we should search into the apostolic mind. Not only in the beginning of the Epistles, but towards their close, and in the middle of them, he used persuasions and admonitions. I hope therefore that, by your prayers, I shall in no respect falsely represent the plan of that holy man. As he was well skilled in these divine matters, and knew the power of the divine teaching, he deemed it necessary, in the first place, to make known the word concerning Christ, and the mystery regarding Him; and then afterwards to point to the correction of habits, so that when they had learned to know the Lord, they might earnestly desire to do those things which He commanded. For when the Guide to the laws is unknown, one does not readily pass on to the observance of them. Faithful Moses, the minister of God, adopted this method; […]

Seek the Lord while He can be found: call upon Him while He is near. Let the ungodly man forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and He will have mercy on him, and to our God: for He is abundant in forgiving. LXX: Seek the Lord: and when you have found Him, call upon Him. And after He has drawn near to you, let the ungodly man forsake his ways and the unrighteous man his thoughts and return to the Lord: and he shall obtain mercy: for He will abundantly forgive your sins. Since, then, as we have already said before, you would not receive the everlasting covenant and the faithful mercies of David, which, when you were unwilling to take them up, the throng of the Gentiles took up, I the Prophet warn you, my own people, and solemnly charge you: while there is time, do penance. Turn to Him who now speaks to you through the Prophets, who afterward will speak in person. Seek Him while He can be found, while you are in the body, while room for repentance is given; […]

How then am I to seek for you, Lord? When I seek for you, my God, my quest is for the happy life. I will seek you that "my soul may live," for my body derives life from my soul, and my soul derives life from you.… Is not the happy life that which all desire, which indeed no one fails to desire?

And yet the prophet Isaiah testifies, that the Lord God can be found when He is sought, when he says: "Seek ye the Lord; and as soon as ye have found Him, call upon Him: and when He has drawn near to you, let the wicked man forsake his ways, and the unrighteous man his thoughts." If, then, when sought, He can be found, why is it said, "Seek ye His face evermore?" Is He perhaps to be sought even when found? For things incomprehensible must so be investigated, as that no one may think he has found nothing, when he has been able to find how incomprehensible that is which he was seeking. Why then does he so seek, if he comprehends that which he seeks to be incomprehensible, unless because he may not give over seeking so long as he makes progress in the inquiry itself into things incomprehensible, and becomes ever better and better while seeking so great a good, which is both sought in order to be found, and found in order to be sought? […]

55:7.t: Nor is it enough to seek the Lord, and to find Him while it is the time of repentance, and to call upon Him while He is near, unless the ungodly man forsakes his former ways and the old thoughts by which he had turned aside from the Lord. For then we shall return to the Lord, who will have mercy on us, and to the most clement father, who is abundant in mercies and ready to forgive, when we have forsaken our former thoughts and ways, so that afterward we may deserve to hear: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered (Ps 31 [32]:1).

55:8.t: Do not want to be more merciful than God, or rather, if you wish it, you will not be able, not even in the least degree. How should you? As far as the heaven is from the earth, Scripture says, so far are My counsels from your counsels: and again, If ye, He says, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more your heavenly Father? But in fact this talk is mere pretext and subterfuge. Let us not prevaricate with God's commandments.

For my thoughts are not your thoughts: nor are your ways my ways, says the Lord. For as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are my ways exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts. LXX: For my thoughts are not as your thoughts: nor are your ways as my ways, says the Lord. But as far as heaven is distant from the earth, so far is my way distant from your ways, and your thoughts from my thought. Do not think, he says, that what I promise is difficult, and let it not seem incredible to you that the ungodly and the unrighteous can be saved, whether the people of the Jews or all those among the nations who did not know God: consider this, that there is a great difference between my counsels and yours, and as great a diversity of will as of nature (Prov 19). For many are the thoughts in the heart of a man, but the counsel of the Lord abides forever. You, as men, often repenting of a promise, have overturned your old will with a new will. […]

See here, I pray, how great is the difference between us and God: for the distance is immeasurable. For He is slow to anger, and long-suffering, and of incomparable gentleness and love to mankind: but we children of earth are quick unto anger, hasty unto impatience, and refuse with indignation to be judged by others when we are found out in committing any wrong act; while we are most ready to find fault with others. And therefore God the Lord of all affirms, saying; "For My thoughts are not as your thoughts, nor your ways as My ways; but as the heaven is far from the earth, so are My ways from your ways, and My thoughts from your thoughts." Such, then, is He Who is Lord of all: but we, as I said, being readily vexed, and easily led into anger, take sometimes severe and intolerable vengeance upon those who have occasioned us some trifling annoyance: and though commanded to live according to the Gospel, we fall short of the practice commanded by the law. For the law indeed said, "Eye for eye; tooth for tooth; […]
55:8.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

55:9.t: Do you wish to know the difference between my counsel and yours? As far as heaven is distant in place from the earth, and the dwelling of the Angels is one thing and that of men another, so far are my thoughts separated from your counsels. For of my thoughts it is said: His judgments are inscrutable, and His ways past finding out (Rom 11:33). But of yours: They devised a counsel which they could not establish (Ps 20 [21]:12). And in another place: Whatever counsel you have entered upon shall be scattered, and whatever you have spoken shall not remain among you (Isa 8:10). Things that are clear need no interpretation; therefore they are touched on briefly rather than discussed.

55:10.t: And concerning all this that I have explained to thee, that those dead persons were raised with two words each, it was because for them two resurrections take place; that former one, and the second, that which is to come. For in that resurrection in which all men shall rise, none shall fall again; and by one word of God, sent forth through Christ, all the dead shall rise in the twinkling of an eye, speedily. For He Who brings it to pass is not feeble or insufficient. For with one word of summons He will cause all the ends (of the world) to hear, and all that are laid (in the grave) shall leap forth and rise up; and no word shall return void to Him that sent it forth, but as it is written in the Prophet Isaiah, who compares the word to rain and snow; […]
55:10.s: Demonstration 8 (Of the Resurrection of the Dead), Section 15

55:10.t: Or certainly this is to be said, that the word of the Gospel's teaching is called rain, and the showers which the spiritual clouds pour upon the good earth, the clouds to which the truth of God reaches. This rain and these showers Moses promises in the Song of Deuteronomy (Deut 32:1, 2): Let the earth hear the words of my mouth: let my speech be awaited as the rain, and let my words come down as the dew; so that those who have sown in tears may reap in joy (Ps 125 [126]). And let those who have sown in righteousness and in the spirit reap the fruit of life everlasting, and receive the bread of the Gospel's teaching, of which it is written in Proverbs and in Ecclesiastes: Open your eyes, and be filled with bread (Prov 20:13); and again: Cast your bread upon the water, for in the multitude of your days you will find it (Eccl 11:1). […]

And as the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and will not return thither again; but they soak the earth, and water it, and make it spring up, and give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be which goes forth from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall do whatever I willed, and shall prosper in the things for which I sent it. LXX: As if the rain or the snow should come down from heaven, and not return until it soaks the earth, and it bring forth and spring up, and give seed to the sower and bread for eating: so shall my word be which has gone forth from my mouth: it shall not return until it accomplishes what I willed, and I will make its ways and my precepts prosperous. What is said hangs on what went before, and briefly the sense is this: let the people of the nations not be incredulous that after such great crimes the ungodly man is suddenly saved. […]
