By means of diffusion, as of brightness out of light, of heat out of fire, of a river out of its headspring, of rain out of a full or humid cloud. In the first diffusion, equality is lacking, for brightness is not the same as light. In the second, closeness is lacking, for heat is not close to fire, since it is the principle neither of its form nor of its origin, but is merely an accident. In the third, simultaneity is lacking, for a spring diffuses itself by flowing, and not all at once. In the fourth, fullness is lacking, for not all of the rain is drawn out of a cloud, but only successive drops. Now, join these four conditions to a single diffusion, one of splendor having equality, of heat having closeness and substantiality, of a river or fountain having simultaneity, and of rain having fullness: and in this way, you will have a trace of the eternal generation.

Hence, the Son is sometimes compared to brightness: "Being the brightness of His glory," etc.; […]

55:11.t: According to the anagogy the understanding is twofold: the word of the Lord is either He of whom it is written: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1), who will not return to Him empty unless He has done the Father's will, and fulfilled all the things for which He had been embodied, and reconciled the world to God. He is said to proceed from the mouth, and from the womb and belly: not that God has these members, but that we may learn the nature of the Lord through our own words.

55:12.t: For you shall go out in gladness, and be led forth in peace. The mountains and the hills shall sing praise before you, and all the trees of the country shall clap their hands. Instead of the saliunca the fir shall come up, and instead of the nettle the myrtle shall grow. And the Lord shall be named for an everlasting sign, which shall not be taken away. LXX: In gladness you shall go out, and in joy you shall be led forth. The mountains and the hills shall leap, awaiting you with joy, and all the trees of the field shall applaud with their branches. And instead of the στοιβὴ (that is, the most worthless stalks) the cypress shall come up: and instead of the conyza the myrtle shall come up. And the Lord shall be for a name and for an everlasting sign, and it shall not fail. My word, he says, shall not return empty, but after it has fulfilled all that I willed, and done my will on earth, then it will come to me; […]

55:13.t: And not only shall the mountains and hills leap and sing, and all the trees of the field which the Lord has blessed clap with their branches and applaud with their hands, but the στοιβή too and the κονύζη, or the saliunca and the nettle, shall be turned into the fir and the myrtle and the cypress. Στοιβή, according to Symmachus and the Seventy, is written in the Hebrew NESUS (נעצוץ), which Aquila and Theodotion interpreted as κονύζην. Now κονύζη is a most worthless and bitter herb, of a very foul smell. And where the Seventy translated κονύζη, the word which in the Hebrew is SARPHOD (סרפד), Symmachus rendered nettle. However the proper sense of the names stands, this is to be said: that evil things are turned into good, and virtues spring up in place of vices, that is, righteousness in place of iniquity, fortitude in place of rashness, temperance in place of luxury, prudence in place of folly. […]

Of the abatement of this heat it is said to her by Isaiah, by promise of the Lord, "Instead of the ground willow shall come up the fir-tree, and instead of the nettle shall come up the myrtle tree." For 'instead of the ground willow there comes up in her the fir-tree,' when in the heart of the Saints, instead of the sunkenness of earthly thought, the elevation of heavenly contemplation rises up. Now the nettle is altogether of a fiery nature. But the myrtle is said to be of cooling virtue, and therefore 'instead of the nettle there comes up the myrtle tree,' when the minds of the righteous are brought from the irritation and heat of bad habits to coolness and quietness of the thoughts, while they now no longer seek earthly things, while they extinguish the flames of the flesh by heavenly aspirations.
55:13.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 18, Section 32

56:1.t: Thus says the Lord: Keep judgment, and do righteousness: for my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed. For righteousness the Seventy translated mercy; the rest alike. The prophecy about the nations being ended, which at the coming of the word of God are to be changed from saliunca and nettle into cypress and myrtle, Isaiah speaks to the hearers of that time, that they should do all things that are right and prepare themselves for the coming of the Savior, because He Himself is the righteousness and mercy of God. For if the thoughts of the Saints are judgments, and we ought to have senses trained for discerning good and evil, why should we not at all times keep judgment, so as not to despise the person of the poor man in judgment, nor be frightened by the power of the rich, but judge the great as we judge the small, knowing, according to Moses, that judgment belongs to the Lord, who judges those who judge (Deut 1)? […]

56:2.t: Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who lays hold of it: keeping the sabbath, so as not to profane it: keeping his hands, so as not to do any evil. LXX: Blessed is the man who shall do these things, and the man who holds them fast, and keeps the sabbaths, so as not to profane them, and guards his hands, so as not to do iniquity. He who can say with the apostle Paul: When I was a little child, I spoke as a little child; I understood as a little child, I thought as a little child; when I became a man, I destroyed the things that belong to a little child (1 Cor 13:11): he obtains the present blessedness, forgetting the things that are past and stretching himself forward to what is to come, until he attains to the unity of the faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, to the perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ; so that that psalm can be fitted to him: Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly (Ps 1:1). […]

56:3.t: What does it mean that the Law calls those accursed who have not left seed in Israel, while through Isaiah it is said that eunuchs suffer no disadvantage, because they cannot generate offspring? — Because it had begun to be understood in a way different from how it was spoken, therefore the prophet Isaiah later showed in what sense it had been said. For since this had been set down in the manner of a sentence of judgment on account of God’s displeasure, because those who abandoned God were struck in this way, that even though they took wives they would not leave offspring, human error seized on this as if those would be guilty before God who either did not want wives, or, having taken them, could not generate children as is usual; as though God sought nothing else but offspring, just as they are criticized through the prophet Malachi. […]
56:3.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 17: ON EUNUCHS AND LEAVING NO SEED IN ISRAEL

56:3.t: And let not the son of the stranger who cleaves to the Lord say: The Lord will divide me from His people with a separation: and let not the eunuch say: Behold, I am a dry tree. LXX: Let not the foreigner who has been joined to the Lord say: Do you think the Lord will separate me from His people? and let not the eunuch say: For I am a dry tree. Those who understand this passage in a lowly way refer what is said to proselytes from the nations and to eunuchs in the literal sense: that both strangers, if they have taken up the law of the Lord and are circumcised, and eunuchs, such as was that eunuch of Queen Candace (Acts 8), who could not be idle even on a journey, and, while he sought an interpreter of his reading, found Christ whom he was seeking, are not strangers to the salvation of God. And this, they say, is said against the Jews, who boast of the nobility of their race, and say that they are sons of Abraham, and think those blessed who have seed in Zion and kinsfolk in Jerusalem (John 8). […]

Those who please me are those who choose to be eunuchs voluntarily.… Who can receive this teaching, let him receive it. It is a matter of great faith and great virtue to be the purest kind of temple of God, in that one dedicates oneself completely to the Lord as a burnt offering and to be holy in body as well as spirit. Those are eunuchs who, thinking themselves to be "dry trees" because of their infertility, hear through Isaiah that instead of sons and daughters they will have a place prepared in heaven. Of this sort were Ebedmelech in Jeremiah and that eunuch of Queen Candace.

56:4.t: For thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: If they keep my sabbaths, and choose the things I have willed, and hold fast my covenant, I will give them in my house and within my walls a place, and a name better than sons and daughters: an everlasting name I will give them, which shall not perish. LXX: Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: Those who keep my sabbaths, and choose the things that I will, and hold fast my testament, I will give them in my house and within my wall a renowned place, better than sons and daughters: an everlasting name I will give them, and it shall not fail. He had set forth two, proselytes and eunuchs. He speaks first of the eunuchs, and gives them precepts for living, and promises them the rewards to come; and after them he comes to the proselytes, promising them also like things. […]

56:5.t: And all the pure virgins who are betrothed to Christ shall light their lamps and with the Bridegroom shall they go into the marriage chamber. All those that are betrothed to Christ are far removed from the curse of the Law, and are redeemed from the condemnation of the daughters of Eve; for they are not wedded to men so as to receive the curses and come into the pains. They take no thought of death, because they do not deliver children to him. And in place of a mortal husband, they are betrothed to Christ. And because they do not bear children, there is Given to them the name that is better than sons and daughters. And instead of the groans of the daughters of Eve, they utter the songs of the Bridegroom. The wedding-feast of the daughters of Eve continues for but seven days; but for these (virgins) is the Bridegroom who departs not for ever. The adornment of the daughters of Eve is wool that wears out and perishes, but the garments of these wear not out. […]

And what could be greater than the reward the Lord bestowed upon His mother, whom He honored above all others? For He deemed no gift more abundant than virginity, as Scripture teaches us. For thus the Lord spoke through Isaiah: Let not the eunuch say, I am but a dry tree. Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: Whoever keeps my commandments, and chooses what I desire, and embraces my covenant, I will give them a place in my house and on my wall, a name better than sons and daughters, an everlasting name will I give them, which shall not be cut off. He promises others that they will not fail: did he allow his mother to fail? But Mary does not fail, the teacher of virginity does not fail; nor could it be possible that she who carried God would think of carrying a human being.
56:5.s: On the Instruction of the Virgin and the Perpetual Virginity of Mary, 6.45

56:6.t: And the sons of the stranger who cleave to the Lord, to worship Him and to love His name, so as to be His servants: everyone who keeps the sabbath so as not to profane it, and holds fast my covenant, I will bring them to my holy mountain, and I will make them joyful in my house of prayer. LXX: And to the foreigners who have been added to the Lord to serve Him, and to love His name, so as to be His servants ÷ and handmaids ⁚ and all who keep my sabbaths so as not to violate them, and hold fast my testament, I will bring them into my holy mountain, and I will make them joyful in my house of prayer. After the eunuchs he passes to the foreigners whom he had named before, and to them also he promises rewards: that if they serve Him, and pass from servitude to the love of His name, they shall be His servants; such as was the Apostle Paul too, who writes at the beginning of his Epistles: Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ (Rom 1:1); and Moses, the servant of God (Heb 3). […]

56:7.t: Whoever, then, does these things, God will bring him to His holy mountain and fill him with gladness in His house of prayer. The holy mountain is either the doctrines of truth and the confession of the Trinity, or the Lord Himself, to whom in the last time (according to this same Isaiah and the prophet Micah) very many nations shall flow together (Isa 2; Mic 4). And the house of prayer is the Church, which is spread throughout the whole world, and not the Temple of the Jews, which was confined within the very narrow bounds of the land of Judea.

Their holocausts and their victims shall please me upon my altar: for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples, says the Lord God, who gathers the scattered of Israel: I will yet gather to him his gathered ones. All you beasts of the field, come to devour, all you beasts of the forest. LXX: Their holocausts and victims shall be acceptable upon my altar. For my house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations, says the Lord, who gathers the scattered of Israel: for I will gather to him a congregation. All you wild beasts, come, eat, all you beasts of the forest. The difference between sacrifices and holocausts we learn more fully in Leviticus. Holocausts are those which are burned whole upon the altar; victims and sacrifices are those of which part is offered to the altar and part is given to the priests. It is not to be believed, then, that the sacrifices of the foreigners and the eunuchs are required according to the Jewish rite. […]

56:8.t: These things the Lord promised would be, He who gathers the scattered of Israel; to whom the Apostle Peter also writes an Epistle; of whom the Evangelist says: This he did not say of himself, but, being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but that He might gather into one the sons of God who were scattered (John 11:51, 52); and that might be fulfilled which was said: The congregation of the peoples shall surround you: for its sake return on high (Ps 7:8).

56:9.t: And when the remnant of Israel had been gathered through the Apostles, and those who before had been scattered had been brought into one flock, all the beasts are summoned to come and devour Israel, namely those who would not believe, of whom the Apostle says: For the end shall come upon them (Phil 3). And the Lord in the Gospel: But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its consummation has come (Luke 21:20). Or this is to be said: that they were handed over to be devoured by the beasts which the Prophet abhors, saying: Do not deliver to the beasts the souls that confess to you (Ps 73 [74]:19). Of these beasts, tropologically, which devoured a certain portion of the Lord, we have read above also (cf. Isa 9): Syria from the rising of the sun, and the Greeks from the West, who devour Israel with their whole mouth. And in Jeremiah: Israel is a wandering sheep, the lions have driven it out: first the king of Assyria devoured it, and last the king of Babylon shall break its bones (Jer 50:17). […]

56:10.t: Great is this mystery, beloved, which he provided and showed (as) His sign to Gideon. For He said to him: "Everyone who laps the water as a dog laps is fit to go to battle." And from every living creature which has been created there is not one which loves his master and keeps watch over him by day and by night as does a dog, and even when his master beats him severely he does not depart from him, and when he goes forth to the hunt with his master and a powerful lion meets his master he delivers himself over to death instead of his master. So are those strong who have been put to the test by the water; they follow their Master as the dogs, and they delivert themselves over to death for Him, and carry on His struggle valiant ly, and keep watch over Him by day and by night, and they roar like the dogs while they meditate upon the law day and night (cf. Heb. Ps. […]

What shall I say about dogs who have a natural instinct to show gratitude and to serve as watchful guardians of their masters’ safety? Hence Scripture cries out to the ungrateful, the slothful, and the craven: ‘Dumb dogs, not able to bark.’ To dogs, therefore, is given the ability to bark in defense of their masters and their homes. Thus you should learn to use your voice for the sake of Christ, when ravening wolves attack His sheepfold. Have the word ready on your lips, lest, like a silent watch-dog, you may appear because of your unfaithfulness to abandon the post entrusted to you. Such a dog was the friend and companion of an angel. Not without reason did Raphael in the prophetic book cause this dog to accompany the son of Tobias when he went on a journey, in order to drive out Asmodeus and thereby confirm the marriage. The demon is driven out as the result of a grateful recognition and the union is stabilized.

His watchmen are all blind, they have all not known: dumb dogs, not able to bark, seeing vain things, sleeping, and loving dreams. And the most shameless dogs have not known fullness: the shepherds themselves have not known understanding: all have turned aside into their own way, each to his own avarice, from the highest to the last. Come, let us take wine, and be filled with drunkenness, and it shall be as today, so also tomorrow, and much more. LXX: See how they have all been blinded: they have all not known, dumb dogs, they will not be able to bark: dreaming of a bed, loving slumbers. And dogs shameless of soul have not known fullness. And they are evil, not knowing understanding: they have all followed their own ways. Each one alike from its summit. Come and let us take wine, and be drunk, and let tomorrow be such a day, great, exceedingly more ⁚. […]

Nor were they content with this end, they who slept in guarding the Lord's flock, and could not bark, and loved their couch, by which the pleasure of the body is indicated; but among their own, shameless of soul, they have not known fullness, they who are never sated with their error; who devour the people of the Lord as a meal of bread, and the houses of widows, and serve gluttony and lust. For they cannot say: The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes (Ps 18 [19]:9), nor know what is written: A man's wisdom enlightens his face (Prov 17:24). And they are dumb dogs against the enemies, of whom it is written: Do not give what is holy to the dogs (Matt 7:6). And sleeping dogs, who do not know the precept: Do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids (Ps 131 [132]); and again: Watch, for you do not know at what hour your Lord will come (Matt 24:42). And therefore, giving place to the devil, they are most shameless dogs, which are never sated. […]

If this is said of the princes of the Jews, because of whom the people of the Lord was devoured by the beasts, let us avoid the examples of the worse; let us not be drunk with wine, in which is luxury, nor be overwhelmed by pleasures; let us not be dumb in speaking and ravening dogs against our adversaries; but let us follow the ways of God rather than our own, and hear the Scripture warning us: Think of the Lord in goodness (Wis 1:1). And again: Understanding is best for those who practice it. And if we have been dogs, let us not despair of salvation, hearing the words of the Canaanite woman saying to the Lord: Yes, Lord, for the little dogs also eat of the crumbs that fall from their masters' table (Matt 15:27). For this reason she obtained mercy, and heard from the Lord: O woman, great is your faith: be it done to you as you will. For she could say with the Prophet: I have run the way of your commandments (Ps 118 [119]:32). And again: Lead me in the right way.

For even some dogs have been reproved by the Prophet Isaiah, not because they were dogs, but because they knew not how to bark, and loved to sleep. In which place indeed he hath shown, that if they had watched and barked for their Lord, they would have been praiseworthy dogs: just as they are praised, of whom is said, “The tongue of Thy dogs.”…

Sometimes in sacred speech preachers are understood by dogs. For the tongue of a dog, when it licks a wound, heals it, because holy teachers too, when they instruct us in the confession of our sin, touch as it were the wound of the mind through their tongue; and because by speaking they rescue us from sins, by touching wounds as it were they restore us to health. For that by the name of dogs the tongue of preachers is signified, the Lord says through the Psalmist: "The tongue of your dogs from enemies, from him." For from the unbelieving Jews the holy preachers were chosen, who, coming against thieves and robbers in defense of the truth, gave great barkings, so to speak, for the Lord. Against this it is said of certain reprobates: "Dumb dogs, not able to bark." Because therefore holy preachers condemn sins, but approve the confession of sins, saying: "Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved," dogs lick the sores of Lazarus.

56:11.t: That these watchmen and dogs are the same as the shepherds the following words show: The shepherds themselves have not known understanding. For the Hebrew word ROIM (רעים), which is written with four letters, res and ain and jod and mem, if it is read roim, means shepherds; if raim, the worst. We have said this to show the causes of the varying interpretation. For all have sought their own things, and not the things that are God's, nor have they walked in the way of the Lord (Phil 2), of which it is written: Seek which is the good way, and walk in it (Jer 6:16). But according to what is read in the volume of Judges: There was no king in Israel; each one did what seemed right to himself (Judg 17:6), and followed his own errors.

And what follows: Each to his own avarice, from the highest to the last: come, let us take wine, and be filled with drunkenness, and it shall be as today, so also tomorrow, and much more, is not found in the Seventy Translators, but has been added from the Hebrew and is marked beforehand with shining stars. In short, none of the Church's interpreters has expounded these little verses, but they leap over them and pass them by, as if a pit lay open in the middle of the road. And what he says is this: since, turning aside from the way of the Lord, they have followed their own paths, therefore they burn with avarice from the highest to the last, from the princes to the common people, so that, after they have begun to beat their fellow servants, and to eat and drink with the drunken, they say: Come, let us take wine, and be filled with drunkenness. Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. And it shall be as today, so also tomorrow, and much more (1 Cor 15:32). […]

For often improvident rulers, fearing to lose human favour, shrink timidly from speaking freely the things that are right; and, according to the voice of the Truth, serve unto the custody of the flock by no means with the zeal of shepherds, but in the way of hirelings; since they fly when the wolf cometh if they hide themselves under silence. For hence it is that the Lord through the prophet upbraids them, saying, "Dumb dogs, that cannot bark." Hence again He complains, saying, "Ye have not gone up against the enemy, neither opposed a wall for the house of Israel, to stand in the battle in the day of the Lord."
56:11.s: The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 2, Chapter 4

57:1.t: The righteous man has perished, and there is none who reflects on it in his heart: and men of mercy are gathered, for there is none who understands: for the righteous man has been gathered away from the face of malice. Let peace come: let him rest in his bed, who walks in his uprightness. LXX: See how the righteous man has perished, and no one takes it to heart: and righteous men are taken away, and no one considers. For the righteous man has been taken away from the face of iniquity: his burial shall be in peace: it has been taken away from the midst. Because of the blind watchmen and the dumb dogs, who are themselves the shepherds, not knowing understanding, who are not sated with present pleasures but are always preparing themselves for future ones, the righteous man has perished, of whom Pilate's wife says: Have nothing to do with that righteous man (Matt 27:19). And Pilate, having washed his hands: I am innocent, he says, of the blood of this righteous man. […]

The Jews think that both this and the rest that follow are to be understood either generally of all the righteous, whose blood Manasseh shed, and filled Jerusalem from gate to gate; or else that Isaiah prophesies of his own death, because he was to be sawn by Manasseh with a wooden saw, which is a most certain tradition among them. Hence most of our own writers also refer what is set down in the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning the passion of the Saints, They were sawn asunder (Heb 11:37), to the passion of Isaiah.

“Deliver,” then, “the poor man, and save the needy from the hands of the ungodly” (ver. 4). This is said that it might be known, that in that nation where Christ was born and put to death, those persons were not guiltless of so great a crime, who being so numerous, that, as the Gospel says, the Jews feared them, and therefore dared not lay hands on Christ, afterwards consented, and permitted Him to be slain by the malicious and envious Jewish rulers: yet if they had so willed, they would still have been feared, so that the hands of the wicked would never have prevailed against Him. For of these it is said elsewhere, “Dumb dogs, they know not how to bark.” Of them too is that said, “Lo, how the righteous perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart.” He perished as far as lay in them who would have Him to perish; for how could He perish by dying, who in that way rather was seeking again what had perished? […]

The malice and wickedness of them that remain behind in the world deserveth that those should quickly be taken away, who by their life might much help us: and for as much as the world draweth towards an end, God's chosen servants are taken out of it, that they fall not into more wicked times: and therefore from hence it cometh that the prophet saith: "The just man doth perish, and there is none that doth ponder it in his heart: and men of mercy are gathered together, because there is none that hath understanding." And yet do I not think that all God's elect servants are so taken out of the world, that none but the wicked remain behind: for sinners would never be converted to the sorrow of true penance, if they had not the examples of some good people to provoke them forward.

57:2.t: And as for what is said according to the Hebrew, Let peace come, let him rest in his bed: let him walk in his uprightness, the sense indeed is clear, but the sequence of the words, which stands in the idiom of its own language, seems disordered in ours. And what he says is this: Let the peace of the Righteous One come, which, ascending to the Father, He left to the Apostles, saying: My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you (John 14:27). And when the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, has come, His Apostles will rest in their beds, and their death will rest. By this he shows that the martyrs do not perish but conquer, and rest in an eternal seat. But He Himself whose peace it is, and whose Apostles rest in their beds, walks in His uprightness, ascending as victor to the Father by a straight road. […]

57:3.t: But draw near hither, you sons of the sorceress, seed of the adulterer and of the harlot. Against whom have you made sport? Against whom have you opened wide the mouth and thrust out the tongue? LXX: But draw near hither, you lawless sons, seed of adulterers and of a harlot. In what have you made sport? Against whom have you opened your mouth, and against whom have you thrust out your tongue? The righteous man having been taken away, whose burial is in peace, or rather having been taken out of the midst, you who are sons of iniquity, draw near to me and hear what I shall say (John 8). For just as he who commits iniquity is a slave of iniquity, so he who, like Judas the traitor, is a son of perdition, can be called a son of iniquity. Indeed it is written of the Lord the Savior: And the son of iniquity shall not proceed to afflict him (Ps 88 [89]:23). […]

57:4.t: Against whom, he says, have you made sport, spitting in his face and plucking his beard; and against whom have you opened wide and opened your mouth, and thrust out your tongue, saying to him: You are a Samaritan and have a demon (John 8:48)? And again: This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, the prince of demons (Matt 12:24). And afterward, at the passion: Crucify, crucify such a one (Luke 23:21). And again: His blood be on us and on our children (Matt 27:25). And elsewhere: Ah, you who destroy the Temple and in three days rebuild it! He saved others; himself he cannot save. Let him come down now from the cross, and we believe him (ibid. 40).

Are you not wicked sons, a lying seed, you who take comfort in gods under every leafy tree, sacrificing little children in the torrents under the overhanging rocks? LXX: Are you not sons of perdition, a lawless seed, you who call upon idols under leafy trees, sacrificing your sons in the valleys in the midst of the rock? You, he says, have done these things which the preceding discourse has related. You who are wicked sons, or sons of perdition, such as was Judas the traitor, who was called the son of perdition (John 17); and a lawless seed, or a lying seed and a seed of falsehood, who delight in gods under every leafy tree, and sacrifice your sons in the torrents (Acts 8). Of this the history of Kings and of Chronicles also tells, that they sacrificed their sons to gods and consecrated them in the fire (2 Kgs 16 and 17). That Ahab king of Israel and Manasseh king of Judah did this is not in doubt; they went on from the murder of their children to the blood of the Prophets. […]

57:6.t: In the parts of the torrent is your portion; this is your lot, and to them you have poured out a libation, you have offered a sacrifice. Shall I not be angry over these things? LXX: This is your portion, this is your lot; and to them you have poured out libations, and to these you have prepared victims. Shall I not then be angry over these things? The things said fit the times of Isaiah. For all the mountains, valleys and torrents were full of the worship of demons, of which Jeremiah speaks: that the fathers and sons gather wood and kindle the fire, to make chavonas for the host of heaven, while the women knead and mix fat with fine flour, in order to provoke the Lord to anger (Jer 7). And no one doubts that he means cakes, or little pastries prepared by the hand of an artisan; for that is what chavonas means in our tongue. […]

57:7.t: Upon a high and lofty mountain you have set your bed, and there you went up to sacrifice victims. And behind the door and back of the post you have set your memorial. LXX likewise. That Israel sacrificed victims to the gods of the nations on high mountains and hills, and like a most shameless harlot spread her feet for all the demons, sacred history relates; and there was no place that was not defiled by the filth of idolatry, so much so that they set idols behind the doors of their houses, which they call the household Lares, and poured out the blood of their souls in public as much as in private. With this error and most evil custom of antiquity the cities of many provinces are afflicted; and Rome herself, the mistress of the world, venerates with wax tapers and lamps, in every tenement block and every house, the image of Tutela, whom they call by that name for the protection of their dwellings, so that, as they enter and as they leave their homes, they may be ever reminded of their inveterate error. […]

57:8.t: For beside me you have uncovered yourself and received the adulterer; you have enlarged your bed, and you have made a covenant with them; you have loved their couch with open hand; and you adorned yourself for the king with ointment, and you have multiplied your perfumes. You sent your envoys far off, and you were humbled even to hell. LXX: You thought that if you had departed from me you would have something more. You have loved those who sleep with you, and you have multiplied your fornication with them, and you have made many to be far from you, and you have sent envoys beyond your borders, and you were humbled even to hell. Let us discuss the Hebrew first, which in this place differs much from the Seventy. […]

According to the Seventy, in the things in which they disagree, the sense seems to me this: Did you think, harlot, that if you had departed from me and joined yourself to your lovers, you would find something more? To her God also speaks through Ezekiel: To all harlots wages are given, but you have given wages, and in you this perverse thing has been done (Ezek 16:33). For not only did you receive nothing from your lovers, but you even lost the things you had received from your husband. What follows, You have enlarged your bed, and you have made a covenant with them, is not found in the Seventy. This woman loved those who sleep with her, the blind watchmen and the dumb dogs, who in their sleep see dreams of vanity. And she multiplied her fornication, so as to have intercourse not once with one, but often and with very many. For this reason she made many depart far from her: the Angels who were her guardians, or the holy men who withdrew from the company of such a harlot. […]

57:9.t: And you adorned yourself for the king with ointment, and you have multiplied your idols. And the sense is: You sought various ornaments, so as to entice the adulterers both by sight and by scent. What is said, you adorned yourself for the king with ointment, is understood in two ways: either for God the king, while you adorn yourself with the things that he had given and prostitute yourself to idols; or certainly for the king who is the idol of the Ammonites, who is called Moloch, which in our tongue means king, and whom according to the Seventy we read in other places as Melchom (Zeph 1). And you sent your envoys far off, so that you might have a zeal for fornication not only with the idols of the neighboring nations, but also with those of nations set far away. He means the gods of Babylon and of Egypt. And you were humbled, he says, even to hell: not with the humility that is praised, but with that by which Amnon had humbled his sister Tamar (2 Sam 13). […]

57:10.t: In the multitude of your way you have labored, and you did not say: I will rest. You have found the life of your hand; therefore you have not asked me. LXX: In your many journeys you have labored, and you did not say: I will leave off. Strengthened, you have done these things; therefore you have not asked me. He who walks in the one royal way does not labor, the way about which God commanded through Moses: You shall walk in the royal way, and you shall not turn aside to the right or to the left (Deut 5:32). There is one way of truth, which says in the Gospel: I am the way, the truth and the life (John 14:6); and many ways of falsehood, in which Jerusalem is now accused of having walked. God, knowing the difference between these ways, speaks above to those who stray: Your ways are not as my ways (Isa 55:8); and they, confessing to the Lord, say: You have made our ways turn aside from your ways (Ps 43 [44]:19). […]

57:11.t: For whom have you been anxious and feared, that you have lied, and have not remembered me, nor thought of me in your heart? For I am silent and as one not seeing, and you have forgotten me. LXX: Whom have you feared and been terrified of, and you have lied to me, and have not remembered me? Nor have you set me in your mind and in your heart. And I, seeing you, will despise you, and you have not feared me. Because, with your barns full, you have confidence in riches and would not ask me, therefore you have feared a great many. For you could not say: The Lord is my helper, and I will look down on my enemies (Ps 117 [118]:7); and again: The Lord is my light and my savior; whom shall I fear? (Ps 26 [27]:1). And even if at some time you wished to say this against the conscience of your mind, you lied. For how could you call upon me, you who had no memory of me, and never thought on the precepts of him who says: Honor the Lord, and you shall be strengthened, and apart from him fear no one (Prov 7:1)? […]

57:12.t: I will declare your righteousness, and your works shall not profit you. When you cry out, let those whom you have gathered deliver you. LXX: I will declare your righteousness and your evils, which shall not profit you. When you cry out, let them rescue you in your tribulation. I who always kept silent, and passed over your sins as though I did not see them, will by no means keep silent any longer, but will say what I already said before: I have kept silent; shall I always keep silent? And I will declare your righteousness and your works. This is to be read as irony, as if someone were to say to a man caught in crimes: See your good works!

57:13.t: Therefore, if ever a time of tribulation comes upon you, and you begin to stretch out your hands not to the idols you have worshiped but to heaven, and to implore the help of God, let those hear you and deliver you from danger whom you worshiped in your security. God speaks to the same woman through Jeremiah also: Where are your gods which you had made? Let them rise and save you in the time of your evils (Jer 2:28). Where the Seventy translated, Let them rescue you in your tribulation, and we have said, Let those whom you have gathered deliver you, Symmachus translated: Let your synagogues rescue you. He therefore speaks properly to the Jews, that the crowd of their synagogues will not be able to deliver them in the time of siege.

But we, joining what is said to what goes before, assert this: that the wind and the tempest take away all the idols which could not deliver them, and they are like the dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth; but that those who have had confidence in the Lord will possess the land of which we shall read in this same Prophet: He will lift you up to the good things of the land. From this it is clear that this land is not below but above, to which the saint will climb as the Lord lifts him up, the land of which we have often spoken: Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land (Matt 5:4); and I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living (Ps 26 [27]:13). The holy mountain of God is to be understood as that of which the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews speaks: You have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to many thousands of Angels, and to the Church of the firstborn who are written in the heavens (Heb 12:22). […]

And the wind shall carry them all away, a breeze shall take them off. But he who has confidence in me shall inherit the land and shall possess my holy mountain. And I will say: Make a way, provide a road, turn aside from the path, take away the stumbling blocks from the way of my people. LXX: For the wind shall take all these away, and the tempest shall carry them off. But those who hope in me shall possess the land and shall obtain my holy mountain by inheritance, and they shall say: Make clean the ways before his face, and take away the stumbling blocks from the way of my people. The Jews assert that these things are prophesied of the Babylonians: that when these have been overcome by the power of God, the people return to Judea and possess Mount Zion, and all the hindrances of the journey are taken away, and they suffer the ambushes of no nation, because the Lord has made the way level for his people. And they contend that these things were fulfilled under Zerubbabel and Ezra.

57:14.t: And the Lord himself commanded the Apostles and all the teachers of the Church to resolve by their interpretation whatever seemed harsh and difficult, and to provide a way for understanding, and to take all stumbling blocks out of the midst, so that the people of the Lord may understand what it reads without any hindrance and may advance in the fear of God. Of these ways John the Baptist too said: Prepare the ways of the Lord, etc. (Matt 3:3). Where we have put, in the person of God, and I will say, the Seventy put and they shall say: namely those who shall possess the land and obtain the holy mountain of God by inheritance. Nor will they be content with their own salvation, but will also call forth the other peoples to teaching. Symmachus interpreted this place thus: But he who trusts in me shall possess the land, and shall obtain my holy mountain by inheritance, and shall say: Make a straight way, and so on; […]

57:15.t: For thus says the high and lofty one who inhabits eternity, and holy is his name: dwelling in the high and holy place, and with the contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble and to revive the heart of the contrite. LXX: Thus says the Most High, who dwells in the heights for ever, Holy among the holy is his name, the Most High resting among the holy, and giving patience to the fainthearted and life to those who are contrite of heart. The prophetic discourse had begun against the people of the Jews, whose teachers he called blind watchmen and dumb dogs and shepherds who know no understanding, and lawless sons, and the seed of adulterers and of a harlot. After this he came to Jerusalem, whom he reproaches for her fornication, because she enlarged her bed for her lovers, and received them with open hand, and adorned herself for all the idols, and sent envoys far off, so as to enjoy foreign lovers too. […]

“Who is like unto the Lord our God, that hath His dwelling so high; and yet beholdeth the humble?” (ver. 5). Any one would think that He dwelleth in the lofty heavens, whence He may behold the humble things on earth; but “He beholdeth the humble things that are in heaven and earth” (ver. 6): what then is His high dwelling, whence He beholdeth the humble things that are in heaven and earth? Are the humble things He beholdeth His own high dwelling itself? For He thus exalteth the humble, so as not to make them proud. He therefore both dwelleth in those whom He raiseth high, and maketh them heaven for Himself, that is, His own abode; and by seeing them not proud, but constantly subject to Himself, He beholdeth even in heaven itself these very humble things, in whom raised on high He dwelleth. For the Spirit thus speaketh through Isaiah: “Thus saith the Highest that dwelleth on high, that inhabiteth eternity; the Lord Most High, dwelling in the holy.” […]

57:16.t: I will not contend for ever, nor will I be angry to the end; for the spirit shall go forth from my face, and I will make the breaths. LXX: I will not take vengeance on you for ever, nor will I always be angry with you. For the spirit shall go forth from me, and I have made every breath. The Lord who dwells in the heights and looks upon the lowly, whose name is holy, and who rests among the holy, who upholds the afflicted and grants life to the oppressed (Ps 112 [113]), has spoken thus: I will not always be angry, nor will I be indignant without end. I strike in order to amend; I kill in order to give life. For I have pity on my creature, and those whom I myself have made I will not allow to perish for ever. My spirit too, which shall go forth from me, or which, according to the Hebrew, Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, surrounds all things (for this is what περιειληθήσεται and περιβαλλεῖ signify), is the quickener of all things. […]

Let her then ask of Him, and hear “Why?” For she is in the Psalm enquiring the cause of her dejection; saying, “Why hast Thou cast me off? and why go I mourning?” Let her hear from Isaiah; let the lesson which has just been read, suggest itself to her. “The spirit shall go forth from me, and every breath have I made. For iniquity have I a little afflicted him; I hid my face from him, and he departed from me sorrowful in the ways of his heart.” Why then didst thou ask, “Why hast Thou cast me off, and why go I mourning?” Thou hast heard, it was “for iniquity.” “Iniquity” is the cause of thy mourning; let “Righteousness” be the cause of thy rejoicing! Thou wouldest sin; and yet thou wouldest fain not suffer; so that it was too little for thee to be thyself unrighteous, without also wishing Him to be unrighteous, in that thou wouldest fain not be punished by Him.

57:17.t: Because of the iniquity of his covetousness I was angry, and I struck him; I hid, and I was indignant; and he walked mourning in the way of his heart. I have seen his ways, and I healed him; and I brought him back, and restored consolations to him and to those who mourn for him. I created the fruit of the lips, peace, peace to him who is far off and to him who is near, said the Lord, and I healed him. But the impious are like the raging sea which cannot rest, and its waves overflow into trampling and mire. There is no peace, said God, for the impious. LXX: Because of sin I grieved him for a little while, and I struck him; and I turned my face away from him, and he was grieved and walked sad in his ways. I have seen his ways, and I healed him; and I comforted him, and gave him true consolation, peace to those who are far off and to those who are near, says the Lord, and I will heal them. But those who are lawless shall be tossed like waves, and shall not be able to rest. […]

Some understand this place specifically of the Savior: that because of the sins of the world he was grieved for a little while, saying: My soul is sorrowful even unto death (Matt 26:38); and that the Father struck him, he who speaks through Zechariah: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered (Zech 13:7); and that he himself said of himself in the sixty-eighth psalm: For they persecuted him whom you struck (Ps 68 [69]:27); and that God turned his face away from him, so that for a little while he took the form of a servant and walked sad, mourning the sins of the people, lamenting and bewailing Jerusalem; and that the Father, who saw his ways, therefore healed him who was free among the dead, and his flesh did not see corruption, so that he who was struck on the cross might be healed in the resurrection. And I comforted him, he says, giving him the whole world in place of the one nation of the Jews. And those who mourn for him, understood, I comforted; […]

57:18.t: Therefore, seeing the ways of his conversion, I healed the wounds with which I had struck him before. And I brought back to me him whom I had first cast out, and restored to him true consolation; for many are the false consolations by which the human race is deceived. Or: I comforted those who mourn for him, saying in the Gospel: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:5).

57:19.t: What follows, I created the fruit of the lips, has this sense: I have fulfilled what I had promised, saying: As I live, says the Lord, I would rather the repentance of the sinner than his death (Ezek 33:11); or: I have granted all that I had promised before. And what is the Lord's promise? My peace I give you; my peace I leave you (John 14:27). And this is what he now says: Peace upon peace; not to one nation only, but to the whole world: namely to those who were far off and to those who were near, that is, first to the nations, and afterward to those of Israel who were willing to believe. Of these the Apostle too says: To you indeed it was necessary that the word of God be preached; but since you judge yourselves unworthy of salvation, behold, we turn to the nations (Acts 13:46). He, writing to the Ephesians and discussing most fully the people of the Circumcision and of the Gentiles, adds: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near in the Blood of Christ. […]

And as to his saying: Coming, he preached peace to you who were far off, that is, to the Gentiles, and peace to those who were near, that is, to the Jews, he seems to me to have brought forward a testimony from Isaiah in other words, and to have used the sense of Scripture as though it were his own. For it is written in him: I have seen his ways, and I have healed him, and I have comforted him, and I have given him true comfort: peace upon peace to those who were far off, and to those who were near (Isa. 57:18). And let this much be said according to the common interpretation.

57:20.t: But the impious, or lawless, shall be tossed like the raging sea, and shall never be able to rest. Although this can be understood of every impious man, yet it refers properly to the people of the Jews, who cried out with one voice and persevered in their impiety, saying: Crucify, crucify such a one. We have no king but Caesar (John 19:15). As, then, the raging sea cannot rest, but its waves overflow and roll up on the shores and are sucked back again, and breaking upon themselves make a mire that is trampled underfoot, so the impious will be subject to eternal trampling; they have no joy, and they rest in no peace, because they persevere in being impious.

57:21.t: For that joy which is after the fashion of the world, is not true joy. Hear the prophet Isaiah: “There is no joy, saith my God, to the wicked.” What the wicked call joy is not joy, such as he knew who made no account of their joy: let us believe him, brethren. He was a man, but he knew both kinds of joy. He certainly knew the joys of the cup, for he was a man, he knew the joy of the table, he knew the joys of marriage, he knew those joys worldly and luxurious. He who knew them saith with confidence, “There is no joy to the wicked, saith the Lord.” But it is not man who speaks, it is the Lord.…

58:1.t: Cry, cease not; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their crimes, and to the house of Jacob their sins. LXX: Cry with strength, and spare not; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to the people their sins, and to the house of Jacob their iniquities. The preceding chapter finished, in which peace is announced to the righteous and no rest to the impious, God commands the prophet Isaiah to cry with strength, and to lift up his voice like a trumpet, and not to fear to tell the sins and crimes of the people of Israel, by no means afraid of death, nor of the threats and abuse of the impious, but rather considering the Lord who commands him. And because they have deaf ears and can scarcely hear, according to Symmachus and Aquila he is to turn his throat into a horn, which in Hebrew is called SOPHAR (שופר), and which they interpreted as κερατίνην, that is, of horn. Above, indeed, where it was said to the Apostles, Go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion; […]

For also when God saw the dying condition of the Jews who of their own will stopped their ears, and blinded their eyes, and made thick their hearts against the remembrance of the knowledge of God, He stirred up Isaiah to rouse them up, and cried to him to cry into their ears, saying, "Cry with thy throat, and spare not, and lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew My people their iniquity, and the house of Jacob their sins".

58:2.t: For they seek me from day to day, and wish to know my ways, as a nation that has done righteousness and has not forsaken the judgment of its God. LXX likewise. This properly fits the Jews, who run every day to the synagogues and meditate on the law of God, desiring to know what Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did, and what the rest of the saints did, and, turning over the books of the Prophets and of Moses by heart, chant the divine commandments. To them this will most rightly be applied: The wicked will seek me and will not find me. For thus it is written: Everyone who seeks finds (Matt 7); whoever does not find is proved to have sought wrongly. For the Lord is found by those who seek him in goodness, and is shown to those who are not unbelieving toward him. […]

They ask of me the judgments of righteousness, and they wish to draw near to God. Why have we fasted, and you have not looked? Why have we humbled our souls, and you have not known? Behold, in the day of your fast shall be found your own will, and you have exacted again from all your debtors. Behold, you fast for lawsuits and contentions, and you strike with the fist wickedly. LXX: They now ask of me righteous judgment, and they desire to draw near to God, saying: Why have we fasted, and you have not seen? Why have we humbled our souls, and you have not known? For in the days of your fasts your own wills are found, and you afflict all who are subject to you, fasting for lawsuits and quarrels, and you strike the lowly with your fists. This is another rashness of the Jews: as though in the confidence of a good conscience, they demand righteous judgment and imitate the words of the saints, who say: Judge me, Lord, for I have walked in my innocence (Ps 25 [26]:1, 2); and again: Prove me, Lord, and try me; […]

Another however, whose heart is wholly buried in the earth and who constantly eats dust with the serpent without caring in any way for the things pleasant to God, who fatigues himself in every respect by the bodily things and is occupied by and constantly cares for intercourse and pleasure and luxury, and who has manifold worldly connections, — when such a man, given to such laxity and indifference regarding excellence, from time to time gets into trouble or want, or the fruits of sinfulness disturb him in any way, and [when he] says as follows: I trust in God, He will work for me without doubt and He will comfort me, — o fool, till now thou hast not recalled God but thou hast disdained Him by the laxity of thy works and His name was slandered among the nations, as the scripture says. And now thou sayest with a full mouth: I confide in Him who will help me and care for me. […]

As a man who sows on thorns and is not able to reap, so is he whose mind is injured by care and wrath and desire of gathering treasures, and who sighs on his bed on account of the frequency of his vigils and abstinence. Witness is the scripture that says: As a nation that did righteousness and forsook not the ordinance of their God: they ask of me the ordinances of justice; they take delight in coming near unto God. Wherefore have we fasted and thou seest not? Have we afflicted our soul and thou takest no knowledge? Behold, in the day of your fast ye find pleasure and sacrifice unto all your idols.

This means: the evil designs and the evil thoughts hold you in yourself in stead of God and sacrifice to them your liberty, a thing esteemed at all times; “the sacrifice which is honoured above all things and which you ought not to omit, consists of your good works and pious inner being. […]

58:3.t: Why have we fasted, they say, and you have not looked? Why have we humbled our souls, and you have not known? They accuse the Lord of unrighteousness, because he does not regard their good works, and they press upon God only the hunger of the belly, without the work of the virtues: not eating the foods which God created for the faithful and for those who know the truth, to be taken with thanksgiving, but those of which it is written in Proverbs: For these are fed with the foods of impiety, and are drunk with the wine of iniquity (Prov 4:17). Glutted with feasts of this kind, the Pharisee, among his other words of pride, boasted that he fasted twice in the week (Luke 18); he had not drunk the wine of the vine of Sorek, but of the vine of Sodom, whose wine is the fury of dragons and the incurable fury of asps, and their grape is a grape of gall. Them God rebukes through the Prophet: They eat the sins of my people (Hos 4:8); […]

Who are willing to enter into judgment with Him, save they who, “being ignorant of the righteousness of God, go about to establish their own?” “Wherefore have we fasted, and Thou hast not seen; wherefore have we afflicted our souls, and Thou takest no knowledge?” As though they would say, “We have done what Thou hast commanded, wherefore dost Thou not render to us what Thou hast promised?” God answereth thee: I will give to thee to receive what I have promised: I have given thee that thou shouldest do that whereby thou mayest receive.

But to those men also will these things be found bad, who are on the lookout for the praises of men by their fasts, and by a foolish show of paleness gain credit for sanctity, of whom the word of the Gospel tells us that they have received their reward in this life, and whose fast the Lord execrates by the prophet. In whose person he first objected to himself and said: "Wherefore have we fasted and Thou hast not regarded: wherefore have we humbled our souls, and Thou hast not known it?" and then at once he answered and explained the reasons why they did not deserve to be heard: "Behold," he says, "in the days of your fast your own will is found and you exact of all your debtors. Behold you fast for debates and strife, and strike with the fist wickedly. Do not fast as ye have done unto this day, to make your cry to be heard on high. Is this such a fast as I have chosen, for a man to afflict his soul for a day? Is it this, to wind his head about like a circle, and to spread sackcloth and ashes? […]
58:3.s: The First Conference of Abbot Theonas, Chapter 14

58:4.t: For what does it profit for the face to grow pale with fasts, and to fast for lawsuits and quarrels, when Scripture says, He who loves sins rejoices in quarrels (Prov 17:19)? The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be gentle (2 Tim 2), and imitate him who says: Learn of me, for I am meek and humble of heart (Matt 11:29), so that the humility be not affected but of the heart, seeking not the glory of men but the conscience of the soul. You fast, he says, and strike the lowly with your fists, and beat them with slaps (1 Tim 3). Hence a bishop must not be a striker. For how can he rein in lust who cannot restrain either his hand or his tongue? Fasts of this kind the Lord rebukes at the beginning of this prophet too, saying: Fasting and idleness, new moons and sabbaths and your other solemnities my soul hates (Isa 1:13). Hence it is commanded through Joel: Sanctify a fast, proclaim a healing (Joel 2:15), so that we may fast from vices, and, by good works and the healing of our sins, our fasts may become holy. […]

Do not fast as you have until this day, so that your cry may be heard on high. Is this such a fast as I have chosen, for a man to afflict his soul for a day? Is it to twist his head round like a ring, and to spread sackcloth and ashes? Will you call this a fast and a day acceptable to the Lord? LXX: Why do you fast to me as today, so that your voice may be heard in clamor? I have not chosen such a fast, and a day for a man to humble his soul. Not even if you bend your neck like a ring and spread under you haircloth and ashes, not even so shall you call it an acceptable fast. Lest he seem to reject the fast which he himself had commanded, he teaches how one should fast; or rather, before teaching what they should pursue, he instructs them in what they ought to avoid. […]

58:5.t: For since, as I before said, there are divers proclamations, listen, as in a figure, to the prophet blowing the trumpet; and further, having turned to the truth, be ready for the announcement of the trumpet, for he saith, ‘Blow ye the trumpet in Sion: sanctify a fast.’ This is a warning trumpet, and commands with great earnestness, that when we fast, we should hallow the fast. For not all those who call upon God, hallow God, since there are some who defile Him; yet not Him—that is impossible—but their own mind concerning Him; for He is holy, and has pleasure in the saints. And therefore the blessed Paul accuses those who dishonour God; ‘Transgressors of the law dishonour God.’ So then, to make a separation from those who pollute the fast, he saith here, ‘sanctify a fast.’ For many, crowding to the fast, pollute themselves in the thoughts of their hearts, sometimes by doing evil against their brethren, sometimes by daring to defraud. […]

If you have fasted two or three days, do not think yourself better than others who do not fast. You fast and are angry; the other eats and wears a smiling face. You work off your irritation and hunger in quarrels. He uses food in moderation and gives God thanks.

For God does not seek only affliction and the humbling of the soul through injury to the body, that a man should twist his body like a ring, and bow his neck, and go about sad, according to what is said in the Psalms: I am afflicted and bowed down to the end; all the day I went about saddened (Ps 37 [38]:7); nor that one should be clothed in sackcloth and sleep in ashes, as we read of David and of Ahab (2 Sam 3; 1 Kgs 21); but that along with these he should do the things that follow. Otherwise the Apostle too says that he fasted often (2 Cor 6 and 11), and the Lord teaches that his disciples will fast when the bridegroom has been taken from them (Matt 9); and in the Psalms the penitent says: I have eaten ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping (Ps 101 [102]:10); And when they were troublesome to me, I put on haircloth (Ps 34 [35]:13). From this we learn that the things the Lord wills must be done first, and the others not passed over.

58:6.t: Is not this rather the fast that I have chosen? Loose the bonds of impiety, undo the bundles that weigh down; let those who are broken go free, and break every burden. Break your bread to the hungry, and bring the needy and the wanderers into the house. When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh. LXX: Is not such a fast what I have chosen, says the Lord? But loose every bond of iniquity. Undo the obligations of violent contracts. Let the broken go in release, and tear up every unjust writing. Break your bread to the hungry, and bring the poor without a roof into your house. If you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise those of the household of your seed. After teaching what kind of fast he rejects, he shows what kind he gladly accepts. Loose, he says, the bonds of impiety; undo the bundles that weigh down; […]

According to tropology we can say this: Let him who fasts from all evils, and wishes his fast to be regarded, not only turn away from evil but also do good, so as to loose every bond of iniquity by which the simple among believers have been bound through the frauds of the heretics; and the στραγγαλιὰς, the obligations of violent treatises, which the Prophet too points out in the psalm, saying: But those who turn aside into obligations the Lord will lead away with the workers of iniquity (Ps 124 [125]:5). For all who are bound with the chains of the heretics turn aside from the Lord, and are like an ox led to the sacrifice; and they choose and exchange falsehood for the truth. Such men, then, who are broken in judgment, let the churchman release and set free; and let him undo and break every writing of the heretics, of whom this same Prophet says: Woe to those who write iniquity; […]

58:7.t: And we shall find many examples also in other places,-as, for instance, respecting prayer: "Good works are an acceptable prayer to the Lord," says the Scripture. And the manner of prayer is described. "If thou seest," it is said, "the naked, cover him; and thou shalt not overlook those who belong to thy seed. Then shall thy light spring forth early, and thy healing shall spring up quickly; and thy righteousness shall go before thee, and the glory of God shall encompass thee." What, then, is the fruit of such prayer? "Then shall thou call, and God will hear thee; whilst thou art yet speaking, He will say, I am here."

WHY IS IT THAT IN THE LAW EVEN AARON HIMSELF IS TOLD THAT HE MUST OFFER BURNT OFFERINGS FOR HIS SINS, WHEN DAVID SAYS, “FOR FAULTS YOU HAVE NOT REQUIRED A BURNT OFFERING” (Ps. 39:7), AND LATER, “YOU WILL NOT TAKE PLEASURE IN BURNT OFFERINGS” (Ps. 50:18)? HOW DID HE COMMAND THAT THERE BE OFFERED WHAT HE DOES NOT TAKE PLEASURE IN? — It is clear that God does not take delight in burnt offerings, but that by way of satisfaction for sin, through the groaning and sorrow of the heart, pardon can be earned. He willed that the sacrifice should be a testimony of sin, so that the sinner, by the offering of the sacrifice, might confess that he had sinned. But how forgiveness might be obtained, He showed in another place, saying, “Break your bread for the hungry; if you see one naked, clothe him, and do not despise your own flesh and blood” (Isa. 58:7), or certainly, “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50:19). First, then, He instructed that the offense must be confessed; […]
58:7.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 12: ON WHY GOD COMMANDS BURNT OFFERINGS HE DOES NOT DESIRE

58:7.t: But it could happen that someone would say: I have no debtors; what must I do for my fast to be accepted? It follows: Break your bread to the hungry. Not many loaves, lest you plead poverty, but one loaf; and not even the whole of it, but a part of the loaf, which you would have eaten if you were not fasting, so that your fast may not be a gain for your purse but a filling of your soul. And he fittingly added your, lest you make alms out of plunder: For the ransom of a man's soul is his own riches (Prov 13:8); and in another place: Honor the Lord from your righteous labors (Prov 3:9). Surely, if you have no bread, and the multitude of the hungry is very great, give something from which you suffer no loss. A thing in which there is no expense: the poor without a roof bring into your house; or, as it is in the Hebrew, into the house, so that, if you have no house of your own, you may bring them into the little lodging which you hold either on rent or by favor. If you see the naked, cover him. […]

Begin, then, to love thy neighbor. "Break thy bread to the hungry, and bring into thy house him that is needy without shelter; if thou seest the naked, clothe him; and despise not those of the household of thy seed." And in doing this, what wilt thou get in consequence? "Then shall thy light break forth as the morning light." Thy light is thy God, a "morning light" to thee, because He shall come to thee after the night of this world: for He neither rises nor sets, because He is ever abiding. He will be a morning light to thee on thy return, He who had set for thee on thy falling away from Him.

You have heard from Isaiah, “Break thy bread to the hungry;” think not that fasting by itself is sufficient. Fasting chasteneth thine own self: it does not refresh others. Thy distress will profit thee, if thou affordest comfort to others. See, thou hast denied thyself; to whom wilt thou give that of which thou hast deprived thyself? Where wilt thou bestow what thou hast denied thyself? How many poor may be filled by the breakfast we have this day given up? Fast in such a way that thou mayest rejoice, that thou hast breakfasted, while another has been eating; fast on account of thy prayers, that thou mayest be heard in them. For He says in that passage, “Whilst thou art yet speaking I will say, Here I am,” provided thou wilt with cheerful mind “break thy bread to the hungry.” For generally this is done by men reluctantly and with murmurs, to rid themselves of the wearisome importunity of the beggar, not to refresh the bowels of him that is needy. But it is “a cheerful giver” that “God loves.” […]

58:8.t: Then your light shall break forth like the morning, and your health shall quickly arise, and your righteousness shall go before your face, and the glory of the Lord shall gather you up. Then you shall call, and the Lord will hear; you shall cry, and he will say: Here I am. LXX: Then your morning light shall break forth, and your healings shall quickly arise, and your righteousness shall go before you in your sight, and the glory of God shall surround you. Then you shall cry, and God will hear you. While you are still speaking, he will say: Here I am. When you have not done the things which the preceding discourse related, and have done these of which we have now spoken, then your fast will be acceptable, and your morning light will break forth: the sun of righteousness, namely, of whom the prophet Malachi speaks in the person of God the Father: For you who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing in his wings (Mal 4:2). He who is called the sun there is called the light here. […]

58:9.t: God is always one and the same; but people have come to be afterwards through the Word, when the Father himself willed it; and God is invisible and inaccessible to originated things, especially to people on earth. When then people in infirmity invoke him, when in persecution they ask help, when they pray as they endure injuries, then the Invisible, being a lover of people, shines forth on them with his beneficence, which he exercises through and in his proper Word. And forthwith the divine manifestation is made to every one according to his need, and is made to the sick, and to the persecuted a "refuge" and "house of defense."

Who was more sympathetic in mind, more bounteous in hand, towards the poor, that most dishonoured portion of the nature to which equal honour is due? For he actually treated his own property as if it were another's, of which he was but the steward, relieving poverty as far as he could, and expending not only his superfluities but his necessities—a manifest proof of love for the poor, giving a portion, not only to seven, according to the injunction of Solomon, but if an eighth came forward, not even in his case being niggardly, but more pleased to dispose of his wealth than we know others are to acquire it; taking away the yoke and election (which means, as I think, all meanness in testing as to whether the recipient is worthy or not) and word of murmuring in benevolence. This is what most men do: they give indeed, but without that readiness, which is a greater and more perfect thing than the mere offering. […]

For were He distant from us in place, thou mightest well doubt, but if He is present everywhere, to him that strives and is in earnest He is near. Wherefore also the prophet said, "I will fear no evil, for Thou art with me;" and God Himself again, "I am a God nigh at hand, and not a God afar off." Then as our sins separate us from Him, so do our righteousnesses draw us nigh unto Him. "For while thou art yet speaking," it is said, "I will say, Here I am." What father would ever be thus obedient to his offspring? What mother is there, so ready, and continually standing, if haply her children call her? There is not one, no father, no mother: but God stands continually waiting, if any of his servants should perchance call Him; and never, when we have called as we ought, hath He refused to hear. Therefore He saith, "While thou art yet speaking," I do not wait for thee to finish, and I straightway hearken.

Let us call Him therefore, as it is His will to be called. But what is this His will? […]
58:9.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 54:8

58:9.t:
[Daniel 9:21] "While I was still speaking in my prayer, behold the man Gabriel, whom I had seen at the beginning of the vision." He calls the previous vision preceding this one the beginning. The effect of his prayer was considerable, and the promise of God was fulfilled which says, "While thou art yet speaking, lo, I am at hand" (Isaiah 58:9). And Gabriel appears not as an angel or archangel, but as a man (vir), a term used to indicate the quality of virtue rather than specifying his sex.

"...he quickly flew to me and touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice." It is stated that he flew, because he had made his appearance as a man. It is said that it was at the time of the evening sacrifice, in order to show that the prophet's prayer had persisted from the morning sacrifice even unto the evening sacrifice, and that God for that reason directed His mercy towards him.
58:9.s: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER NINE

58:9.t: Then you shall call, and the Lord will hear; you shall cry, and he will say: Here I am, not by voice but by deed, not by an answer but by benefits. This is proved according to the letter in the Gospel too, when the leper said to the Lord, If you will, you can make me clean, and the Lord answered, saying: I will; be clean.

If you take away the chain from your midst, and cease to stretch out the finger and to speak what does not profit; when you pour out your soul to the hungry, and fill the afflicted soul, then your light shall rise in the darkness, and your darkness shall be as the noonday. LXX: If you take away from you the bond, and the ordination, and the word of murmuring, and give your bread to the hungry from your soul, and satisfy the humbled soul, then your light shall rise in the darkness, and your darkness shall be as the noonday. The Hebrew word MOTA (מוטה), which in Jeremiah is translated iron collar (Jer 28), is read twice in the present chapter. For in the place where, above, according to the Seventy, we said, Undo the obligations of violent exchanges, let us know that for the one word MOTA they put violent contracts, for which Aquila translated error, Symmachus turning aside, Theodotion κλοιὸν, that is, collar. […]

58:10.t: So if we do not do the things that have been said, and do the things that are to be said, so as to give to the hungry not, as above, our bread, but our soul, so as to help him in whatever ways we can, and to give not as if out of sadness and necessity but from the soul, receiving rather than giving a benefit, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor 9:7); so as not to refresh the hungry or afflicted soul in part but to satisfy it, and to grieve with those who grieve and mourn with those who mourn (Rom 12): then our light will rise in the darkness, he who says: I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness, but may have the light of life (John 12:46). For the lamp of our body is the eye: if it is single, our whole body will be full of light. But if what ought to be light has been turned into darkness, then the whole body will be dark, and it will be said to us: If the light that is in you is darkness, how great is that darkness itself! (Matt 6:23). […]

58:11.t: And the Lord will give you rest always, and will fill your soul with splendors, and will deliver your bones. And you shall be like a watered garden, and like a fountain of waters whose waters shall not fail. LXX: And your God shall be with you always, and you shall be filled as your soul desires, and your bones shall grow fat. And they shall be like a drunken garden, and like a fountain for which the water shall not fail. What has been added in the Alexandrian copies at the beginning of this chapter, And still my praise shall be in you always, and at the end, and your bones shall spring up like grass, and shall grow fat, and they shall possess by inheritance unto generation and generations, is not found in the Hebrew, nor even in the corrected and true copies of the Seventy; hence it must be marked beforehand with an obelus. […]

58:12.t: And the deserts of ages shall be built up in you; you shall raise up the foundations of generation and generation; and there shall be called in you the builder of hedges, turning the paths into rest. LXX: And the places desert from of old shall be built up for you, and your foundations shall be everlasting for generations and generations; and you shall be called the builder of the wall, and you shall make the paths in the midst to rest. Not only, he says, will your light rise in the darkness, and your darkness be like noonday, and the Lord give you rest always, and you be like a watered garden, and the rest, but there shall be built up in you the things that had been desert for a long time; and the foundations of your dwellings will be laid to endure through many generations; so that either you yourself will be called the builder of hedges and walls, or one will arise in you who will be the builder of hedges and will turn the paths into rest, or, according to the Seventy, will make the tracks in the midst to rest. […]

58:13.t: If you turn away your foot from the sabbath, from doing your own will on my holy day, and call the sabbath delightful, and the holy of the Lord glorious, and glorify him while you do not make your own ways, and your own will is not found to speak a word. LXX: If you turn away your foot on the sabbaths, so as not to do your own wills on the holy day; and you shall call the sabbaths delightful, holy to the Lord; you shall not lift your foot to work, nor speak a word ÷ in anger from your mouth ⁚. To the one to whom he had said above, Is not this rather the fast that I have chosen: loose the bond of impiety, undo the bundles that weigh down, and the rest, he now too promises rewards, if he is willing to do the things that follow (Exod 20): namely, that he restrain his foot on the sabbaths, and not do his own wills, nor stain the holy day of the Lord with his wills. […]

The aim indeed of the coenobite is to mortify and crucify all his desires and, according to that salutary command of evangelic perfection, to take no thought for the morrow. And it is perfectly clear that this perfection cannot be attained by any except a coenobite, such a man as the prophet Isaiah describes and blesses and praises as follows: "If thou turn away thy foot from the Sabbath, from doing thy own will in my holy day, and glorify Him, while thou dost not thine own ways, and thine own will is not found to speak a word: then shalt thou be delighted in the Lord, and I will lift thee up above the high places of the earth, and will feed thee with the inheritance of Jacob thy father. For the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it." But the perfection for a hermit is to have his mind freed from all earthly things, and to unite it, as far as human frailty allows, with Christ: and such a man the prophet Jeremiah describes when he says: "Blessed is the man who hath borne the yoke from his youth. […]

Those are certainly worthy of praise as violent, who do violence to their own destruction, for, "A man," as it is written, "that is in sorrow laboureth for himself and does violence to his own destruction." For our destruction is delight in this present life, and to speak more definitely, the performance of our own likes and desires, as, if a man withdraws these from his soul and mortifies them, he straightway does glorious and valuable violence to his own destruction, provided that he refuses to it the pleasantest of its wishes which the Divine word often rebukes by the prophet, saying: "For in the days of your fast your own will is found;" and again: "If thou turn away thy foot from the Sabbath, to do thy will on My holy day, and glorify him, while thou dost not thy own ways, and thy own will is not found, to speak a word." And the great blessedness that is promised to him is at once added by the prophet. […]
