65:17.t: Now the new heaven and the new earth those who think that all things we see will perish interpret by the testimony of the Gospel: Heaven and earth shall pass away (Matt 24:35). And by that of the apostle Paul: For the things that are seen are temporal: but the things that are not seen are eternal (2 Cor 4:18). But those who consider newness to be a change for the better, and not the destruction of the elements, use this example: In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain, and they shall all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you shall roll them up, and they shall be changed (Ps 101 [102]:26, 27). In this it is clearly shown that perdition and destruction mean not an abolition into nothing, but a change for the better. […]

The eighteenth book on Isaiah, or rather the last, is dedicated to your name, O daughter Eustochium, and to that of your holy mother Paula, so that I may now recall with equal remembrance those whom I have looked up to with equal honor: especially since she too, while she lived, often asked for this work together with you, and your brother Pammachius, a most learned man, did not cease, both then and afterwards, to press me with frequent letters; and for me there is one and the same devotion toward friends present and absent, and toward men and women sleeping in Christ, that is, a love of souls, not of bodies. Nor am I unaware how great a diversity of opinions there is among men. I do not speak of the mystery of the Trinity, whose right confession is the ignorance of knowledge, but of the other doctrines of the Church: namely of the Resurrection, of the state of souls and of human flesh, of the Promises of things to come, how they ought to be taken, and in what way the Apocalypse of John is to be understood; […]

65:18.t: For behold, I create Jerusalem an exultation, and its people a joy: and I will exult in Jerusalem, and rejoice in my people. LXX: For behold, I make Jerusalem an exultation, and my people a gladness, and I will exult over Jerusalem, and be glad over my people. You ought, he says, to rejoice and exult with everlasting gladness in the creation of new heavens and a new earth, and not to remember the former things at all, lest any sadness should arise in you from the recollection of the old: for I will create not only new heavens and a new earth, but Jerusalem too in exultation, and its people in joy. Without doubt it will be a gladness for the whole earth, so that the city which, when old, was the joy of one nation, when new may be the gladness of all the nations. […]

65:19.t: And there shall no more be heard in it the voice of weeping, and the voice of crying: there shall no longer be an infant of days, and an old man who does not fill out his days. For the child shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed. LXX: And there shall no more be heard in it the voice of weeping, and the voice of crying: nor shall there be there any more one untimely and an old man who does not fill out his time. For there shall be an infant a hundred years old, and he who dies a sinner at a hundred shall be accursed. For it will not be fitting that in the city of Jerusalem and in the people of God, which will receive the eternal creation of exultation and joy, the voice of weeping and crying should be heard any more, when sorrow, mourning and groaning have gone away. For contraries cannot exist together. […]

65:20.t: In such a city there will not be different ages: an infant and an old man, small and great, who does not fill out his days; but as sons of the resurrection all will come to the perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, so that no one will lack a span of years nor have more than enough, nor will it be that, while one does not yet have firm strength, another ceases to be what he was and withers in decrepit age; and all will come to the number of a hundred, as Abraham was, who at this age received the promise of his son Isaac (Gen 21). Of the praises of this number there is no need to say much, lest the discussion be superfluous. This only we say: that ten decades have equal sides, and possess the firmness of a square form. In the promises too, for the things we have spent, the Lord promises us them multiplied a hundredfold; and the seed falling on good ground has as its first number of most abundant yield the hundred. […]

It is usual for the prophets thus to mingle metaphorical and literal expressions. Yet, anyone with serious purpose and a little useful and salutary effort can discern the prophet's spiritual sense; it is only a lazy and worldly person or one who is ignorant or uneducated who will rest content with the literal and superficial sense and refuse to penetrate the deeper meaning.

The second aspect of the zeal of wisdom is control of the passions, which are the seven affective dispositions of the soul — four principal and three consequent: fear, sorrow, hope and joy; shame and hatred. It is characteristic of these that they go to excess in all matters. But when a child clamors too loudly, he is restrained. Likewise, a man should dominate and restrain these passions with a kind of judicial censure, so that when sorrow comes, he say to himself, "Remain in peace." And the same with the others. And get rid of this childishness and of these infantile dispositions. For children are the pursuers of passions: accursed is the child who is a hundred years old.

65:21.t: And they shall build houses, and dwell in them; and they shall plant vineyards, and eat their fruits. They shall not build, and another dwell: they shall not plant, and another eat. LXX likewise. Of these houses the prophetic word also makes promise in Psalm 68 (69), saying: For God will save Zion: and the cities of Judah shall be built, and they shall dwell there, and acquire it by inheritance, and the seed of his servants shall possess it: and those who love his name shall dwell in it. All this the Jews take carnally, that Jerusalem and the cities of Judea are to be restored to their former state. But if we grant them this, let them hear that this is promised not only to Jerusalem but also to Sodom, as Ezekiel says: Sodom shall be restored to its ancient state (Ezek 16:55). Therefore the houses in which those who build them are to dwell are to be understood either as the Virtues or as the various mansions with the Father, which he who has built them will possess forever. […]

65:22.t: For as the days of the tree, so shall be the days of my people, and the works of their hands shall wear out for my elect. They shall not labor in vain, nor bring forth in trouble: for it is the seed of the blessed of the Lord, and their grandchildren with them. And it shall be that before they cry out, I will hear: while they are still speaking, I will hear. The wolf and the lamb shall feed together, and the lion and the ox shall eat straw, and for the serpent dust shall be its bread. They shall not harm nor kill in all my holy mountain, says the Lord. LXX: For as the days of the tree of life, so the days of my people: the works of their labors my elect shall make old: they shall not labor in vain, nor bring forth sons for a curse: for it is a seed blessed by the Lord, and their grandchildren with them. And it shall be that before they cry out, I will hear them: while they are still speaking I will say, What is it? […]

"As in the days of the tree of life, so shall be the days of my people." Now, anyone who has ever opened the Scriptures knows where God planted the "tree of life." It was from the fruit of this tree that God excluded Adam and Eve.…Of course, it might be argued that those "days of the tree of life" mentioned by Isaiah are the days that are now being spent by Christ's church, since the "tree of life" is simply a prophetic figure for Christ, for that Wisdom of God that Solomon had in mind when he said that Wisdom is "a tree of life to them that laid hold on it."

65:23.t: These shall not labor in vain, as the Jews once labored; but they shall eat the labors of their hands. Nor shall they bring forth in trouble, or for a curse, or, as is put more expressly in the Hebrew, εἰς ἀνυπαρξίαν, which in their language is said LABALA (לבהלה), that is, so that they cease to be and have an end of their substance: for which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion translated haste: so that they may by no means hasten to believe without reason, but may imitate Nathanael, who was praised by the voice of the Lord: Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no guile (John 1:47), who sought Christ by the authority of the Scriptures and longed to recognize him from the Prophets, saying: Can anything good come out of Nazareth? And the sense is: How do you bring me a Messiah from Galilee and Nazareth, whom I know to have been promised from Bethlehem of Judah? […]

65:24.t: When these cry out, they will at once be heard, and while they are speaking the Lord will say, Here I am. All of which we see fulfilled even according to the letter in the Acts of the Apostles. For all the nations could not have believed in so short a time unless their faith had in some way been wrung from them by the miracles of signs. For when the Apostles and apostolic men spoke and cried out, the Lord answered with the greatness of his signs, so that Dorcas rose at the prayers of Peter (Acts 9), so that the father of Publius, on the island of Malta, was healed by the prayers of Paul of fevers and dysentery, which are diseases contrary to each other, and so that the whole world said that they were gods walking among men (Acts 28).

65:25.t: Then the wolf and the lamb fed together, Paul the persecutor and Ananias the disciple (Acts 9). He is the wolf of whom it is written: Benjamin, a ravening wolf, in the morning shall eat the prey, and at evening shall give food (Gen 49:27); or, as it is said in the Hebrew, shall divide the spoils. His teaching was the food of believers, and he triumphed over his vanquished adversaries in the whole world. But the lambs are to be believed to be all who in white garments follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev 14), whom the Lord handed over to Peter to feed, saying: Feed my lambs (John 21:16). The lion too like the ox shall eat straw, when most eloquent men, once powerful in the world, give themselves over to the rusticity of the Scriptures, so that they by no means feed on worldly eloquence, which like honey drips from the lips of a harlot, but follow the plainness and the straw of the history, until by much labor and diligence they deserve to come to the grain of the senses. […]

66:1.t: He has not even built a house for himself! He has nothing to do with space. Even if it is written that "the heaven is his throne," he is not contained as the words suggest.

And He has added hereto by the prophet, "The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: what house will ye build me, and where is the place of my rest?" that He may show that He whom the world does not contain is much less contained in a temple; and He says these things not for boastfulness of Himself, but for our knowledge. For He does not desire from us the glory of His magnitude; but He wishes to confer upon us, even as a father, a religious wisdom.

And although the heavenly Scripture often turns the divine appearance into a human form,—as when it says, "The eyes of the Lord are over the righteous;" or when it says, "The Lord God smelled the smell of a good savour;" or when there are given to Moses the tables "written with the finger of God;" or when the people of the children of Israel are set free from the land of Egypt "with a mighty hand and with a stretched out arm;" or when it says, "The mouth of the Lord hath spoken these things;" or when the earth is set forth as "God's footstool;" or when it says, "Incline thine ear, and hear,"—we who say that the law is spiritual do not include within these lineaments of our bodily nature any mode or figure of the divine majesty, but diffuse that character of unbounded magnitude (so to speak) over its plains without any limit. For it is written, "If I shall ascend into heaven, Thou art there; if I shall descend into hell, Thou art there also; […]

Thou countest tens of thousands, God counts those who are in a state of salvation; thou countest the dust which is without number, I the vessels of election. For nothing is so magnificent in God's sight as pure doctrine, and a soul perfect in all the dogmas of the truth.—For there is nothing worthy of Him Who made all things, of Him by Whom are all things, and for Whom are all things, so that it can be given or offered to God: not merely the handiwork or means of any individual, but even if we wished to honour Him, by uniting together all the property and handiwork of all mankind. Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the Lord! and what house will ye build Me? or what is the place of My rest? But, since man must needs fall short of what is worthy, I ask of you, as approaching it most nearly, piety, the wealth which is common to all and equal in My eyes, wherein the poorest may, if he be nobleminded, surpass the most illustrious. For this kind of glory depends upon purpose, not upon affluence. […]

The Lord is in his holy temple, the Lord's seat is in heaven. Before the bodily temple was built by Solomon, the prophet knows the spiritual temple of the Lord and his throne in heaven. Whereupon it is asked, how it is said elsewhere, "Heaven is my throne." When the throne of the Lord is in heaven, his throne is encompassed by heaven, and the throne of the Lord is in a part of heaven; when heaven is the throne of the Lord, the whole heaven is turned into the throne of the Lord. From which, according to the ἀναγωγήν (higher spiritual sense, anagōgē), the Lord dwelling in his holy temple — that is, in the soul of the believer — dwells either in a part of it or in the whole. When we are still imperfect, and there is in us both something good and something evil, God dwells only in a part of our soul, that is, in heaven. But when we are consummate and perfect, we are wholly turned into a dwelling-place of God, and we are made heaven, his throne.

Thus says the Lord: Heaven is my seat, and earth the footstool of my feet. What is this house that you will build for me, and what is this place of my rest? All these things my hand has made, and all these things have come to be, says the Lord. LXX likewise. Lest we should understand the holy mountain as Zion and be covered with the Jewish error, who think that Jerusalem is to be built up and that all the things the Lord promises are to be fulfilled there carnally, he takes this suspicion away from us, and sets down the testimony which Stephen, the first martyr in Christ, used against the contentiousness of the Jews (Acts 7). Solomon built him a house, without doubt for God; but the Most High does not dwell in things made with hands, as the Prophet says: Heaven is my throne: but earth is the footstool of my feet. And Paul in the same volume: God, who made the world and those who are in it, by no means dwells in temples made with hands (Acts 17:24). […]

Thou art become a heaven, and fearest thou the earth? For the Scripture saith in another passage, that the Lord our God doth declare, “The heaven is My throne.” If therefore even thou by having the fulness of knowledge, and by having love, hast been made the throne of God, thou hast become a heaven. For this heaven which we look up to with these eyes of ours, is not very precious before God. Holy souls are the heaven of God; the minds of the Angels, and all the minds of His servants, are the heaven of God.

But consider, brethren, what he commandeth us to fall down before. In another passage of the Scriptures it is said, “The heaven is My throne, and the earth is My footstool.” Doth he then bid us worship the earth, since in another passage it is said, that it is God’s footstool? How then shall we worship the earth, when the Scripture saith openly, “Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God”? Yet here it saith, “fall down before His footstool:” and, explaining to us what His footstool is, it saith, “The earth is My footstool.” I am in doubt; I fear to worship the earth, lest He who made the heaven and the earth condemn me; again, I fear not to worship the footstool of my Lord, because the Psalm biddeth me, “fall down before His footstool.” I ask, what is His footstool? and the Scripture telleth me, “the earth is My footstool.” In hesitation I turn unto Christ, since I am herein seeking Himself: and I discover how the earth may be worshipped without impiety, how His footstool may be worshipped without impiety. […]

God, then, being immaterial and uncircumscribed, has not place. For He is His own place, filling all things and being above all things, and Himself maintaining all things. Yet we speak of God having place and the place of God where His energy becomes manifest. For He penetrates everything without mixing with it, and imparts to all His energy in proportion to the fitness and receptive power of each: and by this I mean, a purity both natural and voluntary. For the immaterial is purer than the material, and that which is virtuous than that which is linked with vice. Wherefore by the place of God is meant that which has a greater share in His energy and grace. For this reason the Heaven is His throne. For in it are the angels who do His will and are always glorifying Him. For this is His rest and the earth is His footstool. For in it He dwelt in the flesh among men. And His sacred flesh has been named the foot of God. […]
66:1.s: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 1, Chapter 13

66:2.t: Let us therefore, brethren, be of humble mind, laying aside all haughtiness, and pride, and foolishness, and angry feelings; and let us act according to that which is written (for the Holy Spirit saith, "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, neither let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him that glorieth glory in the Lord, in diligently seeking Him, and doing judgment and righteousness" [Jeremiah 9:23-24]), being especially mindful of the words of the Lord Jesus which He spake, teaching us meekness and long-suffering. For thus He spoke: "Be ye merciful, that ye may obtain mercy; forgive, that it may be forgiven to you; as ye do, so shall it be done unto you; as ye judge, so shall ye be judged; as ye are kind, so shall kindness be shown to you; with what measure ye mete, with the same it shall be measured to you." […]
66:2.s: Clement's First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 13

66:2.t: But you also, who desire to receive the sacred baptism and to merit the grace of the Spirit, ought first to be purged by the law, ought first, having heard the word of God, to cut away your inborn vices and to compose your barbarous and savage ways, so that, having taken up gentleness and humility, you may be able also to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit. For thus says the Lord through the prophet: "Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?" If you are not "humble and quiet", the grace of the Holy Spirit cannot dwell in you, if you have not received the divine words with trembling. For the Holy Spirit flees from a proud and stubborn and feigning soul. You ought, therefore, first to meditate on the law of God, so that, if perchance your acts are unrestrained and your ways disordered, the law of God may amend and correct you.

We must preserve in the straight and narrow road of praise and glory; and since peacefulness and humility and the tranquility of a good life are fitting for all Christians, according to the word of the Lord, who looks to no other person than "to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and that trembles at" his word, it the more behooves you confessors, who have been made an example to the rest of the brothers, to observe and fulfill this, as being those whose characters should provoke to imitation the life and conduct of all.

And He, wishing moreover to attract to gentleness our minds, brutish, and swelling, and stubborn with cloddish ferocity, says, "And upon whom shall my Spirit rest, save upon him that is lowly, and quiet, and that trembleth at my words?"—so that in some degree one may recognise how great God is, in learning to fear Him by the Spirit given to him:

Thus also Satan, he has not the knowledge beforehand to know or see when the Spirit will depart, that so he may come to rob the man; but he too listens and watches, and so assails. But if he hears a man in whom Christ dwells speaking shameful words, or enraged, or quarrelling, or contending, then Satan knows that Christ is not with him, and he comes and accomplishes his will in him. For Christ dwells in the peaceful and the meek, and lodges in those that fear His word, as He says through the prophet:—On whom shall I look, and in whom shall I dwell, but in the peaceful and the meek who fear My word? And our Lord said:—Whoever walks in My commandments and keeps My love, We will come to him and make Our abode with him. But if he hears from a man that he is on his guard and is praying and meditating in the Law of his Lord by day and by night, then he turns back from him, for he knows that Christ is with him.

For the prophet says in the person of the Father, "My Hand made all these things," meaning by "Hand," in his dark saying, the power of the Only-begotten. Now the Apostle says that all things are of the Father, and that all things are by the Son, and the prophetic spirit in a way agrees with the Apostolic teaching, which itself also is given through the Spirit. For in the one passage, the prophet, when he says that all things are the work of the Hand of Him Who is over all, sets forth the nature of those things which have come into being in its relation to Him Who made them, while He Who made them is God over all, Who has the Hand, and by It makes all things. […]

Moreover, He did not find rest when He had created such irrational creatures as fish and the various species of wild beasts. He found rest, however, after He had made man to His own image. Give ear to Him as He states on whom He finds rest: ‘Or on whom shall I rest but on him that is humble and gentle and that trembleth at my words?’ Therefore, be humble and gentle, so that God may find rest in your affection.

But to whom shall I look, except to the poor little one and the contrite of spirit, and the one who trembles at my words? He who sacrifices an ox is as one who kills a man. He who slaughters a sheep is as one who brains a dog. He who offers an oblation is as one who offers swine's blood. He who remembers frankincense is as one who blesses an idol. LXX: And upon whom shall I look, except the humble and quiet, and the one who trembles at my words? ÷ But the wicked man ⁚ who sacrifices a calf is as one who strikes down a man. He who sacrifices from the flock is as one who kills a dog. He who offers fine flour is as one who offers swine's blood. He who gives frankincense for a memorial is as a blasphemer. Once the altar and the earthly Temple, which the hand of man had built, have been taken away, the victims of the Jews too are rightly taken away, lest perhaps they should say: We are not so foolish as to think that God can be shut up in a place; […]

"On whom does my Spirit rest, if not on one who is humble and quiet and who trembles at my words?" So when he becomes the occupant, he fills and guides and leads the person, restrains from evil and spurs on to good, makes justice delightful, so that the person does good out of love for what is right, not out of fear of punishment. No one is capable on their own of doing what I have said. But if you have the Holy Spirit as the occupant of your house, you will find him also assisting you in everything good.

Where did he seek a place for the Lord? If he was meek, he sought it in himself. For how is one a place for the Lord? Hear the Prophet: “Upon whom shall My Spirit rest? Even upon him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at My words.” Dost thou wish to be a place for the Lord? Be thou poor in spirit, and contrite, and trembling at the word of God, and thou wilt thyself be made what thou seekest. For if what thou seekest be not realized in thyself, what doth it profit thee in another.…

Wherefore if we wish the summit of our building to be perfect and to rise well-pleasing to God, we should endeavour to lay its foundations not in accordance with the desires of our own lust, but according to the rules of evangelical strictness: which can only be the fear of God and humility, proceeding from kindness and simplicity of heart. But humility cannot possibly be acquired without giving up everything: and as long as a man is a stranger to this, he cannot possibly attain the virtue of obedience, or the strength of patience, or the serenity of kindness, or the perfection of love; without which things our hearts cannot possibly be a habitation for the Holy Spirit: as the Lord says through the prophet: "Upon whom shall My spirit rest, but on him that is humble and quiet and ears My words," or according to those copies which express the Hebrew accurately: "To whom shall I have respect, but to him that is poor and little and of a contrite spirit and that trembleth at My words?"
66:2.s: The Twelve Books on the Institutes of the Coenobia, Book 12, Chapter 31

66:2.t: Differently to be admonished are the humble and the haughty. To the former it is to be insinuated how true is that excellence which they hold in hoping for it; to the latter it is to be intimated how that temporal glory is as nothing which even when embracing it they hold not. Let the humble hear how eternal are the things that they long for, how transitory the things which they despise; let the haughty hear how transitory are the things they court, how eternal the things they lose. Let the humble hear from the authoritative voice of the Truth, Every one that humbleth himself shall be exalted. Let the haughty hear, Every one that exalteth himself shall be humbled. Let the humble hear, Humility goeth before glory; let the haughty hear, The spirit is exalted before a fall. Let the humble hear, Unto whom shall I have respect, but to him that is humble and quiet, and that trembleth at my words?
66:2.s: The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 3, Chapter 17

66:2.t: The first benefit of the fear of God is that the fear of God avails for obtaining the influx of divine grace. Whence Isaiah: "To whom shall I look, except to the poor and contrite of spirit and the one trembling at my words?" However powerful, rich, learned, and strong a man may be, unless he fears God, nothing avails him.

Grace makes a man pleasing to God: but he is pleasing to God who recognizes the gift of divine favor and condescension: yet no one recognizes this except one who is attentive to his own unworthiness: and such a one is truly humble: and hence it is that the grace of the Holy Spirit rests upon the humble alone. Whence in the last chapter of Isaiah: Upon whom does My Spirit rest if not upon the humble, etc.
66:2.s: Disputed Questions on Evangelical Perfection, Question 1

66:3.t: The work of a man who has murmured or has been detected in pride must not be mixed with that done by men humble in heart and of a contrite spirit; it must not be used at all by the pious. “For that which is exalted among men is an abomination before God.” And there is another command of the apostle: “Neither murmur ye, as some of them murmured, and perished by the destroyer.” Then there is this: “Not grudgingly or of necessity.” So the work of such men is unacceptable, like a blemished sacrifice—which it was impious to mingle with the offerings of other men. For if those who brought strange fire to the altar experienced such great wrath, surely it is perilous to accept a work springing from a mind hostile to God to assist us in keeping God’s commandments. “For what fellowship have righteousness and iniquity? Or what portion hath a believer with an unbeliever?” Wherefore it saith: “The lawless, he that sacrificeth a calf for me, is as he that killeth a dog; […]

And what follows in the common edition: But the wicked man, is not found in the Hebrew, but it simply joins on and says: He who sacrifices an ox is as one who kills a man. This is also written in another place: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice: the knowledge of God rather than holocaust (Hos 6:6). And through Malachi: All that I hated, you did: covering my altar with tears: is it fitting that I should look upon your sacrifice, and receive anything acceptable from your hands (Mal 2:13)? Let the Jews hear that God does not seek sacrifices, but the mind of those who offer. And he who slaughters, he says, a sheep is as one who brains a dog. Hence it is also written through Moses: You shall not offer the hire of a harlot, nor the price of a dog, in the house of your God. (Deut 23:18). And the dog and the harlot are fittingly joined, because each animal is prone to lust. And at the same time let us consider that he did not say: He who sacrifices a ram is as one who sacrifices a dog; but as one who kills, he says, a dog. […]

All these things they have chosen in their ways, and in their abominations their soul has delighted. Therefore I too will choose their mockeries, and what they feared I will bring upon them. For I called, and there was none to answer: I spoke, and they did not hear: and they did evil in my eyes: and what I did not will, they chose. LXX: And they themselves have chosen their ways, and their soul has willed their abominations: and I will choose their mockeries, and repay them their sins. For I called them, and they did not hearken: I spoke, and they did not hear. And they did evil in my sight, and what I did not will they chose. To sacrifice an ox, to slaughter a ram, to offer sacrifice, to burn frankincense, which God regards as murder and the offering of a dog, and swine's blood and blasphemy, they themselves chose; and that they should worship such things was of their own choice; according to what he says through Ezekiel: I gave them statutes not good, and precepts not good (Ezek 20:25). […]

66:5.t: Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his speech. Your brothers who hate you, and cast you out for my name's sake, have said: Let the Lord be glorified, and we shall see in your gladness: but they shall be put to shame. LXX: Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his speech. Say to your brothers who hate you and abhor you, that the name of the Lord may be glorified: and may it appear in their gladness: and they shall be put to shame. Those of whom he had already said before: Upon whom shall I look, except upon the humble and quiet, and the one who trembles at my words? he commands that, having despised the victims of the Jews and scorned all the swelling pride of the Scribes and Pharisees, they pass over to the worship of him whom those others would not hear when he called, and despised, and did evil in his sight. […]

66:6.t: A voice of uproar from the city, a voice from the Temple, the voice of the Lord rendering recompense to his enemies. For uproar the LXX put crying, and the rest likewise. We wish to know what the confusion of the Jews is, who said: Let the Lord be glorified, that we may see your gladness, and may behold the triumphs of your king with our eyes, by no means in empty promises. A voice, he says, of crying from the city: without doubt it signifies Jerusalem surrounded by the Roman army and divided within into three parts by sedition, when one held the Temple and possessed all that had formerly been holy, fighting outside against the enemy and inside against his fellow citizens. At that time, both in the city and in the Temple, there was heard the howling of priests and Levites as well as of the common rabble, of women and children, when the Lord rendered recompense to his enemies, fulfilling the threat in which he had said: Your house shall be left to you desolate (Luke 13:35); […]

66:7.t: Now that that parturition was polluted, and stood not in need of expiatory victims, Isaiah is our witness, who proclaims distinctly to the whole earth under the sun: "Before she travailed," he says, "she brought forth before her pains came, she escaped, and brought forth a man-child." Who hath heard such a thing? Who hath seen such things? The most holy virgin mother, therefore, escaped entirely the manner of women even before she brought forth: doubtless, in order that the Holy Spirit, betrothing her unto Himself, and sanctifying her, she might conceive without intercourse with man. She hath brought forth her first-born Son, even the only-begotten Son of God, Him, I say, who in the heavens above shone forth as the only-begotten, without mother, from out His Father's substance, and preserved the virginity of His natural unity undivided and inseparable; […]

Before she was in labor, she brought forth: before her travail came, she brought forth a male. Who has ever heard such a thing? who has seen the like of this ? Shall the earth be in labor in one day: or shall a nation be brought forth at once? for Zion has been in labor and has brought forth her sons: Shall I, who make others bring forth, not bring forth myself, says the Lord? If I, who give generation to the rest, am barren, says the Lord your God. LXX: Before she who travails brings forth: before the pain of those in travail comes, she escapes, and she has brought forth a male. Who has heard such a thing, and who has seen the like? If the earth has travailed in one day; or if a nation has been born at once, because Zion has travailed and brought forth her little ones. But I have given this expectation, and you have not remembered me, says the Lord. Have I not made her who bears and the barren, says your God? […]

For He who was of the Father, yet without mother, was born of woman without a father’s co-operation. And so far as He was born of woman, His birth was in accordance with the laws of parturition, while so far as He had no father, His birth was above the nature of generation: and in that it was at the usual time (for He was born on the completion of the ninth month when the tenth was just beginning), His birth was in accordance with the laws of parturition, while in that it was painless it was above the laws of generation. For, as pleasure did not precede it, pain did not follow it, according to the prophet who says, Before she travailed, she brought forth, and again, before her pain came she was delivered of a man-child.
66:7.s: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 4, Chapter 14

66:8.t: But for God this was no great thing, that the dead should be quickened. Before seed was sown in the earth, the earth produced that which had not been cast into it. Before it had conceived, it bore in its virginity. How then is this difficult, that the earth should cause to spring up again what had been cast into it, and after conception should bear? And lo! her travail-pains are near; as Isaiah said, Who hath seen anything like this and who hath heard such things as these? that the earth should travail in one day, and a people should be born in one hour? For Adam unsown sprang up; unconceived he was born. But lo! now his offspring are sown, and wait for the rain, and shall spring up. And lo! the earth teems with many, and the time of her bringing forth is at hand.
66:8.s: Demonstration 8 (Of the Resurrection of the Dead), Section 6

66:8.t: Zion, then, that is, the remnant from Israel and the faith of the believing Apostles, brought forth a male, the Lord Savior, who was born at once in the whole world: something that no one has heard of, that no history relates, nor the teaching of anyone, that all the nations should believe in a short time, and that out of all the nations there should be made one nation of the Christians, of which Paul too speaks: If anyone is a new creature in Christ, the old things have passed away; behold, they have become new (2 Cor 5:17): according to what is written elsewhere: And all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight: for the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations. For all the nations, he says, which you have made shall come and worship before you, and shall glorify your name (Ps 21 [22]:28ff.). Of him Jacob says: He is the expectation of the nations (Gen 49:10). And the Psalmist: The hope of all the ends of the earth (Ps 64 [65]:6). […]

Further, according to the LXX the sense is this: that at one time, at the preaching of the Gospels, one nation of the whole world should arise. Through many prophets I have often promised, and you have not remembered my promise, O city which is full of cries, O Temple which has been forsaken by the Lord, O people to whom I have rendered its recompense. Have I not, he says, made her who travails and the barren; she who before had been barren afterwards travailed and brought forth? Of her it is written in the psalm: Who makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a mother rejoicing in sons (Ps 112 [113]:9). Or certainly the order of things has been reversed: she who bore has become barren, and she who was once barren has brought forth very many, because this is the sentence of the Lord.

66:9.t: And what follows according to the LXX: But I have given this expectation, and you have not remembered me, says the Lord. Have I not made her who bears and the barren, said your God, is put more plainly in the Hebrew, with which the other translators also agree: Shall I, who make others bring forth, not bring forth myself, says the Lord? If I, who give generation to the rest, am barren, says the Lord your God; according to what is said elsewhere: He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? and he who formed the eye, does he not consider (Ps 93 [94]:9); namely, that he who created all men out of nothing can make out of all the nations one part of those who believe in him, the Church. Finally, in Psalm 28 (29), where we read: The voice of the Lord shaking the desert (Ps 28 [29]:8), in the Hebrew it is written: The voice of the Lord making the desert bring forth (According to the Hebrew), so that the Church, formerly a desert, may bring forth, and the stags may be perfected when the woodlands are opened and crushed.

To that which is objected, that the cause of generation and corruption is to be far distant from the First: it must be said that this is not the whole reason. For man, if he had remained in the state of innocence, would never have been corrupted, and yet he would have generated. Whence generation is rather from the supreme perfection and fecundity and actuality of the first principle itself, than it is for the supplementing of the defect of corruption of the productive principle itself. Therefore the Philosopher speaks of the cause of generation according to the state of deficient nature, not generally and according to the mode of that most complete generation, which is the origin of all production. For the generator of the species constituted all these things, and he himself, who bestows generation upon others, cannot be sterile, according to what is said in the last chapter of Isaiah.
66:9.s: Quaestiones Disputatae, De Mysterio Trinitatis, Question 6

66:10.t: Rejoice with Jerusalem, and exult in her, all you who love her. Rejoice with her with joy, all you who mourn over her, that you may suck and be filled from the breast of her consolation, that you may milk and abound with delights from her glory of every kind. LXX: Rejoice, Jerusalem, and make an assembly, all you who love her. Rejoice with joy, all you who mourn over her, that you may suck and be filled from the breast of her consolation, that, after you have sucked, you may be delighted from the entrance of her glory. It is commanded to the Apostles and to apostolic men, who love both Jerusalems, bewailing and mourning the one that has fallen, and awaiting with all desire the one that is to rise, that they rejoice with her and in her, who has been built of living stones, which roll upon the earth and, in the likeness of the wheels of the Cherubim, follow the spirit going before: not in those stones which have been dissolved into eternal ashes. […]

66:11.t: For it could not be that she who had borne a male and had just given birth should lack an abundance of milk for the rearing of that nation and of the little ones who had been born at once, so that she might offer them two breasts, by no means, as formerly in Egypt, broken and lying low, but whole and standing in virginal beauty, those of the Old and New Instrument, to supply rational milk. Of these the bridegroom speaks to her: Your breasts are better than wine (Song 1:1). These were the ones of whom they specially said: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:5). And this is to be noted: that those who are little ones need the milk of consolation, and are still in a mortal place. But those who after the milk of consolation have advanced to solid food will abound with the delights of truth, and with the knowledge of glory of every kind, which in Hebrew is called ZIZ (זיז). For this the LXX translated entrance; Symmachus fatness; Theodotion multitude. […]

66:12.t: So, then, the Holy Spirit is the river, and the abundant river, which according to the Hebrews flowed from Jesus in the lands, as we have received it prophesied by the mouth of Isaiah. This is the great river that flows always and never fails. And not only a river but also one of the copious stream and overflowing greatness, as also David said, "The stream of the river makes glad the city of God."

For thus says the Lord: Behold, I turn upon her as it were a river of peace, and as an overflowing torrent the glory of the nations, which you shall suck: you shall be carried at the breast, and upon the knees they shall caress you. LXX: For thus says the Lord: Behold, I will turn toward them like a river of peace, and like a torrent overflowing the glory of the nations. Their little ones shall be carried on the shoulders, and upon the knees they shall be comforted. When Jerusalem has been built up by the Apostles and restored to her former state, after her sons and inhabitants have been comforted at her breasts and through the abundance of milk have come to the delights of truth, through which one comes to the glory of God: then the Lord will turn upon her the river of peace, of which we have often said: The river of God is filled with waters (Ps 64 [65]:10). And: The rush of the river gladdens the city of God (Ps 45 [46]:5); […]

66:13.t: A mother draws her children near her; we seek our mother, the church. Whatever is weak and young has an appeal and sweetness and lovableness of its own, just because in its weakness it does stand in need of assistance. But God does not withhold assistance from such an age of life. Just as the male and female parent regard their young tenderly—whether it be horses their colts, or cows their calves, or lions their cubs, or deer their fawn or men and women their children—so, too, does the Father of all draw near to those who seek his aid, giving them a new birth and making them his own adopted children. He recognizes them as his little ones, he loves only them, and he comes to the aid of such as these and defends them. That is why he calls them his children.

As one whom a mother caresses, so will I comfort you, and in Jerusalem you shall be comforted. You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall sprout like grass. And the hand of the Lord shall be known to his servants, and he shall be indignant with his enemies. For servants the LXX put those who fear; for enemies, the unbelieving: the rest likewise. We learn the mercy of the Creator toward his creatures from the example of mothers, who, nursing their children with love in their bosom, surpass every affection. Finally, God, wishing to show how he loves those whom he has created: Shall, he says, a woman forget, so as not to have pity on the offspring of her womb? but even if she should forget, yet I will not forget you (Isa 49:15). The Gospel passage too has this sense, in which the Lord speaks to Jerusalem: How often have I wished to gather your sons, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not (Matt 23:37)? […]

66:14.t: After these have been comforted, it will be said to them: And you shall see, and your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall sprout like grass, or shall spring up, or according to Symmachus, shall flourish (John 16:22). And they shall see, without doubt, God, which is true gladness. Of these the Lord spoke: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8). The vision of him is perfect joy, which dwells in the heart of full faith: and the sprouting of the bones follows, of which we have already spoken before. If the reader has forgotten this, let him go back to the earlier explanation. For it is better for him to read again what was written than for us to repeat what was said. And known, he says, shall be the hand of the Lord to his servants, or to those who fear him, and he shall threaten his enemies, or his unbelieving. […]

66:15.t:
[Passage quoted, Isa. lxvi. 18, 19.]

HERE also the Coming of the Lord to men is exactly foretold. And as it said, "He will come as fire," our Saviour rightly says, "I came to cast fire on the earth, and what will I, if it be already kindled?" You may say His "chariots" are His attendant divine powers, and the holy angels chosen to minister to Him, of whom it is said, "and angels came and ministered to Him," and His holy apostles and disciples, borne up by whom, the Word of God with divine invisible power ran through all the world. One might also literally in another way connect fire and chariots with His coming, through the siege that attacked Jerusalem after our Saviour's Advent, for the Temple was burned with fire not long after, and was reduced to extreme desolation, and the city was encircled by the chariots and camps of the enemy, after which too the promises to the Gentiles were fulfilled in harmony with the prophecy.
66:15.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 25

66:15.t: For behold, the Lord will come in fire: and his chariots like a whirlwind, to render his fury in indignation, and his rebuke in a flame of fire. For in fire the Lord is judged, and with his sword unto all flesh: and those slain by the Lord shall be multiplied. LXX: Behold, the Lord will come as fire, and his chariots as a tempest, to render his vengeance in fury: and his rebuke in a flame of fire. For in the fire of the Lord all the earth shall be judged: and by his sword all flesh shall fall: many shall be wounded by the Lord. The hand of the Lord, which will be made known to his servants and to those who fear him, itself threatens the unbelieving, or his enemies, that if they do not repent they shall endure what follows: For behold, he says, the Lord will come in fire, and his chariots like a whirlwind or tempest. […]

66:16.t: And so in this fire and fury, in these chariots and in the flame of fire all flesh shall be judged, or the Lord himself with his creatures, so that he may be seen to pass sentence not by power but by the truth of judgment, according to what is said at greater length in Micah and more briefly in Psalm 50 (51): That you may be justified in your words, and may prevail when you are judged (Ps 50 [51]:5). And the sword by which all flesh is to be judged is to be taken as that of which we have spoken before, and shall now speak in part: Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword (Ps 7:13). This sword, the punisher of sinful flesh and of all vices, the Israelites complain had been given into the hands of Pharaoh; and they say to Moses and Aaron: May God see you and judge: for you have made our odor abominable before Pharaoh, so that a sword was given into his hand, and he might kill us (Exod 5:21). […]

66:17.t: Those who were sanctified, and thought themselves clean in the gardens behind one within: who ate swine's flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together, says the Lord. LXX: Those who are sanctified and purified in the gardens and on the thresholds: eating pig's flesh, and abominations, and the mouse: they shall be consumed together, says the Lord. Symmachus and Theodotion translated this passage thus: You who are sanctified and cleansed in the gardens one after another, among those who eat swine's flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall fail together, says the Lord, wishing to show that it is not those who are sanctified in the gardens one after another who themselves eat swine's flesh and the abomination and the mouse; but that those who are cleansed associate with those who eat the things that are forbidden. […]

66:18.t:
Who would not wonder hearing the Lord say by the prophet, "I come to bring together all nations and tongues," and then seeing throughout the whole inhabited world the congregations welded together in the Name of Christ through the Coming and the Call of our Saviour Jesus Christ, with the tongues of all nations in varying dialects calling on one God and Lord? To crown all, who beholding all them that believe in Christ using as a seal the sign of salvation, would not rightly be astounded hearing the Lord saying in days of old, "And they shall come and see my glory, and I will leave my sign upon them"?

We see in part, indeed, now with our own eyes the fulfilment of the holy oracles as to the first Epiphany of our Saviour to man. May it be seen completely as well in His second glorious Advent, when all nations shall see His glory, and when He comes in the heavens with power and great glory.

To that day the remainder of the prophecy must be referred, as I shall show in my own argument.
66:18.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 25

66:18.t: The Lord comes, then, to gather the works and thoughts of each. From this we learn that not only works but thoughts too are to be judged on the day of judgment. For he who has looked on a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt 5). Of these it is said: Now their own thoughts have surrounded them: when the Lord will judge the hidden things of men according to the Gospel of Jesus Christ; so that what the Apostle writes may be proved by the truth of the judgment: their thoughts mutually accusing or excusing them, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of men (Rom 2:15): so that all our thoughts, gathered at one time, may be examined by the righteous judge, while our conscience either accuses us or makes satisfaction for the offense, whether the sins are more or the good works, and whether they are old or new, whether blotted out by repentance or renewed by fresh crimes, when the Lord says: I have given their ways upon their heads: and I will render them their […]

Christ makes, as it were, a certain recapitulation of the whole discourse, and of all prophecy through these things, and as in brief and concise terms he announces the things from the beginning to the end, and the power of the economy in the flesh. For he also remembers the calling of the nations, and the appointment of the holy apostles, and that he will be worshipped by all under heaven. For the old law gathered one and only one nation, that is, clearly, the one from Israel, and it called one tongue. But our Lord Jesus Christ did not bestow the power of the economy in the flesh on those of the blood of Israel alone, but indeed on every nation and all tongues. For He said through the lyre of the Psalmist: "Hear these things, all nations: give ear, all you who inhabit the world:" therefore I will gather all, he says: "They shall come, and shall see my glory." For they have been called through faith, and those who were once far off have become near, and they have seen his glory: how, or in what way? […]

66:19.t: But I come to gather their works and their thoughts together with all the nations and tongues: and they shall come and see my glory. And I will set a sign among them, and I will send of those who have been saved to the nations in the sea, to Africa, to Lydia, those who draw the arrow, to Italy and Greece, to the islands far off: to those who have not heard of me, and have not seen my glory. LXX: And I know their works and their thoughts, and I come to gather all the nations and all the tongues: and they shall come and see my glory, and I will let down a sign upon them: and I will send forth of those who have been saved to the nations, to Tharsis and Phud, and Lud and Mosoch and Thobel, and to Greece, and to the islands far off, who have not heard my name, nor seen my glory. Before I explain what the enumeration of so many nations signifies, something must be said briefly about the variety of the translations. Tharsis in the Hebrew language is the name for the sea; […]

And all shall come to see the glory of God: and he will set a sign among them, which is shown at the beginning of Ezekiel under the interpretation of the Hebrew letter THAU (Ezek 9). He who has been stamped with this sign will escape the hand of the smiter. With this the doorposts of the houses in Egypt too were marked, when, as Egypt perished, Israel alone remained unharmed (Exod 12). Of this sign, which Ahaz king of Judah would not accept, the prophet Isaiah testifies: Therefore the Lord will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear (Isa 7:14). Hence the Prophet too entreats for what had been promised: Work with me a sign for good (Ps 85 [86]:17). And in another place: You have given to those who fear you a signal, that they might flee from the face of the bow (Ps 59 [60]:4). This the Lord, ascending to the Father, left us, or set upon our foreheads, so that we might freely say: The light of your countenance has been signed upon us, O Lord (Ps 4:7). […]

66:20.t: And they shall announce my glory among the nations, and they shall bring all your brothers from all the nations as a gift to the Lord, on horses, and in four-horse chariots, and in litters, and on mules, and in carriages, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says the Lord. LXX: And they shall announce my glory among the nations: and they shall bring your brothers from all the nations as a gift to the Lord, with horses and wagons, in the lampenae of mules, with canopies, into the holy city Jerusalem, says the Lord. Those who have been saved and sent to the various nations, and to those who had not heard at first nor seen the glory of the Lord, will announce it to all the nations, and will bring the brothers of the Jewish people, whose remnant has been saved, as an offering to the Lord from all the nations: either those very ones who, despising the error of idolatry, have followed the knowledge of the true God, or those of the people of Israel who have believed throughout the whole world. […]

As if the sons of Israel should bring an offering in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord. And I will take of them for priests and Levites, says the Lord. LXX: As if the sons of Israel should offer their victims to me with Psalms in the house of the Lord: and of them I will take priests and Levites, says the Lord. Those who have been sent to the nations, he says, and have announced my glory to them, will bring your brothers from all the nations as an offering to the Lord, with horses, and four-horse chariots, and litters, and mules, and carriages, and various vehicles, to the holy mountain Jerusalem, in the same way as the sons of Israel used, while their religion stood and the ceremonies of the Temple were kept, to offer victims with Psalms in the house of the Lord. […]

66:21.t: And I will take, he says, of them priests and Levites, says the Lord: so that those who have been saved may preach to the nations. One of these said: So let a man reckon us as ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God (1 Cor 4:1). And Luke the evangelist: As they delivered to us, he says, who from the beginning saw and were ministers of the word. Of these we also read above: You shall be to me priests of the Lord (Isa 61:6). For as he is a Jew in secret who is circumcised in spirit (Rom 2), of whom it is written: We are the Circumcision, who serve God in spirit (Phil 3:3), and we offer spiritual victims pleasing to God, and sing psalms with the spirit and with the understanding: so too they are priests and Levites in secret who follow not the line of descent but the order of faith. […]

66:22.t: For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I make to stand before me, says the Lord: so shall your seed stand, and your name. And it shall be month from month, and sabbath from sabbath: all flesh shall come to worship before my face, says the Lord. LXX: For as the new heaven and the new earth, which I make to remain in my sight, says the Lord: so shall your seed stand and your name. And it shall be month from month, and sabbath from sabbath: all flesh shall come to worship the Lord in my sight in Jerusalem. When he says: I will take of them for priests and Levites, he shows that the old priesthood has been set aside, which was owed to the tribe of Levi, where there is no choice but the order of nature, and a line of family descending through posterity. […]

66:23.t: And it shall be, he says, month from month, and sabbath from sabbath: so that out of carnal sabbaths and months there may come spiritual and delightful sabbaths, which sabbath-rest is reserved for the people of God. And a spiritual month, when the moon is filled from point to point and runs its course, so as to make a month, that is, the kalends, which in Greek are called νεομηνίαι, that is, the beginning of a new month; among whom the beginning of the kalends begins and ends not according to the course of the sun and the different lengths of the months, but according to the circuit of the moon. This is the moon of which it is said in praise of the true Solomon: And he shall remain with the sun and before the moon, for generations of generations (Ps 71 [72]:5). She is called the chosen one in the Song of Songs: Who is this who has come forth like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, and chosen as the sun, wonderful (Song 6:9)? […]

Moreover we should strive that this warning of the prophetic exhortation may not be uttered against us to no purpose: "Celebrate, O Judah, thy festivals, and pay thy vows." For if the occurrence of festival days does not interfere with the continuity of our abstinence, we shall continually enjoy spiritual festivals and so, when we cease from servile work, "there shall be month after month and Sabbath after Sabbath."
66:23.s: The First Conference of Abbot Theonas, Chapter 23

66:24.t: As people who have cut your souls off from this hope, it is necessary that you know how to obtain pardon of your sins and a hope of sharing in the promised blessings. There is no other way than this, that you come to know our Christ, be baptized with the baptism that cleanses you from sin (as Isaiah testified) and thus live a life free of sin.

Also in respect of penalty, I say that all men are not equal. He that has done great wickedness is greatly tormented. And he that has offended not so much is less tormented. Some shall go into outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth. Others shall be cast into the fire, according as they deserve; for it is not written that they shall gnash their teeth, nor that there is darkness there. Some shall be cast into another place, a place where their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall became an astonishment to all flesh. In the faces of others the door shall be closed and the Judge will say to them:—I know you not. And consider that, as the reward for good deeds is not equal for all men, so it is also for evil deeds. Not in one fashion shall men be judged, but every man according to his works shall receive his requital, because the Judge is clothed in righteousness and regards not the persons of men.
66:24.s: Demonstration 22 (Of Death and the Latter Times), Section 22

66:24.t: If heaven and earth are renewed, how can we doubt the possibility of our renewal, for whom heaven and earth were made? If the transgressor is kept for punishment, why should not the just person be preserved for glory? If the worm of sinners does not die, how shall the flesh of the just perish? For the resurrection, as the very form of the word indicates, is this: What has fallen shall rise again, what has died shall live again.

So there is neither any gnashing of bodily teeth, nor any perpetual fire of bodily flames, nor is the worm bodily. But these things are said because, just as from much indigestion both fevers and worms are born, so if anyone does not digest his sins by interposing, as it were, a certain sobriety of abstinence, but, mixing sins with sins, contracts as it were a kind of indigestion of old and recent offenses, he will be scorched by his own fire and consumed by his own worms. Hence Isaiah also says: walk in the light of your fire and in the flame which you have kindled. The fire is that which sorrow for sins begets; the worm is so called because the irrational sins of the soul prick the mind and the sense of the guilty man and eat away certain inward parts of the conscience, sins which are born like worms out of each one, as out of the body of the sinner. Indeed the Lord declared this through Isaiah, saying: and they will see the limbs of the men who have transgressed against me; […]

And they shall go forth, and see the corpses of the men who have transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched. And they shall be a sight to the full for all flesh. LXX likewise. All flesh that is to worship in the sight of the Lord, whether in the heavenly Jerusalem or in every place in which clean hands are lifted up, will go forth to see the corpses of the dead men who have transgressed against God. This can be understood either of the Jews, of whom it was said: I have begotten and exalted sons: but they have despised me; or of all who, having the knowledge of God in their hearts, have turned aside to vanity, so as to worship the creature rather than the Creator. And they will go forth not in place, but in understanding. For the corpses of the dead cannot be within with the Lord. […]

Let us then study to fix the fear of God in our mind, and let us meditate thereupon by day and by night. If the fire of lust kindleth in us, let us set in opposition thereto the fire of Gehenna. If greediness of the belly seize upon us, let us remember the worm which dieth not. If the beauty of the face excite us, let us remember the outer darkness. If the love of mammon fight against us, let us call to mind our own unworthiness. If human benefits stir us, let us be afraid lest we lose the kingdom which abideth for ever. If wrath attacketh us with its violent onset, let us look at the threat of God against those who provoke to wrath. If vainglory raise a tumult within us, let us bring up in our minds the disgrace and contempt [which we shall feel] before our Judge. By fear let us make fear of none effect, and by death let us vanquish death.
66:24.s: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 6 -- First Discourse on the Fear of God

66:24.t:
To this torment of fire will be joined torment according to all the senses; joined to it will be the punishment of the worm and the deprivation of the vision of God, so that in these punishments there will be variety, and with variety severity, and with severity endlessness.

In every actual mortal sin there is a disordered aversion from the highest light and goodness, and an inordinate conversion to a changeable good, and a disorder of the will against the dictate of right reason: hence it is that all who actually sin and will be damned shall be punished with a threefold punishment: on account of their aversion, the deprivation of the vision of God; on account of their conversion, the punishment of material fire; on account of the conflict between will and reason, the punishment of the worm: so that thus afflicted by this multiplicity of punishments they may be tormented both variously and bitterly and eternally, and the smoke of their torments may ascend forever and ever.
